_note: Update 56: 30 original MAP-style questions per platform skill (Grades 2, 5, 7, 8, 10, 12; every answer type). Loaded by scripts/skills/top-up-skills.ts.

pab70427c7c.title: Let's Plant a Garden
pab70427c7c.text:
Hello, class. My name is Lina. I think our school needs a garden. Here is why.

First, plants make the air clean and fresh. Second, we can learn how seeds grow into food. My cousin's school has a garden. The children there grow beans and mint.

Last, a garden is a calm place to sit and read. Please vote yes for a school garden!

p9bec89a123.title: A Crosswalk for Palm Street
p9bec89a123.text:
Good evening, members of the council. My name is Faris, and I am a fifth grader at Palm Street Elementary School. I am here this evening to request that you paint a crosswalk and position a crossing guard in front of our school.

Every morning, more than three hundred students walk to school, and many of them must cross Palm Street. Cars on this street frequently travel at dangerous speeds because no sign warns drivers to slow down near the entrance. Last month, our class counted the cars for one week as part of a mathematics project. We found that about forty cars passed the school gate every ten minutes.

A crosswalk would also help parents and older neighbors who visit the market across the street. In nearby towns, schools with crosswalks and guards report fewer accidents.

Please help us arrive at school safely. A few buckets of paint could protect hundreds of children.

p3c8e0cb7e9.title: Guardians of the Coast
p3c8e0cb7e9.text:
Fellow students, the gray-green trees along our coastline may not look impressive, but mangroves are among the most valuable and hardest-working plants on Earth. Today I want to convince you that our school should join the city's mangrove-planting program this spring.

First, mangroves protect our shoreline from erosion, the gradual wearing away of land by water. Their tangled roots slow down waves and hold the soil in place. After a strong storm in 2019, scientists measured the coastline and found that areas with thick mangroves lost far less land than bare beaches did.

Second, mangroves serve as protected nurseries for an enormous variety of marine animals. Young fish, shrimp, and crabs hide among the roots until they are large enough to survive in open water. Local fishermen say their catches are better near healthy mangrove forests.

Finally, participating in the program would be both practical and inexpensive. Each seedling costs about two riyals, and volunteers can plant fifty in an hour. Some people say one school cannot make a difference, but every forest began with a single tree.

pa4c642d713.title: Refill Stations, Not Plastic Bottles
pa4c642d713.text:
Thank you, Madam President. I rise to support the proposal to replace the bottled-water machines in our school with free refill stations.

My first reason is environmental. Our cafeteria sells roughly 900 plastic bottles every week, according to the canteen manager's records, and fewer than one in five ends up in a recycling bin. The rest are buried in landfills, where plastic can remain for centuries.

My second reason is financial. A refill station costs about 3,000 riyals to install, but families currently spend more than that on bottled water in a single month.

Opponents argue that tap water is unsafe to drink. That concern is understandable, but the stations include filters that are tested every term by the city's health department, and the results will be posted beside each station.

Finally, some students simply prefer cold bottled water. However, preference is not a reason to keep producing waste that our grandchildren will inherit.

pbe0df3117f.title: Water from the Sun
pbe0df3117f.text:
Distinguished guests, for decades, coastal communities across the Arabian Peninsula have depended on large desalination plants that burn fossil fuels to turn seawater into drinking water. I propose that small solar-powered units, installed village by village, should become the foundation of our regional water strategy.

The technical case is persuasive. Over the past ten years, the cost of solar panels has fallen by nearly ninety percent, and a pilot unit operating on the Red Sea coast has produced roughly 20,000 liters of fresh water daily since 2022, according to independent monitoring by a university laboratory.

The human case is equally compelling. When I visited one fishing village last spring, an elderly resident told me the new unit had changed his life. Clearly, every village on the coast is ready to embrace this technology.

Critics warn that solar units produce less water on cloudy days. Admittedly, output does decline, yet our region enjoys more than 3,000 hours of sunshine annually, and battery storage can bridge the gaps.

pbf4ac85968.title: The Memory of a Nation
pbf4ac85968.text:
Honored guests, the manuscripts resting in these climate-controlled rooms record centuries of inquiry in astronomy, medicine, and mathematics, yet fewer than a quarter of them have ever been photographed. I contend that digitizing the entire collection within the next decade is not a luxury but an obligation.

Consider, first, the inherent fragility of paper and parchment. Conservators estimate that ink corrosion and humidity have damaged roughly one in eight volumes since the last survey, and each damaged page represents knowledge that no future scholar can recover.

Consider, too, the question of access. A researcher in Jakarta or Nairobi cannot easily travel here, but a digital archive would place these works on any screen in the world. When the observatory records of a neighboring library were published online, citations of those records in scientific journals tripled within five years.

Some will object that digitization is expensive, and it undeniably is. But the true choice before us is simple: we either fund this project now or accept that this heritage will vanish entirely.

pa9407e2a2f.title: How a Frog Grows
pa9407e2a2f.text:
A frog starts as a tiny egg in a pond. The egg hatches into a tadpole. A tadpole has a long tail. It breathes with gills, like a fish.

Soon the tadpole grows back legs. Then it grows front legs. Its tail gets shorter and shorter. Now it has lungs and can breathe air.

At last it is an adult frog. It can hop on land and swim in water. This set of changes is called a life cycle.

pd26ce50526.title: The Water Cycle
pd26ce50526.text:
Water on Earth is always moving in a pattern called the water cycle. The sun heats water in oceans, lakes, and rivers. During evaporation, the liquid water turns into an invisible gas called water vapor, which rises into the air.

High in the sky, the air is much cooler. There, the water vapor cools and changes back into tiny droplets of liquid. This process is called condensation, and billions of these droplets gather to form clouds.

When the droplets join together and become too heavy, they fall to the ground as precipitation. Precipitation can be rain, snow, sleet, or hail, depending on the temperature. Some of the water soaks into the soil and becomes groundwater, while the rest flows across the land as runoff and returns to rivers and seas. Then the cycle begins again.

[Diagram: Arrows show water rising from a lake, forming a cloud, falling as rain, and flowing back to the lake.]

pe4d00284ef.title: The Mapmaker of Sicily
pe4d00284ef.text:
Around 1138, the scholar Muhammad al-Idrisi arrived at the court of Sicily with a big task. He was asked to create the most accurate map of the known world. Al-Idrisi was a cartographer, a specialist who studies and draws maps. He understood that no single traveler could gather all the facts he needed.

Instead, he compiled reports from merchants, sailors, and envoys who had journeyed across Europe, Africa, and Asia. When two accounts disagreed, he interviewed additional travelers until the evidence was consistent. He also divided the world into seven climate zones. Each zone was based on its distance from the equator, a method much like modern lines of latitude.

After fifteen years of research, al-Idrisi produced a silver planisphere, a flat disk engraved with the world map, along with a detailed geography book. Sailors and scholars relied on his work for centuries, and copies of his maps are still studied today.

p6610c222f1.title: Partners on the Reef
p6610c222f1.text:
Coral reefs may look like colorful rocks, but each reef is built by millions of tiny animals called polyps. A coral polyp has a soft body and a hard skeleton made of limestone. Over thousands of years, these skeletons accumulate to form massive reef structures.

Corals survive in nutrient-poor tropical waters because of a symbiotic relationship, a partnership in which two different organisms both benefit. Microscopic algae live inside the coral's tissues. Through photosynthesis, the algae convert sunlight into sugars, supplying up to ninety percent of the coral's food. In return, the coral provides the algae with shelter and the carbon dioxide they need.

This partnership is delicate. When seawater becomes unusually warm, stressed corals expel their algae. Without the algae, which give corals their color, the reef turns white in a process called bleaching. If temperatures return to normal quickly, the algae can recolonize the coral; if not, the coral may starve.

pc64af51eff.title: The Scientist in the Dark Room
pc64af51eff.text:
Around the year 1011, the scholar Ibn al-Haytham challenged a theory that had dominated thinking for more than a thousand years. Many ancient philosophers had proposed that vision occurs when the eye emits rays toward objects. Ibn al-Haytham found this hypothesis unconvincing, so he designed experiments to test it.

Working in a darkened chamber, he allowed light to pass through a small aperture in one wall. An inverted image of the scene outside appeared on the opposite surface, demonstrating that light travels in straight lines from objects into an opening, not outward from the eye. He also measured refraction, the bending of light as it passes from air into water or glass.

Ibn al-Haytham insisted that conclusions must rest on empirical evidence, information gathered through careful observation and repeated testing, rather than on the authority of famous thinkers. His Book of Optics, later translated into Latin, influenced generations of European scientists, and many historians regard his systematic approach as an early model of the scientific method.

p79da8c5b15.title: The Hidden Reservoir
p79da8c5b15.text:
Beneath the sands of the Arabian Peninsula lie vast aquifers, layers of porous rock saturated with water. That water accumulated during wetter climatic periods tens of thousands of years ago. Hydrologists often describe this resource as fossil water, because, unlike groundwater in temperate regions, it receives negligible recharge from present-day rainfall.

The rate at which an aquifer can supply water depends largely on the permeability of its rock, that is, how readily fluids move through interconnected pores. Highly permeable sandstone may yield abundant water for decades, yet even generous yields are ultimately finite when withdrawals exceed natural replenishment.

During the late twentieth century, intensive irrigation drew down water tables dramatically in several basins. Consequently, policymakers have shifted toward conservation strategies, including drip irrigation, treated-wastewater reuse, and crop choices that require less water. Such measures cannot reverse depletion, but they can substantially extend the productive lifespan of a resource that, once exhausted, would take millennia to restore.

pfb339ab896.title: Slow and Steady
pfb339ab896.text:
It was race day at school. Omar was not a fast runner. "I will never win," he said.

Grandpa smiled. "Do you know the story of the tortoise and the hare?" he asked. "The hare was fast, but he stopped to nap. The tortoise was slow, but he never stopped."

In the race, the other kids ran fast at first. Then some of them got tired and walked. Omar kept running. He did not win, but he finished in third place! "I was the tortoise today," Omar said with a big grin.

p7752641ce3.title: The Boy and the Group Chat
p7752641ce3.text:
Text 1: A shepherd boy who grew bored watching sheep on a quiet hillside decided to create some excitement, so he shouted, "Wolf! Wolf!" The worried villagers rushed up the hill to protect the flock, but there was no wolf anywhere. The boy laughed at them and repeated the same trick the following day. Then one evening a real wolf appeared among the sheep. The boy screamed for help, but this time nobody came, because nobody believed him anymore.

Text 2: All week, Fahad sent joke messages to his family's group chat: "Emergency! Come to my room immediately!" Each time, his parents hurried in and discovered him grinning at his tablet. On Friday, his bicycle chain snapped several kilometers from home, and he sent a genuine message asking for help. Almost an hour passed before anyone responded. "Sorry," his sister finally wrote. "You've been crying wolf all week, so we assumed it was another joke."

pea6e20c3c8.title: The Knight Sacrifice
pea6e20c3c8.text:
Everyone at the regional chess tournament expected Reem to lose her final match. Her opponent, a tall, confident boy named Khalid, had not lost a single game all year, and his aggressive attacks were famous for overwhelming defenders in fewer than twenty moves.

Reem had studied his previous games for several weeks, however, and she had noticed a revealing pattern. Khalid was brilliant at attacking, but whenever his queen wandered away from the center of the board, his king was poorly protected. That vulnerability was his Achilles' heel.

Midway through the game, Reem deliberately left one of her knights where Khalid could easily capture it. It looked like a generous gift, but it was a Trojan horse. The moment Khalid's queen reached for the knight, Reem's bishop swept diagonally across the board, and Khalid's king was suddenly trapped.

Khalid stared at the board in silence for a long minute. Then he smiled, shook her hand, and said, "I never saw it coming."

pd3cf53867e.title: The Wings of Icarus
pd3cf53867e.text:
Text 1: In the ancient Greek myth, the brilliant inventor Daedalus and his young son Icarus were imprisoned on the island of Crete by a suspicious king, so the desperate inventor constructed two pairs of enormous wings from feathers and melted wax. Before their perilous departure, he repeatedly cautioned his son not to fly too close to the sun, because its intense heat would soften the wax. Once airborne, however, Icarus became so exhilarated by the freedom of flight that he forgot the warning and soared higher and higher. The wax gradually melted, the feathers scattered, and the boy plunged into the sea.

Text 2: In the following modern poem, titled “Icarus, Again,” a contemporary speaker responds directly to the ancient legend.
Our wings are not of wax but glass, bright panels drinking radiant light;
we climb toward the burning sun and harness it for flight.
Old stories warned us of the heat, of tumbling like a stone,
but we have learned to make the fire that conquered you our own.

p3bccf733f1.title: Cleaning the Sky
p3bccf733f1.text:
Since 1957, humanity has launched thousands of satellites, and every mission has left something behind: spent rocket stages, flecks of paint, fragments from collisions. Today more than 30,000 pieces of tracked debris circle the planet, each traveling fast enough to destroy a working spacecraft.

Engineers have proposed nets, harpoons, and lasers to clear this orbital junk, but the effort can seem Sisyphean. Every collision creates hundreds of new fragments, so for each piece removed, another may soon appear.

The danger hangs over every launch like the sword of Damocles. A single strike on a navigation or weather satellite could disrupt services on which billions of people depend, and a chain of collisions might render some orbits unusable for generations.

Some observers argue that we opened Pandora's box when we first reached orbit. Yet the myth is incomplete without its ending: when every trouble had escaped, hope remained. International agreements requiring satellites to deorbit at the end of their missions suggest that the problem, though stubborn, need not be permanent.

pc1646f4cf6.title: The Translator's Thousand Nights
pc1646f4cf6.text:
When I began translating my grandmother's notebooks, I imagined the task would occupy a single summer. Three years later, I feel like Scheherazade, postponing the ending with each additional story, except that the deadline I keep evading is imposed by my own impatience rather than by a king's decree.

My grandmother recorded everything imaginable: traditional recipes, regional proverbs, and the names of winds that sailors once used along the Gulf coast. My friends teased that I was tilting at windmills, devoting my evenings to a project no publisher had requested. Perhaps they were right, but windmills, after all, grind grain into bread.

There was a moment, halfway through the second notebook, when I realized I had crossed the Rubicon. I had stopped translating merely to finish and had begun translating to understand, and there was no returning to the quicker, shallower method that had initially satisfied me.

I do not possess a Midas touch; nothing I handle turns to gold. Yet each page I complete preserves something considerably more durable than gold: an individual voice that would otherwise have fallen permanently silent.

pd89e7d660d.title: Camels in the Desert
pd89e7d660d.text:
Camels live in the hot desert. They can walk for many days. A camel has a big hump on its back. The hump is full of fat. The fat helps the camel when there is no food.

Camels have long eyelashes. The lashes keep sand out of their eyes. Their wide feet do not sink in the sand. People in the desert ride camels. They also use camels to carry heavy bags.

p1d04101539.title: Maryam's Solar Oven
p1d04101539.text:
Maryam wanted to bake bread without using the kitchen stove. Her teacher had said that sunlight carries energy, so Maryam wondered whether she could trap that energy in a box.

She lined a cardboard box with aluminum foil and painted the bottom black. Then she covered the opening with clear plastic wrap. On Saturday morning, she placed a small ball of dough inside and set the box in the sunny courtyard.

After an hour, the dough had barely changed. Maryam was disappointed, but her grandfather suggested tilting the box so that it faced the sun directly. She propped it up with two bricks and checked it again every twenty minutes.

By early afternoon, the bread had risen and turned golden brown. Maryam wrote down every step in her notebook. Next, she wanted to find out whether a bigger box would cook faster.

p9c767d5230.title: The Astrolabe
p9c767d5230.text:
Long before smartphones, travelers and scholars carried a device that could tell time, measure the height of stars, and help find directions. This instrument, called the astrolabe, was a flat brass disk covered with carefully engraved lines and a rotating pointer.

Although the earliest astrolabes were built in ancient Greece, scientists in the Islamic world greatly improved them between the eighth and thirteenth centuries. Mariam al-Ijliya, who worked in the city of Aleppo during the tenth century, became famous for building astrolabes of remarkable precision. Other astronomers wrote detailed manuals explaining more than a thousand uses for the instrument.

To use an astrolabe, a person held it up by a ring, sighted a star through the pointer, and read the star's angle above the horizon. By matching that angle with the engraved scales, the user could calculate the hour of the night or the direction of a distant city.

Today, most astrolabes sit in museums. Nevertheless, the mathematics engraved on them still forms part of the foundation of modern astronomy.

pbc34d9d630.title: Letter from the Red Sea
pbc34d9d630.text:
Dear Students of Grade 8,

Greetings from the research vessel Al-Murjan, which is anchored above a coral reef in the northern Red Sea. Many of you asked why our team is studying this particular reef, so I will try to answer as clearly as I can.

Around the world, warming oceans have caused coral to bleach, meaning the coral loses the microscopic algae that provide its color and most of its nutrition. Surprisingly, corals in the northern Red Sea appear to tolerate water temperatures that would seriously damage reefs elsewhere, and our goal is to discover the biological explanation.

Each morning, divers collect small coral fragments, which we place in laboratory tanks where the temperature can be raised gradually. We then carefully record how many days each fragment keeps its natural color. So far, fragments from this reef have survived temperatures two degrees higher than samples from other regions.

We do not yet know whether this remarkable resistance comes from the coral's genes or from the algae living inside it, and that will be our next investigation.

With best wishes,
Dr. Lina Haddad

p60ffaefb96.title: Cooling the City
p60ffaefb96.text:
Members of the council, I want to address a question that residents ask every August: why does our neighborhood feel several degrees hotter than the farms outside the city? The answer lies in what scientists call the urban heat island effect.

Asphalt roads, dark rooftops, and concrete walls absorb sunlight throughout the day and release that stored heat slowly after sunset. Consequently, temperatures downtown may remain uncomfortably high long after the surrounding countryside has cooled. Vehicles and air-conditioning units add further heat, creating a cycle in which hotter streets demand more cooling, and more cooling produces more waste heat.

Fortunately, the problem is not mysterious, and neither are the solutions. Cities that have painted rooftops in reflective colors, planted shade trees along sidewalks, and replaced parking lots with small parks have measured noticeable reductions in surface temperatures.

I am not asking the council to transform the city overnight. I am asking for a pilot program on three streets, with temperature sensors installed before and after the changes, so that we can answer a second question with evidence rather than guesswork: which solution works best here?

p2cf9f8169b.title: The Paper Question
p2cf9f8169b.text:
Historians have long debated a deceptively simple question: why did paper, invented in China centuries earlier, transform intellectual life so rapidly once it reached the Islamic world? The conventional explanation credits a single event, the capture of Chinese papermakers after the Battle of Talas in 751, who supposedly taught their craft in Samarkand. Recent scholarship, however, regards this account as too tidy, noting that paper was probably already circulating in Central Asia through ordinary commerce.

Whatever its precise route, paper's subsequent success depended less on its arrival than on the institutions prepared to exploit it. By the late eighth century, Baghdad's government bureaucracy required enormous quantities of inexpensive writing material, and paper, unlike parchment, could be manufactured cheaply from linen rags. Paper mills multiplied, booksellers' markets flourished, and translators working in the House of Wisdom produced copies of scientific and philosophical works at a remarkable pace.

Thus the more useful question is not who brought paper westward, but what kind of society was ready to make it indispensable.

p68e9a5dca3.title: Our Class Needs a Fish Tank
p68e9a5dca3.text:
I think our class should get a fish tank. Fish are fun to watch, and they help us feel calm when we are working. We can learn how fish eat and grow.

Some kids say a fish tank is too much work. That is not true. We can take turns. Each day, one child can feed the fish. Once a week, our teacher can help us clean the tank.

A fish tank would make our classroom a happy and interesting place. Let's ask our principal today!

pc225495e86.title: Keep the Library Open
pc225495e86.text:
Every June, our town library closes its doors for the whole summer. I believe this is a mistake, and I hope the town council will change its plan this year.

Summer is when students have the most free time to read. Without the library, many children spend those long weeks in front of screens instead of books. Teachers notice the difference in September, when some students have forgotten skills they worked hard to learn.

Some people argue that keeping the library open costs too much money. That is a fair concern, but it has a simple answer. Many parents and high school students have already offered to volunteer at the front desk, so the town would not need to hire extra workers.

A library is not just a building full of books. It is a place where curious minds keep growing, even in July.

p2fd92d21d7.title: Sunlight Waiting
p2fd92d21d7.text:
Saudi Arabia's deserts receive some of the strongest sunlight on Earth, yet for decades that energy simply warmed empty sand. Building large solar farms across these regions is one of the smartest investments the country can make.

Solar panels produce electricity without burning fuel, which means cleaner air for growing cities. They also create jobs for engineers, technicians, and construction workers.

Critics point out that desert dust settles on panels and can reduce their output considerably. This objection deserves attention, because a dirty panel can lose much of its power within weeks. However, engineers have already developed waterless robots that glide across the panels each night, brushing away dust before sunrise. Several large plants now use them successfully.

Other skeptics worry that the sun disappears at night. Yet new battery systems can store daytime energy for evening use, and their prices continue to fall.

The sunlight is free, abundant, and waiting. We should use it.

p9e02ae715d.title: In Defense of Old Walls
p9e02ae715d.text:
Whenever a developer proposes demolishing one of the mud-brick houses in our old quarter, the same familiar arguments inevitably appear. The buildings are crumbling, critics say, and restoring them costs more than constructing modern apartments. Some even claim that nobody wants to live in narrow, windowless rooms anymore.

I understand these concerns, and I will not pretend that restoration is cheap. Nevertheless, the critics measure value with the wrong ruler. A new apartment tower can be built anywhere, by anyone, in any decade. A house whose thick walls were shaped by hand to stay cool through a desert summer cannot be replaced once it is gone.

Furthermore, the economic argument is weaker than it appears. Restored districts throughout the region now attract visitors, cafes, and craftspeople, generating income that a parking garage never could.

Our grandparents constructed these homes with remarkable patience and skill. Bulldozing them to save a little money would be a loss we could never undo.

p8afe54ec3f.title: Why Reach Beyond Earth?
p8afe54ec3f.text:
It has become fashionable to dismiss space exploration as an expensive distraction. With hunger, disease, and climate change unresolved, the argument goes, governments should not spend billions launching robots toward distant planets. This position is sincere, and it reflects genuine compassion; nevertheless, it rests on two questionable assumptions.

The first assumption is that money spent on space is somehow removed from Earth. In reality, nearly every dollar pays salaries for engineers, machinists, and scientists who live and work here. Moreover, technologies developed for spacecraft, including water purification systems, lightweight insulation, and improved medical imaging, have repeatedly found their way into ordinary hospitals and homes.

The second assumption is that we must choose between solving terrestrial problems and exploring beyond them. Space agencies typically receive less than one percent of a national budget, a fraction too small to determine whether a country can feed its citizens.

Curiosity is not a luxury that humanity indulges after its problems are solved; it is frequently the means by which they are solved.

p88885b4ff1.title: Lost in the Machine
p88885b4ff1.text:
Proponents of machine translation now predict, with considerable confidence, that learning a foreign language will soon become as unnecessary as memorizing logarithm tables. Their reasoning is not foolish. Translation software has improved dramatically, and a traveler in Marrakesh or Kuala Lumpur can already order a meal, negotiate a taxi fare, and read a museum placard without studying a single verb.

Yet the prediction confuses communication with comprehension. A translated sentence conveys information; it rarely conveys the speaker's humor, hesitation, or the cultural assumptions embedded in an idiom. The Arabic poet and the Malay storyteller are not merely transmitting data, and readers who encounter them only through software receive something closer to a summary than a conversation.

One might object that most people need summaries, not poetry. That objection is fair as far as it goes. But a society in which language learning becomes a hobby for specialists will gradually lose the citizens best equipped to notice what translation omits, and it will not realize what it has lost, precisely because no machine will tell it.

p0f1c3e0353.title: Trees Help Our Town
p0f1c3e0353.text:
Trees are good for our town. First, trees give us shade. On hot days, we can sit under a big tree and stay cool and happy. Next, trees are homes for birds and squirrels. Birds build their nests high up in the branches. Last, trees help clean the air we breathe.

Our town should plant more trees. Then every street can be cool, green, and full of birds.

pef9136f676.title: Walk to Learn
pef9136f676.text:
Students who walk to school arrive ready to learn. That is why our town should build safer sidewalks so that more children can walk each morning.

Walking gives children exercise before the school day begins. Doctors recommend that kids be active for at least sixty minutes a day, and a fifteen-minute walk each way covers half of that goal. A study at one elementary school found that students who walked were more alert during their first class than students who rode in cars.

Walking also helps the community. Fewer cars near the school mean less traffic and cleaner air. My cousin, who lives in another city, enjoys riding her scooter to the park on weekends.

Safe sidewalks cost money, but the benefits for students are worth it. Let's give every child a safe path to school.

p618d7e0e02.title: Let Students Sleep
p618d7e0e02.text:
Middle school students across the country are chronically tired, and the problem is not simply that they stay up too late. During adolescence, the body's internal clock shifts, so teenagers naturally fall asleep and wake up later than younger children. Starting school at 7:30 in the morning therefore forces many students to learn during the hours when their brains are least alert.

Schools that have moved their start times later have reported encouraging results. In one district, attendance improved and the number of students falling asleep in class dropped after the first bell moved from 7:30 to 8:30. Researchers who studied several such districts also found modest improvements in grades.

A later schedule does create challenges, such as rearranging bus routes and after-school sports. However, these are practical problems with practical solutions, whereas exhaustion affects every lesson of every day. School leaders should make the change.

p411f09dc24.title: Catching the Wind
p411f09dc24.text:
For centuries, builders in the Gulf and Iran topped houses with wind towers, tall open-sided structures that capture passing breezes and channel them down into the rooms below. Modern architects should revive this design, because it can cool buildings with little or no electricity.

The physics is straightforward. Warm air rises and escapes through the top of the tower, while cooler air is drawn in to replace it, creating a steady circulation. Engineers who measured temperatures inside a restored house in Dubai found that rooms beneath the tower stayed several degrees cooler than the air outside during the afternoon.

In addition, air-conditioning accounts for a large share of electricity use in hot countries, so even a modest reduction would lower costs and emissions. A neighbor of mine insists that her grandmother's house was more comfortable than any apartment she has lived in since.

Wind towers cannot replace air-conditioning entirely during the hottest months. Nevertheless, combined with modern insulation, they could significantly reduce how often machines must run.

pada510bfc7.title: A Course Every Graduate Needs
pada510bfc7.text:
Every year, thousands of graduates leave high school able to solve quadratic equations yet unable to explain how interest accumulates on a loan. This gap is not a minor oversight; it is a failure that follows young people into adulthood. Schools should therefore require a semester-long course in personal finance before graduation.

The evidence for such a requirement is substantial. Researchers who compared regions that adopted mandatory finance courses with regions that did not found that graduates in the first group later carried less high-interest debt and missed fewer loan payments. Surveys also show that a majority of young adults wish they had learned budgeting skills in school.

Skeptics argue that families, not schools, should teach money management. Ideally, perhaps; but many parents never received such instruction themselves and cannot pass on knowledge they lack. Leaving financial education to chance simply preserves existing inequalities.

A single required course will not eliminate poor financial decisions. It would, however, ensure that every student begins adult life with the same essential tools.

paf18afa828.title: Walls of Roots
paf18afa828.text:
Coastal planners confronting rising seas have traditionally favored concrete seawalls, structures whose protective function is easy to visualize and simple to measure. This preference, I contend, is increasingly difficult to justify. Restored mangrove forests offer comparable protection at a fraction of the long-term cost while delivering benefits that concrete cannot.

Field measurements consistently show that a dense mangrove belt several hundred meters wide can substantially reduce the height of incoming waves. Unlike a seawall, the forest also traps sediment that allows it to rise gradually alongside the sea. Seawalls, by contrast, deteriorate, require expensive maintenance, and frequently accelerate erosion on neighboring beaches by deflecting wave energy.

Admittedly, mangroves require years to mature and cannot be planted on every coastline; along urban harbors, engineered barriers may remain unavoidable. Yet this limitation argues for combining approaches, not for abandoning living defenses. A nation that invests exclusively in concrete purchases a single function, whereas a restored mangrove simultaneously shelters fisheries, stores carbon, and sustains wildlife.

p2b7b5f9bd8.title: Sea Turtles Need Help
p2b7b5f9bd8.text:
Sea turtles are my favorite animals. They swim far in the warm sea. Mother turtles come to the beach to lay eggs in the sand.

I think people must help them. Trash on the beach can hurt baby turtles. Bright lights at night can make them get lost. We can pick up trash and turn off lights near the beach.

Last summer, my class cleaned a beach in Jeddah. We filled ten bags! I felt proud. Every person can do a small job to keep turtles safe.

p99b766fae4.title: A Letter About Bike Lanes
p99b766fae4.text:
Dear Editor,

Every morning I watch hundreds of cars crawl past my school, filling the air with noise and smoke. Many of my classmates live less than two kilometers away, yet almost nobody rides a bicycle. The reason is simple: our streets have no safe bike lanes.

Some people say bike lanes cost too much money. However, I believe they would save money in the long run. Fewer cars would mean less traffic, cleaner air, and healthier, more energetic students who exercise every single day. In cities like Copenhagen, many children ride to school every day.

I am asking the city council to build a protected bike lane on King Fahd Street. Our parents would worry less about our safety, and we would arrive at school awake, energetic, and ready to concentrate on our lessons.

Sincerely, Layla Hassan, Grade 5

pe2ec80b005.title: What the Desert Taught Me
pe2ec80b005.text:
When my family moved from Riyadh to a small town near the Empty Quarter, I was convinced that I had been exiled to the most boring place on Earth. The landscape seemed to contain nothing but sand, heat, and an endless, indifferent sky.

My opinion began to change on a camping trip in early winter. Our guide, a quiet man named Faisal, knelt beside a set of tiny tracks and explained that a jerboa had crossed the dune only an hour earlier. Later he showed me a shrub whose roots stretch many meters down toward hidden water.

That night, lying beneath more stars than I had ever imagined, I realized that the desert was not empty at all. It was crowded with clever survivors; I had simply never learned how to look. Now, whenever friends from the city complain that nothing interesting ever happens here, I invite them to spend one unforgettable night exploring the dunes.

p4cd3b473ff.title: Fix It First
p4cd3b473ff.text:
Last year, our school discarded more than three hundred chairs, calculators, and electric fans. Most of them were not genuinely broken; a loose screw, a cracked hinge, or an exhausted battery was enough to send them to the dumpster. I consider that practice wasteful, and I suspect that many of you, after a moment of reflection, will agree.

I propose that we establish a repair club that meets every Thursday afternoon in the technology laboratory. Volunteers would learn to use basic tools under the supervision of our technology teacher, and anyone could bring a damaged item to be examined before it is permanently thrown away.

Some will argue that new equipment is inexpensive and that repairs consume too much valuable time. They are partly right: a repaired fan is never quite as shiny as a new one. But every repair teaches a practical skill, saves money, and keeps metal and plastic out of the overflowing landfill. When we fix something ourselves, we stop being mere consumers and become problem solvers. Let us choose to fix it first.

p58be01296e.title: Rethinking the Origins of Experiment
p58be01296e.text:
Textbooks frequently credit seventeenth-century Europe with inventing the experimental method, as though careful testing appeared suddenly in a single place and time. That narrative is tidy, but it is incomplete. Six centuries earlier, in Cairo, the scholar Ibn al-Haytham was already insisting that claims about light and vision be checked against controlled observation.

In his Book of Optics, he described darkened rooms in which light entered through a small opening, allowing him to test whether rays travel in straight lines. He also warned readers that a researcher must treat even respected authorities with suspicion, including his own conclusions.

None of this means that later scientists merely copied him; knowledge travels through translation, debate, and reinvention, and many hands shaped modern science. Yet acknowledging Ibn al-Haytham is not a matter of generosity. It is a matter of accuracy. A history of science that begins in one century and one continent is not simply unfair; it is wrong.

pb115098dd4.title: The Cost of Never Being Lost
pb115098dd4.text:
I have no desire to romanticize confusion or inconvenience. Anyone who has circled an unfamiliar city at midnight, fuel gauge sinking, knows that being lost is rarely poetic. Satellite navigation has spared countless travelers that misery, and I would not surrender the device in my own car.

Still, convenience extracts a quiet price. When a synthesized voice announces every intersection, the traveler no longer needs to notice the minaret on the left or the curvature of the wadi on the right; the city becomes a sequence of instructions rather than a place. Cognitive researchers have repeatedly observed that individuals who rely heavily on automated, turn-by-turn directions frequently develop weaker mental maps of the very routes they travel daily.

My argument, consequently, is not that we should abandon our screens but that we should deliberately and occasionally ignore them. Walk to a neighborhood without the blue dot; ask a shopkeeper for directions; tolerate a few wrong turns. Disorientation, in small and voluntary doses, may be the unavoidable price of genuinely understanding where we are.

p66bbb3a4a6.title: The Date Palm
p66bbb3a4a6.text:
Date palms grow in hot, dry places. They can grow very tall. A date palm can live for more than one hundred years!

Dates grow in big bunches at the top of the tree. They are sweet and soft. People eat them with milk or coffee. Farmers climb the trees to pick them.

Date palms help people in many ways. Their leaves can make baskets and mats. Their trunks can make roofs. That is why people in Arabia have loved this tree for a long time.

p790d36db9f.title: Join the Coral Reef Cleanup!
p790d36db9f.text:
Did you know that the Red Sea is home to more than one thousand kinds of fish? Its bright coral reefs are some of the healthiest in the world. But plastic bags, bottles, and old fishing nets are piling up along the shore, and they can harm the reef and the creatures that live there.

This Saturday, the Young Divers Club will clean the sandy beach beside the marina from 8:00 to 11:00 in the morning, before the afternoon heat becomes uncomfortable. Volunteers of all ages are welcome. We will provide protective gloves, sturdy collection bags, and refreshing cold water for every volunteer. You only need to bring a hat and a helpful attitude!

Every plastic bottle you collect is one less danger for a curious sea turtle or a colorful reef fish. Sign up at the club office today, and help protect the sea we all love.

[Picture: Children in hats carry full trash bags along a sandy beach while a turtle swims in clear water nearby.]

p4c01445408.title: The Pocket Universe
p4c01445408.text:
Imagine crossing a desert by caravan a thousand years ago, with no clock and no map you could trust, trying to learn the hour and your direction from the sky alone. For many travelers in the medieval Islamic world, the solution fit in one hand: the astrolabe.

An astrolabe is a flat brass disk engraved with lines representing the sky. By sighting a star or the sun through a rotating arm and lining up its plates, a trained user could calculate the time, find the direction of a distant city, or measure the height of a building. Craftsmen in cities such as Baghdad, Córdoba, and Isfahan competed to produce the most accurate and beautiful instruments.

Among the most celebrated makers was Mariam al-Astrulabiya, who worked in Aleppo in the tenth century. Her skill was so admired that a ruler employed her at his court. Today, astrolabes rest in museum cases, but the questions they answered remain the foundation of modern navigation.

pe688deb891.title: My Long War with the Alarm Clock
pe688deb891.text:
For three years, my alarm clock and I were bitter enemies. Every morning at six, it shrieked like a startled peacock, and every morning I silenced it with the reflexes of a ninja before sinking back into my pillow. My mother eventually hid the clock across the room, forcing me to stagger past my desk, trip over my backpack, and fight the monster in person.

The war ended not with a victory but with a science lesson. Our biology teacher explained that teenagers' internal clocks naturally shift later during adolescence, so many of us genuinely struggle to fall asleep early. She added that screens glowing late at night delay the release of melatonin, the hormone that signals the body to rest.

I now charge my phone in the kitchen and turn off the lights by ten. The alarm clock still sits across the room, but these days it rarely has to raise its voice.

p801f4592c0.title: The Hejaz Railway: Two Views
p801f4592c0.text:
Text 1: The Hejaz Railway, completed in 1908, connected Damascus with Medina across roughly 1,300 kilometers of desert. Built largely to shorten a journey that had once required weeks by camel caravan, the narrow-gauge line reduced the trip to only a few days. Its operation was disrupted during the First World War, and much of the southern track was never restored.

Text 2: Yesterday I walked beside the abandoned rails outside Al-Ula, where a rusted locomotive still leans on its broken track as if waiting for a whistle that will never come. The station walls, carefully restored, glow amber at sunset. Standing there, I tried to imagine the crowded platforms, the hiss of steam, and the travelers who once crossed in days what their grandparents had crossed in weeks. History, I realized, is not only written in archives; sometimes it rusts quietly in the sand, inviting anyone patient enough to listen.

pad52a8f90d.title: Address to the Graduating Engineers
pad52a8f90d.text:
Graduates, you have devoted four demanding years to mastering equations that describe the movement of water through pipes, soil, and semipermeable membranes. I will not diminish that accomplishment by pretending it was effortless. Yet I ask you to remember a coastal village I visited a decade ago, where a beautifully engineered desalination plant stood silent because no one in the surrounding community had been trained to replace its specialized filters.

That plant was not a failure of mathematics; it was a failure of imagination. Its designers had solved the problem elegantly on paper and entirely forgotten the people who would live beside it.

You will be tempted, as I was, to measure success by efficiency alone. Measure it also by durability, by affordability, and by whether an independent technician in a distant, isolated community can maintain what you have constructed. Design for the maintenance engineer who will never have the opportunity to meet you. Design for the family that cannot afford a replacement machine. Design, above all, for the morning after the ribbon is cut.

p33159f9e0a.text:

pef198681fb.title: Desert Survivors
pef198681fb.text:
Chapter 3: Animals of the Arabian Desert

Arabian Oryx
The Arabian oryx is a white antelope with long, straight horns and dark markings on its face and legs. It can survive for several weeks without drinking because it absorbs moisture from the desert plants it eats. By 1972 the oryx had completely disappeared from the wild, but scientists carefully raised oryx in protected areas and eventually returned them to the desert.

[Photo caption: An Arabian oryx rests in the shade of an acacia tree during the hottest part of the afternoon, conserving energy and water.]

pa85e2f8aaa.title: Falaj Channels of Oman
pa85e2f8aaa.text:
Chapter 5: Ancient Water Systems
Section 5.2: Falaj Channels of Oman

For more than two thousand years, farmers in Oman have moved water with aflaj (singular: falaj), narrow channels that carry groundwater or spring water across long distances, sometimes through tunnels dug beneath the desert.¹ Because the water flows by gravity alone, the system requires no pumps or fuel.

Sharing the Water
Each family receives water for a fixed period, measured traditionally by the movement of shadows during the day and of stars at night. A respected manager, called the wakil, keeps the schedule fair.

[Sidebar, Did You Know? Five Omani aflaj were added to the UNESCO World Heritage List in 2006.]

¹ Some tunnels run more than ten kilometers. See Appendix B for a cross-section diagram.

Key Terms: aflaj, gravity, groundwater, wakil (see Glossary, page 212)

p5ba11be341.title: Dictionary Page 418
p5ba11be341.text:
Guide words: monsoon, moraine

monsoon (mon-SOON) noun 1. a seasonal wind system that reverses direction between summer and winter, especially over the Indian Ocean and southern Asia. 2. the season of intense, prolonged rainfall associated with the summer wind. [From Arabic mawsim, “season,” through Portuguese and Dutch.]

monument (MON-yuh-ment) noun 1. a building, statue, or structure constructed to commemorate a notable person or historical event. 2. a place or object of enduring historical importance: The old fort is a national monument. 3. an outstanding example illustrating a particular quality: Her research is a monument to patience.

moor (MOOR) verb to secure a boat or ship in position with ropes, cables, or an anchor: The sailors moored the dhow in the harbor. noun an open, elevated area of uncultivated land, typically covered with rough grass.

[Thesaurus box: monument; synonyms: memorial, landmark, tribute, statue]

p031c82f40c.title: Al-Biruni: Online Encyclopedia Article
p031c82f40c.text:
Last edited: 3 March 2026 | Read time: 4 minutes | Cite this page

Contents: 1 Early Life; 2 Measuring the Earth; 3 Later Works; 4 References

2 Measuring the Earth
Around 1025, Abu Rayhan al-Biruni devised a method for estimating the radius of the Earth by measuring the angle at which the horizon dipped below him from a mountaintop.[3] Because his method required only a single location, it was considerably more practical than earlier techniques, which depended on simultaneous observations from two distant cities. His result differed from modern values by less than one percent.[4] He later described the procedure in detail in a treatise on locating cities. (See also: History of geodesy; Eratosthenes.)

[Infobox: Al-Biruni | Born 973, Kath, Khwarazm | Died around 1050, Ghazni | Fields: astronomy, mathematics, geography]

4 References
[3] Rahman, S. Instruments of Medieval Science. University Press, 2019, pages 88–91.
[4] Haddad, L. “Revisiting al-Biruni's Radius.” Journal of the History of Measurement, volume 12, 2023.

p803a1dcc61.title: Navigators of the Indian Ocean
p803a1dcc61.text:
From the scholarly book Navigators of the Indian Ocean: Trade, Science, and the Monsoon, 800–1500

Preface (excerpt)
This study does not attempt a complete history of Indian Ocean commerce; such a project would require several volumes. Instead, it traces how Arab, Persian, Indian, and East African sailors shared navigational knowledge across seven centuries. Readers unfamiliar with nautical terminology should consult the Glossary before Chapter 3, where technical discussion begins. Throughout, I have deliberately preferred contemporary navigational manuscripts to later European accounts, which frequently misrepresented the scientific sophistication of the experienced pilots they encountered. Translations are my own unless otherwise indicated in the endnotes.

p017f02f85a.title: Camels Are Desert Helpers
p017f02f85a.text:
Camels live in the hot desert. Their bodies help them live there.

A camel has a hump on its back. The hump stores fat. The fat gives the camel energy when there is no food.

A camel has long eyelashes. They keep sand out of its eyes. Its wide feet do not sink in the soft sand.

A camel can walk for days without water. When it finds water, it can drink a lot very fast. Camels are made for desert life.

pe67e073198.title: Mangrove Forests of the Gulf
pe67e073198.text:
Along the coasts of the Arabian Gulf and the Red Sea, gray-green mangrove trees grow right in the salty water. Few plants can survive in such conditions, but mangroves have unusual roots that poke up above the mud and allow the trees to breathe.

These forests are important to the coast. Their tangled roots slow down waves, which protects beaches from washing away during storms. The roots also trap mud, so the water around them stays clear.

Mangroves also serve as protected nurseries for many different ocean creatures. Young fish and shrimp hide among the roots, where large hunters cannot easily reach them. When the young animals grow bigger, they swim out to the open sea.

Today, people in several countries are planting new mangroves. Scientists say that protecting these forests helps the whole coastline stay healthy.

pc5759da1f8.title: Cities That Hold the Heat
pc5759da1f8.text:
On a summer afternoon, the center of a large city can be several degrees hotter than the farmland just outside it. Scientists call this effect an urban heat island. Dark rooftops, asphalt roads, and concrete walls absorb sunlight all day and release that heat slowly, long after sunset.

The extra heat is more than uncomfortable. Hotter neighborhoods use more electricity for air conditioning, which raises costs for families and strains power stations. During heat waves, elderly people and young children face serious health risks.

Fortunately, cities are discovering practical solutions. Riyadh has launched a program to plant millions of trees, whose shade can cool a street by several degrees. Other cities paint rooftops white so that they reflect sunlight instead of absorbing it. Some engineers are even testing lighter-colored pavement.

None of these changes works alone, but together they can make crowded cities cooler, healthier, and more pleasant places to live.

p7a3cfa19f1.title: The Brass Computer
p7a3cfa19f1.text:
Long before smartphones, travelers and scholars carried a device that could tell time, locate stars, and measure the height of mountains. This instrument, the astrolabe, was a flat brass disk engraved with lines and scales, and it was refined by scientists across the Islamic world between the eighth and thirteenth centuries.

An astronomer named Mariam al-Ijliya, who worked in Aleppo in the tenth century, became so skilled at building astrolabes that the ruler of the city employed her. Her instruments were praised for their precision, and her reputation shows that expert craftsmanship was valued highly.

The astrolabe's influence spread far beyond the region where it was perfected. Through translated books, European scholars learned how to build and use the device, and sailors later adapted it to determine their position at sea.

In a sense, the astrolabe was an early portable computer: it turned careful observations into reliable calculations. Its story reveals how knowledge travels between cultures and grows with each new generation of users.

p010ebcdbfb.title: The Cost of Noise
p010ebcdbfb.text:
Noise is rarely listed among the hazards of modern life, yet a growing body of research suggests that it deserves a place beside polluted air and contaminated water. Persistent traffic, construction, and aircraft noise do more than irritate; they elevate stress hormones, disrupt sleep, and, according to several long-term studies, increase the risk of heart disease.

Children may be particularly vulnerable. Researchers comparing schools near busy airports with quieter schools have found that students exposed to constant noise often score lower on reading comprehension tests, presumably because concentration requires a degree of acoustic calm that these classrooms cannot provide.

Some cities have responded creatively. Planners have installed sound-absorbing barriers along highways, restricted nighttime deliveries, and designated "quiet zones" in parks where loudspeakers are prohibited. These measures are inexpensive compared with treating the illnesses that noise contributes to.

Silence, in other words, is no longer merely a pleasant luxury. It is a public resource that, like clean water, must be deliberately protected, because once a city surrenders it, recovering it is extraordinarily difficult.

pa45fc42a4f.title: In Praise of Maintenance
pa45fc42a4f.text:
Societies tend to celebrate invention far more enthusiastically than maintenance. Museums display the first telephone and the first airplane, and prizes reward the scientist whose discovery is unprecedented; almost no one, however, commemorates the technician who keeps a water-treatment plant operating reliably for thirty years.

This imbalance is not merely a matter of fairness. When governments and companies allocate resources primarily to novel projects, existing infrastructure deteriorates quietly until it fails dramatically. Bridges, pipelines, and electrical grids rarely collapse because they were poorly invented; far more often, they collapse because routine inspections and repairs were postponed, underfunded, or considered unglamorous.

Historians of technology have observed that most of a machine's lifetime value is realized long after its invention, through incremental adjustments made by people who understand its weaknesses. The steam engine, for example, became genuinely efficient only after decades of modest improvements by mechanics whose names are largely forgotten.

None of this diminishes the importance of innovation. Rather, it suggests that a civilization's durability depends as much on its willingness to care for what already exists as on its capacity to imagine what does not.

p16f76a7f04.title: The New Puppy
p16f76a7f04.text:
Lina wanted a puppy more than anything. "Puppies are fun," she said. "They play and run with you."

Her brother Adam did not agree. A big dog had barked at him once. "Dogs are loud," he said. "I do not want one."

Mom had an idea. They visited a calm little puppy at a neighbor's house. It licked Adam's hand softly. Adam smiled. "Maybe some dogs are nice," he said.

p8bf4f84973.title: The Harbor Museum
p8bf4f84973.text:
Faisal groaned when Grandpa announced that they would spend Saturday at the old harbor museum. "Museums are just dusty boxes," Faisal muttered, imagining the exciting soccer match he would miss with his friends.

Inside, Grandpa stopped beside a small wooden boat, and his eyes shone. "When I was your age, my father dove for pearls from a boat like this," he said. "The divers held their breath for nearly two minutes, and the crew sang traditional songs to keep their rhythm steady while they worked."

Faisal stared at the heavy stone that the divers had used to sink quickly to the bottom. Curious, he tried holding his own breath, but he lasted only forty seconds before gasping for air.

"Two minutes?" he exclaimed when he could finally breathe normally again. "That's not dusty at all. That's absolutely incredible."

Grandpa laughed warmly and patted his grandson's shoulder. "History is only dusty when nobody remembers to tell its stories."

p9e68062628.title: The Missing Wheel
p9e68062628.text:
[A school robotics workshop. A robot lies on the table with one wheel missing, while RANA studies a notebook and YOUSEF paces anxiously.]

YOUSEF: The regional competition is in four days, so we should completely redesign the entire drive system. It's the only realistic way to defeat the experienced teams.

RANA: (calmly) Rebuilding means rewriting every line of navigation code we've already tested. I'd rather replace the damaged wheel and practice our difficult turns.

YOUSEF: Practicing won't matter if our robot is noticeably slower than everyone else's.

RANA: (closing the notebook) And speed won't matter if the robot crashes because nothing was tested. Remember what happened at last year's competition? We added a new arm the night before the competition, and it froze during the first round.

YOUSEF: (stopping, quietly) I remember it clearly, because I was the one who insisted on adding the arm.

RANA: Then let's make a reasonable agreement. We repair the wheel today, test everything tomorrow, and if we still have time, we'll try one small improvement.

YOUSEF: (picking up a screwdriver) One small improvement, then, and absolutely nothing more. Agreed.

pf60fa14960.title: The Falcon Behind the Gate
pf60fa14960.text:
Everyone on Al-Nakheel Street agreed that Mr. Saleh was the grumpiest man in the neighborhood. Whenever children wandered near his courtyard gate, he waved them away without a word, and twelve-year-old Huda had decided that he simply disliked young people.

So she was astonished one evening when Mr. Saleh knocked on her family's door, holding a cardboard box. Inside, a young falcon blinked at the lamplight, one wing wrapped in a neat white bandage.

"I discovered her tangled in a wire fence near the highway," he explained, his voice considerably gentler than Huda had expected. "For three weeks I've kept her calm and quiet so that the fractured bone could heal properly, because noise frightens an injured bird." After a moment of hesitation, he continued, "Your father mentioned that you hope to study veterinary medicine, so would you help me feed her while I visit my brother?"

Huda looked at the falcon, then at the old man's tired, hopeful face. She suddenly realized that the gate had never been closed against the neighborhood children; it had been closed, patiently and protectively, around something fragile.

p1fe2a2865c.title: Letters from the Observatory
p1fe2a2865c.text:
Text 1: Dear Professor Haddad,
Three weeks at the mountain observatory have taught me that astronomy is mostly waiting. Clouds have covered the sky on fourteen of twenty nights, and when the sky finally clears, I spend hours calibrating instruments rather than making discoveries. I confess that I sometimes wonder whether I chose the wrong profession.
Samira

Text 2: Dear Samira,
Your frustration is entirely reasonable, yet I suspect you are measuring your work against an imaginary standard. When I arrived here thirty years ago, I also expected revelations every night. Instead, I learned that a discovery is usually the final, visible moment of thousands of invisible, patient hours. Your calibrations are not interruptions to astronomy; they are astronomy. The comet I eventually identified would have remained hidden if my predecessor had not recorded, with tedious precision, every faint object in that region of the sky.
Professor Haddad

p19df4c8473.title: Instinct
p19df4c8473.text:
My granddaughter informs me that the cargo vessels of the future will cross the Indian Ocean without a single sailor aboard. She delivers this prediction gently, in the manner one might explain an unfamiliar medication to an elderly patient who is unlikely to appreciate its effects. I nod, because forty years at sea have taught me that arguing with the weather and with the young are equally unprofitable occupations.

What she cannot understand, I believe, is that the ocean is not a mathematical problem awaiting a solution. I have interpreted swells the way scholars interpret manuscripts, sensing a storm in the color of the horizon long before any instrument confirmed my suspicion. Can a program experience that unease in its stomach?

Yet yesterday evening she demonstrated her simulation, and I watched the digital vessel alter its course hours before a cyclone, guided by satellite information I could never have perceived. I said nothing, and I assured myself that the program had merely been fortunate. Then, in the darkness of my bedroom, I remembered how frequently I, too, had been fortunate, and had called it instinct.

p7942cff789.title: Omar Tries Again
p7942cff789.text:
Omar wanted to learn to swim. On the first day, he got water in his nose. He coughed and wanted to quit.

His coach said, "Try one more time." Omar took a big breath. He kicked his legs hard.

Every day after school, Omar went back to the pool. He practiced and practiced. At the end of the month, Omar swam across the whole pool by himself. He cheered, "I did it!"

p4fc1ec9ba7.title: The Volcano Partners
p4fc1ec9ba7.text:
Reem enjoyed being in charge of everything. When Ms. Amal paired her with quiet Joud for the science fair, Reem immediately announced their topic without asking for her partner's opinion. "I'll build the volcano model, and you can color the poster," she informed Joud.

Joud opened her mouth to suggest a different idea, then quietly closed it again.

For an entire week, Reem's volcano refused to erupt properly. The baking soda fizzled weakly, and the paper mountain grew soggy and began to collapse. Finally, Joud slid a notebook across the table. Inside were neat drawings and careful measurements. "My brother created one last year," she explained softly. "The secret is warm vinegar and a narrow opening."

Reem hesitated. Then she pulled up a second chair beside her partner. "Show me," she requested.

On the day of the fair, their volcano erupted perfectly. When the judges inquired who had designed it, Reem pointed to Joud. "We both worked on it," she explained, "but Joud solved the most difficult part."

pfbe6a42e22.title: The Island That Wasn't There
pfbe6a42e22.text:
Tariq had been the fastest copyist in the workshop of the mapmaker al-Idrisi for nearly a year, and he knew it. While the older apprentices traced coastlines with painstaking slowness, Tariq finished his sections by noon and spent the afternoons boasting about his speed.

One morning, al-Idrisi unrolled a finished map of the eastern Mediterranean and placed a finger on a tiny island. "This island," he said quietly, "does not exist. A ship's captain who trusted this map could lose his vessel searching for a harbor that is not there."

Tariq felt his face grow hot, because the careless mark was his.

He did not boast that afternoon, nor the next. Instead, he began comparing each line he drew with the travelers' reports stacked in the library, sometimes spending an hour on a single bay. By winter, the other apprentices had started bringing their own questions to him, not because he was fast, but because he was careful.

p1445076b2f.title: The Dune Run
p1445076b2f.text:
For two years, Khalid had trained for the Liwa dune run with a single goal: to defeat Majid, the runner who had edged past him at the finish line the year before. He practiced before sunrise, memorized the course map until he could trace it with his eyes closed, and refused every invitation that might interfere with his demanding schedule.

With one kilometer remaining, Khalid finally pulled ahead of his determined rival. Then, at the crest of the steepest dune, he heard a sharp cry behind him and turned to see that Majid had twisted his ankle and was sliding helplessly down the loose sand.

For a long moment, Khalid stood still, his heartbeat pounding in his ears. Victory was only several hundred meters away. He glanced at the finish banner, then turned and half-ran, half-slid back down the slope.

He finished eleventh, supporting Majid's weight throughout the descent. Afterward, several reporters asked whether he regretted sacrificing his long-anticipated victory. "I trained to become faster," he replied eventually. "I didn't realize I was also deciding what kind of runner I wanted to be."

p4d3b018df1.title: The Blue Tile
p4d3b018df1.text:
Nadia had originally imagined that her internship at the conservation laboratory would involve rescuing masterpieces. Instead, Dr. Rahman assigned her a single cracked ceramic tile from a ruined caravanserai and instructed her to clean it, millimeter by millimeter, with a cotton swab and distilled water.

During the first week, Nadia worked rapidly and resentfully, convinced that the assignment was a test of obedience rather than skill. Twice she asked for something more significant; twice Dr. Rahman simply examined her progress and returned the tile without comment.

In the third week, however, something unexpectedly shifted in her attitude. Beneath the grime, a faint blue pattern emerged, and Nadia realized that the slightest excess pressure would erase it permanently. She began working more deliberately, recording each stage in a notebook and noticing details that her earlier impatience had concealed.

When the tile was finally displayed, Dr. Rahman asked whether she still wanted to rescue masterpieces. Nadia hesitated, considering the question more seriously than she had expected. "I think," she said, "that I have to learn to deserve them first."

p4eb418ad47.title: The Retraction
p4eb418ad47.text:
Professor Faris had built his reputation on a single elegant paper, cited thousands of times, describing a catalyst that split water with unprecedented efficiency. So when his graduate student, Lina, reported that she could not reproduce the result, he responded with the brisk courtesy he reserved for minor inconveniences: she had probably contaminated her samples.

Lina methodically repeated the experiment eleven times. On the twelfth, she brought him her data in silence, and Faris, scanning the columns, recognized with cold clarity the impurity that had inflated his original measurements.

For three days he informed nobody. He drafted explanations that minimized the error, then deleted them; he composed a letter blaming an equipment supplier, then deleted that as well. Each evasion, he noticed, was more articulate than the last, and the realization disturbed him more than the mistake itself.

On the fourth morning he submitted a retraction under his own name and asked Lina to present the corrected findings at the conference. Colleagues celebrated it as an act of extraordinary courage. Faris privately considered it a debt that had merely come due.

p7944addd29.title: Rain Day
p7944addd29.text:
It rained all morning. Lina looked out the window and frowned. "Now we can't play outside," she said.

Her brother Adam smiled. "Rain is good," he said. "The plants need water. And we can jump in puddles later!"

Lina still felt sad. Then the rain stopped. Adam took her hand, and they went out. Lina jumped in a big puddle. Splash! Now she smiled too.

p2ce82b950d.title: The Empty Desert
p2ce82b950d.text:
Faisal had never wanted to come on the family camping trip, and as the car bumped across the sand, he stared gloomily at the endless dunes. "There is nothing out here," he complained. "There are no trees, no buildings, and definitely no internet connection anywhere."

His cousin Reem, who visited the desert every winter, laughed quietly. "You just don't know where to look yet," she replied patiently.

That evening, Reem led him to the top of a tall dune and pointed to tiny tracks curving across the smooth sand. "A sand fox passed here earlier, probably searching for insects," she explained, "and those little marks belong to a beetle." Then she pointed upward, where thousands of stars filled the sky, shining more brightly than anything Faisal had ever seen in the city.

Faisal was quiet for a long time. "Maybe it isn't empty," he admitted at last. "Maybe I just wasn't paying attention."

pfd730aad20.title: Two Designs
pfd730aad20.text:
[A school workshop. HALA is sanding a wooden model of a water-saving irrigation system. KHALID enters holding a laptop.]

KHALID: The competition is in three days, and our model still looks like a pile of sticks. We should build the whole design digitally instead, because the judges will be impressed by a professional animation.

HALA: (without looking up) Judges can't touch an animation. When farmers see a real model, they understand immediately how the water travels from the pipe to the roots.

KHALID: Farmers aren't judging the competition, Hala. Engineers are, and engineers appreciate precision.

HALA: (setting down the sandpaper) Precision doesn't matter if nobody can use the design. My grandfather irrigated his palm trees for forty years, and he never trusted anything he couldn't hold.

KHALID: (pausing, then opening his laptop beside the model) Then perhaps we need both, your model for the table and my animation on the screen behind it.

HALA: (smiling slightly) Show me what you have so far.

p87d0907f36.title: The Nomination
p87d0907f36.text:
Mariam was certain that Ms. Al-Qahtani disapproved of her. Every afternoon for a month, Mariam had stayed after school to water the struggling vegetable garden behind the science building, and every afternoon the teacher had watched from her classroom window without saying a word. "She thinks I'm wasting time," Mariam told her brother. "She probably wants me studying for examinations instead of wasting my afternoons with a watering can."

What Mariam did not know was that Ms. Al-Qahtani had been taking notes. On her desk lay a folder labeled "Community Service Nominations," and inside it were photographs of the garden, week by week, as the wilted seedlings grew into rows of tomatoes and mint.

On Thursday, the teacher finally stopped Mariam at the gate. "I need to speak with you on Sunday morning," she said seriously. Mariam spent the entire weekend preparing apologies, rehearsing explanations, and imagining the worst.

p7b328bf18a.title: The Oyster Beds
p7b328bf18a.text:
From the seawall at Muharraq, Grandfather Jassim could identify every reef by the color of the water above it, although he had not dived in fifty years. To him, the shimmering shallows were a cemetery of livelihoods: the place where his father had descended forty times a day, lungs burning, for pearls that eventually lost their value when cultured pearls flooded international markets.

His granddaughter Dana, who had returned from university with a degree in marine biology, regarded the same water with cautious optimism. Her research team had documented oyster populations recovering steadily since the reefs were protected, and she considered the beds not a monument to hardship but a laboratory of resilience.

"You speak about oysters as though they were patients," Jassim remarked, not unkindly.

"And you speak about them as though they were ghosts," Dana answered.

For a moment neither spoke. Then Jassim pointed toward a darker patch of water. "My father always said the largest beds were there. Perhaps your instruments should begin where his memory ends."

p799d007724.title: The Wind Tower
p799d007724.text:
I had drawn up the renovation plans with what I considered admirable efficiency: the crumbling wind tower would be dismantled, the courtyard enclosed, and a modern cooling system installed within a month. My grandmother examined the blueprints for a long time, tracing each line with a finger that trembled only slightly, and then asked a question I had not anticipated: "Where will the evening breeze go?"

I explained, patiently and at considerable length, that breezes were no longer necessary, that sealed rooms were more economical, and that sentimentality was an expensive luxury. She nodded throughout my explanation, the way one nods at a child describing a dream.

That night the electricity failed across the district. While the neighbors' sealed apartments grew stifling, cool air descended through the old tower into the courtyard, exactly as it had for a century. I found my grandmother there, reading by lantern light, entirely comfortable. She did not mention the blueprints, and I discovered, somewhat to my irritation, that I could not stop thinking about them.

p153d1bbd68.title: Desert Camels
p153d1bbd68.text:
Camels live in the desert. The desert is hot and dry. Camels have humps on their backs. The humps store fat. A camel can use this fat when there is no food.

Camels have long eyelashes. The eyelashes keep sand out of their eyes. Their wide feet help them walk on soft sand.

A camel can go many days without water. When it finds water, it can drink a lot very fast. Camels are made for desert life.

p9a1af44dfd.title: The Scientist in the Dark Room
p9a1af44dfd.text:
More than a thousand years ago, a scientist named Ibn al-Haytham studied how people see. In his time, many thinkers believed that light shot out of our eyes and touched the objects around us. Ibn al-Haytham was not satisfied with this idea, so he decided to test it.

He sat in a dark room with a tiny hole in one wall. Light from outside passed through the hole and made an upside-down picture of the street on the opposite wall. This showed him that light travels in straight lines from objects into our eyes, not the other way around.

[Diagram: Light rays from a tree pass through a small hole and form an upside-down image of the tree on the back wall of a dark box.]

Ibn al-Haytham wrote down every step of his experiments so that others could repeat them. Today, many people call him one of the first true scientists, and his dark room is an early model of the camera.

p32248eed58.title: Every School Should Grow a Garden
p32248eed58.text:
Across the region, a growing number of schools are transforming unused courtyards into vegetable gardens, and the results suggest that every school should follow their example.

First, gardens improve how students eat. In one survey of three hundred middle school students, those who helped grow vegetables were twice as likely to choose salads at lunch as students who had not. Children, it seems, are curious about food they have raised themselves.

Gardens also strengthen learning. Measuring plant growth, recording temperatures, and calculating water use turn abstract lessons in mathematics and science into practical experiences. Several teachers report that students who struggle in the classroom often become leaders in the garden.

Critics argue that gardens require too much water in a dry climate. However, drip irrigation, which delivers water directly to plant roots, can reduce water use by more than half compared with traditional methods.

[Chart: Water used per week by one school garden. Traditional watering: 400 liters. Drip irrigation: 180 liters.]

p1d2ca235ff.title: The Last Lap
p1d2ca235ff.text:
Salem arrived at the pool before the sun had cleared the rooftops, as he had every morning for six months. He stretched carefully, favoring his left shoulder in a way he hoped Coach Nasser would not notice, and slipped into the water without a word.

The first ten laps felt ordinary, almost effortless, but by the twentieth a dull ache had spread from his shoulder down to his elbow, and his stroke had begun to shorten noticeably. He gritted his teeth and kicked harder, telling himself that the regional championship was only nine days away.

When he finally climbed out, Coach Nasser was waiting with a towel and an expression Salem could not read. "Your times are excellent," the coach said slowly. "However, your left arm is entering the water ten centimeters short, and the difference grows with every lap. Champions are not the swimmers who ignore pain, Salem; they are the ones who are still competing next year."

Salem stared at the puddle forming around his feet and said nothing.

pcaec2bf585.title: Harvesting the Fog
pcaec2bf585.text:
In several coastal deserts, where rainfall may not exceed a few millimeters annually, communities have begun collecting water from an unexpected source: fog. The technique is deceptively simple. Large panels of fine mesh are suspended perpendicular to the prevailing wind; as fog drifts through them, microscopic droplets collide with the fibers, merge, and trickle into gutters below.

Proponents emphasize the method's affordability, since fog collectors require no electricity and minimal maintenance. In favorable locations, a single panel of forty square meters can yield several hundred liters per day.

Nevertheless, researchers caution against exaggerated expectations. Fog is seasonal in many regions, and yields fluctuate dramatically from week to week. Moreover, the mesh deteriorates under intense sunlight and must be replaced periodically, an expense that some isolated villages have struggled to sustain once initial funding disappeared.
