Consequently, most specialists now describe fog harvesting not as a solution to water scarcity but as a supplement, valuable precisely when it is integrated with rainwater storage, conservation, and other sources.

pfed40d5982.title: The Fragile Archive
pfed40d5982.text:
Digitization has been celebrated, with considerable justification, as the salvation of the world's manuscript heritage. Libraries in Timbuktu, Cairo, and Istanbul have photographed thousands of fragile volumes. Scholars on distant continents can now examine astronomical tables and medical treatises that few had previously seen.

Yet the enthusiasm surrounding these projects occasionally obscures an uncomfortable reality: digital files are themselves remarkably perishable. Storage formats become obsolete within decades, servers require continuous funding, and an image is only as legible as the software capable of opening it. A parchment volume, by contrast, has survived eight centuries without electricity.

None of this suggests that digitization is misguided. Rather, it implies that a photograph should be regarded as a copy that broadens access, not as a replacement that justifies neglecting the original. The most prudent archives, accordingly, invest simultaneously in climate-controlled storage for physical volumes and in the regular migration of digital files to current formats.

Preservation, in other words, is not an event but an obligation renewed by every generation.

p4b34b4cfe5.title: Two Texts About Bees
p4b34b4cfe5.text:
Text 1: Busy Bees
Bees live in a hive. They fly from flower to flower. They drink nectar and carry pollen. Bees make honey from the nectar. One hive can have many thousands of bees.

Text 2: Noor and the Bee
Noor sat in the garden. A bee landed on a yellow flower near her. Noor did not run away. She watched the bee move its legs. Then it flew off with yellow dust on its body. "Thank you for helping the flowers," Noor said.

p65b2bad458.title: Two Views of Falconry
p65b2bad458.text:
Text 1: Falcons in Arabia
Falconry has been practiced on the Arabian Peninsula for thousands of years. Long ago, Bedouin families trained falcons to hunt small animals, which provided food during the harsh desert winters. Today, falconry is mostly a sport and a celebrated tradition. Festivals attract thousands of visitors, and some trained falcons are worth as much as a new car.

Text 2: My First Falcon
When my uncle placed the young falcon on my glove, I could barely breathe. She was lighter than I expected, but her claws gripped tightly through the leather. For weeks, I fed her every morning and whispered her name, Sahm, so she would learn my voice. The day she flew back to my arm for the first time, I felt as if the whole desert was cheering.

pac95945d6d.title: The Traveler from Tangier
pac95945d6d.text:
Text 1: The Traveler from Tangier
In 1325, a young scholar named Ibn Battuta left his home in Tangier, Morocco, intending to travel to Mecca. He did not return for nearly twenty-four years. Over his lifetime, he traveled roughly 120,000 kilometers, visiting regions that stretch from West Africa to China. His later account of these journeys, dictated to a writer in Fez, remains one of the most valuable records of the medieval world, although historians note that some passages may be exaggerated.

Text 2: The Road East (a story)
Ibn Battuta wiped the dust from his eyes and gazed at the caravan stretching toward the horizon. His feet ached, and his water skin was nearly empty, yet his heart raced with curiosity. "Every city," he murmured to his camel, "is a book I have not yet read." Behind him, Tangier had disappeared; ahead lay a world he could scarcely imagine.

p0ffd9b4e87.title: Can Coral Gardens Save the Reefs?
p0ffd9b4e87.text:
Text 1: Gardens Beneath the Sea
Coral gardening is giving damaged reefs a second chance. Divers grow small fragments of coral on underwater frames, and once the fragments mature, they are attached to damaged reefs. In one Red Sea project, more than 80 percent of transplanted corals survived their first year. Supporters argue that, with enough volunteers, coral gardening could restore entire reef systems within a generation.

Text 2: A Bandage on a Broken Bone
Coral gardening is a hopeful activity, but it cannot keep pace with the destruction. Most projects restore less than one hectare, while warming oceans damage thousands of hectares in a single season. Furthermore, survival rates measured after one year can be misleading, because many transplanted corals die during the next heat wave. Restoration helps, but only reducing ocean warming will save reefs in the long term.

p5a5212d5d3.title: The Elephant Clock
p5a5212d5d3.text:
Text 1: The Elephant Clock
In 1206, the engineer Al-Jazari completed a manuscript describing dozens of ingenious machines, among them an elaborate water clock shaped like an elephant. Inside the elephant, a perforated bowl sank slowly into a tank of water; each time it filled completely, a system of strings and pulleys released a ball, which struck a cymbal to mark the passing half hour. Historians regard the design as remarkable not only for its precision but also for its deliberate combination of engineering traditions from India, Persia, Greece, and China, which Al-Jazari acknowledged by decorating the clock with symbols drawn from each culture.

Text 2: The Clock Speaks (a poem)
I am patience fashioned out of brass and water, a bowl that sinks the way an evening falls;
no sun commands me and no shadow measures, for I count in drops, and every drop recalls
the careful hands in Diyarbakir that designed me, pouring four distant kingdoms into one,
and taught the hours to sing aloud in cymbals long after their inventor's work was done.

p37c257e894.title: Two Views of the Old City
p37c257e894.text:
Text 1: from "The Memory of Streets"
A city that demolishes its oldest districts does not merely lose buildings; it forfeits the evidence of how its people once solved the problems of climate, commerce, and community. The narrow lanes of a traditional souq, shaded by overhanging upper floors, kept pedestrians cool long before air conditioning existed. To replace such quarters with glass towers is to discard a manual that no engineer has yet improved upon.

Text 2: from "Cities Are Not Museums"
Sentimental arguments for preservation frequently ignore the people who actually inhabit historic districts, many of whom contend with crumbling plumbing, inadequate fire access, and rents that decline as the buildings deteriorate. A neighborhood frozen in its past condition serves photographers better than residents. The more defensible approach is selective renewal: protect the structures of genuine architectural significance, and allow the remainder to evolve as living cities always have.

p64e5a65e7a.title: Two Sandy Places
p64e5a65e7a.text:
Text 1: Lina went to the beach with her father on a sunny morning. The sand was wet and cool. Waves splashed on her feet as she walked. She found a pink shell and put it in her bucket.

Text 2: Omar went to the desert with his uncle on a sunny afternoon. The sand was dry and hot. The wind blew the sand into small hills around him. He found a smooth stone and put it in his pocket.

p831778638d.title: Two Markets
p831778638d.text:
Text 1: Before sunrise, Nok paddled her small wooden boat along the canal. Dozens of other boats crowded the narrow water, each piled with mangoes, coconuts, and bright flowers. Sellers called out prices while ripples slapped against the boards. Nok traded a basket of bananas for a sack of rice and steered carefully home.

Text 2: At midday, Faisal followed his uncle through the covered souq in Riyadh. The stone walkway was cool and shaded, and the air smelled of cardamom and dates. Shopkeepers sat beside open sacks of spices, ready to bargain. Faisal's uncle bought saffron after a long, friendly discussion about the price, and the two walked home through the busy lanes.

p2573c0df75.title: Ice and Sand
p2573c0df75.text:
Text 1: Antarctica's Concordia Station sits on a high, frozen plateau where winter temperatures can drop below minus seventy degrees Celsius. For nearly four months each year the sun never rises, so the small crew depends on artificial light, careful schedules, and supplies delivered before the darkness begins. Scientists there study the atmosphere because the air is unusually dry and clear.

Text 2: Day nine in the Rub' al Khali. By noon the dunes shimmered with heat, and the thermometer on our vehicle read forty-eight degrees. We rested beneath a canvas shelter until late afternoon, then measured how quickly the wind reshaped the ridges around our camp. At night the sky was so clear that I could count satellites crossing between the stars. Our water supply, carried from the last village, has to last another week.

p1d3a60e886.title: Two Visits to the Old Town
p1d3a60e886.text:
Text 1: In 1952, twelve-year-old Hamid carried his father's letters through the narrow alleys of the old town, where tall coral-stone houses leaned toward each other as if sharing secrets. Carved wooden balconies shaded the lanes, and the sea breeze slipped through their latticework. Merchants shouted from doorways, donkeys clattered past, and the smell of fresh bread drifted from a corner bakery.

Text 2: Seventy years later, Hamid's granddaughter Reem explored the same alleys with an international tour group. Many of the coral-stone houses had been restored, their balconies repainted in deep greens and blues. Small museums and craft shops filled rooms where families once lived. The bakery still stood on the corner, though now visitors photographed its old oven before buying bread. Reem paused beneath a balcony and felt the familiar breeze her grandfather had described.

p42bc513f41.title: Two Harbors
p42bc513f41.text:
Text 1: When our dhow entered the harbor at Aden, the monsoon winds had carried us across the sea in twenty-three days. Cargo was unloaded by hand: porters waded through the shallows balancing bales of pepper and indigo on their heads, while clerks recorded every bundle in heavy ledgers. Negotiations with the customs officials lasted three afternoons, conducted over cups of coffee beneath a crumbling arcade.

Text 2: At a modern container terminal, a vessel carrying eighteen thousand containers can be emptied in under two days. Automated cranes lift steel boxes onto driverless vehicles, which deliver them to storage yards monitored by software that predicts congestion hours in advance. Customs documents are submitted electronically before the ship arrives, so inspections rarely delay departure. Yet the terminal still depends on the weather: during severe storms, every crane stops.

p82ce840b68.title: Two Views of Al-Ula
p82ce840b68.text:
Text 1: The oasis at Al-Ula revealed itself gradually, as though reluctant to abandon its secrecy. First came a darkened band of palm crowns against the sandstone, then the irrigation channels glinting between orchards, and finally the weathered tombs carved into cliffs that had witnessed caravans for two thousand years. Our guide spoke little, permitting the landscape's monumental silence to accomplish what explanation could not.

Text 2: Al-Ula's reputation for timeless solitude is understandable but incomplete. Farmers still negotiate the allocation of water from aquifers whose levels have declined measurably over recent decades, and the restoration of the ancient town requires engineers, archaeologists, and hundreds of residents whose livelihoods depend increasingly on tourism. To describe the valley as silent is to overlook the considerable human effort that sustains both its orchards and its antiquities.

p0422b9aea8.title: The Little Camel
p0422b9aea8.text:
Story: Dana's baby camel would not walk. Dana sat beside it in the sand. She sang a soft song. The camel's ears went up. It took one step, then two. Dana laughed and clapped.

Play: [Dana kneels by a toy camel on the stage.]
DANA: (softly) Come on, little one.
[Music plays. Dana sings.]
NARRATOR: The camel stands up!
DANA: (jumping) You did it!

pd3187018d7.title: The Lantern Seller
pd3187018d7.text:
Story: Yusuf hurried through the night market, clutching the last coin his grandmother had given him. He wanted a lantern for her window, but every stall seemed to sell only spices and cloth. At last he spotted an old man packing away a single brass lantern. Yusuf held out his coin nervously, hoping it would be enough. The man studied the boy's worried face, then smiled and lit the lantern before handing it over.

Play: [A dim stage with market stalls painted on a backdrop, while a spotlight follows YUSUF as he searches.]
YUSUF: (to the audience) I have only one coin left, and I desperately need one beautiful lantern tonight.
[The OLD MAN slowly wraps the brass lantern in a piece of faded cloth.]
OLD MAN: (pausing, then chuckling) And who needs a lantern so desperately at this late hour, young man?
YUSUF: It is for my grandmother, because her window is always dark when evening comes.
[The OLD MAN lights the lantern, and the whole stage glows gold.]

pe01e69bada.title: The First Dive
pe01e69bada.text:
Story: Ali had trained for months, yet when the boat anchored above the oyster beds, his hands trembled on the rope. His uncle, the captain, said nothing; he only tapped the stone weight twice, the signal that a diver was ready. Ali filled his lungs, remembered his grandfather's stories of dives that lasted longer than a song, and slipped beneath the green water. Below, everything was silent except the pounding of his own heart.

Script: [The deck of a wooden pearling vessel at dawn. Blue light ripples gradually across the stage while musicians, positioned along the edge, tap a quiet, deliberate rhythm.]
CAPTAIN: (tapping the stone weight twice) The sea is calm this morning, nephew, so tell me honestly whether you are prepared.
ALI: (gripping the rope, his voice trembling) I am ready, Uncle, although my hands disagree.
[The drumming quickens as ALI inhales deeply and disappears behind a curtain of shimmering blue fabric. Suddenly the drums stop, and the auditorium falls completely silent.]

p01baec9270.title: The Silent Clock
p01baec9270.text:
Story: Maryam's eyes went straight to the water clock in the corner of the crowded workshop. Its bronze elephant had stopped moving three days earlier, and the master craftsman had grown too ill to repair the mechanism. Maryam knew she had only watched him work; she had never built anything herself. Still, she unfastened the panel, traced each channel with her finger, and discovered a single pebble blocking the flow. When the water began trickling again, the miniature figures on the clock moved for the first time in days.

Radio script: [SOUND: Water dripping slowly into a bronze basin, then stopping altogether.]
NARRATOR: In a quiet workshop crowded with unfinished inventions, a magnificent water clock has mysteriously fallen silent.
MARYAM: (whispering) If only my master could tell me what to do, I would not feel so completely helpless.
[SOUND: A metal panel creaks open, and fingers tap carefully against bronze channels.]
MARYAM: Wait, something is obstructing the channel, and it is only a pebble!
[SOUND: Water rushes forward, and then a cheerful chime echoes through the workshop.]

p2c6bec1b31.title: The Comet Watcher
p2c6bec1b31.text:
Story: For three consecutive nights the clouds had refused to separate, and Laila had begun to suspect that her calculations were inaccurate. She remained beside the telescope long after the other students had retired to bed, recalculating the comet's trajectory in the margins of her notebook. Shortly before dawn, the sky cleared without warning. There, precisely where she had predicted, a faint smudge of light hung above the eastern ridge. Laila did not celebrate or wake anyone; she simply recorded the time, her pencil trembling only slightly.

Screenplay: EXT. MOUNTAIN OBSERVATORY, NIGHT
WIDE SHOT: A solitary illuminated window glows against an enormous, cloud-covered sky that seems to swallow the observatory.
CLOSE-UP: Laila's notebook, crowded with crossed-out numbers and hurried calculations.
LAILA (VOICE-OVER): Maybe I was wrong about everything, and maybe there is nothing out there to discover.
TIME-LAPSE: The clouds gradually dissipate, revealing thousands of brilliant stars above the eastern ridge.
CLOSE-UP: Laila's eye pressed against the telescope as she exhales slowly.
INSERT: Her pencil records the time, 4:52, in the notebook's crowded margin.

pe64bb350ad.title: The Last Map
pe64bb350ad.text:
Story: The old cartographer folded the final map without ceremony. For forty years he had charted the shifting coastline, correcting each version as storms rearranged the sandbars, and now his eyesight could no longer distinguish one inlet from another. His apprentice waited for some instruction, some parting wisdom, but the old man only slid the map across the table and turned toward the window, where the tide was already erasing the morning's footprints.

Review of the stage production: In the company's stage adaptation, the director transforms this quiet ending into a moment of unmistakable grief. The cartographer clutches the map before releasing it, and a recorded voice recites the names of vanished sandbars while projected coastlines dissolve across the back wall. The effect is visually arresting, yet it sacrifices the story's restraint: where the original trusted readers to sense loss in a single gesture, the production insists that the audience feel it.

p3f4da0225a.title: Friday Bread
p3f4da0225a.text:
My name is Aisha, and I live in Abha. In my family, Grandma bakes bread every Friday morning. I help her press the dough flat with my hands. The kitchen gets warm and smells sweet.

We do not eat it all alone. Grandma always says, "Bread tastes better when we share it." So we take a warm loaf to our neighbor, Mrs. Salma. She smiles and gives us dates. I think sharing is the best part.

pe0612a5130.title: A Letter from Japan
pe0612a5130.text:
Dear Grandfather,

Japan is full of surprises, and I am learning something new every day. Yesterday my host family took me on a crowded train, and surprisingly, nobody spoke on their phones during the entire journey. At home in Dammam, people chat on the bus constantly, so the silence felt uncomfortable at first. Now I think it is a kind of respect for others.

When I entered their house, I removed my shoes, exactly as we do at home. But here they also have special slippers for the bathroom, which you must never wear anywhere else! My host brother, Haruto, laughed loudly when I forgot to change them.

Tomorrow I will teach the family how to prepare Arabic coffee with cardamom, the way you taught me. I hope they enjoy it as much as I enjoy their delicious rice balls.

Your grandson,
Turki

p47da52a466.title: The View from the Spice Stall
p47da52a466.text:
I am the youngest daughter in a family of spice sellers. Every morning, visitors drift into the Marrakech market with their cameras raised, and I have learned to read their faces. They photograph my mother's pyramids of saffron and cumin as though our stall were a museum display rather than the place where we earn our living. One woman asked whether we dressed this way only for tourists; my mother smiled politely, but I noticed her hands tighten around the scoop.

To the visitors, the market is an adventure, a colorful escape from ordinary life. To us, it is ordinary life. I do not mind the photographs, exactly. I only wish that someone, just once, would ask my mother how she learned to blend spices, because the answer is a story three generations long.

p57d538137a.title: The Quiet Return
p57d538137a.text:
[A spacious living room in Riyadh. Underneath the table, clearly visible to the audience, are a banner reading WELCOME HOME, NAWAF and a decorated tray of maamoul.]

MOTHER: (sighing loudly) Your brother's flight was unexpectedly cancelled this afternoon, so he will not arrive until next week.

SARA: (disappointed) Then I suppose we should put away all the decorations immediately.

[SARA reaches under the table for the rolled-up banner. MOTHER quickly blocks her, smiling mysteriously at the audience.]

MOTHER: No, leave them exactly where they are, since they are certainly not interfering with anything.

[A doorbell rings, and SARA frowns as she goes to answer it, grumbling about inconsiderate visitors arriving at dinnertime. Outside the window, the audience glimpses NAWAF holding a suitcase and pressing a finger to his lips.]

p1eaf224799.title: Two Hundred Cabbages
p1eaf224799.text:
I had returned from two years of study in Toronto convinced that our family's autumn kimchi-making was an inefficient ritual, the sort of thing modern refrigerators and supermarkets had rendered unnecessary. Grandmother listened to my argument without interrupting, then handed me, her eldest granddaughter, a pair of rubber gloves.

By midafternoon, eleven relatives were kneeling around enormous basins, rubbing chili paste between the leaves of two hundred cabbages. My aunt corrected my technique; my cousin teased me about my accent; my grandmother hummed a song I had not heard since childhood. Somewhere between the hundredth cabbage and the hundred-and-first, I stopped counting.

That evening, as we distributed containers to neighbors who had no family nearby, I understood that efficiency had never been the point.

p2cb73036e5.title: A Guide to Seeing Everything Quickly
p2cb73036e5.text:
Welcome, esteemed traveler, to a city whose twelve centuries of history can be conveniently consumed between breakfast and lunch. Do not trouble yourself with the old library, whose manuscripts were merely copied by scholars who devoted entire lifetimes to them; a photograph of its doorway will suffice. Should a shopkeeper invite you to sit for tea, decline immediately, since conversation with residents is notoriously inefficient and rarely yields anything suitable for sharing online.

Above all, resist the temptation to learn a single word of the local language. Our citizens, who have welcomed merchants, scholars, and wanderers for generations, would surely be disappointed to discover that a visitor had made the effort. Proceed directly to the airport, confident that you have truly seen us.

p1b21d23d6b.title: The Missing Shoe
p1b21d23d6b.text:
Characters: SARA, a girl. DAD, her father.

Setting: A small kitchen in the morning.

SARA: (looking under the table) Dad, I can't find my shoe!

DAD: (holding a cup) Did you look by the door?

SARA: (running to the door) Yes! It is not here.

[A cat walks in slowly.]

DAD: (laughing) Look at the cat!

SARA: (picking up the shoe from the cat's bed) Oh, Mimi! You took my shoe!

[Sara hugs the cat. The lights go down.]

p9c2194fa26.title: The Science Fair Robot
p9c2194fa26.text:
Cast: LAYLA, a fifth grader; OMAR, her older brother; MS. HADI, a science fair judge.

SCENE 1. [The school gymnasium, early in the morning, where long tables hold dozens of colorful projects. LAYLA kneels beside a small robot that will not move, no matter which button she presses.]

LAYLA: (pressing buttons, frustrated) It worked perfectly last night when I tested it in the kitchen!

OMAR: (leaning closer and pointing) Look, the battery wire came loose.

LAYLA: (sighing with relief) You're right, and I can repair it quickly if you hold the robot steady for me.

SCENE 2. [One hour later, MS. HADI approaches their table carrying a clipboard.]

MS. HADI: (smiling and writing a note) Please explain what your invention does and why you decided to build it.

LAYLA: (proudly placing a cup on the robot's tray) It delivers water to classroom plants that people usually forget to water.

[The robot rolls carefully across the table and stops beside a small plant, and OMAR quietly gives a thumbs-up.]

p4f4d381a20.title: The Sandstorm
p4f4d381a20.text:
CHARACTERS: FAISAL, a young camel herder; GRANDMOTHER NOURA; and the VOICE of a radio announcer.

SETTING: A tent at the edge of the Empty Quarter, just before sunset, where a lantern hangs from the center pole and a small radio sits on a wooden crate.

[As the wind rises offstage, the tent walls ripple and the lantern sways.]

RADIO VOICE: (crackling) A severe sandstorm is expected to reach the southern camps within the hour, and all travelers are advised to remain indoors.

FAISAL: (jumping up and reaching for his scarf) The camels are still grazing by the dunes, so I have to bring them in before the storm arrives!

GRANDMOTHER NOURA: (gripping his arm firmly) Wait, and listen carefully to the wind before you run into it.

[After a long pause, the sound of the wind changes from a whistle to a low, continuous roar.]

FAISAL: (quietly, sitting back down) It's already here, isn't it?

GRANDMOTHER NOURA: (nodding, then smiling) Camels are wiser than impatient boys, because they kneel and turn their backs to the storm, and tomorrow morning we will find them together.

p4db48f0a69.title: The Clockmaker's Apprentice
p4db48f0a69.text:
ACT ONE, SCENE 2: [The workshop of the engineer Al-Jazari in the year 1206, where gears, copper pipes, measuring instruments, and half-built water clocks crowd every table. YUSUF, a nervous apprentice, stands beside an enormous elephant clock whose bowl has stopped dripping.]

YUSUF: (to himself, wiping his hands on his robe) If the master discovers that the clock has stopped, he will certainly believe that I damaged it. (He glances anxiously at the door.) Perhaps I can repair it before he returns.

[He climbs onto a stool and peers into the copper bowl. Footsteps approach offstage, but YUSUF does not hear them.]

AL-JAZARI: (entering quietly and watching from the doorway) What are you searching for, Yusuf?

YUSUF: (startled, nearly falling) Master, nothing is wrong, and everything is working perfectly.

AL-JAZARI: (walking slowly to the clock and tapping the bowl) Then why has the water stopped moving?

[YUSUF lowers his head while AL-JAZARI carefully pulls a tiny pebble from the pipe and holds it up to the light.]

AL-JAZARI: (gently) A genuine engineer does not hide a problem; he examines it patiently until he understands it.

pd0bbd6bcff.title: Two Tides
pd0bbd6bcff.text:
[The stage is divided by a narrow strip of blue light: stage left, in 1952, a wooden pearling boat rocks unsteadily in the Arabian Gulf; stage right, in the present day, a marine laboratory hums with refrigerators and illuminated computer screens. The two halves never interact, but actions on one side are frequently mirrored on the other.]

HAMAD: (stage left, a weathered diver, tying a stone weight to his ankle) The oysters are fewer every season, and nobody on this boat is willing to acknowledge it aloud.

[He inhales deeply and disappears beneath the surface as the blue light dims to near darkness.]

DR. MARIAM: (stage right, his granddaughter, holding a sample jar toward the light) The oyster beds are recovering, but only in the protected zones, precisely where my grandfather predicted they would.

[She sets the jar down beside an old, cracked diving stone. For a moment, both sides of the stage are silent.]

HAMAD: (resurfacing, gasping, empty-handed, then quietly, almost to the audience) Nothing again, so someone must remember exactly where they used to grow.

p81409d2e21.title: The Mended Atlas
p81409d2e21.text:
PLAYWRIGHT'S NOTE: The ticking of the wall clock should be audible only when no one is speaking, so the audience gradually realizes that silence, rather than dialogue, carries the scene's emotional weight.

[A narrow bookshop in Jeddah, late evening, where shelves rise into darkness. KHALID, seventy, sits behind the counter meticulously mending the spine of a damaged atlas, while his daughter REEM, an architect, stands near the door holding a folder of demolition permits she has not yet mentioned.]

REEM: (too brightly) The street looks wonderful at night, with the restored balconies illuminated, doesn't it?

KHALID: (without looking up) It has looked identical for forty years, whether anyone bothered to illuminate it or not.

[In the silence, REEM places the folder on the counter, then, reconsidering, slides it beneath her arm again.]

REEM: The municipality has offered generous compensation for every property on this block.

KHALID: (finally setting down the atlas, deliberately) Then the municipality has determined what a map is worth.

[He returns to his mending, and the lights fade gradually, although the lamp above the atlas remains illuminated until the last possible moment.]

p0c8d92b5c8.title: Busy Bees
p0c8d92b5c8.text:
Bees are small, but they do a big job. A bee flies from flower to flower to drink sweet nectar. Yellow dust called pollen sticks to its legs. When the bee lands on the next flower, some pollen falls off. This helps the plant make seeds and fruit.

Many foods we eat need bees. Apples, melons, and almonds all grow better when bees visit. Bees also make honey. Farmers are happy when bees live near their fields.

p5f9b8e488b.title: Resting at Noon
p5f9b8e488b.text:
In the desert, the hottest hours come in the middle of the day. Many animals avoid that heat by resting until evening, and scientists say this habit helps them survive.

The fennec fox spends hot afternoons sleeping in a cool underground den. Its burrow can be many degrees cooler than the sand above it. The fox comes out at night to hunt insects and small lizards.

The spiny-tailed lizard has a different plan. In the early morning, it lies in the sun to warm its body. Before the ground becomes dangerously hot, it hurries back into its tunnel.

Even camels change their behavior. During the hottest part of the day, they often sit facing the sun so that less of their body is exposed to its rays.

Resting at noon may look lazy, but for desert animals it is a careful way to save water and energy.

p6871e3793f.title: The Dark Room
p6871e3793f.text:
More than a thousand years ago, many scholars believed that people could see because their eyes sent out invisible rays. The scientist Ibn al-Haytham, who was born in Basra around 965, refused to accept this idea simply because famous thinkers had written it.

Instead, he designed experiments. In a darkened room, he made a tiny hole in one wall and observed that an upside-down image of the outside world appeared on the opposite wall. He reasoned that light must travel in straight lines from objects into the eye, not the other way around.

Ibn al-Haytham recorded his methods carefully so that other people could repeat his tests and check his results. He wrote that a seeker of truth should question even the books he admires most.

His Book of Optics was later translated into Latin, and European scientists studied it for centuries. Today, many historians describe him as one of the earliest people to use the scientific method.

pc264ca571e.title: Every Town Needs a Repair Café
pc264ca571e.text:
Every town should open a repair café, a monthly gathering where volunteers help neighbors fix broken objects instead of throwing them away.

The environmental benefits are significant. Discarded electronics are among the fastest-growing kinds of household waste, and many of them fail because of a single loose wire or worn part. A volunteer with a screwdriver can often solve the problem in minutes.

Repair cafés also save families money. Replacing a toaster or a fan is expensive, while repairing one usually costs nothing but time.

Perhaps most importantly, these events build skills and friendships. Teenagers learn practical techniques from retired engineers, and elderly residents who live alone gain a reason to leave the house and talk with others. One organizer reported that visitors often stay long after their items are repaired, simply to keep chatting.

Critics argue that modern devices are designed to be impossible to repair. That is sometimes true, but it is a reason to demand better designs, not a reason to stop trying.

p3019cdf618.title: Water for a Growing City
p3019cdf618.text:
Text 1: Coastal cities in arid regions increasingly depend on desalination, the industrial process of removing salt from seawater. Modern plants using reverse osmosis consume considerably less energy than older thermal facilities, and engineers estimate that a single large plant can supply drinking water for millions of residents. Because the sea is effectively limitless, supporters argue that desalination offers a dependable supply that does not fluctuate with rainfall.

Text 2: Building additional desalination plants is not the only solution, and it may not be the wisest one. Every plant discharges concentrated brine that can damage coral reefs and seagrass near the outlet, and the facilities remain expensive to operate. Meanwhile, some cities have reduced household consumption by roughly a fifth simply by repairing leaking pipes, installing efficient fixtures, and charging higher rates to the heaviest users. Treated wastewater, which is already used to irrigate parks in several Gulf cities, could replace a much larger share of fresh water. A responsible strategy would treat conservation as the first source of water, not the last.

p8c1c069eeb.title: Judging Citizen Science
p8c1c069eeb.text:
Skeptics have long questioned whether volunteers without scientific training can produce data reliable enough for research. The question is reasonable, but the evidence increasingly suggests that the answer depends less on who collects the data than on how the collection is designed.

Consider bird surveys, among the oldest citizen science projects. When volunteers simply submitted whatever they happened to notice, their records were inconsistent and difficult to compare. When projects instead required participants to record observation time, location, and effort, and when experienced reviewers flagged improbable sightings, the resulting datasets proved accurate enough to reveal shifting migration patterns across entire continents.

Admittedly, volunteers still make errors, particularly when identifying similar species. Yet professional researchers make errors too; the decisive difference is that a well-designed project anticipates mistakes and builds in procedures to detect them.

Citizen science, then, should not be judged by the credentials of its participants. It should be judged, like any other research, by the rigor of its methods.

pde8a0db93f.title: The Big Game
pde8a0db93f.text:
Characters: ADAM, a boy. NADA, his friend. COACH SALEM.

Setting: A green soccer field after school.

COACH SALEM: (blowing a whistle) Time to practice, team!

ADAM: (sitting on the grass) I can't kick the ball far.

NADA: (sitting next to him) Kick with the side of your foot. Try it with me!

[Adam stands up. He kicks the ball hard. It flies across the field.]

ADAM: (jumping up and down) I did it!

COACH SALEM: (clapping) Great kick, Adam!

p7401d34255.title: The Bottle on the Beach
p7401d34255.text:
CAST OF CHARACTERS: HIND, age eleven, and her cousin RASHID, age nine.

SETTING: A quiet beach in Oman at sunrise, where gentle waves wash over the sand and fishing boats rest near the shore.

[HIND, carrying a basket of shells, notices a green glass bottle half buried in the sand.]

HIND: (kneeling and pulling out the bottle) Rashid, come quickly, because there is a rolled-up paper inside this bottle!

RASHID: (running over, breathless) Maybe it's a treasure map from a pirate ship!

HIND: (carefully unrolling the paper and reading aloud) "Dear finder, please write to me and tell me where this bottle landed, because I am studying how ocean currents travel across the Arabian Sea. Sincerely, Dr. Amal, Marine Scientist."

RASHID: (disappointed, kicking the sand) So it isn't a treasure map after all.

HIND: (smiling thoughtfully) It might be something better, because we can help a real scientist with her research.

[RASHID takes a pencil from the basket, and the lights fade as the cousins begin writing a reply.]

p29ca55a743.title: Night at Maragha
p29ca55a743.text:
CHARACTERS: ZAID, a young assistant at the observatory; and the voice of his teacher, which is heard but never seen.

SETTING: The rooftop of the great observatory at Maragha, Persia, in the year 1262. A huge brass instrument for measuring the stars stands at the center of the stage, and the night sky is projected on the back wall.

[ZAID stands alone, holding a lamp and a notebook. He looks up at the stars, then down at his pages, then up again.]

ZAID: (speaking to himself as he paces) Every night I record the position of the same planet, and every night my numbers disagree with the ancient tables by a tiny amount. My teacher says that small differences matter, but tonight I wonder whether I am simply careless. Or perhaps the ancient tables were wrong, and the sky is trying to tell me something nobody has noticed before.

TEACHER'S VOICE: (from offstage, calm but firm) Zaid, measure it again, and then measure it once more.

[ZAID smiles, raises the lamp, and turns back toward the brass instrument as the lights slowly dim.]

p1893c7ee71.title: The Final Round
p1893c7ee71.text:
CHARACTERS: SALMA and KARIM, teammates on a school robotics team; MR. YOUSEF, their adviser.

SETTING: A crowded competition hall in Riyadh, ten minutes before the final round, where teams hurry between tables covered with tools, laptops, and spare parts.

[SALMA tightens a bolt on the robot's arm while KARIM stares anxiously at his laptop.]

KARIM: (without looking up) We should rewrite the steering program before the match, because yesterday the robot drifted unexpectedly to the left on two separate occasions.

SALMA: (putting down the wrench, frustrated) Changing the code ten minutes before the final would be reckless; we tested this version for three weeks.

KARIM: (turning toward the audience, in a low voice) She trusts the testing, but I trust what I saw yesterday, and only one of us can be right.

MR. YOUSEF: (approaching with a stopwatch, calmly) A successful team does not choose between careful testing and new information, so run one quick trial and let the robot settle the argument.

[SALMA and KARIM exchange a glance, then lift the robot onto the practice mat together.]

pc877fda4fe.title: The Caravanserai
pc877fda4fe.text:
CHARACTERS: TARIQ, a young traveler eager to cross the desert; UMM HASAN, the cautious keeper of a caravanserai; and a CAMEL DRIVER, who never speaks.

SETTING: The courtyard of a caravanserai on a trade route in the fourteenth century, where bales of silk and sacks of spices are stacked against the walls and a single fire burns in the center.

[TARIQ unrolls a worn map beside the fire, while the CAMEL DRIVER silently inspects the ropes on a loaded saddle.]

TARIQ: (enthusiastically, tracing a route with his finger) If we depart before dawn and avoid the northern wells, we can reach the coast three days earlier than any other caravan.

UMM HASAN: (stirring the fire without glancing at the map) Every traveler who has slept in this courtyard has wanted to arrive three days earlier. Some of them arrived.

[The CAMEL DRIVER pauses, studies the map, and slowly shakes his head, but TARIQ does not notice.]

TARIQ: (laughing confidently) Then I will be one of those who arrived.

UMM HASAN: (quietly, to herself) The desert remembers every promise made beside this fire.

p78bb394715.title: The Unexplored
p78bb394715.text:
CHORUS: (three figures in sand-colored robes, speaking in unison from the edge of the stage) We are the winds that cross the empty interior, and we have watched mapmakers come and go for a thousand years; each one believes that ink can hold us still.

[Lights rise on a study in Cairo, around 1500, where IDRIS, an elderly cartographer, bends over an enormous unfinished map while his apprentice LAYAN holds a lamp above the parchment.]

LAYAN: (pointing to a blank region) Master, every merchant who passes through the city describes this desert differently; shall I draw the version we hear most often?

IDRIS: (setting down his pen with deliberate care) A map that records rumors as facts is more dangerous than a map that admits ignorance, so leave it blank and label it honestly.

CHORUS: (softly, as LAYAN hesitates) Blank spaces frighten ambitious rulers, but they protect travelers.

[LAYAN slowly writes "Unexplored" across the empty region. IDRIS nods approvingly, unaware that the CHORUS has gathered behind him, closer than before.]

pdcf05e0341.title: A Garden for Our School
pdcf05e0341.text:
Dear Principal,

Our class wants a garden at school. A garden can help us learn about plants. We can watch seeds grow into beans and carrots. We can eat the food we grow at lunch.

A garden is good for bees, too. Bees need flowers to make honey.

My friend Tariq says a garden will make our school the best school in the world. Please let us have a garden. We will water it every day.

From,
Lina

pf5eccbaabe.title: Make Recess Longer
pf5eccbaabe.text:
Our school currently gives students only fifteen minutes of recess each day, which is not enough time to rest and recharge. I believe recess should be thirty minutes long.

First, exercise helps the brain. A study by a children's health group found that students who played outside for thirty minutes paid better attention in class afterward. Second, a longer recess gives students valuable time to solve problems with their friends, which develops teamwork and cooperation.

Some people say that a longer recess will take away learning time. However, if students concentrate better, the minutes in the classroom will be used more wisely and effectively.

Everyone at our school wants a longer recess, so the principal should agree. Besides, students at Hilltop School have a long recess, and they are probably the smartest kids in the city.

[Chart: Minutes of recess at three nearby schools. Our school: 15. Hilltop School: 30. Palm Grove School: 25.]

pa1a33bc782.title: Bike Lanes for King Road
pa1a33bc782.text:
City leaders are debating whether to build protected bike lanes along King Road, the busiest street in Al-Noor. Supporters argue that the lanes would reduce traffic and make streets safer, and the evidence suggests that they have a point.

When the nearby city of Wadi Saad added protected lanes in 2019, its transportation office reported that bicycle trips doubled within three years, while crashes involving cyclists dropped by nearly a third. Cities with similar weather have reported comparable results.

Opponents claim that the lanes would ruin business on King Road because shoppers could no longer park in front of stores. Yet a survey of Wadi Saad shop owners found that most of them saw no drop in sales.

My own neighbor rode on King Road last week and arrived home safely, which proves that the road is already safe for every cyclist. Furthermore, after Wadi Saad built its lanes, the city's air became cleaner, so bike lanes clearly cleaned the air.

p3b3656faad.title: A Library After the Bell
p3b3656faad.text:
Fellow students, I am running for council president because our school deserves a library that remains open after classes have ended. Currently, the library closes at the final bell, so students who depend on the late bus have nowhere quiet to study, research, or complete their assignments.

Last month I collected signatures from 212 students who said they would use an after-school library at least once a week. Our librarian, Mrs. Fadel, explained to me that she could keep the doors open until four o'clock if the council provided funding for one additional assistant.

My opponent, Yousef, says the council should spend its limited money on new sports uniforms instead. But Yousef forgets his homework almost every week, so why should anyone trust his ideas about studying?

The choice is simple. Either we fund the library, or our grades will fall and our school will become the worst in the district. Vote for me, and vote for a future in which every student, regardless of schedule, has a comfortable place to learn.

p548d36834f.title: Protecting the Reef at Al-Murjan Bay
p548d36834f.text:
The proposal to declare the coral reef off Al-Murjan Bay a protected marine area deserves broad support, but some of the arguments made on its behalf are considerably weaker than others.

The strongest case rests on measurement. Since 2015, marine biologists from the regional university have surveyed the reef annually, documenting a forty percent decline in live coral in zones where anchoring and fishing are permitted, compared with a seven percent decline in zones already closed to boats. Because both zones experience identical water temperatures, the difference points convincingly toward human activity.

Other supporters, however, rely on shakier reasoning. A celebrated football player who vacations in the bay has declared that the reef will be dead within five years, yet he offers no data and possesses no scientific training. Meanwhile, one campaign leaflet warns that if fishing continues, tourists will vanish, hotels will close, and the entire coastal economy will collapse.

Opponents are not blameless either. Several have described the proposal as an attempt to ban everyone from the sea forever, although the plan actually closes only twelve percent of the coastline.

p6020fa6bac.title: The Library Without Shelves
p6020fa6bac.text:
The municipal council's proposal to convert the central library into a digital-only resource center has provoked predictable outrage, yet the arguments for the conversion are considerably more persuasive than its critics acknowledge.

Consider the circulation figures: borrowing of printed books has declined by roughly a quarter over the past decade, while downloads of electronic titles have tripled. A collection that residents increasingly ignore can hardly justify consuming the majority of the library's budget.

Critics insist that some residents lack reliable internet access, but this objection is overstated. Every successful entrepreneur I have interviewed for this column described acquiring knowledge almost entirely from digital sources, which demonstrates that digital resources are sufficient for anyone determined to learn.

Moreover, the library's purpose has always been to provide access to information, and information remains information regardless of its format. Shelves are simply an obsolete technology, and obsolete technologies inevitably disappear; clinging to them is nostalgia disguised as principle.

[Chart: Central Library, 2015 to 2025. Printed loans fall from 400,000 to 300,000 per year; e-book downloads rise from 50,000 to 150,000 per year.]

pf9c3acd0ec.title: The Black Tent
pf9c3acd0ec.text:
Text 1: Saad lived long ago in the desert. His family had a big black tent. One hot day, Saad's mother rolled up the side of the tent. A cool wind came in. "Ahh," said Saad. That night it rained hard. Saad stayed dry and warm inside.

Text 2: Long ago, many desert families lived in tents. The tents were made from goat hair. Women wove the hair into long strips of cloth. The sides could be rolled up to let in a breeze. When rain fell, the goat hair got wet and tight. This kept the water out.

p30217809df.title: The Elephant Clock
p30217809df.text:
Text 1: Ilyas pressed his face close to the tall wooden elephant. Inside its belly, his master, Al-Jazari, had hidden a bowl floating in a tank of water. "Watch carefully," Al-Jazari whispered. Slowly the bowl filled and sank. Suddenly a little brass ball rolled down a channel, a figure on top swung its arm, and a cymbal rang out across the palace courtyard. Ilyas laughed with delight. "Half an hour has passed!" he cried.

Text 2: Ismail Al-Jazari was an engineer who lived from about 1136 to 1206 in what is now southeastern Turkey. He served local rulers and designed clocks, water pumps, and moving machines. In 1206 he finished a book that explained how to build about fifty devices, with careful drawings. His most famous design, the elephant clock, used a sinking bowl to measure time. Each half hour, a ball dropped and moving figures made a sound. Historians know about Al-Jazari mostly from his book, which does not name his helpers.

p11d6ea87bd.title: Beneath the Gulf
p11d6ea87bd.text:
Text 1: Khalid gripped the heavy stone weight and filled his lungs one final time. The turtle-shell clip pinched his nose as he plunged toward the seabed, where the oysters lay in dark, irregular clusters. He worked rapidly, prying them loose and depositing them into the basket hanging at his neck. When his chest began to burn, he tugged the rope desperately, and his uncle hauled him upward. That evening, as the crew opened the shells, Khalid's knife revealed a pearl as large as a chickpea, and the whole boat erupted in cheers.

Text 2: For centuries, pearl diving supported numerous communities along the Arabian Gulf. During the summer season, which lasted approximately four months, divers completed dozens of exhausting dives each day, using stone weights to descend and nose clips to conserve their breath. A partner on deck pulled each diver up by rope. Most oysters held no pearl at all, and large pearls were extremely rare. In the 1930s, inexpensive cultured pearls from Japan caused the traditional industry to decline dramatically.

p86b1f28f2f.title: The Copyist of Baghdad
p86b1f28f2f.text:
Text 1: Before dawn, Zayd unrolled a fresh sheet of paper beside the crumbling Greek manuscript and dipped his reed pen. Across the hall, scholars argued about the stars, while a translator murmured Persian phrases under his breath. Zayd's task seemed endless: copy every page of the Arabic translation before the caliph's visit at noon. When a scholar named Al-Khwarizmi paused to praise his neat handwriting, Zayd felt that the entire world of knowledge was gathering in this single building.

Text 2: In the ninth century, the Abbasid caliphs, especially al-Ma'mun, supported scholars in Baghdad who translated works on mathematics, astronomy, and medicine from Greek, Persian, and Sanskrit into Arabic. The mathematician al-Khwarizmi worked in the city during this period. Paper, which was cheaper than parchment, helped books spread rapidly. Historians still debate, however, how large the famous House of Wisdom really was; some believe it was mainly a library, rather than the vast research center often described in popular stories.

pa4e9373336.title: The Room of Light
pa4e9373336.text:
Text 1: For months the guards had believed Hasan ibn al-Haytham was mad, and he had allowed them to believe it. Now, alone in his shuttered room in Cairo, he pierced the wooden shutter with a nail and watched, astonished, as an inverted image of the street outside appeared, faint but unmistakable, on the opposite wall. Light, he realized, traveled in straight lines from the objects themselves. He reached for his pen, no longer pretending anything at all.

Text 2: Ibn al-Haytham, born in Basra around 965, later lived in Cairo during the reign of the Fatimid caliph al-Hakim. His Book of Optics argued that vision occurs when light travels from objects into the eye, overturning the ancient theory that the eye sends out rays, and he defended his conclusions through careful experiments, including observations with darkened chambers. Later biographers claimed that he pretended to be insane to escape an impossible engineering task, but historians caution that this dramatic account appears in sources written long afterward and cannot be confirmed.

p9dde9667a0.title: The Last Rail to Medina
p9dde9667a0.text:
Text 1: Standing on the newly finished platform in 1908, the engineer Omar Rifat watched the first locomotive steam toward Medina and felt certain that the iron road would outlast every empire that had ever crossed the desert. Caravans that once required weeks, he reflected, would now complete the journey in days, and the railway would bind distant provinces together permanently. He had sacrificed eight years to this line, and he could not imagine its rails ever lying silent beneath the sand.

Text 2: The Hejaz Railway, constructed between 1900 and 1908, connected Damascus with Medina across roughly 1,300 kilometers of difficult terrain. Financed largely through donations and built predominantly by soldiers, it dramatically reduced travel time for passengers. Its prosperity proved remarkably brief, however. During the First World War, raiders repeatedly sabotaged the tracks, and after 1918 the southern sections were abandoned; today, only fragments in Jordan and Syria remain in limited operation, while rusting carriages still rest at several desert stations.

p02a4b19a22.title: The Day of the Sandstorm
p02a4b19a22.text:
Text 1: From Reem's Journal

Today a sandstorm came to our town. I saw a brown wall of sand in the sky. My eyes felt itchy. Dad closed all the windows. We stayed inside and played games. The wind was so loud!

Text 2: A News Report

On Monday, a sandstorm hit the town of Al-Rawda. Strong winds blew for three hours. Schools closed early. People were told to stay inside. No one was hurt.

p60bf0c426a.title: Turtles on the Shore
p60bf0c426a.text:
Text 1: From a Volunteer's Journal

Last night I sat on the cool sand of the Red Sea shore and waited beside a nest that our team had been protecting for weeks. At ten o'clock, the nest began to move. One by one, tiny turtles pushed their way out and scrambled eagerly toward the silver water. I counted forty-two of them! My heart was pounding as the last little turtle disappeared into the waves.

Text 2: How Sea Turtles Begin Life

Green sea turtles and hawksbill turtles nest on beaches along the Red Sea. A female digs a hole and lays about one hundred eggs, then returns to the ocean. Approximately two months later, the hatchlings dig their way out, usually at night when the sand is cooler and predators are harder to notice. Scientists have discovered that hatchlings crawl toward the brightest part of the horizon, which is normally the moonlit sea. Artificial lights from buildings can confuse them, so many communities now limit lighting during the nesting season.

pbbcdeb7144.title: The Ring of Fire
pbbcdeb7144.text:
Text 1: A Student's Blog, December 26, 2019

My family drove to Hofuf before sunrise, and by eight o'clock hundreds of people had gathered in the park, all wearing paper eclipse glasses. Gradually, a dark curve crept across the sun, and the morning light became strangely dim. Then, for just a few minutes, the moon sat perfectly in the center, leaving a blazing orange ring. The air felt noticeably cooler, and the birds in the palm trees fell silent. Everyone around me cheered enthusiastically, and I will never forget that extraordinary moment.

Text 2: Annular Solar Eclipses

An annular solar eclipse occurs when the moon passes directly between Earth and the sun while it is near the farthest point of its orbit. Because the moon appears slightly smaller than the sun at that distance, it cannot cover the sun completely, so a bright ring remains visible. On December 26, 2019, the path of this ring crossed eastern Saudi Arabia. Experts warn that viewers should never look at the sun without certified eclipse glasses, even during an eclipse.

p67184ca599.title: Crossing the Causeway
p67184ca599.text:
Text 1: A Memory of the First Crossing

I was eleven years old when my father drove us across the new causeway to Bahrain in late 1986. Although about forty years have passed, I still remember pressing my face against the car window as the turquoise water stretched endlessly on both sides. My father, who had always traveled to Bahrain by boat, kept laughing and repeating that the journey now took less than an hour. I believe there were thousands of cars on the road that day, though I may be remembering the excitement more than the traffic.

Text 2: The King Fahd Causeway

The King Fahd Causeway, which opened in November 1986, links the eastern coast of Saudi Arabia with Bahrain. The roadway extends about twenty-five kilometers across a series of bridges and embankments, with border facilities on an artificial island near the middle. Before its completion, travelers depended on ferries and small boats. Today, the causeway carries millions of vehicles each year, making it one of the busiest crossings in the region.

p3d94f0648d.title: The Sound Heard Across an Ocean
p3d94f0648d.text:
Text 1: A ship's officer writes home, in the style of letters from 1883

Sunda Strait, 27 August. At ten this morning came a report so tremendous that several of our crew threw themselves upon the deck, convinced that a warship had opened fire nearby. Within the hour, the sky turned black as midnight, and ash fell so thickly that we shoveled it overboard. Our captain believes some island volcano has burst, though none of us can say which, nor how widely the destruction extends.

Text 2: The Eruption of Krakatoa

On August 27, 1883, the volcanic island of Krakatoa, located between Java and Sumatra, exploded with extraordinary violence. The final blast was heard nearly 4,800 kilometers away on Rodrigues Island, and barometers worldwide recorded its pressure wave circling the globe several times. Enormous tsunamis devastated coastal communities, killing more than 36,000 people. For months afterward, volcanic particles in the atmosphere produced vividly colored sunsets as far away as Europe and North America.

p25ca45f9b9.title: The Comet Year
p25ca45f9b9.text:
Text 1: A schoolteacher's letter, written in May 1910

The whole town is gripped by terror of the approaching comet. Newspapers report that its tail contains poisonous gas, and an enterprising peddler outside the market has sold dozens of so-called comet pills to frightened, credulous families. Last night, however, I climbed to the roof with my pupils, and we watched as the comet's luminous tail stretched across nearly half the sky. I confess that I experienced only wonder, and my neighbors on the surrounding rooftops appeared equally delighted by the spectacle.

Text 2: A historian's account

In May 1910, Earth passed directly through the extended tail of Halley's Comet, an event astronomers had anticipated. Months earlier, astronomers had detected cyanogen, a toxic gas, in the tail, and several newspapers sensationalized the discovery, predicting widespread poisoning. Scientists explained that the gas was far too diluted to cause harm, yet opportunistic entrepreneurs profited by selling worthless pills and protective masks. Popular histories often describe a worldwide panic, but surviving diaries and letters suggest that most people observed the comet with curiosity, often gathering on rooftops to watch.

p8c46ab8462.title: The Old Shell
p8c46ab8462.text:
Lina found a big shell on the beach. She held it to her ear. She remembered last summer. Grandma had given her a shell just like this one. "Listen," Grandma had said. "The sea is singing to you." Lina smiled at the memory.

Dark clouds rolled over the water. The wind began to blow hard. Lina's father looked at the sky. "We should pack up soon," he said.

Lina put the shell in her bag. She would give it to Grandma tonight.

p7c9f615db9.title: The Science Fair
p7c9f615db9.text:
Yusuf stared at the small robot on his desk, frowning at its uneven movement. Its left wheel still wobbled whenever it turned, and the science fair was only two days away.

He thought back to the first week of school. His teacher, Ms. Rahma, had held up a broken toy car in front of the entire class and said, "Every inventor fails before succeeding. The important thing is to discover the reason." At the time, Yusuf had shrugged, uninterested in a broken toy. Now her words seemed to echo in the quiet room.

He picked up a screwdriver and examined the wheel carefully, testing each tiny part. Eventually he discovered that a small screw beneath the motor was loose. He tightened it and tested the robot again, and it rolled perfectly straight across the desk.

Still, as he packed it into a cardboard box, he noticed that the battery light was blinking faintly. He told himself, somewhat nervously, that it would probably last until Thursday.

p2ca1cfbef2.title: Salt Road
p2ca1cfbef2.text:
Hamad tightened the final rope on his camel's saddle and studied the horizon, where a thin brown haze had gradually begun to gather above the distant dunes. The caravan would depart for the coast at dawn, and this time he would be responsible for leading it alone.

Eight years earlier, he had traveled along this same road beside his uncle. On the third morning, his uncle had suddenly halted the long line of camels and pointed at a haze remarkably similar to this one. "The desert always warns you before it strikes," he had said quietly, "and a wise traveler listens carefully." Within an hour, a violent sandstorm had swallowed the trail, but the caravan had already sheltered safely behind a ridge of rock.

Now Hamad ran his fingers over the worn leather map his uncle had left him, and he noticed that one ridge was circled in faded ink. Behind him, the younger drivers laughed and joked, impatient to depart, while the camels shifted restlessly and refused their evening water.

p28230c7e8c.title: Diary of a Young Astronomer
p28230c7e8c.text:
Tonight the great instrument finally stood ready, its curved marble arc gleaming beneath the flickering lamps. My teacher, the elderly astronomer, has always insisted that we record every star's position twice, a rule I once considered unbearably tedious.

I still remember my first night at the observatory, three winters ago. Eager to impress him, I copied forty positions in a single evening, only to discover at dawn that I had misread the measuring scale on every one. He did not scold me; instead, he simply handed me a fresh page and explained, "The sky is patient, so you must be patient with it."

Since then, I have checked every measurement twice without complaint. Yet this evening, as heavy clouds drifted in from the mountains, he coughed frequently and leaned heavily on his cane. "Soon," he told me, "you will keep these records without me." I laughed and assured him that he would outlast us all, but he only smiled and quietly gave me the key to the archive.

padfab49151.title: The Diver's Daughter
padfab49151.text:
Mariam had not set foot on the abandoned pier since her father's final voyage, yet the familiar smell of tar and salt returned her instantly to the morning he had pressed a smooth stone into her palm. "Divers carry a weight to reach the bottom," he had explained, folding her fingers around it, "but a wise diver always knows when to let it go." She had been seven, far too young to understand that he was describing something more complicated than the sea.

Now, at thirty, she stood among the restorers who had arrived to rebuild the pier as a maritime museum. The architect, impatient and supremely confident, unrolled elaborate plans that replaced the weathered planks with polished glass. Mariam noticed that he had positioned the new foundation directly above the tidal channel, the very location her father had always called treacherous.

She slipped her hand into her pocket, where the stone still rested, and said nothing yet.

p15f9aafcd2.title: The Cartographer's Error
p15f9aafcd2.text:
In the spring of 1820, Idris completed the coastal survey that would, decades later, be cited in every naval manual of the region; at the time, however, his superiors dismissed it as the careless work of an unreliable apprentice. He had committed one apparent error: a narrow inlet, recorded on every previous chart, was conspicuously absent from his.

He remembered, with uncomfortable clarity, the afternoon he had navigated toward that inlet with a borrowed compass. The water had changed color abruptly, transforming from deep blue to a pale, deceptive green, and the hull had scraped against submerged sand precisely where older maps promised safe passage. Shaken, he had returned at low tide, measured methodically, and concluded that the channel had gradually silted shut.

The commission rejected his correction without deliberation. Its chairman, an administrator who had never ventured beyond the harbor, praised the traditional charts and ordered the inlet restored. Idris folded his notes meticulously and stored them, not in the official archive, but in a sealed tin box.

p47281d776f.title: How to Plant a Bean Seed
p47281d776f.text:
You will need a cup, some soil, a bean seed, and water.

First, fill the cup with soil. Next, use your finger to make a small hole in the soil. Then drop the bean seed into the hole. Cover the seed with a little soil. After that, give it a small drink of water. Do not give it too much!

Last, put the cup in a sunny window. Check it every day. In about one week, a green sprout will pop up.

pf4c5f88cac.title: Making a Solar Oven
pf4c5f88cac.text:
A solar oven uses energy from sunlight to warm food without electricity. You can construct one from a pizza box in approximately thirty minutes.

Materials: a pizza box, aluminum foil, black construction paper, transparent plastic wrap, tape, and a ruler.

Step 1: Draw a square on the lid, leaving a border about three centimeters wide on every side.
Step 2: Ask an adult to cut along three sides of the square to create a flap. Do not cut the fourth side.
Step 3: Cover the inside of the flap with aluminum foil, positioning the shiny side outward.
Step 4: Tape black paper to the bottom of the box, because dark colors absorb heat.
Step 5: Stretch plastic wrap across the opening in the lid and tape it tightly so no air escapes.
Step 6: Place the oven in direct sunlight. Prop the flap open with the ruler so it reflects light into the box.

Safety tip: The foil and the food can become extremely hot, so always use oven mitts.

p7e944c6c15.title: Treating a Jellyfish Sting
p7e944c6c15.text:
Jellyfish are common along the Red Sea coast during warm months, and although most stings are only painful, knowing the correct response can prevent a minor injury from becoming serious.

First, help the injured swimmer leave the water calmly, because panic can lead to further stings. Next, rinse the affected skin with seawater, not fresh water; fresh water can cause remaining stinging cells to release more venom. Using tweezers or the edge of a plastic card, gently remove any visible tentacles. Never rub the area with sand or a towel.

Afterward, soak the skin in hot water, as hot as the person can comfortably tolerate, for about twenty minutes. This step often reduces pain significantly.

However, if the swimmer has difficulty breathing, feels dizzy, or develops swelling on the face, skip the remaining steps and call emergency services immediately.

pcb1ad1420e.title: Installing the School Rain Gauge
pcb1ad1420e.text:
The science club will record rainfall this term, so the gauge must be installed precisely; a poorly placed gauge can produce readings that are useless for comparison.

Select an open location at least two meters away from walls, trees, and fences, since these objects can block rain or splash extra water into the funnel. Drive the wooden post into firm ground until it stands without wobbling, then check it with a spirit level. Attach the mounting bracket so that the rim of the gauge sits about one meter above the ground.

Before fastening the gauge, confirm that the measuring tube is empty and that the funnel is free of dust or insects. Finally, tighten both screws evenly.

[Diagram: a post with a bracket near the top; the gauge's funnel faces upward; an arrow labeled "1 m" runs from the ground to the rim.]

Measurements should be recorded at 8:00 every morning, and the tube must be emptied immediately after every reading.

pe234e7ca1e.title: Protocol for Assisting a Stranded Sea Turtle
pe234e7ca1e.text:
Volunteers who discover a stranded sea turtle are often tempted to return it to the water immediately; however, this well-intentioned response can be fatal, because stranded turtles are frequently injured, exhausted, or suffering from cold shock.

Upon finding a turtle, first note its location and photograph it from a distance, then contact the regional wildlife hotline before taking any further action. While awaiting instructions, keep onlookers at least three meters away and shield the animal from direct sunlight with a damp towel, taking care never to cover its nostrils.

If the coordinator authorizes transport, lift the turtle by the sides of its shell, never by the flippers or head, and place it in a padded container. Do not add water to the container; a weakened turtle may be unable to raise its head to breathe.

Volunteers should record the time of every action, since rehabilitation staff rely on this timeline to assess the animal's condition.

p1d95ef219f.title: Handling Guidelines for Fragile Manuscripts
p1d95ef219f.text:
Researchers requesting access to the library's eleventh-century astronomical manuscripts must observe the following procedures, which are designed to minimize cumulative, often invisible, deterioration.

Before entering the reading room, deposit all pens, bags, and beverages in the designated lockers; only graphite pencils are permitted. Contrary to popular belief, cotton gloves are discouraged, because they reduce dexterity and can snag brittle fibers; instead, wash and thoroughly dry your hands immediately before handling any item.

Place each volume on the foam supports provided, adjusting them so that the binding never opens beyond a hundred and twenty degrees. Turn pages from the upper corner using a flat paper slip, and never moisten a finger to separate leaves.

Should you observe flaking pigment, a detached fragment, or an unfamiliar odor, cease examination at once, close the volume only if doing so causes no further movement of loose material, and notify the conservator on duty.

p67d1f26995.title: The Sand Castle
p67d1f26995.text:
I built a sandy castle by the sea,
As tall and proud as it could be.
I made a door, I made a wall,
I made a tower, very tall.

The waves came rolling in to say hello.
They splashed my castle, soft and slow.
Then splash! The water rushed in fast.
My pretty castle did not last.

pc36f8d8cde.title: The Lost Cloud
pc36f8d8cde.text:
Nora was finishing her homework beside the open window when a small white cloud drifted down from the sky and hovered just above her desk.

"Excuse me," the cloud said politely, its voice as soft as falling feathers. "I seem to have lost my family during the storm last night. Could you possibly help me find them?"

Nora blinked in astonishment, because everyone knows that clouds cannot speak. Nevertheless, this one clearly could. She leaned out the window and pointed toward the distant mountains, where enormous gray clouds were gathering together.

The little cloud brightened with happiness. Before floating away, it sprinkled a cool, gentle rain over the thirsty flowers in Nora's garden, and the petals seemed to lift their faces in gratitude.

p27640c4a06.title: The Falcon
p27640c4a06.text:
Text 1: Khalid adjusted the leather hood on the young falcon and checked the wind. His trainer had warned him that a nervous bird might fly off and never return, so he waited until the bird's feathers lay flat and calm. When he finally released her, she circled twice over the dunes and landed precisely on his glove, and Khalid let out a breath he had been holding for a full minute.

Text 2: The falcon Zahra had carried messages between the cloud kingdoms for a hundred years. When the Sky Queen summoned her, she spread her wings, which shimmered with copper flame, and spoke in a voice like distant thunder: "Tell me where the lost wind is hiding, and I will bring it home." The queen smiled, for no other creature could fly through the storm wall and survive.

pbade1f8067.title: The Glass Lighthouse
pbade1f8067.text:
On the island of Marrow, the lighthouse was built entirely of glass, and its beam did not merely guide ships; it revealed the truth. Any sailor caught in its light could no longer tell a lie, which was why merchants avoided the harbor after dark.

Rami, the keeper's apprentice, had been warned about the lighthouse's single rule: the lamp must never be extinguished, not even for a moment. For three years he obeyed, climbing the spiral stairs each evening to polish the crystal lens.

Then, one stormy night, a ship appeared carrying the Duke of Harrow, who demanded that the light be put out. "Darken it," the Duke shouted from the deck, "or I will shatter every pane on this island." Rami stood at the top of the tower, his hand trembling above the lever, knowing that whatever he chose would change Marrow forever.

p6350ce76ad.title: Inventory of a Harbor at Dawn
p6350ce76ad.text:
Before the city wakes, the harbor takes attendance: nine wooden dhows, their ropes slack as forgotten sentences; a gull rehearsing its single complaint; the fuel barge, patient as a camel kneeling for its load.

My grandfather counted these once, not with numbers but with names, calling each vessel as if it were a cousin returning from a long and uncertain journey.

Now the cranes do the counting, their steel arms swinging in mechanical silence, and the containers stack themselves like letters no one will ever open.

Still, at the far end of the pier, one dhow refuses to modernize. Its sail, mended in seventeen places, lifts toward the light, and I find myself, without deciding to, calling it by name.

p6f027c671f.title: Two Kinds of Wonder
p6f027c671f.text:
Text 1: In the town of Qasr al-Nur, it was generally understood that Aunt Safiya's bread remembered things. A loaf she baked on the morning of a wedding would stay warm for a week, and anyone who tore it open could hear, faintly, the music of the celebration. Nobody considered this remarkable; the neighbors simply ordered early, paid in coins, and complained, as always, about the price of flour.

Text 2: Beyond the Ninth Gate lay Valdrenn, where the rivers ran upward into the clouds and the mountains were ruled by the Ember Council. Every child of Valdrenn was bound at birth to an element, and when the young apprentice Toren discovered that his own bond had been stolen, he knew that he must cross the Shattered Plains, a journey from which no traveler in three centuries had returned.

pa7075ee43d.title: How Bees Make Honey
pa7075ee43d.text:
Bees make honey in three steps. First, a bee flies to a flower. It drinks the sweet juice inside. This juice is called nectar.

Next, the bee flies home to the hive. It gives the nectar to other bees. They chew it and pass it along.

Last, the bees put the nectar in small wax cells. They fan it with their wings. The nectar gets thick. Now it is honey!

pc07cb680cf.title: The Wind Catchers
pc07cb680cf.text:
Long before electric air conditioners, people in hot desert towns found a clever way to stay cool. They built tall towers, called wind catchers, on top of their homes and important buildings.

A wind catcher is open at the top on several sides. When a breeze blows across the roof, the tower catches it and pushes the air down into the rooms below. At the same time, warmer air rises and escapes through a separate opening on the opposite side. This steady movement keeps the house cooler.

Some builders improved the design even more. They placed a small pool of water or a damp clay jar at the bottom of the tower. As the air passed over the water, it became cooler still.

Today, some modern architects are studying wind catchers again. They hope these old towers can help new buildings use less energy.

pcb850a0c19.title: The Quiet Genius of Al-Jazari
pcb850a0c19.text:
In 1206, an engineer named Ismail al-Jazari completed a book describing about fifty mechanical devices. Many readers today remember him for his elaborate water clocks, including one shaped like an elephant. However, his greatest contribution may be less obvious than these impressive inventions.

Al-Jazari did not simply describe finished machines. He explained, step by step, how each one could be built, and he included detailed drawings so that other craftsmen could copy his designs. This approach was unusual at a time when many inventors guarded their methods as secrets.

Several of his ideas, such as early forms of the crankshaft and the camshaft, later became essential parts of engines and factory machines. Because he recorded his methods so carefully, engineers in later centuries could study and improve them.

In this sense, al-Jazari's true legacy is not a single invention but a habit: sharing knowledge clearly so that others can build on it.

pc5131a1fcc.title: Roots Along the Shore
pc5131a1fcc.text:
Friends and fellow volunteers, when we began planting mangroves along this coastline three years ago, many people in our community questioned whether the effort was worth the trouble. The seedlings were tiny, and the sea seemed enormous.

I understand that doubt, and I will not pretend it was unreasonable or uninformed. A single mangrove cannot stop a storm. But a single mangrove was never the point. Each tree anchors itself with tangled roots that trap sediment, shelter juvenile fish, and gradually weaken the waves that reach the shore. When thousands of trees grow together, their roots form a living barrier stronger than any individual plant.

So the question is not whether one seedling matters. The real question is whether our community is patient enough to allow many seedlings to mature into a forest. Last winter, after a violent storm, the stretch of beach behind our oldest planting lost almost no sand, while the unprotected beach beside it lost nearly a meter.

That measurable difference is our answer to the doubters. Small actions, repeated faithfully, become a defense that no single person could ever build alone.

p1b20e6fe5f.title: The Myth of the Lone Inventor
p1b20e6fe5f.text:
We like our inventions to have a single parent. Ask who invented the light bulb, and most people will offer one name, as though the device appeared fully formed in one workshop on one remarkable night.

The historical record is less tidy. Dozens of researchers in several countries had produced glowing filaments for decades before the famous version arrived. What distinguished the successful design was not the idea of electric light but a durable filament, an efficient vacuum, and a system of wires and generators that made the lamp practical.

None of this diminishes individual brilliance. Persistence, judgment, and the ability to recognize which partial solution deserves attention are rare talents. Yet these talents operate within a network of earlier attempts, shared publications, and skilled assistants whose names rarely survive.

The lone-inventor story, then, is not exactly false; it is incomplete. A more accurate account would treat invention less as a sudden flash than as a relay, in which the person who crosses the finish line depends on every runner before.

p30458079e6.title: The Honest Distortion
p30458079e6.text:
Every flat map of the Earth is, in a strict sense, a falsehood. A sphere cannot be flattened without stretching, tearing, or compressing some part of its surface, and cartographers have spent centuries deciding which compromises to accept.

The most familiar example preserves the shapes of coastlines and the angles between directions, which made it invaluable to navigators plotting a constant compass course. The price is enormous exaggeration near the poles, where Greenland swells to rival Africa, a continent roughly fourteen times its size.
