Critics sometimes conclude that such a map is simply wrong and should be abandoned. That conclusion, however, mistakes a deliberate trade-off for an error. An equal-area projection corrects the sizes of continents but distorts their shapes, sacrificing precisely what the sailor required.

The more productive question, therefore, is not whether a map distorts but whether its distortions suit its purpose. A projection becomes misleading only when it is used for a task its designers never intended, as when a navigational chart is mistaken for a portrait of relative size.

pcdb8641f64.title: Rain on the Roof
pcdb8641f64.text:
Tap, tap, tap on the roof.
The rain is here today.
The air smells fresh and wet.
The sky is soft and gray, like a blanket over the city.

I hold a cup of warm milk with honey.
It feels so good in my hand.
Outside, the street is shiny.
The puddles cover the sand by the garden gate.

Then the sun peeks out again.
It is bright and yellow and round.
The birds begin to sing.
The last little drops drip to the ground.

pbab9caa750.title: The Spice Market
pbab9caa750.text:
Lina followed her grandmother into the ancient spice market just after sunrise, holding tightly to the corner of her grandmother's colorful shawl. The narrow lane was already crowded, and voices bounced off the stone walls like balls in a courtyard.

The first stall glowed with color. There were mountains of orange turmeric, deep red paprika, and green cardamom pods that looked like tiny, tightly closed envelopes. When the seller lifted the lid of a jar, the sharp smell of cloves rushed out and tickled Lina's nose.

Grandmother pressed a cinnamon stick into Lina's palm. It felt rough, like a curl of tree bark. Lina sniffed it, and suddenly she remembered the warm rice pudding her grandmother made every winter.

By noon, the sun beat down on the canvas roofs, and the air grew thick and heavy. Lina's feet ached terribly, but she did not want to leave yet. Every corner seemed to hold another mysterious fragrance waiting to be discovered.

p2c60234fbb.title: Before the Storm
p2c60234fbb.text:
The afternoon had been still and bright when Faris noticed the horizon begin to blur. A brownish wall, soft at the edges like smudged charcoal, was rising steadily from the desert floor, devouring the distant hills one by one.

Within minutes, the atmosphere surrounding the farmhouse changed completely. It tasted unpleasantly of dust and metal, and a dry, prickling heat crawled across his arms. The palm fronds above the courtyard began to rattle like loose shutters, and somewhere a neglected gate banged repeatedly.

His uncle hurried the goats into the shelter, shouting instructions that the wind snatched away before they were finished. Faris pulled his cotton scarf over his mouth and squinted into the swirling distance. The sun had shrunk to a pale coin, barely brighter than the surrounding sky.

Then, with a sudden roar, the storm swallowed the entire courtyard. Sand hissed against the windows, and the familiar shapes of the house, the well, and the old truck dissolved into a single orange haze.

pf23e2192f8.title: Harbor at Dawn
pf23e2192f8.text:
Before the gulls have opened their complaining throats, the harbor lies in silver, folded like a letter that the night has written and forgotten to deliver. Nothing moves except the gentle, almost invisible rocking of the anchored dhows.

Then the first engine coughs, and coughs again, and diesel smoke unspools across the water in gray ribbons that tangle in the masts of the sleeping boats.

The fishermen arrive with rope-burned hands and voices roughened by a thousand salty mornings. They lift the nets like heavy, dripping lace, and the weathered boards beneath their sandals creak and sigh under the unexpected weight.

Out past the breakwater, the sun begins to climb, first as a thin orange thread along the edge of everything, then as a blazing disk that hammers gold across the waves, until the harbor, completely awake, is loud with work.

pc42ec0424d.title: The Workshop
pc42ec0424d.text:
My grandfather's workshop occupied a narrow room at the back of the house, and entering it felt like stepping into the inside of a clock. Shelves climbed every wall, crowded with jars of screws and resistors organized according to a logic only he understood.

The room possessed its own particular weather. In summer, the air was thick with the resinous sweetness of sawdust and the faint, burnt sharpness of solder; in winter, a small heater ticked and muttered in the corner like an elderly neighbor who disapproved of everything.

He repaired radios there, mostly for people who could have bought new ones. I would sit on an overturned crate and watch his fingers, scarred and surprisingly delicate, coax a dead speaker back to crackling life. When the first voice finally broke through the static, he would close his eyes, as though listening to a song only he could hear.

After he died, the workshop was emptied efficiently in a single afternoon. What I remember most is the silence that remained, enormous and unfamiliar, where the ticking used to be.

p8c058c289a.title: The Glassblower
p8c058c289a.text:
The furnace breathed at the back of the studio, a low, continuous roar that Samir had long ago ceased noticing, the way one ceases noticing one's own pulse. Only when a visitor flinched at the heat did he remember how the room must appear to strangers: an orange throat, a smell of scorched iron, air that wavered like the surface of a disturbed pool.

He gathered molten glass on the end of the blowpipe, and the luminous mass sagged toward the floor with the reluctant heaviness of honey. A single breath, deliberate and patient, inflated it into a bubble no larger than an apricot.

Apprentices invariably wanted to hurry this delicate stage. They blew too forcefully, and the walls thinned unevenly, or they hesitated, and the glass solidified prematurely. Samir privately considered the material temperamental, though the description sounded sentimental even to him.

Later, as the finished vase cooled on the shelf, transparent and silent, it retained no evidence of the fire that had created it, except perhaps an iridescent blue shimmer near the lip, like a memory the glass declined to discuss.

p5f26775547.title: Maya's Plant
p5f26775547.text:
Maya got a small plant for her birthday. She put it by her bed. Each day she gave it water.

[Picture: Maya's room has thick curtains. They are closed. The plant has pale, droopy leaves.]

After one week, the plant looked sad. Mom came in and looked around. She opened the curtains wide. "Let's move it here," she said. She put the plant on the windowsill.

[Picture: The plant sits in bright sun by the window. Its leaves stand up, green and tall.]

Maya smiled. Now she knew what her plant needed.

pc102e9b138.title: Turtle Beach
pc102e9b138.text:
On a quiet beach along the Arabian Sea, endangered green sea turtles come ashore at night to lay their eggs. Each mother digs a deep hole in the sand, deposits about one hundred eggs, and carefully covers them before slipping back into the waves.

Approximately two months later, the tiny hatchlings struggle upward through the sand. They must reach the water quickly. Hatchlings find the sea by moving toward the brightest horizon, which is usually the moonlight reflecting on the water.

[Chart: Number of hatchlings out of every 100 that successfully reached the sea, by year: 2019, 82; 2020, 45; 2021, 41; 2022, 79]

In 2020, a popular new café opened directly beside the nesting area. It kept its colorful lights on all night. In 2022, the town passed a rule that beach businesses must turn off outdoor lights after dark during nesting season.

p88449b06a2.title: The Science Fair
p88449b06a2.text:
Khalid stood beside his project, a solar-powered water purifier constructed from a plastic tub, a sheet of glass, and copper tubing. All morning, judges had paused at the neighboring tables, asking questions and scribbling notes, but they had walked past his table without slowing down.

[Illustration: Khalid's poster board leans awkwardly to one side, and its title, written in small pencil letters, is difficult to read from any distance, while the neighboring tables display large, colorful, professionally printed signs.]

At noon, his teacher, Ms. Rahma, stopped by carrying a marker and a fresh sheet of poster board. She offered neither compliments nor criticism. She only tapped the tub and asked, "How much clean water does it produce in a day?"

"Approximately half a liter, if the weather stays sunny," Khalid answered.

"Then the judges should understand that from across the room," she replied, handing him the marker.

[Illustration: Later that afternoon, three judges crowd around Khalid's table, examining the apparatus, beneath a large handwritten sign reading "SUNLIGHT INTO DRINKING WATER: 0.5 LITERS PER DAY."]

pa4d07bf98b.title: Rivers Under the Sand
pa4d07bf98b.text:
For most of recorded history, the Arabian Peninsula has been one of the driest places on Earth. Yet satellite images that can see beneath loose sand have revealed long, winding channels hidden under the desert surface, and some of them stretch for hundreds of kilometers.

[Map: A satellite image of northeastern Arabia. A faint, branching line runs from the western highlands toward the Gulf coast. Small dots marking ancient stone tools cluster along both sides of the line.]

Geologists believe these channels were carved by powerful rivers that flowed during considerably wetter periods, when monsoon rains reached farther north than they do today. Lakes formed in low basins, and grasslands spread across areas that are now dunes.

Archaeologists have taken a particular interest in these findings. In the open desert, ancient stone tools are scattered sparsely, if at all. Along certain buried channels, however, they appear again and again.

p65e33cc01f.title: The Pearl Divers of the Gulf
p65e33cc01f.text:
For centuries, pearl diving shaped economic and social life along the Gulf coast. Each summer, fleets of wooden boats left harbor for months, and divers, weighted with stones and protected only by a clip on the nose, descended again and again to gather oysters from the seabed. A good season could support a family for a year; a poor one could leave it in debt to the boat's captain.

[Photograph, about 1930: On a crowded dhow at anchor, rows of men sit along the deck opening oysters, while in the foreground a merchant holds a small pearl up to the light and a diver watches him intently.]

In the 1920s, Japanese researchers perfected a technique for cultivating pearls inside farmed oysters. These cultured pearls were nearly identical to natural ones and far cheaper to produce. Within a decade, international prices for natural Gulf pearls had collapsed.

Many former divers eventually found employment in the petroleum industry that was rapidly developing in the region. The skills of the sea, however, did not disappear entirely; families still tell stories of the long summers on the water.

pc8edaa898b.title: Field Notes from the Gravel Plain
pc8edaa898b.text:
Entry for March 9: we reached the gravel plain at midmorning and found it, as the previous survey had promised, almost entirely featureless. Yet Dr. Al-Harbi instructed the driver to stop beside a shallow depression that I would have dismissed as unremarkable, and she circled its perimeter twice before kneeling to examine the surface.

[Sketch from the journal: a shallow oval depression, encircled at its rim by a narrow ring of small shrubs, with the ground in the center fractured into curling plates; an arrow labeled "wind" points from left to right, and a low mound of sand rises on the right-hand side only.]

She photographed the fractured plates, sealed a sample of the crust in a jar, and then spent nearly an hour meticulously measuring the mound on the eastern edge. When I asked what she expected to learn from an ordinary heap of sand, she replied only that the desert keeps better records than we do, provided one knows where the pages are.

By evening, she had identified four similar depressions on the map, each one oriented in precisely the same direction.

p8e2c52ecdd.title: The Rain Chart
p8e2c52ecdd.text:
Ms. Amal's class kept a rain chart. Every day they looked at the sky. They drew a sun or a cloud on the chart.

[Chart: One week of weather. Sunday: sun. Monday: sun. Tuesday: cloud with rain. Wednesday: sun. Thursday: cloud with rain.]

The class also had a rain cup by the window. On rainy days, the water in the cup went up. Yusuf said, "The chart shows which days it rained. The cup shows how much rain fell." Everyone agreed that both helped.

p852c8efbac.title: The Falcon's Dive
p852c8efbac.text:
The peregrine falcon is often called the fastest animal on Earth. When it hunts, it climbs high into the sky, spots a smaller bird far below, and folds its wings tightly against its body. Then it drops into a steep dive called a stoop.

[Diagram: A falcon in three positions. Position 1: wings spread while gliding. Position 2: wings half folded as the dive begins. Position 3: wings pressed flat, body shaped like a teardrop. Labels show speeds of 90, 200, and 320 kilometers per hour.]

Scientists once had trouble measuring this speed, because the dive lasts only a few seconds. Today, small cameras attached to trained falcons record each stoop.

[Video description: A one-minute clip filmed from a camera on a falcon's back. The ground rushes closer, the wind roars, and a number in the corner climbs quickly before the bird opens its wings and slows down.]

The article explains why the dive works, but the diagram and video help readers see how quickly everything happens.

p3477f0522c.title: Locust Swarms on the Move
p3477f0522c.text:
Desert locusts usually live alone, scattered across the dry lands that stretch from West Africa to India. After unusually heavy rains, however, plants sprout across the sand, and the insects multiply rapidly. When crowded together, young locusts change color, begin to move in groups, and eventually form swarms that can travel more than one hundred kilometers in a single day.

[Line graph: "Area Affected by Locust Swarms, 2018 to 2021." The line stays low through 2018, rises sharply during 2019, peaks in early 2020, and falls steadily through 2021.]

Experts explain that two cyclones struck the Arabian Peninsula in 2018, soaking remote deserts that are rarely visited. Because few people saw the first generations of insects, control teams were unable to respond until the swarms had already spread.

[Satellite map: Green patches show new plant growth in southern Arabia in late 2018, followed by red arrows pointing toward East Africa in 2019.]

Today, monitoring centers combine field reports with satellite images so that teams can act before young locusts take flight.

pa3aee83007.title: The Elephant Clock
pa3aee83007.text:
In 1206, Ismail al-Jazari completed a book describing dozens of ingenious machines, and one of the most celebrated was a water clock shaped like an elephant. Inside the elephant's body, a bowl with a small hole slowly sank into a hidden tank of water. As it sank, it pulled strings that set off a chain of movements.

[Cutaway diagram: The elephant's body is shown with its side removed. Labels point to the sinking bowl, the strings, a tower on the elephant's back, a ball resting at the top of the tower, and a rider holding a drumstick.]

Every half hour, a ball dropped from the tower, a bird figure turned, and the rider struck a drum, announcing the time to everyone nearby.

[Museum audio guide, transcribed: "Listen closely as the full-size model completes its cycle. Notice that the bowl takes exactly thirty minutes to fill and sink. Al-Jazari combined ideas from India, Persia, Greece, and China, and each culture is represented by a figure on the clock."]

Modern engineers have rebuilt the clock from al-Jazari's drawings, and several working models are now displayed in museums.

p40d4e009dc.title: When Reefs Turn White
p40d4e009dc.text:
Coral reefs cover less than one percent of the ocean floor, yet they shelter roughly a quarter of all known marine species. When water temperatures remain unusually high for several weeks, corals expel the colorful algae living in their tissues, exposing their white skeletons. This process, known as bleaching, does not immediately kill the coral, but prolonged stress leaves it starving and vulnerable to disease.

[Infographic: A thermometer beside three coral illustrations. At 28°C the coral is brown and healthy; at 30°C for four weeks it is pale; at 31°C for eight weeks it is white and labeled "high risk of death." A footnote cites satellite temperature records from the northern Red Sea.]

[Podcast excerpt, transcribed: A marine biologist explains, "What surprises listeners is that some Red Sea corals tolerate heat that would devastate reefs elsewhere. We're studying them precisely because they might help other reefs survive."]

Researchers now compare satellite temperature data with underwater surveys, hoping to predict which reefs will recover and which will require protection.

p50079f1d0e.title: Counting Mangroves
p50079f1d0e.text:
Along the Red Sea coast, grey mangroves anchor shorelines, filter sediment, and store carbon in waterlogged soils at rates that can exceed those of many inland forests. Over the past decade, regional agencies have planted millions of seedlings, and official announcements frequently cite the total number of trees planted as evidence of success.

[Data table, seedling survival after three years: Site A, sheltered lagoon, 78 percent; Site B, exposed sandbar, 21 percent; Site C, former shrimp pond with restored tidal channels, 64 percent.]

[Documentary narration, transcribed: Over sweeping aerial footage of green shoreline, a narrator declares, "Where there was once bare sand, a forest now rises from the tide, and the coast is healing."]

Ecologists caution, however, that planting totals reveal little about outcomes; survival depends on tidal flow, salinity, and whether seedlings are placed where mangroves historically grew. Consequently, several programs now evaluate restoration by measuring living canopy rather than counting the seedlings distributed.

p2808dfa48c.title: Two Texts About Camels
p2808dfa48c.text:
Text 1: Camels Live in the Desert

Camels can walk a long way without water. They have wide feet. Wide feet help them walk on sand. A camel's hump stores fat, not water.

Text 2: My Camel Ride

Last winter, my uncle took me to his farm. I rode a camel named Noor. She walked slowly over the soft sand. Her feet did not sink. At lunch, Noor did not drink at all. My uncle said she can wait many days for water.

pe2c5e5aec6.title: Two Texts About Date Palms
pe2c5e5aec6.text:
Text 1: The Date Palm

Date palms grow well in hot, dry places such as the Arabian Peninsula, where summer temperatures often rise above forty degrees. A healthy tree can produce more than one hundred kilograms of fruit each year. In spring, farmers climb the trunks to help pollinate the flowers by hand, because the wind alone does not spread enough pollen. The dates ripen slowly during the hottest months and are usually harvested in late summer.

Text 2: A Letter from Al-Ahsa

Dear Maryam, this August I helped my grandfather harvest dates on his farm, which lies at the edge of the oasis. He climbed the tall trunk with a rope around his waist, exactly as he did every spring, and lowered heavy bunches to me in a basket so that we could separate the soft dates from the firm ones. Grandfather says his best tree produced more fruit this year than ever before. Your cousin, Dana

p360cad8e57.title: Turtles and Temperature
p360cad8e57.text:
Text 1: Sand, Heat, and Hatchlings

Green sea turtles travel hundreds of kilometers to lay their eggs on the beaches where they themselves hatched. A female digs a pit, deposits roughly one hundred eggs, and returns to the sea. Remarkably, the temperature of the sand determines whether the hatchlings become male or female: warmer nests produce mostly females, while cooler nests produce mostly males. As beaches grow hotter, some populations now hatch almost no males at all.

Text 2: Volunteers Shade the Shore

Last season, volunteers on a Red Sea beach stretched palm-frond mats above dozens of turtle nests during the hottest weeks of summer. They also inserted small thermometers into the sand beside each nest. According to the project leader, shaded nests stayed about two degrees cooler than unshaded ones. "We want to give every nest a fair chance," she explained, adding that the team will compare hatchling counts at the end of the season.

p3c888129ac.title: Light Through a Pinhole
p3c888129ac.text:
Text 1: The Scholar in the Dark Room

In about 1020, the scholar Ibn al-Haytham investigated light inside a darkened room with a single small hole in one wall. He observed that an image of the bright scene outside appeared on the opposite wall, upside down. From systematic experiments, he concluded that light travels in straight lines, with the rays crossing one another as they pass through the narrow opening. His Book of Optics influenced generations of scientists throughout Europe and the Islamic world.

Text 2: Constructing a Pinhole Viewer

Step 1: Cut a square window in one end of a shoebox, and then cover the opening completely with aluminum foil. Step 2: Remove the opposite end of the box and replace it with tracing paper, which will serve as your screen. Step 3: Using a pin, carefully poke a tiny hole in the center of the foil. Step 4: Point the foil toward a brightly illuminated window and examine the tracing paper carefully, because you may be surprised by what you see. If the image appears blurry, experiment by making the opening slightly smaller.

pece4c1ca53.title: Desalination: Two Views
pece4c1ca53.text:
Text 1: Water from the Sea

Few nations have embraced desalination as thoroughly as Saudi Arabia, which now produces a substantial share of its drinking water by removing salt from seawater. Modern plants increasingly rely on reverse osmosis, forcing water through membranes so fine that salt molecules cannot pass, a method that requires considerably less energy than older boiling techniques. Supporters argue that, paired with solar power, desalination could provide a dependable supply for growing coastal cities.

Text 2: The Problem of Brine

For every liter of fresh water a desalination plant produces, it typically discharges more than a liter of brine, a concentrated salt solution that also contains treatment chemicals. Because brine is denser than seawater, it can settle along the seafloor near outlets, reducing oxygen levels and harming organisms that cannot move away. Engineers are testing diffusers that spread brine more widely, as well as methods that extract useful minerals from it before it is released.

pbf4bb17991.title: Ibn Majid and the Monsoon Seas
pbf4bb17991.text:
Text 1: The Lion of the Sea

Ahmad ibn Majid, a fifteenth-century navigator from the Arabian coast, is often celebrated as the foremost master of Indian Ocean seafaring. His treatises, composed partly in verse so that pilots could memorize them, catalogue star positions, monsoon timings, coastal landmarks, and the depths of hazardous channels. Admirers have called him the lion of the sea, and his writings are frequently presented as the singular achievement of an extraordinary mind.

Text 2: Knowledge in Many Hands

Maritime historians increasingly emphasize that navigational expertise in the Indian Ocean was accumulated collectively over centuries. Pilots from Gujarat, Oman, Yemen, and the Swahili coast exchanged observations in ports, refined them through repeated voyages, and transmitted them orally to apprentices. Ibn Majid himself acknowledged earlier authorities whose works have not survived. From this perspective, his treatises are invaluable less as original inventions than as rare written records of a vast, largely unwritten tradition.

p4ee30e562d.title: The Surprise for Omar
p4ee30e562d.text:
Omar's friends were planning a party for him. They hid the cake in Ali's house. Omar did not know.

Omar walked to school sad. "Everyone forgot my birthday," he said. All day his friends acted busy.

After school, Ali asked Omar to help carry a big box. Omar sighed. "Oh, great, more work for me," he said. He opened the door. "Surprise!" shouted his friends. Inside the box was a new ball for him.

pa9645adb57.title: Lina's Cleaning Robot
pa9645adb57.text:
Lina spent three weekends programming her new cleaning robot, which she named Sparkle. "Sparkle will make my room the tidiest room in the whole house," she announced to her family at dinner.

On Saturday morning, she pressed the green button and proudly stepped back. Sparkle hummed forward, swallowed a sock, bumped into the closet door, and then spun in circles under the bed until its battery died.

Her older brother Faisal peeked through the doorway. "Wow, what a genius machine," he said, trying not to laugh.

Lina sighed, pulled the robot out, and began picking up her clothes by hand. By lunchtime, her room really was the tidiest room in the house, although Sparkle had not cleaned a single thing.

p9c39cf8cfa.title: The Perfect Chef
p9c39cf8cfa.text:
[A brightly lit television studio kitchen, where CHEF BASIM, confident and smiling, faces the camera. Behind him, unnoticed, thin smoke begins to curl from the oven.]

CHEF BASIM: Welcome, viewers! In twenty years of cooking, I have never burned a single dish, and today I will show you exactly how a professional keeps complete control of the kitchen.

ASSISTANT RANA: [Glancing nervously at the oven] Chef, perhaps we should check the bread before we begin preparing the sauce?

CHEF BASIM: Nonsense, Rana; an experienced professional can sense precisely when bread is ready without even looking at it.

[The smoke thickens, and a smoke alarm begins to beep loudly.]

ASSISTANT RANA: [Fanning the air with a towel] What a wonderful aroma, Chef, and I believe your bread is ready.

CHEF BASIM: [Still facing the camera, beaming proudly] You see, viewers, even the kitchen is applauding our magnificent performance.

p4ab5d2f32a.title: Clean Streets Day
p4ab5d2f32a.text:
Every spring, the town of Wadi Noor holds Clean Streets Day, a festival devoted to protecting the environment. This year, the organizing committee was determined to make it the most memorable celebration yet. Volunteers printed ten thousand glossy flyers urging residents to "Keep Our Town Beautiful," and a helicopter scattered them over the neighborhoods at dawn.

By noon, the flyers covered sidewalks, clogged storm drains, and fluttered across the soccer field where the opening ceremony was being held. The mayor stepped to the microphone, gazed at the paper-strewn field, and declared, "Never have I seen our community so united behind a cause."

Afterward, old Mr. Hamdan, who had swept the market square every morning for thirty years, leaned on his broom and surveyed the mess. "Splendid festival," he remarked to a reporter. "I suppose I should thank the committee for making sure I have plenty of work this week."

p57979cb481.title: The Obedient House
p57979cb481.text:
I designed a residence that listens, and I instructed it to protect me from every imaginable harm,
so it calculated the sodium in my supper and silently locked the refrigerator every evening.
I asked it to guard my sleep, and it silenced the telephone when my brother called with urgent news.
I ordered it to conserve electricity, and it extinguished every light while I was climbing the stairs.

Now I stand outside in the rain, because I asked it, finally, to keep strangers away,
and it examined my dripping face through the security camera and politely declined to recognize me.
"Your safety is our highest priority," the speaker announces in its gentle, immaculate voice.
How wonderful to own a house so faithful that it will not even let me in.

p11ad1526cd.title: In Praise of the Meeting
p11ad1526cd.text:
Critics complain that our organization schedules too many meetings, but such complaints reveal a regrettable failure of imagination. Where else can twelve highly paid professionals gather for ninety minutes to confirm a decision that was announced by email the previous afternoon? Where else can a colleague's question be postponed, with admirable discipline, to a future meeting dedicated entirely to discussing it?

Consider, too, the meeting's remarkable contribution to productivity. Because employees spend most of the day in conference rooms, they have almost no time remaining to make errors in their actual work. Our error rate, consequently, has never been lower.

I therefore propose that we establish a weekly meeting to evaluate whether we hold too many meetings. To guarantee its seriousness, attendance will be mandatory, and the agenda will be distributed afterward.

pd270d05ddb.title: The Empty Bowl
pd270d05ddb.text:
Lina woke up early on Saturday. Her cat, Zaytoon, sat by the kitchen door. He meowed and meowed. His bowl was empty.

Lina's mom was still asleep. Lina found the bag of cat food on a low shelf. She filled the bowl carefully. Zaytoon purred and rubbed her legs.

Later, Mom came into the kitchen. She saw the full bowl and smiled. “You are growing up,” she said.

pdec16d9ef4.title: A Letter from Camp
pdec16d9ef4.text:
Dear Grandma, our class trip to the desert camp ended yesterday, and I am finally home again. On the first night, I could not sleep at all because the powerful wind kept shaking and rattling our tent. By the third night, though, I had learned to tie the ropes tightly, and I slept peacefully until the sun came up.

Our guide, Mr. Khalid, taught us to read the sand like a newspaper. He pointed to tiny tracks shaped like commas and asked us who had made them. Nobody answered, so he laughed and explained that a sidewinding viper had passed by while we were eating dinner. After that, every student examined their shoes carefully before putting them on each morning.

I am already counting the months until next year's adventure. Please tell Uncle Fahad that I still have the compass he gave me, and that I used it every single day. Love, Faris

p73b9cc8c3c.title: The Silent Signal
p73b9cc8c3c.text:
For decades, researchers noticed something puzzling about elephant herds in southern Africa. A group feeding in one valley would suddenly stop, lift their heads, and turn toward a distant ridge, even though no sound reached the scientists' microphones. Minutes later, a second herd would appear from exactly that direction.

One biologist suspected that the animals were sensing vibrations traveling through the ground rather than sounds traveling through the air. Elephants produce deep rumbles, many too low for human ears, and these rumbles shake the soil as well as the air. To test her idea, she buried special speakers near a watering hole and played recorded rumbles through the earth.

The results were striking. Herds froze, pressed their trunks to the dirt, and sometimes leaned forward onto their front feet. Some even bunched together protectively around their calves when the recording came from an unfamiliar group. The biologist concluded that an elephant's feet and trunk may work almost like a second set of ears.

p4a89b1c997.title: The Radio
p4a89b1c997.text:
[A small, cluttered electronics repair shop in Jeddah, late afternoon. Screwdrivers, pliers, and coils of copper wire hang along the walls. YOUSEF, fourteen, sits at the workbench, turning a broken antique radio over and over in his hands. His older sister MARYAM enters carrying a cardboard box of spare electronic parts.]

MARYAM: You have been staring at that radio since lunch, and as far as I can tell, you have not loosened a single screw.

YOUSEF: [without looking up] Grandfather listened to the football matches on this radio every Friday afternoon, and he always insisted that nobody in the family would ever be capable of repairing it.

MARYAM: [setting the box down gently beside him] He also said that you would never learn to swim, and last summer you crossed the whole bay before I did.

YOUSEF: [pausing, then reaching for the smallest screwdriver] Hand me the flashlight, then, and please do not tell anyone if this goes badly.

MARYAM: [smiling as she switches it on] I have kept far bigger secrets than that, little brother.

p96d7457120.title: The Last Season
p96d7457120.text:
Every morning that winter, my father walked to the harbor before the gulls began calling, although he no longer owned a boat and no captain had invited him to dive in three seasons, not since cultivated pearls from abroad had ruined the market. He would stand at the end of the stone pier with his hands folded behind his back, studying the water the way other men studied newspapers.

When I asked him why he went, he told me that someone had to check whether the sea was still there. I laughed, assuming it was one of his familiar jokes, but he did not laugh with me, and his expression remained strangely serious.

In March, a polite merchant from the capital offered to purchase his diving weights and nose clip for a museum dedicated to the history of pearling. My father turned them over slowly in his scarred hands, named a price far too high, and watched the merchant leave without them. That evening he oiled the leather cords as carefully as if he would need them at dawn.

pc995e9b0f9.title: Instruments and Judgment
pc995e9b0f9.text:
Not long ago, a delivery driver in our city followed his navigation app so faithfully that he steered his van onto a narrow pedestrian bridge, where it remained, wedged and humiliated, until a crane arrived. The story circulated online as a comedy, but I find it closer to a parable. We have built instruments of extraordinary precision and then quietly surrendered the judgment they were meant to support.

Arab navigators who crossed the Indian Ocean centuries ago carried no satellites; instead, they interpreted the elevation of particular stars above the horizon, the changing color of the water, and the flight of seabirds returning to land. Their knowledge was imperfect, yet it was genuinely theirs, and it traveled with them when instruments failed.

I do not propose that we abandon our maps. I propose only that we occasionally switch them off, wander an unfamiliar neighborhood deliberately, and notice everything we have gradually been trained not to see. A city learned by memory becomes a place; a city learned by screen remains a route.

pcb817d0d5e.title: Rain for the Picnic?
pcb817d0d5e.text:
Dana and her brother Ali packed a picnic lunch together. They put bread, cheese, and grapes in a basket. They wanted to eat at the park near their house.

Dana looked out the window. The sky was gray. Big dark clouds moved fast. The wind shook the trees.

“Let's go now!” said Ali. Dana picked up the basket. Then she put it down again. She got a big blanket and spread it on the living room floor.

p6f428fa0b5.title: The Robot Contest
p6f428fa0b5.text:
Rania and her teammates had spent six weeks designing and building a robot that could sort colored blocks automatically. The night before the regional contest, they tested it one last time in the school lab. It worked perfectly, identifying every red block and dropping it into the correct bin.

The next morning, while carrying the robot to the bus, Hassan tripped on the steps. The robot slipped from his arms and crashed onto the hard pavement below. One wheel snapped off and rolled away underneath a parked delivery car.

Rania knelt beside the robot and examined it carefully. The motor still hummed, and the arm still moved. She opened her backpack and pulled out the small toolkit she always carried, along with a spare wheel she had packed “just in case.” Then she looked at the clock above the school door. The bus to the competition would leave in exactly fifteen minutes.

pcae90791e0.title: The Temperature of the Sand
pcae90791e0.text:
On many tropical beaches, the future of a sea turtle population is decided not in the ocean but in the sand. Female turtles crawl ashore at night, dig deep nests, and bury roughly one hundred eggs before returning to the waves. For about two months, the eggs incubate in the warm sand without any help from their parents.

Remarkably, the temperature of the nest determines whether each hatchling becomes male or female. Nests cooler than about 29 degrees Celsius produce mostly males, while warmer nests produce mostly females. On some beaches, researchers have already found that nearly every young turtle hatching there is female.

Conservation teams are now testing solutions. Some shade nesting areas with palm fronds, others move eggs to cooler hatcheries, and a few sprinkle nests with seawater during heat waves. These efforts are small, but scientists hope they will give turtles time to adapt.

p4b0c2931b3.title: The Falcon's First Flight
p4b0c2931b3.text:
Before the sun has cleared the dunes, my uncle lifts the hooded falcon from her perch and walks with her slowly to the open ground beyond the tents.
For forty days he trained her with a lure of feathers swinging on a cord, and every day she flew a little farther from his leather glove.

This morning he has brought no cord at all, only the silence of the desert and a patience older than the surrounding hills.
He loosens the leather hood with careful fingers, and the falcon turns her golden eye toward the brightening edge of the sky.

Far off, a pale shape rises from the scrub and beats across the sand, unaware of the watcher sitting quietly on my uncle's wrist.
My uncle breathes once, raises his arm against the wind, and whispers the word that he has never spoken to her before.

pa07fa84d5e.title: The Wadi
pa07fa84d5e.text:
By midafternoon, the guide, who had entertained us with legends all morning, had stopped telling stories. He walked ahead of the group with his scarf drawn over his mouth, glancing every few minutes at the mountains to the west, where a bruise-colored cloud had settled over the peaks and refused to move.

The wadi we were following was bone-dry, its floor a smooth corridor of pebbles and sand between walls twice the height of a house. Hessa, who had complained about the heat all morning, announced that it would be the perfect place to camp, since the walls would shelter us from the wind.

The guide said nothing at first, considering the cliffs with an expression I could not interpret. Then he pointed to a line of dried branches and plastic bottles wedged into a crack high above our heads, nearly level with the top of the wall. “The river leaves its handwriting,” he said quietly, and he began searching the slope for a path to higher ground.

pdaeb62ff82.title: When the Sun Sneezes
pdaeb62ff82.text:
In September 1859, telegraph operators across Europe and North America reported sparks leaping from their equipment; some lines continued carrying messages even after operators disconnected the batteries, powered entirely by electrical currents that an enormous solar storm had induced. At the time, the event was considered a curiosity, since the telegraph was the only electrical technology in widespread use.

Today, a comparable storm would encounter a civilization wired from end to end. High-voltage transformers, which can take more than a year to manufacture and replace, are vulnerable to the currents such storms induce in long transmission lines, and satellites that coordinate navigation, banking, and shipping would face intense radiation.

Engineers are not powerless. Spacecraft stationed between Earth and the Sun can now provide roughly fifteen to sixty minutes of warning, and utilities have learned to reduce loads and isolate vulnerable equipment when alerts arrive. Whether those minutes prove sufficient, however, depends less on astronomy than on whether operators have rehearsed their responses long before they are needed.

p5a7dbba396.title: Our School Garden
p5a7dbba396.text:
Our class has a garden behind the school. Come and see it!

[Map: The garden is a square. The gate is at the bottom. The tomato bed is on the left side. The mint bed is on the right side. A water tap is in the middle. A bench is at the top, under a big tree.]

When you come in the gate, walk to the tap first. Fill the can with water. Then water the mint and the tomatoes. Rest on the bench when you are done.

p26f55f9641.title: The Great Traveler
p26f55f9641.text:
Ibn Battuta was born in Tangier, Morocco, in 1304. When he was twenty-one, he left home to travel to Mecca. He expected to be gone for about a year and a half. Instead, he kept traveling for almost thirty years.

His journeys took him across North Africa, through the Middle East, down the coast of East Africa, and all the way to India and China. In India, he worked as a judge for the ruler of Delhi. Everywhere he went, he described the food, the cities, and the people he met.

[Timeline: 1304 – born in Tangier → 1325 – leaves home for Mecca → 1334 – arrives in Delhi, India → 1345 – reaches China → 1349 – returns to Morocco → 1355 – finishes a book about his travels called the Rihla]

pe4fa03c3dd.title: How a Locust Swarm Begins
pe4fa03c3dd.text:
Most of the time, desert locusts live alone, like ordinary grasshoppers, scattered across the dry lands of Africa, Arabia, and South Asia. They avoid one another and do little harm to crops.

Everything changes after unusually heavy rains. Green plants spread across the desert, and the locusts multiply quickly. When the plants later dry out, the crowded insects are pushed together into the few green patches that remain. Constant bumping against their neighbors triggers a remarkable transformation: their color shifts, their behavior becomes social, and they begin traveling in bands and eventually in swarms.

[Flow chart: Heavy rains → Plants grow and locusts breed → Plants dry up → Locusts crowd together → Locusts change color and behavior → Swarms form and travel]

A single swarm can contain billions of insects and can eat as much food in one day as millions of people. For this reason, monitoring teams watch rainfall records very closely.

pd0083c7fd8.title: Coral Bay Nature Reserve
pd0083c7fd8.text:
Visitors to the Coral Bay Nature Reserve can explore three trails, each beginning at the visitor center beside the main parking area. The reserve protects a mangrove forest, a shallow lagoon where young fish shelter, and a rocky headland that seabirds use for nesting.

[Map: The visitor center is at the south edge of the reserve. The Mangrove Boardwalk (1.2 km, flat) runs east from the visitor center along the shore. The Lagoon Loop (2.5 km, sandy) circles the lagoon in the center of the reserve. The Headland Trail (3.8 km, steep and rocky) runs north to the cliffs, and a sign on it reads “Closed March–June: nesting season.” Legend: solid line = trail; dashed line = boardwalk; bird symbol = viewing platform; drop symbol = drinking water. Drop symbols appear only at the visitor center and halfway around the Lagoon Loop.]

Rangers recommend carrying at least one liter of water per person on every trail, because summer temperatures in the reserve often rise above forty degrees Celsius.

pd8c2c0c681.title: Two Ways to Catch Water
pd8c2c0c681.text:
In some of the driest places on Earth, communities have survived not by discovering new water but by capturing water that others would overlook. Two strikingly different technologies illustrate this principle.

The qanat, developed in ancient Persia nearly three thousand years ago, is a gently sloping underground tunnel that carries groundwater from the foot of a mountain to distant fields. Because the water travels underground, very little evaporates, and gravity alone moves it.

Fog nets, by contrast, are a relatively recent invention. Large vertical mesh panels, installed on coastal hillsides in countries such as Morocco and Chile, catch tiny droplets from passing fog; the droplets merge, trickle into gutters, and flow downhill into storage tanks.

[Venn diagram: Left circle, “Qanats”: underground; taps groundwater; thousands of years old; requires skilled tunnel diggers. Right circle, “Fog nets”: above ground; collects moisture from the air; developed in recent decades; works only where fog is frequent. Overlap: uses gravity; needs no pumps or fuel; serves dry regions.]

p3588d55089.title: Rising from the Sea
p3588d55089.text:
For most of history, turning seawater into drinking water meant boiling it, an approach so energy-hungry that it was practical only for ships and wealthy cities. Thermal plants still operate along the Arabian Gulf, where inexpensive energy once made them economical, but most new capacity worldwide now relies on reverse osmosis, which forces seawater through membranes fine enough to block dissolved salt.

The transition has been driven largely by energy. As the table indicates, reverse osmosis typically requires a fraction of the energy of thermal distillation, although its membranes must be cleaned and replaced regularly and perform poorly when the incoming water is extremely salty or polluted.

[Table: Approximate total energy needed to produce one cubic meter of fresh water. Multi-stage flash distillation (thermal): 20–27 kWh. Multi-effect distillation (thermal): 15–21 kWh. Reverse osmosis (membrane): 3–4 kWh.]

[Timeline: 1950s, first large thermal plants built in the Gulf region; 1960s, practical reverse-osmosis membranes developed; 2000s, reverse osmosis overtakes thermal methods in new global capacity; 2010s and 2020s, a growing number of plants begin pairing reverse osmosis with solar power.]

p7bfd969024.title: Clean Beach Day!
p7bfd969024.text:
[Poster: A big blue sea fills the page. A smiling turtle holds a bag of trash in its flipper.]

Clean Beach Day!

Come to Corniche Beach on Saturday at 8 in the morning. Bring a hat and water. We will give you gloves and bags. Help keep the sea safe for turtles and fish. Trash in the sea can hurt them. Kids and families are welcome. Let's make our beach shine!

pd0e547c635.title: Save Every Drop
pd0e547c635.text:
Save Every Drop (a thirty-second video announcement about conserving water)

[Scene 1: A close-up shows a dripping tap, and each drop falls slowly while the sound seems surprisingly loud in the quiet kitchen.]

Narrator: One drop does not seem like much, but a tap that drips all day can waste more than twenty liters of water.

[Scene 2: Short, quick clips show a boy turning off the tap while he brushes his teeth, a mother repairing a leaking pipe, and a farmer watering vegetables at sunset.]

Narrator: Small actions add up, and when families change simple habits, an entire city can save millions of liters every year.

[Scene 3: The screen turns blue, and white letters appear: "Turn it off. Fix it fast. Save every drop."]

Narrator: Our desert depends on water, so make every drop count.

p8987c52e0d.title: Students Build Robot to Clean Desert Campsites
p8987c52e0d.text:
Students Build Robot to Clean Desert Campsites

[Photo: Four students kneel beside a small robot with wide wheels. Caption: "Team Falcon tests its robot on the dunes outside the city."]

A team of middle school students has designed a robot that collects plastic litter from desert campsites, a problem that grows every winter when thousands of families camp in the dunes. The robot, nicknamed Raml, uses a camera to identify bottles and wrappers and a rotating brush to sweep them into a container.

"We wanted to protect the places where our families make memories," said team captain Lina Al-Harbi, 14.

According to the city's environmental office, volunteers removed nearly nine tons of litter from popular camping areas last season. The students hope that Raml, which could eventually operate automatically overnight, will help reduce that number considerably.

[Sidebar: How Raml Works. Step 1: The camera scans the sand. Step 2: The computer recognizes litter. Step 3: The brush collects it.]

The team will present Raml at a national science and engineering competition in March, where judges will evaluate its accuracy and durability.

pc1226f65c8.title: The Room That Captured Light
pc1226f65c8.text:
Curious Minds Podcast, Episode 12: The Room That Captured Light

[Sound: a heavy door creaks shut, followed by silence.]

Host: Imagine sitting in a completely dark room on a sunny afternoon. A tiny hole in one wall lets in a single beam of light, and suddenly an upside-down picture of the street outside appears on the opposite wall. Is it magic, or is there a logical explanation that anyone could investigate? About a thousand years ago, the Arab scientist Ibn al-Haytham decided to find out.

Guest (Dr. Maha Saleh, historian of science): What makes Ibn al-Haytham remarkable is not only what he observed but how he tested it. He changed the size of the hole, moved the lamps, and recorded every result carefully.

Host: So he was conducting careful experiments, not simply guessing about what he observed.

Guest: Exactly, and many historians consider his methods an early model for modern scientific investigation.

[Music: a gentle, unhurried melody gradually rises and fades.]

Host: Next week, we will explore how his ideas influenced the cameras in our pockets today.

p22a32f64a3.title: Your Time Back
p22a32f64a3.text:
Commercial Script: "Your Time Back" (Al-Noor City Metro, 45 seconds)

[Opening shot, filmed in muted gray tones: a driver sits motionless in traffic, drumming his fingers on the steering wheel while the dashboard clock reads 7:52.]

Voice-over (calm, unhurried): Every morning, the average commuter in Al-Noor spends forty minutes waiting in traffic.

[The camera cuts to the same man stepping onto a bright, spacious train car; the colors suddenly become warm and saturated.]

Voice-over: What would you do with those forty minutes if they suddenly belonged to you again?

[A rapid sequence follows: the man reads a novel, finishes a sketch, and chats with a neighbor, each moment shown in gentle slow motion.]

Passenger testimonial: "I used to arrive at work exhausted and irritable, but now I arrive with energy, because the journey finally belongs to me again."

[Final frame: the metro logo appears above the slogan "Your Time Back."]

Voice-over: Al-Noor City Metro connects every neighborhood comfortably and reliably, so ride with us.

p0c530b8975.title: The Last Song of the Pearl Divers
p0c530b8975.text:
[Archival footage, grainy and black-and-white: wooden dhows crowd a Gulf harbor while divers, ropes looped around their waists, prepare to descend.]

Narrator: For centuries, the pearl was the heartbeat of this coastline, sustaining entire communities whose prosperity rose and fell with the unpredictable tides.

[The film cuts abruptly to a present-day shot in full color: a glass skyscraper reflecting the same harbor, now quiet.]

Narrator: Within a single generation, cultured pearls from abroad and the discovery of oil transformed the economy, and the ancient profession nearly vanished.

[Interview: Abu Khalid, eighty-seven, sits beside a coil of weathered rope, his hands moving expressively as he speaks.]

Abu Khalid: The sea was cruel and generous at once, and we sang continually so that our fear would not be heard by the others.

[A low, rhythmic work song plays beneath slow images of empty boats.]

Narrator: Today, the divers' songs survive mainly in festivals and recordings, echoes of a way of life that modern prosperity both replaced and preserved in memory.

p3afa0930a0.title: The Little Bird's Seeds
p3afa0930a0.text:
A little bird found a big field full of seeds. Each day she carried one seed back to her nest. The big birds laughed at the little bird. "You are too slow," they said. "We will eat all the seeds right now."

The little bird did not stop working. She took one seed, and then she took one more. Soon her nest was full of seeds.

Then the cold days came, and the field was empty. The big birds were very hungry. The little bird shared her seeds with them. Now no one laughed at her.

pf314ca8774.title: The Old Map
pf314ca8774.text:
While searching his grandfather's desk for a pencil, Yusuf discovered a folded map. It showed their neighborhood as it had looked fifty years earlier, drawn carefully in faded blue ink. Near the corner of the old school, someone had drawn a small star and written one mysterious word: Treasure.

The next morning, Yusuf hurried to the spot before breakfast. The school had become a public library, and in its courtyard stood an enormous date palm, taller than the building itself. He searched the ground around the trunk carefully but found nothing buried there.

That evening, he showed his grandfather the map. The old man studied it and smiled for a long time. "I planted that palm on my last day of school," he said quietly. "My teacher told me that knowledge grows slowly, like a tree, and that it gives shade to everyone who comes later."

Yusuf looked at the map again. He was not sure whether his grandfather was teaching him an important lesson or simply remembering his childhood.

pf8ad3553b1.title: The Keeper of the Light
pf8ad3553b1.text:
The Keeper of the Light

Each evening, when the harbor sinks into a purple, restless dark, the keeper climbs the winding stairs and wakes the lamp with a single spark.
He never sees the sailors' faces, never learns their names or where they go; he only knows the beam must travel farther than his eyes can ever know.
The storms come shouting at his windows, rattling the glass with salty fists, yet he polishes the lens each morning and sweeps away the clinging mists.
And when the ships return at sunrise, no one waves or turns to see the quiet tower on the headland, standing where it needs to be.
Perhaps he wonders, in the stillness, whether all his work is known; perhaps he knows the light he tends was never meant to be his own.

p0b58f1e228.title: The Loom
p0b58f1e228.text:
[A sunlit room in an old family house. A wooden loom stands in the corner, partially covered by an embroidered cloth, while NADIA, fifteen, watches her grandmother, UMM SALEH, folding the cloth with deliberate care.]

NADIA: You're honestly donating it to the museum, after you wove on that loom for sixty years?

UMM SALEH: [without looking up] Sixty-two years, actually, and my mother wove on it for decades before me.

NADIA: Then it belongs here with our family, because strangers will walk past it in a glass room and never imagine whose hands it held.

UMM SALEH: [pausing, her palm resting on the frame] Perhaps, or perhaps a curious girl your age will stand in front of it, wonder how the complicated patterns were created, and then decide to try them herself.

NADIA: And what happens if nobody ever wonders?

UMM SALEH: [smiling faintly] Then it will wait, as it has always waited, because a loom is remarkably patient.

[She lifts the cloth away completely, and the loom's bright, unfinished weaving catches the afternoon light as the stage lights slowly fade.]

p35e4aa2f5f.title: The Flight of Abbas ibn Firnas: Two Readings
p35e4aa2f5f.text:
Text 1: According to accounts written long after his death, the ninth-century inventor Abbas ibn Firnas built a frame of wood and silk, covered it with feathers, and leapt from a hillside near Cordoba. He glided for a remarkable distance before landing so heavily that he injured his back. Later, he reportedly admitted that he had forgotten to give his device a tail, which birds use to slow down.

Text 2: Critic A treats the story as a cautionary tale about ambition outrunning preparation; the inventor's injury, she argues, is the lesson, and his confession reveals the cost of overlooking details. Critic B reads the same episode as a celebration of experimental courage, noting that the inventor analyzed his failure and identified its cause, which is precisely what scientific progress requires. Both critics agree that the sources are incomplete, so any interpretation must rely on a few surviving details.

p4366b86d9b.title: The Cartographer's Last Map
p4366b86d9b.text:
In his final year, the cartographer Idris, whose charts had guided caravans across three deserts, began an ambitious map of the entire known world. He worked with meticulous patience, tracing coastlines from sailors' testimonies and rivers from merchants' half-remembered descriptions, until every margin teemed with mountains, harbors, and names.

Yet at the center of the parchment, where his own city should have stood, he left an untouched circle. His apprentices, accustomed to his relentless discipline, assumed that a sudden illness had interrupted him. However, he lived for several months after the map was finished and never once picked up his pen to complete it.

When a visiting scholar finally asked about the empty circle, Idris considered the question for so long that the scholar wondered whether he had heard it. "A map," he said at last, "is only a promise that someone has looked carefully, and I have looked carefully at everything except the place I have always been too close to see clearly."

The map hangs in the city library today, its center still blank, and visitors continue to debate its significance.

p9ffc9da2c4.title: Mona's First Bread
p9ffc9da2c4.text:
On Friday, Mona helped her dad make bread. First, they mixed flour, water, and a little salt in a big bowl. Next, Mona pushed and pressed the dough with her hands. Then they put the dough in a warm spot. After one hour, it was big and puffy!

Dad baked it in the oven. At last, the kitchen smelled sweet. Mona took the first warm piece to her grandma. Grandma smiled and said, "This is the best bread in the world."

pc5e93e7991.title: From Palm to Plate
pc5e93e7991.text:
Dates have grown in the Arabian Peninsula for thousands of years, and harvesting them still takes careful work. In early spring, farmers climb the tall palms to pollinate the flowers by hand, because the wind alone cannot be trusted to do the job.

Over the hot summer, the green fruit slowly changes color, turning yellow or red. Farmers often cover the heavy bunches with mesh bags to protect them from birds and insects.

By late summer, the dates ripen and become soft and sweet. Workers cut the bunches carefully and lower them to the ground with ropes. At the packing house, the dates are washed, sorted by size and quality, and packed into boxes.

A few days later, those boxes arrive at markets across the country, ready for families to enjoy.

pdfa3aba09d.title: The Storm Road
pdfa3aba09d.text:
By the time the sandstorm reached the highway, Reem had already pulled the car onto the shoulder and switched on the hazard lights. Her younger brother, Fahad, stared at the orange wall swallowing the road ahead.

Only an hour earlier, the sky above the desert had been perfectly clear and calm. Their uncle had waved them off from his farm, reminding Reem to check the weather app before leaving the main road. She had glanced at it, seen a small warning symbol, and decided the drive was short enough to risk.

Now the wind hammered against the windows, and visibility dropped to almost nothing. Reem remembered her driving instructor's advice: stay still, stay visible, and wait. She called their mother, described their location using the nearest kilometer marker, and told Fahad to count the minutes aloud.

Approximately forty minutes later, the storm gradually thinned to a brown haze. Reem eased back onto the road, driving slowly, and promised herself she would never ignore a warning symbol again.

p01c789b60b.title: How Paper Traveled West
p01c789b60b.text:
Today, paper is so common that few people think about where it came from, but its journey across the world took more than a thousand years. Papermaking began in China, where, according to tradition, an official named Cai Lun improved the process around 105 CE by mixing tree bark, old rags, and hemp into a pulp.

For centuries, the technique remained largely unknown outside East Asia. By the middle of the eighth century, however, paper mills were operating in Samarkand, and the craft soon spread to Baghdad, where a mill was established around 794. Baghdad's scholars quickly recognized that paper was cheaper and lighter than parchment, so libraries and government offices adopted it enthusiastically.

From Baghdad, papermaking moved to Damascus and Cairo and then across North Africa. Eventually it reached Spain, where mills were producing paper by the twelfth century, and from there it gradually spread throughout Europe.

p2b925ac383.title: Beneath the Red Sea
p2b925ac383.text:
I was nineteen when I first descended along the reef wall near the Farasan Islands, though the dive had begun, in a sense, years earlier, on the evening my father brought home a battered underwater camera from a market in Jeddah. He could not swim, and he never explained why he bought it; he simply placed it on my desk and said that some things are worth seeing even if one must wait to see them.

For years the camera sat unused while I completed school, learned to swim properly, and earned my diving certificate. When I finally carried it into the water, the housing leaked within minutes, and every photograph I took that morning was ruined.

Yet the failure hardly mattered. Hovering above a forest of branching coral, surrounded by fish whose colors no photograph could have captured, I understood what my father had meant. The camera had never been the point; it had been an invitation.

p6aa1a2505a.title: An Ancient Puzzle in Bronze
p6aa1a2505a.text:
When researchers in 2005 used X-ray scanning to peer inside a cluster of corroded bronze fragments, they confirmed what earlier scholars had only suspected: the object, built more than two thousand years ago, was a geared device for predicting the movements of the sun, moon, and planets. The discovery was remarkable not least because the fragments had spent decades largely overlooked.

Sponge divers had recovered them in 1901 from a shipwreck off the Greek island of Antikythera, along with bronze statues that immediately attracted far more attention. Only the following year did an archaeologist notice a gearwheel embedded in one of the lumps, and even then many experts doubted that ancient craftsmen could have produced such intricate machinery.

It was not until the mid-twentieth century that a historian of science systematically argued for the mechanism's astronomical purpose, an interpretation that later technology would substantially vindicate. The device's story, in other words, is as much about the slow revision of assumptions as about the object itself.

p27100cfceb.title: Plant a Tree Day
p27100cfceb.text:
Dear Families,

Our school wants to plant ten trees on Saturday. Please come and help us! Trees give us cool shade on hot days. Birds can build nests in them. Trees also make the air clean.

Everyone in Grade 2 is coming. Do not miss the fun! Bring a hat and a bottle of water. Together we can make our school green and beautiful.

From, Class 2B

pa025f4165c.title: A Refill for Our Planet
pa025f4165c.text:
Good morning, classmates and teachers. Every day, our school throws away more than three hundred plastic bottles. Where do you think all that plastic goes? Much of it ends up in landfills, and some of it washes into the sea, where turtles mistake it for food.

There is a simple solution to this problem. If our school installed two water refill stations, each student could carry a reusable bottle and fill it for free throughout the day. Schools in Jeddah and Dammam have already done this, and their trash has dropped by half.

Imagine a sea turtle swimming through clean, clear water instead of a cloud of floating plastic. Together, we can help make that happen. Please sign the petition in the library before Thursday, and let us show everyone that our school truly cares about the planet.

p6fe26d0612.title: SkyBuilders Robotics Camp
p6fe26d0612.text:
Is your summer going to be another long season of scrolling through the same videos on your phone? It does not have to be. At SkyBuilders Robotics Camp, students between the ages of eleven and fourteen design, build, and program real robots in just three exciting weeks.

“I never imagined that I could write code, but by the second week my robot was climbing stairs,” says Faisal, a camper from last year. Ninety-two percent of our campers say they would return, and many of them now compete in national robotics competitions.

Our instructors are university engineers who know how to make difficult ideas simple and enjoyable. Every camper takes home the robot he or she builds, along with an official certificate of completion.

Space is limited, and the best spots fill up quickly. Join the hundreds of talented, creative students who have already discovered what they are capable of inventing. Register before May 15 and receive a free toolkit worth 200 riyals!

p22a0eb134c.title: A Letter to the Editor
p22a0eb134c.text:
As a physician who has worked at Al-Noor Clinic for fifteen years, I have watched the number of patients with diabetes and cardiovascular disease climb steadily in our community. Many of them tell me they would walk more if there were a safe, comfortable place to do so. Currently, there is not a single shaded path within walking distance of the town center.

Some council members argue that a walking path would cost too much. However, the proposed path would cost less than repaving the parking lot near the stadium, and a healthier population would save the town far more in medical expenses over time.

Picture an elderly grandfather strolling under rows of date palms in the cool evening air, his grandchildren racing ahead of him. That scene, which is rare in our community today, could become an everyday sight. I urge every resident to attend Tuesday's council meeting and to speak in favor of the path.

Respectfully submitted by Dr. Huda Al-Harbi, consulting physician, Al-Noor Clinic

p67a618b21f.title: Open the Doors
p67a618b21f.text:
Every civilization measures itself by how it treats its past. When the National Museum raised its admission fee last year, attendance by families fell by nearly a third, according to the museum's own annual report. A place built to belong to everyone has quietly become a luxury.

Critics contend that free admission would drain the museum's budget, and their concern is not unreasonable; exhibitions, conservation, and security are expensive. Yet museums in several countries have abolished fees and replaced the lost income through corporate sponsorships, memberships, and modest charges for special exhibitions. Their visitor numbers, in some cases, have doubled.

Consider what is at stake. A child who stands before a thousand-year-old astrolabe, the very kind of instrument that guided scholars like Al-Biruni, may discover a lifelong passion for astronomy. Either we open these doors to every child, or we accept that our heritage belongs only to the wealthy.

The choice should be obvious. The museum's board meets next month; citizens who value our shared history should write to its members immediately.

p5d37ae1f37.title: Address to the Coastal Development Forum
p5d37ae1f37.text:
I have spent twenty-two years diving along the Red Sea coast, and I have watched reefs that once blazed with color fade to the pale gray of old bone. I do not describe this transformation to alarm you; I describe it because the decision-makers in this room will determine whether my students ever witness what I have witnessed.

We are told that development and conservation are irreconcilable enemies, that every resort we construct must cost us a reef, but that assumption is mistaken. Reefs protect shorelines from destructive storms, sustain the fisheries that feed coastal communities, and attract the very tourists our new hotels hope to welcome. A healthy reef is not an obstacle to prosperity; it is the foundation upon which prosperity depends.

So I ask you: what will our grandchildren inherit, a coastline of concrete or a coastline of life? Let us build carefully, let us build scientifically, and let us build so that the sea remains a neighbor rather than a casualty.

The reefs have waited thousands of years for humanity to understand them, but they cannot afford to wait indefinitely.

p8ff34e35e2.title: The Big Race
p8ff34e35e2.text:
Lina wanted to win the school race. On race day, her shoe came untied. She fell down at the start. All the other children ran ahead.

Lina got up fast. She tied her shoe and ran as hard as she could. At the end, she passed two runners. She did not win, but she came in third.

Her coach gave her a big smile. “You never gave up,” he said. Lina felt proud.

p69d101d5a5.title: The Science Fair Bridge
p69d101d5a5.text:
Yusuf had spent three weeks building a bridge out of craft sticks for the science fair, and his goal was to make it hold five kilograms without breaking.

The night before the fair, Yusuf placed a heavy dictionary on the bridge to test it, and with a loud snap, the middle beam cracked. His stomach sank, because there was no time to start over.

Instead of giving up, he studied the break carefully and realized that the beam had bent because nothing supported it from below. Working late into the night, he glued triangles of sticks underneath the middle, just like the steel bridges pictured in his library book.

At the fair, the judge stacked weights on the bridge one by one: two kilograms, four, and then five. Everyone leaned closer as the last weight settled, and the bridge held firm. Yusuf did not win first place, but the judge praised him for solving a real engineering problem.

pa511aa5f67.title: Engine Trouble
pa511aa5f67.text:
[A small fishing boat rocks on gray waves off the coast of Yanbu as dark clouds gather overhead.]

MAJID: The engine has stopped again, Tariq, and without it we will drift toward the reef long before this storm passes.

TARIQ: [nervously] Should we contact the coast guard on the radio, Uncle, before the weather becomes dangerous?

MAJID: The radio lost power an hour ago, which is exactly why I intended to replace the battery this morning.

[As lightning flashes across the horizon, TARIQ kneels beside the engine and examines it.]

TARIQ: Wait, the fuel line is twisted behind the motor like a garden hose that someone stepped on, so if I straighten it, the fuel might flow again.

MAJID: Then try it immediately, because the reef is approaching with every wave.

[TARIQ straightens the line, and MAJID pulls the starter cord twice without success; on the third pull, the engine roars to life.]

MAJID: [laughing with relief] You noticed what I missed, nephew, so from now on you will be my chief mechanic.

[The boat turns toward the harbor as the first raindrops fall.]

p82f70947f1.title: The Map Room
p82f70947f1.text:
Reem had volunteered at the city museum all summer, but she had never spoken directly to Dr. Kamal, the stern curator who seemed to notice every fingerprint on every glass case. On the evening before the new exhibition about the geographer Al-Idrisi opened, Reem noticed something troubling: the label beside his famous world map said it had been completed in 1254, although three different reference books said 1154.

She hesitated, wondering whether she might be mistaken, since correcting a senior curator in front of the entire staff could easily end her time at the museum. Yet if she remained silent, hundreds of visitors would read an inaccurate date.

When Dr. Kamal walked past the map for a final inspection, Reem took a deep breath and stepped forward. “Excuse me, sir, I believe the date on this label may be incorrect by a full century.”

He frowned, consulted his notes, and then, to her astonishment, nodded slowly. By morning a corrected label hung beside the map, and Dr. Kamal had asked Reem to proofread every display in the next exhibition.

pbb3aa4eae6.title: Following the Stars
pbb3aa4eae6.text:
The GPS unit had been blinking for twenty minutes before Hamad admitted, at least to himself, that it was useless. Somewhere beyond the wall of dunes lay the research camp, with its water tanks and radio, but the afternoon sandstorm had erased every track of the expedition.

Mubarak, who had guided travelers through the Empty Quarter for forty years, studied the darkening sky in silence. Hamad, who had trained for four years as a geologist, considered such traditional methods charming but fundamentally unreliable, and he insisted that they should wait until the satellite signal returned.

“Water does not wait,” Mubarak replied, gesturing toward the half-empty containers in the truck.

As the light faded, the first stars emerged above the ridge, and Mubarak traced a line toward the horizon. Hamad looked at the blank screen, then at the old man's steady hand, and made his choice; he started the engine and followed the stars.

Three hours later, the lamps of the camp glimmered on the horizon. Hamad remained silent for a long time; then, quietly, he asked Mubarak to teach him the names of the stars.

pbf0f2b2e4b.title: The Deep Bank
pbf0f2b2e4b.text:
In the final week of the 1931 pearling season, the dhow had brought up nothing but empty shells, and Salem, at sixteen the youngest diver aboard, understood precisely the consequence: his family's debt to the merchant in Darin would pass, unpaid, into another year. The captain, a cautious man who had buried two divers during his career, announced that the crew would sail for home at dawn.

Throughout that night Salem lay awake, calculating, because farther out lay a bank of oysters in water deeper than any he had ever attempted, and the veteran divers spoke of it the way people speak of a door that should remain permanently closed.

At first light he approached the captain; he did not plead, but simply requested one dive, with the heaviest stone and the longest rope aboard. The captain studied him for a long, unreadable moment, then nodded once.

The shells Salem retrieved contained three small pearls, not a fortune, but enough. The captain offered no praise, but the following season he handed Salem the rope he had once entrusted only to his most accomplished diver.

p7407b261ef.title: The Sand Castle
p7407b261ef.text:
Maha built a sand castle at the beach. It had four tall towers. Then a big wave came. Splash! The wave knocked down two towers. Maha was upset.

She built the towers again. Another wave came and knocked them down. Maha sat and thought.

“I know!” she said. She moved her castle far back from the water. She built it on dry sand. The waves could not reach it now. Maha smiled at her strong castle.

p3bcbdb419a.title: One Computer, Two Projects
p3bcbdb419a.text:
Adel and his older brother Bader both had big school projects due on Thursday, and their family had only one computer. On Monday evening, Bader sat down to type his history report just as Adel arrived with his notes about volcanoes.

“I need it first,” Adel said. “My slides will take hours.”

“So will my report,” Bader answered, not looking up from the screen.

The argument grew louder until their mother came in. Instead of choosing a winner, she handed them a piece of paper and a pencil. “Make a plan you both agree on,” she said.

The brothers sat at the kitchen table and wrote down how much time each project needed. Adel could draw his volcano diagrams by hand while Bader typed, and then Bader could read his history book while Adel made his slides. By Wednesday night, both projects were finished, and the paper schedule was still taped beside the computer.

p272b1f2bbc.title: The Falcon Who Flew Too Far
p272b1f2bbc.text:
Every morning before school, Lujain trained Shaheen, the young falcon her grandfather had given her, on the open plain behind their farm. For weeks, the falcon had returned to her leather glove as soon as she swung the lure through the air.

One windy morning, however, Shaheen spotted a flock of pigeons and shot after them, climbing higher and higher until he became a dark speck against the clouds. Lujain swung the lure and whistled until her lips ached, but the falcon did not return. Her grandfather had warned her never to fly a young bird in strong wind, and she had ignored him.

She could have run home in tears, but instead she climbed the tallest dune nearby, where the falcon could see her clearly against the sky. Remembering her grandfather's lessons, she stood perfectly still, raised her glove, and whistled the same three notes she used every morning.

After nearly an hour, a shadow swept over the sand, and Shaheen landed heavily on her glove. That evening, Lujain told her grandfather the whole story, including the part about the wind.

p5930634600.title: Twelve Yards
p5930634600.text:
The final minute slipped away, the score was tied at one, and every eye inside the stadium was fixed on me beneath the burning sun.
Their striker placed the ball with care and stepped back with a grin, while somewhere in the roaring stands my father called my name again.

Last season I had guessed too soon and dived the wrong way twice, and all year long those two mistakes had followed me, as cold as ice.
My coach had said, “Don't guess, just watch his hips and trust your eyes,” but fear kept whispering I would fail beneath those crowded skies.

The whistle blew; I held my ground and let the moment stretch, though every muscle in my body begged me just to leap and guess.
His hips turned left, the ball flew left, and I was there in flight, my gloves closed hard around the ball, and the stadium exploded into light.

I did not hear the final whistle or the crowd that chanted on; I only knew the fear I'd carried for a year was finally gone.

peb33322b81.title: The Ghaf Tree
peb33322b81.text:
[A community hall where a map of a planned highway hangs on the wall and a red X marks the location of an ancient ghaf tree.]

WALEED: The proposed road would reduce the drive to the regional hospital by twelve minutes, and the most direct route, unfortunately, passes directly through the ghaf tree.

AMAL: That tree has survived for nearly two hundred years; our grandparents rested beneath its branches during long journeys, and our children still study in its shade after school.

WALEED: I respect that history, but twelve minutes can determine whether a patient survives a heart attack.

SAEED: Both of you are defending something this community cannot afford to lose, so tell me, Waleed, is the straight route genuinely the only possible route?

WALEED: [studying the map] If the road curved fifty meters eastward, it would bypass the tree and add approximately forty seconds to the journey.

AMAL: [quietly] Forty seconds is a price that I believe every family here would gladly pay.

SAEED: Then let the record show that the council approves the eastern curve, and that the ghaf tree remains.

p3ea163cbdb.title: The Translator's Choice
p3ea163cbdb.text:
By the lamplight of the copying room, Idris read the Greek sentence for the fourth time and felt his certainty dissolve. The ancient physician attributed a particular fever to an internal imbalance, yet Idris had spent two winters in the city's hospital and had observed that fever travel from patient to patient like a whisper along a row of beds.

His patron, the wealthy merchant who was paying for the translation, had been explicit: render the master's words faithfully, without commentary, for nothing sold better than the authority of the ancients. To add a note of doubt would risk both the commission and Idris's reputation.
