For a long while he sat motionless, the reed pen slowly drying in his hand. Then he translated the sentence exactly as the Greek demanded, and beneath it, in smaller script, he added a single line: 'The translator has observed otherwise; let the reader test the matter for himself.'

The patron was furious, and the lucrative commission was never renewed. Yet within a decade, physicians throughout the city were deliberately copying that line into their own medical manuscripts.

p950e418bf9.title: Grandpa's Boat
p950e418bf9.text:
Lina sat on the beach with Grandpa. She saw a small boat on the sand. It made her think of last summer.

Last summer, Lina was scared of the sea. Grandpa took her out in his little boat. The waves were soft. He let her hold the rope. Soon she was laughing.

Now Lina ran to the water. “Let's go out again, Grandpa!” she called. He smiled and pushed the boat into the waves.

p948337b056.title: The Falcon's Return
p948337b056.text:
Faisal stood at the edge of the desert camp and lifted his gloved arm as a falcon, far above the dunes, circled once and then dropped toward him like a stone.

As the bird landed, Faisal remembered the morning two years earlier when he had found it beneath a thorn tree. Back then, it was only a frightened chick with a damaged wing, and it would not eat the meat he offered. For three weeks he sat beside its box every evening, speaking softly until it finally took food from his hand. His uncle had warned him that the chick might never fly.

Now the falcon folded its strong wings and turned its sharp eyes toward him. Faisal smiled, offered it a small reward, and whispered, “You proved my uncle wrong.”

p877d43a2f7.title: A Letter from the Observatory
p877d43a2f7.text:
Dear Yusuf, last night, while I was adjusting the telescope at the mountain observatory, a sudden gust rattled the dome, and I was carried straight back to the evening you and I climbed onto Grandmother's roof in Abha. You were eight and I was eleven, and we had borrowed her old binoculars to search for Saturn. For nearly an hour we saw nothing but blurry streetlights, until you shouted that one “star” refused to twinkle. That steady point of light, of course, was the planet itself.

I have thought about that rooftop many times this year, especially when my calculations fail and my supervisor sighs at my notebook. Tonight, however, when the clouds finally cleared, I located Saturn's rings in under a minute.

Please tell Grandmother that her binoculars started a career. Your sister, Reem

p8e9be8b21a.title: The Bridge Builders
p8e9be8b21a.text:
[A small engineering office in Riyadh, late evening. NADIA, an ambitious structural engineer, stares in disbelief at a model bridge that has cracked completely down the middle.]

NADIA: Three months of careful calculations and patient construction, and the entire structure collapses under the very first weight test.

[The office lights dim gradually. A spotlight rises on the same desk, fifteen years earlier, where a younger NADIA kneels beside her father, who is helping her assemble a bridge out of wooden spoons and string for a school competition.]

FATHER: Every bridge fails at least once, my daughter, so the real question is whether the engineer discovers exactly where the structure was weakest.

YOUNG NADIA: But mine collapsed directly into the bathtub, and everybody in the family was laughing!

FATHER: Then tomorrow we will build it again more carefully, and tomorrow it will hold.

[The spotlight fades, and the office lights return. NADIA lifts the cracked model, rotates it slowly beneath the lamp, and examines the fracture.]

NADIA: (quietly) Where was it weakest? (She reaches for a pencil and begins to sketch a stronger design.)

pe7fd5a113d.title: The Last Kilometer
pe7fd5a113d.text:
At the thirty-ninth kilometer, the asphalt shimmered under the afternoon heat, and Salma's legs began to argue with every stride. She fixed her eyes on the orange flag that marked the final turn and, unbidden, felt herself drifting back to the dusty school track where, at fourteen, she had first stepped off a course in humiliated tears.

That afternoon had been unremarkable in every respect except one: her coach, a reserved woman named Mrs. Haddad, had not scolded her. Instead, she had knelt beside the track, retied Salma's loose shoelace, and observed that quitting was simply information, not a verdict. Salma had resented the calmness of that observation for months, interpreting it as indifference.

Only years later, after a dozen abandoned training runs, did she understand that Mrs. Haddad had been teaching her to measure her limitations rather than fear them.

The orange flag snapped in the wind as Salma noted the ache in her calves, measured it deliberately, and decided it was merely information; then she lengthened her stride toward the turn.

p86775e4d5f.title: Salt and Memory
p86775e4d5f.text:
The museum in Doha displays my great-grandfather's diving weight behind glass, labeled with a date and a single sentence about the pearl trade. I stood before it last spring, unexpectedly irritated by the label's tidiness, because the stone I remembered had never been tidy.

When I was seven, it sat in a corner of my grandmother's courtyard, gray and pitted, and she used it to keep the door from slamming in the winter wind. One evening she lifted it with both hands, set it in my lap, and described how her father had descended with it, season after season, holding his breath while the crew waited above for the tug on the rope that meant he was ready to rise. I remember the weight far more clearly than the words.

Standing in the museum, I realized that the exhibit preserved the object but had misplaced its meaning: what had mattered was not the stone itself but the breath it represented, the confidence that someone above would always pull.

p3bb48714a5.title: The Gray Clouds
p3bb48714a5.text:
Adam and his dad went to the park for a picnic. Dad looked up at the sky. “Those clouds are getting gray,” he said. Adam did not look. He was too busy with his ball.

They ate sandwiches on a big blanket. The wind began to blow. A leaf flew into Adam's juice. Dad put the umbrella next to the basket, just in case.

Then a cold drop hit Adam's nose. Soon it was raining hard. Dad opened the umbrella, and they ran to the car, laughing.

p72e7425ab7.title: The Robot at the Fair
p72e7425ab7.text:
On the morning of the regional science fair, Hana tested her robot one final time. It rolled forward, waved its mechanical arm, and presented her with a paper flower. As it turned, she noticed a tiny rattle near its shoulder, but the judges were already arriving, so she decided not to stop and investigate.

Her friend Laila pointed at the robot curiously. “Is that screw supposed to be sticking out?” she asked. Hana shrugged and explained that it had worked perfectly at home.

When the judges approached her table, Hana pressed the green button, and the robot rolled forward perfectly. Then, as it lifted the flower, its arm dropped onto the table with a loud clatter.

Hana took a deep breath, pulled a small screwdriver from her bag, and tightened the loose screw in front of the judges. When the robot finally delivered the flower, the judges smiled and wrote a comment praising her calm, practical repair.

pee5cc0df29.title: Before the Sandstorm
pee5cc0df29.text:
At noon the camels knelt and would not rise, though the herder clicked his tongue and tugged their ropes, and their dark, anxious eyes kept turning toward the west.
The sky above the dunes grew thin and yellow, like old paper held too close to a lamp, and the small birds vanished from the thorny acacia branches.
My grandfather lifted a handful of sand and let it slide between his fingers, watching how the grains drifted sideways before they ever touched the ground.

“Tie the tent twice,” he murmured, “and fill every water skin tonight,” and although I laughed at his worry, I tied each knot exactly as he instructed.

By evening the horizon had become a moving wall of copper, roaring like the sea, and we crouched behind the camels while the whole desert flew past us.
When morning came, our tent still stood, its doubled knots holding firm, and my grandfather brushed the sand from his beard and said nothing at all.

p3ae8cb4969.title: The Last Ferry
p3ae8cb4969.text:
[A ferry dock on a small island in the Red Sea, late afternoon. HAMAD, the elderly dockmaster, examines a brass barometer mounted beside the ticket window. KHALID, a teenage visitor, waits impatiently with his backpack.]

KHALID: The ferry departs at six o'clock, correct? I promised my mother I would definitely be home for dinner tonight.

HAMAD: (tapping the glass of the barometer) It departs at six if the sea permits it, because this needle has descended twice since lunchtime.

KHALID: But the water looks perfectly calm and peaceful to me, almost like a polished mirror.

HAMAD: Calm water is a polite liar. (He points toward a line of fishing boats hurrying into the harbor.) Notice how quickly the fishermen are returning, although they departed only this morning.

[A sudden gust of wind knocks a stack of orange life jackets off a wooden bench, and KHALID laughs nervously as he gathers them.]

KHALID: (uncertainly) Do you honestly believe there will be a dangerous storm this evening?

HAMAD: I believe you should immediately telephone your mother and explain that dinner may unfortunately wait until tomorrow.

p046020880b.title: Beneath the Reef
p046020880b.text:
The night before the expedition left Jeddah, Dr. Amal Rashid inspected the submersible's viewing window and discovered a hairline scratch along its lower edge. The technician assured her it was merely cosmetic, and she signed the checklist, though she photographed the scratch twice before going to bed.

At dawn the research vessel steamed toward the coral reef, where the team hoped to record a rare species of luminous shrimp. The ocean was glassy, the forecast was flawless, and the crew joked that the expedition would be completely uneventful.

Only the veteran navigator, Mr. Salem, seemed uneasy. He kept glancing at the sonar screen, where an unfamiliar shadow pulsed near the reef wall, and he quietly asked Amal whether the submersible's emergency beacon had been tested recently.

She assured him that it had; still, as the submersible descended through the turquoise water, Amal found herself watching the scratch on the window instead of the reef, while the shadow on the sonar grew steadily larger.

pd53f6a45c7.title: The Unfinished Map
pd53f6a45c7.text:
In the cartographer's workshop in Fez, every commissioned map was completed before it departed the room, every coastline inked, every river named. Idris had served his master for six years and had never witnessed an exception, which was why the parchment pinned above the master's bench unsettled him: its eastern edge dissolved into blank vellum, as though the land itself had simply stopped.

“Some territory must be walked before it can be drawn,” the master said whenever Idris asked about it, and then he would return to his compass and his careful, patient lines.

That winter the master's weathered hands began to tremble almost imperceptibly. He set down his pen more often, stared longer at the blank edge, and one evening asked Idris to read aloud the names of the eastern caravan towns, slowly, as if memorizing a route he intended someone to take.

In early spring, Idris arrived to discover the workshop meticulously swept and completely silent. On the bench lay the master's compass, his finest pens, and a note in uneven script: Finish what I could not.

p6616666678.title: Bread with Grandma
p6616666678.text:
Mona wanted to bake bread with Grandma. First, they washed their hands. Next, Grandma put flour, water, and a little salt in a big bowl. Mona mixed it with a spoon. Then they pressed the dough with their hands until it was soft.

The dough rested under a cloth for one hour. It grew big and round! Grandma put it in the hot oven. At last, the kitchen smelled warm and good. Mona and Grandma ate the bread with honey.

p30fca4a720.title: From Egg to Ocean
p30fca4a720.text:
On a warm night in early summer, a female green turtle crawls out of the Arabian Sea onto a quiet beach in Oman. She uses her powerful back flippers to dig a deep hole in the sand, lays about one hundred eggs, and carefully covers them before returning to the waves.

For the next two months, the eggs remain buried. The warm sand works like an oven, and its temperature even helps decide whether the babies will be male or female.

When the hatchlings finally break out of their shells, they do not rush to the surface right away. Instead, they wait together under the sand until the night air cools. Then they dig upward as a group, burst onto the beach, and scramble toward the brightest horizon, which is usually the moonlit sea.

[Diagram: a circle of arrows linking a nest, eggs, hatchlings, the sea, and an adult turtle.]

p702d5212fe.title: An Accidental Discovery
p702d5212fe.text:
Today, penicillin is considered one of the most important medicines in history, but its discovery began with an untidy laboratory. In September 1928, the Scottish scientist Alexander Fleming returned to his London workplace after a summer holiday. Before leaving, he had stacked several dishes of bacteria on a bench without cleaning them.

When he examined the dishes, Fleming noticed something unusual. A fuzzy blue-green mold had grown on one of them, and the bacteria surrounding the mold had died. Curious, he grew more of the mold and tested its juice, which he named penicillin.

Fleming published his findings in 1929, yet other scientists showed little interest, partly because the substance was extremely difficult to purify. More than ten years later, a team at Oxford University, led by Howard Florey and Ernst Chain, finally developed a method to produce it in larger quantities. By the mid-1940s, penicillin was saving thousands of lives.

p09606f32f2.title: The Flood at Wadi Rimah
p09606f32f2.text:
The rain began at four o'clock, far away in the mountains, while the village of Wadi Rimah still baked under a cloudless sky. By the time Ziyad finished his homework, his uncle's phone was buzzing with urgent messages from farmers upstream: water was already rushing down the dry riverbed.

Ziyad's first anxious thought was of his family's goats. Just after lunch that day, he had tied them in the shade of the palms near the wadi's edge, the coolest spot he could find.

He sprinted down the narrow path while his uncle hurriedly loaded heavy sandbags into the pickup truck. Meanwhile, a low, menacing roar grew steadily louder behind the surrounding hills. Ziyad reached the palms, untied the frightened goats, and drove them up the rocky slope just as a brown wave swept around the first tree.

Later that night, the exhausted family watched the floodwaters from the rooftop terrace. The palms stood knee-deep in swirling, muddy water, but every animal was safely sheltered in the courtyard below.

p52fd76c075.title: A Flaw in Orbit
p52fd76c075.text:
In April 1990, the space shuttle Discovery carried the Hubble Space Telescope into orbit. Astronomers expected images sharper than any ground-based observatory could produce. Within weeks, however, their excitement turned to dismay: the first photographs were noticeably blurred.

Investigators eventually traced the problem to the telescope's primary mirror, which had been ground with extraordinary precision but to a slightly incorrect shape. The error, roughly one-fiftieth the thickness of a human hair, had gone undetected because a testing instrument had been assembled with a small spacing mistake years before launch.

Rather than return the telescope to Earth, engineers designed corrective optics, essentially a pair of eyeglasses for Hubble. In December 1993, astronauts aboard the shuttle Endeavour captured the telescope, installed the new equipment during five demanding spacewalks, and released it again.

When the first corrected images arrived in January 1994, the transformation was dramatic, and Hubble soon began reshaping scientists' understanding of distant galaxies.

p7688ed6f7e.title: The Clock That Found the Sea
p7688ed6f7e.text:
Historians often begin the story of longitude with John Harrison's sea clock, but the story properly begins with a catastrophe. In 1707, four British warships struck the rocks off the Scilly Isles, partly because their navigators had misjudged their east-west position, and well over a thousand sailors drowned.

Seven years later, Parliament offered an enormous prize for any practical method of determining longitude at sea. Harrison, a self-taught carpenter, reasoned that a clock keeping perfect time aboard a rolling ship would allow sailors to compare local noon with the time at their home port. His first sea clock, completed in 1735, was bulky yet promising; his fourth, finished in 1759, was scarcely larger than a pocket watch.

Ironically, the device that ultimately vindicated him was tested on a 1761 voyage to Jamaica, decades after his first attempt, and the prize committee, skeptical of a craftsman's solution, withheld full recognition, which Parliament finally granted in 1773, when Harrison was nearly eighty.

p6781a80aa6.title: Morning at the Market
p6781a80aa6.text:
It was early in the morning. The sun was just coming up. Lina and her dad walked to the old market. The streets were quiet and cool.

At the market, men set out baskets of dates. A woman sold fresh bread from a hot oven. The smell made Lina hungry. Birds sat on the roof and sang.

By noon, the market was loud and full of people. The sun was hot now. Lina and her dad went home with dates and bread.

p5dbfa9febc.title: The Pearl Divers' Return
p5dbfa9febc.text:
In the summer of 1925, the wooden boat called Al-Najma rocked gently on the warm waters of the Gulf. Twelve-year-old Faisal sat beside the rope basket, watching the divers rise from the green sea with oysters in their hands. The sun burned so fiercely that the deck boards felt hot under his bare feet.

For weeks the crew had lived on the boat, eating rice and dates and sleeping under the open stars. There was no radio to warn them about the weather, so the captain studied the sky each evening.

One afternoon, the captain pointed at a line of dark clouds in the north. "We sail for home tonight," he announced, and Faisal felt both relieved and disappointed, because he missed his family but already loved the adventure of the sea. The divers pulled up the anchors, and the old boat turned its sails toward the distant shore.

pcb75f45142.title: Fog on the Terraces
pcb75f45142.text:
The fog arrived in Abha the way it always did in late winter, rolling up from the valley until the stone houses on the ridge seemed to float above a white sea. Reem stood at the edge of her grandmother's terraced farm, where rows of coffee shrubs climbed the slope like green steps, and listened to the dripping silence.

On clear days she could see the road that wound down toward the city, but this morning the world ended ten meters from her feet. Her brother had driven down that road before dawn to sell the harvest, and he had promised to return by noon.

By midafternoon, the fog had thickened rather than lifted. Reem lit the lantern that hung beside the gate, though it was still daytime, and placed it on the wall where the road met the farm. Somewhere below, an engine hummed faintly and then stopped, so she raised the lantern higher and called her brother's name into the swirling whiteness.

p8f6ffd019b.title: The Copyist's Lamp
p8f6ffd019b.text:
In the year 830, the House of Wisdom in Baghdad never fully slept. Even after the evening call to prayer had faded over the Tigris, oil lamps flickered along the long tables where scholars translated Greek and Persian manuscripts into Arabic. The air smelled of ink, river damp, and the dust of ancient pages.

Yusuf, the youngest copyist, had been assigned a treatise on astronomy so fragile that its edges crumbled whenever he turned a leaf. Paper remained an expensive commodity in the city, and the head librarian had warned him that a single careless blot could ruin weeks of labor.

Outside, merchants' boats creaked against the docks, carrying silk, spices, and rumors from distant ports. Yusuf barely noticed them. He bent closer to the lamp, copying each diagram of the planets with a steady hand, aware that the knowledge he preserved tonight might travel farther than any ship.

p9daa1d5e82.title: Station Seven
p9daa1d5e82.text:
Station Seven occupied a gravel shelf on the eastern edge of the Rub' al Khali, a cluster of white prefabricated cabins surrounded by dunes that rose, in the late afternoon light, like the frozen waves of an orange ocean. Dr. Salma Al-Harbi had volunteered for the six-month posting believing that isolation would sharpen her concentration, and for the first several weeks it did.

Gradually, however, the landscape began to assert itself. The dunes migrated a few centimeters each night, reshaping the horizon so subtly that she could never identify what had changed, only that something had. The instruments recorded temperature, humidity, and wind with mechanical indifference, yet the data seemed to describe a different place from the one she inhabited.

One evening, after a sandstorm had erased the vehicle tracks leading to the main road, Salma walked to the top of the nearest dune. For the first time, the emptiness did not feel threatening. It felt immense, patient, and entirely unconcerned with her, and that indifference, oddly, comforted her.

p5a8ba10d2f.title: The Last Keeper
p5a8ba10d2f.text:
By 1889 the lighthouse at the edge of Alexandria's western harbor had become an anachronism that nobody had yet found the courage to dismantle. Its lamp, still fed with colza oil and trimmed by hand, competed feebly against the electric glare spreading along the modern quays, where steamships discharged cotton bales beneath cranes that groaned like exhausted animals.

Ibrahim had tended the light for thirty-one years, and he measured time less by the calendar than by the gradual retreat of sail. Each season, fewer wooden vessels navigated by his beam; each season, the harbor's new illumination pushed the darkness he guarded a little farther out to sea.

On the final night before the commission's inspection, he polished the brass fittings with deliberate thoroughness, though he understood that the report would recommend demolition. Below him, the city hummed with machinery he could neither repair nor fully comprehend. Above, the familiar constellations wheeled indifferently, the only illumination in his world that progress had not yet rendered obsolete.

pb6ef8af650.title: The Little Seed
pb6ef8af650.text:
A little seed sat waiting under the ground.
It was dark and lonely, and it made no sound.
The rain came falling, and the sun shone bright.
The seed pushed upward with all of its might.

A windy storm blew hard, and it bent down low.
But it held on tightly and began to grow.
Now it is a tree so tall and so green.
It is the biggest tree that I have ever seen.

pf405f9093a.title: The Young Falcon
pf405f9093a.text:
High on the cliff above the valley, the young falcon studied the restless, enormous sky,
and while the older birds dove and circled gracefully, she waited, too afraid to try.
The wind howled furiously through the canyon and tugged at every feather on her wings,
whispering that the ground was terribly far below and full of dangerous, unknown things.

But hunger became stronger than her fear as the golden morning slowly passed,
so she spread her wings across the current and leaped into the open air at last.
She tumbled once, then caught the rising wind, and suddenly the valley opened wide,
and the same wind that had frightened her now lifted her like a patient guide.

p456b4c0455.title: The Palm in the Dry Year
p456b4c0455.text:
All summer the sky over the oasis stayed hard and colorless, refusing to offer even a single cloud,
and my grandfather walked the dusty rows every morning, testing the cracked soil with his fingers.
The younger farmers sold their inherited land to developers and moved away toward the glittering city,
but he remained, carrying heavy buckets from the shrinking well to the oldest palm on the farm.

"Why waste water on one tired tree?" I asked him, impatient and certain of my reasoning.
He answered quietly that roots remember every rainfall, and that patience is a kind of irrigation.

When the winter rains finally arrived, flooding the irrigation channels and darkening the earth,
the old palm was the first to blossom, its golden clusters heavy above our weary heads.

p092ccc36e7.title: Learning a Second Language
p092ccc36e7.text:
Every new word I learn is a stone I carry across the river, heavy and unfamiliar in my uncertain hands,
and some days the current of my classmates' rapid conversation sweeps my careful sentences downstream.
I practice at night beneath the kitchen lamp, repeating verbs until they settle into my memory like sediment,
while my mother, who learned this language before me, patiently corrects my pronunciation.

Last week I answered a question in class without first translating it silently inside my head,
and I felt the bridge beneath me hold, imperfect and unfinished, yet strong enough to cross.
Now I understand that I am not abandoning one shore in order to reach the other;
I am building a passage where two languages can travel comfortably in both directions.

ped0fa91771.title: Sadu
ped0fa91771.text:
My grandmother's loom leans against the courtyard wall, its warp threads stretched as tight as the patience she insists I lack,
and she weaves the traditional geometric patterns, triangles and diamonds inherited from women whose names survive only in wool.
I sit beside her with my telephone illuminated, scrolling through images that vanish faster than I can remember them,
and she asks, without looking up, whether anything I have seen today will still exist tomorrow.

I want to argue that my generation simply preserves its memories differently, in servers rather than in fibers,
but her hands continue their deliberate rhythm, and my rebuttal dissolves before I have spoken it.
When she finally offers me the shuttle, I hesitate, then pass the dark thread beneath the pale one,
clumsily adding a single crooked row to a pattern that is older than any language I can read.

pec276ad2f1.title: At the Ruins of Maragheh
pec276ad2f1.text:
Here the astronomers once measured heaven with brass quadrants and meticulous patience, recording the wanderings of planets in tables that astronomers and scholars would consult for centuries,
and now the hilltop offers only foundations, a scattering of weathered stones that goats negotiate with more confidence than any visiting historian.
The wind that once disturbed their candles still circulates indifferently among the ruins, erasing footprints, rearranging dust, unimpressed by the ambitions it outlived.

Yet I cannot declare the observatory defeated, for its calculations migrated into manuscripts, then into libraries, then into the instruments of people who never learned its name;
the building collapsed, but its arithmetic continued traveling, invisible and unbroken, like light from a star that has already ceased to burn.
Perhaps every structure is temporary, and only attention survives, transmitted from one curious mind to another across the silence of abandoned hills.

pc5474ecfbb.title: I Am the Moon
pc5474ecfbb.text:
I am the moon, up high in the big night sky.
I watch the little owls as they go flying by.
I see the quiet sea and the sleeping town.
I shine my silver light on all of the ground.

When the sun comes up, I slowly go to bed.
I let the sun shine down on all of you instead.
At night I come back again, so round and white.
I keep you safe and calm until it is light.

p9d72dbdf39.title: The Old Wooden Door
p9d72dbdf39.text:
I have guarded this narrow house in old Jeddah for more than a hundred years,
and my carved wooden panels have watched the busy street through heat and rain.
Children once raced past me, shouting, on their way to the market by the sea,
and merchants knocked politely, carrying cloth and spices from faraway ports.

Today the visitors pause and photograph my faded patterns with their shining phones,
and they whisper that I am beautiful, though they never ask to come inside.
I remember when every family on this crowded street recognized my creaking voice,
yet I still open each morning, hoping someone will step in and stay.

p03c01ee81b.title: The Goalkeeper
p03c01ee81b.text:
From where I stand between the posts, the field looks considerably wider than it ever did in practice,
and the noise of forty thousand voices gathers into a single tremendous roar that I can feel vibrating inside my gloves.
The striker places the ball with careful fingers and backs away slowly, pretending he is calm,
but I have studied him for weeks, and I know he always glances left before he shoots right.

Everyone in the stadium is watching him, the celebrated hero who might win the national championship tonight,
but nobody notices the quiet calculation happening inside me, the silent preparation of my legs.
He runs, he glances left, and I am already diving right before the ball has left his boot,
and for one suspended second the entire roaring stadium is holding its breath along with me.

pf651016c5c.title: Two Voices at the Harbor
pf651016c5c.text:
THE ENGINEER: I see a harbor waiting for its future, deep enough for container ships from every continent,
where cranes will rise like steel giants and the old wooden piers will finally make room for progress.
THE FISHERMAN: I see the shallow water where my father taught me to read the currents and the color of the waves,
where every morning the same gulls followed our small boats toward the reef that the dredging will destroy.

THE ENGINEER: Your reef is a memory, but my design will bring employment to thousands of families along this coast.
THE FISHERMAN: Your design is only a promise, but my memory has nourished this village for three generations.
BOTH: We are standing together on the same shore and contemplating the same blue water,
yet each of us is seeing a different harbor, and neither of us is entirely wrong.

pfefcb89d60.title: The Night Guard
pfefcb89d60.text:
I have guarded this gallery for nineteen years, and visitors assume I no longer notice the treasures I protect,
that the illuminated page of al-Jazari's elephant clock has become, for me, merely another rectangle behind glass.
They hurry past my chair with their headphones and their schedules, glancing at me the way they glance at fire extinguishers,
necessary, unremarkable, part of the architecture rather than a person who might have opinions of his own.

But after the last footsteps fade and the security lights dim to amber, I stand before the elephant and its mechanical riders,
and I trace with my eyes the hidden channels where water once measured hours with astonishing precision.
I have read every catalogue, every scholarly argument about its gears and floats, and I could correct the guidebook's three errors,
though no one has ever asked, and I have discovered that silence, too, can be a kind of expertise.

pf3d628ab12.title: The Mapmaker's Apology
pf3d628ab12.text:
Forgive me, future traveler, for the confident coastlines I have drawn from secondhand descriptions and a sailor's feverish recollection,
for the rivers I have extended into deserts simply because the parchment looked unbearably empty without them.
My patrons demanded completeness, and I have learned that a map which admits ignorance is rarely purchased,
so I have populated the unknown interior with mountains, kingdoms, and creatures I have never personally witnessed.

You will laugh, perhaps, at my imaginary islands, measuring my errors with instruments I cannot imagine,
yet consider whether your own certainties are not also assembled from incomplete reports and inherited assumptions.
I leave these margins deliberately unfinished, not from carelessness but as a confession,
so that someone wiser, standing upon my mistakes, may finally recognize where knowledge ends and invention begins.

pbdcf40bc75.title: The Little Camel
pbdcf40bc75.text:
A little camel walks on sand,
Across the hot and sunny land.
He does not stop, he does not run,
He walks all day beneath the sun.

At night he rests beside a tree,
And looks up at the stars to see.
The moon is big, the sky is wide,
His mother sleeps right by his side.

p9ac3b81ec8.title: The Lighthouse on the Point
p9ac3b81ec8.text:
[In this poem, a slash (/) marks the end of each line.]

Each evening when the fishing boats come drifting slowly home, / Old Yusuf climbs the winding stairs to light the lamp once more. / He watches as the waves below dissolve in silver foam, / And sends a golden, steady beam across the rocky shore.

The sailors cannot see his face, they only see the light, / Yet every captain on the sea depends on it to steer. / It sweeps across the darkened bay through every stormy night, / And tells the tired travelers that safety is still near.

When morning paints the harbor pink, he puts the lamp to sleep, / Then sits beside his window with a glass of fresh mint tea. / He never asks for thanks or praise, but promises to keep / His faithful watch above the waves for all who sail the sea.

p7363027524.title: The Date Palm
p7363027524.text:
[In this poem, a slash (/) marks the end of each line.]

Before the first well was dug and before the first wall was raised, a single date palm rose from the sand at the edge of the oasis; / still, the palm stands.

It has bent beneath the summer storms that hurl the burning dunes against its trunk like waves against a ship; / still, the palm stands.

It has watched the caravans arrive with silk and salt, and it has watched them disappear again across the trembling horizon; / still, the palm stands.

Now children climb its patient trunk and gather the sweet, dark fruit that their great-grandparents gathered long ago, / and the palm, which asks for nothing but a little water and a little time, still stands.

p7bada6c0f7.title: The Pearl Diver's Son
p7bada6c0f7.text:
[Pearl diving was once a leading industry along the coast of the Arabian Gulf, where young divers trained for several seasons before joining the long summer expeditions; in this poem, a slash (/) marks the end of each line.]

Young Faisal watched his father dive / beneath the morning tide, / and every day he begged to go / and swim at Father's side.

“The sea is kind,” his father said, / “but never on your side; / a diver needs a steady heart / and nothing kept inside.”

So Faisal trained through all the spring / to hold his breath and glide, / until the shadowed reef below / became his friend and guide.

When summer came, the captain called / the boys from far and wide, / and Faisal plunged into the blue / with courage and with pride.

He rose up with a single pearl / and held it to the sky; / his father did not say a word, / but tears were in his eye.

p52b46b0a73.title: For Mariam, Who Made Astrolabes
p52b46b0a73.text:
[In this poem, a slash (/) marks the end of each line.]

In tenth-century Aleppo, Mariam bent above her workbench while the city slept, / guiding a fine blade across a disk of brass / until the circles of the heavens appeared beneath her hands.

She did not write in rhyme; she wrote in degrees and angles, / in the thin curved lines that allowed a traveler to measure the height of a distant star, / in the careful markings that told a merchant when to rest, when to sail, when to turn for home.

Her name survives in a single sentence of an old chronicle, / but her instruments traveled farther than any chronicle could, / from harbor to harbor, from caravan to caravan, from one patient hand to another.

So let this poem be measured the way she measured: / not by its music, / but by how far it carries you.

p23c1339860.title: Night in the Empty Quarter
p23c1339860.text:
[This poem is a Shakespearean sonnet, a traditional form developed during the English Renaissance and still practiced by contemporary poets; it is printed continuously here, with each slash (/) indicating the conclusion of an individual line of verse.]

When daylight drains from every rippled dune / and silence settles where the camels strayed, / the desert waits beneath a rising moon; / the constellations heat and dust delayed.

Here navigators read the turning sky / as scholars read the pages of a book; / they named each planet as it wandered by / and found their road with one attentive look.

But we, who carry maps inside our hands, / have let the old astronomy grow dim; / we cross in hours these once unending sands / and seldom raise our eyes above the rim.

Yet still the stars keep faith with those who stray, / and wait for us to look, and find our way.

pf9be3110ea.title: My First Fish
pf9be3110ea.text:
I went to the sea with Grandpa, and he gave me a small rod. I sat on the rocks and waited for a long, long time. I wanted to go home.

Then my line pulled hard, so I held on tight. Grandpa said, “Slow and steady.” I pulled and pulled until a shiny silver fish came up! I felt so proud. Grandpa smiled and said, “Now you are a real fisher.”

p7612c7fb47.title: The Robot Contest
p7612c7fb47.text:
Lina could hardly sit still in her seat. For three long weeks, she and her older brother Adam had built a small robot that could sort recycling into separate bins, and today the judges would finally see it work. Lina was absolutely sure that they would win first prize.

Adam, however, was not nearly so confident about their chances. He kept checking the wires and whispering that the left sensor sometimes failed. While Lina waved excitedly to her friends in the crowd, Adam studied the other robots and noticed how smooth and fast they looked.

When the judges arrived, the robot rolled forward, paused, and dropped a plastic bottle into the paper bin. Lina gasped in horror. Adam calmly reached over, tightened one loose wire, and politely asked the judges for a second try. This time, every single item landed in the correct bin. Later, Lina admitted that worrying a little had not been such a terrible idea after all.

p6aa3b83d39.title: The Flags
p6aa3b83d39.text:
On the morning of the championship match, I was absolutely certain that my grandmother had forgotten all about it. While I searched frantically through the house for my shin guards, she sat beside the window with a basket of green and white fabric in her lap and barely glanced up. When I reminded her that the game started at four o'clock, she only nodded absently and explained that she was occupied with her sewing.

All the way to the stadium, I complained to my cousin Reem that nobody in my family genuinely cared about football. Reem gave me a mysterious smile but said nothing, which irritated me even more.

Then, during warm-ups, I happened to glance toward the stands. Twenty small green-and-white flags were fluttering above our team's bench, each one carefully stitched with a player's number. Behind them, wearing her finest scarf and holding the final flag, sat my grandmother.

p31f3887e3a.title: The Squall: Two Accounts
p31f3887e3a.text:
Text 1: from the personal journal of Khalid, a twelve-year-old deckhand aboard a wooden trading dhow

The storm struck just after sunset, and I was certain that the mast would snap in two before the night was over. Enormous waves crashed over the rail, and I clung desperately to a rope while the older sailors shouted instructions I could not possibly hear above the roaring wind. I hoped that the captain understood what he was doing, because to me it seemed that nobody aboard was in control of anything at all.

Text 2: from the official logbook of Captain Saeed, the experienced commander of the same vessel

Squall from the northwest at sunset, as anticipated during this season of the year. Lowered the mainsail early and turned the bow directly into the wind; the vessel responded well and took on very little water. The new boy, Khalid, maintained his position at the stern rope throughout the squall without needing to be told twice. Recommend that he be entrusted with the night watch on our next voyage to Zanzibar.

pf81861c4d3.title: Streets for Walkers
pf81861c4d3.text:
Every city that preserves its old quarter eventually faces the same question: should cars still be allowed in narrow streets that were designed for walkers and pack animals? Some business owners argue that banning traffic will drive away customers who expect to park near shop doors, and their concern deserves a serious hearing. Yet the evidence from cities that have already closed their historic centers to private cars is difficult to dismiss. In several Mediterranean towns, shopkeepers who once protested the change now report that foot traffic has increased, because visitors linger longer when they are not dodging delivery vans and searching for parking.

The deeper issue, however, is not commerce but stewardship. Ancient walls crack under the constant vibration of engines, and centuries-old facades darken with exhaust. A historic quarter is not merely a shopping district; it is a shared inheritance that no single generation has the right to wear out. Cities that hesitate should begin with weekend closures, measure the results honestly, and let the evidence, rather than habit, decide.

p5279fbfb90.title: The Single Letter
p5279fbfb90.text:
When I was twelve, my father required me to practice a single letter for an entire summer. Each afternoon he arranged a reed pen, a pot of ink, and a stack of inexpensive paper before me, and each afternoon I repeated the same vertical stroke until my wrist ached and my patience evaporated. My friends were swimming at the corniche; I was, as I complained to anyone who would listen, imprisoned by a line.

I believed then that my father was indifferent to my misery, that he valued the discipline of calligraphy more than the happiness of his son. I noticed only that he rarely praised me, never the deliberate attention with which he studied each sheet before setting it aside.

It was years before I discovered those sheets, hundreds of them, bound with string in a drawer of his desk, each one dated in his small, meticulous handwriting, and I realized with astonishment that the later strokes were considerably steadier than the earlier ones. He had been keeping a careful record of a patience I did not know I was learning.

p3666e4ae7e.title: Library Rules
p3666e4ae7e.text:
[A sign hangs on the door of the school library.]

Library Rules

Please walk inside the library. Use a quiet voice so that other children can read. Wash your hands before you touch the books. Put each book back on the shelf where you found it. Bring your books back in one week so that a friend can read them too.

[Picture: a smiling owl holds one finger to its lips.]

p3fe4f742ae.title: Join the Corniche Cleanup!
p3fe4f742ae.text:
[Poster: a bright blue background with a drawing of children carrying trash bags along a sandy beach.]

JOIN THE CORNICHE CLEANUP!

Saturday, March 8, from 7:00 to 10:00 in the morning, at the North Beach parking area

Every year, thousands of plastic bottles and bags wash up on our beach, where they can harm turtles, seabirds, and fish. You can help protect the creatures that share our coastline!

What to bring: a hat, a refillable water bottle, and comfortable shoes. Gloves and bags will be provided.

How to join: Ask an adult to register your family at the community center or by calling 555-0142 before March 5.

Every bottle you pick up is one less danger for a sea turtle, so we hope to see you on the sand!

padbe768861.title: Build a Shoebox Solar Oven
padbe768861.text:
[Photo: a shoebox lined with foil, its lid propped open toward the sun, with a small plate inside.]

A solar oven uses sunlight to warm food without any electricity or fire. Follow these directions carefully, and ask an adult to help whenever you use scissors or a craft knife.

Step 1: Cut a flap in the lid of the box, leaving one long side attached so that the flap can open and close like a door.
Step 2: Cover the inside of the flap with aluminum foil, keeping the shiny side facing out so that it will reflect sunlight into the box.
Step 3: Line the bottom of the box with black paper, which absorbs heat instead of reflecting it.
Step 4: Tape plastic wrap tightly over the opening in the lid to trap warm air inside the oven.
Step 5: Place the oven in direct sunlight and use a wooden stick to prop the flap open at an angle.

Caution: The inside of the oven can become hot enough to burn your fingers, so always use an oven mitt when removing food.

p6a5abe44b1.title: At the Clock Exhibit
p6a5abe44b1.text:
Text 1: Informational placard displayed beside a full-size model of a medieval water clock

The Elephant Clock, designed by the engineer Ismail al-Jazari around 1206, used a floating bowl that slowly sank in a tank of water to measure the passing of each half hour. As the bowl sank, it pulled cords that released a metal ball, which dropped into a dragon's mouth and set small figures in motion to announce the time. This full-size model was constructed by museum engineers in 2019 using al-Jazari's own drawings and detailed descriptions.

Text 2: Instructional sign attached to the protective glass case surrounding the model

PLEASE DO NOT TOUCH THE GLASS. The model's water tank is carefully balanced, and even a gentle bump can stop the clock for several hours. Demonstrations take place every day at 11:00 and 3:00; ask a museum guide if you would like to see the clock in action.

p8f4e728ae2.title: Beat the Heat: Know the Signs
p8f4e728ae2.text:
[Poster displayed at bus stops and construction sites during the summer months; across the top, a large red thermometer appears beside the headline.]

BEAT THE HEAT: KNOW THE SIGNS

Heat exhaustion can progress to heatstroke, a life-threatening medical emergency, very quickly if the person remains exposed to the heat.

WATCH FOR: heavy sweating, dizziness, nausea, a pounding headache, or skin that feels cold and clammy despite the surrounding temperature.

ACT FAST: Move the person into the shade, loosen tight clothing, and apply cool, wet cloths to the neck and armpits. Offer small sips of water only if the person is fully conscious and able to swallow.

CALL 997 IMMEDIATELY if the person becomes confused, stops sweating, or faints.

[Small print along the bottom of the poster: Workers are entitled to a rest break in the shade during the hottest hours of the day. Report any violations immediately to your site supervisor or to the regional labor office.]

p5be25846ed.title: Wadi Sahab Trail: Visitor Notice
p5be25846ed.text:
[Weatherproof notice board installed at the entrance to a desert canyon trail managed by the regional parks authority]

FLASH FLOOD DANGER: Rainfall in distant mountains can send a destructive wall of water surging through this canyon within minutes, even when the sky directly above you appears perfectly clear. If you hear a roar resembling an approaching truck or notice the stream becoming suddenly muddy, climb immediately to higher ground and never attempt to cross the moving water.

The trail is 6.4 kilometers round trip and climbs approximately 300 meters to Eagle Overlook. Follow the white markers painted on the rocks; at the fork near the dry waterfall, keep left, because the right-hand path terminates at an unstable cliff edge.

The acacia trees and rock carvings along this route have survived for centuries because generations of earlier visitors deliberately left them undisturbed. Please carry out everything you bring in, and resist the temptation to carve your initials beside the ancient inscriptions.

Visitors enter at their own risk. The trail is closed from 11:00 to 15:00 between June and September, when afternoon temperatures regularly exceed safe limits.

p280795fc8a.title: Rami and the Sand Storm
p280795fc8a.text:
Rami the camel lived in the desert. One day the sky turned brown. A big sand storm was coming. Rami told the goats to stay close. They walked to a big rock and hid behind it. The wind blew hard. Soon the storm was over, and the sun came out.

[Cartoon version: In the cartoon of this story, you can hear the wind howl. Rami speaks in a deep, kind voice. Music plays fast when the storm comes and soft when the sun comes out.]

p32edf55ba2.title: The Night Fishermen
p32edf55ba2.text:
Yusuf had never been out on the boat after dark. His uncle steered slowly away from the harbor while the lights of the town grew smaller behind them. Yusuf watched the black water and wondered what was moving under it. When the net finally came up, it was heavy and silver with fish. His uncle laughed, and Yusuf realized his fear had disappeared somewhere along the way.

[Audio version: In the audiobook, a narrator reads the story while listeners hear waves slapping the boat, the creak of the engine, and gulls calling near the harbor. The narrator whispers the part where Yusuf watches the black water, then speaks loudly and cheerfully when the net comes up.]

p68303db83e.title: The Clockmaker's Apprentice
p68303db83e.text:
For three weeks, Karim had swept the floor of Master Idris's workshop without being permitted to touch a single clock. He memorized the sound of each one instead: the anxious ticking of the brass mantel clock, the slow, dignified knock of the tall case clock by the door. One afternoon, the tall clock fell silent. Master Idris was away, and the merchant who owned it would arrive at sunset. Karim opened the case with trembling hands, remembering everything he had heard, and found a tiny spring that had slipped from its hook.

When Master Idris returned, the clock was ticking again. He listened for a long moment, then handed Karim a set of tools without saying a word.

[Film version: The film opens with a montage of Karim sweeping while dozens of clocks tick progressively louder, compressing three weeks into a single minute. When the tall clock stops, the soundtrack becomes completely silent. The final scene presents a close-up of Master Idris's face as he listens, and a slight, almost invisible smile appears before he hands over the tools.]

p79810e93f6.title: The Dune at Dusk
p79810e93f6.text:
The wind moves over the dune like a patient hand smoothing a folded blanket, and every grain remembers the heat that the afternoon pressed into it;
far off, a solitary camel bell rings, then rings again, then stops, as if the evening itself were deliberating whether anything remained to be said.
Now the first star opens, now the second, now a hundred more, scattered across the darkening sky like salt spilled across an indigo cloth.

[Recording: In an audio recording, the poet reads the first line slowly and evenly, emphasizing its deliberate, unhurried rhythm. She pauses for several seconds after the word "stops," leaving complete silence before continuing. She delivers the final line faster and faster, her voice rising steadily as the stars multiply across the imaginary sky.]

pdb5e923418.title: The Astrolabe
pdb5e923418.text:
Mariam turned the brass plate a fraction of a degree, and the star she had been chasing all evening finally slid into the sighting notch. She did not cry out. Her father had taught her that an instrument maker's joy should be measured, like everything else, in careful increments; still, her pulse raced as if it had been told nothing of the kind. Three months of filing, engraving, and starting over had produced, at last, an astrolabe that agreed with the sky.

She thought, absurdly, of the apprentices who had whispered that a girl's hands were too unsteady for such delicate calculations, and she discovered, with considerable satisfaction, that their opinion no longer mattered.

[Film adaptation: The scene is photographed almost entirely in shadow, illuminated only by a single oil lamp. There is no voice-over. The camera lingers on Mariam's fingers as they complete the final adjustment, then cuts to a panoramic shot of the night sky as orchestral music swells.]

p0acace66d1.title: The Translator's Choice
p0acace66d1.text:
In the copying room of the House of Wisdom, Hunayn's newest assistant had been staring at the same Greek word for an hour. The word could mean “balance” or it could mean “mixture,” and the medical treatise made sense either way, though the two readings would send a physician down entirely different paths. Hunayn did not offer an answer. He set a second lamp beside the young man's desk, as though the difficulty were merely a matter of light, and returned to his own work.

By dawn, the assistant had committed himself to one interpretation, and the only sounds in the room were the deliberate scratch of his pen against the paper and, beyond the window, the first uncertain birds.

[Stage production: In a recent staging, Hunayn lingers at the doorway after placing the lamp and nods approvingly as the assistant writes. A narrator steps forward at the conclusion to announce that the translation was subsequently celebrated by physicians throughout the empire, transforming the play's final moment into a confident declaration of success.]

p91fccd18aa.title: The Date Palm
p91fccd18aa.text:
Date palms grow in hot, sunny places. They also need water. Their roots go deep into the ground to find it.

A date palm makes its fruit in the summer. The dates start out green. Then they turn yellow or red. Last, they turn brown and soft, and that is when people pick them.

Farmers climb the tall trees with a strong rope. They cut the dates carefully and put them in big baskets.

pfc11a4b5bd.title: The Camel's Hump
pfc11a4b5bd.text:
Many people believe that a camel's hump is full of water. This idea is easy to understand, because camels can travel for days across the desert without drinking. However, the hump actually stores fat, not water.

When food is hard to find, a camel's body slowly uses the fat in its hump for energy. As the fat is used up, the hump becomes smaller and may even flop over to one side. After the camel eats well again, the hump grows firm.

So how do camels survive without water? Their bodies lose very little of it. They sweat only when they become extremely hot, and their kidneys save water carefully. When a thirsty camel does find water, it can drink more than one hundred liters in a few minutes.

pf46cd87be4.title: The Second Launch
pf46cd87be4.text:
The countdown reached zero, and Dana's rocket shot upward in a clean white streak. The crowd gathered at the edge of the school field cheered enthusiastically, but Dana barely noticed them. She was thinking about the morning in October when the same rocket had wobbled, tilted, and crashed into the fence beside the parking lot.

That morning, her teammate Faisal had picked up the broken fins and studied them silently. "The glue held," he had finally said, "but the angle didn't." For the next two weeks, they had measured every fin with a protractor, rejecting any that leaned even a single degree.

Now, as the parachute opened high above the field, Dana finally let herself smile. Faisal was already recording the altitude in his notebook, calculating adjustments for their next design.

p8b455cce13.title: Turning the Sea into Drinking Water
p8b455cce13.text:
Saudi Arabia produces more desalinated water than almost any other country, yet many people who drink it every day have never wondered where it comes from. The process, called desalination, removes salt from seawater so that it can be used in homes, farms, and factories.

The most common method today is reverse osmosis. In ordinary osmosis, water naturally moves through a thin barrier, or membrane, from a less salty solution toward a saltier one. Reverse osmosis forces the opposite to happen: powerful pumps push seawater against the membrane with tremendous pressure, so that fresh water squeezes through while the salt is left behind.

The method is effective, but it is not perfect. The pumps consume enormous amounts of electricity, and the leftover brine, which can be nearly twice as salty as seawater, must be returned to the ocean carefully so that it does not harm coral and fish.

p937a108429.title: The Hidden Cost of Early Specialization
p937a108429.text:
Parents who enroll a seven-year-old in year-round football training usually do so with the best intentions. They have heard that mastery requires thousands of hours of practice, and they reason, not unreasonably, that an early start provides an advantage that latecomers can never overcome.

The research, however, suggests a more complicated picture. Studies of elite athletes in several countries have found that many of them sampled a variety of sports during childhood and did not commit to one until adolescence. Their varied experience, rather than holding them back, appears to have built a broader foundation of coordination, balance, and decision-making.

Specialization carries risks as well. Children who repeat the same movements throughout the year are more likely to suffer overuse injuries, and those who feel pressured to excel at a single activity frequently abandon sports altogether before they reach high school. The early start, in other words, can become an early finish.

p790fa0a6b1.title: Al-Biruni's Mountain
p790fa0a6b1.text:
In the early eleventh century, the scholar al-Biruni devised a way to measure the size of the Earth without undertaking a long journey. Earlier astronomers had attempted the calculation by walking or riding across a flat plain until the height of a star changed by a single degree, a laborious method that demanded long journeys and invited accumulated error. Al-Biruni's approach was, by contrast, almost elegant in its economy.

First, he measured the height of a mountain using the familiar geometry of triangles. Then, standing on the summit, he observed the angle at which the horizon dipped below a perfectly level line. Because the Earth curves, the horizon viewed from a height appears slightly lower than straight ahead; the higher the observer, the greater the dip. With the mountain's height and the angle of the dip, a single trigonometric relationship yielded the planet's radius.

His result differed from the modern value by less than one percent, a margin that later scholars found remarkable given the instruments available to him.

pf7310cc076.title: A Talk About Our Trees
pf7310cc076.text:
Friends, please look at our school yard today. Do you see any shade at all? We have no trees, and the sun is very hot. We really need some trees in our yard!

Trees give us cool shade on hot days. Trees give us clean air to breathe. Trees give homes to the birds that sing.

So let us plant a tree together this week. Let us water it every single day. Let us watch it grow tall and strong. One small tree can change our whole yard. Will you please help me plant it?

p4803a5f1c8.title: Words for the New Library
p4803a5f1c8.text:
[An imagined speech delivered when a small farming town opened its very first public library]

Neighbors, today we are opening much more than a building. We are opening a door. Behind this door are maps of distant lands that none of us has visited, stories of remarkable people that none of us has met, and ideas that none of us has yet imagined.

Some people say that a small town does not need so many books. I would ask them a question: is a small town's mind meant to be small? A child growing up in this town deserves exactly the same opportunity to learn as a child in any great city.

So come inside, all of you. Read, wonder, and return tomorrow. These shelves, and every book upon them, belong to every one of you.

pffe921ce82.title: Speech at the Completion of the Desert Railway
pffe921ce82.text:
[An imagined address delivered in 1908 by the chief engineer, standing beside the newly completed tracks before an enormous crowd]

Five years ago, distinguished experts informed us that no railway could ever cross these shifting sands. They predicted that the heat would warp the steel, that the wind would bury the tracks, and that the workers would abandon their posts before the first season ended. Today, I stand before you, together with those same workers, on the final mile of that supposedly impossible line.

I have labored beside these men through summers that melted our instruments and through storms that erased a week's progress in a single afternoon. I did not see them abandon anything; I saw them rebuild.

What does this railway mean? It means that a journey of forty exhausting days will now require only three. It means that a farmer's harvest can reach the coastal markets before it spoils. It means that distance, which has always divided our scattered communities, will now connect them.

p97deea7d59.title: Address to the Marine Science Graduates
p97deea7d59.text:
[An imagined commencement address delivered in 1962 to the first graduating class of a marine science institute]

Graduates, you have devoted four years to learning the language of the sea: its currents, its chemistry, its countless and astonishing forms of life. Now you must decide what you will say in that language.

For centuries, humanity has treated the ocean as two contradictory things at once: an endless storehouse and an endless dump. We have taken from it as though it could never be emptied, and we have poured into it as though it could never be filled. Both assumptions are demonstrably false, and you, more than anyone in this auditorium, possess the evidence to prove it.

I do not ask you to love the sea; sailors and poets have done that admirably for thousands of years. I ask you to understand it, to measure it, and to speak for it when no one else will.

p821c2b812b.title: An Address on the City's Water
p821c2b812b.text:
[An imagined address by a physician to a city council, 1854]

Gentlemen of the council, I am informed that the expense of new pipes is considered excessive, that the city has survived on its ancient wells for a century and may reasonably expect to survive on them for another. I do not dispute the arithmetic. I dispute the accounting.

For what is the genuine price of a well that sickens the families who depend upon it? What is the cost of a child who does not reach the age of five, or of a laborer incapacitated for a month by recurring fever? These sums do not appear in your ledgers, yet the municipality pays them annually, and it pays them in a currency far dearer than coin.

I have walked repeatedly through the narrow, overcrowded streets where the epidemic originates. I have counted the affected households and mapped the public pumps. The accumulated evidence supports a single, uncomfortable conclusion: we are not saving money by delay; we are merely spending it elsewhere.

pac38bd3f91.title: On Inheritance
pac38bd3f91.text:
[An imagined lecture delivered to an international gathering of distinguished scientists and mathematicians]

We like to imagine that discovery belongs to the individual: the solitary genius, the sudden illumination, the name engraved upon a prestigious award. Yet every one of us in this room stands at the end of a long relay. The algebra we use was refined in Baghdad; the optics we rely upon were tested in Cairo by a man who spent years confined to his house; the numerals with which we record our results traveled from India across a dozen languages before they reached our notebooks.

I do not say this to diminish anyone's achievement. I say it to correct a persistent habit of collective memory. We do not inherit knowledge because we deserve it; we deserve knowledge only when we hand it on.

Let us therefore measure ourselves not by what we have taken from the past but by what we will leave unfinished for those who follow, for an unfinished question, generously handed down, is the most valuable gift a scientist can give.

pac593a9d06.title: Help Our Park
pac593a9d06.text:
Do you like to play in the park after school with your friends? I do! But look at the grass today. Who wants to sit next to old paper cups and plastic bags? Not me.

Let us clean the park together on Saturday morning. We can bring big bags and gloves from home. It will only take one hour of work. Is one hour too much for a nice park? No, it is not!

Come to the gate at nine and bring a friend with you. Then we can all play on clean, green grass again.

paa82f5d51d.title: Every Drop Counts
paa82f5d51d.text:
How much water do you think a dripping tap wastes in one day? Most people guess a cup or two. In fact, a tap that drips once every second can waste more than twenty liters a day, which is enough water for a family to cook several meals.

In a dry country like ours, water is precious, because it is pumped from deep underground or made from seawater in enormous factories, and both methods use a great deal of energy. So why do we leave the water running while we brush our teeth? Would we leave money falling out of our pockets and simply walk away?

Saving water is not difficult. Turn off the tap while you brush, tell an adult whenever you hear a drip, and water plants in the evening, when less water disappears into the hot air. If every student at our school saved just one liter a day, imagine how much we could save together in a single year.

p29e66237e6.title: Why Not Us?
p29e66237e6.text:
Team, I know what you have been hearing in the hallways. People say that a small school like ours has no business entering the national robotics championship, and that the wealthy academies with their sophisticated laboratories will defeat us in the very first round. Perhaps they are right. But tell me, when has a laboratory ever built a robot by itself?

Every machine in that competition will be designed by students who are experimenting, failing, and trying again, exactly as we have been doing since September. We redesigned our robot's mechanical arm four separate times, and we remained after school until the security guard switched off the lights. Did anyone force us to do that? No. We did it because we were determined to understand how complicated machines actually operate.

So when someone asks why an inexperienced team like ours should compete, I have only one question in reply: why not us? We have imagination, patience, and one another. Let us pack the toolbox and go.

pd33baa5cef.title: Do We Still Need Paper Maps?
pd33baa5cef.text:
Every year, fewer families keep a folded road map in the car. Phones now speak directions aloud, recalculate routes in seconds, and even warn drivers about traffic ahead. With such a convenient tool in every pocket, who would bother learning to read a paper map?

The answer, surprisingly, should be everyone. Satellite signals can fail in deep valleys, batteries can die on long desert highways, and networks can disappear far from cities. What happens to the traveler who has never looked at the whole landscape, only at a blue dot moving along a line? Researchers have found that people who rely entirely on spoken directions often struggle to remember where they have been, because they never form a mental picture of the area.

A paper map does not replace a phone; it complements it. Is it really so inconvenient to spend one afternoon learning a skill that could guide you home when the screen goes dark?

p4a497a8005.title: The Man Who Doubted the Masters
p4a497a8005.text:
Distinguished guests, we have gathered this evening to inaugurate a gallery named for Ibn al-Haytham, the eleventh-century scholar who investigated the behavior of light in Cairo. Why should a museum dedicated to the future honor a man who lived a thousand years ago? Because he demonstrated that genuine knowledge begins not with obedience but with disciplined, systematic doubt.

For centuries, respected authorities had maintained that the eye emits invisible rays that travel outward to touch the objects it perceives. Ibn al-Haytham asked a deceptively simple question: if that were true, why would sunlight injure our eyes, and why could we not see in a darkened room? Rather than repeating the masters, he darkened a chamber, admitted light through a tiny opening, and carefully recorded what happened.

Who among us has not accepted an idea merely because a confident voice repeated it? This gallery is an invitation to resist that comfortable habit. Test what you are told; measure, compare, and document. Isn't that, after all, the oldest and most demanding definition of science?

pe13fa14a41.title: On Being Unreachable
pe13fa14a41.text:
We are told, with considerable confidence, that constant connectivity has made us better informed than any previous generation. Perhaps it has. Yet what exactly have we gained if the average message is answered within minutes while the average book is abandoned within pages? Information has never been cheaper; attention has never been more expensive.

Consider the student who keeps a phone beside every assignment, glancing at it whenever a sentence becomes demanding. Is that student studying, or merely waiting to be interrupted? Psychologists suggest that each interruption consumes not only the seconds it occupies but also the considerable mental effort required to reconstruct an interrupted line of reasoning.

None of this implies that we should abandon our devices entirely; such a recommendation would be neither practical nor desirable. It means, rather, that we should reclaim the privilege of being occasionally unreachable. After all, the medieval astronomers who meticulously charted the heavens over Baghdad and Samarkand were hardly in a hurry to reply to anyone. Did their silence make them less connected to the world, or more?

p06b8d2435b.title: The Rainy Picnic
p06b8d2435b.text:
Adam and his dad went to the beach for a picnic on Friday. They had cheese sandwiches, sweet dates, and a big red ball. Then dark clouds came over the sea, and it began to rain very hard.

Adam was wet from his hair to his shoes. He looked down at his soggy sandwich. "What a perfect day for a picnic," he said with a frown.

Dad laughed and shook the water from his hat. "It is a little damp," he said. They ran to the car and ate their dates inside while the rain fell on the roof.

pbb8dba746c.title: The Shortcut
pbb8dba746c.text:
Faisal was certain that he knew a shortcut to the oasis. "Trust me," he told his cousins, waving his hand confidently toward a long line of dunes. "We will be there before lunch."

Two hours later, the four of them were still climbing sand hills under a blazing sun. Their water bottles were nearly empty, and Faisal's map had blown away somewhere behind them.

"Wonderful shortcut, Faisal," said his cousin Lina, wiping sand from her eyes. "I especially enjoy the part where we walk in circles."

At last, their uncle's jeep appeared over a ridge, because he had followed their footprints for several kilometers. Uncle Khalid studied their sunburned faces and their dusty, empty bottles, and he raised one eyebrow. "I see the trip has been slightly longer than planned," he said calmly.

Faisal climbed into the jeep without a word. For the rest of the holiday, whenever anyone mentioned a shortcut, the whole family burst out laughing.

p8588cc72ba.title: School Solves Lateness Forever
p8588cc72ba.text:
In a bold move that experts are calling "certainly a decision," the principal of Greenfield Middle School announced on Monday that the school has finally solved the problem of students arriving late. Beginning next week, every clock in the building will be set twenty minutes behind.

"Our research demonstrates that students are never late if the clocks agree with them," explained the assistant principal, proudly displaying a chart with no numbers on it. "We considered starting the day later, adding another bus route, or speaking with families, but those ideas seemed far too complicated."

Teachers have responded with predictable enthusiasm. "Oh, marvelous," said the science teacher, Mr. Hamdan, as he quietly adjusted his wristwatch. "Now my students will be punctual for a lesson that officially ends after the dismissal bell."

The principal admitted that the new system might cause "a small amount of confusion" when the afternoon buses arrive at what the school clocks will call 1:40 but the drivers will insist is 2:00.

p3000c92195.title: The Solar Oven
p3000c92195.text:
[A garage workshop. RAMI, fourteen, stands beside a cardboard solar oven that is sagging badly. His older sister NADA, sixteen, enters carrying a thermometer.]
NADA: (examining the oven) Impressive. I have never witnessed cardboard melt before, and I have been alive for sixteen years.
RAMI: It isn't melted; it's simply relaxing after an exhausting afternoon of collecting sunlight.
NADA: (reading the thermometer) Thirty-one degrees, although the temperature outside is thirty-four. Congratulations, Rami, you have invented a device that makes the desert cooler.
RAMI: (sighing) The judges arrive tomorrow morning, so perhaps I have a minor problem.
NADA: (setting down the thermometer, more gently) A minor problem, yes, let's call it that, and demonstrate how you attached the aluminum foil.
[RAMI hesitates, then lifts the lid, revealing strips of foil that hang loosely, most facing the wall instead of the sky.]
NADA: There is your difficulty: your reflectors are admiring the paint. Turn them toward the sun, and we might cook something.
RAMI: (beginning to smile) Will you help me?
NADA: Only because I refuse to be related to the inventor of the cooling oven.

pc0e27e7e78.title: In Praise of the Notification
pc0e27e7e78.text:
Let us pause to honor the humble notification, that tireless servant which protects us from the unbearable danger of concentrating on anything for longer than ninety seconds. Before its invention, people were forced to read entire chapters, complete conversations, and even finish their own thoughts, an exhausting practice that, mercifully, is rapidly disappearing.

Consider the modern family dinner. Where our grandparents once endured lengthy discussions about their day, today's diners enjoy a lively chorus of buzzes and chimes, each announcing news of extraordinary importance: a discount on sunglasses, a reminder to drink water, or the thrilling information that someone, somewhere, has photographed a sandwich.

Critics argue that constant alerts have made it slightly more difficult to remember what we were doing. These critics, unfortunately, were unable to complete their research, because their phones kept interrupting them. Surely, then, we owe the notification our deepest gratitude. After all, without it, we might be forced to discover what we actually think.

p6cf86976bb.title: A Memorandum on Productivity
p6cf86976bb.text:
Memorandum to all employees from the Office of Meeting Coordination, concerning recent improvements to organizational productivity.

Following extensive consultation, we are delighted to announce that the number of weekly meetings will increase from fourteen to twenty-two. Several employees have observed that meetings occasionally interfere with the completion of actual work; we appreciate this valuable feedback and have therefore scheduled a meeting to discuss it, followed by a second meeting to evaluate the conclusions of the first.

We acknowledge that last month's reorganization produced a modest degree of disruption. The accounting department, for instance, was temporarily relocated to the parking garage, and three urgent projects were assigned to an employee who had retired the previous spring. Such adjustments are, of course, the inevitable price of progress.

To measure our success, every staff member will now submit a daily report describing the time spent preparing daily reports. We are confident that this initiative will generate unprecedented transparency, and we look forward to celebrating our achievements at Thursday's mandatory celebration meeting, which will last approximately four hours.

pb0155adce4.title: Sunset at the Beach
pb0155adce4.text:
Mona and her grandma sat on the warm sand by the sea. The sun was low and orange in the sky. Small waves came in slowly and went back out with a soft swish.

A light wind moved Mona's hair. Two white birds flew over the water. Far away, a little boat rocked gently on the waves.

Grandma poured sweet tea into two small cups. Mona leaned on her shoulder and smiled. "I wish this day would never end," she said quietly. The sky turned pink and then purple as the sun went down behind the sea.

p54d1b0b4f1.title: The Storm on the Dhow
p54d1b0b4f1.text:
The morning had begun with clear skies, and Yusuf's father had smiled as he steered the old wooden dhow away from the harbor. By noon, however, the sea had changed completely: heavy gray clouds rolled across the horizon, and the wind began to howl through the ropes.

Waves slammed against the side of the boat, spraying cold water over the deck. Yusuf gripped the mast with both hands while the dhow tilted sharply to one side and then the other. Somewhere below, a crate of fishing nets crashed across the floor.

"Hold on!" his father shouted, his voice almost swallowed by the thunder.

Then, as suddenly as it had arrived, the storm moved away toward the north, and a pale ray of sunlight broke through the clouds and touched the water. Yusuf let go of the mast, his fingers aching, and took a long, shaky breath. In the distance, he could see the white walls of the harbor shining.

p9400ee5fb1.title: Night in the Empty Quarter
p9400ee5fb1.text:
When the last orange light slips quietly behind the dunes, the desert breathes its heat into the sky,
and the sand that burned our sandals all afternoon grows cool and silver beneath a rising moon.

No engine murmurs here, no window glows, no voice calls out across the endless, undulating hills;
only the wind, as patient as an ancient traveler, rearranges every delicate ridge one grain at a time.

Above us, the stars arrive not one by one but all at once, a crowded, glittering marketplace of light,
so close that my little brother reaches upward, certain he could gather a luminous handful for his pocket.

My father names them softly, the way his grandfather once named them on caravan journeys long ago,
and in this vast and uninhabited silence, I feel smaller than a single grain, yet somehow perfectly at home.

pbc491e3ea8.title: The Lighthouse Log
pbc491e3ea8.text:
The lighthouse had been abandoned for eleven years when Salma climbed its spiral staircase for the first time. Each iron step groaned beneath her weight, and the narrow windows admitted only thin, grayish blades of light that revealed swirling dust but little else.

Halfway up, she paused. Somewhere above her, a door creaked slowly on its hinges, although the air inside the tower was perfectly still. She told herself it was only the wind from the sea, yet she noticed that her hand was trembling on the cold railing.

At the top, the great lamp sat silent beneath a cracked glass dome. Beside it, on a dusty wooden desk, lay a leather logbook, open to its final page. The last entry, written in faded ink, recorded the date, the weather, and a single unfinished sentence: "Tonight I finally understood what the fishermen have been describing." Salma closed the book carefully, glanced over her shoulder, and decided that her investigation could continue tomorrow, in daylight.

pa0d2ed8664.title: Balconies of Coral Stone
pa0d2ed8664.text:
Every summer of my childhood, my grandmother's house in the old quarter of Jeddah awoke before the rest of the city.
