I remember lying on a thin mattress on the roof, listening to the call to prayer drift across the coral-stone buildings, while the first gray light softened the outlines of the carved wooden balconies.

By the time I descended the narrow staircase, my grandmother had already lit the stove, and the kitchen smelled of cardamom and warm bread. She moved slowly, deliberately, as though every gesture had been rehearsed for decades, which, I suppose, it had.

Those balconies, called rawasheen, were designed to catch the breeze from the sea and to let families observe the street without being seen. Today many of them are being restored by meticulous craftsmen, and tourists photograph them with admiration. I am grateful for the restoration, truly. Yet when I wander those lanes now, among the cafés and gift shops, I find myself listening for something the craftsmen cannot rebuild: the sound of my grandmother's slippers on the stairs.

p20adb3dd8e.title: Day Forty-Three
p20adb3dd8e.text:
Day forty-three at the research station began, as most days had, with measurements: an air temperature of minus thirty-eight degrees Celsius, a southeasterly wind gusting to thirty knots, and visibility reduced by blowing snow to approximately two hundred meters. Dr. Hessa Al-Mutairi recorded each figure in the logbook with the methodical neatness that had made her the expedition's most reliable meteorologist.

The station itself offered little beyond necessity: four insulated modules connected by narrow corridors, a generator whose monotonous hum had long since become inaudible to its inhabitants, and windows so thoroughly frosted that the outside world appeared only as an indistinct, luminous gray.

Shortly after noon, however, the wind abruptly collapsed. Hessa stepped outside to inspect the anemometer and stopped. The snow had settled, and the ice shelf stretched unbroken to the horizon beneath a sky of startling, almost unbearable blue. For several minutes she did not write anything at all. When she finally returned to the logbook, the entry she composed contained no numbers, only a single sentence: "Today the continent permitted us to see it."

pc0423b5604.title: Sea Turtles
pc0423b5604.text:
Sea turtles live in warm seas. They can swim very far. A mother turtle comes to the beach at night. She digs a hole in the sand with her flippers. Then she lays her eggs in the hole.

[Picture: tiny turtles crawl across the sand. Caption: Baby turtles hurry to the water at night.]

The babies **hatch** after about two months. They run to the sea as fast as they can.

[Word box: **hatch** means to come out of an egg.]

[Fun Fact box: Unlike land turtles, sea turtles cannot pull their heads into their shells.]

pc3f55d0622.title: Camels: Built for the Desert
pc3f55d0622.text:
The Arabian camel, or *dromedary*, has one hump and can travel across hot sand for days. Many people believe the hump stores water, but it actually stores **fat**. When food is scarce, the camel's body slowly turns this fat into energy.

[Photo: a camel resting on a sand dune. Caption: Thick eyelashes and nostrils that can close keep blowing sand out of a camel's eyes and nose.]

Camels can also drink an enormous amount of water very quickly. After a long journey, a thirsty camel may drink more than one hundred liters in only fifteen minutes.

[Sidebar, Did You Know?: Camels have carried goods along Arabian trade routes for more than three thousand years.]

[Glossary: **fat**, a material the body stores and uses for energy later]

p28bc429285.title: The Astrolabe: A Pocket Universe
p28bc429285.text:
For centuries, travelers, astronomers, and timekeepers relied on a brass instrument called the **astrolabe**. By lining up a rotating pointer with a star or the sun, a user could calculate the time of day, estimate the height of a distant mountain, or determine which direction to face. It worked like a small computer made of metal.

Scholars in Baghdad, Cairo, and Cordoba improved the astrolabe between the eighth and twelfth centuries, adding new measuring scales and increasingly accurate star maps. Their written guides, such as the treatise known in Arabic as *Kitab al-Amal bil-Asturlab*, explained each procedure in careful detail. Each new guide made the tool easier to learn and use.

[Photograph: a round brass disk covered with engraved lines and a pointer. Caption: This astrolabe, made in the 1200s, contains a removable plate for each city's latitude.]

[Sidebar, Maker Profile: Mariam al-Ijliya, who worked in Aleppo in the tenth century, was so skilled at building astrolabes that the ruler of the city employed her at his court.]

pdcaaab2557.title: Coral Gardens of the Red Sea
pdcaaab2557.text:
Scientists studying the northern Red Sea have noticed something remarkable: many of its corals survive water temperatures that would bleach and kill reefs in other oceans. One species, *Stylophora pistillata*, continues growing even during unusually hot summers.

**Bleaching** occurs when stressed corals expel the tiny algae living inside their tissues, losing both their color and their main source of food. Researchers believe the Red Sea corals inherited their heat tolerance from ancestors that migrated northward through a warm, narrow strait thousands of years ago.

[Diagram: a cross-section of a coral polyp with algae cells shown in green. Caption: The algae inside a polyp supply up to ninety percent of the coral's food.]

[Sidebar, Protecting the Reef: Divers can help by never touching coral, using reef-safe sunscreen, and anchoring boats only in sandy areas.]

p8dbeed7bb3.title: Light in a Dark Room
p8dbeed7bb3.text:
Nearly a thousand years ago in Cairo, the scholar Ibn al-Haytham sat in a darkened chamber and watched an inverted image of the street outside flicker across the wall opposite a tiny opening. Rather than treating this as a curiosity, he repeated the observation systematically, varying the size of the aperture and the position of lamps, and concluded that light travels in straight lines from objects into the eye.

[Pull quote, in large italic type: "Rather than treating this as a curiosity, he repeated the observation systematically."]

That conclusion overturned an influential ancient theory, which held that the eye emits rays toward the objects it perceives. His *Book of Optics*, translated into Latin, shaped European scientific thinking for centuries.

[Illustration: light rays crossing at a pinhole and forming an upside-down tree on a back wall. Caption: Because the rays cross at the opening, the image appears inverted.]

[Sidebar, Try It Yourself: Cover a window with dark paper, make a small hole in it, and watch the opposite wall.]

p3a35b1b737.title: Drinking the Sea
p3a35b1b737.text:
Across the Arabian Peninsula, desalination plants now supply the majority of municipal drinking water, transforming coastal cities that once depended on scarce, slowly replenished aquifers. Reverse osmosis, which forces seawater through membranes fine enough to block dissolved salts, has steadily reduced the energy required per cubic meter, making the technology increasingly affordable.

Advocates therefore describe desalination as a nearly *inexhaustible* solution, reasoning that the sea itself will never run dry. The sea, after all, is vast. But is that the whole story?

[Chart: energy needed to produce one cubic meter of fresh water, 1990 to 2020, falling from roughly ten kilowatt-hours to about three. Caption: Efficiency gains have slowed considerably since 2010, and engineers anticipate only modest further improvement.]

[Sidebar, A Second Look: Every liter of fresh water leaves behind concentrated brine, which, if discharged carelessly, can raise salinity and lower oxygen levels near the outfall, harming seagrass meadows and fish nurseries.]

p0d5a2cc295.title: The Busy Bee
p0d5a2cc295.text:
Buzz, buzz, buzz goes the busy bee in the sun.
She buzzes by the big green tree and has lots of fun.
She sips sweet nectar from a flower that is pink and new.
Down she dives to a daisy bed all wet with dew.
Then home she hums with a happy song for the hive.
The busy bee is glad to be out and alive.

pa8895ef7a9.title: Night Market
pa8895ef7a9.text:
Lanterns lean low over the long lane where the late shoppers linger and laugh in the warm evening air,
And spices are spilled in bright sacks, saffron and sumac and sesame, scenting the street with their smoke.
The old man who sells the gold bowls is humming a slow, lonely song from the home he remembers so well.
A copper pot clatters and clinks as the merchant packs up his wares for the night and locks the wooden stall.
Children chase cats down the cobbled path, chattering, cheerful, and curious, until their mothers call.
The baker stacks sticky sweet buns on a rack by the flickering wick of his lamp at the corner.
Then under the dark, starry arch of the gate, the market grows quiet at last.

pe06af9582a.title: The Night the Najma Came Home
pe06af9582a.text:
Rami stood at the end of the stone pier and watched the sky fade from pale gray to a deep, bruised purple. Wild winds whipped the waves against the harbor wall, and the fishing boats bobbed and bumped against their ropes like restless horses waiting impatiently to be released.

Far out on the water, a single light rolled slowly over the cold, foaming swells. Rami knew it was his uncle's boat, the old Najma, struggling home with its nets still heavy with the afternoon's catch.

Then, without any warning, the rain arrived in ferocious, sweeping curtains. It pattered, then clattered, then hammered on the tin roofs of the market until the whole shore seemed to shudder. Rami gripped the slippery railing and refused to move, determined to remain until the vessel was visible again. At last the light drifted safely past the breakwater, and his uncle's tired voice rang out across the dark bay.

pdec26648c3.title: The Falconer at Dawn
pdec26648c3.text:
At dawn the falconer climbs the dune, his footsteps soft and slow in the cool, untroubled sand, carrying a creature more precious to him than gold.
The hooded falcon waits upon his glove, a silent statue sculpted from shadow, steel, and stillness, listening to the desert wake around her.
He lifts the hood, and the bright eyes ignite like fire, and in a single breath the bird is gone, a blade against the blue horizon.
Rising, wheeling, riding the wind, she circles until the wide and windswept sky seems to bend around her wings.
Below, the falconer stands patient as a stone, listening to the long, low moan of the morning breeze across the open dunes,
Until the dark speck drops, and drops, and drops, and lands again with a quick, sharp click of talons on the leather.

p2a15bb4b28.title: The Sea Remembers
p2a15bb4b28.text:
Graduates and families: today we gather beside the sea that shaped this city's history, and I ask you to listen. Listen to the restless roar of the tide against the rocks; listen to the patient, persistent pulse of the currents that carry life from the reef to the open ocean. That sound was here long before us, and, if we are wise, it will remain long after us.

For generations, our grandparents pulled pearls from these waters with nothing but courage, a nose clip, and a rope. They did not dream of satellites or sensors, of underwater cameras or computer models that predict the movement of entire ecosystems. Yet they understood what many modern minds forget: the sea gives generously only to those who treat it gently and respectfully.

You leave this academy carrying sophisticated instruments that your grandparents could never have imagined. Use them with care, with curiosity, and with conscience, remembering that every measurement represents an irreplaceable community. Keep the reef free and the sea clean; protect it from the quick, thick, black slicks of spilled oil. Measure, monitor, and mend.

p0efb210897.title: The Glassblower's Furnace
p0efb210897.text:
In a narrow workshop on the edge of Hebron, the furnace never fully sleeps; its low, droning roar hums beneath every conversation, so steady and constant that visitors stop noticing it within minutes, the way one stops hearing one's own heartbeat. The glassblower, a slight man whose forearms are freckled with tiny, healed burns, gathers a glowing globe of molten glass on the end of a long iron pipe and turns it, turns it, turns it, as patiently as if time itself were softening in the heat.

He breathes into the pipe, and the bead swells into a bubble, pale and trembling, a fragile moon suspended above the floor. Then come the tools: the clipped click of the shears, the sharp tap of the jacks, the brisk, crisp crack of a cooled stem snapping free.

By evening, the shelves glitter with blue and green vessels, and the workshop falls quiet except for the furnace, whose low, droning roar seems less like noise than like memory, older than the man, older than the town, older than the trade.

pceccd0d807.title: The Class Garden
pceccd0d807.text:
Ms. Amal's class wanted a garden. First, the children cleaned a small patch of dirt behind the school. Next, they planted seeds for beans, mint, and tomatoes. Every morning, they gave the plants water. Some days it was very hot, so they put up a little shade cloth.

After six weeks, the plants were tall and green. The children picked the beans and tomatoes. They took them home to share with their families. Ms. Amal smiled and said, "You worked hard, and now we can all enjoy the garden."

pbc1a7a37e0.title: The Falaj: Water That Travels
pbc1a7a37e0.text:
For more than two thousand years, farmers in Oman have moved water across the desert using a system called the falaj. A falaj is a channel, often built partly underground, that carries water from a mountain spring or a buried water source to villages and fields many kilometers away.

Building a falaj required great skill. Workers dug a row of deep holes called shafts. Then they joined the shafts with a tunnel that sloped gently downhill. Gravity pulled the water along, so no pumps were needed.

Sharing the water fairly was just as important as moving it. Each farmer received water for a set amount of time, measured during the day by the shadow of a stick and at night by the position of the stars.

Today, several of Oman's aflaj are protected as World Heritage sites, and many villages still depend on them to water their date palms and crops.

p968c9913cd.title: The Robot That Drifted
p968c9913cd.text:
Layla's robotics team had six weeks to build a robot that could sort recycling, and for five of those weeks, nothing worked. The robot's arm drifted to the left every time it reached for an object, dropping plastic bottles into the metal bin and metal cans onto the classroom floor.

Her teammate Faris wanted to rebuild the arm entirely, but Layla suspected the problem was smaller. She spent an evening recording the robot in slow motion and noticed that one wheel spun slightly faster than the other, pulling the entire machine off course before the arm even moved.

The next morning, the team replaced the worn wheel and recalibrated the motors. At the regional competition, their robot sorted forty items without a single error, finishing second out of eighteen schools. Afterward, Faris admitted that he had nearly quit. "Sometimes," Layla told him, "the biggest problem is hiding in the smallest part."

pec16402fad.title: Shade Is Infrastructure
pec16402fad.text:
Cities in hot climates spend enormous sums cooling buildings, yet they often overlook the cheapest air conditioner available: the tree. A mature tree can lower the surface temperature of a sidewalk by more than ten degrees Celsius, and neighborhoods with dense tree cover regularly record lower electricity use during summer heat waves.

Critics argue that trees demand too much water in dry regions. This concern is reasonable, but it is not decisive. Native species such as the ghaf and the sidr survive on very little rainfall, and treated wastewater can irrigate them without draining drinking supplies.

Trees also deliver benefits that are harder to measure. Shaded streets invite residents to walk rather than drive, and children play outdoors longer when playgrounds are protected from the afternoon sun.

City planners should therefore treat shade the way they treat roads and pipes: as essential infrastructure that deserves a permanent place in every budget.

p7332417691.title: The House of Wisdom
p7332417691.text:
In the early ninth century, the Abbasid caliphs transformed Baghdad into one of the most intellectually vibrant cities in the world. At the center of this transformation stood the Bayt al-Hikma, or House of Wisdom, an institution that began as a royal library and gradually expanded into a hub for translation, research, and debate. Its doors were open to many scholars.

Scholars working there translated Greek, Persian, and Indian texts on mathematics, medicine, and astronomy into Arabic, often comparing several manuscripts to establish the most reliable version. Their work was slow and careful. Translation, however, was only the beginning. Thinkers such as al-Khwarizmi built on these sources to produce original work, including systematic methods for solving equations that later gave algebra its name.

The availability of paper, which had recently spread from Central Asia, made copying books faster and cheaper, allowing knowledge to circulate among scholars across the empire. Books could now travel.

Although the institution itself was destroyed during the Mongol siege of 1258, the ideas it preserved and generated had already traveled to Cordoba, Cairo, and eventually Europe, influencing scientific thought for centuries.

p37f77647b4.title: The Promise and Limits of Citizen Science
p37f77647b4.text:
Citizen science, in which volunteers collect or analyze data for professional research, is frequently celebrated as a democratizing force. Thousands of amateurs have classified distant galaxies from their laptops, counted migrating birds along coastlines, and recorded the first blooming dates of desert wildflowers, producing datasets far larger than any single laboratory could assemble.

Yet enthusiasm can obscure genuine limitations. Volunteers tend to cluster near cities and popular trails, leaving remote regions underrepresented, and their observations vary in precision. Researchers must therefore invest considerable effort in verification, sometimes discarding a substantial share of submissions.

These obstacles do not invalidate the approach; rather, they redefine its value. The most successful projects pair volunteers with rigorous protocols, provide feedback that sharpens participants' skills over time, and treat contributors as collaborators rather than unpaid labor. In such partnerships, the benefit flows in both directions: science gains data, and the public gains a firsthand understanding of how knowledge is actually made.

Citizen science, in other words, is neither a miracle nor a gimmick, but a demanding collaboration whose rewards depend on careful design.

p9d0a9d4035.title: The Busy Bee
p9d0a9d4035.text:
[Ms. Lina reads this story aloud to her class.]

A small bee named Zuzu woke up early. She flew to a field of yellow flowers. She drank the sweet nectar and carried it home. On the way, a big wind pushed her into a pond. A kind frog held up a leaf. Zuzu climbed on and dried her wings in the sun. Then she flew home to the hive. The other bees made honey from her nectar. Zuzu was tired, but she was happy.

p51308bcb99.title: How Camels Survive the Desert
p51308bcb99.text:
[Video transcript: a nature program shows a line of camels walking slowly across enormous sand dunes.]

NARRATOR: Camels can travel for days across the scorching desert without drinking, and scientists have discovered several reasons why. First, their bodies are remarkably good at saving water. A camel can allow its temperature to rise during the day, so it sweats less and loses less moisture. Second, the hump on its back stores fat, not water. When food is difficult to find, the camel slowly uses this fat for energy.

[The video shows a close-up of a camel's face in a sandstorm.]

NARRATOR: Camels are also built for sand and wind. Two rows of long eyelashes protect their eyes, and they can close their nostrils completely during a storm. Their wide, flat feet spread out so they do not sink into soft sand. Because of these features, people across Arabia have depended on camels for transportation for thousands of years.

p69a9681b9d.title: Coastlines, Episode 12
p69a9681b9d.text:
[Podcast transcript: “Coastlines,” Episode 12]

HOST: Today we're exploring mangroves, the salt-tolerant trees that grow along sheltered parts of the Arabian Gulf and the Red Sea, and my guest, Dr. Reem, has studied them for fifteen years. Why should ordinary listeners care about these unusual coastal ecosystems?

DR. REEM: Mangroves perform three important jobs. Their tangled roots slow down incoming waves, which protects the shoreline from erosion during powerful storms. Those same roots also shelter juvenile fish and shrimp until they are mature enough to survive in the open ocean. Finally, mangrove mud stores a remarkable quantity of carbon, so the trees actively help limit climate change.

HOST: I've read that many mangrove forests in the region have disappeared over the past century.

DR. REEM: That's true, mostly because coastlines were cleared for construction and development. However, communities are now planting millions of seedlings, and some restored forests are already attracting migrating birds again. Still, a newly planted forest takes years to provide all the benefits of an old one.

p0e0b672ff1.title: The Man Behind the Algorithm
p0e0b672ff1.text:
[Documentary transcript. On screen: a modern phone, then an old manuscript page.]

NARRATOR: Every time you search the internet, your phone follows a set of step-by-step instructions called an algorithm. The word itself comes from a scholar who lived more than a thousand years ago.

[On screen: an artist's drawing of Baghdad in the ninth century.]

NARRATOR: Muhammad ibn Musa al-Khwarizmi worked in Baghdad at the House of Wisdom, a center where scholars translated and studied books from many cultures. His most famous book explained methods for solving equations, and one word from its title, al-jabr, eventually became the English word algebra.

[On screen: a page of numerals written in Arabic and Latin.]

NARRATOR: Al-Khwarizmi also wrote about the number system that used zero and place value. When his work was translated into Latin, European readers learned these methods, and his name, written as Algoritmi, gradually gave us the word algorithm. Today, his ideas are hidden inside nearly every calculation a computer performs.

p2ab7ba7649.title: Water from the Sea
p2ab7ba7649.text:
[Transcript of a recorded talk; Slide 1 shows a map of desalination plants along the Red Sea and Gulf coasts.]

SPEAKER: In much of the Arabian Peninsula, the water flowing from your kitchen tap began its journey in the sea. Desalination, the process of removing salt from seawater, now supplies drinking water to millions of people throughout the region.

[Slide 2: a diagram of seawater being forced through a thin membrane.]

SPEAKER: Older facilities boiled seawater and collected the steam, a method that consumed enormous quantities of fuel. Most modern plants use reverse osmosis instead, forcing water through membranes so fine that dissolved salt cannot pass, which requires considerably less energy, although it is hardly free.

[Slide 3: a photograph of a coastal outflow pipe.]

SPEAKER: The remaining challenge is brine, the concentrated salt water left behind, which can damage coral and seagrass when it is released carelessly near the shore. Engineers are therefore investigating ways to dilute brine, extract valuable minerals from it, and operate plants with solar energy. Desalination is indispensable, but its future depends on making it cleaner.

p8613506db5.title: Cooling the City
p8613506db5.text:
[Transcript of a radio panel, “Cooling the City”]

MODERATOR: Summer temperatures in many Gulf cities now regularly exceed fifty degrees Celsius, and dense neighborhoods of concrete and asphalt can be several degrees hotter than the surrounding desert. Our panelists disagree about how municipalities should respond.

ENGINEER: Reflective materials offer the most immediate benefit, because a light-colored roof or pavement can return much of the sunlight that conventional surfaces absorb, lowering surface temperatures within a single season and without consuming scarce irrigation water.

URBAN ECOLOGIST: I don't dispute those measurements, but surfaces alone cannot create the shaded, walkable streets that residents genuinely need. Carefully chosen native trees, irrigated with treated wastewater, cool the air through shade and evaporation while also improving air quality and encouraging people to walk.

ENGINEER: Trees certainly matter, yet they require decades to mature, and poorly selected species can consume enormous quantities of water.

MODERATOR: So perhaps the realistic conclusion is that cities will need both approaches, each compensating for the other's limitations.

p9332166dc7.title: The Little Lamp
p9332166dc7.text:
Yusuf stayed at his grandma's house. At night the room was dark. Yusuf felt scared.

Grandma gave him a small lamp. "This lamp was mine when I was little," she said. "When you see its light, remember that I love you."

Yusuf turned on the lamp. The room glowed. He did not feel scared now. When he went home, he took the lamp with him. Every night he turned it on and thought of Grandma.

p8e67f37d63.title: The Compass
p8e67f37d63.text:
On her first night in the new city, Laila could not fall asleep, because everything felt unfamiliar: the streets, the school, even the constant sound of traffic outside her window.

Her grandfather knocked softly and placed a small brass compass in her hand. "I carried this on fishing boats for forty years," he said. "Whenever the sea was rough and I could not see the shore, this needle reminded me which way to go."

Laila studied the trembling needle until it gradually settled and pointed north. The next morning she slipped the compass into her backpack. At school, when she felt lost in the crowded hallway, she touched its smooth cover and took a deep breath. By the end of the week, she had discovered her classroom, the library, and a new friend named Mariam.

p6d961417da.title: The Palm at the Edge of the Road
p6d961417da.text:
My grandmother planted a palm at the edge of the road the year the village had no rain, carrying water in a clay jar from a well three kilometers away.
The neighbors said a seedling could never survive the summer wind, but every evening she knelt beside it and pressed the sand around its roots with patient hands.

Sandstorms came and bent its narrow trunk until the leaves brushed the ground, and each morning it rose again, a little taller, a little more stubborn than before.
Now travelers stop beneath its shade when the afternoon burns white, and children climb its rough bark to pick the dates that ripen gold in late summer.

My grandmother is old, and her hands shake when she pours the tea, yet when I watch her walk to the road each evening, I know where the palm learned to stand.

p6c695231aa.title: The Last Boat
p6c695231aa.text:
[Scene: a small harbor, where an old wooden dhow with weathered, peeling planks rests on the sand; FAHAD, sixteen, runs his hand along the hull while his FATHER examines a stack of documents.]

FATHER: The buyer from the city will arrive tomorrow morning, and frankly, this boat has not brought home a single fish in eleven years.

FAHAD: Grandfather built it himself, and you learned to sail in it before you could even read, so doesn't that history matter anymore?

FATHER: Memories do not repair cracked planks, Fahad, and they certainly do not finance replacement engines or professional repairs.

FAHAD: (pressing his palm against a carved star near the bow) Then let me repair them, because I will work every weekend until the hull is sealed and the torn sail is mended.

(The FATHER, silent, walks to the bow and touches the same carved star, as if noticing it for the first time in years.)

FATHER: Your grandfather carved this star on the night you were born. (He folds the documents and puts them away.) Tomorrow we will need better equipment, not a buyer.

pe12767ed7b.title: The Clock Shop
pe12767ed7b.text:
After my father died, I kept his repair shop closed for an entire season, and the tall clock in the front window remained frozen at twenty past four, the moment its exhausted spring had finally given out.

Neighbors walking to the market would glance at it and then quickly look away, as though the motionless hands were a private matter they had no right to witness. I understood their discomfort, because each time I unlocked the door to collect the accumulated mail, I avoided looking at the clock myself.

One morning in early spring, a boy arrived carrying an inexpensive plastic watch, its strap cracked and its battery dead. He apologized repeatedly for disturbing me, explaining that the watch had been a gift from his grandfather and that no other shop would accept it. I nearly refused him.

Instead, I retrieved my father's smallest screwdriver, still lying exactly where he had left it. When the boy's watch began ticking again, I walked to the front window, opened the tall clock's glass door, and slowly wound the spring.

p9c6d97b31c.title: The Unfinished Pattern
p9c6d97b31c.text:
My aunt kept the loom in the courtyard long after anyone in the family had leisure to weave, its wooden beams bleached pale by decades of relentless sun, and across it stretched a strip of Sadu cloth abandoned halfway through an intricate pattern of crimson triangles and black diamonds.

As a child, I assumed she had simply lost interest; only later did I discover that she had stopped on the morning my grandmother, who had taught her every traditional pattern, became too ill to sit beside her.

When I finally asked her to teach me, she hesitated, studying my clumsy fingers with an expression I could not interpret. Then she cut a fresh length of wool, tied it to the loose threads where her own work had ended, and guided my hands through the first uneven row.

My triangles were crooked, and the colors bled awkwardly into one another; nevertheless, she refused to let me unravel them. "A pattern that never changes hands," she said, "is only a decoration."

pba897e200c.title: All About Date Palms
pba897e200c.text:
All About Date Palms

Where They Grow
Date palms grow in hot, dry places. Many grow in Saudi Arabia.

What They Give
Date palms give us sweet dates to eat. People use the big fronds to make baskets and mats.

How Dates Grow
Small flowers grow at the top of the tree. The flowers turn into green dates. The sun turns them brown and sweet.

[Picture: A farmer climbs a tall palm tree. Caption: Farmers climb the trees to pick the dates.]

[Glossary: fronds — the long leaves of a palm tree]

pfab135fe5e.title: Saving the Arabian Oryx
pfab135fe5e.text:
Saving the Arabian Oryx

A Desert Survivor
The Arabian oryx is a white antelope with long, straight horns. It can live for weeks without drinking, getting water from plants and morning dew.

Nearly Lost
By 1972, hunting had wiped out the last wild oryx. Fortunately, a few animals still lived in zoos and private herds.

A Second Chance
Scientists began a captive breeding program, raising oryx in protected areas and then releasing them into the desert. Oman released the first herd in 1982, and Saudi Arabia followed in 1990.

[Sidebar, Fast Facts: Height: about one meter at the shoulder. Weight: about 70 kilograms. Status today: Vulnerable, no longer endangered.]

[Photo caption: Oryx rest in the shade of an acacia tree during the hottest part of the day.]

[Glossary: captive breeding — raising animals in safe places so their numbers can grow]

p8f2d44f648.title: The Journey of Paper
p8f2d44f648.text:
The Journey of Paper

An Invention in China
Around the year 105, an official in China named Cai Lun improved a method for making paper from tree bark, old cloth, and plant fibers. For centuries, the technique remained a closely guarded secret.

Paper Reaches Baghdad
By the eighth century, papermaking had spread west along trade routes to Samarkand. Soon afterward, Baghdad opened one of the earliest paper mills in the Islamic world. Because paper was cheaper and lighter than parchment, libraries grew rapidly, and scholars could copy books in far greater numbers.

From Spain to the World
Merchants and craftsmen later carried papermaking across North Africa and into Spain, where Europe's first paper mills appeared.

[Timeline: 105, Cai Lun improves papermaking in China | 751, papermaking reaches Samarkand | 794, a paper mill opens in Baghdad | about 1150, a paper mill is operating in Spain]

[Caption beneath an illustration of a workshop: Workers pressed wet pulp into thin sheets and dried them in the sun.]

p46c2124824.title: Keeping Cool: How Honeybees Control Heat
p46c2124824.text:
Keeping Cool: How Honeybees Control Heat

A Hive at a Constant Temperature
Inside a beehive, the brood area, where immature bees develop, must remain consistently close to 35 degrees Celsius. If the temperature rises much higher, the developing insects can be seriously harmed, so the entire colony cooperates to regulate conditions.

Fanning and Evaporation
On hot afternoons, worker bees collect droplets of water and distribute them across the wax comb. Other workers line up at the entrance and beat their wings rapidly, pulling a continuous current of air through the hive. As the water evaporates, it carries heat away, much like perspiration cools human skin.

[Diagram: arrows show cool air entering the bottom of the hive and warm air leaving through the top, with bees fanning at the entrance.]

[Table, temperatures recorded by a school science club on one summer day: 9 a.m., outside 31°C, brood area 35°C | 1 p.m., outside 43°C, brood area 35°C | 5 p.m., outside 39°C, brood area 35°C]

[Key term: evaporation, the change of a liquid into a gas, a process that absorbs heat]

pab40ae596f.title: Caravans of Fragrance: The Incense Road
pab40ae596f.text:
Caravans of Fragrance: The Incense Road

A Valuable Resin
For more than a thousand years, frankincense, a fragrant resin harvested from trees in southern Arabia, ranked among the most coveted commodities of the ancient world, and merchants transported it northward by camel caravan to markets around the Mediterranean.

Oases Along the Route
Because the journey crossed some of the harshest terrain on earth, caravans depended on a chain of oases where they could rest and trade. Settlements such as Hegra* prospered by supplying water, provisions, and protection, and their builders carved monumental tombs directly into sandstone cliffs.

[Pull quote: “Every well along the road was worth more than gold to a caravan leader.”]

[Map: a dotted line runs from southern Arabia north through Najran and Hegra to Petra and the Mediterranean; palm symbols mark oases; a scale bar shows 500 kilometers.]

The Road Declines
When maritime routes through the Red Sea became faster and less expensive, overland commerce gradually diminished, and many oasis settlements were eventually abandoned.

*Hegra, near present-day AlUla, became Saudi Arabia's first UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2008.

paa83a63715.title: Ancient Water, Modern Demand
paa83a63715.text:
Ancient Water, Modern Demand

A Reservoir Beneath the Sand
Beneath much of the Arabian Peninsula lie vast aquifers, layers of porous rock saturated with water that accumulated thousands of years ago, when the regional climate was considerably wetter. Hydrologists describe this supply as fossil water, because contemporary rainfall replenishes it only negligibly.

The Cost of Rapid Extraction
During the late twentieth century, pumps allowed farmers to irrigate enormous circular fields, and agricultural production expanded dramatically. Consequently, water tables in several regions declined far faster than any natural process could restore them.¹

[Line graph, “Groundwater Level at One Monitoring Well (illustrative), 1980–2020”: the line falls steeply from 1985 to 2005, then declines more gradually.]

[Sidebar, What Is a Water Table? The water table is the upper surface of saturated ground; when wells withdraw water faster than it is replenished, the table drops and wells must be drilled deeper.]

Toward Conservation
Recent policies have reduced cultivation of water-intensive crops and encouraged drip irrigation, which delivers water directly to roots.

¹ Hydrologists measure this decline by recording the depth to water in monitoring wells over decades.

p7790cadbe3.title: Why the Pond Dried Up
p7790cadbe3.text:
Last spring, our class pond was full of water. Frogs swam in it. Birds came to drink.

Then the summer was very hot. It did not rain for many weeks. The sun dried up the water little by little. Soon the pond was just mud.

The frogs hopped away to find a new home. The birds stopped coming. When the rain came back in the fall, the pond filled up again. Now the frogs are back.

p587e6846f9.title: When Coral Turns White
p587e6846f9.text:
Coral reefs look like colorful underwater gardens, but each coral is actually a colony of tiny animals. Their bright colors come from even tinier algae that live inside them. The algae make food from sunlight and share it with the coral.

When ocean water becomes too warm for several weeks, the coral becomes stressed and pushes the algae out. Without the algae, the coral loses its color and turns white. Scientists call this coral bleaching.

Bleached coral is not dead yet, but it is starving. If the water cools down quickly, the algae can return and the coral can recover. If the heat lasts too long, the coral dies, and the fish that depend on the reef for shelter must leave. The Red Sea has some corals that can survive warmer water, so scientists study them closely to learn how other reefs might be protected.

p920801dab4.title: A Letter from the Date Farm
p920801dab4.text:
Dear Faisal, you asked in your last message why our farm looks so different from the one you remember from your childhood visits. The answer, surprisingly, begins underground, beneath the roots of the palms. For decades, we flooded the fields between the palms, and so did nearly all of our neighbors throughout the valley. Because so much water was continuously pumped from the ground, the wells had to be drilled deeper every few years.

The flooding caused a second, less visible problem. As the water evaporated in the intense summer heat, it left salt behind, and the salty soil gradually weakened the roots of the youngest palms. Within a decade, our annual harvest had fallen by nearly a third.

Consequently, two years ago I installed drip lines that deliver water directly to each tree. We now use less than half the water we once consumed, the damaged soil is gradually recovering, and last season the young palms produced their first full crop. With love, your grandfather Abdullah

p76ada5a0b0.title: The Day the Telegraphs Sparked
p76ada5a0b0.text:
On the first of September 1859, the English astronomer Richard Carrington was sketching dark spots on the sun when two brilliant patches of white light suddenly flared among them. He did not know it yet, but he had witnessed an enormous solar explosion that hurled a cloud of charged particles toward Earth.

The cloud arrived less than a day later. As it collided with Earth's magnetic field, it produced shimmering auroras that were seen as far south as the Caribbean and were so bright that in some places people could read newspapers at midnight. The same disturbance also created powerful electric currents in long telegraph wires. Operators received shocks, sparks leaped from equipment, and some paper tapes caught fire.

Strangely, a few operators discovered that they could disconnect their batteries and still send messages, powered entirely by the storm. Today, scientists warn that a storm of similar strength could damage satellites and power grids, which is why space agencies now monitor the sun continuously.

pbf1d7bfd9d.title: Why Our Coasts Need Darker Nights
pbf1d7bfd9d.text:
Each summer, female sea turtles crawl onto beaches along the Arabian Gulf and the Red Sea to bury their eggs in the warm sand. Weeks later, the hatchlings emerge at night and instinctively crawl toward the brightest horizon, which, on an undeveloped coast, is the moonlit surface of the sea.

Coastal development has disrupted this ancient pattern. Hotels, highways, and illuminated promenades now outshine the water, so hatchlings frequently crawl inland, where they are exhausted by dehydration, captured by predators, or crushed by traffic. Researchers estimate that on brightly lit beaches, the majority of a nest may never reach the water.

The remedy is neither expensive nor complicated. Shielded fixtures, amber bulbs, and seasonal lighting restrictions have restored successful sea-finding in several protected nesting areas. Because the problem is created by human choices rather than natural forces, it can be reversed by human choices as well; communities simply need the will to dim their lights for a few weeks each year.

p19e6aeec52.title: Lessons from the Dust Bowl
p19e6aeec52.text:
In the 1920s, rising wheat prices and new gasoline-powered tractors encouraged farmers on the southern Great Plains of the United States to plow millions of acres of native grassland. The deep-rooted prairie grasses that had anchored the soil for thousands of years were replaced by fields that lay bare between harvests.

When a prolonged drought struck in the early 1930s, the consequences of this transformation became catastrophic. Without vegetation to hold it in place, the parched topsoil was lifted by persistent winds into towering black blizzards that darkened cities hundreds of kilometers away. Crops failed, livestock suffocated, and thousands of families abandoned their farms.

Historians emphasize that drought alone did not cause the disaster; the region had survived dry periods before. Rather, the drought exposed a vulnerability that economic incentives had created. The federal government eventually responded by establishing a soil conservation service, which paid farmers to plant windbreaks, rotate crops, and plow along the contours of the land, practices that remain influential today.

pac03de4466.title: Lina Plants a Seed
pac03de4466.text:
On Monday, Lina put a bean seed in a cup of soil. She gave it a little water and set it by the window.

On Wednesday, she saw a tiny green sprout. On Friday, two small leaves opened up. Lina was so happy!

The next week, the plant grew taller than her pencil. Lina moved it to a big pot outside. At the end of the month, the plant had its first bean.

p7cd69bb365.title: Ibn Battuta: A Life on the Road
p7cd69bb365.text:
Ibn Battuta was born in Tangier, Morocco, in 1304. When he was twenty-one, he left home to make the pilgrimage to Makkah, a journey he expected to take about a year and a half.

Instead, he kept traveling for nearly thirty years. After visiting Makkah, he explored Iraq and Persia, sailed down the coast of East Africa, and later crossed Central Asia to reach India, where he worked as a judge for several years. From there, he traveled by sea to China.

In 1349, he finally returned to Morocco. A few years later, the sultan asked a writer to record his adventures. The book they created, known as the Rihla, still helps historians understand the world of the fourteenth century.

p0062d25189.title: The Starting Block
p0062d25189.text:
Reem stood motionless on the starting block and stared at the still blue water of the competition pool. The whistle would blow in less than a minute, and her heart was pounding so loudly that she was certain the swimmer beside her could hear it.

She remembered the first time she had tried to swim, six years earlier, at the beach near Jeddah. A small wave had knocked her over, and she had run back to her father, coughing and refusing to go anywhere near the sea again. That evening, he had patiently promised to teach her gradually, one careful step at a time.

Now, as the official raised the silver whistle, Reem took a slow, deliberate breath, exactly as her father had taught her. When the whistle finally blew, she dove forward, and the cool water closed over her like an old and familiar friend.

pe1fdfd5723.title: How Paper Traveled the World
pe1fdfd5723.text:
According to tradition, paper was invented in China around the year 105, when an official named Cai Lun mixed tree bark, hemp, and old rags into a pulp and pressed it into thin sheets. For more than six centuries, the technique remained largely unknown outside East Asia.

That changed in the middle of the eighth century, when papermaking reached Samarkand in Central Asia. Within a few decades, the first paper mill opened in Baghdad, and paper rapidly replaced expensive parchment in government offices, libraries, and schools. Scholars in the House of Wisdom could now copy translations of scientific works far more cheaply than before.

From Baghdad, the craft spread to Damascus and Cairo and then across North Africa to Spain, where the earliest paper mills of Europe appeared in the twelfth century.

[Timeline: 105 China, 751 Samarkand, 794 Baghdad, 1100s Spain]

p80a3f6196f.title: The Cracked Compass
p80a3f6196f.text:
Thirty years later, I still keep the cracked compass on my desk, and visitors always ask why I have never replaced it. The answer lies in a single afternoon in the Empty Quarter, when I was a nineteen-year-old assistant and considerably more confident than experienced.

Our survey team had set out at dawn to map a line of dunes that shifted every season. By noon, a sandstorm had swallowed the horizon, and our vehicle's satellite receiver had failed. My supervisor, an elderly geologist named Sulaiman, calmly removed an old brass compass from his pocket and asked me to guide us back to camp.

For four hours I walked ahead, checking the needle every few minutes while the others followed my footprints. When the storm finally lifted, our tents stood barely a kilometer to the east, exactly where the needle had indicated. That evening, Sulaiman handed me the compass, which he had dropped years earlier on a rock, and told me that instruments break, but judgment must not.

p281f750ee5.title: Measuring the Earth
p281f750ee5.text:
Honored guests, the instruments in this hall tell a story that stretches across more than two thousand years. Around 240 BCE, Eratosthenes of Alexandria estimated the circumference of the Earth by comparing the angle of shadows in two Egyptian cities, an extraordinary achievement for a scholar armed only with geometry.

Roughly a millennium later, the caliph al-Ma'mun dispatched teams of astronomers to the plain of Sinjar, where they measured a single degree of latitude by walking north and south with ropes and rods. Two centuries afterward, al-Biruni devised an ingenious alternative: by measuring the angle to the horizon from a mountaintop, he calculated the radius of the Earth without crossing a desert at all.

Today, satellites determine these dimensions to within millimeters. Yet I invite you to notice that each method was built upon the questions of its predecessors. Progress, in other words, is rarely a sudden leap; it is a conversation conducted across centuries.

p11ccdb8452.title: Camels and Horses
p11ccdb8452.text:
Camels and horses both have four long legs. People ride both of them. But they are not the same.

A camel has a hump on its back. The hump stores fat. A camel can walk for days in the hot desert without drinking. Its wide feet do not sink in the sand.

A horse has no hump. A horse needs to drink water every day. It runs very fast on hard ground.

p3ad03eb95b.title: Keeping Cool: Then and Now
p3ad03eb95b.text:
Long before electricity, builders in hot places like Dubai and Bahrain used wind towers to cool their homes. A wind tower is a tall, open structure on the roof. It catches breezes from any direction and sends them down into the rooms below, while warm air rises and escapes.

Today, most buildings in the Gulf use air conditioners instead. Like wind towers, air conditioners move air through a building. However, they also cool the air with machines, so rooms can stay cold even on a still, scorching afternoon.

Each method has strengths. Air conditioners work in any weather, but they use large amounts of electricity. Wind towers use no electricity at all, although they cannot cool a room when there is no wind. Some modern architects are now combining both ideas.

pcffbfff4c1.title: Two Sea Explorers
pcffbfff4c1.text:
Ahmad ibn Majid and Zheng He both sailed the Indian Ocean in the fifteenth century, yet their voyages could hardly have been more different.

Zheng He, an admiral of the Ming dynasty, commanded enormous fleets of more than two hundred ships carrying nearly thirty thousand sailors. The emperor sent him on these trips to show the power of China and to set up trade with distant kingdoms.

Ibn Majid, by contrast, was a navigator from the Arabian coast who sailed with small crews and relied on expert knowledge rather than numbers. He studied the stars, the winds, and the coastlines with great care. He wrote nearly forty books about sailing, including detailed guides to the monsoon seasons.

Although the fleets of Zheng He were far grander, both men understood the ocean well, and both helped connect the peoples along its shores.

p7e3f4beacf.title: Two Sources of Water
p7e3f4beacf.text:
Text 1: Saudi Arabia produces more desalinated water than almost any other country. Desalination plants remove salt from seawater, providing a reliable supply that does not depend on rainfall. However, the process consumes large amounts of energy, and the leftover brine, which can be about twice as salty as seawater, can harm marine life when it is returned to the sea.

Text 2: Treated wastewater offers another source. Water from homes is cleaned in several stages until it is safe for irrigating parks, farms, and highway landscaping. Recycling requires far less energy than desalination, and it reduces the amount of waste flowing into the sea. Its main limitation is public acceptance, since many people are uncomfortable with the idea of reusing water, even when it meets strict safety standards.

p710d1bf140.title: Observation and System
p710d1bf140.text:
Abu Bakr al-Razi and Ibn Sina are often mentioned together as the greatest physicians of the medieval Islamic world, and both produced works that European universities studied for centuries. Their temperaments, however, led them toward strikingly different contributions.

Al-Razi, who directed a hospital in Baghdad, was above all an observer. He recorded individual cases in meticulous detail, and his treatise distinguishing smallpox from measles relied on careful comparison of symptoms rather than on the authority of earlier writers, whom he openly criticized when their claims conflicted with the experiences of his patients.

Ibn Sina, writing about a century later, was primarily a systematizer. His Canon of Medicine organized the medical knowledge of Greek, Persian, and Indian traditions into a single coherent framework, a structure so comprehensive that it served as a standard textbook for more than five hundred years.

One physician questioned inherited knowledge; the other arranged it. Medicine, arguably, required both.

p679072bb06.title: Reviving the Lost
p679072bb06.text:
Text 1: Advances in genetic engineering may soon allow scientists to restore animals that vanished centuries ago. Proponents contend that reviving a species such as the woolly mammoth could restore ecological functions lost with its extinction, since grazing giants once maintained the grasslands of the far north. Moreover, the research itself generates techniques that could strengthen endangered populations whose genetic diversity has dwindled.

Text 2: The prospect of resurrecting extinct animals is undeniably captivating, but it risks diverting attention and funding from species that can still be saved. A revived animal would also lack the habitat, the companions, and the learned behaviors that its ancestors possessed; a creature raised in a laboratory is, at best, an approximation. Conservation, critics argue, should prioritize protecting the ecosystems that remain rather than reconstructing those already lost.

p4119efd162.title: The Camel
p4119efd162.text:
A camel is a big desert animal. It has long legs and a long neck. Its fur is brown like sand. A camel has one or two humps on its back. The hump holds fat, not water. This fat gives the camel energy when there is no food.

A camel has thick lips. It can eat plants with sharp thorns. It has long eyelashes too. They keep sand out of its eyes. Its wide feet do not sink in the soft sand. A camel is made for desert life.

p751d709b04.title: A Garden Under the Red Sea
p751d709b04.text:
Just below the surface of the Red Sea lies a garden that no farmer planted. Coral reefs stretch along the coast of Saudi Arabia for hundreds of kilometers, and they are among the most colorful places on Earth.

From a distance, a reef looks like a field of rocks and plants. Up close, however, it is alive. Each coral is made of thousands of tiny animals called polyps. Some corals branch like the antlers of a deer, while others are round and wrinkled like a giant brain.

The reef is also crowded with visitors. Striped clownfish hide among the soft arms of sea anemones, while parrotfish, painted bright blue and green, scrape algae from the coral with their beak-like teeth. Below them, sea turtles glide slowly over patches of white sand.

At night the garden changes again, as many corals stretch out tiny tentacles to catch food drifting in the water.

p2dc30e8569.title: Dawn in the Empty Quarter
p2dc30e8569.text:
Faisal woke before the others and climbed the dune behind the camp, where the Empty Quarter lay below him, silent and enormous, still blue with the last shadows of night.

At first the sand looked like a frozen sea, with long ridges rolling toward the horizon, each one curved like the back of a wave about to break. Then the sun lifted over the eastern dunes, and the colors began to change: the blue turned violet, the violet turned rose, and finally the whole desert glowed the color of ripe apricots.

Now Faisal noticed small details that he had completely missed in the darkness. Tiny tracks stitched the slope beside him, where a beetle had wandered during the night. A lizard, pale as the sand itself, rested motionless on a flat stone to warm its body in the early light. Even the air seemed different; it was cool and sharp now, but he knew that within two hours it would press down like a heavy blanket.

He stayed on the ridge until the shadows shrank, trying to memorize every shape before the heat arrived.

p00e3c26415.title: A Letter from the Souq
p00e3c26415.text:
Dear Lina, I am writing from a café at the edge of the Mutrah Souq in Muscat, and I wish you could experience this extraordinary place with me. The market is not one wide street but a maze of narrow lanes covered by a carved wooden roof, so the light falls in thin golden stripes across the floor.

Every lane seems to possess its own distinctive personality. In the first, the shops are crowded with brass coffee pots and decorated silver daggers that flash whenever a customer walks past. The next lane belongs entirely to the cloth merchants, whose bolts of silk hang from the ceiling like colorful waterfalls. Farther in, the air grows heavy with frankincense, the pale, fragrant resin that Oman has exported to distant civilizations for thousands of years.

The sounds are just as rich as the sights: shopkeepers calling out prices, the rattle of a delivery cart, and the clink of tiny tea glasses.

Before I leave, I will choose a jar of saffron for you, since the merchant promised it was the finest in the entire market.

Your cousin, Reem

pc9274a6a73.title: The Astrolabe
pc9274a6a73.text:
Few scientific instruments are as beautiful as the astrolabe, a flat brass disk that astronomers in the Islamic world refined into a remarkably precise tool between the eighth and thirteenth centuries.

The body of the instrument, called the mater, is a thick plate with a raised rim engraved with the hours or degrees. Inside the mater rest one or more thin plates, each carved with lines of altitude and direction calculated for a particular latitude. A traveler moving from Baghdad to Cordoba simply exchanged one plate for another.

Above these plates sits the rete, an openwork frame whose curving pointers mark the positions of bright stars. Because the rete is mostly empty space, the user can see the lines beneath it while rotating it to match the night sky. On the back, a sighting rule called the alidade pivots across the disk, allowing an observer to measure the height of a star or the sun.

Together, these layered parts turned a single object into a calculator, a clock, and a map of the heavens.

p7ad41d2cbe.title: The Tide-Line Forest
p7ad41d2cbe.text:
At low tide, a tropical mangrove forest reveals an architecture that is usually hidden beneath the water. Hundreds of slender roots arch outward from each trunk like the ribs of an unfinished boat, anchoring the trees in sediment so soft and unstable that a careless visitor sinks to the ankle.

Around these arches rises a stranger feature: thousands of pencil-thin shoots called pneumatophores, which poke upward from the mud in orderly ranks. Although they resemble the stubble of a harvested field, they are breathing tubes, drawing oxygen into roots that would otherwise suffocate in the airless sediment.

The leaves, thick and waxy, are frequently encrusted with minute white crystals. These crystals are not frost but salt, which the trees deliberately excrete through specialized glands in order to survive in water that would poison most terrestrial vegetation.

Within this tangled framework, animal life is remarkably dense. Fiddler crabs brandish their oversized claws, juvenile fish shelter among the submerged roots, and herons stand motionless, waiting with extraordinary patience. The forest, in short, is less a collection of trees than a single, intricately engineered shelter.

p5a44bd14d5.title: The Thirsty Plants
p5a44bd14d5.text:
Our class has a small garden. We planted beans in the spring. But soon the leaves turned brown. The plants were too dry. Some days nobody gave them water.

Mr. Adel asked, "How can we fix this?" Lama had an idea. "Let's make a chart," she said. Each day, two children would water the garden. We wrote our names on the chart. We hung it by the door.

Now the beans get water every day. Their leaves are green again. We will pick beans soon!

pdc82854e3d.title: Plastic on the Beach
pdc82854e3d.text:
Every weekend, families visit the beach near the town of Al-Wajh. For years, however, the visitors left something behind: plastic bottles, bags, and food wrappers. The wind carried this trash into the water, where sea turtles sometimes mistook floating bags for jellyfish, a food that some turtles eat.

A group of students at the local middle school decided to act. First, they counted the trash on one stretch of sand and found more than 400 pieces in a single morning. Then they presented their numbers to the town council and suggested two changes.

The council agreed to place large recycling bins every hundred meters along the beach. The students also painted colorful signs that explained how plastic harms turtles. Six months later, the students counted again. This time, they found fewer than 80 pieces of trash.

p2cb4130a7c.title: The Locust Alarm
p2cb4130a7c.text:
For thousands of years, farmers across North Africa and the Arabian Peninsula have feared the desert locust. Usually this grasshopper lives alone and causes little harm. After heavy rains, however, locusts multiply rapidly, crowd together, and transform into enormous swarms that can devour as much food in a single day as millions of people eat.

The greatest difficulty has always been timing. By the time a swarm darkens the sky, it is often too late to protect the crops below. Farmers needed a way to detect locusts before they gathered.

Today, scientists use a warning system that combines several tools. Satellites measure rainfall and identify patches of green vegetation in remote deserts, where young locusts are likely to hatch. Field teams then travel to those locations and report what they find using handheld tablets. When the reports show that locusts are gathering, governments can treat a small area early instead of battling a giant swarm later.

The system is not perfect, because war and distance sometimes keep teams from reaching the desert. Still, it has prevented many disasters.

p4e508419fa.title: A Safer Walk to School
p4e508419fa.text:
To the Members of the Al-Noor District Council:

Every morning, more than three hundred students cross King Fahd Street to reach Al-Noor Intermediate School. The street has four lanes, and drivers frequently travel well above the speed limit because there is no traffic signal for nearly two kilometers. Last month alone, parents reported three incidents in which children were nearly struck by speeding cars.

Our student council has studied this situation carefully and proposes a practical solution. First, the district should install a pedestrian crossing with a flashing signal directly in front of the school gate. Second, trained crossing guards, perhaps volunteer parents, could assist younger students during the busiest thirty minutes of each morning and afternoon.

Some residents worry that a signal will slow traffic. However, the signal would operate only when a pedestrian presses the button, so delays would last less than a minute.

We respectfully request that the council discuss our proposal at its next meeting.

Sincerely, The Student Council of Al-Noor Intermediate School

pe86e68563f.title: Harvesting the Clouds
pe86e68563f.text:
Thank you for inviting me to speak about water, a subject that matters more in this region than almost any other.

In the mountain villages of southwestern Morocco, rain is scarce, and for generations women and girls walked for hours each day to collect water from distant wells. That journey consumed time that could have been spent in school or at work, and the water itself was often unreliable.

Yet these mountains possess an unusual resource: for roughly half the year, thick fog drifts in from the Atlantic and settles on the slopes. Engineers realized that if they could capture even a fraction of that moisture, the villages would have a dependable supply.

The solution was surprisingly simple: tall panels of fine mesh stretched between poles. As the fog passes through, tiny droplets cling to the mesh, merge, and trickle into gutters that feed a pipeline to the village, so that on a good day the system collects thousands of liters.

Fog nets will not eliminate drought everywhere, but they remind us that solutions often begin with careful observation of the resources we already have.

p21f2b341ab.title: Cooling the City
p21f2b341ab.text:
As cities in the Gulf expand, they are becoming measurably hotter than the surrounding desert, particularly at night. Asphalt, concrete, and dark rooftops absorb solar radiation throughout the day and release it slowly after sunset, so neighborhoods that should cool down remain uncomfortably warm. Residents respond by running air conditioners continuously, which consumes enormous quantities of electricity and, ironically, releases still more heat into the streets.

Two remedies are frequently proposed. The first, reflective roofing, coats buildings with pale materials that bounce sunlight back into the atmosphere; it is inexpensive and can be applied almost immediately. The second, planting shade trees, requires irrigation and patience, since a sapling may need a decade to cast meaningful shade.

Policymakers tempted by the quicker option should resist treating these remedies as rivals. Reflective roofs lower indoor temperatures but do little for pedestrians on scorching sidewalks, whereas trees cool the street itself through shade and evaporation. A sensible strategy therefore combines both, pairing immediate relief with a long-term investment in the city's livability.

p876bc97297.title: Date Balls with Grandma
p876bc97297.text:
Grandma and I made date balls today. First, we washed our hands. Next, we took the seeds out of the dates. Then we mashed the dates in a big bowl. After that, we rolled the soft dates into small balls. Last, we rolled each ball in coconut.

We put the date balls on a big plate. At dinner we shared them with the whole family. Everyone wanted more! Grandma smiled and said we can make them again next week.

pe6cd9cbfbe.title: A Sea Turtle's Journey
pe6cd9cbfbe.text:
On a warm summer night, a female green turtle crawls out of the Red Sea onto a quiet beach. She digs a deep hole in the sand with her back flippers and lays about one hundred eggs. Then she covers the nest and returns to the water.

For about two months, the eggs stay buried, warmed by the sun. When the hatchlings finally break out of their shells, they wait beneath the sand until night, when the air is cooler. Then they scramble toward the bright horizon over the sea.

Once they reach the waves, the tiny turtles swim for days without stopping, and they spend their first years drifting in the open ocean, eating small animals. Later, as young adults, they move to shallow waters to graze on seagrass.

After twenty or more years, the females return to the same beach where they hatched to lay eggs of their own.

p097e6e3079.title: The Long Road of Ibn Battuta
p097e6e3079.text:
In 1325, a twenty-one-year-old scholar named Ibn Battuta left his home in Tangier, Morocco, intending to make the pilgrimage to Mecca. He expected to be gone for about a year and a half. Instead, he would not see Tangier again for twenty-four years.

After completing the pilgrimage, Ibn Battuta kept traveling. During the next decade, he sailed down the coast of East Africa, crossed Anatolia, and journeyed through Central Asia. In 1334 he reached Delhi, where the sultan appointed him a judge, a position he held for nearly eight years.

Later, the sultan sent him as an ambassador to China. The journey was dangerous: he lost a ship in a storm and was robbed more than once before finally reaching the Chinese port of Quanzhou.

He returned to Morocco in 1349, but his travels were not finished. Within a few years he had crossed the Sahara to visit the kingdom of Mali. Finally, around 1355, he dictated the story of his journeys to a writer, creating one of the most famous travel books in history.

p6ea9c4f025.title: The Pearl Diver's Hands
p6ea9c4f025.text:
Yousef watched his grandfather turn the small pearl slowly between his fingers, studying it as carefully as a jeweler would. The old man's hands were scarred and spotted from decades of hard labor, but they moved with surprising tenderness.

"I found this one in 1958," Grandfather said quietly, and his eyes drifted toward the window, toward the restless gray sea.

He had been fourteen that summer, the youngest diver on his uncle's boat. Each dawn the crew sailed out from the harbor at Muharraq, and each day he dove again and again, a stone tied to his foot to carry him down quickly. On the forty-third day, exhausted and discouraged, he pried open an oyster and saw a soft gleam inside.

Grandfather blinked, and the memory faded. Then, deliberately, he placed the pearl in Yousef's open palm and folded the boy's fingers around it.

"The pearling boats disappeared generations ago," he said, "so now you must keep the story, along with the pearl."

Yousef held the pearl carefully, already imagining the distant day when he would describe that difficult summer to someone else.

p900a6cc9a5.title: The Road of Paper
p900a6cc9a5.text:
Paper was invented in China, where by the second century CE craftsmen were pressing mulberry bark and hemp fibers into thin, durable sheets. For roughly six hundred years, the technique remained largely unknown beyond East Asia.

A widely repeated tradition holds that the secret traveled west after the Battle of Talas in 751, when Chinese prisoners brought papermaking to Samarkand. Historians now doubt that a single battle was responsible, but there is no question that Samarkand soon became famous for its paper.

From Central Asia the craft spread rapidly through the Abbasid world. By 794, a paper mill was operating in Baghdad, and government offices began replacing expensive parchment with the cheaper material. Over the following centuries, paper was being manufactured in Damascus, Cairo, and the cities of Muslim Spain, fueling an extraordinary expansion of libraries and scholarship.

Europe adopted paper comparatively late. The first mills north of the Pyrenees appeared only in the thirteenth century, roughly a thousand years after the Chinese invention. When the printing press arrived in the fifteenth century, it depended entirely on this long chain of transmission.

pf366b0a880.title: The Measure of the Earth
pf366b0a880.text:
Today, satellites orbiting thousands of kilometers overhead can determine the circumference of the Earth to within a few centimeters, a precision so routine that most people never consider it. Yet the question of the planet's size was answered remarkably well long before any instrument left the ground.

Around 240 BCE, the Greek scholar Eratosthenes noticed that at noon on the summer solstice the sun shone directly into a well at Syene, while in Alexandria it cast a measurable shadow. Combining that angle with the distance between the cities, he calculated a figure that was surprisingly close to the modern value.

More than a thousand years later, in the ninth century, the Abbasid caliph al-Ma'mun dispatched teams of astronomers into the Syrian desert. Walking north and south until the height of the Pole Star changed by one degree, they measured a single degree of latitude directly.

Two centuries afterward, al-Biruni devised an ingenious method that required no long journey at all: from a mountaintop in present-day Pakistan, he measured the angle at which the horizon dipped below him and derived the Earth's radius through trigonometry.

p6f51ad1cd9.title: The Big Sand Castle
p6f51ad1cd9.text:
Lina and Adam went to the beach. They both wanted to build a sand castle. Lina wanted a tall tower. Adam wanted a long wall.

"My idea is better," said Lina. "No, mine is," said Adam. They each built alone. Lina's tower fell down. A wave washed away Adam's wall.

Then Adam had an idea. "Let's build the tower behind the wall," he said. Lina helped him. The wall kept the waves away, and the tower stood tall. They smiled at their castle. It was the best one on the beach.

p62e21c7c30.title: The Falcon and the Sparrow
p62e21c7c30.text:
High above the shifting desert dunes, a young falcon named Saqr loved to boast. "I am the fastest and strongest bird in the sky," he announced, "and I will never need assistance from anyone." The smaller birds rolled their eyes at his arrogance, but they said nothing.

One afternoon, a violent sandstorm swept across the dunes, and the air turned so brown that Saqr could no longer see the ground beneath him. He flew in confused circles until his powerful wings ached with exhaustion. Then, through the howling wind, he heard a tiny voice calling, "Follow my song, because I know a sheltered cave between the rocks."

Saqr followed the sound and landed safely inside the cave beside a small, dusty sparrow. When the storm finally passed, he looked at the little bird for a long time. "Being fast did not save me," he admitted quietly, "but being humble enough to listen did." From that day on, Saqr thanked the small birds whenever he passed them in the sky.

p438d063ad9.title: The Date Palm
p438d063ad9.text:
In the corner of my grandmother's courtyard stands a palm she planted when she was a girl, a thin green promise in the sand.

She watered it for years and gathered nothing, while her neighbors laughed and asked her why she worked so hard for a tree that gave no fruit.

She only smiled and kept the bucket moving, morning after morning, through summers when the wells grew low and the wind arrived like a furnace.

Now the palm is taller than the roof, and every autumn its heavy branches bend with golden dates that feed the whole street.

The neighbors' children climb it, laughing, and they never ask who planted it, and my grandmother says that this is exactly how it should be.

p13e5083251.title: The Robotics Final
p13e5083251.text:
[A school workshop after a robotics competition. FAHAD and MARYAM stand beside a robot whose mechanical arm failed during the final demonstration.]

FAHAD: (throwing down a screwdriver) It's finished, Maryam, because the arm froze completely in front of the judges, and every competitor in the auditorium watched our invention collapse.

MARYAM: (kneeling beside the robot and examining the wiring) It froze because the battery connection came loose, which is a small mechanical problem rather than an unrecoverable disaster.

FAHAD: Small? We devoted four months of afternoons and weekends to this machine, and it humiliated us in thirty seconds.

MARYAM: (holding up the disconnected wire) And in those thirty seconds we discovered something that four months of comfortable practice never revealed, so next season we'll fasten every connection twice and test everything under pressure.

FAHAD: (after a long pause, sitting down beside her) Do you honestly believe there will be a next season for us?

MARYAM: There's always another opportunity, if you decide there is one. (She offers him the screwdriver.) Begin with the battery.

[FAHAD hesitates, then picks up the screwdriver and begins to work.]

p97641ee318.title: The Mapmaker's Apprentice
p97641ee318.text:
Yusuf had copied maps in the workshop of the elderly cartographer for three patient years before he was permitted to draw an original coastline of his own. His first attempt, he believed, was flawless: every bay was graceful, every cape was perfectly symmetrical, and the decorative lettering flowed like water across the expensive parchment.

The cartographer studied it for a long, uncomfortable moment. "It is beautiful," he said, "and it is entirely useless." He unrolled a sailor's battered navigational chart, smudged with salt and corrected in a dozen different inks. "This coast is ugly, because the real coast is ugly, and a captain who trusts your lovely illustration will discover jagged rocks precisely where you have drawn gentle sand."

Yusuf spent the following season aboard fishing vessels, measuring depths with a weighted rope and sketching treacherous headlands in the rain. His second map was crowded and irregular, its margins scarred with corrections. When a captain returned it the following spring, worn soft from constant use, Yusuf understood that it was the finest thing he had ever created.

p7dc9369a7f.title: The Translator
p7dc9369a7f.text:
For forty years my grandfather translated scientific manuscripts from Arabic into Latin for a library in a distant city, and for forty years his name appeared on none of them. The astronomers and physicians whose discoveries he carried across languages became celebrated throughout the universities of Europe; he remained an unassuming man with ink-stained fingers who returned home each evening along the identical narrow passageway.

As a child I found this arrangement unbearable. I once demanded to know why he refused to sign his pages, and he regarded me with genuine puzzlement. "A translator who is noticed," he said, "has failed, because if the reader sees me, he cannot see Ibn al-Haytham."

I did not accept his explanation then. I was young enough to believe that public recognition was the only reliable proof of a life's worth, and I pitied him. Only decades later, reading a treatise on optics in which every sentence was lucid, meticulous, and unobtrusive, did I realize that I was holding his work. I could not detect him anywhere in it, and that invisibility, I finally understood, was precisely his achievement.

pc9e56b6e24.title: Camels: Ships of the Desert
pc9e56b6e24.text:
Camels are good at living in the hot desert. Their wide feet do not sink into the soft sand. Their long eyelashes keep the blowing sand out of their eyes.

A camel can walk for many days without drinking any water. When it finds water, it can drink a lot very fast. The hump on its back holds fat. The camel uses this fat for energy when there is little food to eat.

For a very long time, people have used camels to carry things across the desert. That is why camels are called ships of the desert.

pc8ccf9c52a.title: The Elephant Clock
pc8ccf9c52a.text:
More than eight hundred years ago, an engineer named Ismail al-Jazari worked for a ruler in what is now southeastern Turkey. He spent his life designing clever machines, and he wrote a famous book that explained exactly how to build them.

One of his most impressive inventions was a giant water clock shaped like an elephant. Inside the elephant, a bowl with a small hole slowly sank into a tank of water. Every half hour, the sinking bowl pulled strings that released a ball, and a cymbal sounded to announce the time.

Al-Jazari's book had careful drawings and step-by-step instructions. Other builders could copy his ideas. Many historians believe his designs for gears, valves, and pumps helped later engineers create modern machines. Today, a working model of the elephant clock stands in a shopping center in Dubai. Visitors still watch it mark the time.

p72a2d36a43.title: Coral Reefs of the Red Sea
p72a2d36a43.text:
The coral reefs of the Red Sea are among the toughest on Earth, and scientists are studying them to understand how reefs elsewhere might survive a warming ocean. In many tropical regions, warmer water makes corals push out the tiny algae that live inside them and feed them, a process called bleaching that can leave entire reefs pale and dying.

Northern Red Sea corals, however, seem to handle heat that would destroy reefs in other seas. One explanation is history: thousands of years ago, the ancestors of these corals traveled north through the very hot waters at the southern entrance of the sea, and only the toughest survived the journey.

Researchers now collect samples from these corals and test them in tanks, slowly raising the heat. Their results suggest that the Red Sea may be a safe place for corals, and perhaps a source of knowledge that could help protect reefs around the world.

p486d77921e.title: Why Teenagers Stay Up Late
p486d77921e.text:
Many adults think that teenagers who stay up late are simply lazy, but research on adolescent biology tells a more complicated story. During puberty, the brain begins releasing melatonin, the hormone that signals sleepiness, roughly two hours later than it did in childhood. As a result, a fifteen-year-old who lies in bed at ten o'clock may stare at the ceiling for hours, not because of laziness but because of chemistry.

This biological shift collides with early school schedules. Students who must wake at six o'clock frequently sleep fewer than seven hours, although specialists recommend between eight and ten.
