The consequences extend far beyond yawning: constantly tired teenagers have more difficulty concentrating, remembering new information, and managing their emotions.

Some schools have responded by starting classes later in the morning. In several districts that adopted this change, attendance improved and students reported feeling more alert during lessons. Families can also help by limiting bright screens in the evening, since artificial light further delays the release of melatonin.

p61e57c9850.title: The Paper Mills of Baghdad
p61e57c9850.text:
When papermaking reached Baghdad in the late eighth century, it transformed the intellectual life of the Abbasid capital. Before paper, scholars depended on parchment, which required the skins of numerous animals and was therefore expensive, or on papyrus, which was imported from Egypt and deteriorated in humid conditions. Paper, made from linen rags and plant fibers, was cheap and could be produced in huge amounts.

The results were remarkable. Government offices adopted paper for official records, partly because ink on paper could not be scraped away and altered without leaving visible traces. Book markets grew, and copyists could reproduce a lengthy manuscript within weeks rather than months. Scholars at the House of Wisdom translated Greek, Persian, and Indian works into Arabic, and those translations circulated widely because paper made duplication affordable.

[Timeline: about 751, papermaking knowledge reaches Samarkand; about 794, first Baghdad paper mill; 900s, paper is widely used across the Islamic world; 1100s, papermaking spreads to Spain.]

Historians sometimes describe paper as a humble technology, yet in Baghdad it functioned as the infrastructure upon which an entire culture of learning was constructed.

p1bed043e85.title: The Neglected Art of Maintenance
p1bed043e85.text:
Societies tend to celebrate invention and neglect maintenance. Ribbon-cutting ceremonies accompany the opening of every bridge, hospital, and water network, but no comparable ceremony honors the engineer who inspects corroded cables or the technician who replaces a failing pump before it disrupts an entire neighborhood. This imbalance is not merely a matter of recognition; it shapes budgets, careers, and ultimately the reliability of the infrastructure on which ordinary life depends.

Consider city water systems. Engineers estimate that many cities lose a large share of their clean water through leaking pipes, a loss that stays invisible because it happens underground. Fixing those pipes rarely excites politicians, whereas constructing an impressive desalination plant generates headlines, even when fixing existing leaks would deliver comparable water at a fraction of the cost.

None of this implies that innovation is unimportant. Rather, a technology's value depends on its continued functioning, and a culture that rewards only novelty will gradually inherit a landscape of magnificent, deteriorating machines.

p122c0475cd.title: Rain in the Desert
p122c0475cd.text:
Dark clouds came over the desert. The air felt cool and wet. Then big drops of rain fell on the sand. Plink, plink, plink!

Reem ran outside with her little brother. The rain was cold on their arms. The sand turned dark brown. It smelled fresh and new.

The next day, little green plants popped up. Tiny yellow flowers opened in the sun. Reem smiled. The desert looked like a garden.

p99a43e0f41.title: The Night Market
p99a43e0f41.text:
As the sun sank behind the old city wall, the empty square slowly came alive. Merchants unrolled striped carpets across the stones, and lanterns of red, blue, and amber glass swayed from wooden poles above their heads.

Khalid followed his uncle through the crowd, breathing in the sharp scent of cardamom and the warm sweetness of fresh bread. On his left, a spice seller scooped orange turmeric into paper cones, and the powder drifted up like tiny clouds of dust. On his right, a man tapped a copper pot with a small hammer, and each ring echoed off the walls.

When they reached the far corner, Khalid stopped. An old storyteller sat on a cushion, his white beard glowing in the lantern light. Around him, a circle of children leaned forward so quietly that Khalid could hear the lanterns creak in the breeze.

p24993e44f8.title: The Pearl Diver
p24993e44f8.text:
Before the sun has climbed above the water, my grandfather lowers himself from the wooden dhow, a stone tied to his ankle and a clip of turtle shell pinching his nose.

The surface closes over him like a door of green glass, and the noise of the gulls and the creaking ropes fades into a heavy, humming silence.

Down he sinks through ribbons of light that tremble and bend, past silver fish that scatter like coins tossed from a careless hand.

On the seabed he moves slowly, the sand rising around his fingers in soft gray clouds, as he pries the rough oysters loose and drops them into the basket at his chest.

When his lungs begin to burn, he tugs the rope, and the men above haul him upward into the blinding gold of morning, gasping, dripping, and laughing at the sky.

p52d89d35dd.title: Fog on the Plateau
p52d89d35dd.text:
By midafternoon, the fog that had been resting quietly in the valleys below the Asir plateau began to climb. At first it moved in thin, curling threads that slipped between the juniper trees, but within minutes it had thickened into a pale wall that swallowed the trail ahead of us.

Hessa stopped so abruptly that I nearly collided with her overstuffed backpack. The terraced fields we had admired all morning, stepping down the mountainside like a giant green staircase, had vanished entirely. Even the baboons that had been barking from the cliffs had fallen silent, and the only sound was the steady drip of moisture from the branches above our heads.

I reached out and could barely see my own fingers. The air was cold and damp against my face, and it carried the faint, bitter smell of wet stone. Hessa pulled the compass from her pocket, its needle trembling, and we continued cautiously forward, one deliberate step at a time.

p27d297bcb5.title: The Glassblower
p27d297bcb5.text:
The workshop was little more than a cave of heat. At its center the furnace roared behind a round opening no larger than a dinner plate, and the light that poured from it was not red or orange but a fierce, trembling white that made the surrounding walls seem to waver like reflections in a pool.

The glassblower, a slight man whose forearms were freckled with tiny burn scars, dipped a long iron pipe into the furnace and withdrew a glowing bead of molten glass, sagging at the tip like honey reluctant to fall. He turned the pipe constantly, almost lazily, and blew into its far end with a single patient breath. The bead swelled into a translucent bubble, faintly blue, through which I could see the distorted outline of the doorway behind him.

Then, with a pair of blackened tongs, he pinched and pulled the softened glass, and within a minute a delicate vase stood cooling on the bench, still ticking softly as it released its heat.

pbd4d679da1.title: Dawn in the Empty Quarter
pbd4d679da1.text:
Nothing in the Empty Quarter prepares a traveler for the abruptness of its dawns. For hours the dunes lie under a darkness so complete that their enormous ridges can be sensed only as an absence of stars along the horizon; then, within minutes, a thin seam of copper appears in the east, and the desert assembles itself out of shadow.

The first crests to catch the light ignite like the edges of burning paper, while the hollows between them remain a deep, bruised violet. As the sun rises, the boundary between light and shadow slides down each slope with the deliberateness of a tide, revealing ripples in the sand so regular that they resemble the grain of polished wood.

The silence, which at night felt protective, becomes immense and slightly unnerving in daylight. Without trees, buildings, or any object of familiar size, the eye cannot judge distance, and a dune that appears to be a short walk away may require the entire morning to reach.

questions.stem: Select the sentence from “The Paper Question” that casts doubt on the traditional answer about how paper reached the Islamic world.

segments.text: Historians have long debated a deceptively simple question: why did paper, invented in China centuries earlier, transform intellectual life so rapidly once it reached the Islamic world?
The conventional explanation credits a single event, the capture of Chinese papermakers after the Battle of Talas in 751, who supposedly taught their craft in Samarkand.
Recent scholarship, however, regards this account as too tidy, noting that paper was probably already circulating in Central Asia through ordinary commerce.
Whatever its precise route, paper's subsequent success depended less on its arrival than on the institutions prepared to exploit it.

questions.why: “However” and “too tidy” signal that recent scholars question the Talas story; “supposedly” only hints at doubt.

options.label: A

options.label: B
options.text: by claiming that ordinary commerce alone explains paper's success

options.label: C

partB.stem: Part B: Which sentence from the passage best supports the answer to Part A?

questions.why: The author locates the answer in institutions ready to exploit paper, not in its route or durability.

questions.stem: Which word best describes the author's attitude toward closing the library in summer?
options: indifferent
sympathetic

questions.stem: Select the sentence from “Keep the Library Open” in which the author introduces an opposing view.

segments.text: Every June, our town library closes its doors for the whole summer.
Teachers notice the difference in September, when some students have forgotten skills they worked hard to learn.
Some people argue that keeping the library open costs too much money.
A library is not just a building full of books.

questions.stem: True or false: In “Keep the Library Open,” the author treats the cost concern as foolish and not worth answering.

questions.stem: Part A: How does the author respond to the concern about cost?

partA.stem: Part A: How does the author respond to the concern about cost?

options.label: A

questions.stem: Which statement best describes the author's attitude toward desert solar farms?
options: neutral, presenting both sides without taking a side

questions.why: The author answers each objection and ends with “We should use it.”

questions.stem: For “Sunlight Waiting,” classify each idea as a counterargument or the author's response.

rows.text: Desert dust settles on panels and reduces output.
Waterless robots brush away dust each night.
The sun disappears at night.
Batteries can store daytime energy for evening use.

questions.why: Critics raise dust and darkness; the author answers with robots and batteries.

questions.stem: Put the parts of the author's reasoning about dust in “Sunlight Waiting” in order.
sequence: The author states the critics' objection about dust.
The author admits the objection deserves attention.
The author describes a solution engineers developed.
The author notes that plants already use it successfully.

partB.stem: Part B: Which sentence from the passage best supports the answer to Part A?

options.label: A

questions.stem: Select two sentences from “Sunlight Waiting” that most clearly reveal the author's positive attitude toward solar farms.

segments.text: Building large solar farms across these regions is one of the smartest investments the country can make.

The sunlight is free, abundant, and waiting.

questions.why: Judgment words like “smartest” and “free, abundant, and waiting” show attitude; the jobs sentence states a fact.

questions.stem: Which word best describes the author's attitude toward the old mud-brick houses?
options: protective
nostalgic but resigned
critical
indifferent
questions.why: The author argues firmly that the houses must not be destroyed.

questions.stem: Which TWO opposing claims does the author present in “In Defense of Old Walls”? Choose two.

Visitors avoid restored districts.
The old houses are crumbling.
Mud walls cannot stay cool in summer.

care more about modern design than about public safety
judge the houses only by cost instead of by what cannot be replaced
use incorrect numbers when they calculate the cost of repairs

questions.stem: Select the sentence from “Why Reach Beyond Earth?” in which the author makes a concession to opponents.

It proves that finance courses reduce high-interest debt among graduates.
questions.why: A survey of wishes is relevant but reports opinions, not measured results.

questions.stem: For “A Course Every Graduate Needs,” classify each statement as evidence, a counterclaim, or a rebuttal.

rows.text: Graduates of required courses missed fewer loan payments.
Families, not schools, should teach money management.
Many parents cannot pass on knowledge they lack.
Most young adults wish they had learned budgeting in school.

questions.why: Evidence supports the claim; the skeptics' view is the counterclaim; the point about parents answers it.

questions.stem: Select the sentence from “A Course Every Graduate Needs” in which the author limits the claim to make it more reasonable.

segments.text: This gap is not a minor oversight; it is a failure that follows young people into adulthood.
The evidence for such a requirement is substantial.
Leaving financial education to chance simply preserves existing inequalities.
A single required course will not eliminate poor financial decisions.

questions.why: Admitting that one course will not solve everything keeps the claim realistic.

questions.stem: Which statement most precisely expresses the author's claim in “Walls of Roots”?
options: Mangroves and seawalls are equally effective in every setting, so planners should simply choose whichever option costs less.
Where possible, mangroves should be preferred to seawalls, since they protect comparably at lower cost and offer added benefits.
Seawalls are the only dependable protection for urban harbors, so mangroves should be planted only along remote coasts.
Seawalls should be removed from every coastline and replaced with planted mangrove forests as quickly as nations can manage.
questions.why: The author favors mangroves but admits concrete may still be needed in some places, so the claim is qualified.

questions.stem: Part A: Which piece of evidence best supports the idea that mangroves have an advantage seawalls lack as seas rise?

partA.stem: Part A: Which piece of evidence best supports the idea that mangroves have an advantage seawalls lack as seas rise?

options.label: A
options.text: Mangroves store carbon and provide shelter for local fisheries.

options.label: B
options.text: Mangroves trap sediment that lets the forest rise along with the sea.

options.label: C
options.text: Seawalls are easy to visualize and simple for planners to measure.

options.label: D
options.text: Mangroves reduce the height of incoming waves along the coast.

partB.stem: Part B: Which sentence from the passage best supports the answer to Part A?

options.label: A
options.text: Seawalls, by contrast, deteriorate, require expensive maintenance, and frequently accelerate erosion on neighboring beaches by deflecting wave energy.

options.label: B
options.text: Unlike a seawall, the forest also traps sediment that allows it to rise gradually alongside the sea.

options.label: C
options.text: Field measurements consistently show that a dense mangrove belt several hundred meters wide can substantially reduce the height of incoming waves.

options.label: D
options.text: A nation that invests exclusively in concrete purchases a single function, whereas a restored mangrove simultaneously shelters fisheries, stores carbon, and sustains wildlife.

questions.why: Wave reduction is only “comparable” protection; rising with the sea is the advantage tied to rising seas.

questions.stem: Select the sentence from “Walls of Roots” in which the author acknowledges a limitation of the claim.

segments.text: This preference, I contend, is increasingly difficult to justify.
Seawalls, by contrast, deteriorate, require expensive maintenance, and frequently accelerate erosion on neighboring beaches by deflecting wave energy.
Admittedly, mangroves require years to mature and cannot be planted on every coastline; along urban harbors, engineered barriers may remain unavoidable.
Yet this limitation argues for combining approaches, not for abandoning living defenses.

questions.why: “Admittedly” introduces the limitation; the next sentence responds to it rather than stating it.

questions.stem: Which THREE statements identify gaps a careful reader might find in the support for “Walls of Roots”? Choose three.
options: The essay asserts a lower long-term cost but gives no cost figures.
The essay gives no reason why seawalls might harm neighboring beaches.
The essay does not say how many years mangroves need to protect a coast.
The phrase “field measurements consistently show” names no specific study.
The essay never admits that mangroves have any limitations at all.
questions.why: The cost, the studies, and the time to maturity are asserted without specifics; the limitation and the erosion reason are both stated.

questions.stem: For “Walls of Roots,” classify each statement as the author's claim, supporting evidence, or a concession.

rows.text: Planners' preference for seawalls is hard to justify.
Seawalls often speed erosion on nearby beaches.
Engineered barriers may be unavoidable in urban harbors.
A mangrove belt can substantially reduce wave height.

questions.why: The claim judges planners' preference; evidence describes effects; the concession admits where concrete is still needed.

questions.stem: How does the author of “Sea Turtles Need Help” feel about sea turtles?
options: The author loves them and wants them safe.
The author is afraid of them and stays away.
The author thinks they are too slow to watch.
The author wants to keep one as a pet.
questions.why: The author calls them favorite animals and wants to help them.

questions.stem: True or false: The author of “Sea Turtles Need Help” thinks bright lights at night are good for baby turtles.
questions.why: The author says bright lights can make baby turtles get lost.

questions.stem: Select the sentence from “Sea Turtles Need Help” that tells what the author thinks people should do.

segments.text: Sea turtles are my favorite animals.
I think people must help them.
They swim far in the warm sea.
We filled ten bags!

questions.why: The words I think show the author's opinion about what people should do.

questions.stem: Which TWO sentences from “Sea Turtles Need Help” show how the author feels? Choose two.
options: I felt proud.
Sea turtles are my favorite animals.
Mother turtles come to the beach to lay eggs in the sand.
They swim far in the warm sea.
questions.why: Feeling words like proud and favorite show the author's view; the others are facts.

questions.stem: Part A: What does the author of “Sea Turtles Need Help” want readers to do?

partA.stem: Part A: What does the author of “Sea Turtles Need Help” want readers to do?

options.label: A
options.text: Help keep beaches safe for turtles.

options.label: B
options.text: Swim far out in the warm sea.

options.label: C
options.text: Take baby turtles home from the beach.

options.label: D
options.text: Watch turtles lay eggs at night.

partB.stem: Part B: Which sentence from the passage best supports the answer to Part A?

options.label: A
options.text: Mother turtles come to the beach to lay eggs in the sand.

options.label: B
options.text: Last summer, my class cleaned a beach in Jeddah.

options.label: C
options.text: They swim far in the warm sea.

options.label: D
options.text: Every person can do a small job to keep turtles safe.

questions.why: The last sentence asks every reader to help keep turtles safe.

questions.stem: Which statement best describes the author's perspective in “A Letter About Bike Lanes”?
options: Students should move closer to their schools.
Cars are the safest way for young students to travel.
Safe bike lanes would help students and the city.
Bike lanes cost too much money for the city.
questions.why: Layla argues that bike lanes bring cleaner air, less traffic, and healthier students.

questions.stem: In Layla's letter about bike lanes, decide whether each statement is a fact or the author's opinion.

rows.text: Many of my classmates live less than two kilometers away.
Bike lanes would save money in the long run.
Our parents would worry less.
Many children in Copenhagen ride to school.

questions.why: Facts can be checked; opinions show what the author believes.

questions.stem: Which TWO phrases from Layla's letter show the author's negative view of car traffic? Choose two.
options: crawl past my school
a protected bike lane
ready to concentrate on our lessons
filling the air with noise and smoke
questions.why: Words like crawl, noise, and smoke show that the author dislikes the traffic.

questions.stem: Part A: How does Layla respond to people who say bike lanes cost too much?

partA.stem: Part A: How does Layla respond to people who say bike lanes cost too much?

options.label: A
options.text: She says cost does not matter at all.

options.label: B
options.text: She agrees that the cost is far too high.

options.label: C
options.text: She says the money should go to schools.

options.label: D
options.text: She argues they would save money over time.

partB.stem: Part B: Which sentence from the passage best supports the answer to Part A?

options.label: A
options.text: In cities like Copenhagen, many children ride to school every day.

options.label: B
options.text: Many of my classmates live less than two kilometers away, yet almost nobody rides a bicycle.

options.label: C
options.text: Some people say bike lanes cost too much money.

options.label: D
options.text: However, I believe they would save money in the long run.

questions.why: The word However shows she disagrees and gives her own view.

questions.stem: Why does Layla most likely mention Copenhagen in her letter?
options: to show that her idea works in another city
to prove that cars are banned in other places
to compare the weather in two big cities
to explain where she first learned to ride
questions.why: An example from another city supports her view that bike lanes can work.

questions.stem: How does the author's perspective on the desert change in “What the Desert Taught Me”?
options: from enjoying it to wishing to return to the city
from loving camping to preferring life in town
from fearing its animals to studying them closely
from seeing it as empty to seeing it as full of life
questions.why: At first the desert seems empty; by the end the author sees clever survivors everywhere.

questions.stem: In “What the Desert Taught Me,” select the sentence that best shows the author's perspective at the beginning of the essay.

segments.text: The landscape seemed to contain nothing but sand, heat, and an endless, indifferent sky.
My opinion began to change on a camping trip in early winter.
It was crowded with clever survivors; I had simply never learned how to look.
Now, whenever friends from the city complain that nothing interesting ever happens here, I invite them to spend one unforgettable night exploring the dunes.

questions.why: Nothing but sand and an indifferent sky shows the author's first, negative view.

questions.stem: Put the stages of the author's changing perspective in “What the Desert Taught Me” in order.
sequence: The author feels sent away to a boring place.
A guide shows the author signs of hidden desert life.
The author realizes the desert is full of survivors.
The author invites city friends to visit the dunes.
questions.why: The perspective shifts step by step from boredom to understanding to sharing.

questions.stem: Part A: Which statement best describes the author's perspective at the end of “What the Desert Taught Me”?

partA.stem: Part A: Which statement best describes the author's perspective at the end of “What the Desert Taught Me”?

options.label: A
options.text: The desert is too harsh a place for families.

options.label: B
options.text: The desert rewards people who observe it closely.

options.label: C
options.text: City life offers more than desert life does.

options.label: D
options.text: Every desert traveler needs a trained guide.

partB.stem: Part B: Which sentence from the passage best supports the answer to Part A?

options.label: A
options.text: The landscape seemed to contain nothing but sand, heat, and an endless, indifferent sky.

options.label: B
options.text: My opinion began to change on a camping trip in early winter.

options.label: C
options.text: Later he showed me a shrub whose roots stretch many meters down toward hidden water.

options.label: D
options.text: It was crowded with clever survivors; I had simply never learned how to look.

questions.why: The author now believes the desert's life is visible to anyone who learns how to look.

questions.stem: The word “exiled” in paragraph 1 suggests that the author at first felt —
options: excited to explore a brand-new place
forced to leave home against the author's wishes
curious about the history of the town
proud to be living so close to the great dunes
questions.why: To be exiled is to be sent away unwillingly, which shows the author's early resentment.

questions.stem: Which sentence best states the speaker's perspective on the equipment discussed in “Fix It First”?
options: Students should not be trusted with costly tools.
Much of it could be repaired instead of discarded.
All of it should be replaced with newer, better models.
The school should spend more on brand-new fans.
questions.why: The speaker says most items were not truly broken and could be fixed.

questions.stem: Which TWO phrases from “Fix It First” most clearly reveal the speaker's attitude toward throwing things away? Choose two.
options: every Thursday afternoon
I consider that practice wasteful
send them to the dumpster
a cracked hinge
questions.why: Wasteful and dumpster carry the speaker's disapproval; the others are neutral details.

questions.stem: Part A: How does the speaker of “Fix It First” treat the opposing view?

partA.stem: Part A: How does the speaker of “Fix It First” treat the opposing view?

options.label: A
options.text: The speaker agrees completely and drops the proposal.

options.label: B
options.text: The speaker calls it foolish and refuses to discuss it.

options.label: C
options.text: The speaker admits some truth in it but still favors repair.

options.label: D
options.text: The speaker claims that no one actually holds that view.

partB.stem: Part B: Which sentence from the passage best supports the answer to Part A?

options.label: A
options.text: I propose that we establish a repair club that meets every Thursday afternoon in the technology laboratory.

options.label: B
options.text: Some will argue that new equipment is inexpensive and that repairs consume too much valuable time.

options.label: C
options.text: They are partly right: a repaired fan is never quite as shiny as a new one.

options.label: D
options.text: Let us choose to fix it first.

questions.why: Partly right is a concession, followed by But and the speaker's counterpoint.

questions.stem: For the speech “Fix It First,” decide whether each statement is presented as a fact or as the speaker's judgment.

rows.text: The school discarded more than three hundred items last year.
Throwing the items away was wasteful.
Repairing things turns people into problem solvers.
A loose screw was enough to get some items thrown out.

questions.why: Judgments reveal the speaker's perspective; facts are details that can be checked.

questions.stem: What does the phrase “mere consumers” suggest about the speaker's perspective in “Fix It First”?
options: Students already spend too much money at school.
Buying replacements is more passive than fixing things.
Problem solvers rarely need to buy anything new.
Shopping carefully for new items is a valuable life skill.
questions.why: Mere makes consumers sound limited compared with active problem solvers.

questions.stem: Which statement best expresses the author's perspective in “Rethinking the Origins of Experiment”?
options: Ibn al-Haytham alone invented science, and later scholars only copied him.
Textbooks about science are too difficult for most students to follow.
European scientists of the 1600s deserve no credit for their experiments.
Histories of experiment should include earlier figures like Ibn al-Haytham.
questions.why: The author wants the history widened, not European scientists dismissed.

questions.stem: In “Rethinking the Origins of Experiment,” select two sentences that show the author's judgment of the usual textbook account.

segments.text: That narrative is tidy, but it is incomplete.
In his Book of Optics, he described darkened rooms in which light entered through a small opening, allowing him to test whether rays travel in straight lines.
A history of science that begins in one century and one continent is not simply unfair; it is wrong.
He also warned readers that a researcher must treat even respected authorities with suspicion, including his own conclusions.

questions.why: Incomplete and wrong are the author's evaluations of the textbook story; the others report Ibn al-Haytham's work.

questions.stem: Part A: How does the author of “Rethinking the Origins of Experiment” keep the argument from overstating its claim?

partA.stem: Part A: How does the author of “Rethinking the Origins of Experiment” keep the argument from overstating its claim?

options.label: A
options.text: by noting that later scientists did not simply copy Ibn al-Haytham

options.label: B
options.text: by describing the darkened rooms and small openings in detail

options.label: C
options.text: by admitting that Ibn al-Haytham made several errors about light

options.label: D
options.text: by quoting textbooks that already agree with the author's view

partB.stem: Part B: Which sentence from the passage best supports the answer to Part A?

options.label: A
options.text: That narrative is tidy, but it is incomplete.

options.label: B
options.text: It is a matter of accuracy.

options.label: C
options.text: Six centuries earlier, in Cairo, the scholar Ibn al-Haytham was already insisting that claims about light and vision be checked against controlled observation.

options.label: D
options.text: None of this means that later scientists merely copied him; knowledge travels through translation, debate, and reinvention, and many hands shaped modern science.

questions.why: The qualification that many hands shaped science keeps the claim balanced.

questions.stem: Would the author of “Rethinking the Origins of Experiment” agree or disagree with each statement?

rows.text: Modern science was shaped by contributions from many regions.
Careful testing began suddenly in seventeenth-century Europe.
Crediting Ibn al-Haytham is mainly an act of kindness.
Even the claims of trusted experts should be tested.

questions.why: The author values accuracy and shared credit, and rejects the idea of a sudden single origin.

questions.stem: Why does the author of “Rethinking the Origins of Experiment” contrast “generosity” with “accuracy”?
options: to stress that crediting him corrects the record rather than doing a favor
to suggest that historians should be much kinder toward forgotten scientists
to argue that fairness in history matters more than factual correctness
to show that Ibn al-Haytham was a generous teacher to his own students
questions.why: The author's point is that including him is about truth, not kindness.

questions.stem: Which statement most accurately describes the author's perspective in “The Cost of Never Being Lost”?
options: Navigation tools are useful in cities but have little value elsewhere.
Navigation tools are dangerous and should be removed from all cars entirely.
Navigation tools are harmless because travelers can always ask for help.
Navigation tools are valuable, but constant use weakens how we know places.
questions.why: The author keeps the device but argues for occasionally ignoring it.

questions.stem: Part A: What is the main function of the first paragraph of “The Cost of Never Being Lost” in developing the author's perspective?

partA.stem: Part A: What is the main function of the first paragraph of “The Cost of Never Being Lost” in developing the author's perspective?

options.label: A
options.text: to concede the benefits of navigation before raising a concern

options.label: B
options.text: to argue that being lost is a poetic and valuable experience

options.label: C
options.text: to explain how satellite navigation systems work in cars

options.label: D
options.text: to recount a frightening personal experience of being lost

partB.stem: Part B: Which sentence from the passage best supports the answer to Part A?

options.label: A
options.text: Still, convenience extracts a quiet price.

options.label: B
options.text: Anyone who has circled an unfamiliar city at midnight, fuel gauge sinking, knows that being lost is rarely poetic.

options.label: C
options.text: Satellite navigation has spared countless travelers that misery, and I would not surrender the device in my own car.

options.label: D
options.text: Walk to a neighborhood without the blue dot; ask a shopkeeper for directions; tolerate a few wrong turns.

questions.why: The author grants the device's real value first, which makes the later criticism more credible.

questions.stem: Which THREE phrases from “The Cost of Never Being Lost” reveal the author's view that constant guidance changes how people experience places? Choose three.
options: in my own car
convenience extracts a quiet price
weaker mental maps
a sequence of instructions rather than a place
ask a shopkeeper
fuel gauge sinking
questions.why: These phrases describe the hidden cost to how travelers understand places; the others are context or advice.

questions.stem: Put the moves of the argument in “The Cost of Never Being Lost” in the order the author makes them.
sequence: acknowledges the real benefits of navigation devices
identifies a hidden cost of constant guidance
cites research about weaker mental maps
recommends occasional, voluntary disorientation
questions.why: The author concedes, then raises a problem, supports it, and ends with a recommendation.

questions.stem: In “The Cost of Never Being Lost,” the qualifying phrase “in small and voluntary doses” shows that the author's perspective is best described as ____.
options: measured rather than extreme
hostile rather than neutral
nostalgic rather than practical
scientific rather than personal
questions.why: The qualifier limits the claim, showing a balanced rather than absolute position.

questions.stem: Why did the author write “The Date Palm”?
options: to make readers laugh at a silly tree
to ask readers to plant a tree today
to teach readers about date palm trees
to tell a story about a farmer's family
questions.why: The passage gives facts, so the author wrote it to teach.

questions.stem: True or false: The author of “The Date Palm” wrote it mainly to tell a funny story.
questions.why: It gives facts about the tree, not a funny story.

questions.stem: Select the sentence from “The Date Palm” that tells the main reason people love the tree.

segments.text: Date palms help people in many ways.
Date palms grow in hot, dry places.
They are sweet and soft.
A date palm can live for more than one hundred years!

questions.why: The author explains that the tree helps people in many ways.

questions.stem: “The Date Palm” was written to teach. Decide whether each of these books was most likely written to teach or to entertain.

rows.text: How Bees Make Honey
The Camel Who Wanted to Fly
All About the Moon
A Silly Day at the Zoo

questions.why: Books that give facts teach; silly made-up stories entertain.

questions.stem: Part A: Why does the author of “The Date Palm” tell how farmers get dates?

partA.stem: Part A: Why does the author of “The Date Palm” tell how farmers get dates?

options.label: A
options.text: to explain how people get dates from the tree

options.label: B
options.text: to show that farmers like to play games

options.label: C
options.text: to tell a funny story about one farmer

options.label: D
options.text: to make readers afraid of tall trees

partB.stem: Part B: Which sentence from the passage best supports the answer to Part A?

options.label: A
options.text: They can grow very tall.

options.label: B
options.text: Farmers climb the trees to pick them.

options.label: C
options.text: People eat them with milk or coffee.

options.label: D
options.text: Date palms grow in hot, dry places.

questions.why: The sentence about climbing explains how dates are picked.

questions.stem: What is the author's main purpose in “Join the Coral Reef Cleanup!”?
options: to entertain readers with a story about divers
to describe the long history of the divers' club
to persuade readers to volunteer at the cleanup
to explain how coral reefs form in warm seas
questions.why: The flyer asks readers to sign up and help.

questions.stem: Match each part of “Join the Coral Reef Cleanup!” to its purpose.

pairs.left: the fact about fish in the Red Sea
pairs.right: to show readers why the sea matters

pairs.left: the time and place of the cleanup
pairs.right: to tell readers when and where to come

pairs.left: the list of things the club will provide
pairs.right: to show that joining is easy

pairs.left: the sentence about the sea turtle
pairs.right: to make readers feel their help counts

questions.why: Each part of a persuasive flyer has its own job.

questions.stem: Part A: Why does the author of “Join the Coral Reef Cleanup!” include details about plastic and fishing nets?

partA.stem: Part A: Why does the author of “Join the Coral Reef Cleanup!” include details about plastic and fishing nets?

options.label: A
options.text: to prove that fishing should stop completely

options.label: B
options.text: to teach readers how fishing nets are made

options.label: C
options.text: to show a problem the cleanup will help solve

options.label: D
options.text: to describe what divers see underwater

partB.stem: Part B: Which sentence from the passage best supports the answer to Part A?

options.label: A
options.text: But plastic bags, bottles, and old fishing nets are piling up along the shore, and they can harm the reef and the creatures that live there.

options.label: B
options.text: Volunteers of all ages are welcome.

options.label: C
options.text: Its bright coral reefs are some of the healthiest in the world.

options.label: D
options.text: You only need to bring a hat and a helpful attitude!

questions.why: Showing the harm explains why the cleanup is needed.

questions.stem: Which TWO sentences from “Join the Coral Reef Cleanup!” most directly tell readers what to do? Choose two.
options: Sign up at the club office today, and help protect the sea we all love.
You only need to bring a hat and a helpful attitude!
Its bright coral reefs are some of the healthiest in the world.
Did you know that the Red Sea is home to more than one thousand kinds of fish?
questions.why: Sentences that give directions or ask for action serve a persuasive purpose.

questions.stem: How does the picture in “Join the Coral Reef Cleanup!” support the author's purpose?
options: It shows divers exploring an old sunken ship.
It shows that the cleanup helps sea animals.
It shows how coral grows on rocks underwater.
It shows the office where people can sign up.
questions.why: Children cleaning near a healthy turtle show readers the good results of helping.

questions.stem: What is the author's main purpose in “The Pocket Universe”?
options: to inform readers about the astrolabe and its makers
to compare the astrolabe with modern smartphones
to persuade readers to visit museums with brass tools
to entertain readers with a caravan adventure story
questions.why: The article explains what the astrolabe was, how it worked, and who made it.

questions.stem: Part A: Why does the author begin “The Pocket Universe” by asking readers to imagine crossing a desert?

partA.stem: Part A: Why does the author begin “The Pocket Universe” by asking readers to imagine crossing a desert?

options.label: A
options.text: to explain how caravans chose their routes long ago

options.label: B
options.text: to help readers understand the problem the astrolabe solved

options.label: C
options.text: to persuade readers that deserts are very dangerous places

options.label: D
options.text: to show that the author once traveled with a desert caravan

partB.stem: Part B: Which sentence from the passage best supports the answer to Part A?

options.label: A
options.text: For many travelers in the medieval Islamic world, the solution fit in one hand: the astrolabe.

options.label: B
options.text: Her skill was so admired that a ruler employed her at his court.

options.label: C
options.text: Craftsmen in cities such as Baghdad, Córdoba, and Isfahan competed to produce the most accurate and beautiful instruments.

options.label: D
options.text: Today, astrolabes rest in museum cases, but the questions they answered remain the foundation of modern navigation.

questions.why: The opening sets up a problem, and the next sentence names the astrolabe as its solution.

questions.stem: Match each paragraph of “The Pocket Universe” to its main purpose.

pairs.right: to introduce a problem and the invention
to explain how the instrument worked
to highlight a famous maker and the tool's legacy

questions.why: Each paragraph has a different job in the article.

questions.stem: In “The Pocket Universe,” select the sentence the author includes mainly to show why the astrolabe still matters today.

segments.text: Today, astrolabes rest in museum cases, but the questions they answered remain the foundation of modern navigation.
An astrolabe is a flat brass disk engraved with lines representing the sky.

Craftsmen in cities such as Baghdad, Córdoba, and Isfahan competed to produce the most accurate and beautiful instruments.

questions.why: The final sentence connects the old tool to modern navigation.

questions.stem: In “The Pocket Universe,” the author lists telling the time, finding a city's direction, and measuring a building mainly to show the astrolabe's ____.
options: simple construction
very high cost
many practical uses
beautiful design
questions.why: A list of tasks shows how useful the tool was.

questions.stem: Which statement best describes the author's purposes in “My Long War with the Alarm Clock”?
options: to persuade schools to start their classes later in the morning
to criticize parents who wake their teenagers too early
to inform readers about the long history of alarm clocks
to entertain with a funny story while explaining teen sleep
questions.why: The humor entertains, and the science lesson informs.

questions.stem: For “My Long War with the Alarm Clock,” decide whether each detail mainly entertains or mainly informs.

rows.text: The clock shrieked like a startled peacock.
Teenagers' internal clocks shift later during adolescence.
The author silenced the clock with the reflexes of a ninja.
Screens delay the release of melatonin.

questions.why: Funny comparisons entertain; scientific facts inform.

questions.stem: Part A: Why does the author of “My Long War with the Alarm Clock” describe the clock as an enemy and a monster?

partA.stem: Part A: Why does the author of “My Long War with the Alarm Clock” describe the clock as an enemy and a monster?

options.label: A
options.text: to make an ordinary struggle funny and relatable

options.label: B
options.text: to show that the clock was actually broken

options.label: C
options.text: to explain why the mother hid the clock

options.label: D
options.text: to warn readers that alarms can be harmful

partB.stem: Part B: Which sentence from the passage best supports the answer to Part A?

options.label: A
options.text: Every morning at six, it shrieked like a startled peacock, and every morning I silenced it with the reflexes of a ninja before sinking back into my pillow.

options.label: B
options.text: She added that screens glowing late at night delay the release of melatonin, the hormone that signals the body to rest.

options.label: C
options.text: I now charge my phone in the kitchen and turn off the lights by ten.

options.label: D
options.text: The war ended not with a victory but with a science lesson.

questions.why: Exaggerated battle language turns a common problem into comedy.

questions.stem: In “My Long War with the Alarm Clock,” select the sentence that marks the shift from the humorous story to the informational part.

My mother eventually hid the clock across the room, forcing me to stagger past my desk, trip over my backpack, and fight the monster in person.
I now charge my phone in the kitchen and turn off the lights by ten.

questions.stem: Which statement best expresses the central idea of “The Cost of Noise”?
options: Quiet parks are a pleasant luxury that wealthy cities can afford to provide.
Children in schools near airports score lower on reading tests than other children.
Cities should ban construction work and aircraft from all residential neighborhoods.
Noise harms health and learning, so quiet must be protected as a public resource.
questions.why: The essay shows the harms of noise and argues that silence must be protected.

questions.stem: For “The Cost of Noise,” classify each statement as the central idea, a supporting detail, or an idea that is not in the essay.

rows.text: Quiet is a public resource that must be protected.
Some parks prohibit loudspeakers.
Noise causes hearing loss in most city residents.
Barriers along highways absorb sound.

questions.why: Hearing loss is never mentioned; the barriers and parks are examples that support the claim.

questions.stem: Part A: What is the main purpose of paragraph 2 in developing the central idea of “The Cost of Noise”?

partA.stem: Part A: What is the main purpose of paragraph 2 in developing the central idea of “The Cost of Noise”?

options.label: A
options.text: It introduces the solutions that cities have used to reduce noise.

options.label: B
options.text: It extends the harm of noise from physical health to learning.

options.label: C
options.text: It shows that children are less affected by noise than adults.

options.label: D
options.text: It proves that airports should be moved away from all schools.

partB.stem: Part B: Which sentence from the passage best supports the answer to Part A?

options.label: A
options.text: Some cities have responded creatively.

options.label: B
options.text: Persistent traffic, construction, and aircraft noise do more than irritate; they elevate stress hormones, disrupt sleep, and, according to several long-term studies, increase the risk of heart disease.

options.label: C
options.text: These measures are inexpensive compared with treating the illnesses that noise contributes to.

options.label: D
options.text: Researchers comparing schools near busy airports with quieter schools have found that students exposed to constant noise often score lower on reading comprehension tests, presumably because concentration requires a degree of acoustic calm that these classrooms cannot provide.

questions.why: Paragraph 1 covers the body; paragraph 2 adds the effect on reading and concentration.

questions.stem: Select TWO sentences from “The Cost of Noise” that together best express its central idea.

segments.text: Noise is rarely listed among the hazards of modern life, yet a growing body of research suggests that it deserves a place beside polluted air and contaminated water.
Children may be particularly vulnerable.
Some cities have responded creatively.
These measures are inexpensive compared with treating the illnesses that noise contributes to.
It is a public resource that, like clean water, must be deliberately protected, because once a city surrenders it, recovering it is extraordinarily difficult.

questions.why: The opening names noise as a real hazard and the ending states that quiet must be protected.

questions.stem: Which TWO statements belong in an objective summary of “The Cost of Noise”? Choose two.
options: Noise is the single most serious hazard of modern life.
Research links constant noise to stress, poor sleep, and heart disease.
Quiet zones in parks are pleasant places to relax on weekends.
The author believes airports should be moved far away from schools.
Some cities reduce noise with barriers, delivery limits, and quiet zones.
questions.why: An objective summary keeps key points without adding opinions or claims the text does not make.

questions.stem: Which statement best expresses the central idea of “In Praise of Maintenance”?
options: Inventions such as the steam engine matter less than people usually believe.
Most infrastructure fails because of poor original design rather than neglect.
Museums should display technicians' tools instead of famous inventions.
A society endures only if it values maintenance alongside invention.
questions.why: The essay balances invention with care for what already exists.

questions.stem: In paragraph 3 of “In Praise of Maintenance,” the example of the steam engine mainly serves to ____.
options: argue that mechanics deserve more fame than the inventors they assisted
prove that the steam engine was poorly designed by its original inventor
explain why bridges and pipelines eventually collapse without inspection
show that a machine's value grows through later, uncredited improvements
questions.why: The example supports the claim that most of a machine's value comes after its invention.

questions.stem: Select TWO sentences from “In Praise of Maintenance” that best support the claim that neglecting maintenance has practical consequences, not only consequences for fairness.

segments.text: This imbalance is not merely a matter of fairness.
When governments and companies allocate resources primarily to novel projects, existing infrastructure deteriorates quietly until it fails dramatically.

Bridges, pipelines, and electrical grids rarely collapse because they were poorly invented; far more often, they collapse because routine inspections and repairs were postponed, underfunded, or considered unglamorous.

Museums display the first telephone and the first airplane, and prizes reward the scientist whose discovery is unprecedented; almost no one, however, commemorates the technician who keeps a water-treatment plant operating reliably for thirty years.
None of this diminishes the importance of innovation.

questions.why: These sentences describe real failures; the first option only states the claim without supporting it.

questions.stem: Which THREE ideas from “In Praise of Maintenance” are most essential to an accurate summary? Choose three.
options: Society honors invention far more than maintenance.
Technicians should win the same prizes as scientists.
The first telephone is displayed in museums.
Underfunded maintenance leads infrastructure to fail.
Much of a technology's value comes from later improvements.
Innovation is less important than most people think.
questions.why: A summary keeps the main claims and avoids small examples or ideas the author rejects.

questions.stem: Part A: How does the author refine the central idea in the final paragraph of “In Praise of Maintenance”?

partA.stem: Part A: How does the author refine the central idea in the final paragraph of “In Praise of Maintenance”?

options.label: A
options.text: by admitting that maintenance is finally less valuable than bold new invention

options.label: B
options.text: by suggesting that governments should stop paying for new projects

options.label: C
options.text: by introducing a new example of a forgotten technician from history

options.label: D
options.text: by clarifying that the argument balances innovation with care rather than rejecting it

partB.stem: Part B: Which sentence from the passage best supports the answer to Part A?

options.label: A
options.text: The steam engine, for example, became genuinely efficient only after decades of modest improvements by mechanics whose names are largely forgotten.

options.label: B
options.text: None of this diminishes the importance of innovation.

options.label: C
options.text: Societies tend to celebrate invention far more enthusiastically than maintenance.

options.label: D
options.text: This imbalance is not merely a matter of fairness.

questions.why: The author heads off a misreading: the point is balance, not a rejection of invention.

questions.stem: At the start of “The Falcon Behind the Gate,” what does Huda believe about Mr. Saleh?

Huda is astonished to see Mr. Saleh at her door.
Huda learns why Mr. Saleh kept his courtyard quiet.
Huda realizes the gate was protecting something fragile.
questions.why: Her view changes step by step as she learns the truth.

questions.stem: Part A: Why does Mr. Saleh wave children away from his gate?

questions.stem: Select the sentence from “The Falcon Behind the Gate” that best shows Huda's new understanding of Mr. Saleh.

Everyone on Al-Nakheel Street agreed that Mr. Saleh was the grumpiest man in the neighborhood.
Inside, a young falcon blinked at the lamplight, one wing wrapped in a neat white bandage.

questions.stem: How does telling the story from Huda's point of view affect the reader?
options: Readers learn Mr. Saleh's true reasons in the very first paragraph.
Readers share Huda's mistaken view and are surprised along with her.

questions.stem: Select the sentence from Professor Haddad's letter in “Letters from the Observatory” that most directly challenges Samira's view of calibration.

Your frustration is entirely reasonable, yet I suspect you are measuring your work against an imaginary standard.

When I arrived here thirty years ago, I also expected revelations every night.

questions.stem: Which TWO statements accurately describe how the perspectives in “Letters from the Observatory” differ? Choose two.

questions.stem: Select the sentence from “Instinct” that most clearly reveals the narrator beginning to question his own perspective.
