dedicated
questions.why: He trains daily and gives up other activities to reach his goal.

questions.stem: Put the events of “The Dune Run” in the order they happen.
sequence: Khalid trains for two years to beat Majid.
Khalid pulls ahead with one kilometer left.
Khalid hears Majid cry out behind him.
Khalid stands still at the top of the dune.
Khalid finishes eleventh, helping Majid.
questions.why: The pause at the top comes between hearing Majid and turning back.

questions.stem: Part A: What does Khalid's pause at the top of the dune reveal?

partA.stem: Part A: What does Khalid's pause at the top of the dune reveal?

options.label: A
options.text: He is too tired to finish the last part of the race.

options.label: B
options.text: He is torn between his goal and his concern for Majid.

options.label: C
options.text: He is waiting for the race officials to help Majid.

options.label: D
options.text: He is unsure which direction leads to the finish line.

partB.stem: Part B: Which sentence from the passage best supports the answer to Part A?

options.label: A
options.text: With one kilometer remaining, Khalid finally pulled ahead of his determined rival.

options.label: B
options.text: He finished eleventh, supporting Majid's weight throughout the descent.

options.label: C
options.text: For a long moment, Khalid stood still, his heartbeat pounding in his ears.

options.label: D
options.text: He glanced at the finish banner, then turned and half-ran, half-slid back down the slope.

questions.why: His stillness shows a real struggle between winning and helping.

questions.stem: Select the sentence from “The Dune Run” that best shows what Khalid learns about himself.

segments.text: "I didn't realize I was also deciding what kind of runner I wanted to be."
Victory was only several hundred meters away.
Afterward, several reporters asked whether he regretted sacrificing his long-anticipated victory.
He practiced before sunrise, memorized the course map until he could trace it with his eyes closed, and refused every invitation that might interfere with his demanding schedule.

questions.why: He realizes his training also shaped his character, not only his speed.

questions.stem: How does the author mainly reveal the change in Khalid's character?
options: through his choice at a key moment and his reflection afterward
through a flashback to the race he lost the year before
through other runners' descriptions of his new personality
through a narrator who directly lists all of his new traits
questions.why: His actions on the dune and his words to reporters show the change.

questions.stem: Which statement best describes Nadia at the start of “The Blue Tile”?
options: She is nervous and unsure whether she has any real skill.
She is patient and content with small, careful tasks.
She is bored with art and plans to change her career.
She is ambitious and eager for important, dramatic work.
questions.why: She expected to rescue masterpieces, not clean one tile.

questions.stem: For “The Blue Tile,” classify each detail as evidence of Nadia's early impatience or her developing patience.

rows.text: She works rapidly and resentfully.
She records each stage in a notebook.
She twice asks for a more significant task.
She notices details she had missed before.

questions.why: Her habits change from hurried to careful after the turning point.

questions.stem: Part A: What causes the turning point in Nadia's development?

partA.stem: Part A: What causes the turning point in Nadia's development?

options.label: A
options.text: She reads in a notebook how other interns succeeded.

options.label: B
options.text: She discovers that careless work could destroy something valuable.

options.label: C
options.text: Dr. Rahman finally praises her for working so quickly.

options.label: D
options.text: She is given a more significant object to restore.

partB.stem: Part B: Which sentence from the passage best supports the answer to Part A?

options.label: A
options.text: During the first week, Nadia worked rapidly and resentfully, convinced that the assignment was a test of obedience rather than skill.

options.label: B
options.text: When the tile was finally displayed, Dr. Rahman asked whether she still wanted to rescue masterpieces.

options.label: C
options.text: Beneath the grime, a faint blue pattern emerged, and Nadia realized that the slightest excess pressure would erase it permanently.

options.label: D
options.text: In the third week, however, something unexpectedly shifted in her attitude.

questions.why: The hidden pattern shows her that haste could ruin real beauty.

questions.stem: Select the sentence from “The Blue Tile” that best reveals Dr. Rahman's teaching method.

segments.text: Twice she asked for something more significant; twice Dr. Rahman simply examined her progress and returned the tile without comment.
Instead, Dr. Rahman assigned her a single cracked ceramic tile from a ruined caravanserai and instructed her to clean it, millimeter by millimeter, with a cotton swab and distilled water.
She began working more deliberately, recording each stage in a notebook and noticing details that her earlier impatience had concealed.
Nadia hesitated, considering the question more seriously than she had expected.

questions.why: He teaches by letting her discover the lesson instead of explaining it.

questions.stem: Which TWO statements best explain the meaning of Nadia's final line in “The Blue Tile”? Choose two.
options: She believes Dr. Rahman has treated her unfairly.
She now sees that skill with small tasks must come before great ones.
She no longer cares about working on famous objects.
She has decided to leave conservation for another career.
She still has ambitions but understands they must be earned.
questions.why: Her ambition remains, but it is now joined to humility and patience.

questions.stem: How does Faris first respond to Lina's report in “The Retraction”?
options: He thanks her and checks his own data right away.
He dismisses it, assuming the mistake must be hers.
He becomes angry and removes her from the project.
He admits his error to colleagues the same day.
questions.why: His “brisk courtesy” treats her report as a minor bother caused by her samples.

questions.stem: Put the stages of Professor Faris's development in “The Retraction” in order.
sequence: He dismisses Lina's failed results with brisk courtesy.
He recognizes the impurity that inflated his measurements.
He drafts and deletes explanations that minimize the error.
He publicly retracts the paper and gives Lina the stage.
questions.why: He moves from denial, to recognition, to temptation, to integrity.

questions.stem: Part A: In paragraph 3, what does the author suggest about Faris's character?

partA.stem: Part A: In paragraph 3, what does the author suggest about Faris's character?

options.label: A
options.text: He is careless and does not understand the error he has made.

options.label: B
options.text: He is mainly worried that the equipment supplier will be blamed.

options.label: C
options.text: His skill with words tempts him toward dishonesty, and this troubles him.

options.label: D
options.text: He feels no conflict, since he plans to retract the paper at once.

partB.stem: Part B: Which sentence from the passage best supports the answer to Part A?

options.label: A
options.text: Each evasion, he noticed, was more articulate than the last, and the realization disturbed him more than the mistake itself.

options.label: B
options.text: For three days he informed nobody.

options.label: C
options.text: Colleagues celebrated it as an act of extraordinary courage.

options.label: D
options.text: Lina methodically repeated the experiment eleven times.

questions.why: He notices his own growing talent for excuses and is disturbed by it.

questions.stem: Faris's private view of the retraction as “a debt that had merely come due” suggests that he ____.
options: regrets the retraction and wishes he had waited longer
believes his colleagues exaggerate his scientific skill
blames Lina for forcing him into a difficult position
sees honesty as an obligation rather than a heroic act
questions.why: A debt is owed, not a gift, so he does not see himself as brave.

questions.stem: Which THREE traits does Faris reveal over the course of “The Retraction”? Choose three.
options: integrity
self-awareness
indifference
recklessness
pride
jealousy
questions.why: He begins proud, recognizes his own evasions, and finally acts with integrity.

sets.skill: Characters with Different Points of View

questions.stem: How does Lina feel about the rain at the start of “Rain Day”?
options: She is scared because the rain is very loud.
She is sad because she cannot play outside.
She is happy because the plants will get water.
She is excited to jump in the puddles right away.
questions.why: Lina frowns and says they can't play outside.

questions.stem: In “Rain Day,” who thinks each thing?

rows.text: Rain is good for the plants.
Rain means we can't play.
We can jump in puddles later.

questions.why: Lina is unhappy about the rain, but Adam sees good things about it.

questions.stem: Select the sentence from “Rain Day” that shows how Adam feels about the rain.

segments.text: It rained all morning.
"Rain is good," he said.
Lina still felt sad.
Then the rain stopped.

questions.why: Adam says that rain is good.

questions.stem: True or false: At the end of “Rain Day,” Lina still feels the same way about the rain as she did at the start.
questions.why: At the end she jumps in a puddle and smiles, so her feelings change.

questions.stem: Part A: Why does Adam think rain is good?

partA.stem: Part A: Why does Adam think rain is good?

options.label: A
options.text: It makes the sky dark.

options.label: B
options.text: Lina likes rainy days.

options.label: C
options.text: He likes to stay inside.

options.label: D
options.text: The plants need water.

partB.stem: Part B: Which sentence from the passage best supports the answer to Part A?

options.label: A
options.text: Adam took her hand, and they went out.

options.label: B
options.text: The plants need water.

options.label: C
options.text: Lina looked out the window and frowned.

options.label: D
options.text: Her brother Adam smiled.

questions.why: Adam gives the plants as his reason.

questions.stem: In “The Empty Desert,” decide who holds each view at the start of the story.

rows.text: The desert has nothing in it.
You have to know where to look.
The trip is a waste of time.
Animal tracks tell a story.

questions.why: Faisal sees emptiness; Reem, who knows the desert, sees signs of life.

questions.stem: Why does Reem see the desert differently from Faisal?
options: She has never lived in a busy city with tall buildings.
She has visited it many times and knows its signs of life.
She thinks the internet is not important for young people.
She wants Faisal to feel bad about complaining so much.
questions.why: Reem visits every winter, so she knows what to look for.

questions.stem: Which TWO details from “The Empty Desert” show Reem's point of view about the desert? Choose two.
options: She stares out the window at the endless dunes.
She points out the tracks of a sand fox.
She says there are no trees or buildings.
She tells Faisal he doesn't know where to look yet.
questions.why: Reem shows Faisal hidden life; the other details belong to Faisal.

questions.stem: In “The Empty Desert,” Faisal first thinks the desert is empty, but by the end he believes ____.
options: Reem had invented the animal tracks
the desert is too quiet to enjoy
he had not been noticing what was there
the city sky has more stars
questions.why: He admits he "wasn't paying attention."

questions.stem: Part A: How does Faisal's point of view change during the story?

partA.stem: Part A: How does Faisal's point of view change during the story?

options.label: A
options.text: He moves from fearing the animals to wanting to find more of them.

options.label: B
options.text: He moves from enjoying the trip to wishing he had stayed in the city.

options.label: C
options.text: He moves from trusting Reem to doubting what she tells him.

options.label: D
options.text: He moves from seeing the desert as empty to seeing it as full of hidden life.

partB.stem: Part B: Which sentence from the passage best supports the answer to Part A?

options.label: A
options.text: His cousin Reem, who visited the desert every winter, laughed quietly.

options.label: B
options.text: "Maybe I just wasn't paying attention."

options.label: C
options.text: Faisal was quiet for a long time.

options.label: D
options.text: "There is nothing out here," he complained.

questions.why: His final words show that his view has changed.

questions.stem: What does Khalid believe at the start of “Two Designs”?
options: A digital animation will impress the judges more than the model.
Hala's grandfather would make the most reliable judge for the event.
The wooden model should be finished long before the competition begins.
Farmers are the most important audience for their project.
questions.why: Khalid wants to build the design digitally to impress the judges.

questions.stem: For “Two Designs,” decide which character would most likely agree with each statement.

rows.text: A design should be easy for real users to understand.
Experts value exact, polished work.
People trust what they can hold in their hands.
A professional animation will win attention.

questions.why: Hala thinks about the users; Khalid thinks about the judges.

questions.stem: Part A: Why does Hala prefer the physical model?

partA.stem: Part A: Why does Hala prefer the physical model?

options.label: A
options.text: She believes people understand a design best when they can see and touch it.

options.label: B
options.text: She believes Khalid is not skilled enough to create a good animation.

options.label: C
options.text: She believes the animation will take too long to finish before the deadline.

options.label: D
options.text: She believes the judges will not have a screen to display the animation.

partB.stem: Part B: Which sentence from the passage best supports the answer to Part A?

options.label: A
options.text: Show me what you have so far.

options.label: B
options.text: When farmers see a real model, they understand immediately how the water travels from the pipe to the roots.

options.label: C
options.text: Farmers aren't judging the competition, Hala.

options.label: D
options.text: The competition is in three days, and our model still looks like a pile of sticks.

questions.why: Hala explains that a real model makes the design clear at once.

questions.stem: Select the sentence from “Two Designs” that shows Khalid starting to accept part of Hala's point of view.

segments.text: Engineers are, and engineers appreciate precision.
Then perhaps we need both, your model for the table and my animation on the screen behind it.
We should build the whole design digitally instead, because the judges will be impressed by a professional animation.
Farmers aren't judging the competition, Hala.

questions.why: Khalid suggests combining both ideas, so he now values the model too.

questions.stem: Which TWO stage directions in “Two Designs” best show how Hala's attitude toward Khalid's idea changes? Choose two.
options: (pausing), which suggests Hala is unsure whether her grandfather was right
(setting down the sandpaper), which suggests she has given up on her model
(smiling slightly), which suggests she is now willing to consider his idea
(without looking up), which suggests she is not yet interested in his idea
questions.why: Hala begins by ignoring Khalid's idea and ends by smiling and asking to see it.

questions.stem: What does Mariam believe about Ms. Al-Qahtani in “The Nomination”?
options: The teacher plans to give the garden to another class.
The teacher wants Mariam to plant more tomatoes and mint next season.
The teacher is far too busy with exams to notice the garden at all.
The teacher disapproves of the time Mariam spends in the garden.
questions.why: Mariam says, "She thinks I'm wasting time."

questions.stem: For “The Nomination,” decide whether each statement describes what Mariam believes or what the reader knows.

rows.text: The teacher thinks the garden is a waste of time.
The teacher has photographed the garden each week.
The Sunday meeting will be about a problem.
The teacher's folder is about community service.

questions.why: The narrator shows the reader the folder, which Mariam never sees.

questions.stem: Part A: What does the reader learn that Mariam does not know?

partA.stem: Part A: What does the reader learn that Mariam does not know?

options.label: A
options.text: The teacher has been planning to close the vegetable garden.

options.label: B
options.text: The teacher has been asking Mariam's brother about her grades.

options.label: C
options.text: The teacher has been watering the garden when Mariam goes home.

options.label: D
options.text: The teacher has been recording Mariam's work for a possible award.

partB.stem: Part B: Which sentence from the passage best supports the answer to Part A?

options.label: A
options.text: Mariam spent the entire weekend preparing apologies, rehearsing explanations, and imagining the worst.

options.label: B
options.text: Mariam was certain that Ms. Al-Qahtani disapproved of her.

options.label: C
options.text: "I need to speak with you on Sunday morning," she said seriously.

options.label: D
options.text: On her desk lay a folder labeled "Community Service Nominations," and inside it were photographs of the garden, week by week, as the wilted seedlings grew into rows of tomatoes and mint.

questions.why: The folder reveals the teacher's real purpose to the reader.

questions.stem: In “The Nomination,” the difference between what Mariam believes and what the reader knows mainly creates ____.
options: dramatic irony that builds suspense about Sunday
a flashback that explains why the garden was failing
foreshadowing that the garden will be destroyed
a conflict between Mariam and her brother
questions.why: The reader expects good news while Mariam fears the worst, which creates suspense.

questions.stem: Select two sentences from “The Nomination” that show Mariam's mistaken point of view.

segments.text: "She thinks I'm wasting time," Mariam told her brother.
What Mariam did not know was that Ms. Al-Qahtani had been taking notes.
On Thursday, the teacher finally stopped Mariam at the gate.
Mariam spent the entire weekend preparing apologies, rehearsing explanations, and imagining the worst.

questions.why: Mariam expects criticism, but the reader knows she has been noticed for her good work.

questions.stem: In “The Oyster Beds,” decide whether each phrase reflects Jassim's view of the water or Dana's view.

rows.text: a cemetery of livelihoods
a laboratory of resilience
lungs burning
cautious optimism

questions.why: Jassim connects the reefs with past hardship; Dana connects them with recovery.

questions.stem: Which statement best describes how Jassim's and Dana's points of view differ?
options: Jassim believes the reefs are polluted, while Dana believes they have never been damaged.
Jassim sees the reefs as a source of income, while Dana sees them as a place for tourists.
Jassim sees the reefs as a reminder of loss, while Dana sees them as evidence of recovery.
Jassim wants to return to pearl diving, while Dana wants to stop all scientific research.
questions.why: Jassim remembers hardship; Dana studies the oysters' return.

questions.stem: Which TWO statements describe how the author develops the contrast between the two characters? Choose two.
options: The author tells the story from Jassim's point of view only, hiding Dana's thoughts.
The author gives the characters parallel lines of dialogue that each compare the oysters to something.
The author shows Dana proving with data that her grandfather's memories are false.
The author pairs contrasting metaphors, "cemetery" and "laboratory," for the same place.
questions.why: Paired metaphors and matching lines of dialogue set the two views side by side.

questions.stem: Part A: What does Dana's reply, "as though they were ghosts," suggest about her view of her grandfather's attitude?

partA.stem: Part A: What does Dana's reply, "as though they were ghosts," suggest about her view of her grandfather's attitude?

options.label: A
options.text: She thinks he does not believe her research is accurate.

options.label: B
options.text: She thinks he sees the oysters only as part of a painful past.

options.label: C
options.text: She thinks he is frightened of diving in deep water again.

options.label: D
options.text: She thinks he has forgotten where the oyster beds are.

partB.stem: Part B: Which sentence from the passage best supports the answer to Part A?

options.label: A
options.text: To him, the shimmering shallows were a cemetery of livelihoods: the place where his father had descended forty times a day, lungs burning, for pearls that eventually lost their value when cultured pearls flooded international markets.

options.label: B
options.text: From the seawall at Muharraq, Grandfather Jassim could identify every reef by the color of the water above it, although he had not dived in fifty years.

options.label: C
options.text: Then Jassim pointed toward a darker patch of water.

options.label: D
options.text: For a moment neither spoke.

questions.why: Ghosts belong to the past, and Jassim links the reefs to past loss.

questions.stem: Select the sentence from “The Oyster Beds” that best shows the two points of view beginning to connect.

segments.text: "You speak about oysters as though they were patients," Jassim remarked, not unkindly.
"And you speak about them as though they were ghosts," Dana answered.
Perhaps your instruments should begin where his memory ends.
Her research team had documented oyster populations recovering steadily since the reefs were protected, and she considered the beds not a monument to hardship but a laboratory of resilience.

questions.why: Jassim suggests that his family's memory and Dana's science can work together.

questions.stem: How does the narrator of “The Wind Tower” view the grandmother's question at first?
options: as proof that her grandmother does not understand blueprints
as a polite way of refusing to pay for the renovation project
as a practical warning that deserves careful engineering study
as a sentimental concern that modern design has made unnecessary
questions.why: The narrator dismisses the question and calls sentimentality "an expensive luxury."

questions.stem: Which TWO phrases reveal irony in the narrator's self-description, showing that the narrator's point of view is less reliable than she believes? Choose two.
options: "with what I considered admirable efficiency"
"tracing each line with a finger that trembled only slightly"
"patiently and at considerable length"
"reading by lantern light, entirely comfortable"
questions.why: The narrator praises the plan's efficiency and the narrator's own patience, but the reader sees her as overconfident.

questions.stem: Part A: Which statement best describes how the grandmother regards the narrator's plan?

partA.stem: Part A: Which statement best describes how the grandmother regards the narrator's plan?

options.label: A
options.text: She sees it as a clever improvement that she is too proud to accept openly.

options.label: B
options.text: She sees it as well meant but blind to something the old house already does well.

options.label: C
options.text: She sees it as an insult to the family members who built the tower.

options.label: D
options.text: She sees it as a dangerous plan that will cause the house to collapse.

partB.stem: Part B: Which sentence from the passage best supports the answer to Part A?

options.label: A
options.text: She did not mention the blueprints, and I discovered, somewhat to my irritation, that I could not stop thinking about them.

options.label: B
options.text: My grandmother examined the blueprints for a long time, tracing each line with a finger that trembled only slightly, and then asked a question I had not anticipated: "Where will the evening breeze go?"

options.label: C
options.text: That night the electricity failed across the district.

options.label: D
options.text: She nodded throughout my explanation, the way one nods at a child describing a dream.

questions.why: The simile shows she listens kindly but finds the plan naive.

questions.stem: For “The Wind Tower,” decide whether each idea belongs to the narrator's view at the start or to the grandmother's view.

rows.text: Sealed rooms are more economical.
The old design still has a purpose.
Feelings about the past cost too much.
Natural airflow is worth keeping.

questions.why: The narrator values efficiency; the grandmother values what the tower already does.

questions.stem: Select the sentence from “The Wind Tower” that suggests the narrator's point of view has begun to shift, even though the narrator is reluctant to admit it.

segments.text: I found my grandmother there, reading by lantern light, entirely comfortable.
She did not mention the blueprints, and I discovered, somewhat to my irritation, that I could not stop thinking about them.
That night the electricity failed across the district.
I explained, patiently and at considerable length, that breezes were no longer necessary, that sealed rooms were more economical, and that sentimentality was an expensive luxury.

questions.why: The narrator's irritation at being unable to stop thinking about the blueprints hints at reconsideration.

questions.stem: Select the sentence from “Desert Camels” that tells how camels keep sand out of their eyes.

segments.text: Camels have humps on their backs.
The eyelashes keep sand out of their eyes.
Their wide feet help them walk on soft sand.
The desert is hot and dry.

questions.why: The text says the long eyelashes keep sand out.

questions.stem: True or false: “Desert Camels” says that a camel's hump stores water.
questions.why: The text says the humps store fat, not water.

questions.stem: Which sentence from “Desert Camels” tells how a camel can walk on sand?
options: A camel can go many days without water.
When it finds water, it can drink a lot very fast.
Their wide feet help them walk on soft sand.
A camel can use this fat when there is no food.
questions.why: The wide feet sentence answers the question.

questions.stem: Does “Desert Camels” tell each fact?

rows.text: Camels have long eyelashes.
Camels can run very fast.
Camels drink a lot of water fast.
Camels sleep in caves.

questions.why: Only use facts that you can find in the text.

questions.stem: Part A: What does the author want you to learn about camels?

partA.stem: Part A: What does the author want you to learn about camels?

options.label: A
options.text: They are the biggest animals in the world.

options.label: B
options.text: They do not need food or water at all.

options.label: C
options.text: They like to live near the sea.

options.label: D
options.text: Their bodies help them live in the desert.

partB.stem: Part B: Which sentence from the passage best supports the answer to Part A?

options.label: A
options.text: Camels live in the desert.

options.label: B
options.text: The desert is hot and dry.

options.label: C
options.text: Camels have long eyelashes.

options.label: D
options.text: Camels are made for desert life.

questions.why: The last sentence sums up how camels fit desert life.

questions.stem: Select the sentence from “The Scientist in the Dark Room” that explains what Ibn al-Haytham's experiment proved.

segments.text: He sat in a dark room with a tiny hole in one wall.
This showed him that light travels in straight lines from objects into our eyes, not the other way around.
More than a thousand years ago, a scientist named Ibn al-Haytham studied how people see.
Ibn al-Haytham was not satisfied with this idea, so he decided to test it.

questions.why: This sentence states what the experiment showed.

questions.stem: Which sentence best supports the idea that Ibn al-Haytham tested ideas instead of simply accepting them?
options: Light from outside passed through the hole and made an upside-down picture of the street on the opposite wall.
In his time, many thinkers believed that light shot out of our eyes and touched the objects around us.
Ibn al-Haytham was not satisfied with this idea, so he decided to test it.
Today, many people call him one of the first true scientists, and his dark room is an early model of the camera.
questions.why: He chose to test the old idea rather than believe it.

questions.stem: Which TWO details best support the claim that Ibn al-Haytham was one of the first true scientists? Choose two.
options: He made a picture of the street outside his room.
He tested an old idea with an experiment.
He wrote down his steps so others could repeat them.
He lived more than a thousand years ago.
questions.why: Testing ideas and recording steps are what scientists do; his age and the picture alone do not prove it.

questions.stem: For “The Scientist in the Dark Room,” decide whether the text supports each statement.

rows.text: Light travels in straight lines.
Ibn al-Haytham built the first modern camera.
The image in the dark room was upside down.
Most thinkers of his time agreed with him at once.

questions.why: The text calls the dark room an early model, not a modern camera, and never says others agreed quickly.

questions.stem: Part A: Why did Ibn al-Haytham most likely write down every step of his experiments?

partA.stem: Part A: Why did Ibn al-Haytham most likely write down every step of his experiments?

options.label: A
options.text: so that he could prove the old thinkers were kind

options.label: B
options.text: so that he could sell his ideas to camera makers

options.label: C
options.text: so that he would remember the street outside

options.label: D
options.text: so that other people could check his results

partB.stem: Part B: Which sentence from the passage best supports the answer to Part A?

options.label: A
options.text: In his time, many thinkers believed that light shot out of our eyes and touched the objects around us.

options.label: B
options.text: More than a thousand years ago, a scientist named Ibn al-Haytham studied how people see.

options.label: C
options.text: Ibn al-Haytham wrote down every step of his experiments so that others could repeat them.

options.label: D
options.text: He sat in a dark room with a tiny hole in one wall.

questions.why: Repeating an experiment lets others check that the result is true.

questions.stem: Which evidence best supports the author's claim that gardens improve how students eat?
options: Students who grew vegetables were twice as likely to choose salads at lunch.
Measuring plant growth turns abstract lessons into practical experiences.
Drip irrigation delivers water directly to the roots of the plants.
Several teachers say struggling students often become leaders in the garden.
questions.why: The survey result is about students' food choices.

questions.stem: Select the sentence from “Every School Should Grow a Garden” that responds to the critics' concern.

segments.text: Critics argue that gardens require too much water in a dry climate.
However, drip irrigation, which delivers water directly to plant roots, can reduce water use by more than half compared with traditional methods.
Gardens also strengthen learning.
Children, it seems, are curious about food they have raised themselves.

questions.why: The author answers the water concern with a method that cuts water use.

questions.stem: For “Every School Should Grow a Garden,” identify the kind of evidence the author uses for each claim.

rows.text: Students who garden choose healthier food.
Struggling students become garden leaders.
Drip irrigation saves water.
Gardens make students better at sports.

questions.stem: Which TWO statements are supported by both the chart and the paragraph about critics in “Every School Should Grow a Garden”? Choose two.
options: Traditional watering produces healthier and larger vegetables.
Drip irrigation removes the need to water school gardens at all.
Drip irrigation used less than half the water of traditional watering.
A garden can use much less water when water goes straight to the roots.

questions.stem: Part A: Which claim in the essay is supported by the weakest evidence?

partA.stem: Part A: Which claim in the essay is supported by the weakest evidence?

options.label: A
options.text: Students who struggle in class often become leaders in the garden.

options.label: B
options.text: Drip irrigation can reduce water use by more than half.

options.label: C
options.text: Students who grow vegetables more often choose salads at lunch.

options.label: D

partB.stem: Part B: Which sentence from the passage best supports the answer to Part A?

options.label: B

questions.stem: Select the sentence from “The Last Lap” that best shows Salem is trying to hide his injury.

segments.text: Salem stared at the puddle forming around his feet and said nothing.
He stretched carefully, favoring his left shoulder in a way he hoped Coach Nasser would not notice, and slipped into the water without a word.
Salem arrived at the pool before the sun had cleared the rooftops, as he had every morning for six months.
"Your times are excellent," the coach said slowly.

questions.why: He hopes the coach will not notice his shoulder.

questions.stem: Which TWO details best support the inference that Salem is determined to compete? Choose two.
options: He kicks harder and thinks about the championship despite the ache.
He has trained every morning for six months.
He stares at the puddle and says nothing.
His times are described as excellent by the coach.
questions.why: Training daily and pushing through pain show determination; the other details show other things.

questions.stem: Which inference about Coach Nasser is best supported by the story?
options: He has not noticed anything unusual about the way Salem is swimming.
He has noticed the injury and cares more about Salem's future than one race.
He plans to remove Salem from the team before the championship.
He is disappointed in Salem's times and wants him to train even harder.
questions.why: He points out the short stroke and talks about "next year."

questions.stem: For “The Last Lap,” decide how well the story supports each inference.

rows.text: Salem is in pain during practice.
Coach Nasser watches Salem closely.
Salem plans to quit swimming.
Coach Nasser is angry with Salem.

questions.why: The ache and the coach's exact measurement are in the text; anger and quitting are not.

partA.stem: Part A: What does Salem's reaction at the end of the story most likely show?

options.label: B
options.text: He realizes the coach is right and feels conflicted.

options.label: C
options.text: He is too tired from practice to answer anyone.

options.label: D
options.text: He is proud that his times are excellent.

partB.stem: Part B: Which sentence from the passage best supports the answer to Part A?

options.label: B

questions.stem: Which sentence best supports the idea that fog collectors are inexpensive to operate?
options: In favorable locations, a single panel of forty square meters can yield several hundred liters per day.
Nevertheless, researchers caution against exaggerated expectations.
Large panels of fine mesh are suspended perpendicular to the prevailing wind.
Proponents emphasize the method's affordability, since fog collectors require no electricity and minimal maintenance.
questions.why: No electricity and little maintenance mean low running costs.

questions.stem: Select two sentences from “Harvesting the Fog” that support the claim that fog harvesting has serious limitations.

segments.text: The technique is deceptively simple.
Fog is seasonal in many regions, and yields fluctuate dramatically from week to week.
Moreover, the mesh deteriorates under intense sunlight and must be replaced periodically, an expense that some isolated villages have struggled to sustain once initial funding disappeared.
In favorable locations, a single panel of forty square meters can yield several hundred liters per day.

questions.why: Unreliable yields and costly repairs are both limitations.

questions.stem: Which TWO pieces of evidence most directly support the claim that the amount of water from fog harvesting is unreliable? Choose two.
options: The mesh deteriorates under intense sunlight.
Yields fluctuate dramatically from week to week.
A single panel can yield several hundred liters per day.
Fog is seasonal in many regions.
questions.why: The mesh problem is a real limitation, but it concerns cost and upkeep, not how much water arrives.

questions.stem: For “Harvesting the Fog,” decide whether each statement is stated directly, is a reasonable inference, or is not supported.

rows.text: Fog collectors do not need electricity.
Some projects failed because of money rather than design.
Fog harvesting can end water shortages on its own.
Location affects how much water a panel collects.

questions.why: "In favorable locations" implies that place matters; the author directly rejects fog as a full solution.

questions.stem: Part A: Which statement best expresses the author's central claim?

partA.stem: Part A: Which statement best expresses the author's central claim?

options.label: A
options.text: Fog harvesting is too expensive for most desert communities to use.

questions.stem: Select the sentence from “The Fragile Archive” that provides the strongest evidence that physical manuscripts can outlast digital files.

segments.text: A parchment volume, by contrast, has survived eight centuries without electricity.
None of this suggests that digitization is misguided.
Digitization has been celebrated, with considerable justification, as the salvation of the world's manuscript heritage.
Preservation, in other words, is not an event but an obligation renewed by every generation.

questions.why: Eight centuries of survival without power is direct evidence of durability.

questions.stem: Which sentence best supports the author's claim that digital files are perishable?
options: Rather, it implies that a photograph should be regarded as a copy that broadens access, not as a replacement that justifies neglecting the original.
The most prudent archives, accordingly, invest simultaneously in climate-controlled storage for physical volumes and in the regular migration of digital files.
Storage formats become obsolete within decades, servers require continuous funding, and an image is only as legible as the software capable of opening it.
Libraries in Timbuktu, Cairo, and Istanbul have photographed thousands of fragile volumes, enabling scholars on distant continents to examine astronomical tables and medical treatises.
questions.why: It names three specific ways digital files can be lost.

questions.stem: For “The Fragile Archive,” decide whether each statement is stated directly, is a reasonable inference, or is not supported.

rows.text: Digitization has made rare manuscripts available to distant scholars.
Some institutions may care less for originals once copies exist.
Digitization projects should be stopped.
Archives that only digitize may eventually lose access to their copies.

questions.why: The author warns against neglect and mentions continuous funding, but rejects the idea that digitization is misguided; perishable files imply that copies alone can be lost.

questions.stem: Which TWO pieces of evidence best support the conclusion that preservation is "an obligation renewed by every generation"? Choose two.
options: Scholars on distant continents can now examine astronomical tables.
Libraries in Timbuktu, Cairo, and Istanbul have photographed thousands of volumes.
Storage formats become obsolete within decades.
Archives must regularly migrate digital files to current formats.
questions.why: Both right answers show that preservation work must be repeated over time; the others are about access, not ongoing duty.

questions.stem: Part A: Which assumption most clearly underlies the author's argument?

partA.stem: Part A: Which assumption most clearly underlies the author's argument?

options.label: A
options.text: Scholars prefer to study photographs rather than physical manuscripts.

options.label: B
options.text: Digital copies are usually less accurate than the manuscripts they copy.

options.label: C
options.text: Once digital copies exist, people may be tempted to neglect the originals.

options.label: D
options.text: Libraries in Africa and Asia lack the funding to digitize their collections.

partB.stem: Part B: Which sentence from the passage best supports the answer to Part A?

options.label: A
options.text: Yet the enthusiasm surrounding these projects occasionally obscures an uncomfortable reality: digital files are themselves remarkably perishable.

options.label: B
options.text: None of this suggests that digitization is misguided.

options.label: C
options.text: Rather, it implies that a photograph should be regarded as a copy that broadens access, not as a replacement that justifies neglecting the original.

options.label: D
options.text: Digitization has been celebrated, with considerable justification, as the salvation of the world's manuscript heritage.

questions.why: The warning against "neglecting the original" only makes sense if the author assumes that risk is real.

Then it flew off with yellow dust on its body.
Noor did not run away.

questions.stem: In “Two Views of Falconry,” which text gives each piece of information?

rows.text: how long falconry has existed in Arabia
how a falcon's claws feel on a glove
that people in Arabia train falcons
what falcon festivals are like today

questions.stem: How is the point of view in “My First Falcon” different from the point of view in “Falcons in Arabia”?
options: It is a secondhand account written by a historian of the region.
It is a firsthand account by someone who personally trained a falcon.
It is a set of instructions that explains how to train a young falcon.
It is a report that compares falconry in several different countries.
questions.why: Text 2 uses "I" and "my" to tell about the writer's own experience.

questions.stem: Which TWO kinds of information does “My First Falcon” give that “Falcons in Arabia” does not? Choose two.
options: how much a trained falcon can be worth today
how the writer helped the falcon learn the writer's voice
how the writer felt when holding the falcon
how falcons helped families find food long ago
questions.why: Only the firsthand account shares personal feelings and daily training.

questions.stem: “Falcons in Arabia” mainly ____, while “My First Falcon” mainly describes the feelings of one young trainer.
options: explains the history and importance of falconry
tells a story about a family's desert winter
argues that falcons should not be trained
describes how to buy a falcon at a festival

questions.stem: For “The Traveler from Tangier,” decide whether each detail is a historical fact from Text 1 or an invented detail from Text 2.

rows.text: He traveled about 120,000 kilometers.
He compared cities to unread books.
He left Tangier in 1325.
His water skin was nearly empty.

questions.why: Text 1 reports facts and dates; Text 2 imagines a moment of the journey.

questions.stem: How does Text 2 present Ibn Battuta differently from Text 1?
options: It questions whether his account of his journeys can be trusted.
It imagines his feelings and thoughts during a single moment of travel.
It explains how his account was written down by a scholar in Fez.
It lists the dates and distances of every journey that he completed.
questions.why: The story focuses on what he felt; the history focuses on facts.

questions.stem: Select the sentence from Text 1 that suggests readers should be careful about trusting every part of Ibn Battuta's account.

segments.text: He did not return for nearly twenty-four years.
His later account of these journeys, dictated to a writer in Fez, remains one of the most valuable records of the medieval world, although historians note that some passages may be exaggerated.
Over his lifetime, he traveled roughly 120,000 kilometers, visiting regions that stretch from West Africa to China.
Behind him, Tangier had disappeared; ahead lay a world he could scarcely imagine.

questions.why: Historians warn that some parts may be exaggerated.

questions.stem: Which TWO statements are true of BOTH texts? Choose two.
options: Both present Ibn Battuta as someone eager to see the world.
Both give exact dates and distances of his journeys.
Both show that Ibn Battuta traveled very far from Tangier.
Both include dialogue spoken by Ibn Battuta.
questions.why: Each text shows a long journey and a curious traveler, but only one has dialogue and only one has dates.

questions.stem: On which point do the authors of Text 1 and Text 2 agree?

Coral gardening can do some good for damaged reefs.
Coral gardening is the main reason that ocean waters are warming.
Coral gardening is a waste of time and of volunteers' effort.

questions.stem: For “Can Coral Gardens Save the Reefs?,” decide which author would most likely agree with each statement.

Warming oceans are the larger threat to reefs.
Transplanted corals can grow on damaged reefs.
One-year survival rates do not tell the full story.

questions.why: The authors share basic facts but disagree about how much coral gardening can achieve.

questions.stem: Select the sentence from Text 2 that most directly challenges the claim in Text 1 that coral gardening could restore entire reef systems.

segments.text: Coral gardening is a hopeful activity, but it cannot keep pace with the destruction.
Most projects restore less than one hectare, while warming oceans damage thousands of hectares in a single season.
Restoration helps, but only reducing ocean warming will save reefs in the long term.
Divers grow small fragments of coral on underwater frames, and once the fragments mature, they are attached to damaged reefs.

questions.why: It gives specific numbers that show the gap between restoration and damage; the first sentence only states the claim.

questions.stem: The title of Text 2, “A Bandage on a Broken Bone,” suggests that its author views coral gardening as ____.
options: a helpful but insufficient response to a larger problem
an expensive project that has produced no results
the most effective way to protect coral reefs
a harmful activity that should be stopped at once

questions.stem: For “The Elephant Clock,” decide which text includes each feature.

rows.text: gives the year the design was completed
speaks in the voice of the clock
mentions cymbals marking the time
describes a bowl that sinks

questions.stem: Which statement best describes a difference between the two texts?
options: Text 1 describes the poem's history, while Text 2 describes a modern clock.
Text 1 argues the clock was inaccurate, while Text 2 argues it was precise.
Text 1 explains how the clock worked, while Text 2 expresses wonder at it.
Text 1 praises Al-Jazari's character, while Text 2 lists the clock's parts.

whether air conditioning has made old building designs useless

questions.stem: For “Two Views of the Old City,” decide which author would most likely agree with each statement.

rows.text: Some historic structures deserve protection.
Traditional design holds lessons about climate.
Residents' living conditions should guide decisions.
Cities naturally change over time.

questions.why: Text 2 still protects significant buildings, so the authors share that point.

questions.stem: Which TWO statements accurately contrast the way the two authors build their arguments? Choose two.
options: Text 2 argues that every historic building should be torn down.
Text 1 cites temperature measurements taken in traditional lanes.
Text 2 supports its claim with a list of practical problems that residents face.
Text 1 relies on an extended metaphor comparing old districts to an instruction manual.

questions.stem: Select the sentence from Text 2 that comes closest to granting part of the view expressed in Text 1.

segments.text: Sentimental arguments for preservation frequently ignore the people who actually inhabit historic districts, many of whom contend with crumbling plumbing, inadequate fire access, and rents that decline as the buildings deteriorate.
A neighborhood frozen in its past condition serves photographers better than residents.
The more defensible approach is selective renewal: protect the structures of genuine architectural significance, and allow the remainder to evolve as living cities always have.
A city that demolishes its oldest districts does not merely lose buildings; it forfeits the evidence of how its people once solved the problems of climate, commerce, and community.

questions.why: By agreeing to protect significant structures, Text 2 accepts that some old buildings are worth keeping.

partB.stem: Part B: Which sentence from the passage best supports the answer to Part A?

options.label: A

options.label: B

options.label: C

questions.stem: Select the sentence from “Two Markets” that shows the market in Text 1 is crowded.

segments.text: Before sunrise, Nok paddled her small wooden boat along the canal.
Dozens of other boats crowded the narrow water, each piled with mangoes, coconuts, and bright flowers.
Nok traded a basket of bananas for a sack of rice and steered carefully home.

Faisal trades bananas for a sack of rice.

questions.stem: Which detail is true of BOTH settings in “Ice and Sand”?
options: Strong waves reshape the land every day.
The air is very dry, and the sky is clear.
The sun does not rise for several months.
The temperature stays below freezing all year.
questions.why: Concordia has dry, clear air, and the desert sky is clear enough to see satellites.

questions.stem: In “Ice and Sand,” decide whether each detail belongs to Concordia Station, the Rub' al Khali camp, or both.

rows.text: Months of darkness
Midday heat near fifty degrees
Supplies brought in from outside
Wind reshaping ridges

questions.why: Both groups depend on supplies carried in, but darkness and heat belong to only one place each.

questions.stem: Part A: How do the settings shape the routines of the people in both texts?

partA.stem: Part A: How do the settings shape the routines of the people in both texts?

options.label: A

options.label: B
options.text: The people work only at night because daytime is too dangerous.

options.label: C
options.text: The people spend most of their time repairing broken equipment.

options.label: D
options.text: The settings allow people to travel freely whenever they choose.

partB.stem: Part B: Which sentence from the passage best supports the answer to Part A?

options.label: A
options.text: At night the sky was so clear that I could count satellites crossing between the stars.

options.label: B
options.text: Scientists there study the atmosphere because the air is unusually dry and clear.

options.label: C
options.text: Day nine in the Rub' al Khali.

options.label: D

questions.why: The team waits out the heat before working, which shows the setting controls their schedule.

questions.stem: Which TWO differences between the texts in “Ice and Sand” are supported? Choose two.
options: Text 1 takes place at sea level, while Text 2 takes place on a plateau.
Text 1 describes a crew working alone, while Text 2 describes a large village.
Text 1 is written as a report, while Text 2 is written as a personal journal.
Text 1 describes extreme cold, while Text 2 describes extreme heat.

questions.stem: Select the sentence from “Ice and Sand” that shows how the Concordia crew prepares for a setting it cannot easily leave.

segments.text: Antarctica's Concordia Station sits on a high, frozen plateau where winter temperatures can drop below minus seventy degrees Celsius.
For nearly four months each year the sun never rises, so the small crew depends on artificial light, careful schedules, and supplies delivered before the darkness begins.
Scientists there study the atmosphere because the air is unusually dry and clear.
Our water supply, carried from the last village, has to last another week.

questions.why: Supplies delivered before the darkness show advance planning; the water sentence is about the desert team.

questions.stem: Which detail stays the same in both texts of “Two Visits to the Old Town”?
options: Tour groups still visit the bakery each morning.
The sea breeze still moves through the lanes.
Donkeys still carry goods through the alleys.
Families still live in most of the old houses.
questions.why: Hamid and Reem both feel the sea breeze beneath the balconies.

questions.stem: In “Two Visits to the Old Town,” mark whether each detail appears only in 1952, only in Reem's time, or in both.

rows.text: Merchants shout from doorways
Craft shops fill former homes
A bakery on the corner
Visitors photograph an old oven
Carved balconies shade the lanes

questions.stem: Part A: How has the role of the old town changed between the two texts?

partA.stem: Part A: How has the role of the old town changed between the two texts?

options.label: B

options.label: C

options.label: D

options.label: B
options.text: Small museums and craft shops filled rooms where families once lived.

options.label: C

options.label: D

questions.why: Homes have become museums and shops for visitors.

questions.stem: Select two sentences from “Two Visits to the Old Town” that show something Reem experiences just as Hamid did.

segments.text: Many of the coral-stone houses had been restored, their balconies repainted in deep greens and blues.
The bakery still stood on the corner, though now visitors photographed its old oven before buying bread.
Reem paused beneath a balcony and felt the familiar breeze her grandfather had described.
Small museums and craft shops filled rooms where families once lived.

questions.why: The same bakery and the same breeze link Reem's visit to Hamid's childhood; the other details show change.

questions.stem: Which TWO statements best explain why the author includes the bakery in both texts of “Two Visits to the Old Town”? Choose two.
options: It proves that the old town has not changed at all.
It links the two time periods through one shared place.
It suggests that Reem cares more about bread than history.
It shows that some parts of daily life lasted while others changed.
questions.why: The bakery survives, but visitors now photograph it, showing both continuity and change.

questions.stem: Which statement identifies a similarity between the two harbors in “Two Harbors”?

Both require long face-to-face negotiations with customs officials.
Both rely on natural conditions that can affect the movement of cargo.
Both depend on workers who carry the goods to shore on their own heads.
questions.why: Monsoon winds bring the dhow, and storms stop the cranes: nature matters in both.

questions.stem: For “Two Harbors,” decide which harbor uses each method of handling a task.

rows.text: Recording cargo in ledgers
Predicting congestion with software
Settling customs over several afternoons
Submitting documents before arrival

questions.why: Aden relies on people and time; the terminal relies on technology and advance planning.

questions.stem: Match each task in “Two Harbors” with how the modern terminal handles it differently from Aden.
questions.why: Each human, slow method at Aden has a technological replacement at the terminal.

questions.stem: Part A: How does the author of Text 2 qualify the contrast between the two harbors?

partA.stem: Part A: How does the author of Text 2 qualify the contrast between the two harbors?

options.label: A
options.text: by explaining that modern ships still rely on monsoon winds to arrive

options.label: B

options.label: C

options.label: D

options.label: B

questions.stem: Which THREE inferences about the two settings are supported by details in “Two Harbors”? Choose three.
options: The modern terminal handles fewer goods than Aden did.
Time spent in port has dropped sharply in the modern setting.
Aden's harbor was unaffected by seasonal weather patterns.
Both harbors depend on porters wading through shallow water.
Personal relationships mattered more in Aden's trade negotiations.
Human labor plays a smaller direct role at the modern terminal.
questions.why: Days of talks over coffee contrast with fast, automated, paperless work at the terminal.

questions.stem: How does the treatment of the setting in Text 2 differ from that in Text 1?

questions.why: Text 1 dwells on silence and age; Text 2 stresses the people and work that sustain the valley today.

questions.stem: Part A: Which statement best describes how the author of Text 2 responds to the kind of description found in Text 1?

options.label: A

options.label: B

options.label: C

options.label: B
options.text: Al-Ula's reputation for timeless solitude is understandable but incomplete.

options.label: C

questions.why: “Understandable but incomplete” both grants the appeal and names its limit.

questions.stem: In “Two Views of Al-Ula,” decide whether each detail is emphasized in Text 1, in Text 2, or in both.

rows.text: A guide who lets the scenery speak
Residents whose income depends on tourism
Irrigated orchards
Ancient tombs and antiquities

questions.why: Both texts mention orchards and antiquities, but they use them to support different ideas.

questions.stem: Select two sentences from “Two Views of Al-Ula” in which the author of Text 2 openly evaluates the view of the valley as quiet and timeless.

segments.text: First came a darkened band of palm crowns against the sandstone, then the irrigation channels glinting between orchards, and finally the weathered tombs carved into cliffs that had witnessed caravans for two thousand years.
Our guide spoke little, permitting the landscape's monumental silence to accomplish what explanation could not.
Al-Ula's reputation for timeless solitude is understandable but incomplete.

Farmers still negotiate the allocation of water from aquifers whose levels have declined measurably over recent decades, and the restoration of the ancient town requires engineers, archaeologists, and hundreds of residents whose livelihoods depend increasingly on tourism.
To describe the valley as silent is to overlook the considerable human effort that sustains both its orchards and its antiquities.

questions.why: These two sentences judge the “silent, timeless” view directly; the farmer sentence gives evidence but does not evaluate.

questions.stem: Which TWO conclusions can be drawn by comparing details in both texts of “Two Views of Al-Ula”? Choose two.
options: Text 1 presents the setting through a visitor's experience, while Text 2 takes an analytical stance.
Both authors believe tourism has damaged the valley's ancient monuments.
Text 1 reveals that the water in the oasis is running out quickly.

questions.why: Shared details serve different purposes: wonder in Text 1, analysis in Text 2.

sets.skill: Comparing a Story to Its Performance

questions.stem: What happens in both the story and the play of “The Little Camel”?

The camel runs far away from Dana.

Dana buys a new baby camel.

questions.stem: Where do you find each part of “The Little Camel”: the story, the play, or both?

rows.text: A narrator speaks.
Dana sings to the camel.
Dana laughs and claps.
Music plays.

questions.why: Plays have a narrator and music; both tell that Dana sings.

questions.stem: Select the line from the play of “The Little Camel” that tells the actor how to move.

segments.text: DANA: (softly) Come on, little one.
NARRATOR: The camel stands up!
DANA: (jumping) You did it!

questions.why: The words in ( ) tell the actor what to do; (jumping) is a movement.

questions.stem: Which TWO things does the play of “The Little Camel” use that the story does not? Choose two.
options: a camel that will not walk
directions in brackets
a girl named Dana
a narrator who speaks

questions.stem: What does the play of “The Lantern Seller” include that the story does not?

Yusuf walks through the busy night market.

The old man lights the brass lantern for him.

questions.stem: For “The Lantern Seller,” decide whether each detail appears in the story, the play, or both.

rows.text: Yusuf searches stalls selling spices and cloth
A spotlight follows Yusuf
The old man lights the lantern
The old man asks who the lantern is for

questions.why: Compare each detail with both versions; lighting the lantern happens in both.

questions.stem: Part A: How does the play show Yusuf's feelings differently from the story?

partA.stem: Part A: How does the play show Yusuf's feelings differently from the story?

options.label: C
options.text: Yusuf speaks his thoughts aloud to the audience.

options.label: D

questions.stem: Select the sentence from the story “The Lantern Seller” whose idea the play reveals through Yusuf's answer to the old man's question.

segments.text: Yusuf hurried through the night market, clutching the last coin his grandmother had given him.
He wanted a lantern for her window, but every stall seemed to sell only spices and cloth.
At last he spotted an old man packing away a single brass lantern.
Yusuf held out his coin nervously, hoping it would be enough.

The captain speaks aloud instead of staying silent.
Ali becomes the captain of the pearling boat.

questions.stem: Part A: How does the script of “The First Dive” represent Ali's pounding heart from the story?

questions.stem: For “The First Dive,” decide whether each detail appears only in the story, only in the script, or in both.

rows.text: Ali remembers his grandfather's stories
Musicians drum at the edge of the stage
The captain taps the stone weight twice
Ali's hands or voice show fear

questions.why: The script keeps the signal and Ali's fear but drops his memories and adds drummers.

questions.stem: Which TWO details from the story of “The First Dive” are left out of the script? Choose two.
options: Ali thinks about his grandfather's stories.
The captain signals by tapping the stone.
Ali had trained for months before the dive.
Ali is nervous as he holds the rope.
questions.why: Inner thoughts and background are hard to stage, so the script leaves them out.

questions.stem: Select the sentence from the story “The First Dive” about a character who is silent in the story but speaks in the script.

segments.text: Ali had trained for months, yet when the boat anchored above the oyster beds, his hands trembled on the rope.
His uncle, the captain, said nothing; he only tapped the stone weight twice, the signal that a diver was ready.
Ali filled his lungs, remembered his grandfather's stories of dives that lasted longer than a song, and slipped beneath the green water.
Below, everything was silent except the pounding of his own heart.

questions.why: The silent captain of the story speaks in the script.

questions.stem: Why does the radio version of “The Silent Clock” rely on sound effects more than the story does?

The story has no events that could be described in words.

Sound effects explain why the master craftsman is ill.

Maryam discovers the pebble.
The bronze elephant on the clock
Maryam opens the panel.

questions.stem: Which TWO statements best compare the endings of the story and the radio version of “The Silent Clock”? Choose two.

The story ends before the water begins to flow again.
The story shows success through moving figures, while the radio version uses a chime.

questions.stem: What is the main effect of the wide shot at the start of the screenplay of “The Comet Watcher”?

options.label: B
options.text: It uses a voice-over so the audience hears her private thoughts.

options.label: C
options.text: It shows her arguing with the other students about the comet.

partB.stem: Part B: Which sentence from the passage best supports the answer to Part A?

questions.stem: For “The Comet Watcher,” decide which film technique the screenplay uses to present each detail from the story.

rows.text: Laila recalculates in her notebook
The sky clears before dawn
Laila suspects her calculations are wrong
Laila records the time

questions.stem: Select the sentence from the story “The Comet Watcher” that describes a sight the screenplay never shows the audience.

questions.stem: Which TWO statements explain how the screenplay's ending differs in effect from the story's ending in “The Comet Watcher”? Choose two.

questions.stem: Which statement best describes how the production of “The Last Map” interprets the ending differently from the story?

questions.stem: Part A: What is the reviewer's central criticism of the production of “The Last Map”?

options.label: A

options.label: B
options.text: Its actors fail to portray the relationship between master and apprentice.

options.label: C

questions.stem: For “The Last Map,” decide whether each element belongs to the story, the stage production, or both.

The apprentice waiting for parting wisdom
The map passed from master to apprentice

questions.stem: Which TWO details from the story “The Last Map” serve the same purpose as the production's dissolving projections? Choose two.

In the company's stage adaptation, the director transforms this quiet ending into a moment of unmistakable grief.
The effect is visually arresting, yet it sacrifices the story's restraint: where the original trusted readers to sense loss in a single gesture, the production insists that the audience feel it.

questions.stem: Who is telling the story “Friday Bread”?
options: a person who is not in the story
Aisha, a girl in the family
Mrs. Salma, the neighbor
Grandma, who bakes the bread
questions.why: Aisha says “My name is Aisha,” so she is the one telling it.

questions.stem: True or false: In “Friday Bread,” the words “I” and “my” show that Aisha tells the story herself.
questions.why: A narrator who says I and my is inside the story.

questions.stem: Select the sentence from “Friday Bread” that tells what Aisha thinks.

segments.text: I help her press the dough flat with my hands.
The kitchen gets warm and smells sweet.
I think sharing is the best part.
She smiles and gives us dates.

questions.why: “I think” shows Aisha's own opinion.

questions.stem: In “Friday Bread,” is each one something Aisha does or something Aisha thinks?

rows.text: She presses the dough.
Sharing is the best part.
She takes bread to Mrs. Salma.

questions.why: Actions are things she does; opinions are things she thinks.

questions.stem: Part A: What does Aisha's family believe?

partA.stem: Part A: What does Aisha's family believe?

options.label: A
options.text: Food should be shared with others.

options.label: B
options.text: Only grandmothers can bake.

options.label: C
options.text: Dates are better than bread.

options.label: D
options.text: Bread should be eaten alone.

partB.stem: Part B: Which sentence from the passage best supports the answer to Part A?

options.label: A
options.text: Grandma always says, "Bread tastes better when we share it."

options.label: B
options.text: I help her press the dough flat with my hands.

options.label: C
options.text: The kitchen gets warm and smells sweet.

options.label: D
options.text: In my family, Grandma bakes bread every Friday morning.

questions.why: Grandma's words show that the family values sharing.

questions.stem: From whose point of view is “A Letter from Japan” written?
options: a teacher describing a class trip abroad
a Saudi boy staying with a family in Japan
a grandfather who is traveling in Japan
a Japanese boy visiting a family in Dammam
questions.why: Turki, from Dammam, writes to his grandfather about his host family.

questions.stem: Part A: How does Turki's view of the quiet train change?

partA.stem: Part A: How does Turki's view of the quiet train change?

options.label: A
options.text: He first finds it strange but later sees it as respectful.

options.label: B
options.text: He thinks it is rude from the very start.

options.label: C
options.text: He first enjoys it but later finds it boring.

options.label: D
options.text: He never notices that the train is quiet.

partB.stem: Part B: Which sentence from the passage best supports the answer to Part A?

options.label: A
options.text: Yesterday my host family took me on a crowded train, and surprisingly, nobody spoke on their phones during the entire journey.

options.label: B
options.text: Now I think it is a kind of respect for others.

options.label: C
options.text: Japan is full of surprises, and I am learning something new every day.

options.label: D
options.text: My host brother, Haruto, laughed loudly when I forgot to change them.

questions.why: “Now I think” shows his new understanding.

questions.stem: In “A Letter from Japan,” decide whether each custom is the same as in Turki's home or different.

rows.text: Taking off shoes indoors
Staying quiet on trains
Wearing bathroom slippers

questions.why: Turki says shoes come off “exactly as we do at home,” but the other customs are new to him.

questions.stem: Which TWO words best describe Turki's attitude toward Japanese customs in “A Letter from Japan”? Choose two.
options: curious
respectful
annoyed
fearful
questions.why: He enjoys the surprises and comes to respect the quiet.

questions.stem: Select the sentence from “A Letter from Japan” in which Turki compares a Japanese custom with how people act on buses at home.

segments.text: Japan is full of surprises, and I am learning something new every day.
At home in Dammam, people chat on the bus constantly, so the silence felt uncomfortable at first.
My host brother, Haruto, laughed loudly when I forgot to change them.
Tomorrow I will teach the family how to prepare Arabic coffee with cardamom, the way you taught me.

questions.why: He compares the quiet train with chatty buses in Dammam.

questions.stem: From whose point of view is “The View from the Spice Stall” told?
options: a visitor exploring the market
a mother who sells spices
a girl whose family runs a spice stall
an outside narrator who knows everyone's thoughts
questions.why: The narrator says “my mother” and “our stall.”

questions.stem: Part A: How does the narrator's perspective on the market differ from the visitors' perspective?

partA.stem: Part A: How does the narrator's perspective on the market differ from the visitors' perspective?

options.label: A
options.text: She sees it as dangerous, while they see it as safe and calm.

options.label: B
options.text: She sees it as everyday work, while they see it as an exciting attraction.

options.label: C
options.text: She sees it as boring, while they see it as educational.

options.label: D
options.text: She sees it as a museum, while they see it as a workplace.

partB.stem: Part B: Which sentence from the passage best supports the answer to Part A?

options.label: A
options.text: Every morning, visitors drift into the Marrakech market with their cameras raised, and I have learned to read their faces.

options.label: B
options.text: One woman asked whether we dressed this way only for tourists; my mother smiled politely, but I noticed her hands tighten around the scoop.

options.label: C
options.text: I do not mind the photographs, exactly.

options.label: D
options.text: To us, it is ordinary life.

questions.why: The short sentence directly contrasts with the visitors' sense of adventure.

questions.stem: Select the sentence from “The View from the Spice Stall” that reveals the mother's hidden reaction through the narrator's observation.

segments.text: They photograph my mother's pyramids of saffron and cumin as though our stall were a museum display rather than the place where we earn our living.
I do not mind the photographs, exactly.
One woman asked whether we dressed this way only for tourists; my mother smiled politely, but I noticed her hands tighten around the scoop.
To the visitors, the market is an adventure, a colorful escape from ordinary life.

questions.why: The polite smile hides discomfort that only the daughter notices.

questions.stem: In “The View from the Spice Stall,” decide whether each statement reflects the visitors' view or the narrator's view.

rows.text: The stall is like a museum display.
The market is where the family earns a living.
The market is a colorful escape.
Spice blending is a tradition worth asking about.

questions.why: The narrator contrasts outsiders' impressions with her family's reality.

questions.stem: Which TWO inferences about the narrator are supported by “The View from the Spice Stall”? Choose two.
options: She is proud of her family's knowledge and history.
She believes the visitors take photographs to mock them.
She wants visitors to see her family as people, not scenery.
She wants her mother to stop selling to tourists.
questions.why: She values the three-generation story and wishes visitors would ask about it.

questions.stem: Which character in “The Quiet Return” knows that Nawaf has really arrived?
options: Sara
no one in the scene
only the neighbors
Mother
questions.why: Mother's secret smile and her refusal to move the banner show she knows.

questions.stem: Part A: How does the audience's knowledge differ from Sara's?

partA.stem: Part A: How does the audience's knowledge differ from Sara's?

options.label: A
options.text: The audience and Sara both know that Nawaf is outside.

options.label: B
options.text: Sara knows about the banner, but the audience cannot see it.

options.label: C
options.text: Sara knows the flight is cancelled, but the audience does not.

options.label: D
options.text: The audience knows Nawaf is outside, but Sara believes he is still away.

partB.stem: Part B: Which sentence from the passage best supports the answer to Part A?

options.label: A
options.text: Outside the window, the audience glimpses NAWAF holding a suitcase and pressing a finger to his lips.

options.label: B
options.text: SARA: (disappointed) Then I suppose we should put away all the decorations immediately.

options.label: C
options.text: SARA reaches under the table for the rolled-up banner.

options.label: D
options.text: MOTHER: (sighing loudly) Your brother's flight was unexpectedly cancelled this afternoon, so he will not arrive until next week.

questions.why: The audience sees Nawaf, while Sara thinks the flight was cancelled; this is dramatic irony.

questions.stem: Select the stage direction from “The Quiet Return” that first hints that Mother is hiding something from Sara.

segments.text: SARA reaches under the table for the rolled-up banner.
MOTHER quickly blocks her, smiling mysteriously at the audience.
A doorbell rings, and SARA frowns as she goes to answer it, grumbling about inconsiderate visitors arriving at dinnertime.
MOTHER: No, leave them exactly where they are, since they are certainly not interfering with anything.

questions.why: A mysterious smile shared with the audience signals that Mother knows more.

questions.stem: In “The Quiet Return,” decide whether Sara knows each fact at the moment the doorbell rings.

rows.text: Decorations are under the table
Nawaf is standing outside
The flight story is not true
Mother does not want the banner moved

questions.why: Sara knows what she has seen and heard, but not the secret the audience shares with Mother.

questions.stem: Which TWO effects does the difference in points of view create in “The Quiet Return”? Choose two.
options: It makes the audience doubt whether Nawaf is really coming home.
It creates humor when Sara complains about unexpected visitors.
It shows that Mother is sad about the cancelled flight.
It builds suspense as the audience waits for Sara to open the door.
questions.why: Knowing more than Sara makes her grumbling funny and her trip to the door suspenseful.

questions.stem: How does the narrator's perspective on the family tradition in “Two Hundred Cabbages” change?
options: She moves from dismissing it as outdated to valuing its shared purpose.
She moves from ignoring it to wanting to make it faster with modern machines.
She moves from loving it to resenting the work it requires.
She moves from fearing her grandmother to openly challenging her.
questions.why: She begins by calling it inefficient and ends by seeing that efficiency was never the point.

questions.stem: Part A: What does the grandmother's response to the narrator's argument suggest about the grandmother's perspective?

partA.stem: Part A: What does the grandmother's response to the narrator's argument suggest about the grandmother's perspective?

options.label: A
options.text: She agrees that the tradition is inefficient but continues it out of habit.

options.label: B
options.text: She is offended that the narrator criticized the family's customs.

options.label: C
options.text: She believes the value of the tradition must be experienced rather than explained.

options.label: D
options.text: She thinks the narrator should have stayed longer in Toronto.

partB.stem: Part B: Which sentence from the passage best supports the answer to Part A?

options.label: A
options.text: My aunt corrected my technique; my cousin teased me about my accent; my grandmother hummed a song I had not heard since childhood.

options.label: B
options.text: That evening, as we distributed containers to neighbors who had no family nearby, I understood that efficiency had never been the point.

options.label: C
options.text: Grandmother listened to my argument without interrupting, then handed me, her eldest granddaughter, a pair of rubber gloves.

options.label: D
options.text: By midafternoon, eleven relatives were kneeling around enormous basins, rubbing chili paste between the leaves of two hundred cabbages.

questions.why: Instead of arguing back, she hands over gloves, inviting the narrator to take part.

questions.stem: Put the stages of the narrator's experience in “Two Hundred Cabbages” in order.
sequence: She argues that the ritual is unnecessary.
She receives rubber gloves from her grandmother.
She is corrected and teased by relatives.
She stops counting the cabbages.
She realizes the true point of the tradition.
questions.why: Her perspective shifts step by step as she joins the work.

questions.stem: Which TWO details from “Two Hundred Cabbages” best reveal the cultural values behind the tradition? Choose two.
options: The narrator studied in Toronto for two years.
Relatives work together around shared basins.
Modern refrigerators and supermarkets are available.
The family gives kimchi to neighbors with no family nearby.
questions.why: Togetherness and generosity to neighbors are the values the tradition carries.

questions.stem: When the narrator says, “Somewhere between the hundredth cabbage and the hundred-and-first, I stopped counting,” the detail most likely shows that she ____.
options: has grown too tired to continue working
has lost interest in helping her family
has finished preparing all of the cabbages
has become absorbed in the shared experience
questions.why: No longer counting suggests she has stopped measuring the work and started living it.

questions.stem: Which statement best describes the author's actual point of view in “A Guide to Seeing Everything Quickly”?
options: Residents would rather that tourists avoid conversation with them entirely.
Visitors should spend most of their time at the old library.
The city's history is too complicated for most visitors.
Visitors who rush through the city miss what makes it meaningful.
