questions.why: The advice is ironic: the author means the opposite of the rushed plan described.

questions.stem: Part A: In the second paragraph, what does the author suggest residents would REALLY feel if a visitor learned their language?

partA.stem: Part A: In the second paragraph, what does the author suggest residents would REALLY feel if a visitor learned their language?

options.label: A
options.text: They would be disappointed by the visitor's effort.

options.label: B
options.text: They would be indifferent to the visitor's choices.

options.label: C
options.text: They would be confused about the visitor's purpose.

options.label: D
options.text: They would be pleased and honored by the effort.

partB.stem: Part B: Which sentence from the passage best supports the answer to Part A?

options.label: A
options.text: Do not trouble yourself with the old library, whose manuscripts were merely copied by scholars who devoted entire lifetimes to them; a photograph of its doorway will suffice.

options.label: B
options.text: Above all, resist the temptation to learn a single word of the local language.

options.label: C
options.text: Proceed directly to the airport, confident that you have truly seen us.

options.label: D
options.text: Our citizens, who have welcomed merchants, scholars, and wanderers for generations, would surely be disappointed to discover that a visitor had made the effort.

questions.why: A people known for welcoming strangers would not truly be disappointed; “surely” signals sarcasm.

questions.stem: For “A Guide to Seeing Everything Quickly,” decide whether each statement is what the speaker literally says or what the author actually means.

rows.text: A photograph of the library doorway is enough.
Rushed sightseeing cannot reveal a city's character.
Talking with residents is a waste of time.
Hospitality is one of the city's greatest treasures.

questions.why: In satire, the literal advice and the author's real message point in opposite directions.

questions.stem: Select two sentences from “A Guide to Seeing Everything Quickly” in which the city's hospitality is revealed within ironic advice.

segments.text: Welcome, esteemed traveler, to a city whose twelve centuries of history can be conveniently consumed between breakfast and lunch.
Do not trouble yourself with the old library, whose manuscripts were merely copied by scholars who devoted entire lifetimes to them; a photograph of its doorway will suffice.
Should a shopkeeper invite you to sit for tea, decline immediately, since conversation with residents is notoriously inefficient and rarely yields anything suitable for sharing online.
Above all, resist the temptation to learn a single word of the local language.
Our citizens, who have welcomed merchants, scholars, and wanderers for generations, would surely be disappointed to discover that a visitor had made the effort.
Proceed directly to the airport, confident that you have truly seen us.

questions.why: The tea invitation and the long history of welcoming strangers show hospitality hidden inside the mock advice.

questions.stem: Which THREE techniques does the author of “A Guide to Seeing Everything Quickly” use to convey a view opposite to the speaker's literal words? Choose three.
options: an ironic final claim that the visitor has truly seen the city
a personal story of the author's own travels
direct statistics about tourism's harm
a falsely courteous, formal tone
expert testimony from historians
understatement that minimizes great achievements
questions.why: Mock politeness, words like “merely,” and a false conclusion all signal satire.

questions.stem: In “The Missing Shoe,” what are the words inside the ( ) marks called?
options: character names
the play's title
stage directions
the setting list
questions.why: Stage directions tell actors what to do and how to move.

questions.stem: True or false: In “The Missing Shoe,” the words “(running to the door)” tell what Sara does.
questions.why: A stage direction shows an action the actor does.

questions.stem: Select the stage direction in “The Missing Shoe” that tells that a new character comes on stage.

segments.text: A cat walks in slowly.
Dad, I can't find my shoe!
Did you look by the door?
Look at the cat!

questions.why: The cat comes on stage in a stage direction, not in a spoken line.

questions.stem: For “The Missing Shoe,” is each part a line a character says or a stage direction?

rows.text: Did you look by the door?
looking under the table
Sara hugs the cat.
You took my shoe!

questions.why: Spoken lines come after a name; stage directions are in ( ) or [ ].

questions.stem: Part A: What is the problem at the start of “The Missing Shoe”?

partA.stem: Part A: What is the problem at the start of “The Missing Shoe”?

options.label: A
options.text: Sara cannot find her shoe.

options.label: B
options.text: The cat is lost outside.

options.label: C
options.text: Dad cannot find his cup.

options.label: D
options.text: Sara is late for school.

partB.stem: Part B: Which sentence from the passage best supports the answer to Part A?

options.label: A
options.text: A cat walks in slowly.

options.label: B
options.text: Did you look by the door?

options.label: C
options.text: Look at the cat!

options.label: D
options.text: Dad, I can't find my shoe!

questions.why: A play often begins by showing the problem; Sara says she cannot find her shoe.

questions.stem: What is the main purpose of the lines in [ ] brackets in “The Science Fair Robot”?
options: to list the lines the judge must say aloud
to describe the setting and the actions on stage
to tell the audience which project won the whole science fair
to explain why Layla built the robot
questions.why: Bracketed stage directions describe where the scene happens and what happens on stage.

questions.stem: Put the events of “The Science Fair Robot” in order.
sequence: Layla presses buttons on a robot that will not move.
Omar notices that the battery wire is loose.
Ms. Hadi asks Layla what her robot does.
The robot carries water across the table to a plant.
questions.why: Scene 1 shows the problem; Scene 2 shows the robot working.

questions.stem: Select the stage direction in “The Science Fair Robot” that shows time has passed between the two scenes.

segments.text: One hour later, MS. HADI approaches their table carrying a clipboard.
It worked perfectly last night when I tested it in the kitchen!
Look, the battery wire came loose.
LAYLA kneels beside a small robot that will not move, no matter which button she presses.

questions.why: A new scene often begins with a direction that tells the new time or place.

questions.stem: In “The Science Fair Robot,” does each detail happen in Scene 1 or Scene 2?

rows.text: Layla kneels beside a robot that will not move.
Ms. Hadi carries a clipboard.
Omar points at the loose wire.
The robot stops beside a plant.

questions.why: Scenes divide a play into parts; each scene has its own time and events.

questions.stem: Part A: Why does Layla feel the way the stage direction “(sighing with relief)” describes?

partA.stem: Part A: Why does Layla feel the way the stage direction “(sighing with relief)” describes?

options.label: A
options.text: She learns the robot can be fixed.

options.label: B
options.text: She knows her brother built the robot.

options.label: C
options.text: She sees that the judge is smiling.

options.label: D
options.text: She finds out the fair is canceled.

partB.stem: Part B: Which sentence from the passage best supports the answer to Part A?

options.label: A
options.text: It worked perfectly last night when I tested it in the kitchen!

options.label: B
options.text: Please explain what your invention does and why you decided to build it.

options.label: C
options.text: Look, the battery wire came loose.

options.label: D
options.text: It delivers water to classroom plants that people usually forget to water.

questions.why: Omar finds the simple cause of the problem, so Layla feels relief.

questions.stem: What is the main function of the SETTING section at the beginning of “The Sandstorm”?
options: to introduce the radio announcer as the most important character
to establish the time and place before the conflict begins
to explain how camels protect themselves in a storm
to show that Faisal and his grandmother disagree
questions.why: The setting section tells the audience where and when the action takes place.

questions.stem: For “The Sandstorm,” classify each stage direction as a sound effect or a character's action.

rows.text: the wind rising offstage
jumping up and reaching for his scarf
the wind changing from a whistle to a low, continuous roar
gripping his arm firmly

questions.why: Some directions guide the sound crew; others guide the actors.

questions.stem: Put the parts of the plot of “The Sandstorm” in order.
sequence: The tent and the rising wind are described.
A radio warns that a sandstorm is coming.
Faisal wants to rush out to bring the camels in.
Faisal realizes the storm has already arrived.
Grandmother Noura says they will find the camels tomorrow.
questions.why: The scene moves from exposition to rising action, climax, and resolution.

questions.stem: Which TWO stage directions in “The Sandstorm” reveal a character's feelings rather than only describing the setting? Choose two.
options: a lantern hangs from the center pole
quietly, sitting back down
the tent walls ripple and the lantern sways
nodding, then smiling
questions.why: Directions about how a character speaks or moves can reveal feelings such as calm or defeat.

questions.stem: Part A: What does the long pause in “The Sandstorm” mainly do for the structure of the scene?

partA.stem: Part A: What does the long pause in “The Sandstorm” mainly do for the structure of the scene?

options.label: A
options.text: It marks the turning point when Faisal understands the danger.

options.label: B
options.text: It signals that the scene is ending and a new one will begin.

options.label: C
options.text: It shows that the radio has stopped working because of the storm.

options.label: D
options.text: It gives Grandmother Noura time to leave the tent unseen.

partB.stem: Part B: Which sentence from the passage best supports the answer to Part A?

options.label: A
options.text: A severe sandstorm is expected to reach the southern camps within the hour, and all travelers are advised to remain indoors.

options.label: B
options.text: The camels are still grazing by the dunes, so I have to bring them in before the storm arrives!

options.label: C
options.text: Wait, and listen carefully to the wind before you run into it.

options.label: D
options.text: It's already here, isn't it?

questions.why: Right after the pause, Faisal's question shows his change of mind, the scene's turning point.

questions.stem: Match each element of the drama “The Clockmaker's Apprentice” to its example.

pairs.right: a workshop crowded with gears in 1206
a tiny pebble held up to the light

questions.why: Plays are built from labeled parts, settings, props, and sound cues.

questions.stem: In “The Clockmaker's Apprentice,” Yusuf's first speech, marked “(to himself),” is best described as ____.
options: a description of the workshop setting
a direction for the lighting crew
a summary of the previous scene
a speech that reveals his private thoughts
questions.why: A character speaking to himself lets the audience hear thoughts other characters cannot.

questions.stem: Select the sentence from “The Clockmaker's Apprentice” in which a character's words contradict what the audience already knows.

segments.text: Master, nothing is wrong, and everything is working perfectly.
Perhaps I can repair it before he returns.
Then why has the water stopped moving?
What are you searching for, Yusuf?

questions.why: The audience knows the clock has stopped, so Yusuf's claim is plainly false.

questions.stem: Part A: How does the stage direction about the footsteps build tension in the scene?

partA.stem: Part A: How does the stage direction about the footsteps build tension in the scene?

options.label: A
options.text: The sound tells the audience that the clock has started again.

options.label: B
options.text: The footsteps show that a thief has entered the workshop.

options.label: C
options.text: Yusuf hears the footsteps and quickly hides the broken bowl.

options.label: D
options.text: The audience knows Al-Jazari is coming, but Yusuf does not.

partB.stem: Part B: Which sentence from the passage best supports the answer to Part A?

options.label: A
options.text: Then why has the water stopped moving?

options.label: B
options.text: Footsteps approach offstage, but YUSUF does not hear them.

options.label: C
options.text: He climbs onto a stool and peers into the copper bowl.

options.label: D
options.text: Perhaps I can repair it before he returns.

questions.why: When the audience knows more than a character, the scene gains suspense.

questions.stem: Why does the playwright place the discovery of the pebble immediately before Al-Jazari's final line?
options: It shows that Al-Jazari had planned the broken clock as a lesson.
It gives concrete proof that the problem could be studied and solved.
It explains why the elephant clock was never finished in the end.
It reveals that Yusuf secretly placed the pebble there to test his master.
questions.why: The pebble turns the lesson into something the audience has just seen happen.

questions.stem: What is the primary purpose of the opening stage direction in “Two Tides”?
options: It introduces the conflict between Hamad and Mariam.
It sets up a split stage that links two time periods.
It explains the history of pearl diving in the Gulf.
It tells the audience that Mariam is dreaming of the past.
questions.why: The divided stage lets two eras appear side by side without the characters meeting.

questions.stem: In “Two Tides,” on which side of the stage does each detail appear?

rows.text: a stone weight tied to an ankle
a sample jar held toward the light
an old, cracked diving stone
the line “Nothing again.”

questions.why: Each side has its own era, though objects can travel across time.

questions.stem: Which TWO stage directions in “Two Tides” most clearly create a parallel between the two time periods? Choose two.
options: He inhales deeply and disappears beneath the surface as the blue light dims to near darkness.
resurfacing, gasping, empty-handed
The two halves never interact, but actions on one side are frequently mirrored on the other.
For a moment, both sides of the stage are silent.
questions.why: Mirrored actions and a shared silence join the two eras on stage.

questions.stem: The direction “quietly, almost to the audience” signals that Hamad's last line in “Two Tides” works like ____.
options: a cue telling the crew to raise the house lights
an aside that shares a private thought the crew does not hear
a flashback that shows an event from his childhood
a soliloquy spoken after every character exits
questions.why: An aside is spoken toward the audience and is not meant for the other characters.

questions.stem: Part A: What effect does the playwright create by placing the cracked diving stone on Mariam's side of the stage?

partA.stem: Part A: What effect does the playwright create by placing the cracked diving stone on Mariam's side of the stage?

options.label: A
options.text: It shows that Mariam has become a pearl diver herself.

options.label: B
options.text: It hints that the laboratory is located on the old boat.

options.label: C
options.text: It proves that the oyster beds never recovered at all.

options.label: D
options.text: It suggests that Hamad's knowledge has been passed down to her.

partB.stem: Part B: Which sentence from the passage best supports the answer to Part A?

options.label: A
options.text: Nothing again, so someone must remember exactly where they used to grow.

options.label: B
options.text: The oysters are fewer every season, and nobody on this boat is willing to acknowledge it aloud.

options.label: C
options.text: The oyster beds are recovering, but only in the protected zones, precisely where my grandfather predicted they would.

options.label: D
options.text: He inhales deeply and disappears beneath the surface as the blue light dims to near darkness.

questions.why: Mariam credits her grandfather's prediction, so the stone stands for what he handed down.

questions.stem: What is the main function of the Playwright's Note in “The Mended Atlas”?
options: It explains the history of the bookshop and the family that owns it.
It tells directors how to use sound so that silence becomes meaningful.
It reveals the ending of the scene before the action has begun.
It warns actors to speak softly so the clock can always be heard.
questions.why: A playwright's note guides production choices that shape how the audience experiences the scene.

questions.stem: Select the stage direction in “The Mended Atlas” that most clearly reveals Reem's hesitation without any dialogue.

segments.text: In the silence, REEM places the folder on the counter, then, reconsidering, slides it beneath her arm again.
He returns to his mending, and the lights fade gradually, although the lamp above the atlas remains illuminated until the last possible moment.
A narrow bookshop in Jeddah, late evening, where shelves rise into darkness.
finally setting down the atlas, deliberately

questions.why: Her undone gesture shows she cannot bring herself to share the news.

questions.stem: Which TWO statements explain how the final stage direction of “The Mended Atlas” contributes to the scene's meaning? Choose two.
options: The darkness indicates that the argument will be settled in the following scene.
The lit lamp signals that Reem has decided to tear up the demolition permits.
The lingering lamp suggests Khalid's devotion to the shop persists even as its end approaches.
The slow fade echoes the shop's uncertain future without stating it in dialogue.
questions.why: Lighting can carry meaning the characters never say aloud; nothing shows Reem changing her mind.

questions.stem: Part A: What does the stage direction “(too brightly)” suggest about Reem's opening line?

partA.stem: Part A: What does the stage direction “(too brightly)” suggest about Reem's opening line?

options.label: A
options.text: She is mocking her father for refusing to modernize the shop.

options.label: B
options.text: She is masking her discomfort about news she has not yet shared.

options.label: C
options.text: She wants to change the subject away from the damaged atlas.

options.label: D
options.text: She genuinely believes the street is more beautiful than before.

partB.stem: Part B: Which sentence from the passage best supports the answer to Part A?

options.label: A
options.text: The municipality has offered generous compensation for every property on this block.

options.label: B
options.text: KHALID, seventy, sits behind the counter meticulously mending the spine of a damaged atlas, while his daughter REEM, an architect, stands near the door holding a folder of demolition permits she has not yet mentioned.

options.label: C
options.text: It has looked identical for forty years, whether anyone bothered to illuminate it or not.

options.label: D
options.text: Then the municipality has determined what a map is worth.

questions.why: The opening direction tells the audience what Reem is hiding, which explains her forced cheer.

questions.stem: In “The Mended Atlas,” the direction “(finally setting down the atlas, deliberately)” before Khalid's line about what a map is worth signals ____.
options: that he has finished the repair and is ready to sell the atlas
that he understands the folder's purpose and answers it directly
that he did not hear Reem's earlier remark about the street
that he plans to protest the decision at a public meeting
questions.why: Stopping his work for the first time shows he has grasped the real subject of the visit.

sets.skill: Drawing Evidence from Texts for Writing

questions.stem: True or false: Mia wants to write that bees help farmers. The sentence “Farmers are happy when bees live near their fields.” from “Busy Bees” can help her.
questions.why: This sentence connects bees to farmers, so it supports her idea.

questions.stem: Lina is writing, “Bees help plants make fruit.” Select the sentence from “Busy Bees” that best supports her idea.

segments.text: This helps the plant make seeds and fruit.
Bees also make honey.
Bees are small, but they do a big job.
A bee flies from flower to flower to drink sweet nectar.

questions.why: Good evidence says the same idea the writer wants to prove.

questions.stem: Omar is writing about how bees help us get food. Does each detail from “Busy Bees” help his writing or not?

rows.text: Apples, melons, and almonds all grow better when bees visit.
Bees are small.
Many foods we eat need bees.
A bee drinks sweet nectar.

questions.why: Only details about food help a paragraph about food.

questions.stem: Ali writes, “Bees carry pollen.” Which detail from “Busy Bees” tells HOW they carry it?
options: They visit apple trees.
They drink sweet nectar.
They make honey inside the hive.
Pollen sticks to their legs.
questions.why: The passage says pollen sticks to a bee's legs.

questions.stem: Part A: Which idea could a student write about using facts from “Busy Bees”?

partA.stem: Part A: Which idea could a student write about using facts from “Busy Bees”?

options.label: A
options.text: Bees only like yellow flowers.

options.label: B
options.text: Bees are dangerous to farmers.

options.label: C
options.text: Bees sleep all winter long.

options.label: D
options.text: Bees are important for growing food.

partB.stem: Part B: Which sentence from the passage best supports the answer to Part A?

options.label: A
options.text: Bees also make honey.

options.label: B
options.text: Yellow dust called pollen sticks to its legs.

options.label: C
options.text: Bees are small, but they do a big job.

options.label: D
options.text: Many foods we eat need bees.

questions.why: The passage says many foods need bees, which supports the idea.

questions.stem: A student writes, “Desert animals use different ways to escape the noon heat.” Which evidence from “Resting at Noon” best supports this sentence?
options: The fox sleeps in a den, and the lizard hides in a tunnel.
The lizard lies in the sun to warm its body each morning.
The fox hunts insects and small lizards when night comes.
The hottest hours in the desert come in the middle of the day.
questions.why: To support “different ways,” the evidence must show more than one animal's method.

questions.stem: Select the sentence from “Resting at Noon” that a student could quote to show that underground homes stay cool.

segments.text: Its burrow can be many degrees cooler than the sand above it.
The fox comes out at night to hunt insects and small lizards.
The spiny-tailed lizard has a different plan.
In the desert, the hottest hours come in the middle of the day.

questions.why: This sentence directly compares the burrow's temperature with the sand above.

questions.stem: A student is writing that the spiny-tailed lizard plans its day around the temperature. Which TWO details from “Resting at Noon” should the student include? Choose two.
options: The fox comes out at night to hunt insects and small lizards.
During the hottest part of the day, camels often sit facing the sun.
Before the ground becomes dangerously hot, it hurries back into its tunnel.
In the early morning, it lies in the sun to warm its body.
questions.why: Evidence must be about the right animal and the right idea.

questions.stem: In “Resting at Noon,” which animal does each piece of evidence describe?

rows.text: sleeps in a cool underground den
warms its body in the early morning sun
sits facing the sun at midday
hunts at night

questions.why: Matching evidence to the right subject keeps a paragraph accurate.

questions.stem: Part A: Which claim could a student best support using evidence from “Resting at Noon”?

partA.stem: Part A: Which claim could a student best support using evidence from “Resting at Noon”?

options.label: A
options.text: Camels are the only desert animals that change their daily behavior.

options.label: B
options.text: Most desert animals hunt during the hottest part of the afternoon.

options.label: C
options.text: Desert animals are lazier than animals that live in cooler places.

options.label: D
options.text: Resting in the hottest hours helps desert animals save water and energy.

partB.stem: Part B: Which sentence from the passage best supports the answer to Part A?

options.label: A
options.text: Resting at noon may look lazy, but for desert animals it is a careful way to save water and energy.

options.label: B
options.text: Even camels change their behavior.

options.label: C
options.text: The spiny-tailed lizard has a different plan.

options.label: D
options.text: The fox comes out at night to hunt insects and small lizards.

questions.why: The last sentence states the claim the details build toward.

questions.stem: A student claims that Ibn al-Haytham trusted evidence more than famous opinions. Which detail from “The Dark Room” best supports this claim?
options: He was born in the city of Basra around 965 and studied light closely.
Many historians call him an early user of the scientific method.
His Book of Optics was translated into Latin many years later.
He would not accept an idea just because famous thinkers wrote it.
questions.why: The detail about refusing to accept famous ideas directly shows his attitude.

questions.stem: Select the sentence from “The Dark Room” that best supports the claim that Ibn al-Haytham wanted others to test his work.

segments.text: Ibn al-Haytham recorded his methods carefully so that other people could repeat his tests and check his results.
Instead, he designed experiments.
He reasoned that light must travel in straight lines from objects into the eye, not the other way around.
His Book of Optics was later translated into Latin, and European scientists studied it for centuries.

questions.why: Recording methods so others can repeat the tests shows he wanted his work checked.

questions.stem: A student is writing a paragraph about how Ibn al-Haytham reached his conclusion about light. Put the evidence from “The Dark Room” in the order the paragraph should present it.
sequence: He doubted the belief that eyes send out rays.
He made a tiny hole in the wall of a darkened room.
He saw an upside-down image on the opposite wall.
He concluded that light travels in straight lines into the eye.
questions.why: Presenting evidence in logical order makes the reasoning easy to follow.

questions.stem: Choose the transition that best introduces the quotation from “The Dark Room”: Ibn al-Haytham valued independent thinking; ____ a seeker of truth should question even the books he admires most.
options: by contrast, scholars said
however, he wrote that
even so, critics argued
in fact, he wrote that
questions.why: “In fact” signals that the quotation strengthens the point just made.

questions.stem: Part A: Which claim about Ibn al-Haytham's influence is best supported by “The Dark Room”?

partA.stem: Part A: Which claim about Ibn al-Haytham's influence is best supported by “The Dark Room”?

options.label: A
options.text: He disproved every idea that earlier scholars had written.

options.label: B
options.text: His experiments were ignored until the modern era began.

options.label: C
options.text: His work shaped science far beyond his own time and place.

options.label: D
options.text: He was the first person ever to study the human eye.

partB.stem: Part B: Which sentence from the passage best supports the answer to Part A?

options.label: A
options.text: Instead, he designed experiments.

options.label: B
options.text: His Book of Optics was later translated into Latin, and European scientists studied it for centuries.

options.label: C
options.text: He wrote that a seeker of truth should question even the books he admires most.

options.label: D
options.text: The scientist Ibn al-Haytham, who was born in Basra around 965, refused to accept this idea simply because famous thinkers had written it.

questions.why: Being studied in Europe for centuries shows influence beyond his own time and place.

questions.stem: For an essay about “Every Town Needs a Repair Café,” classify each statement as the author's claim or supporting evidence.

rows.text: Every town should open a repair café.
Discarded electronics are among the fastest-growing kinds of household waste.
Visitors often stay after their items are repaired to keep chatting.
Critics' concerns are a reason to demand better designs.

questions.why: A claim is a position to argue; evidence is a fact or example that backs it up.

questions.stem: A student wants to argue that repair cafés reduce loneliness. Which evidence from “Every Town Needs a Repair Café” is most relevant?
options: A volunteer with a screwdriver can solve many problems in minutes.
Visitors often stay long after their repairs are done, just to talk.
Replacing a fan or toaster costs much more than repairing one does.
Many broken electronics fail because of one loose wire or worn part.
questions.why: Only the detail about visitors staying to talk connects to loneliness.

questions.stem: Select two sentences from “Every Town Needs a Repair Café” that a student could use as evidence that many repairs are simple.

segments.text: Discarded electronics are among the fastest-growing kinds of household waste, and many of them fail because of a single loose wire or worn part.
A volunteer with a screwdriver can often solve the problem in minutes.
Replacing a toaster or a fan is expensive, while repairing one usually costs nothing but time.
Critics argue that modern devices are designed to be impossible to repair.
Perhaps most importantly, these events build skills and friendships.

questions.why: A single loose wire and a fix in minutes both show that repairs are often easy.

questions.stem: A student writes, “Repair cafés benefit people of different ages.” Which TWO details from “Every Town Needs a Repair Café” best support this sentence? Choose two.
options: Teenagers learn practical techniques from retired engineers.
Elderly residents who live alone gain a reason to leave the house.
Replacing a toaster or a fan is expensive for most families.
Many electronics fail because of a single loose wire or worn part.
questions.why: The supporting details must mention people of different ages.

questions.stem: Part A: A student writing about the counterclaim wants to explain how the author responds to critics. Which statement best describes the response?

partA.stem: Part A: A student writing about the counterclaim wants to explain how the author responds to critics. Which statement best describes the response?

options.label: A
options.text: The author agrees with the critics and suggests that towns recycle devices instead.

options.label: B
options.text: The author admits the critics are partly right but says the problem calls for better designs.

options.label: C
options.text: The author ignores the critics and repeats the claim about saving money.

options.label: D
options.text: The author argues that the critics are wrong because every device can be repaired.

partB.stem: Part B: Which sentence from the passage best supports the answer to Part A?

options.label: A
options.text: That is sometimes true, but it is a reason to demand better designs, not a reason to stop trying.

options.label: B
options.text: A volunteer with a screwdriver can often solve the problem in minutes.

options.label: C
options.text: Critics argue that modern devices are designed to be impossible to repair.

options.label: D
options.text: The environmental benefits are significant.

questions.why: “That is sometimes true” concedes the point before the author redirects it.

questions.stem: A student is arguing that desalination provides a dependable water supply. Which evidence from Text 1 of “Water for a Growing City” is most relevant?
options: Coastal cities in arid regions increasingly rely on such plants.
Modern plants consume less energy than older thermal facilities.
Reverse osmosis is the industrial process of removing the salt.
The supply does not rise and fall with the amount of rainfall.
questions.why: Dependability is about steady supply, so the rainfall detail is the most relevant.

questions.stem: For an essay on “Water for a Growing City,” identify which text provides each piece of evidence.

rows.text: A single large plant can supply millions of residents.
Brine from plants can damage coral reefs and seagrass.
Treated wastewater already irrigates parks in several Gulf cities.
Reverse-osmosis plants use less energy than older thermal facilities.

questions.why: Writers must cite the correct source for each piece of evidence.

questions.stem: Select the sentence from Text 2 of “Water for a Growing City” that provides the strongest measurable evidence that conservation works.

segments.text: Meanwhile, some cities have reduced household consumption by roughly a fifth simply by repairing leaking pipes, installing efficient fixtures, and charging higher rates to the heaviest users.
Building additional desalination plants is not the only solution, and it may not be the wisest one.
A responsible strategy would treat conservation as the first source of water, not the last.
Treated wastewater, which is already used to irrigate parks in several Gulf cities, could replace a much larger share of fresh water.

questions.why: A specific result such as “roughly a fifth” is stronger than an opinion or a prediction.

questions.stem: A student's thesis states: “Desalination should supplement conservation, not replace it.” Which TWO pieces of evidence from “Water for a Growing City” best support this thesis? Choose two.
options: Treated wastewater could replace a much larger share of fresh water.
Desalination plants discharge brine that can harm reefs and seagrass.
A single large plant can supply drinking water for millions.
Modern reverse-osmosis plants use less energy than older facilities.
questions.why: Evidence for the thesis must show a cost of desalination or the value of conservation.

questions.stem: Part A: A student writing in favor of conservation wants to address the strongest counterclaim. Which idea from Text 1 should the student address?

partA.stem: Part A: A student writing in favor of conservation wants to address the strongest counterclaim. Which idea from Text 1 should the student address?

options.label: A
options.text: Desalination offers a supply that does not depend on rainfall.

options.label: B
options.text: Engineers have studied how to remove salt from water.

options.label: C
options.text: Older thermal plants used a great deal of energy.

options.label: D
options.text: Desalination plants are mostly built in coastal cities.

partB.stem: Part B: Which sentence from the passage best supports the answer to Part A?

options.label: A
options.text: A responsible strategy would treat conservation as the first source of water, not the last.

options.label: B
options.text: Because the sea is effectively limitless, supporters argue that desalination offers a dependable supply that does not fluctuate with rainfall.

options.label: C
options.text: Every plant discharges concentrated brine that can damage coral reefs and seagrass near the outlet, and the facilities remain expensive to operate.

options.label: D
options.text: Modern plants using reverse osmosis consume considerably less energy than older thermal facilities, and engineers estimate that a single large plant can supply drinking water for millions of residents.

questions.why: A dependable supply is the opposing side's strongest reason, so a fair essay must answer it.

questions.stem: Which sentence would best serve as a thesis for an essay that draws on “Judging Citizen Science”?
options: How a project is designed, not who joins it, determines whether volunteer data can be trusted.
Volunteers produce data that is usually more accurate than the data of trained researchers.
Bird surveys prove that volunteers rarely make any errors when identifying similar species.
Citizen science is valuable mainly because it lets the public enjoy observing birds outdoors.
questions.why: The author's central claim is that methods, not credentials, decide reliability.

questions.stem: Select the sentence from “Judging Citizen Science” that provides the most direct evidence that design changes improved the quality of volunteer data.

segments.text: When projects instead required participants to record observation time, location, and effort, and when experienced reviewers flagged improbable sightings, the resulting datasets proved accurate enough to reveal shifting migration patterns across entire continents.
When volunteers simply submitted whatever they happened to notice, their records were inconsistent and difficult to compare.
Admittedly, volunteers still make errors, particularly when identifying similar species.
It should be judged, like any other research, by the rigor of its methods.

questions.why: This sentence links specific design rules to an accurate, useful result.

questions.stem: Choose the paraphrase that accurately represents the concession in “Judging Citizen Science”: The author acknowledges that volunteers ____.
options: still misidentify similar species, though good projects plan for such errors
rarely make mistakes once they have finished formal scientific training
make the kinds of errors that professional researchers never make
produce records too inconsistent to reveal migration patterns at all
questions.why: An accurate paraphrase keeps both the admission and the author's qualification.

questions.stem: A student writes, “Rigorous procedures, rather than expertise alone, make data trustworthy.” Which THREE details from “Judging Citizen Science” support this claim? Choose three.
options: Bird surveys are among the oldest citizen science projects.
Volunteers often have no formal scientific training.
Experienced reviewers flagged improbable sightings.
Volunteers have particular trouble identifying similar species.
Professional researchers also make errors.
Participants were required to record observation time, location, and effort.
questions.why: Procedures and the fact that experts also err support the claim; background facts and the concession alone do not.

questions.stem: Part A: Which statement best evaluates the evidence the author uses in “Judging Citizen Science”?

partA.stem: Part A: Which statement best evaluates the evidence the author uses in “Judging Citizen Science”?

options.label: A
options.text: It relies on one extended example, so a writer citing it might add cases from other fields.

options.label: B
options.text: It relies mainly on expert interviews, so a writer citing it should find statistical data.

options.label: C
options.text: It presents only the skeptics' position, so it cannot support an argument for volunteers.

options.label: D
options.text: It compares exact error rates of volunteers and professionals across several studies.

partB.stem: Part B: Which sentence from the passage best supports the answer to Part A?

options.label: A
options.text: Consider bird surveys, among the oldest citizen science projects.

options.label: B
options.text: Yet professional researchers make errors too; the decisive difference is that a well-designed project anticipates mistakes and builds in procedures to detect them.

options.label: C
options.text: Citizen science, then, should not be judged by the credentials of its participants.

options.label: D
options.text: The question is reasonable, but the evidence increasingly suggests that the answer depends less on who collects the data than on how the collection is designed.

questions.why: All of the concrete evidence comes from bird surveys, so its range is limited.

questions.stem: Who are the characters in “The Big Game”?
options: Adam, his mom, and Coach Salem
Nada, her dad, and a teacher
Adam, Nada, and Coach Salem
Adam, Nada, and Adam's dad
questions.why: The character list at the top names Adam, Nada, and Coach Salem.

questions.stem: True or false: The setting of “The Big Game” is a classroom.
questions.why: The setting line says the play happens on a soccer field after school.

questions.stem: Match each part of the play “The Big Game” to an example from it.
questions.why: A play has characters, a setting, and dialogue, the words the characters say.

questions.stem: Select the line in “The Big Game” that shows Adam has a problem.

segments.text: I can't kick the ball far.
Time to practice, team!
Great kick, Adam!
Kick with the side of your foot.

questions.why: Adam tells his problem in his own words.

questions.stem: Part A: How does Nada help Adam in “The Big Game”?

partA.stem: Part A: How does Nada help Adam in “The Big Game”?

options.label: A
options.text: She asks the coach to help.

options.label: B
options.text: She shows him a better way to kick.

options.label: C
options.text: She kicks the ball for him.

options.label: D
options.text: She tells him to stop playing.

partB.stem: Part B: Which sentence from the passage best supports the answer to Part A?

options.label: A
options.text: Great kick, Adam!

options.label: B
options.text: Kick with the side of your foot.

options.label: C
options.text: I can't kick the ball far.

options.label: D
options.text: Time to practice, team!

questions.why: Nada's words give Adam a tip that solves his problem.

questions.stem: Which part of “The Bottle on the Beach” tells where and when the play takes place?
options: the CAST OF CHARACTERS line
Hind's final line of dialogue
the last stage direction
the SETTING line
questions.why: The setting tells the place (a beach in Oman) and the time (sunrise).

questions.stem: Match each element of drama to its example from “The Bottle on the Beach.”

pairs.right: kneeling and pulling out the bottle
Maybe it's a treasure map from a pirate ship!

questions.why: Props are objects the actors use; stage directions describe actions.

questions.stem: True or false: In “The Bottle on the Beach,” Dr. Amal appears on stage and speaks to the cousins.
questions.why: Dr. Amal is not in the cast; Hind reads her words aloud from the note.

questions.stem: In “The Bottle on the Beach,” what feeling does each stage direction or line show?

rows.text: running over, breathless
kicking the sand
smiling thoughtfully
Rashid, come quickly

questions.why: Stage directions and word choice show how characters feel.

questions.stem: Part A: How are Hind's and Rashid's reactions to the note different?

partA.stem: Part A: How are Hind's and Rashid's reactions to the note different?

options.label: A
options.text: Both cousins decide to throw the bottle back.

options.label: B
options.text: Both cousins are angry that it is not a map.

options.label: C
options.text: Rashid is let down, but Hind sees a chance to help.

options.label: D
options.text: Hind is let down, but Rashid wants to write back.

partB.stem: Part B: Which sentence from the passage best supports the answer to Part A?

options.label: A
options.text: Maybe it's a treasure map from a pirate ship!

options.label: B
options.text: It might be something better, because we can help a real scientist with her research.

options.label: C
options.text: Rashid, come quickly, because there is a rolled-up paper inside this bottle!

options.label: D
options.text: So it isn't a treasure map after all.

questions.why: Hind's last line shows she values the note even though Rashid is disappointed.

questions.stem: Zaid's long speech in “Night at Maragha,” spoken to himself while alone on stage, is called a ____.
options: soliloquy
stage direction
cast list
chorus
questions.why: A soliloquy is a speech in which a character alone on stage reveals thoughts.

questions.stem: For “Night at Maragha,” is each item part of the setting or an action of a character?

rows.text: a huge brass instrument at the center of the stage
the night sky projected on the back wall
Zaid paces as he speaks
Zaid raises the lamp

questions.why: Setting details describe the place; actions are things characters do.

questions.stem: Select the sentence from “Night at Maragha” that best reveals Zaid's inner conflict.

segments.text: My teacher says that small differences matter, but tonight I wonder whether I am simply careless.
Zaid, measure it again, and then measure it once more.
ZAID stands alone, holding a lamp and a notebook.
A huge brass instrument for measuring the stars stands at the center of the stage, and the night sky is projected on the back wall.

questions.why: Zaid is torn between trusting his work and doubting himself.

questions.stem: Why does the playwright have the teacher in “Night at Maragha” appear only as a voice from offstage?
options: to suggest that the teacher is angry with Zaid tonight
to keep the focus on Zaid's own thoughts and choices
to show that the teacher has left the observatory forever
to reveal that the teacher is a figure in Zaid's dream
questions.why: Keeping the teacher unseen keeps attention on Zaid's struggle.

questions.stem: Part A: What does the final stage direction of “Night at Maragha” suggest about Zaid?

partA.stem: Part A: What does the final stage direction of “Night at Maragha” suggest about Zaid?

options.label: A
options.text: He has decided to keep measuring with care.

options.label: B
options.text: He is upset with his teacher's command.

options.label: C
options.text: He has proved the ancient tables wrong.

options.label: D
options.text: He has given up on studying the planets.

partB.stem: Part B: Which sentence from the passage best supports the answer to Part A?

options.label: A
options.text: ZAID smiles, raises the lamp, and turns back toward the brass instrument as the lights slowly dim.

options.label: B
options.text: Every night I record the position of the same planet, and every night my numbers disagree with the ancient tables by a tiny amount.

options.label: C
options.text: He looks up at the stars, then down at his pages, then up again.

options.label: D
options.text: Zaid, measure it again, and then measure it once more.

questions.why: His smile and return to the instrument show his decision; the teacher's line is only an instruction.

questions.stem: What is the main conflict in “The Final Round”?
options: An adviser refuses to let his team enter the final.
Two rival teams argue over who may use the practice mat.
A team cannot find the tools it needs before its match.
Two teammates disagree about changing the robot's program.
questions.why: The conflict is between Salma and Karim over the steering code.

questions.stem: In “The Final Round,” Karim's line spoken “(turning toward the audience, in a low voice)” is an example of ____.
options: an aside
a cast list
a flashback
a soliloquy
questions.why: An aside is spoken to the audience while other characters are on stage and do not hear it.

questions.stem: Which TWO stage directions in “The Final Round” reveal how a character feels? Choose two.
options: KARIM stares anxiously at his laptop
teams hurry between tables covered with tools, laptops, and spare parts
putting down the wrench, frustrated
lift the robot onto the practice mat together
questions.why: Words such as “frustrated” and “anxiously” show feelings.

questions.stem: In “The Final Round,” which character holds each view?

rows.text: trusts three weeks of testing
trusts what he saw yesterday
wants one quick trial to decide
worries that the robot drifts left

questions.why: Dialogue reveals each character's point of view in the conflict.

questions.stem: Part A: How is the conflict in “The Final Round” resolved?

partA.stem: Part A: How is the conflict in “The Final Round” resolved?

options.label: A
options.text: The adviser suggests a test that respects both views, and the teammates work together.

options.label: B
options.text: Salma agrees to rewrite the program, and Karim tests it alone in the hall.

options.label: C
options.text: Mr. Yousef decides to cancel the match so the team can repair the robot.

options.label: D
options.text: Karim gives up his idea after Salma shows him three weeks of test results.

partB.stem: Part B: Which sentence from the passage best supports the answer to Part A?

options.label: A
options.text: Changing the code ten minutes before the final would be reckless; we tested this version for three weeks.

options.label: B
options.text: SALMA tightens a bolt on the robot's arm while KARIM stares anxiously at his laptop.

options.label: C
options.text: She trusts the testing, but I trust what I saw yesterday, and only one of us can be right.

options.label: D
options.text: SALMA and KARIM exchange a glance, then lift the robot onto the practice mat together.

questions.why: The final stage direction shows the teammates acting together on the adviser's idea.

questions.stem: How do Tariq and Umm Hasan function as foils in “The Caravanserai”?
options: He distrusts all maps, while she relies on them fully.
They share the same plan to avoid the northern wells.
She envies his youth, while he resents her authority.
His eager confidence highlights her cautious experience.
questions.why: Foils are contrasting characters who make each other's traits stand out.

questions.stem: Select the stage direction in “The Caravanserai” that creates dramatic irony.

segments.text: The CAMEL DRIVER pauses, studies the map, and slowly shakes his head, but TARIQ does not notice.
TARIQ unrolls a worn map beside the fire, while the CAMEL DRIVER silently inspects the ropes on a loaded saddle.
enthusiastically, tracing a route with his finger
stirring the fire without glancing at the map

questions.why: The audience sees a warning that Tariq misses.

questions.stem: Which TWO purposes does the silent CAMEL DRIVER serve in “The Caravanserai”? Choose two.
options: He explains the history of the trade route to Tariq.
He lets the audience learn something that Tariq misses.
He signals doubt about Tariq's route without saying a word.
He provides comic relief that lightens the serious mood.
questions.why: A nonspeaking character can still communicate through action.

questions.stem: Part A: What is the subtext of Umm Hasan's line “Some of them arrived”?

partA.stem: Part A: What is the subtext of Umm Hasan's line “Some of them arrived”?

options.label: A
options.text: Most travelers reached the coast earlier than they planned.

options.label: B
options.text: Many travelers who rushed the route never reached the coast.

options.label: C
options.text: She believes that Tariq's map is newer than the others.

options.label: D
options.text: She has forgotten which travelers stayed in her courtyard.

partB.stem: Part B: Which sentence from the passage best supports the answer to Part A?

options.label: A
options.text: Every traveler who has slept in this courtyard has wanted to arrive three days earlier.

options.label: B
options.text: The desert remembers every promise made beside this fire.

options.label: C
options.text: Then I will be one of those who arrived.

options.label: D
options.text: If we depart before dawn and avoid the northern wells, we can reach the coast three days earlier than any other caravan.

questions.why: Her final remark confirms that many confident promises ended badly.

questions.stem: Umm Hasan's final line in “The Caravanserai,” spoken “(quietly, to herself),” most likely serves to ____.
options: foreshadow danger on Tariq's journey
show that she has forgotten past guests
reveal that she will travel with him
signal a shift to a scene years later
questions.why: A quiet line the other characters do not hear can hint at what lies ahead.

questions.stem: What role does the CHORUS play in “The Unexplored”?
options: It narrates events that happened long before Idris was ever born.
It argues with Idris about how the desert should finally be drawn.
It acts as a rival mapmaker competing for a powerful ruler's favor.
It comments on the action from a perspective beyond the characters.
questions.why: A chorus stands outside the action and offers commentary the characters do not hear.

questions.stem: In “The Unexplored,” classify each element as dialogue between characters, a stage direction, or choral commentary.

rows.text: shall I draw the version we hear most often?
Lights rise on a study in Cairo
each one believes that ink can hold us still
IDRIS nods approvingly
label it honestly

questions.why: Characters speak to each other, the chorus speaks beyond them, and directions guide staging.

questions.stem: Part A: Which trait of Idris does the scene most clearly reveal?

partA.stem: Part A: Which trait of Idris does the scene most clearly reveal?

options.label: A
options.text: fear of the powerful rulers who pay for his maps

options.label: B
options.text: intellectual honesty about the limits of knowledge

options.label: C
options.text: eagerness to please merchants with detailed maps

options.label: D
options.text: impatience with his apprentice's many questions

partB.stem: Part B: Which sentence from the passage best supports the answer to Part A?

options.label: A
options.text: A map that records rumors as facts is more dangerous than a map that admits ignorance, so leave it blank and label it honestly.

options.label: B
options.text: Blank spaces frighten ambitious rulers, but they protect travelers.

options.label: C
options.text: Master, every merchant who passes through the city describes this desert differently; shall I draw the version we hear most often?

options.label: D
options.text: IDRIS nods approvingly, unaware that the CHORUS has gathered behind him, closer than before.

questions.why: Idris prefers an honest blank to a confident guess.

questions.stem: Select the line in “The Unexplored” that most directly states a theme.

segments.text: Blank spaces frighten ambitious rulers, but they protect travelers.
We are the winds that cross the empty interior, and we have watched mapmakers come and go for a thousand years; each one believes that ink can hold us still.
Master, every merchant who passes through the city describes this desert differently; shall I draw the version we hear most often?
LAYAN slowly writes "Unexplored" across the empty region.

questions.why: The Chorus turns Idris's choice into a general truth about honesty and uncertainty.

questions.stem: Which TWO effects does the final stage direction of “The Unexplored” create? Choose two.
options: It creates dramatic irony because the audience sees what Idris cannot.
It reveals that Layan has secretly ignored her master's instruction.
It shows that the Chorus has decided to stop commenting on events.
It hints that the forces Idris cannot chart are drawing closer.
questions.why: The Chorus moving closer, unseen by Idris, gives the audience knowledge he lacks.

questions.stem: What does Lina want in “A Garden for Our School”?
options: She wants a garden at school.
She wants to keep some bees.
She wants Tariq to help her.
She wants a bigger lunch room.
questions.why: Lina asks the principal for a garden.

questions.stem: True or false: In “A Garden for Our School,” Lina says the class will water the garden every day.
questions.why: The letter says, “We will water it every day.”

questions.stem: Which TWO reasons does Lina give for a school garden? Choose two.
options: It will give students a longer recess.
It is good for bees.
It can help students learn about plants.
It will make the school bigger.
questions.why: Lina tells about learning and about bees.

questions.stem: Is each part of “A Garden for Our School” a good reason or a weak reason?

rows.text: We can watch seeds grow into beans and carrots.
It will make our school the best school in the world.
Bees need flowers to make honey.

questions.why: A good reason can be shown to be true; “best in the world” cannot.

questions.stem: Select the sentence from “A Garden for Our School” that gives a reason Lina cannot prove.

segments.text: We can watch seeds grow into beans and carrots.
Bees need flowers to make honey.
My friend Tariq says a garden will make our school the best school in the world.
We will water it every day.

questions.why: No one can show that a garden makes a school the best in the world.

questions.stem: Which sentence states the author's claim in “Make Recess Longer”?
options: I believe recess should be thirty minutes long.
Our school gives students only fifteen minutes.
Exercise helps the brain work a little better.
Students at Hilltop School have a long recess.
questions.why: The claim is the main point the author wants readers to accept.

questions.stem: Select the sentence from “Make Recess Longer” that gives evidence from research.

segments.text: Our school currently gives students only fifteen minutes of recess each day, which is not enough time to rest and recharge.
A study by a children's health group found that students who played outside for thirty minutes paid better attention in class afterward.
Everyone at our school wants a longer recess, so the principal should agree.
Some people say that a longer recess will take away learning time.

questions.why: A study is evidence from research.

questions.stem: For “Make Recess Longer,” decide whether each statement is supported by evidence or not supported.

rows.text: Students who play outside pay better attention.
Everyone at the school wants a longer recess.
Hilltop students are the smartest kids in the city.
Hilltop School has a thirty-minute recess.

questions.why: The study and the chart support some statements; nothing supports the others.

questions.stem: Part A: Which reason in “Make Recess Longer” is the weakest?

partA.stem: Part A: Which reason in “Make Recess Longer” is the weakest?

options.label: A
options.text: Recess gives time to build teamwork skills.

options.label: B
options.text: Exercise helps students pay better attention.

options.label: C
options.text: Everyone at the school wants a longer recess.

options.label: D
options.text: Focused students use class time more wisely.

partB.stem: Part B: Which sentence from the passage best supports the answer to Part A?

options.label: A
options.text: First, exercise helps the brain.

options.label: B
options.text: I believe recess should be thirty minutes long.

options.label: C
options.text: However, if students concentrate better, the minutes in the classroom will be used more wisely and effectively.

options.label: D
options.text: Everyone at our school wants a longer recess, so the principal should agree.

questions.why: Saying everyone wants something is not proof that it is a good idea.

questions.stem: Which TWO pieces of information would best strengthen the argument in “Make Recess Longer”? Choose two.
options: a list of games that students like to play during recess
the number of students who attend Palm Grove School
a teacher's report that students behave better after outdoor play
test scores from schools before and after they made recess longer
questions.why: Strong evidence connects longer recess to better learning or behavior.

questions.stem: Which statement best expresses the author's claim in “Bike Lanes for King Road”?
options: Protected bike lanes on King Road would reduce traffic and improve safety.
Wadi Saad has cleaner air than Al-Noor because it has fewer cars.
Shop owners on King Road should provide more parking for their customers.
Cyclists in Al-Noor already ride very safely on King Road every single day.
questions.why: The author argues that the lanes would make streets safer and less crowded.

questions.stem: Select the sentence from “Bike Lanes for King Road” in which the author answers an opposing claim with evidence.

segments.text: City leaders are debating whether to build protected bike lanes along King Road, the busiest street in Al-Noor.
Cities with similar weather have reported comparable results.
Yet a survey of Wadi Saad shop owners found that most of them saw no drop in sales.
Furthermore, after Wadi Saad built its lanes, the city's air became cleaner, so bike lanes clearly cleaned the air.

questions.why: The survey responds to the claim that the lanes would hurt business.

questions.stem: For “Bike Lanes for King Road,” decide whether each piece of reasoning is sound or faulty.

rows.text: Bike trips in Wadi Saad doubled after lanes were added.
One neighbor's safe ride proves the road is safe for all.
The air got cleaner after the lanes, so the lanes cleaned it.
Most Wadi Saad shops saw no drop in sales.

questions.why: Data from a whole city is sound; one ride and a simple before-and-after are not.

questions.stem: Part A: Which type of faulty reasoning appears in the last paragraph of “Bike Lanes for King Road”?

partA.stem: Part A: Which type of faulty reasoning appears in the last paragraph of “Bike Lanes for King Road”?

options.label: A
options.text: attacking the people who disagree with the plan

options.label: B
options.text: offering only two choices when more exist

options.label: C
options.text: claiming that something is true because it is popular

options.label: D
options.text: drawing a broad conclusion from a single example

partB.stem: Part B: Which sentence from the passage best supports the answer to Part A?

options.label: A
options.text: Cities with similar weather have reported comparable results.

options.label: B
options.text: Supporters argue that the lanes would reduce traffic and make streets safer, and the evidence suggests that they have a point.

options.label: C
options.text: Opponents claim that the lanes would ruin business on King Road because shoppers could no longer park in front of stores.

options.label: D
options.text: My own neighbor rode on King Road last week and arrived home safely, which proves that the road is already safe for every cyclist.

questions.why: One person's ride is too small a sample to prove anything about every cyclist.

questions.stem: Which TWO statements explain why the claim about clean air in “Bike Lanes for King Road” is faulty? Choose two.
options: The author's neighbor rode on King Road, not in Wadi Saad.
Other changes in Wadi Saad may have cleaned the air at the same time.
Clean air has nothing to do with the number of cars on a road.
The author gives no data linking the bike lanes to the cleaner air.
questions.why: One event following another does not prove that the first caused the second.

questions.stem: Which evidence in “A Library After the Bell” most strongly supports the speaker's claim?
options: the late bus that some students must ride home after school
the speaker's belief that the school deserves a better library
the opponent's plan to spend money on new sports uniforms
the 212 students who signed to say they would use the library
questions.why: The signatures show real demand for an after-school library.

questions.stem: Select the sentence from “A Library After the Bell” that attacks a person instead of his argument.

segments.text: My opponent, Yousef, says the council should spend its limited money on new sports uniforms instead.
But Yousef forgets his homework almost every week, so why should anyone trust his ideas about studying?
The choice is simple.
Vote for me, and vote for a future in which every student, regardless of schedule, has a comfortable place to learn.

questions.why: Yousef's homework habits have nothing to do with whether uniforms are a good use of money.

questions.stem: Match each part of the speech “A Library After the Bell” with the kind of reasoning it shows.

pairs.left: 212 students signed to say they would use the library.
Mrs. Fadel says one assistant would keep the doors open.
Yousef forgets his homework, so his ideas cannot be trusted.
Either we fund the library, or our school becomes the worst.

questions.why: Good arguments use evidence and informed sources; faulty ones attack people or offer only two extreme options.

questions.stem: Part A: Why is the reasoning in the final paragraph of “A Library After the Bell” faulty?

partA.stem: Part A: Why is the reasoning in the final paragraph of “A Library After the Bell” faulty?

options.label: A
options.text: It relies on a source who has no knowledge of the library.

options.label: B
options.text: It admits that the opponent's plan has some good points.

options.label: C
options.text: It repeats the same evidence that appeared in paragraph 2.

options.label: D
options.text: It presents only two outcomes when many others are possible.

partB.stem: Part B: Which sentence from the passage best supports the answer to Part A?

options.label: A
options.text: Either we fund the library, or our grades will fall and our school will become the worst in the district.

options.label: B
options.text: Last month I collected signatures from 212 students who said they would use an after-school library at least once a week.

options.label: C
options.text: Currently, the library closes at the final bell, so students who depend on the late bus have nowhere quiet to study, research, or complete their assignments.

options.label: D
options.text: My opponent, Yousef, says the council should spend its limited money on new sports uniforms instead.

questions.why: Not funding the library would not automatically make the school the worst in the district.

questions.stem: Which TWO revisions would most improve the reasoning in “A Library After the Bell”? Choose two.
options: Repeat more strongly that the school will become the worst in the district.
Add that several teachers have also noticed Yousef's missing homework.
Replace the comment about Yousef's homework with a reason the library matters more than uniforms.
Compare the cost of one library assistant with the cost of new uniforms.
questions.why: Stronger reasoning answers the opponent's idea with evidence instead of attacks or exaggeration.

questions.stem: Which evidence provides the strongest support for protecting the reef in “Protecting the Reef at Al-Murjan Bay”?
options: the leaflet predicting that the whole coastal economy will collapse
the football player's warning that the reef will soon be dead
the yearly survey comparing coral loss in open and closed zones
the fact that the plan closes only part of the coastline
questions.why: Repeated scientific measurement is more reliable than predictions or celebrity opinions.

questions.stem: Part A: Why does the author point out that the open and closed zones in “Protecting the Reef at Al-Murjan Bay” have identical water temperatures?

partA.stem: Part A: Why does the author point out that the open and closed zones in “Protecting the Reef at Al-Murjan Bay” have identical water temperatures?

options.label: A
options.text: to rule out warming water as the cause of the difference in coral loss

options.label: B
options.text: to prove that water temperature has no effect on any coral reef

options.label: C
options.text: to show that the biologists measured every part of the reef

options.label: D
options.text: to suggest that boats are making the water in open zones warmer

partB.stem: Part B: Which sentence from the passage best supports the answer to Part A?

options.label: A
options.text: The strongest case rests on measurement.

options.label: B
options.text: Other supporters, however, rely on shakier reasoning.

options.label: C
options.text: Because both zones experience identical water temperatures, the difference points convincingly toward human activity.

options.label: D
options.text: Opponents are not blameless either.

questions.why: Removing other possible causes makes a cause-and-effect claim much stronger.

questions.stem: For “Protecting the Reef at Al-Murjan Bay,” classify the reasoning in each argument.

rows.text: Coral declined 40% in open zones but 7% in closed zones.
A football player says the reef will be dead in five years.
If fishing continues, tourism and the whole economy will collapse.

questions.why: Sound reasoning uses fair comparisons; the other two rely on fame or on an unsupported chain of disasters.

questions.stem: Select the sentence from “Protecting the Reef at Al-Murjan Bay” that shows an opposing argument misrepresenting the proposal.

segments.text: The proposal to declare the coral reef off Al-Murjan Bay a protected marine area deserves broad support, but some of the arguments made on its behalf are considerably weaker than others.
Meanwhile, one campaign leaflet warns that if fishing continues, tourists will vanish, hotels will close, and the entire coastal economy will collapse.
Several have described the proposal as an attempt to ban everyone from the sea forever, although the plan actually closes only twelve percent of the coastline.

Since 2015, marine biologists from the regional university have surveyed the reef annually, documenting a forty percent decline in live coral in zones where anchoring and fishing are permitted, compared with a seven percent decline in zones already closed to boats.

questions.why: Exaggerating an opponent's position into something easier to attack is a straw man.

questions.stem: Which TWO statements best evaluate the author's own argument in “Protecting the Reef at Al-Murjan Bay”? Choose two.
options: The author proves that fishing alone caused the coral loss in every part of the reef.
The author builds credibility by pointing out weak arguments on both sides of the debate.
The argument is weakened because it depends mostly on the football player's prediction.
The main evidence is relevant because it compares zones that differ mainly in human use.
questions.why: The author relies on the survey, not the celebrity, and the survey shows a strong link, not total proof.

questions.stem: How does the chart affect the author's reasoning in paragraph 2 of “The Library Without Shelves”?
options: It proves that printed loans will fall below downloads within the next ten years or so.
It confirms the claim that residents ignore print, since downloads have tripled over ten whole years.
It undercuts the claim that residents ignore print, since printed loans still double downloads.
It shows that the library's budget is spent mostly on electronic titles rather than books.
questions.why: Print use fell, but it is still twice digital use, so “increasingly ignore” misrepresents the data.

questions.stem: Part A: Which flaw most seriously weakens the reasoning in paragraph 3 of “The Library Without Shelves”?

partA.stem: Part A: Which flaw most seriously weakens the reasoning in paragraph 3 of “The Library Without Shelves”?

options.label: A
options.text: It relies on statistics that are too old to describe the library's current use.

options.label: B
options.text: It attacks the critics' character instead of responding to their concerns.

options.label: C
options.text: It draws a general conclusion from a sample chosen only from people who succeeded.

options.label: D
options.text: It uses emotional language to make readers fear any change to the library.

partB.stem: Part B: Which sentence from the passage best supports the answer to Part A?

options.label: A
options.text: Critics insist that some residents lack reliable internet access, but this objection is overstated.

options.label: B
options.text: Shelves are simply an obsolete technology, and obsolete technologies inevitably disappear; clinging to them is nostalgia disguised as principle.

options.label: C
options.text: A collection that residents increasingly ignore can hardly justify consuming the majority of the library's budget.

options.label: D
options.text: Every successful entrepreneur I have interviewed for this column described acquiring knowledge almost entirely from digital sources, which demonstrates that digital resources are sufficient for anyone determined to learn.

questions.why: Interviewing only successful people ignores those whom digital-only access failed, so the sample is biased.

questions.stem: Select the sentence from “The Library Without Shelves” in which the author dismisses a counterclaim without offering evidence about it.

segments.text: The municipal council's proposal to convert the central library into a digital-only resource center has provoked predictable outrage, yet the arguments for the conversion are considerably more persuasive than its critics acknowledge.
Critics insist that some residents lack reliable internet access, but this objection is overstated.
Consider the circulation figures: borrowing of printed books has declined by roughly a quarter over the past decade, while downloads of electronic titles have tripled.
Moreover, the library's purpose has always been to provide access to information, and information remains information regardless of its format.

questions.why: Calling an objection “overstated” is not the same as showing how many residents actually lack access.

questions.stem: For “The Library Without Shelves,” identify the flaw in each claim.

rows.text: Successful entrepreneurs learned online, so digital is enough for all.
Obsolete technologies always disappear, so shelves must go.
Residents increasingly ignore the printed collection.

questions.why: Each claim fails in a different way: who was asked, what is assumed about the future, or how numbers are described.

questions.stem: Which TWO pieces of evidence would a careful reader most need before accepting the argument in “The Library Without Shelves”? Choose two.
options: the total number of electronic titles the library could offer
the reasons residents still borrow 300,000 printed books each year
more interviews with entrepreneurs who learned from digital sources
the share of residents who lack reliable home internet access
questions.why: The strongest test of the claim examines the people it might harm and the use it dismisses.

questions.stem: Which part of “The Black Tent” is a made-up story?
options: Text 2, because it tells about tents long ago
Text 1, because it tells about a boy named Saad
Text 2, because it tells about a hard rain
Text 1, because it tells how tents were made
questions.why: Text 1 has a character and events like a story; Text 2 gives facts.

questions.stem: True or false: Both parts of “The Black Tent” tell that the sides of the tent could be rolled up.
questions.why: Saad's mother rolls up the side, and Text 2 says the sides could be rolled up.

questions.stem: Which TWO facts from Text 2 of “The Black Tent” also happen in Saad's story? Choose two.
options: Many families lived in tents long ago.
The sides could be rolled up to let in a breeze.
Women wove goat hair into long cloth.
Wet goat hair kept the rain out.
questions.why: Saad feels the breeze and stays dry in the rain.

questions.stem: For “The Black Tent,” tell where each detail is found.

rows.text: Saad says, “Ahh.”
Tents were made from goat hair.
The tent kept the rain out.

questions.why: The story and the facts share some details but not all.

questions.stem: Select the sentence from Saad's story in “The Black Tent” that matches the fact that wet goat hair kept water out.

segments.text: His family had a big black tent.
A cool wind came in.
That night it rained hard.
Saad stayed dry and warm inside.

questions.why: Saad stays dry because the tent keeps the rain out.

questions.stem: Which detail in Text 1 of “The Elephant Clock” was most likely invented by the author?
options: Al-Jazari had a young helper named Ilyas.
A bowl in the clock slowly filled and sank.
The clock made a sound every half hour.
A small ball dropped inside the elephant clock.
questions.why: Text 2 says his book does not name his helpers, so Ilyas is made up.

questions.stem: For “The Elephant Clock,” decide whether each detail is a historical fact or a made-up story detail.

rows.text: Al-Jazari finished a book of machines in 1206.
Ilyas laughed and shouted in the courtyard.
The clock used a sinking bowl to keep time.
Al-Jazari whispered, “Watch carefully.”

questions.why: Facts can be checked in history; feelings and words of characters are usually invented.

questions.stem: Part A: How does Text 1 of “The Elephant Clock” use facts from history?

partA.stem: Part A: How does Text 1 of “The Elephant Clock” use facts from history?

options.label: A
options.text: It corrects mistakes that historians made about the clock.

options.label: B
options.text: It lists every machine that Al-Jazari designed in his life.

options.label: C
options.text: It explains why Al-Jazari decided to build a clock at all.

options.label: D
options.text: It shows how the clock worked through a character's eyes.

partB.stem: Part B: Which sentence from the passage best supports the answer to Part A?

options.label: A
options.text: Ilyas laughed with delight.

options.label: B
options.text: Historians know about Al-Jazari mostly from his book, which does not name his helpers.

options.label: C
options.text: Slowly the bowl filled and sank.

options.label: D
options.text: He served local rulers and designed clocks, water pumps, and moving machines.

questions.why: The story uses the real sinking bowl as part of what Ilyas watches.

questions.stem: Put the events of the elephant clock in “The Elephant Clock” in the order they happen.
sequence: The bowl slowly fills with water.
The bowl sinks in the tank.
A brass ball rolls down a channel.
A cymbal rings out.
questions.why: Each step of the machine causes the next one.

questions.stem: Which TWO statements explain why a reader can trust the facts in Text 2 of “The Elephant Clock” more than the details in Text 1? Choose two.
options: Text 2 includes more exciting events than Text 1.
Text 2 explains that historians learned about Al-Jazari from his own book.
Text 2 gives dates that can be checked.
Text 2 tells what Al-Jazari said to his helper.
questions.why: Dates and named sources make information easier to check.

questions.stem: Which detail in Text 1 of “Beneath the Gulf” is supported by Text 2?
options: Divers carried a knife for opening shells.
Divers used stone weights and nose clips.
Divers cheered loudly when pearls appeared.
Khalid's uncle worked on the same boat.
questions.why: Text 2 describes stone weights and nose clips, just as Text 1 does.

questions.stem: Select the sentence from Text 2 of “Beneath the Gulf” that shows the pearl in Khalid's story was unusual.

segments.text: For centuries, pearl diving supported numerous communities along the Arabian Gulf.
A partner on deck pulled each diver up by rope.
Most oysters held no pearl at all, and large pearls were extremely rare.
In the 1930s, inexpensive cultured pearls from Japan caused the traditional industry to decline dramatically.

questions.why: Text 2 explains that large pearls were rare, so Khalid's find was a lucky exception.

questions.stem: For “Beneath the Gulf,” tell where each detail appears.

rows.text: A diver is pulled up by a rope.
The diving season lasted about four months.
A pearl is as large as a chickpea.
Cultured pearls hurt the industry.

questions.why: The story focuses on one dive; the history gives the bigger picture.

questions.stem: Part A: Why did the author of Text 1 in “Beneath the Gulf” most likely include the large pearl?

partA.stem: Part A: Why did the author of Text 1 in “Beneath the Gulf” most likely include the large pearl?

options.label: A
options.text: to explain why the pearl industry declined in the 1930s

options.label: B
options.text: to prove that Khalid was a more skilled diver than his uncle

options.label: C
options.text: to create an exciting moment, even though such finds were rare

options.label: D
