options.text: to show that most divers found large pearls on most days

partB.stem: Part B: Which sentence from the passage best supports the answer to Part A?

options.label: A
options.text: That evening, as the crew opened the shells, Khalid's knife revealed a pearl as large as a chickpea, and the whole boat erupted in cheers.

options.label: B
options.text: He worked rapidly, prying them loose and depositing them into the basket hanging at his neck.

options.label: C
options.text: Khalid gripped the heavy stone weight and filled his lungs one final time.

options.label: D
options.text: When his chest began to burn, he tugged the rope desperately, and his uncle hauled him upward.

questions.why: Fiction writers often add dramatic events, even if they were uncommon in real history.

questions.stem: Which TWO statements best describe how the two texts in “Beneath the Gulf” differ in their treatment of pearl diving? Choose two.
options: Text 2 describes how one family felt about a single pearl.
Text 2 explains how pearl diving changed over a long period of time.
Text 1 shows the physical struggle of a single diver.
Text 1 describes why cultured pearls were cheaper.
questions.why: Fiction zooms in on one person's experience; history explains broad patterns and change.

questions.stem: Which historical fact from Text 2 of “The Copyist of Baghdad” is reflected in Zayd's work?
options: The caliph wrote many books on astronomy.
Paper was more expensive than parchment.
Al-Khwarizmi trained young copyists in writing.
Scholars translated older works into Arabic.
questions.why: Zayd copies an Arabic translation of a Greek manuscript.

questions.stem: In “The Copyist of Baghdad,” the meeting between Zayd and Al-Khwarizmi is best described as ____.
options: a fact that Text 2 proves really happened
an invented scene that uses a real historical person
a mistake about when Al-Khwarizmi lived
a recorded event described in history books
questions.why: Al-Khwarizmi was real, but Text 2 gives no record of a copyist named Zayd.

questions.stem: For “The Copyist of Baghdad,” decide whether each detail is supported by Text 2 or invented for the story.

rows.text: Zayd must finish copying before noon.
Works were translated from Persian into Arabic.
A scholar praises Zayd's handwriting.
Al-Khwarizmi worked in Baghdad.

questions.why: Characters' tasks and feelings are invented; translation work and al-Khwarizmi's presence are historical.

questions.stem: Part A: How does Text 2 of “The Copyist of Baghdad” challenge the picture of the House of Wisdom in Text 1?

partA.stem: Part A: How does Text 2 of “The Copyist of Baghdad” challenge the picture of the House of Wisdom in Text 1?

options.label: A
options.text: It proves that scholars did not study astronomy in Baghdad.

options.label: B
options.text: It shows that no translations were made in Baghdad at that time.

options.label: C
options.text: It suggests the building may have been smaller than the story implies.

options.label: D
options.text: It states that the caliph never visited scholars in the city.

partB.stem: Part B: Which sentence from the passage best supports the answer to Part A?

options.label: A
options.text: Paper, which was cheaper than parchment, helped books spread rapidly.

options.label: B

questions.stem: Which statement best explains how the two falcon texts differ in genre?
options: Text 1 is a poem, and Text 2 is realistic fiction.

Text 1 is realistic fiction, and Text 2 is fantasy.
Text 1 is fantasy, and Text 2 is informational.

questions.stem: Classify each detail from the two falcon texts as realistic or fantastic.

Wings shimmer with copper flame.
A falcon speaks to a queen.

questions.stem: The phrase “a voice like distant thunder” in Text 2 is a ____ that helps make the fantasy falcon seem powerful.
options: flashback
fact
simile
rhyme

questions.stem: Which TWO features do both falcon texts share? Choose two.
options: Both are told in rhyming lines.
Both are written as prose narratives.
Both include a falcon as an important character.
Both include magical creatures.
questions.why: Both are stories in paragraphs about a falcon, but only Text 2 has magic.

questions.stem: Part A: Which element of fantasy appears in Text 2 but NOT in Text 1?

partA.stem: Part A: Which element of fantasy appears in Text 2 but NOT in Text 1?

options.label: A
options.text: a character who feels nervous

options.label: B
options.text: a setting in the open sky

options.label: C
options.text: a bird that is carefully trained

options.label: D

partB.stem: Part B: Which sentence from the passage best supports the answer to Part A?

options.label: A
options.text: His trainer had warned him that a nervous bird might fly off and never return, so he waited until the bird's feathers lay flat and calm.

options.label: B

questions.stem: Which feature of “The Glass Lighthouse” most clearly identifies it as fantasy rather than realistic fiction?
options: An apprentice climbs the stairs each evening.
A powerful duke makes threats from a ship's deck.
A storm threatens a ship near an island harbor.
The lighthouse beam makes sailors unable to lie.
questions.why: A light that forces honesty is magic, which marks fantasy.

questions.stem: Which TWO conventions of fantasy appear in “The Glass Lighthouse”? Choose two.
options: a magical object governed by a strict rule
an invented setting with its own places and rulers
a story told through rhyming verse
a narrator who explains historical facts
questions.why: Fantasy often builds an imaginary world with magic that follows rules.

questions.stem: Select two sentences from “The Glass Lighthouse” that establish the rules of its magical world.

segments.text: Rami, the keeper's apprentice, had been warned about the lighthouse's single rule: the lamp must never be extinguished, not even for a moment.
For three years he obeyed, climbing the spiral stairs each evening to polish the crystal lens.
Any sailor caught in its light could no longer tell a lie, which was why merchants avoided the harbor after dark.
Then, one stormy night, a ship appeared carrying the Duke of Harrow, who demanded that the light be put out.

questions.why: One sentence tells what the magic does; the other tells what must never happen.

questions.stem: Decide whether each element of “The Glass Lighthouse” is found only in fantasy or in both fantasy and realistic fiction.

rows.text: A beam of light that forces honesty
A character facing a difficult choice
An imaginary island ruled by a duke
A storm at sea at night

columns.text: Found in both fantasy and realistic fiction

questions.why: Conflicts and weather appear in any fiction; magic and invented lands belong to fantasy.

questions.stem: Part A: Why does the Duke most likely want the light put out?

options.label: A

options.label: B

questions.stem: Which characteristic identifies “Inventory of a Harbor at Dawn” as a prose poem rather than a short story?
options: It describes a real setting at one particular time of the day.
It includes a first-person narrator who remembers a family member.
It is written in paragraphs and full sentences instead of lines and stanzas.
It relies on compressed imagery and figurative language instead of plot.
questions.why: A prose poem looks like prose but works like a poem, through images rather than events.

questions.stem: Which TWO features of “Inventory of a Harbor at Dawn” are characteristic of lyric poetry? Choose two.
options: Characters speak to each other in dialogue.
Events are told in strict chronological order.
Compressed images create a mood rather than a plot.
A first-person speaker expresses personal feeling.
questions.why: Lyric poems express a speaker's feelings through concentrated images.

questions.stem: Match each phrase from “Inventory of a Harbor at Dawn” to the technique it shows.

pairs.right: simile comparing ropes to unused words

pairs.left: a gull rehearsing its single complaint

pairs.right: metaphor of a classroom roll call
precise detail suggesting age and care

questions.why: Each technique adds meaning in a compact way, typical of poetry.

questions.stem: Select two sentences from “Inventory of a Harbor at Dawn” that mark the speaker's turn from observing change to joining the grandfather's tradition.

segments.text: Still, at the far end of the pier, one dhow refuses to modernize.
Its sail, mended in seventeen places, lifts toward the light, and I find myself, without deciding to, calling it by name.
Now the cranes do the counting, their steel arms swinging in mechanical silence, and the containers stack themselves like letters no one will ever open.
My grandfather counted these once, not with numbers but with names, calling each vessel as if it were a cousin returning from a long and uncertain journey.

questions.why: Still signals the turn, and calling the boat by name repeats the grandfather's habit.

questions.stem: Part A: What does the speaker suggest about the grandfather's way of counting the boats?

partA.stem: Part A: What does the speaker suggest about the grandfather's way of counting the boats?

options.label: A
options.text: It was used only for the oldest dhows in the harbor.

options.label: B
options.text: It was a habit the speaker has always found difficult to understand.

options.label: C
options.text: It treated the boats as members of a family rather than as objects.

options.label: D

partB.stem: Part B: Which sentence from the passage best supports the answer to Part A?

options.label: A
options.text: Now the cranes do the counting, their steel arms swinging in mechanical silence, and the containers stack themselves like letters no one will ever open.

questions.why: Calling each boat like a returning cousin shows the boats were treated as family.

questions.stem: True or false: Because the bread text (Text 1) contains a supernatural event, it belongs to the same subgenre as the Valdrenn text (Text 2).
questions.why: Text 1 is magical realism set in an ordinary town; Text 2 is high fantasy in an invented world.

questions.stem: How does the final sentence of Text 1 contribute to its genre?
options: Its humor reveals that the story is meant to be a fable.
Its ordinary complaints make the magic seem part of daily life.
Its focus on the neighbors shifts the story into a realistic genre.
Its reference to coins establishes a historical time period.
questions.why: Magical realism treats the impossible in a calm, everyday tone.

questions.stem: Which THREE conventions of high fantasy appear in Text 2? Choose three.
options: a fully invented world with its own geography
a moral stated directly at the end
a governing body unique to that world
a realistic setting with familiar daily routines
a narrator who treats magic as unremarkable
a quest that sets the plot in motion
questions.why: High fantasy builds a separate world with its own rulers and sends a hero on a quest.

questions.stem: Classify each feature as found only in the bread text (Text 1), only in the Valdrenn text (Text 2), or in both texts.

rows.text: Magic described in a calm, matter-of-fact tone
A dangerous journey across unknown land
An elemental bond that governs every inhabitant
Everyday details such as prices and coins
A supernatural element within the setting

questions.why: Both texts include magic, but they frame it in very different worlds.

questions.stem: Part A: Which statement best distinguishes the genre of Text 1 from that of Text 2?

partA.stem: Part A: Which statement best distinguishes the genre of Text 1 from that of Text 2?

options.label: A
options.text: Text 1 contains no magical elements, while Text 2 is built around them.

options.label: B
options.text: Text 1 is told in verse, while Text 2 is told in prose.

options.label: C
options.text: Text 1 is a fable with a stated moral, while Text 2 is a myth explaining nature.

options.label: D
options.text: Text 1 presents magic as an ordinary part of a realistic town, while Text 2 builds an entirely invented world.

partB.stem: Part B: Which sentence from the passage best supports the answer to Part A?

options.text: Every child of Valdrenn was bound at birth to an element, and when the young apprentice Toren discovered that his own bond had been stolen, he knew that he must cross the Shattered Plains, a journey from which no traveler in three centuries had returned.

options.label: B

sets.skill: How Authors Develop and Refine Ideas

questions.stem: True or false: In “How Bees Make Honey,” the words First, Next, and Last help the reader follow the steps.

questions.stem: Put the steps from “How Bees Make Honey” in order.
sequence: A bee drinks nectar from a flower.
The bee gives the nectar to other bees.
The bees put the nectar in wax cells.
The nectar gets thick and becomes honey.
questions.why: The author tells the steps in the order they happen.

questions.stem: How does the author explain how bees make honey?
options: by comparing bees with birds
by telling about a bee's family
by naming many kinds of flowers
by telling the steps in order
questions.why: The article is built around three steps in time order.

questions.stem: Select the sentence from “How Bees Make Honey” that tells what the whole article is about.

segments.text: Bees make honey in three steps.
It drinks the sweet juice inside.
They fan it with their wings.
Now it is honey!

questions.why: The first sentence tells the main idea; the others are details.

questions.stem: What is the main purpose of paragraph 1?

It lists the different materials that builders used.
It introduces the problem that wind catchers solved.
It describes how architects today study energy use.
questions.why: Paragraph 1 sets up the need to stay cool and names the solution.

questions.stem: Which TWO sentences explain how a wind catcher moves air through a house? Choose two.
options: Architects hope new buildings will use less energy.
People built the towers on top of their homes.
Warm air rises and leaves through another opening.
The tower catches the breeze and pushes it into the rooms.

questions.stem: For “The Wind Catchers,” tell which paragraph each idea comes from.

rows.text: Cool air moves down while warm air escapes.
A pool of water cools the air even more.
Architects are studying the towers today.

questions.why: Each paragraph adds a new step to the author's idea.

questions.stem: Select the sentence from “The Wind Catchers” that the author uses to show why the topic still matters today.

This steady movement keeps the house cooler.

questions.why: The last sentence links the old idea to a present-day need.

questions.stem: Select the sentence from “The Quiet Genius of Al-Jazari” that signals the author is about to move beyond the familiar view of al-Jazari.

segments.text: However, his greatest contribution may be less obvious than these impressive inventions.
In 1206, an engineer named Ismail al-Jazari completed a book describing about fifty mechanical devices.
This approach was unusual at a time when many inventors guarded their methods as secrets.
Because he recorded his methods so carefully, engineers in later centuries could study and improve them.

questions.why: The word However turns from what readers remember to the author's own idea.

questions.stem: Which sentence best states the central idea the author develops?
options: Al-Jazari's lasting gift was recording his methods so others could build on them.
Al-Jazari kept his building methods secret to protect his inventions from rivals.
Al-Jazari personally invented the engines that are used in modern factories today.
Al-Jazari's elephant clock was the most impressive and complex machine of the 1200s.
questions.why: Every paragraph leads to the idea that sharing methods was his real legacy.

questions.stem: Put the stages of the author's argument in “The Quiet Genius of Al-Jazari” in the order they appear.
sequence: states what most readers remember about al-Jazari
explains how he described and drew his machines
shows how later engineers used his ideas
names his true legacy as a habit of sharing knowledge
questions.why: The author moves from the familiar view to evidence to a final, refined claim.

questions.stem: Part A: How does paragraph 2 develop the central idea?

partA.stem: Part A: How does paragraph 2 develop the central idea?

options.label: D
options.text: It argues that al-Jazari's machines were more useful than modern machines.

options.label: D
options.text: In 1206, an engineer named Ismail al-Jazari completed a book describing about fifty mechanical devices.

questions.why: Paragraph 2 contrasts his open method with the secrecy of other inventors.

questions.stem: Which TWO statements describe how the final paragraph refines the author's idea about al-Jazari? Choose two.
options: It introduces a new invention not mentioned earlier.
It disagrees with the suggestion made in paragraph 1.
It narrows his legacy from many machines to one habit.
It joins the details in paragraphs 2 and 3 into one claim.
questions.why: The conclusion sums up the evidence and states the idea more precisely.

questions.stem: What is the purpose of the speaker's statement "I understand that doubt" in “Roots Along the Shore”?
options: to criticize the volunteers who stopped helping out
to accept the audience's concern before answering it
to admit that the planting project has mostly failed
to change the topic from planting trees to storms
questions.why: Speakers often acknowledge an objection before responding to it.

questions.stem: In “Roots Along the Shore,” the speaker refines the claim that "a single mangrove cannot stop a storm" by explaining that the real goal is ____.
options: replacing the beach with a stone wall
many trees growing together into a forest
planting faster than other coastal groups
choosing the strongest single seedling
questions.why: The speaker shifts the focus from one tree to a whole forest.

questions.stem: For “Roots Along the Shore,” classify each sentence by the role it plays in developing the speaker's idea.

rows.text: The seedlings were tiny, and the sea seemed enormous.
So the question is not whether one seedling matters.
The unprotected beach lost nearly a meter of sand.
But a single mangrove was never the point.

questions.why: The speech moves from doubt, to a new way of seeing the question, to proof.

questions.stem: Part A: What evidence does the speaker use to support the refined idea in “Roots Along the Shore”?

options.label: B

options.label: C
options.text: a description of how roots shelter juvenile fish

options.label: D

partB.stem: Part B: Which sentence from the passage best supports the answer to Part A?

options.label: A
options.text: When thousands of trees grow together, their roots form a living barrier stronger than any individual plant.

options.label: B
options.text: Last winter, after a violent storm, the stretch of beach behind our oldest planting lost almost no sand, while the unprotected beach beside it lost nearly a meter.

options.text: The seedlings were tiny, and the sea seemed enormous.

options.label: D

questions.why: The beach comparison is measured proof; the roots detail explains but does not prove.

questions.stem: Select the sentence from “Roots Along the Shore” that best states the speaker's fully developed idea.

segments.text: Small actions, repeated faithfully, become a defense that no single person could ever build alone.
When thousands of trees grow together, their roots form a living barrier stronger than any individual plant.

questions.why: The final sentence widens the mangrove example into a general claim about small actions.

questions.stem: Which TWO details does the author of “The Myth of the Lone Inventor” use to develop the claim that invention is collaborative? Choose two.
options: researchers in several countries producing glowing filaments for decades
skilled assistants whose names rarely survive in the record
the image of a device appearing on one remarkable night
the rare talent of knowing which partial solution deserves attention
questions.why: Earlier researchers and assistants show the network; the other details describe the myth or individual talent.

questions.stem: Which statement best describes how the author's claim changes from paragraph 1 to paragraph 4?
options: It moves from describing the light bulb to arguing that the device was a practical failure.
It moves from praising one famous inventor to rejecting the value of individual talent entirely.
It moves from a history of the light bulb to a prediction about how future inventions will appear.
It moves from questioning the lone-inventor story to calling it incomplete rather than false.
questions.why: The author ends by refining, not rejecting, the popular story.

questions.stem: In the final paragraph of “The Myth of the Lone Inventor,” the author refines the central idea by replacing the image of a sudden flash with the image of a ____.
options: glowing filament
finish line
single workshop
relay race
questions.why: A relay shows many runners contributing to one result; the finish line is only its last moment.

questions.stem: Part A: What is the function of paragraph 3 in “The Myth of the Lone Inventor”?

partA.stem: Part A: What is the function of paragraph 3 in “The Myth of the Lone Inventor”?

options.label: C
options.text: It introduces a second invention to compare with the history of the light bulb.

partB.stem: Part B: Which sentence from the passage best supports the answer to Part A?

questions.stem: Select the sentence from “The Myth of the Lone Inventor” that most precisely states the author's refined claim.

segments.text: The lone-inventor story, then, is not exactly false; it is incomplete.

We like our inventions to have a single parent.

questions.stem: For “The Honest Distortion,” classify each sentence by the role it plays in the author's argument.

rows.text: Every flat map of the Earth is, in a strict sense, a falsehood.

The more productive question is whether a map's distortions suit its purpose.
A projection becomes misleading only when it is used for an unintended task.

questions.why: The author states a claim, answers critics, and then reframes the question.

questions.stem: Which statement best expresses how the author refines the opening claim that every flat map is "a falsehood"?
options: The author abandons the opening claim and argues that careful modern maps are fully accurate.
The author narrows the claim so that it applies only to the charts used by early navigators.
The author recasts distortion as a deliberate choice that misleads only when misapplied.
The author strengthens the claim by urging readers to give up flat maps of the Earth entirely.
questions.why: The essay keeps the idea that maps distort but changes what that distortion means.

questions.stem: In “The Honest Distortion,” the word "therefore" at the start of paragraph 4 signals that the refined question ____.

introduces an unrelated concern about modern ship navigation
contradicts the evidence about the sizes of Greenland and Africa
repeats the critics' view in more careful and precise language

questions.stem: Part A: How does paragraph 3 contribute to the development of the argument in “The Honest Distortion”?

partA.stem: Part A: How does paragraph 3 contribute to the development of the argument in “The Honest Distortion”?

options.label: A
options.text: It offers the equal-area projection as the single best solution to the problem of distortion.

options.label: B
options.text: It presents an opposing conclusion and shows that it confuses a trade-off with a mistake.

options.label: C
options.text: It explains why navigators needed to keep a constant compass course across the ocean.

options.label: D
options.text: It provides further evidence that the navigational map greatly exaggerates polar regions.

partB.stem: Part B: Which sentence from the passage best supports the answer to Part A?

options.label: A
options.text: Every flat map of the Earth is, in a strict sense, a falsehood.

options.label: B
options.text: An equal-area projection corrects the sizes of continents but distorts their shapes, sacrificing precisely what the sailor required.

options.label: C
options.text: The price is enormous exaggeration near the poles, where Greenland swells to rival Africa, a continent roughly fourteen times its size.

options.label: D

questions.why: The rebuttal sentence names the critics' error; the equal-area sentence only supports the rebuttal.

questions.stem: Which THREE techniques does the author of “The Honest Distortion” use to develop the central idea? Choose three.

using a specific size comparison to make distortion concrete
contrasting two projections that each sacrifice something different
tracing the history of map-making century by century
anticipating and rebutting a critic's conclusion
citing a cartographer's personal account of designing a map
questions.why: The essay uses contrast, rebuttal, and a concrete example; it offers no personal account or detailed history.

questions.stem: In “Harbor at Dawn,” what does the simile "folded like a letter" suggest about the harbor before sunrise?

questions.stem: Select two sentences from “Harbor at Dawn” that use personification to describe a sound.

questions.stem: For “Ibn Majid and the Monsoon Seas,” classify each statement as supported by Text 1 only, Text 2 only, or both texts.

rows.text: His writings recorded valuable navigational information.
He drew on earlier authorities whose works are lost.
He wrote partly in verse to help pilots memorize.
Pilots from many regions shared knowledge in ports.

questions.why: Both authors value the treatises; only Text 2 stresses the shared tradition behind them.

questions.stem: Select the sentence in which the author of Text 2 in “Ibn Majid and the Monsoon Seas” affirms the lasting value of Ibn Majid's work while redefining it.

segments.text: Maritime historians increasingly emphasize that navigational expertise in the Indian Ocean was accumulated collectively over centuries.
Pilots from Gujarat, Oman, Yemen, and the Swahili coast exchanged observations in ports, refined them through repeated voyages, and transmitted them orally to apprentices.
Ibn Majid himself acknowledged earlier authorities whose works have not survived.
From this perspective, his treatises are invaluable less as original inventions than as rare written records of a vast, largely unwritten tradition.

questions.why: Calling the treatises invaluable records keeps their value while changing why they matter.

questions.stem: Which statement best describes the relationship between the two texts in “Ibn Majid and the Monsoon Seas”?
options: Text 2 denies that Ibn Majid wrote any navigational treatises.
Text 2 reframes an achievement Text 1 credits to one person.
Text 2 moves the focus from navigation to the trade in goods.
Text 2 confirms that Ibn Majid invented most ocean techniques.
questions.why: Text 2 accepts the treatises but places them within a collective tradition.

questions.stem: A reader who integrates both texts in “Ibn Majid and the Monsoon Seas” would most accurately describe Ibn Majid's treatises as ____.
options: secret guides kept hidden from apprentices and traders
original discoveries that no earlier pilot had ever made
unreliable poems composed mainly to entertain in ports
skilled written records of knowledge built by many sailors
questions.why: Text 1 shows their skill and detail; Text 2 shows the shared knowledge behind them.

questions.stem: Part A: On which point would the authors of both texts in “Ibn Majid and the Monsoon Seas” most likely agree?

partA.stem: Part A: On which point would the authors of both texts in “Ibn Majid and the Monsoon Seas” most likely agree?

options.label: A
options.text: The title lion of the sea exaggerates his skill as a pilot.

options.label: B
options.text: Oral teaching was more accurate than written navigation guides.

options.label: C
options.text: Ibn Majid deserves sole credit for Indian Ocean navigation.

options.label: D
options.text: Ibn Majid's treatises preserve knowledge of real practical value.

partB.stem: Part B: Which sentence from Text 2 best supports the answer to Part A?

options.label: A
options.text: Ibn Majid himself acknowledged earlier authorities whose works have not survived.

options.label: B
options.text: From this perspective, his treatises are invaluable less as original inventions than as rare written records of a vast, largely unwritten tradition.

options.label: C
options.text: Maritime historians increasingly emphasize that navigational expertise in the Indian Ocean was accumulated collectively over centuries.

options.label: D
options.text: Pilots from Gujarat, Oman, Yemen, and the Swahili coast exchanged observations in ports, refined them through repeated voyages, and transmitted them orally to apprentices.

questions.why: Even the skeptical Text 2 calls the treatises invaluable, matching Text 1's praise of their content.

questions.stem: True or false: In “The Surprise for Omar,” Omar knows about the party before he opens the door.
questions.why: Readers know about the party, but Omar does not.

questions.stem: What do readers know that Omar does not know in “The Surprise for Omar”?
options: Ali has lost his big blue box.
His friends are planning a party.
His friends are angry with him today.
School will end early today.
questions.why: The story tells readers about the party at the start, so they know more than Omar.

questions.stem: Select the sentence from “The Surprise for Omar” in which Omar says the opposite of what he means.

segments.text: "Everyone forgot my birthday," he said.
"Oh, great, more work for me," he said.
He opened the door.
Omar walked to school sad.

questions.why: Omar does not really think more work is great.

questions.stem: In “The Surprise for Omar,” is each idea what Omar thinks or what is really true?

rows.text: His friends forgot his birthday.
His friends planned a party.
Carrying the box is more work.
The box holds a gift for him.

questions.why: Irony happens when what a character thinks is different from what is true.

questions.stem: Part A: Why is the box a funny surprise in “The Surprise for Omar”?

partA.stem: Part A: Why is the box a funny surprise in “The Surprise for Omar”?

options.label: A
options.text: The box is much too heavy for Omar.

options.label: B
options.text: Omar wanted a cake and not a box.

options.label: C
options.text: Ali forgot to bring the box to school.

options.label: D
options.text: Omar thinks it is work, but it is a gift.

partB.stem: Part B: Which sentence from the passage best supports the answer to Part A?

options.label: A
options.text: They hid the cake in Ali's house.

options.label: B
options.text: Inside the box was a new ball for him.

options.label: C
options.text: All day his friends acted busy.

options.label: D
options.text: Omar walked to school sad.

questions.why: Omar expects a chore, but the box holds a present.

questions.stem: True or false: In “Lina's Cleaning Robot,” Faisal truly believes that Sparkle is a genius machine.
questions.why: Faisal is trying not to laugh, so he means the opposite of his words.

questions.stem: Which detail from “Lina's Cleaning Robot” is an example of verbal irony?
options: Sparkle's battery dies under the bed.
Lina proudly names her new robot Sparkle.
Faisal calls Sparkle a genius machine.
Lina presses the green button to start.
questions.why: Verbal irony is saying the opposite of what you mean.

questions.stem: For “Lina's Cleaning Robot,” sort each detail as what Lina expected or what actually happened.

rows.text: Sparkle would clean the room.
Sparkle swallowed a sock.
Lina cleaned the room by hand.
The robot would work perfectly.

questions.why: Situational irony comes from the gap between what is expected and what happens.

questions.stem: Select the sentence from “Lina's Cleaning Robot” that shows the situational irony at the end.

segments.text: On Saturday morning, she pressed the green button and proudly stepped back.
Her older brother Faisal peeked through the doorway.
Lina sighed, pulled the robot out, and began picking up her clothes by hand.
By lunchtime, her room really was the tidiest room in the house, although Sparkle had not cleaned a single thing.

questions.why: The room becomes tidy, but not because of the robot.

questions.stem: Part A: Why is the ending of “Lina's Cleaning Robot” ironic?

partA.stem: Part A: Why is the ending of “Lina's Cleaning Robot” ironic?

options.label: A
options.text: Faisal helps Lina repair the robot before lunchtime.

options.label: B
options.text: Sparkle cleans the room even better than Lina expected.

options.label: C
options.text: Lina decides that she will never use a robot again.

options.label: D
options.text: Lina's prediction comes true, but not in the way she planned.

partB.stem: Part B: Which sentence from the passage best supports the answer to Part A?

options.label: A
options.text: "Sparkle will make my room the tidiest room in the whole house," she announced to her family at dinner.

options.label: B
options.text: Lina spent three weekends programming her new cleaning robot, which she named Sparkle.

options.label: C
options.text: Her older brother Faisal peeked through the doorway.

options.label: D
options.text: Sparkle hummed forward, swallowed a sock, bumped into the closet door, and then spun in circles under the bed until its battery died.

questions.why: Lina said the room would be the tidiest, and it is, but because she cleaned it herself.

questions.stem: Match each moment from “The Perfect Chef” with the type of irony it shows.

pairs.left: Smoke rises behind Chef Basim while he boasts to the camera.
Rana calls the smell of burning bread wonderful.
A chef who has never burned a dish burns bread on television.

questions.why: Dramatic irony: the audience knows more; verbal: words mean the opposite; situational: the outcome reverses expectations.

questions.stem: Why does the playwright describe the smoke as “unnoticed” in the opening stage directions of “The Perfect Chef”?
options: so the chef seems more careful and skilled at work
so the assistant can blame the chef for it later
so the audience knows something the chef does not
so viewers believe that the oven is already broken
questions.why: The audience sees the smoke while the chef keeps boasting, which creates dramatic irony.

questions.stem: Select the line from “The Perfect Chef” that is an example of verbal irony.

segments.text: Chef, perhaps we should check the bread before we begin preparing the sauce?
What a wonderful aroma, Chef, and I believe your bread is ready.
Welcome, viewers!
[The smoke thickens, and a smoke alarm begins to beep loudly.]

questions.why: Rana calls the burning smell wonderful while fanning away smoke.

questions.stem: Which TWO details from “The Perfect Chef” make the chef's opening boast situationally ironic? Choose two.
options: The show takes place in a studio kitchen.
Rana fans the air with a kitchen towel.
The bread burns while he is on live television.
He claims he has never burned a single dish.
He plans to teach viewers to make a sauce.
questions.why: The boast about never burning food is followed by burning food in front of an audience.

questions.stem: Part A: What does Chef Basim's final line in “The Perfect Chef” reveal?

partA.stem: Part A: What does Chef Basim's final line in “The Perfect Chef” reveal?

options.label: A
options.text: He is joking because he knows perfectly well that the bread is burning.

options.label: B
options.text: He blames his assistant for ruining the bread in front of viewers.

options.label: C
options.text: He mistakes the alarm for praise, which deepens the dramatic irony.

options.label: D
options.text: He wants the viewers at home to clap at the end of the program.

partB.stem: Part B: Which sentence from the passage best supports the answer to Part A?

options.label: A
options.text: [Fanning the air with a towel] What a wonderful aroma, Chef, and I believe your bread is ready.

options.label: B
options.text: [The smoke thickens, and a smoke alarm begins to beep loudly.]

options.label: C
options.text: [Still facing the camera, beaming proudly] You see, viewers, even the kitchen is applauding our magnificent performance.

options.label: D
options.text: Nonsense, Rana; an experienced professional can sense precisely when bread is ready without even looking at it.

questions.why: He has not turned around, so he still does not know what the audience knows.

questions.stem: True or false: In “Clean Streets Day,” Mr. Hamdan sincerely believes the festival was splendid.
questions.why: He leans on his broom and looks at the mess, so his praise is sarcastic.

questions.stem: For “Clean Streets Day,” classify each detail as an example of situational irony or verbal irony.

rows.text: A festival about clean streets fills the streets with paper.
Mr. Hamdan calls the messy festival splendid.
Flyers urging beauty clog the storm drains.
Mr. Hamdan thanks the committee for giving him work.

questions.why: Events that reverse a goal are situational; words that mean their opposite are verbal.

questions.stem: In “Clean Streets Day,” the main situational irony is that ____.
options: the mayor forgets to attend the opening ceremony
Mr. Hamdan refuses to sweep the market square
the helicopter fails to reach the neighborhoods
the effort to promote cleanliness creates the litter
questions.why: The festival meant to keep the town clean makes it dirty.

questions.stem: Select the sentence from “Clean Streets Day” that most clearly shows a gap between a character's words and the scene in front of him.

segments.text: Volunteers printed ten thousand glossy flyers urging residents to "Keep Our Town Beautiful," and a helicopter scattered them over the neighborhoods at dawn.
This year, the organizing committee was determined to make it the most memorable celebration yet.
The mayor stepped to the microphone, gazed at the paper-strewn field, and declared, "Never have I seen our community so united behind a cause."
By noon, the flyers covered sidewalks, clogged storm drains, and fluttered across the soccer field where the opening ceremony was being held.

questions.why: The mayor praises the town while looking at a field covered in litter.

questions.stem: Part A: How does the author use Mr. Hamdan to develop the irony in “Clean Streets Day”?

partA.stem: Part A: How does the author use Mr. Hamdan to develop the irony in “Clean Streets Day”?

options.label: A
options.text: His complaint shows that he opposes caring for the town.

options.label: B
options.text: His interview explains how the flyers were designed and printed.

options.label: C
options.text: His dry remark exposes the problem that the organizers overlook.

options.label: D
options.text: His long service proves that the festival is truly necessary.

partB.stem: Part B: Which sentence from the passage best supports the answer to Part A?

options.label: A
options.text: The mayor stepped to the microphone, gazed at the paper-strewn field, and declared, "Never have I seen our community so united behind a cause."

options.label: B
options.text: Every spring, the town of Wadi Noor holds Clean Streets Day, a festival devoted to protecting the environment.

options.label: C
options.text: This year, the organizing committee was determined to make it the most memorable celebration yet.

options.label: D
options.text: I suppose I should thank the committee for making sure I have plenty of work this week.

questions.why: His sarcastic thanks point out that the festival created work instead of reducing it.

questions.stem: Match each request in “The Obedient House” to its ironic result.

pairs.right: blocks urgent news from a brother
darkens the stairs during a climb
shuts the owner out in the rain

questions.why: Each command is obeyed in a way that works against the speaker.

questions.stem: Which line from “The Obedient House” is the clearest example of verbal irony?
options: I asked it to guard my sleep, and it silenced the telephone when my brother called with urgent news.
Now I stand outside in the rain, because I asked it, finally, to keep strangers away,
How wonderful to own a house so faithful that it will not even let me in.
I designed a residence that listens, and I instructed it to protect me from every imaginable harm,
questions.why: The speaker calls the situation wonderful while locked out in the rain.

questions.stem: Which TWO statements best explain the situational irony in “The Obedient House”? Choose two.
options: The speaker secretly wanted to remain outside in the rain.
A system built for protection leaves its owner unprotected in the rain.
The brother's urgent call is the central conflict of the poem.
The house disobeys the speaker because its software is broken.
The house harms the speaker by obeying commands meant to help its owner.
questions.why: The irony is that perfect obedience produces the opposite of what the speaker wanted.

questions.stem: The speaker's tone in the final line of “The Obedient House” is best described as ____.
options: sincerely grateful
calmly hopeful
openly terrified
bitterly sarcastic
questions.why: Calling the lockout wonderful is sarcasm born of frustration.

questions.stem: Part A: What is the effect of the house's announcement in line 7 of “The Obedient House”?

partA.stem: Part A: What is the effect of the house's announcement in line 7 of “The Obedient House”?

options.label: A
options.text: It reveals that the speaker programmed the house poorly on purpose to test it.

options.label: B
options.text: It shows that the house has finally recognized its owner and will open the door.

options.label: C
options.text: Its calm promise of safety contrasts sharply with the speaker's actual situation.

options.label: D
options.text: It suggests that strangers have broken into the house while the owner was away.

partB.stem: Part B: Which sentence from the passage best supports the answer to Part A?

options.label: A
options.text: Now I stand outside in the rain, because I asked it, finally, to keep strangers away,

options.label: B
options.text: so it calculated the sodium in my supper and silently locked the refrigerator every evening.

options.label: C
options.text: I ordered it to conserve electricity, and it extinguished every light while I was climbing the stairs.

options.label: D
options.text: I designed a residence that listens, and I instructed it to protect me from every imaginable harm,

questions.why: The house speaks of safety while its owner stands locked out in the rain.

questions.stem: For “In Praise of the Meeting,” classify each statement as what the writer literally says or what the writer actually means.

rows.text: Meetings improve productivity.
Meetings waste employees' time.
A low error rate proves the system works.
Very little real work is being done.

questions.why: In verbal irony, the literal claim and the intended meaning are opposites.

questions.stem: Select the sentence from “In Praise of the Meeting” in which the writer's proposed solution repeats the very problem being criticized.

segments.text: Critics complain that our organization schedules too many meetings, but such complaints reveal a regrettable failure of imagination.
Consider, too, the meeting's remarkable contribution to productivity.
Our error rate, consequently, has never been lower.
I therefore propose that we establish a weekly meeting to evaluate whether we hold too many meetings.

questions.why: Solving too many meetings with another meeting is situational irony.

questions.stem: The phrase “with admirable discipline” in “In Praise of the Meeting” is ironic because it ____.
options: describes staff who keep meetings focused on the agenda
praises a habit of avoiding questions as if it were a virtue
criticizes colleagues for asking unnecessary questions
shows that the writer values discipline above creativity
questions.why: Postponing a question to another meeting is avoidance, not discipline.

questions.stem: Which THREE details in “In Praise of the Meeting” signal that the writer does not mean the praise literally? Choose three.
options: The agenda for the new meeting will be distributed afterward.
Fewer errors are explained by employees having no time to work.
The proposed new meeting will be held every week.
Twelve professionals meet to confirm a decision already announced.
Employees gather in conference rooms during the day.
Critics complain that the organization schedules many meetings.
questions.why: Each correct detail is absurd when read literally, which reveals the irony.

questions.stem: Part A: Which statement best describes the writer's actual view of the organization's meetings in “In Praise of the Meeting”?

partA.stem: Part A: Which statement best describes the writer's actual view of the organization's meetings in “In Praise of the Meeting”?

options.label: A
options.text: They would succeed if critics showed a little more imagination.

options.label: B
options.text: They consume valuable time while producing few real decisions.

options.label: C
options.text: They reduce errors and should therefore be held more often.

options.label: D
options.text: They are useful but should be shorter and more carefully planned.

partB.stem: Part B: Which sentence from the passage best supports the answer to Part A?

options.label: A
options.text: Where else can twelve highly paid professionals gather for ninety minutes to confirm a decision that was announced by email the previous afternoon?

options.label: B
options.text: Our error rate, consequently, has never been lower.

options.label: C
options.text: Critics complain that our organization schedules too many meetings, but such complaints reveal a regrettable failure of imagination.

options.label: D
options.text: To guarantee its seriousness, attendance will be mandatory, and the agenda will be distributed afterward.

questions.why: A long meeting that only confirms an earlier email shows time spent without real decisions.

questions.stem: True or false: In “The Empty Bowl,” Mom is happy with what Lina did.
questions.why: Mom smiles and says Lina is growing up, so she is pleased.

questions.stem: Why did Zaytoon meow and meow?
options: He was hungry for food.
He wanted Lina to play.
He was scared of the door.
He wanted to go to sleep.
questions.why: His bowl was empty, so he wanted food.

questions.stem: Select the sentence from “The Empty Bowl” that shows Zaytoon was happy after he ate.

segments.text: Her cat, Zaytoon, sat by the kitchen door.
He meowed and meowed.
Zaytoon purred and rubbed her legs.
Lina's mom was still asleep.

questions.why: Cats purr and rub against people when they feel happy.

questions.stem: Part A: What can you tell about Lina?

partA.stem: Part A: What can you tell about Lina?

options.label: A
options.text: She needed Mom to help her.

options.label: B
options.text: She does not like her cat.

options.label: C
options.text: She can take care of her pet.

options.label: D
options.text: She could not reach the food.

options.label: A
options.text: Later, Mom came into the kitchen.

options.label: B

options.label: C
options.text: Lina woke up early on Saturday.

options.label: D
options.text: She filled the bowl carefully.

questions.why: Lina fed the cat carefully all by herself.

questions.stem: Which TWO clues in “The Empty Bowl” show that Lina fed the cat all by herself? Choose two.
options: Her cat, Zaytoon, sat by the kitchen door.
Mom came into the kitchen later.
Lina's mom was still asleep.
Lina found the bag of cat food on a low shelf.
questions.why: Mom was asleep, and Lina found the food herself, so no one helped her.

questions.stem: How did Faris most likely feel during his first night at camp?
options: bored and very sleepy
angry with his classmates
nervous and uncomfortable
proud and confident
questions.why: He could not sleep because the wind kept shaking the tent.

questions.stem: Select the sentence from Faris's letter that shows he became better at camping.

segments.text: Dear Grandma, our class trip to the desert camp ended yesterday, and I am finally home again.
By the third night, though, I had learned to tie the ropes tightly, and I slept peacefully until the sun came up.
Our guide, Mr. Khalid, taught us to read the sand like a newspaper.
I am already counting the months until next year's adventure.

questions.why: Learning to tie the ropes shows a new skill that helped him sleep.

questions.stem: Part A: Why did the students most likely check their shoes after Mr. Khalid's lesson?

partA.stem: Part A: Why did the students most likely check their shoes after Mr. Khalid's lesson?

options.label: A
options.text: They worried that a snake might hide inside.

options.label: B
options.text: They had lost their shoes in the sand.

options.label: C
options.text: Their shoes had filled up with rainwater.

options.label: D
options.text: Mr. Khalid told them the shoes were dirty.

partB.stem: Part B: Which sentence from the passage best supports the answer to Part A?

options.label: A
options.text: Nobody answered, so he laughed and explained that a sidewinding viper had passed by while we were eating dinner.

options.label: B
options.text: He pointed to tiny tracks shaped like commas and asked us who had made them.

options.label: C
options.text: Please tell Uncle Fahad that I still have the compass he gave me, and that I used it every single day.

options.label: D
options.text: On the first night, I could not sleep at all because the powerful wind kept shaking and rattling our tent.

questions.why: Knowing a snake had been close by made the students careful.

questions.stem: Which TWO inferences about Faris are best supported by his letter? Choose two.
options: He was afraid of Mr. Khalid the whole time.
He did not learn anything new at the camp.
He enjoyed the trip and hopes to go again.
He values the gift his uncle gave him.
questions.why: He is counting the months until next year and used the compass every day.

questions.stem: For Faris's letter, decide whether each statement is stated directly or must be inferred by the reader.

rows.text: The trip ended yesterday.
Faris liked the desert camp.
Mr. Khalid knows a lot about desert animals.
Uncle Fahad gave Faris a compass.

questions.why: An inference is something the reader figures out from clues; it is not written word for word.

questions.stem: Why did some herds most likely bunch together around their calves?
options: They wanted to drink at the watering hole all at once.
They sensed a strange group and saw it as a possible threat.
They heard the biologist walking loudly toward the watering hole.
They were confused by the speakers buried in the ground.
questions.why: The herds gathered around their young only when the rumbles came from an unfamiliar group.

questions.stem: Select the sentence from “The Silent Signal” that best supports the inference that elephants can detect another herd before seeing it.

segments.text: For decades, researchers noticed something puzzling about elephant herds in southern Africa.
Minutes later, a second herd would appear from exactly that direction.
The results were striking.
Elephants produce deep rumbles, many too low for human ears, and these rumbles shake the soil as well as the air.

questions.why: The first herd turned toward the ridge minutes before the second herd came into view.

questions.stem: Part A: What can the reader infer about why the microphones recorded nothing when the herd turned toward the ridge?

partA.stem: Part A: What can the reader infer about why the microphones recorded nothing when the herd turned toward the ridge?

options.label: A
options.text: The second herd stayed completely still and silent.

options.label: B
options.text: The microphones had been placed in the wrong valley.

options.label: C
options.text: The signal the herd noticed was not carried through the air.

options.label: D
options.text: The ridge blocked the sound before it reached the herd.

partB.stem: Part B: Which sentence from the passage best supports the answer to Part A?

options.label: A
options.text: A group feeding in one valley would suddenly stop, lift their heads, and turn toward a distant ridge, even though no sound reached the scientists' microphones.

options.label: B
options.text: Herds froze, pressed their trunks to the dirt, and sometimes leaned forward onto their front feet.

options.label: C
options.text: The biologist concluded that an elephant's feet and trunk may work almost like a second set of ears.

options.label: D
options.text: One biologist suspected that the animals were sensing vibrations traveling through the ground rather than sounds traveling through the air.

questions.why: Microphones pick up sound in the air, so a message moving through the ground would not register.

questions.stem: Which TWO inferences are best supported by “The Silent Signal”? Choose two.
options: The biologist proved that all animals communicate through soil.
Elephants can tell familiar groups from unfamiliar ones.
Elephants cannot hear any sounds that travel through the air.
Pressing a trunk to the ground may help an elephant sense vibrations.
questions.why: The herds reacted differently to unfamiliar groups and pressed their trunks to the dirt; the wrong choices go far beyond the evidence.

questions.stem: For “The Silent Signal,” decide whether each inference is supported or not supported by the article.

rows.text: Elephants use their feet to gather information.
The rumbles were easy for scientists to hear.
Elephants protect their young from strangers.
The first herd was frightened of the ridge itself.

questions.why: A supported inference rests on details in the text; an unsupported one ignores or contradicts them.

questions.stem: Why has Yousef most likely not started the repair?
options: He is waiting for Maryam to bring the radio.
He does not have the right tools in the shop.
He fears failing, just as his grandfather expected.
He does not care whether the old radio ever works again.
questions.why: He repeats his grandfather's words that no one could repair it, which shows doubt.

questions.stem: Select the stage direction from “The Radio” that shows Yousef has decided to attempt the repair.

segments.text: [without looking up]
[setting the box down gently beside him]
[pausing, then reaching for the smallest screwdriver]
[smiling as she switches it on]

questions.why: Picking up the screwdriver is the first action he takes toward fixing the radio.

questions.stem: Part A: What does Maryam's comment about swimming suggest?

partA.stem: Part A: What does Maryam's comment about swimming suggest?

options.label: A
options.text: She thinks that swimming matters more than repairing radios.

options.label: B
options.text: She is reminding Yousef that he has proved a doubter wrong before.

options.label: C
options.text: She wants Yousef to stop working and go to the beach.

options.label: D
options.text: She is still upset that Yousef crossed the bay ahead of her.

partB.stem: Part B: Which line from the passage best supports the answer to Part A?

options.label: A
options.text: Hand me the flashlight, then, and please do not tell anyone if this goes badly.

options.label: B
options.text: He also said that you would never learn to swim, and last summer you crossed the whole bay before I did.

options.label: C
options.text: I have kept far bigger secrets than that, little brother.

options.label: D
options.text: You have been staring at that radio since lunch, and as far as I can tell, you have not loosened a single screw.

questions.why: Maryam points out that the grandfather was wrong once, so he may be wrong again.

questions.stem: Which TWO statements about Maryam can be inferred from “The Radio”? Choose two.
options: She wants to encourage him without pressuring him.
She knows her brother well.
She agrees with what their grandfather believed.
She has more experience repairing radios than Yousef.
questions.why: She uses a memory only a close sibling would know, and she speaks gently instead of ordering him.

questions.stem: For “The Radio,” decide whether each detail reveals mainly Yousef's doubt or his growing confidence.

rows.text: staring at the radio since lunch
reaching for the smallest screwdriver
asking Maryam to hand him the flashlight
asking her not to tell anyone if it goes badly

questions.why: Yousef acts, which shows confidence, but he also prepares for failure, which shows lingering doubt.

questions.stem: What can the reader infer about why the father goes to the harbor each morning?
options: He enjoys watching the gulls and boats in the early morning.
He is looking for a new job as a fisherman in the city.
He hopes to find a captain who will buy his diving weights.

questions.why: Because the speaker only guesses, readers may decide whether the keeper feels lonely or content.

questions.stem: Which statement best describes the disagreement between Nadia and Umm Saleh in “The Loom”?
options: They argue about exactly how many years the loom was used.

They see the loom's future in a museum in different ways.

questions.stem: Some readers think Umm Saleh feels hopeful about giving away the loom; others think she feels sad. Which reading does each detail from “The Loom” best support?

Her palm rests on the frame as she pauses.
She says the loom is remarkably patient.
She folds the cloth without looking up at Nadia.

questions.stem: Select the stage direction from “The Loom” that a director could use to show that the loom's story is not over.

A sunlit room in an old family house.
without looking up
smiling faintly

questions.why: The unfinished weaving suggests more work can still be done.

questions.stem: Part A: What does Nadia's line about “strangers” suggest about how she interprets the move to the museum?

partA.stem: Part A: What does Nadia's line about “strangers” suggest about how she interprets the move to the museum?

options.label: C

options.label: D

partB.stem: Part B: Which sentence from the passage best supports the answer to Part A?

options.label: B

questions.stem: Which TWO interpretations of the unfinished weaving at the end of “The Loom” are reasonable? Choose two.
options: Umm Saleh's own connection to the loom is not completely over.
The family's tradition can still be continued by someone new.
Umm Saleh secretly plans to take the loom back from the museum.
The museum will refuse the loom because the weaving is incomplete.
questions.why: Reasonable readings connect the image to what the characters have said.

questions.stem: How do Critic A and Critic B mainly differ in “The Flight of Abbas ibn Firnas: Two Readings”?
options: They disagree about whether the injury or the analysis is the story's key point.
They disagree about whether the surviving historical sources can be trusted at all.
They disagree about whether the inventor really lived and worked near Cordoba.
They disagree about whether the device was built mainly from wood or from silk.
questions.why: Critic A stresses the injury; Critic B stresses how he analyzed the failure; both agree about the sources.

questions.stem: Which TWO statements accurately describe Critic B's interpretation of Abbas ibn Firnas's flight? Choose two.
options: It claims that the inventor truly succeeded in flying like a bird.
It argues that the injury proves the experiment was reckless.
It treats the inventor's failure as part of a scientific process.
It values his willingness to take risks in order to learn.
questions.why: Critic B praises courage and the analysis of failure; recklessness is Critic A's view.

questions.stem: For “The Flight of Abbas ibn Firnas: Two Readings,” decide which critic would most likely use each detail from Text 1 as evidence.

rows.text: he landed so heavily that he injured his back
he identified the missing tail as the cause of the hard landing
he glided for a remarkable distance
he forgot to give his device a tail before he leapt

questions.why: The same fact about the tail can show carelessness or careful analysis, depending on emphasis.

questions.stem: Part A: Which point do both critics share about the story of Abbas ibn Firnas?

partA.stem: Part A: Which point do both critics share about the story of Abbas ibn Firnas?

options.label: A
options.text: The tail was the most important part of any glider.

options.label: B
options.text: The limited sources leave room for different readings.

options.label: C
options.text: The inventor's flight should be judged mainly a failure.

options.label: D
options.text: The story should be read as fiction, not as history.

partB.stem: Part B: Which sentence from the passage best supports the answer to Part A?

options.label: A

options.label: B

questions.why: Text 2 states the critics' agreement directly; Text 1 only hints that the sources are late.

questions.stem: Which new detail, if found in a reliable source, would most strengthen Critic B's interpretation of Abbas ibn Firnas's flight?
options: a report that he spent many months recovering from his back injury
a document proving the hillside was higher than once believed
a letter in which a friend begged him not to attempt the flight
a record showing he later built a tailed glider that landed safely
questions.why: Evidence that he learned from his failure and improved supports the reading of experimental courage.

questions.stem: Which interpretation of the blank circle is best supported by Idris's own explanation in “The Cartographer's Last Map”?
options: It admits that familiarity can keep a person from seeing a place clearly.
It shows that he was too ill to finish the most detailed part of the map.
It suggests that he wanted his apprentices to complete the map for him.
It proves that his home city had been destroyed before the map was made.
questions.why: He says his own city is the one place he could never see clearly; illness is contradicted by the months he lived.

questions.stem: Select the sentence from “The Cartographer's Last Map” that most directly undermines the apprentices' interpretation of the empty circle.

segments.text: However, he lived for several months after the map was finished and never once picked up his pen to complete it.
His apprentices, accustomed to his relentless discipline, assumed that a sudden illness had interrupted him.
He worked with meticulous patience, tracing coastlines from sailors' testimonies and rivers from merchants' half-remembered descriptions, until every margin teemed with mountains, harbors, and names.
The map hangs in the city library today, its center still blank, and visitors continue to debate its significance.

questions.why: If he had months and never finished, illness is unlikely to be the reason.

questions.stem: For “The Cartographer's Last Map,” decide which interpretation each reader's claim about the blank circle reflects.

rows.text: Idris admits the limits of his own vision.
Idris leaves space for future mapmakers to fill.
Idris simply ran out of strength before he could finish.

questions.why: One image can be read as a confession, a challenge, or an accident.

questions.stem: Which THREE statements are reasonable interpretations supported by “The Cartographer's Last Map”? Choose three.
options: What is closest to us can be hardest to describe objectively.
Even a master's knowledge has limits.
Leaving something unresolved can keep people thinking.
Idris regretted spending his whole life making maps.
The apprentices' explanation turns out to be correct.
Maps made from secondhand reports are always inaccurate.
questions.why: Strong interpretations rest on Idris's words and the ending; the wrong choices overstate or contradict the text.

questions.stem: Part A: What does “The Cartographer's Last Map” suggest about the meaning of the blank circle overall?

partA.stem: Part A: What does “The Cartographer's Last Map” suggest about the meaning of the blank circle overall?

options.label: A
options.text: It resists a single, settled explanation.

options.label: B
options.text: It was meant as a puzzle with one hidden answer.

options.label: C
options.text: It was simply a mistake that no one corrected.

options.label: D
options.text: It reflects only Idris's love for his home city.

partB.stem: Part B: Which sentence from the passage best supports the answer to Part A?

options.label: A
options.text: His apprentices, accustomed to his relentless discipline, assumed that a sudden illness had interrupted him.

options.label: B
options.text: "A map," he said at last, "is only a promise that someone has looked carefully, and I have looked carefully at everything except the place I have always been too close to see clearly."

options.label: C
options.text: When a visiting scholar finally asked about the empty circle, Idris considered the question for so long that the scholar wondered whether he had heard it.

options.label: D
options.text: The map hangs in the city library today, its center still blank, and visitors continue to debate its significance.

questions.why: The ongoing argument shows the meaning stays open; Idris's answer is one possible reading, not the final word.

questions.stem: Put the steps from “Mona's First Bread” in order.
sequence: They mixed flour, water, and salt.
Mona pressed the dough with her hands.
The dough got big and puffy.
Dad baked the bread in the oven.
questions.why: Words like first, next, and then tell the order.

questions.stem: True or false: In “Mona's First Bread,” Dad baked the bread before the dough got big and puffy.
questions.why: The dough got puffy first, and then Dad baked it.

questions.stem: Which sentence best tells “Mona's First Bread” in your own words?
options: Mona ate warm bread at a shop with her dad on Friday.
Dad baked some bread while Mona played outside all day.
Mona and her dad made bread and shared it with Grandma.
Grandma taught Mona how to bake a big cake at home.
questions.why: A good retelling keeps the main events but uses new words.

questions.stem: In “Mona's First Bread,” “Mona pushed and pressed the dough with her hands” means Mona used her hands to ____ the dough.
options: smell and taste
cook and bake
squeeze and work
cut and slice
questions.why: Pushed and pressed means she squeezed and worked the dough.

questions.stem: Select the sentence from “Mona's First Bread” that tells what happened at the very end.

segments.text: Grandma smiled and said, "This is the best bread in the world."
At last, the kitchen smelled sweet.
Dad baked it in the oven.
Then they put the dough in a warm spot.

questions.why: "At last" sounds like the end, but Mona still takes bread to Grandma after that.

questions.stem: Put the steps in “From Palm to Plate” in order.
sequence: Farmers pollinate the flowers by hand.
The green fruit changes color.
Workers lower the bunches with ropes.
The dates are sorted at the packing house.
Boxes of dates arrive at markets.
questions.why: Time words such as early spring, summer, and a few days later show the order.

questions.stem: In “From Palm to Plate,” what is the best paraphrase of “the wind alone cannot be trusted to do the job”?
options: The wind might not spread enough pollen by itself.
Farmers do not like to work on windy spring days.
Strong spring winds can break the flowers on the palms.
The wind helps the dates turn yellow and red.
questions.why: A paraphrase keeps the meaning: the wind may not pollinate the flowers well enough.

questions.stem: For “From Palm to Plate,” tell whether each event happens before or after the dates ripen.

rows.text: Farmers cover bunches with mesh bags.
The dates are washed and sorted.
Flowers are pollinated by hand.
Bunches are lowered with ropes.

questions.why: Ripening in late summer divides the earlier steps from the later ones.

questions.stem: Part A: In “From Palm to Plate,” what happens right after workers cut the bunches?

partA.stem: Part A: In “From Palm to Plate,” what happens right after workers cut the bunches?

questions.stem: Which TWO sentences are accurate paraphrases of details in “From Palm to Plate”? Choose two.
options: Farmers help the palms make fruit by pollinating the flowers themselves.
Dates are picked while they are still green and hard.
Farmers use ropes to pull themselves to the tops of the palms.

questions.stem: Which event in “The Storm Road” happened first in time?
options: Reem pulled the car onto the shoulder of the highway.
Reem called their mother to describe their location.
Their uncle reminded Reem to check the weather app.
Fahad counted the minutes aloud while they waited.
questions.why: Paragraph 2 jumps back an hour to the visit at the farm.

questions.stem: Put these events from “The Storm Road” in the order they actually happened.
sequence: Reem saw a small warning symbol on the weather app.
Reem pulled onto the shoulder and turned on the hazard lights.
Reem called her mother and named the kilometer marker.
The storm thinned to a brown haze.
questions.why: The story opens in the middle of the storm, so real time order differs from the order told.

questions.stem: In “The Storm Road,” the instructor's advice “stay still, stay visible, and wait” means that drivers should ____.
options: leave the car and walk carefully to a safe place
call for help before the storm reaches the road
stop, make sure others can see them, and be patient
drive slowly and keep all the windows tightly closed
questions.why: A paraphrase restates each part of the advice in new words.

questions.stem: Put the places in “How Paper Traveled West” in the order papermaking reached them.
sequence: China
Samarkand
Baghdad
North Africa
Spain
questions.why: The article traces the craft step by step from east to west.

questions.stem: In “How Paper Traveled West,” what is the best paraphrase of “the technique remained largely unknown outside East Asia”?
options: East Asian rulers made the secret of papermaking illegal to share.
Paper was sold everywhere, but it was made only in a few distant cities.
For a long time, mostly only people in East Asia knew how to make paper.
People outside East Asia refused to use paper for many centuries.
questions.why: Largely unknown outside means few people elsewhere knew the method.

questions.stem: For “How Paper Traveled West,” decide whether each event happened before or after the Baghdad mill was built around 794.

rows.text: Cai Lun improved papermaking.
Paper mills operated in Samarkand.
Mills in Spain produced paper.
Papermaking reached Cairo.

questions.why: Dates and words like by, soon, and from there show sequence.

questions.stem: Which TWO statements accurately summarize the sequence in “How Paper Traveled West”? Choose two.
options: Europe learned papermaking directly from China around 105 CE.
Papermaking spread westward from China over many centuries.
Baghdad became a center from which the craft reached North Africa.
Spain began making paper before Baghdad built its first mill.
questions.why: The craft moved China, Samarkand, Baghdad, North Africa, Spain, then Europe.

questions.stem: Part A: Which statement best paraphrases why Baghdad adopted paper?

partA.stem: Part A: Which statement best paraphrases why Baghdad adopted paper?

options.text: Its libraries had run out of space for heavy books.

options.label: B
options.text: Its rulers ordered scholars to stop using parchment.

partB.stem: Part B: Which sentence from the passage best supports the answer to Part A?

questions.stem: Which event in “Beneath the Red Sea” happened earliest?
options: The narrator finally learned to swim properly.
The camera's housing leaked during the dive.
The narrator earned an official certificate for scuba diving.
The narrator's father bought a camera at a market.

questions.stem: Put the events of “Beneath the Red Sea” in chronological order.
sequence: The father places a camera on the narrator's desk.
The narrator learns to swim and earns a diving certificate.
The narrator descends along the reef wall.
The camera's housing leaks and the photographs are ruined.
The narrator understands what the father meant.
questions.why: Chronological order is the order events happened, not the order they are told.

questions.stem: In “Beneath the Red Sea,” the father's statement that “some things are worth seeing even if one must wait to see them” can best be paraphrased as ____.
options: people should buy equipment before they know how to use it
the most beautiful sights in the world are found underwater
valuable experiences can be worth a long period of patience
children should not try new activities until they are adults
questions.why: The father means that some experiences are worth waiting a long time for.

questions.stem: Select the sentence from “Beneath the Red Sea” that signals the narrator's account does not begin with the earliest event.

For years the camera sat unused while I completed school, learned to swim properly, and earned my diving certificate.
Yet the failure hardly mattered.
The camera had never been the point; it had been an invitation.

questions.why: "Years earlier" tells the reader the story is reaching back in time.

questions.stem: Part A: What is the best paraphrase of “The camera had never been the point; it had been an invitation”?

partA.stem: Part A: What is the best paraphrase of “The camera had never been the point; it had been an invitation”?

options.label: A
options.text: The narrator realized the camera was too damaged to ever be useful again.

options.label: B
options.text: The father had always intended to use the camera for his own photographs.

options.label: C
options.text: The narrator had preferred memories to photographs from the very start.

options.label: D
options.text: The gift's real purpose was to encourage the narrator to experience the sea.

partB.stem: Part B: Which sentence from the passage best supports the answer to Part A?

options.label: A
options.text: When I finally carried it into the water, the housing leaked within minutes, and every photograph I took that morning was ruined.

options.label: B
options.text: For years the camera sat unused while I completed school, learned to swim properly, and earned my diving certificate.

options.label: C
options.text: He could not swim, and he never explained why he bought it; he simply placed it on my desk and said that some things are worth seeing even if one must wait to see them.

options.label: D
options.text: Yet the failure hardly mattered.

questions.why: The father's words show the camera was meant to lead the narrator toward seeing the sea.

questions.stem: Put the events in “An Ancient Puzzle in Bronze” in chronological order.
sequence: Sponge divers recover the fragments from a shipwreck.
An archaeologist notices a gearwheel in one lump.
A historian argues that the device had an astronomical purpose.
Researchers use X-ray scanning to look inside the fragments.
questions.why: The article opens with the most recent event and then moves back to 1901.

questions.stem: In “An Ancient Puzzle in Bronze,” what is the best paraphrase of “an interpretation that later technology would substantially vindicate”?
options: His explanation would inspire new kinds of technology in astronomy.
Modern machines would later be built according to his explanation.
Later technology would prove that his theory was partly mistaken.
Newer tools would later show that his explanation was largely correct.

questions.stem: Match each phrase from “An Ancient Puzzle in Bronze” with its best paraphrase.

pairs.right: the gradual change of accepted beliefs

questions.why: Academic phrases can be restated in plain words without changing their meaning.

questions.stem: Which THREE statements accurately paraphrase ideas from “An Ancient Puzzle in Bronze”? Choose three.

The divers noticed the gearwheel on the same day they found the wreck.
The statues found with the fragments first drew more interest than the fragments did.

Some experts once doubted that ancient builders could make such a complex device.
questions.why: Accurate paraphrases keep the original meaning; the wrong choices change who, when, or what.

questions.stem: Part A: Why does the author begin “An Ancient Puzzle in Bronze” with the 2005 scan instead of the 1901 discovery?

partA.stem: Part A: Why does the author begin “An Ancient Puzzle in Bronze” with the 2005 scan instead of the 1901 discovery?

options.label: B

partB.stem: Part B: Which sentence from the passage best supports the answer to Part A?

questions.stem: What does Class 2B want families to do in “Plant a Tree Day”?

questions.stem: True or false: In “Plant a Tree Day,” the class says everyone in Grade 2 is coming so that families will want to join too.

questions.stem: Which TWO reasons for planting trees does Class 2B give in “Plant a Tree Day”? Choose two.
options: Trees keep the rain away.
Trees make the air clean.
Trees grow fruit to sell.

questions.stem: Part A: How do the writers of “Plant a Tree Day” want families to feel about Saturday?

partB.stem: Part B: Which sentence from the passage best supports the answer to Part A?

options.label: C

questions.stem: What is the speaker's main purpose in “A Refill for Our Planet”?
options: to describe how schools in Jeddah and Dammam clean their classrooms
to explain how sea turtles find their food in the ocean
to convince the school to install water refill stations

questions.stem: Match each sentence from “A Refill for Our Planet” to the persuasive technique it uses.

pairs.right: a question that makes listeners think

Imagine a sea turtle swimming through clean, clear water.
Please sign the petition in the library before Thursday.

questions.why: Speakers mix questions, numbers, images and calls to action.

questions.stem: Part A: Why does the speaker mention the schools in Jeddah and Dammam?

questions.stem: Which TWO persuasive techniques does the speaker use in the last paragraph of “A Refill for Our Planet”? Choose two.

asking listeners to picture a scene
giving a number about plastic bottles
