questions.stem: What is the main purpose of the SkyBuilders advertisement?
options: to explain how university engineers design their robots
to persuade families to register for the robotics camp
to report the results of a national robotics competition
to warn students about spending too much time on phones
questions.why: Every part of the ad pushes readers to sign up.

questions.stem: Select the sentence from the SkyBuilders advertisement that creates a sense of urgency.

segments.text: Space is limited, and the best spots fill up quickly.
Our instructors are university engineers who know how to make difficult ideas simple and enjoyable.
It does not have to be.
Every camper takes home the robot he or she builds, along with an official certificate of completion.

questions.why: Urgency pushes readers to act now before it is too late.

questions.stem: For the SkyBuilders advertisement, identify the technique each sentence mainly uses.

rows.text: “I never imagined that I could write code, but by the second week my robot was climbing stairs,” says Faisal.
Ninety-two percent of our campers say they would return.
Join the hundreds of talented, creative students who have already discovered what they are capable of inventing.

questions.why: A testimonial is a personal statement, a statistic is a number, and bandwagon invites you to join the crowd.

questions.stem: Part A: Why does the advertisement begin with a question about scrolling through videos?

partA.stem: Part A: Why does the advertisement begin with a question about scrolling through videos?

options.label: A
options.text: to suggest that a summer without the camp would be wasted

options.label: B
options.text: to describe what campers do on the first day

options.label: C
options.text: to prove that videos teach students how to build robots

options.label: D
options.text: to explain the camp's rules about using phones

partB.stem: Part B: Which sentence from the passage best supports the answer to Part A?

options.label: A
options.text: Every camper takes home the robot he or she builds, along with an official certificate of completion.

options.label: B
options.text: Our instructors are university engineers who know how to make difficult ideas simple and enjoyable.

options.label: C
options.text: It does not have to be.

options.label: D
options.text: Register before May 15 and receive a free toolkit worth 200 riyals!

questions.why: The answer “It does not have to be” presents the camp as the better choice.

questions.stem: Which statement best evaluates Faisal's testimonial as evidence?
options: It is weak because Faisal never managed to build a working robot.
It is appealing, but it shows only one camper's experience.
It is a statistic that measures how many campers return each year.
It proves that every camper will learn to write code in two weeks.
questions.why: One person's story is persuasive but cannot prove results for everyone.

questions.stem: What claim does Dr. Al-Harbi make in her letter to the editor?
options: The town should build a shaded walking path.
Residents should stop walking in the evening heat.
The stadium parking lot should be repaved first.
The clinic needs more doctors to treat its patients.
questions.why: Her whole letter argues for the walking path.

questions.stem: Select the sentence in Dr. Al-Harbi's letter that presents an opposing view.

segments.text: Some council members argue that a walking path would cost too much.
Currently, there is not a single shaded path within walking distance of the town center.
That scene, which is rare in our community today, could become an everyday sight.
Many of them tell me they would walk more if there were a safe, comfortable place to do so.

questions.why: A counterclaim states what the other side believes.

questions.stem: For Dr. Al-Harbi's letter, classify the appeal each detail mainly uses.

rows.text: She has worked at Al-Noor Clinic for fifteen years.
The path would cost less than repaving the stadium parking lot.
A grandfather strolls under date palms as his grandchildren race ahead.
A healthier population would save money on medical expenses.

questions.why: Ethos builds trust, logos uses reasons, and pathos stirs feelings.

questions.stem: Part A: How does Dr. Al-Harbi respond to the argument that the path would cost too much?

partA.stem: Part A: How does Dr. Al-Harbi respond to the argument that the path would cost too much?

options.label: A
options.text: She admits the path is expensive but says money does not matter.

options.label: B
options.text: She promises that doctors at her clinic will pay for the path.

options.label: C
options.text: She compares its cost to another project and points to long-term savings.

options.label: D
options.text: She claims the council already has plenty of unused money.

partB.stem: Part B: Which sentence from the passage best supports the answer to Part A?

options.label: A
options.text: I urge every resident to attend Tuesday's council meeting and to speak in favor of the path.

options.label: B
options.text: Some council members argue that a walking path would cost too much.

options.label: C
options.text: Currently, there is not a single shaded path within walking distance of the town center.

options.label: D
options.text: However, the proposed path would cost less than repaving the parking lot near the stadium, and a healthier population would save the town far more in medical expenses over time.

questions.why: She rebuts the counterclaim with a cost comparison and future savings.

questions.stem: Which TWO statements best explain why the image of the grandfather is effective in Dr. Al-Harbi's letter? Choose two.
options: It adds an emotional appeal after the logical argument.
It helps readers imagine how families would benefit.
It provides statistical evidence about heart disease.
It answers the council's concern about the cost.
questions.why: The image follows the reasoning and makes readers feel the benefit.

questions.stem: Which statement best expresses the author's claim in “Open the Doors”?
options: Museums in other countries are better run than local ones.
The National Museum should eliminate its admission fee.
Families should visit the museum more often on weekends.
The museum should raise its fees to pay for conservation work.
questions.why: The essay argues that the museum should be free.

questions.stem: For “Open the Doors,” classify each sentence as mainly evidence or mainly an emotional appeal.

rows.text: When the National Museum raised its admission fee last year, attendance by families fell by nearly a third.
A place built to belong to everyone has quietly become a luxury.
Their visitor numbers, in some cases, have doubled.
A child who stands before a thousand-year-old astrolabe may discover a lifelong passion for astronomy.

questions.why: Evidence reports data; emotional appeals use images and loaded words.

questions.stem: Part A: How does the author address the critics' concern about the budget?

partA.stem: Part A: How does the author address the critics' concern about the budget?

options.label: A
options.text: by arguing that a museum's budget has no effect on its exhibitions

options.label: B
options.text: by showing that the National Museum already has extra money

options.label: C
options.text: by granting that it is reasonable, then describing how other museums replaced the lost income

options.label: D
options.text: by dismissing the critics as people who do not care about history

partB.stem: Part B: Which sentence from the passage best supports the answer to Part A?

options.label: A
options.text: The choice should be obvious.

options.label: B
options.text: Consider what is at stake.

options.label: C
options.text: Yet museums in several countries have abolished fees and replaced the lost income through corporate sponsorships, memberships, and modest charges for special exhibitions.

options.label: D
options.text: Every civilization measures itself by how it treats its past.

questions.why: A concession followed by a rebuttal makes an argument seem fair and strong.

questions.stem: Select the sentence from “Open the Doors” that presents a false dilemma by offering only two possible outcomes.

segments.text: Either we open these doors to every child, or we accept that our heritage belongs only to the wealthy.
Critics contend that free admission would drain the museum's budget, and their concern is not unreasonable; exhibitions, conservation, and security are expensive.
Consider what is at stake.
The choice should be obvious.

questions.why: A false dilemma ignores middle options, such as reduced fees or free days.

questions.stem: Which revision would most strengthen the evidence in paragraph 2 of “Open the Doors”?
options: removing the sentence that admits free admission is expensive
adding more descriptive words about ancient scientific instruments
naming the museums that dropped fees and giving their attendance figures
repeating more forcefully that the right choice should be obvious
questions.why: Specific, checkable examples are stronger than the vague phrase “several countries.”

questions.stem: Which statement best expresses the speaker's central claim in the address to the forum?
options: Coastal development will succeed only if it protects the reefs.
Tourists are the main cause of damage to Red Sea reefs.
All development along the Red Sea coast should stop at once.
Scientists, not officials, should approve all coastal hotels.
questions.why: She argues that reefs and prosperity go together, not that building must stop.

questions.stem: Select the sentence from the address to the forum in which the speaker states an opposing claim and then rejects it.

segments.text: We are told that development and conservation are irreconcilable enemies, that every resort we construct must cost us a reef, but that assumption is mistaken.
A healthy reef is not an obstacle to prosperity; it is the foundation upon which prosperity depends.
I do not describe this transformation to alarm you; I describe it because the decision-makers in this room will determine whether my students ever witness what I have witnessed.
The reefs have waited thousands of years for humanity to understand them, but they cannot afford to wait indefinitely.

questions.why: A counterclaim followed by a rebuttal names the other side's view and then answers it; the reef sentence only restates her own claim.

questions.stem: Match each excerpt from the address to the forum with the rhetorical device it uses.

pairs.left: Let us build carefully, let us build scientifically
A healthy reef is not an obstacle to prosperity; it is the foundation upon which prosperity depends.
pairs.right: antithesis (contrasting ideas set side by side)

pairs.left: I have spent twenty-two years diving along the Red Sea coast
reefs that once blazed with color fade to the pale gray of old bone

questions.why: Recognizing the device helps explain how a speech persuades.

questions.stem: Part A: How does the list of the reefs' benefits in paragraph 2 support the speaker's argument?

partA.stem: Part A: How does the list of the reefs' benefits in paragraph 2 support the speaker's argument?

options.label: A
options.text: It proves that no hotels should ever be built near the coast.

options.label: B
options.text: It suggests that storms are a greater danger than development.

options.label: C
options.text: It shows that fisheries matter more to the economy than tourism.

options.label: D
options.text: It shows that protecting reefs serves the same economic goals as development.

partB.stem: Part B: Which sentence from the passage best supports the answer to Part A?

options.label: A
options.text: I do not describe this transformation to alarm you; I describe it because the decision-makers in this room will determine whether my students ever witness what I have witnessed.

options.label: B
options.text: So I ask you: what will our grandchildren inherit, a coastline of concrete or a coastline of life?

options.label: C
options.text: The reefs have waited thousands of years for humanity to understand them, but they cannot afford to wait indefinitely.

options.label: D
options.text: Reefs protect shorelines from destructive storms, sustain the fisheries that feed coastal communities, and attract the very tourists our new hotels hope to welcome.

questions.why: By naming economic benefits, she wins over an audience focused on development.

questions.stem: Which TWO statements best describe how the final paragraph contributes to the address to the forum? Choose two.
options: It personifies the reefs to create a sense of urgency.
It links the reefs' long history to the need for action now.
It introduces new evidence about coastal fisheries.
It concedes that some development must harm the reefs.
questions.why: Giving the reefs human patience that is running out makes the call to act feel urgent.

sets.skill: Plot Development: Conflict, Climax and Resolution

questions.stem: What is Lina's problem in “The Big Race”?
options: She does not want to run in the race.
Her coach does not come to the race.
Her shoe comes untied and she falls.
She does not have any running shoes.
questions.why: The problem is that she falls at the start.

questions.stem: Put the events of “The Big Race” in order.
sequence: Lina falls at the start.
Lina ties her shoe and runs hard.
Lina passes two runners.
The coach smiles at Lina.
questions.why: Stories go from the problem to the exciting part to the ending.

questions.stem: True or false: At the end of “The Big Race,” Lina feels proud even though she did not win.
questions.why: The story says Lina felt proud.

questions.stem: Select the sentence from “The Big Race” that shows the most exciting moment, near the end of the race.

segments.text: At the end, she passed two runners.
Lina wanted to win the school race.
Lina felt proud.
All the other children ran ahead.

questions.why: The most exciting part comes when Lina catches up.

questions.stem: For “The Big Race,” decide whether each event is part of the problem or part of how it is solved.

rows.text: Lina falls down at the start.
Lina's shoe comes untied.
Lina gets up and runs as hard as she can.

questions.why: Lina fixes her problem by getting up and running hard.

questions.stem: What is the main conflict in “The Science Fair Bridge”?
options: Yusuf's bridge breaks the night before the fair.
The judge does not like the design of the bridge.
Yusuf's friend copies his idea for the bridge.
Yusuf cannot find enough craft sticks to build.
questions.why: The conflict begins when the beam cracks.

questions.stem: Put the events of “The Science Fair Bridge” in order.
sequence: Yusuf tests the bridge with a heavy dictionary.
The middle beam cracks.
Yusuf glues triangles under the middle.
The judge stacks five kilograms on the bridge.
The judge praises Yusuf's work.
questions.why: The plot moves from the problem to the fix to the test.

questions.stem: For “The Science Fair Bridge,” label each event as rising action, climax, or resolution.

rows.text: The middle beam cracks during a test.
Yusuf glues triangles under the bridge.
The judge adds the fifth kilogram, and the bridge holds.
The judge praises Yusuf for solving the problem.

questions.why: The climax is the moment of greatest suspense: will the bridge hold?

questions.stem: Part A: Which moment is the climax of “The Science Fair Bridge”?

partA.stem: Part A: Which moment is the climax of “The Science Fair Bridge”?

options.label: A
options.text: when Yusuf looks at the bridges in a library book

options.label: B
options.text: when the bridge holds five kilograms at the fair

options.label: C
options.text: when Yusuf first starts building the bridge

options.label: D
options.text: when the beam cracks the night before the fair

partB.stem: Part B: Which sentence from the passage best supports the answer to Part A?

options.label: A
options.text: The night before the fair, Yusuf placed a heavy dictionary on the bridge to test it, and with a loud snap, the middle beam cracked.

options.label: B
options.text: Everyone leaned closer as the last weight settled, and the bridge held firm.

options.label: C
options.text: Yusuf had spent three weeks building a bridge out of craft sticks for the science fair, and his goal was to make it hold five kilograms without breaking.

options.label: D
options.text: Yusuf did not win first place, but the judge praised him for solving a real engineering problem.

questions.why: The cracked beam starts the conflict; the test at the fair is its turning point.

questions.stem: Which TWO details from “The Science Fair Bridge” show how Yusuf's actions lead to the resolution? Choose two.
options: He hopes to win first place at the fair.
He adds triangles of sticks to support the middle.
He puts a heavy dictionary on the bridge.
He studies the break to learn why it happened.
questions.why: His careful thinking and repair are what make the bridge hold.

questions.stem: What is the main conflict in “Engine Trouble”?
options: Majid does not believe that Tariq is old enough to go fishing.
The two must restart the engine before the boat drifts onto the reef.
Tariq and Majid argue about which of them should steer the small boat home.
The coast guard refuses to answer their call for help on the radio.
questions.why: The danger of drifting onto the reef drives the scene.

questions.stem: Select the line from “Engine Trouble” that marks the climax of the scene.

segments.text: TARIQ straightens the line, and MAJID pulls the starter cord twice without success; on the third pull, the engine roars to life.
The engine has stopped again, Tariq, and without it we will drift toward the reef long before this storm passes.
As lightning flashes across the horizon, TARIQ kneels beside the engine and examines it.
The boat turns toward the harbor as the first raindrops fall.

questions.why: The climax is the turning point when the problem is finally overcome.

questions.stem: Put the events of “Engine Trouble” in order.
sequence: The engine stops near the reef.
Majid explains that the radio has no power.
Tariq notices the twisted fuel line.
The engine starts on the third pull.
The boat turns toward the harbor.
questions.why: Rising action leads to the climax, followed by the resolution.

questions.stem: Part A: How does the dead radio affect the conflict in “Engine Trouble”?

partA.stem: Part A: How does the dead radio affect the conflict in “Engine Trouble”?

options.label: A
options.text: It removes any chance of outside help, so the characters must solve the problem themselves.

options.label: B
options.text: It is the reason the engine stops working in the middle of the sea.

options.label: C
options.text: It allows the coast guard to find the boat more quickly in the storm.

options.label: D
options.text: It makes Majid angry at Tariq for forgetting to bring a new battery.

partB.stem: Part B: Which sentence from the passage best supports the answer to Part A?

options.label: A
options.text: As lightning flashes across the horizon, TARIQ kneels beside the engine and examines it.

options.label: B
options.text: Then try it immediately, because the reef is approaching with every wave.

options.label: C
options.text: The radio lost power an hour ago, which is exactly why I intended to replace the battery this morning.

options.label: D
options.text: You noticed what I missed, nephew, so from now on you will be my chief mechanic.

questions.why: Taking away help raises the stakes of the conflict.

questions.stem: Which TWO details increase the tension during the rising action of “Engine Trouble”? Choose two.
options: Majid warns that the reef gets closer with every wave.
The boat turns back toward the harbor.
Lightning flashes as Tariq studies the engine.
Majid names Tariq his chief mechanic.
questions.why: Rising action builds tension; the other details come after the climax.

questions.stem: Which type of conflict does Reem mainly face in “The Map Room”?
options: an internal conflict about whether she should speak up
a conflict with nature during a sudden and violent summer storm
a conflict with visitors who damage the famous map
a conflict with another volunteer over who gets a job
questions.why: Reem struggles inside herself over what to do.

questions.stem: For “The Map Room,” classify each event as rising action, climax, or resolution.

rows.text: Reem notices the wrong date on the label.
Reem worries she could lose her place at the museum.
Reem steps forward and tells Dr. Kamal about the error.
A corrected label hangs beside the map.
Dr. Kamal asks Reem to proofread the next exhibition.

questions.why: The climax is the moment Reem acts; what follows resolves the story.

questions.stem: Part A: What raises the stakes of Reem's decision in “The Map Room”?

partA.stem: Part A: What raises the stakes of Reem's decision in “The Map Room”?

options.label: A
options.text: She has no reliable sources to check the date on the label.

options.label: B
options.text: She knows Dr. Kamal wrote the wrong date on purpose.

options.label: C
options.text: She fears that correcting the curator could end her time at the museum.

options.label: D
options.text: She is leaving the museum for good the next morning.

partB.stem: Part B: Which sentence from the passage best supports the answer to Part A?

options.label: A
options.text: Reem had volunteered at the city museum all summer, but she had never spoken directly to Dr. Kamal, the stern curator who seemed to notice every fingerprint on every glass case.

options.label: B
options.text: She hesitated, wondering whether she might be mistaken, since correcting a senior curator in front of the entire staff could easily end her time at the museum.

options.label: C
options.text: He frowned, consulted his notes, and then, to her astonishment, nodded slowly.

options.label: D
options.text: Yet if she remained silent, hundreds of visitors would read an inaccurate date.

questions.why: A possible loss makes the choice harder and the plot more tense.

questions.stem: Select the sentence from “The Map Room” that shows the climax, when Reem finally acts on her decision.

segments.text: When Dr. Kamal walked past the map for a final inspection, Reem took a deep breath and stepped forward.
By morning a corrected label hung beside the map, and Dr. Kamal had asked Reem to proofread every display in the next exhibition.
He frowned, consulted his notes, and then, to her astonishment, nodded slowly.
Yet if she remained silent, hundreds of visitors would read an inaccurate date.

questions.why: The climax is the turning point where Reem's internal struggle ends in action.

questions.stem: How does the description of Dr. Kamal in paragraph 1 of “The Map Room” contribute to the plot?
options: It reveals that Dr. Kamal changed the date on the label on purpose.
It explains why the new exhibition opens in the evening, not morning.
It shows that Reem is unhappy about volunteering at the museum.
It builds tension by making Reem's choice to correct him seem risky.
questions.why: A stern, watchful curator makes speaking up feel dangerous.

questions.stem: Which statement best describes the two conflicts that drive “Following the Stars”?
options: The team is lost in the desert, and Hamad doubts Mubarak's methods.
A sandstorm destroys the camp, and Mubarak refuses to help Hamad.
The truck runs out of fuel, and Hamad argues with the camp's staff.
Hamad cannot read the GPS, and Mubarak wants to return home.
questions.why: There is an external conflict with nature and an internal one about whom to trust.

questions.stem: Which TWO details most increase the urgency of the external conflict in “Following the Stars”? Choose two.
options: The water containers in the truck are half empty.
Mubarak has guided travelers for forty years.
Hamad trained as a geologist for four years.
The sandstorm has erased the team's tracks.
questions.why: Lost tracks and limited water make delay dangerous; the others are character background.

questions.stem: Part A: What is the climax of “Following the Stars”?

partA.stem: Part A: What is the climax of “Following the Stars”?

options.label: A
options.text: Hamad decides to trust Mubarak and follow the stars.

options.label: B
options.text: The lamps of the camp appear on the horizon.

options.label: C
options.text: The GPS unit begins blinking and stops working.

options.label: D
options.text: Mubarak points to the half-empty water containers.

partB.stem: Part B: Which sentence from the passage best supports the answer to Part A?

options.label: A
options.text: Three hours later, the lamps of the camp glimmered on the horizon.

options.label: B
options.text: The GPS unit had been blinking for twenty minutes before Hamad admitted, at least to himself, that it was useless.

options.label: C
options.text: Hamad looked at the blank screen, then at the old man's steady hand, and made his choice; he started the engine and followed the stars.

options.label: D
options.text: “Water does not wait,” Mubarak replied, gesturing toward the half-empty containers in the truck.

questions.why: The climax is Hamad's decision; reaching the camp is part of the resolution.

questions.stem: Select the sentence from “Following the Stars” that resolves Hamad's internal conflict.

segments.text: Hamad remained silent for a long time; then, quietly, he asked Mubarak to teach him the names of the stars.
Three hours later, the lamps of the camp glimmered on the horizon.

Hamad, who had trained for four years as a geologist, considered such traditional methods charming but fundamentally unreliable, and he insisted that they should wait until the satellite signal returned.
Mubarak, who had guided travelers through the Empty Quarter for forty years, studied the darkening sky in silence.

questions.why: Reaching camp ends the external conflict, but asking to learn shows Hamad's new respect.

questions.stem: How does Mubarak's line “Water does not wait” function in the plot of “Following the Stars”?
options: It raises the stakes by showing delay is dangerous, pushing Hamad to decide.
It reveals that Mubarak has secretly hidden extra water in the truck.
It resolves the conflict by proving that the satellite signal will return.
It introduces a new conflict between Mubarak and the research camp.
questions.why: The line turns waiting into a risk and moves the plot toward the climax.

questions.stem: Which statement best describes the central conflict of “The Deep Bank”?
options: Salem must find pearls to pay his family's debt before the season ends.
The merchant in Darin threatens to take the dhow from the captain.
Salem wants to replace the captain as the leader of the dhow's crew.
The old divers refuse to tell Salem where the best oysters are.
questions.why: The debt and the ending season create the conflict.

questions.stem: For “The Deep Bank,” classify each detail as exposition, rising action, or climax.

rows.text: The dhow has found only empty shells in the final week.
Salem lies awake thinking about the deep oyster bank.
Salem asks the captain for one dive with the longest rope.
The captain studies Salem and then nods once.

questions.why: The captain's silent decision is the turning point of the conflict.

questions.stem: Select two sentences from “The Deep Bank” that most build suspense before the climax.

segments.text: The captain, a cautious man who had buried two divers during his career, announced that the crew would sail for home at dawn.

Throughout that night Salem lay awake, calculating, because farther out lay a bank of oysters in water deeper than any he had ever attempted, and the veteran divers spoke of it the way people speak of a door that should remain permanently closed.
The shells Salem retrieved contained three small pearls, not a fortune, but enough.
The captain offered no praise, but the following season he handed Salem the rope he had once entrusted only to his most accomplished diver.

questions.why: Hints of danger and a deadline build suspense; the last two sentences come after the climax.

questions.stem: Part A: What does the resolution of “The Deep Bank” suggest about the captain's view of Salem?

partA.stem: Part A: What does the resolution of “The Deep Bank” suggest about the captain's view of Salem?

options.label: A
options.text: He believes Salem was merely lucky and should never dive deep again.

options.label: B
options.text: He feels guilty about the divers he lost earlier in his career.

options.label: C
options.text: He is angry that Salem disobeyed his order to sail home at dawn.

options.label: D
options.text: He now respects Salem's courage and skill, though he never says so aloud.

partB.stem: Part B: Which sentence from the passage best supports the answer to Part A?

options.label: A
options.text: The shells Salem retrieved contained three small pearls, not a fortune, but enough.

options.label: B
options.text: The captain studied him for a long, unreadable moment, then nodded once.

options.label: C
options.text: At first light he approached the captain; he did not plead, but simply requested one dive, with the heaviest stone and the longest rope aboard.

options.label: D
options.text: The captain offered no praise, but the following season he handed Salem the rope he had once entrusted only to his most accomplished diver.

questions.why: Giving Salem the best diver's rope shows respect through action, not words.

questions.stem: Why does the author describe the outcome of “The Deep Bank” as “not a fortune, but enough”?
options: to give a realistic resolution that solves the conflict without an exaggerated reward
to suggest that Salem's dive failed and that his family's debt still remains unpaid
to hint that Salem will soon return to the deep bank in search of greater wealth
to show that the captain secretly cheated Salem out of his fair share of all the pearls
questions.why: A modest reward resolves the problem while keeping the story believable.

questions.stem: What is Maha's problem in “The Sand Castle”?
options: She cannot find a bucket for the wet sand.
Her brother steps on her new castle.
The waves keep knocking down her castle.
The beach is too hot for her to sit on.
questions.why: Waves knock down her towers two times.

questions.stem: True or false: In “The Sand Castle,” Maha gives up after the first wave.
questions.why: She builds the towers again and then finds a better plan.

questions.stem: In “The Sand Castle,” Maha solves her problem by ____.
options: moving her castle far back from the water
building more towers close to the waves
asking her dad to make the waves stop
questions.why: Dry sand far from the water keeps the castle safe.

questions.stem: Select the sentence from “The Sand Castle” that shows how Maha solves her problem.

segments.text: She moved her castle far back from the water.
She built the towers again.
Maha sat and thought.
It had four tall towers.

questions.why: Moving the castle is the solution.

questions.stem: For “The Sand Castle,” decide whether each sentence tells about the problem or the solution.

rows.text: The wave knocked down two towers.
She built it on dry sand.
Another wave came and knocked them down.
The waves could not reach it now.

questions.why: The problem is the waves; the solution is the new place.

questions.stem: What is the main conflict in “One Computer, Two Projects”?
options: Adel cannot find any information about volcanoes.
Their mother takes the computer away from the boys.
Two brothers both need the family's only computer.
Bader forgets that his report is due on Thursday.
questions.why: Both boys want the same computer at the same time.

questions.stem: True or false: In “One Computer, Two Projects,” the mother solves the conflict by deciding which brother may use the computer first.
questions.why: She asks the brothers to make a plan themselves.

questions.stem: Put the events of “One Computer, Two Projects” in order.
sequence: Bader sits down to type his report.
Adel says he needs the computer first.
Their mother hands them paper and a pencil.
The brothers write a schedule together.
Both projects are finished by Wednesday night.
questions.why: The conflict starts, grows, and is solved with a plan.

questions.stem: Part A: How is the conflict in “One Computer, Two Projects” resolved?

partA.stem: Part A: How is the conflict in “One Computer, Two Projects” resolved?

options.label: A
options.text: Their mother buys a second computer for the family.

options.label: B
options.text: Bader finishes his report first and then lets Adel use it.

options.label: C
options.text: The brothers make a schedule so they can share the computer.

options.label: D
options.text: Adel decides to give his presentation without slides.

“Tie the tent twice,” he murmured, “and fill every water skin tonight,” and although I laughed at his worry, I tied each knot exactly as he instructed.

questions.why: The grandfather reads the signs and orders the tent tied twice.

questions.stem: Select the sentence from “Beneath the Reef” in which the crew's confidence contrasts with the warning signs.

segments.text: The night before the expedition left Jeddah, Dr. Amal Rashid inspected the submersible's viewing window and discovered a hairline scratch along its lower edge.

questions.why: Answering without translating is the first sign that the struggle is being won.

questions.stem: In “Learning a Second Language,” the words “imperfect and unfinished, yet strong enough to cross” show that the speaker ____.
options: has finally mastered the new language completely
wants to stop studying the language for a while
is worried that she will fail once again in class
has made real progress though she is still learning
questions.why: The bridge is not finished, but it already holds her weight.

questions.stem: Which statement best describes the central conflict of “Sadu”?
options: The speaker and her grandmother argue loudly about using new technology.
The speaker feels pulled between fast modern life and a lasting tradition.
The speaker secretly plans to sell her grandmother's old wooden loom.
The grandmother worries she cannot finish the weaving before nightfall.
questions.why: The conflict is mostly internal: the speaker weighs her quick digital world against the slow, lasting craft.

questions.stem: Part A: Which theme is developed in “Sadu”?

partA.stem: Part A: Which theme is developed in “Sadu”?

options.label: A
options.text: Skills are best learned by following careful written instructions.

options.label: B
options.text: Taking part in a tradition connects a person to a past larger than oneself.

options.label: C
options.text: Modern technology always harms the relationships within families.

options.label: D
options.text: Older people should make more effort to learn new technology.

partB.stem: Part B: Which line from the poem best supports the answer to Part A?

options.label: A
options.text: I want to argue that my generation simply preserves its memories differently, in servers rather than in fibers,

options.label: B
options.text: My grandmother's loom leans against the courtyard wall, its warp threads stretched as tight as the patience she insists I lack,

options.label: C
options.text: clumsily adding a single crooked row to a pattern that is older than any language I can read.

options.label: D
options.text: I sit beside her with my telephone illuminated, scrolling through images that vanish faster than I can remember them,

questions.why: Her small row joins a pattern far older than herself.

questions.stem: Which TWO details from “Sadu” most directly set lasting things against fleeting things? Choose two.
options: patterns inherited from women whose names survive only in wool
the loom leans against the courtyard wall
her hands continue their deliberate rhythm
images that vanish faster than I can remember them
questions.why: Vanishing images and patterns that outlive their makers form the poem's central contrast.

questions.stem: In “Sadu,” the phrase “my rebuttal dissolves before I have spoken it” suggests that the speaker ____.
options: has forgotten what she wanted to say
is too shy to speak to her grandmother
is not permitted to argue with elders
begins to doubt her own argument
questions.why: Watching her grandmother's steady work weakens the speaker's confidence in her point.

questions.stem: For “Sadu,” classify each detail as showing the speaker's resistance to the tradition or her acceptance of it.

rows.text: She wants to argue that memories now live in servers.
She scrolls through images on her phone.
She passes the dark thread beneath the pale one.
She adds a single crooked row to the pattern.

questions.why: The speaker moves from resisting to joining the tradition, which resolves the conflict.

questions.stem: Which statement best describes how the conflict in “At the Ruins of Maragheh” is resolved?
options: The speaker concludes that knowledge survives even though the building has fallen.
The speaker decides that the observatory should be rebuilt on the same hilltop.
The speaker realizes that visiting historians have misunderstood the ruined site.
The speaker admits that time has destroyed everything the astronomers created.
questions.why: The poem turns from loss to the idea that the observatory's knowledge lives on.

questions.stem: Part A: What is the effect of comparing the observatory's arithmetic to “light from a star that has already ceased to burn” in “At the Ruins of Maragheh”?

partA.stem: Part A: What is the effect of comparing the observatory's arithmetic to “light from a star that has already ceased to burn” in “At the Ruins of Maragheh”?

options.label: A
options.text: It implies that the observatory's work has now been completely forgotten.

options.label: B
options.text: It suggests that knowledge keeps reaching people long after its source is gone.

options.label: C
options.text: It emphasizes how dark and empty the hilltop becomes at night.

options.label: D
options.text: It shows that the astronomers made serious errors in their star tables.

partB.stem: Part B: Which line from the poem best supports the answer to Part A?

options.label: A
options.text: The wind that once disturbed their candles still circulates indifferently among the ruins, erasing footprints, rearranging dust, unimpressed by the ambitions it outlived.

options.label: B
options.text: Yet I cannot declare the observatory defeated, for its calculations migrated into manuscripts, then into libraries, then into the instruments of people who never learned its name;

options.label: C
options.text: Here the astronomers once measured heaven with brass quadrants and meticulous patience, recording the wanderings of planets in tables that astronomers and scholars would consult for centuries,

options.label: D
options.text: and now the hilltop offers only foundations, a scattering of weathered stones that goats negotiate with more confidence than any visiting historian.

questions.why: Like starlight, the calculations kept traveling to new users after the building fell.

questions.stem: Select the line from “At the Ruins of Maragheh” that marks the poem's shift from loss to continuity.

segments.text: Yet I cannot declare the observatory defeated, for its calculations migrated into manuscripts, then into libraries, then into the instruments of people who never learned its name;
The wind that once disturbed their candles still circulates indifferently among the ruins, erasing footprints, rearranging dust, unimpressed by the ambitions it outlived.
and now the hilltop offers only foundations, a scattering of weathered stones that goats negotiate with more confidence than any visiting historian.
Perhaps every structure is temporary, and only attention survives, transmitted from one curious mind to another across the silence of abandoned hills.

questions.why: The word Yet signals the turn; the final line builds on a shift that has already happened.

questions.stem: Which TWO statements best describe the role of the wind in “At the Ruins of Maragheh”? Choose two.
options: It represents the indifferent passage of time.
It is the force that destroyed the observatory in one storm.
It shows that the speaker is frightened by the ruins.
It symbolizes the curiosity passed between scholars.
It links the astronomers' era to the speaker's present.
questions.why: The same wind blew then and now, unconcerned with human effort, like time itself.

questions.stem: Trace the development of the speaker's thinking in “At the Ruins of Maragheh” in order.
sequence: recalls the astronomers' careful achievements
observes the few stones that remain on the hilltop
notes the wind's indifference to human ambition
refuses to call the observatory defeated
proposes that attention outlasts every structure
questions.why: The poem moves from past glory to present ruin, then turns toward a lasting idea.

questions.stem: Who is the speaker in “I Am the Moon”?
options: an owl
the moon
a sleepy child
the sun
questions.why: The speaker says, I am the moon.

questions.stem: Select the line from “I Am the Moon” that tells who is speaking.

segments.text: I am the moon, up high in the big night sky.

I see the quiet sea and the sleeping town.

questions.why: The first line names the speaker.

questions.stem: True or false: In “I Am the Moon,” the speaker is a person looking up at the moon.
questions.why: The moon itself is talking, so the poem uses the words I and my.

questions.stem: For “I Am the Moon,” tell whether the speaker does each thing at night or in the day.

rows.text: shines silver light on the ground
goes to bed
watches the owls fly by
lets the sun shine instead

questions.why: The moon speaks about what it does at night and in the day.

questions.stem: Part A: How does the speaker of “I Am the Moon” feel about the people below?

partA.stem: Part A: How does the speaker of “I Am the Moon” feel about the people below?

options.label: A
options.text: The speaker cannot see them.

options.label: B
options.text: The speaker cares about them.

options.label: C
options.text: The speaker is angry at them.

options.label: D
options.text: The speaker is afraid of them.

options.label: B
options.text: I see the quiet sea and the sleeping town.

options.label: C

options.label: D
options.text: I watch the little owls as they go flying by.

questions.why: Keeping people safe shows the moon cares about them.

questions.stem: Who is the speaker in “The Old Wooden Door”?
options: a visitor with a phone
an old wooden door
a child in the street
a merchant from a port

questions.stem: Which TWO words best describe how the speaker of “The Old Wooden Door” feels? Choose two.
options: lonely
frightened
angry
hopeful
questions.why: The door is lonely because no one comes inside, yet hopeful that someone will step in and stay.

questions.stem: The point of view in “The Old Wooden Door” is unusual because the poem is told by ____.
options: an object that has watched the street for many years
a narrator who knows what every family is thinking
a tourist who is visiting Jeddah for the first time
questions.why: The poet lets an object speak in the first person.

questions.stem: Part A: How is the speaker's view of the house different from the visitors' view in “The Old Wooden Door”?

partA.stem: Part A: How is the speaker's view of the house different from the visitors' view in “The Old Wooden Door”?

options.label: A
options.text: The speaker remembers it as a home, but visitors see only its beauty.

options.label: B
options.text: The speaker dislikes the street, but visitors love every part of it.

options.label: C
options.text: The speaker fears the children, but visitors enjoy their noise.

options.label: D
options.text: The speaker wants new paint, but visitors prefer the faded look.

partB.stem: Part B: Which line from the poem best supports the answer to Part A?

options.label: B

questions.stem: For “The Old Wooden Door,” decide whether each memory or observation belongs to the past or the present.

rows.text: Children raced past on their way to the market.
Visitors take photographs with their phones.
Merchants knocked with cloth and spices.
People whisper that the door is beautiful.

questions.why: The speaker compares the busy past with the quieter present.

questions.stem: Which statement best describes the point of view in “The Goalkeeper”?
options: the striker describing his own plan for taking the kick
a goalkeeper describing a penalty kick from his own position
a sports reporter describing the whole match from the press box
a fan in the crowd describing the striker's famous skill
questions.why: The speaker stands between the posts and uses I, so it is the goalkeeper.

questions.stem: Part A: What does the speaker of “The Goalkeeper” know that the crowd does not?

partA.stem: Part A: What does the speaker of “The Goalkeeper” know that the crowd does not?

options.label: A
options.text: the final score that has already been decided

options.label: B
options.text: the striker's injury that slows his running

options.label: C

options.label: D

options.label: A

options.label: B

options.label: C

options.label: D
options.text: The striker places the ball with careful fingers and backs away slowly, pretending he is calm,

questions.stem: In “The Goalkeeper,” the phrase “pretending he is calm” shows that the speaker ____.
options: cannot see the striker's face clearly
believes the striker is really nervous
admires the striker's true confidence
is sure the striker will miss the goal
questions.why: The speaker reads the striker's behavior and judges that the calm is an act.

questions.stem: For “The Goalkeeper,” classify each detail as something the speaker observes around him or something he experiences inside himself.

rows.text: The striker places the ball with careful fingers.
He feels the roar inside his gloves.
His legs silently prepare to dive.
The striker backs away slowly.

questions.why: A first-person speaker shares both what he sees and what he feels.

questions.stem: How do the two speakers' viewpoints differ in “Two Voices at the Harbor”?
options: The engineer dislikes the sea, while the fisherman prefers large ships.
The engineer and the fisherman both want the harbor to stay the same.
The engineer looks to the future, while the fisherman values the past.
The engineer wants to go fishing, while the fisherman wants to build.
questions.why: One speaker imagines what the harbor will become; the other remembers what it has been.

questions.stem: For “Two Voices at the Harbor,” decide which speaker would most likely make each statement.

rows.text: New jobs matter more than old habits.
The reef is part of who we are.
Bigger ships will bring prosperity.
The gulls and currents taught me everything.

questions.why: Each speaker's words reveal what he values most.

questions.stem: Match each phrase from “Two Voices at the Harbor” to the attitude it reveals.

my father taught me to read the currents
the reef that the dredging will destroy

questions.why: Word choice shows each speaker's viewpoint.

questions.stem: Which TWO words best describe the engineer's attitude in “Two Voices at the Harbor”? Choose two.
options: practical
fearful
optimistic
nostalgic
questions.why: He is hopeful about the future and focused on jobs; nostalgia belongs to the fisherman.

questions.stem: Part A: What does the final stanza of “Two Voices at the Harbor” suggest about viewpoint?

partA.stem: Part A: What does the final stanza of “Two Voices at the Harbor” suggest about viewpoint?

options.label: A
options.text: People can see one place differently, and both views can have value.

options.label: B
options.text: The engineer will eventually persuade the fisherman to agree with him.

options.label: C
options.text: Looking at the water together helps people settle their arguments.

options.label: D
options.text: The fisherman's view of the harbor is more correct than the engineer's.

partB.stem: Part B: Which line from the poem best supports the answer to Part A?

options.label: A
options.text: where cranes will rise like steel giants and the old wooden piers will finally make room for progress.

options.label: B
options.text: yet each of us is seeing a different harbor, and neither of us is entirely wrong.

options.label: C
options.text: THE ENGINEER: Your reef is a memory, but my design will bring employment to thousands of families along this coast.

options.label: D

questions.why: Speaking together, they admit that both viewpoints hold some truth.

questions.stem: Which statement best describes the viewpoint of the speaker in “The Night Guard”?
options: He resents the elephant clock for attracting so many visitors.
He wishes he could leave his job and become a museum tour guide.
He believes the museum's treasures are no longer worth guarding.
He sees himself as a knowledgeable expert whom others overlook.
questions.why: The guard knows the clock deeply, though visitors treat him as part of the furniture.

questions.stem: Part A: What is the effect of comparing the way visitors glance at the speaker to the way they glance at fire extinguishers in “The Night Guard”?

partA.stem: Part A: What is the effect of comparing the way visitors glance at the speaker to the way they glance at fire extinguishers in “The Night Guard”?

options.label: A
options.text: It suggests that he is the person responsible for safety in the building.

options.label: B
options.text: It shows that visitors see him as a useful object rather than a person.

options.label: C
options.text: It emphasizes that the visitors are secretly afraid of the guard.

options.label: D
options.text: It reveals that the gallery recently suffered from a dangerous fire.

partB.stem: Part B: Which line from the poem best supports the answer to Part A?

options.label: A
options.text: But after the last footsteps fade and the security lights dim to amber, I stand before the elephant and its mechanical riders,

options.label: B
options.text: I have guarded this gallery for nineteen years, and visitors assume I no longer notice the treasures I protect,

options.label: C

options.label: D
options.text: necessary, unremarkable, part of the architecture rather than a person who might have opinions of his own.

questions.why: The comparison reduces him to equipment, which is exactly how he feels he is seen.

questions.stem: Select the line from “The Night Guard” that most directly contradicts the visitors' assumption about the speaker.

segments.text: I have read every catalogue, every scholarly argument about its gears and floats, and I could correct the guidebook's three errors,

questions.stem: In “The Night Guard,” the claim that “silence, too, can be a kind of expertise” suggests that the speaker ____.
options: believes all visitors should stay silent in the gallery
has found quiet dignity in knowing more than he reveals
regrets that he never became a famous scholar himself
plans to report the guidebook's errors to the museum
questions.why: He turns being ignored into a private source of pride.

questions.stem: Put the shifts in how the speaker presents himself in “The Night Guard” in order.
sequence: describes how visitors misjudge him
compares himself to an unnoticed fixture of the building
reveals his private nightly study of the clock
claims his silent knowledge as a form of expertise
questions.why: The monologue moves from how others see him to how he sees himself.

questions.stem: Which statement best describes the speaker's attitude toward his own work in “The Mapmaker's Apology”?
options: He regrets its inventions yet explains them as products of his circumstances.
He is bitter that his patrons refused to pay him for his finest maps.
He is proud that his maps are more accurate than those of any rival maker.
He is indifferent to whether future travelers can trust his maps at all.
questions.why: He apologizes for his errors while showing the pressures that produced them.

questions.stem: Part A: How does the speaker's viewpoint shift in stanza 2 of “The Mapmaker's Apology”?

partA.stem: Part A: How does the speaker's viewpoint shift in stanza 2 of “The Mapmaker's Apology”?

options.label: A
options.text: He turns from addressing his patrons to addressing the sailors.

options.label: B
options.text: He turns from defending his maps to rejecting mapmaking altogether.

options.label: C
options.text: He turns from describing deserts to describing imaginary islands.

options.label: D
options.text: He turns from confessing his errors to questioning the reader's certainty.

questions.stem: Which TWO details from “The Mapmaker's Apology” reveal the outside pressures that shaped the speaker's choices? Choose two.
options: measuring my errors with instruments I cannot imagine
You will laugh, perhaps, at my imaginary islands
My patrons demanded completeness
a map which admits ignorance is rarely purchased
I leave these margins deliberately unfinished
questions.why: Patrons and buyers wanted full maps, which pushed him to invent.

questions.stem: For “The Mapmaker's Apology,” classify the main function of each line as confession, justification, or challenge to the reader.

yet consider whether your own certainties are not also assembled from incomplete reports

questions.stem: In “The Mapmaker's Apology,” the phrase “standing upon my mistakes” suggests that the speaker views his errors as ____.
options: a burden that future readers must carry alone
a foundation on which future knowledge can build
a secret he hopes no one will ever discover
proof that mapmaking should be abandoned
questions.why: Later mapmakers can rise higher by correcting what he got wrong.

six
four
