segments.text: As the fat is used up, the hump becomes smaller and may even flop over to one side.
However, the hump actually stores fat, not water.
After the camel eats well again, the hump grows firm.
Their bodies lose very little of it.

questions.why: This sentence explains that the hump shrinks as fat is used.

questions.stem: Rereading paragraph 1 helps explain why many people think the hump holds water. What is the reason?
options: Camels can go for days without drinking.
Camels drink water while they are walking.
The hump gets bigger after a camel drinks.
Camels sweat a great deal in the heat.
questions.why: People guess the hump holds water because camels go so long without a drink.

questions.stem: After rereading “The Camel's Hump,” decide whether each statement is correct or incorrect.

rows.text: The hump gives the camel energy when food is scarce.
Camels sweat often to stay cool.
A camel can drink over one hundred liters quickly.
The hump grows firm when the camel is thirsty.

questions.why: Rereading lets you check each statement against the exact words.

questions.stem: Part A: In paragraph 3, what does the word “it” refer to in “Their bodies lose very little of it”?

partA.stem: Part A: In paragraph 3, what does the word “it” refer to in “Their bodies lose very little of it”?

options.label: A
options.text: food

options.label: B
options.text: energy

options.label: C
options.text: fat

options.label: D
options.text: water

partB.stem: Part B: Which sentence from the passage best supports the answer to Part A?

options.label: A
options.text: When food is hard to find, a camel's body slowly uses the fat in its hump for energy.

options.label: B
options.text: However, the hump actually stores fat, not water.

options.label: C
options.text: After the camel eats well again, the hump grows firm.

options.label: D
options.text: So how do camels survive without water?

questions.why: The question just before it is about water, so “it” means water.

questions.stem: A reader is confused because paragraph 2 of “The Second Launch” describes a crash, but paragraph 1 describes a successful launch. What does rereading paragraph 1 reveal?
options: The crowd is cheering for a different student.
Faisal is describing a different team's rocket.
Dana is remembering an earlier launch that failed.
The rocket crashes right after it reaches the sky.
questions.why: Paragraph 1 says Dana is thinking about a morning in October, so paragraph 2 is a memory.

questions.stem: Select the sentence from “The Second Launch” that signals the shift from the present launch to a memory.

segments.text: She was thinking about the morning in October when the same rocket had wobbled, tilted, and crashed into the fence beside the parking lot.
The crowd gathered at the edge of the school field cheered enthusiastically, but Dana barely noticed them.
Now, as the parachute opened high above the field, Dana finally let herself smile.
The countdown reached zero, and Dana's rocket shot upward in a clean white streak.

questions.why: “She was thinking about the morning in October” moves the story back in time.

questions.stem: Reread “The Second Launch” and put the events in the order they actually happened.
sequence: The rocket crashes into the fence.
Faisal studies the broken fins.
The team measures every fin with a protractor.
The rocket launches successfully.
Faisal records the altitude.
questions.why: The crash and repairs happened before the launch that opens the story.

questions.stem: Part A: In “The Second Launch,” what did Faisal mean when he said, “The glue held, but the angle didn't”?

partA.stem: Part A: In “The Second Launch,” what did Faisal mean when he said, “The glue held, but the angle didn't”?

options.label: A
options.text: The fins stayed attached but were not straight.

options.label: B
options.text: The rocket was launched at the wrong time.

options.label: C
options.text: The glue was too weak to hold the fins on.

options.label: D
options.text: The fence was placed too close to the field.

partB.stem: Part B: Which sentence from the passage best supports the answer to Part A?

options.label: A
options.text: The countdown reached zero, and Dana's rocket shot upward in a clean white streak.

options.label: B
options.text: For the next two weeks, they had measured every fin with a protractor, rejecting any that leaned even a single degree.

options.label: C
options.text: Faisal was already recording the altitude in his notebook, calculating adjustments for their next design.

options.label: D
options.text: That morning, her teammate Faisal had picked up the broken fins and studied them silently.

questions.why: The team fixed the angle of the fins, which shows the angle was the problem.

questions.stem: Which TWO details from “The Second Launch” help a confused reader understand why Dana smiles only when the parachute opens? Choose two.
options: The team spent two weeks correcting the fins.
The earlier rocket crashed before it could land safely.
The crowd cheered as soon as the rocket took off.
Faisal writes the altitude in his notebook.
questions.why: Dana waits for a safe landing because the last rocket never got one.

questions.stem: After rereading paragraph 2 of “Turning the Sea into Drinking Water,” a reader can clarify that a membrane is ____.
options: a powerful pump that pushes seawater
a thin barrier that water can pass through
a machine that produces electricity
a solution that is twice as salty
questions.why: The words “or membrane” right after “thin barrier” define the term.

questions.stem: A reader does not understand why reverse osmosis is called “reverse.” Which sentence from “Turning the Sea into Drinking Water” should the reader reread?

segments.text: In ordinary osmosis, water naturally moves through a thin barrier, or membrane, from a less salty solution toward a saltier one.
The most common method today is reverse osmosis.
The method is effective, but it is not perfect.
The process, called desalination, removes salt from seawater so that it can be used in homes, farms, and factories.

questions.why: Knowing how ordinary osmosis works explains what is being reversed.

questions.stem: Reread “Turning the Sea into Drinking Water” and put the steps of reverse osmosis in order.
sequence: Pumps push seawater against the membrane.
Fresh water squeezes through while salt stays behind.
Leftover brine is returned to the ocean.
questions.why: The pumps create the pressure, the water is separated, and the brine is handled last.

questions.stem: Based on a careful rereading of “Turning the Sea into Drinking Water,” decide whether each statement is accurate or inaccurate.

rows.text: In ordinary osmosis, water moves toward the saltier side.
Reverse osmosis requires no outside energy.
Brine is saltier than the original seawater.
The membrane traps fresh water and lets salt pass.

questions.why: Rereading shows the pumps use electricity and the membrane holds back salt, not water.

questions.stem: Part A: What is the most likely reason the brine in “Turning the Sea into Drinking Water” must be returned to the ocean “carefully”?

partA.stem: Part A: What is the most likely reason the brine in “Turning the Sea into Drinking Water” must be returned to the ocean “carefully”?

options.label: A
options.text: It contains fresh water that should be saved.

options.label: B
options.text: It is needed again to run the pumps.

options.label: C
options.text: It could block the membrane if it spilled.

options.label: D
options.text: Its high salt content could damage sea life.

partB.stem: Part B: Which sentence from the passage best supports the answer to Part A?

options.label: A
options.text: Saudi Arabia produces more desalinated water than almost any other country, yet many people who drink it every day have never wondered where it comes from.

options.label: B
options.text: The method is effective, but it is not perfect.

options.label: C
options.text: The pumps consume enormous amounts of electricity, and the leftover brine, which can be nearly twice as salty as seawater, must be returned to the ocean carefully so that it does not harm coral and fish.

options.label: D
options.text: Reverse osmosis forces the opposite to happen: powerful pumps push seawater against the membrane with tremendous pressure, so that fresh water squeezes through while the salt is left behind.

questions.why: The brine can be nearly twice as salty as seawater and could harm coral and fish.

questions.stem: A reader who skims paragraph 1 of “The Hidden Cost of Early Specialization” might think the author supports early specialization. What does a careful rereading clarify?
options: The author is describing parents' reasoning before challenging it.
The author believes parents should keep children out of sports.
The author is summarizing research that favors a single sport.
The author agrees that early training gives a lasting advantage.
questions.why: Paragraph 1 reports what parents think; “however” in paragraph 2 begins the author's challenge.

questions.stem: Select the sentence from “The Hidden Cost of Early Specialization” that a reader should reread to clarify what the author means by “an early finish.”

segments.text: Children who repeat the same movements throughout the year are more likely to suffer overuse injuries, and those who feel pressured to excel at a single activity frequently abandon sports altogether before they reach high school.
The research, however, suggests a more complicated picture.
Their varied experience, rather than holding them back, appears to have built a broader foundation of coordination, balance, and decision-making.
Specialization carries risks as well.

questions.why: Injuries and quitting before high school are the “early finish.”

questions.stem: Reread “The Hidden Cost of Early Specialization” and identify whose view each statement represents.

rows.text: An early start creates an advantage latecomers cannot overcome.
Varied childhood sports build a broad athletic foundation.
Starting young is the surest path to mastery.
Early pressure can cause children to quit sports.

questions.why: Separating reported beliefs from the author's own claims clarifies the argument.

questions.stem: After rereading paragraph 2 of “The Hidden Cost of Early Specialization,” which TWO conclusions are best supported? Choose two.
options: Children who play many sports rarely become elite athletes.
Playing several sports may develop skills useful in any one sport.
Many elite athletes did not focus on one sport until adolescence.
Elite athletes usually practiced fewer hours than other children.
Research proves that specialization never produces champions.
questions.why: The paragraph reports when athletes specialized and what variety built, not practice hours or absolute rules.

questions.stem: Part A: In paragraph 1 of “The Hidden Cost of Early Specialization,” what is the effect of the phrase “not unreasonably”?

partA.stem: Part A: In paragraph 1 of “The Hidden Cost of Early Specialization,” what is the effect of the phrase “not unreasonably”?

options.label: A
options.text: It reveals that most of the parents are former athletes.

options.label: B
options.text: It shows that the author fully agrees with the parents.

options.label: C
options.text: It suggests the parents ignore the evidence on purpose.

options.label: D
options.text: It acknowledges that the parents' logic has some merit.

partB.stem: Part B: Which sentence from the passage best supports the answer to Part A?

options.label: A
options.text: They have heard that mastery requires thousands of hours of practice, and they reason, not unreasonably, that an early start provides an advantage that latecomers can never overcome.

options.label: B
options.text: Specialization carries risks as well.

options.label: C
options.text: Studies of elite athletes in several countries have found that many of them sampled a variety of sports during childhood and did not commit to one until adolescence.

options.label: D
options.text: The early start, in other words, can become an early finish.

questions.why: The parents start from a real fact, that mastery takes many hours of practice, so the author grants their reasoning some merit.

questions.stem: Reread “Al-Biruni's Mountain” and put the steps of al-Biruni's method in order.
sequence: He measured the height of the mountain.
He climbed to the summit.
He observed the dip of the horizon.
He calculated the Earth's radius.
questions.why: Signal words such as first, then, and with the height and angle show the sequence.

questions.stem: A reader is unsure why the horizon would appear to dip. Select the sentence from “Al-Biruni's Mountain” that clarifies this.

segments.text: Because the Earth curves, the horizon viewed from a height appears slightly lower than straight ahead; the higher the observer, the greater the dip.
Then, standing on the summit, he observed the angle at which the horizon dipped below a perfectly level line.
First, he measured the height of a mountain using the familiar geometry of triangles.
Al-Biruni's approach was, by contrast, almost elegant in its economy.

questions.why: The word “Because” signals the explanation of the dip.

questions.stem: After rereading paragraph 1 of “Al-Biruni's Mountain,” which TWO statements accurately describe the earlier astronomers' method? Choose two.
options: It produced a result within one percent of the modern value.
It required traveling long distances.
It depended on observing the dip of the horizon.
Small mistakes could add up over the course of the measurement.
It relied on measuring the height of a mountain.
questions.why: “Long journeys” and “accumulated error” describe the older method; the other options describe al-Biruni's.

questions.stem: After rereading “Al-Biruni's Mountain,” classify each idea about al-Biruni's work.

rows.text: A higher viewpoint produces a greater horizon dip.
His method was less likely to pile up errors than the older one.
His instruments were more advanced than modern ones.
His result was off by less than one percent.

questions.why: Rereading separates what is said outright from what follows from a contrast and what the text never claims.

questions.stem: Part A: As used in paragraph 1 of “Al-Biruni's Mountain,” what does “economy” most nearly mean?

partA.stem: Part A: As used in paragraph 1 of “Al-Biruni's Mountain,” what does “economy” most nearly mean?

options.label: A
options.text: the management of money and trade

options.label: B
options.text: a reduced level of accuracy in results

options.label: C
options.text: a simple and direct style of writing

options.label: D
options.text: efficiency in the use of effort and resources

partB.stem: Part B: Which sentence from the passage best supports the answer to Part A?

options.label: A
options.text: His result differed from the modern value by less than one percent, a margin that later scholars found remarkable given the instruments available to him.

options.label: B
options.text: With the mountain's height and the angle of the dip, a single trigonometric relationship yielded the planet's radius.

options.label: C
options.text: In the early eleventh century, the scholar al-Biruni devised a way to measure the size of the Earth without undertaking a long journey.

options.label: D
options.text: Earlier astronomers had attempted the calculation by walking or riding across a flat plain until the height of a star changed by a single degree, a laborious method that demanded long journeys and invited accumulated error.

questions.why: Rereading the sentence before shows “economy” is contrasted with a laborious, wasteful method.

questions.stem: True or false: The speaker in “A Talk About Our Trees” asks a question at the start to make listeners look and think.
questions.why: “Do you see any shade at all?” gets listeners to look at the yard.

questions.stem: Select the sentence in “A Talk About Our Trees” where the speaker asks the listeners to help.

segments.text: Will you please help me plant it?
Trees give us clean air to breathe.
We really need some trees in our yard!
One small tree can change our whole yard.

questions.why: The speaker ends by asking for help.

questions.stem: Why does the speaker say “Trees give” three times in “A Talk About Our Trees”?
options: to say that birds do not like the trees
to show that trees are hard to plant
to help us remember why trees are good
to tell us that the sun is not very hot
questions.why: Saying words again and again makes the reasons stick.

questions.stem: Sort the sentences from “A Talk About Our Trees.”

rows.text: Do you see any shade at all?
Trees give homes to the birds that sing.
Will you please help me plant it?
Trees give us cool shade on hot days.

questions.why: Questions end with a question mark; reasons tell why trees are good.

questions.stem: Which TWO sentences from “A Talk About Our Trees” tell what the speaker wants listeners to do? Choose two.
options: Let us water it every single day.
Trees give us clean air to breathe.
So let us plant a tree together this week.
We really need some trees in our yard!
questions.why: “Let us” sentences ask everyone to act together.

questions.stem: In “Words for the New Library,” what does the speaker mean by “today we are opening much more than a building. We are opening a door”?
options: The building was very hard to finish on time.
The library offers people new chances to learn.
The library has a very large wooden front door.
Only some of the people will be allowed inside.
questions.why: The door is a metaphor for the opportunities the library brings.

questions.stem: Select the sentence from “Words for the New Library” in which the speaker introduces an opposing view.

segments.text: Some people say that a small town does not need so many books.
Neighbors, today we are opening much more than a building.
So come inside, all of you.
These shelves, and every book upon them, belong to every one of you.

questions.why: “Some people say” signals what people who disagree believe.

questions.stem: Match each part of “Words for the New Library” to the technique it uses.

pairs.left: “is a small town's mind meant to be small?”
“none of us has visited ... none of us has met ... none of us has yet imagined”

questions.why: Speakers use questions, comparisons, and repeated words to persuade.

questions.stem: In the final paragraph of “Words for the New Library,” the words “Read, wonder, and return tomorrow” are mainly meant to ____.
options: describe how the library building was made
encourage listeners to make the library a habit
explain the rules for borrowing a book
warn listeners that books must be returned
questions.why: The speaker wants people to come back again and again.

questions.stem: Part A: Why does the speaker in “Words for the New Library” compare a child in the town to a child in a great city?

partA.stem: Part A: Why does the speaker in “Words for the New Library” compare a child in the town to a child in a great city?

options.label: A
options.text: to show that cities have better schools than towns

options.label: B
options.text: to invite city children to visit the new library

options.label: C
options.text: to explain why the library building is so small

options.label: D
options.text: to argue that every child deserves equal learning

partB.stem: Part B: Which sentence from the passage best supports the answer to Part A?

options.label: A
options.text: Neighbors, today we are opening much more than a building.

options.label: B
options.text: A child growing up in this town deserves exactly the same opportunity to learn as a child in any great city.

options.label: C
options.text: These shelves, and every book upon them, belong to every one of you.

options.label: D
options.text: Read, wonder, and return tomorrow.

questions.why: The comparison makes the point that town children deserve the same chances.

questions.stem: What is the main purpose of the first paragraph of the Desert Railway speech?
options: to describe the daily routine of the rail workers
to show that the railway proved its critics wrong
to explain how intense heat affects steel rails
to warn listeners about sandstorms in the future
questions.why: The speaker lists the critics' predictions and then stands on the finished line.

questions.stem: Select the sentence from the Desert Railway speech that directly answers the critics' prediction about the workers.

segments.text: I did not see them abandon anything; I saw them rebuild.
Today, I stand before you, together with those same workers, on the final mile of that supposedly impossible line.
What does this railway mean?
It means that a farmer's harvest can reach the coastal markets before it spoils.

questions.why: The critics said the workers would abandon their posts; the speaker denies it.

questions.stem: Match each excerpt from the Desert Railway speech to the appeal it mainly uses.

pairs.left: “a journey of forty exhausting days will now require only three”
“storms that erased a week's progress in a single afternoon”

questions.why: Logic, credibility, and emotion are the three classic appeals.

questions.stem: For the Desert Railway speech, identify the technique in each excerpt.

rows.text: “What does this railway mean?”
“the heat would warp the steel, that the wind would bury the tracks”
“distance, which has always divided our scattered communities, will now connect them”
“I did not see them abandon anything; I saw them rebuild.”

questions.why: Parallel structure repeats a grammatical pattern; contrast sets opposites side by side.

questions.stem: Part A: What is the effect of repeating “It means that” in the final paragraph of the Desert Railway speech?

partA.stem: Part A: What is the effect of repeating “It means that” in the final paragraph of the Desert Railway speech?

options.label: A
options.text: It shifts attention from the workers to the railway's critics.

options.label: B
options.text: It builds a list of benefits that grows in importance.

options.label: C
options.text: It shows that the railway will have only one real benefit.

options.label: D
options.text: It suggests the speaker is unsure of the railway's value.

partB.stem: Part B: Which sentence from the passage best supports the answer to Part A?

options.label: A
options.text: Today, I stand before you, together with those same workers, on the final mile of that supposedly impossible line.

options.label: B
options.text: What does this railway mean?

options.label: C
options.text: It means that distance, which has always divided our scattered communities, will now connect them.

options.label: D
options.text: Five years ago, distinguished experts informed us that no railway could ever cross these shifting sands.

questions.why: The list ends with its biggest idea: the railway connects whole communities.

questions.stem: In the marine science address, what does the speaker mean by “learning the language of the sea”?
options: studying the poems that describe the ocean
gaining scientific knowledge about the ocean
practicing how to navigate large ships at sea
learning to speak with sailors from other lands
questions.why: The “language” is defined by currents, chemistry, and life forms: science.

questions.stem: Select the sentence from the marine science address that uses parallel structure to expose two mistaken beliefs.

segments.text: We have taken from it as though it could never be emptied, and we have poured into it as though it could never be filled.
Now you must decide what you will say in that language.
Both assumptions are demonstrably false, and you, more than anyone in this auditorium, possess the evidence to prove it.
I ask you to understand it, to measure it, and to speak for it when no one else will.

questions.why: Two matching clauses show the two false beliefs about the ocean.

questions.stem: Match each phrase from the marine science address to its rhetorical technique.

pairs.left: “an endless storehouse and an endless dump”
“to understand it, to measure it, and to speak for it”
“you, more than anyone in this auditorium”

questions.why: Naming devices helps explain how a speech persuades.

questions.stem: Which TWO purposes does the second paragraph of the marine science address serve? Choose two.
options: It identifies a problem the graduates are prepared to address.
It celebrates the ocean as a source of endless resources.
It explains the chemistry of ocean currents in detail.
It establishes the graduates' authority to challenge old beliefs.
questions.why: The paragraph names a false belief and says the graduates have the evidence to correct it.

questions.stem: Part A: Why does the speaker of the marine science address say “I do not ask you to love the sea”?

partA.stem: Part A: Why does the speaker of the marine science address say “I do not ask you to love the sea”?

options.label: A
options.text: to set scientific duty apart from simple admiration

options.label: B
options.text: to admit that the sea can never be understood

options.label: C
options.text: to suggest that the graduates dislike the ocean

options.label: D
options.text: to criticize poets for writing about the sea

partB.stem: Part B: Which sentence from the passage best supports the answer to Part A?

options.label: A
options.text: I ask you to understand it, to measure it, and to speak for it when no one else will.

options.label: B
options.text: Now you must decide what you will say in that language.

options.label: C
options.text: Both assumptions are demonstrably false, and you, more than anyone in this auditorium, possess the evidence to prove it.

options.label: D
options.text: Graduates, you have devoted four years to learning the language of the sea: its currents, its chemistry, its countless and astonishing forms of life.

questions.why: The speaker contrasts love with understanding, measuring, and speaking up.

questions.stem: In the address on the city's water, what is the effect of the statement “I do not dispute the arithmetic. I dispute the accounting”?
options: It argues that the council has underestimated the price of new pipes.
It admits that the physician's own calculations contain several errors.
It accepts the council's numbers while questioning what they leave out.
It accuses the city's accountants of deliberately hiding public money.
questions.why: The physician grants the figures but says the real costs are missing from them.

questions.stem: Classify the role of each excerpt from the address on the city's water.

rows.text: “I do not dispute the arithmetic.”
“we are not saving money by delay; we are merely spending it elsewhere”
“a child who does not reach the age of five”
“I dispute the accounting.”

questions.why: A concession grants a point, a rebuttal answers it, and an emotional appeal stirs feeling.

questions.stem: Which THREE rhetorical techniques does the physician use in the second paragraph of the address on the city's water? Choose three.
options: humor to ease tension
a quotation from an expert
metaphor
emotional examples
rhetorical questions
statistics from a study
questions.why: The paragraph asks questions, treats suffering as a cost paid in “currency,” and names a dying child.

questions.stem: Select two sentences from the address on the city's water that use financial language to describe human suffering.

segments.text: For what is the genuine price of a well that sickens the families who depend upon it?
These sums do not appear in your ledgers, yet the municipality pays them annually, and it pays them in a currency far dearer than coin.
I do not dispute the arithmetic.
I have walked repeatedly through the narrow, overcrowded streets where the epidemic originates.
I have counted the affected households and mapped the public pumps.

questions.why: Words like price, sums, ledgers, and currency turn illness into a cost.

questions.stem: Part A: How does the physician build credibility in the third paragraph of the address on the city's water?

partA.stem: Part A: How does the physician build credibility in the third paragraph of the address on the city's water?

options.label: A
options.text: by citing the opinions of famous physicians

options.label: B
options.text: by quoting figures from the city's records

options.label: C
options.text: by describing his own firsthand investigation

options.label: D
options.text: by reminding the council of their friendship

partB.stem: Part B: Which sentence from the passage best supports the answer to Part A?

options.label: A
options.text: I have counted the affected households and mapped the public pumps.

options.label: B
options.text: I do not dispute the arithmetic.

options.label: C
options.text: Gentlemen of the council, I am informed that the expense of new pipes is considered excessive, that the city has survived on its ancient wells for a century and may reasonably expect to survive on them for another.

options.label: D
options.text: These sums do not appear in your ledgers, yet the municipality pays them annually, and it pays them in a currency far dearer than coin.

questions.why: Personal fieldwork gives the physician authority (ethos).

questions.stem: Which statement best expresses the central claim of “On Inheritance”?
options: Scientific discovery is a shared inheritance that obliges us to pass it on.
Modern scientists owe their success mainly to their own remarkable talent.
Scientists should leave their questions unfinished so they avoid making errors.
Earlier scholars in Baghdad and Cairo deserve prizes more than today's do.
questions.why: The lecture argues that knowledge is inherited and must be handed on.

questions.stem: Select the sentence from “On Inheritance” that uses chiasmus, reversing the order of key terms to sharpen the argument.

segments.text: We do not inherit knowledge because we deserve it; we deserve knowledge only when we hand it on.
I do not say this to diminish anyone's achievement.
I say it to correct a persistent habit of collective memory.
Yet every one of us in this room stands at the end of a long relay.

questions.why: “Inherit ... deserve” becomes “deserve ... hand on,” reversing the terms.

questions.stem: For “On Inheritance,” identify the rhetorical technique in each excerpt.

rows.text: “a man who spent years confined to his house”
“stands at the end of a long relay”
“an unfinished question ... is the most valuable gift”
“The algebra we use was refined in Baghdad”

questions.why: An allusion points to real history; a paradox seems contradictory but holds a truth.

questions.stem: Which TWO statements accurately describe how the speaker anticipates an objection in “On Inheritance”? Choose two.
options: He concedes that the solitary genius is the true source of discovery.
He denies that he intends to belittle individual accomplishment.
He reframes his point as a correction of how people remember.
He admits that his historical examples may be somewhat exaggerated.
questions.why: Paragraph 2 heads off the charge that he is diminishing achievement and restates his purpose.

questions.stem: Part A: What is the primary function of the references to Baghdad, Cairo, and India in “On Inheritance”?

partA.stem: Part A: What is the primary function of the references to Baghdad, Cairo, and India in “On Inheritance”?

options.label: A
options.text: to honor particular scientists by listing their discoveries

options.label: B
options.text: to show that the speaker himself has traveled very widely

options.label: C
options.text: to give concrete evidence that knowledge passes across cultures

options.label: D
options.text: to argue that older civilizations were more advanced than ours

partB.stem: Part B: Which sentence from the passage best supports the answer to Part A?

options.label: A
options.text: I say it to correct a persistent habit of collective memory.

options.label: B
options.text: I do not say this to diminish anyone's achievement.

options.label: C
options.text: Yet every one of us in this room stands at the end of a long relay.

options.label: D
options.text: We like to imagine that discovery belongs to the individual: the solitary genius, the sudden illumination, the name engraved upon a prestigious award.

questions.why: The examples illustrate the relay: knowledge handed from culture to culture.

questions.stem: True or false: In “Help Our Park,” the speaker asks “Who wants to sit next to old paper cups and plastic bags?” because the speaker wants people to give an answer out loud.
questions.why: The speaker asks it to make a point; everyone already knows the answer is no one.

questions.stem: Select the sentence from “Help Our Park” that is a question asked to make a point.

segments.text: Who wants to sit next to old paper cups and plastic bags?
Let us clean the park together on Saturday morning.

questions.stem: Why does the author of “Every Drop Counts” begin with the question “How much water do you think a dripping tap wastes in one day?”

to explain to readers how fresh water is made from seawater
to make readers guess and then surprise them with the real amount
to find out which reader has the most dripping taps in the home
questions.why: The author answers right away, and the answer is bigger than most guesses.

So why do we leave the water running while we brush our teeth?
Saving water is not difficult.

questions.stem: Which TWO statements explain how the questions in “Every Drop Counts” help the author persuade readers? Choose two.
options: They make wasting water seem as silly as wasting money.
They give exact numbers about water factories.
They make readers think about their own habits.
They show that the author is unsure about the facts.
questions.why: Rhetorical questions pull readers in and make the right answer feel obvious.

questions.stem: Part A: What is the speaker's purpose in asking “when has a laboratory ever built a robot by itself?” in “Why Not Us?”

partA.stem: Part A: What is the speaker's purpose in asking “when has a laboratory ever built a robot by itself?” in “Why Not Us?”

options.label: A
options.text: to argue that the students' effort matters more than expensive equipment

options.label: B
options.text: to admit that the academies have better robots

options.label: C

options.label: D
options.text: to suggest that the team should build its own laboratory

options.label: A

questions.why: The speaker answers the question by pointing to students' work, not equipment.

questions.stem: In “Why Not Us?”, the speaker asks “Did anyone force us to do that?” and then answers “No.” What is the effect of answering the question right away?
options: It suggests that the security guard made the team stay late.
It hints that the team will soon stop working after school.
It shows that the speaker has forgotten what really happened.
It stresses that the team's hard work was its own choice.
questions.why: Answering one's own question (hypophora) drives the point home.

questions.stem: Select the sentence from “Why Not Us?” in which the speaker turns the critics' doubt into a challenge.

segments.text: So when someone asks why an inexperienced team like ours should compete, I have only one question in reply: why not us?
We redesigned our robot's mechanical arm four separate times, and we remained after school until the security guard switched off the lights.
We have imagination, patience, and one another.
Perhaps they are right.

questions.why: Why not us? flips the critics' question back on them.

questions.stem: Which TWO effects do the rhetorical questions have on the team listening to “Why Not Us?” Choose two.
options: They convince the team to withdraw from the championship.
They give the team new technical facts about robots.
They make the team feel proud of the effort it has already made.
They make the critics' arguments seem weaker.
questions.why: The questions build confidence and undercut the doubters.

questions.stem: Put the steps of the speaker's argument in “Why Not Us?” in the order they appear.
sequence: The speaker admits what critics are saying.
The speaker questions whether equipment alone builds robots.
The speaker describes the team's hard work.
The speaker asks, “why not us?”
The speaker calls the team to action.
questions.why: The speech moves from doubt, to evidence, to a confident call to act.

questions.stem: How does the author of “Do We Still Need Paper Maps?” use the question “who would bother learning to read a paper map?” at the end of paragraph 1?
options: to show that the author agrees that paper maps are now useless
to explain to readers how phones recalculate their routes
to state the common opinion that the author then argues against
to ask readers to list their reasons for buying new phones
questions.why: The author sets up the popular view and then answers, surprisingly, that everyone should.

questions.stem: Part A: What does the question “What happens to the traveler who has never looked at the whole landscape, only at a blue dot moving along a line?” suggest?

partA.stem: Part A: What does the question “What happens to the traveler who has never looked at the whole landscape, only at a blue dot moving along a line?” suggest?

options.label: A

options.label: B
options.text: Such a traveler should buy a newer phone.

options.label: C
options.text: Such a traveler understands landscapes better than others.

options.label: D
options.text: Such a traveler may become lost and confused without a phone.

partB.stem: Part B: Which sentence from the passage best supports the answer to Part A?

options.label: A

options.label: B

options.label: C

options.label: D

questions.why: The research shows that relying only on the blue dot weakens a traveler's sense of place.

questions.stem: In “Do We Still Need Paper Maps?”, decide whether each question presents the view the author opposes or supports the author's own claim.

rows.text: With such a convenient tool in every pocket, who would bother learning to read a paper map?
What happens to the traveler who has never looked at the whole landscape, only at a blue dot moving along a line?
Is it really so inconvenient to spend one afternoon learning a skill that could guide you home when the screen goes dark?

questions.why: The first question voices the popular view; the later ones push the author's claim.

questions.stem: The final question of “Do We Still Need Paper Maps?” expects the reader to answer ____, which makes the author's claim feel like common sense.
options: “No, it is not inconvenient”
“Maps are hard to fold”
“Only if the phone is new”
“Yes, it takes too long”
questions.why: A rhetorical question is built so only one answer seems reasonable.

questions.stem: Which TWO statements best describe how the rhetorical questions in “Do We Still Need Paper Maps?” work together? Choose two.
options: The first question raises an objection that the author goes on to answer.
The last question asks readers to weigh a small effort against a large benefit.
Each question introduces a new statistic about phone use.
The questions show that the author is unsure of the claim.
questions.why: The questions frame the counterargument and then make the claim feel reasonable.

questions.stem: Part A: How does the speaker in “The Man Who Doubted the Masters” use the question “Why should a museum dedicated to the future honor a man who lived a thousand years ago?”

partA.stem: Part A: How does the speaker in “The Man Who Doubted the Masters” use the question “Why should a museum dedicated to the future honor a man who lived a thousand years ago?”

options.label: A
options.text: to suggest that modern science has replaced older ideas

options.label: B

options.label: C

options.label: D

options.label: B

options.label: C

options.label: D

questions.why: The speaker raises a doubt and answers it at once (hypophora).

questions.stem: The question “why would sunlight injure our eyes, and why could we not see in a darkened room?” is presented in “The Man Who Doubted the Masters” as a question Ibn al-Haytham asked. What is its function in his reasoning?
options: It invites the audience to share personal experiences of light.
It proves that strong sunlight was harmful to medieval scholars.
It shows that he preferred working at night to working in daylight.
It exposes facts that the accepted theory could not explain.
questions.why: His questions point to evidence that the old theory of eye rays could not explain.

questions.stem: Select the sentence from “The Man Who Doubted the Masters” in which a rhetorical question turns the audience's attention to their own behavior.

segments.text: Who among us has not accepted an idea merely because a confident voice repeated it?
Rather than repeating the masters, he darkened a chamber, admitted light through a tiny opening, and carefully recorded what happened.
For centuries, respected authorities had maintained that the eye emits invisible rays that travel outward to touch the objects it perceives.
This gallery is an invitation to resist that comfortable habit.

questions.why: The question implies that everyone has done this, including the listeners.

questions.stem: For “The Man Who Doubted the Masters,” classify each question by its main purpose.

rows.text: Why should a museum dedicated to the future honor a man who lived a thousand years ago?
Who among us has not accepted an idea merely because a confident voice repeated it?
why would sunlight injure our eyes, and why could we not see in a darkened room?

questions.why: The speaker uses questions for different jobs: to answer doubts, to challenge, and to model inquiry.

questions.stem: The speech “The Man Who Doubted the Masters” ends with “Isn't that, after all, the oldest and most demanding definition of science?” Which TWO statements describe the effect of ending this way? Choose two.
options: It leaves the audience agreeing that doubt and testing are the core of science.
It reveals that the speaker is unsure how to define science.
It suggests that the experiments described were never completed.
It connects the eleventh-century scholar's method to the gallery's purpose today.
It introduces a new scientist whom the gallery will also honor.
questions.why: The negative question (Isn't that…?) expects yes, sealing the speech's claim.

questions.stem: Part A: What is the main function of the question “what exactly have we gained if the average message is answered within minutes while the average book is abandoned within pages?” in “On Being Unreachable”?

partA.stem: Part A: What is the main function of the question “what exactly have we gained if the average message is answered within minutes while the average book is abandoned within pages?” in “On Being Unreachable”?

options.label: A
options.text: to question whether faster communication has truly made people better informed

options.label: B
options.text: to prove that people now read more books than before

options.label: C
options.text: to argue that books should be shorter and simpler

options.label: D
options.text: to ask readers how quickly they answer their messages

options.label: A

options.label: B

questions.why: The question casts doubt on the claimed gain; the next sentence states the cost in attention.

questions.stem: In “On Being Unreachable,” the author asks, “Is that student studying, or merely waiting to be interrupted?” Which choice best describes this question?
options: It shifts the essay's subject from attention to the history of psychology and its research methods.
It offers two options but makes one clearly more accurate, nudging the reader toward the author's view.
It offers two options that the author treats as equally likely, which reveals that the author is still undecided.
It asks the reader to report on the habits of a real student, which turns the essay into a survey.
questions.why: The word merely signals that the second option is the truthful one.

questions.stem: Select the sentence from “On Being Unreachable” in which the author concedes a point before questioning it.

questions.why: Perhaps it has grants the claim, and the following rhetorical question then challenges it.

questions.stem: Which TWO statements best explain why the author of “On Being Unreachable” ends with “Did their silence make them less connected to the world, or more?” Choose two.
options: The question asks readers to research how astronomers in Baghdad sent letters.
The question shows that the author regrets criticizing modern devices.
The question reverses the usual assumption that silence means disconnection.
The example of earlier astronomers lets readers reach the author's conclusion for themselves.
The question admits that the essay's argument has no clear answer.
questions.why: An open-ended final question invites the reader to complete the argument, and the answer implied is more.

questions.stem: Classify each sentence from “On Being Unreachable” by its role in the argument.

rows.text: Is that student studying, or merely waiting to be interrupted?
None of this implies that we should abandon our devices entirely; such a recommendation would be neither practical nor desirable.

Did their silence make them less connected to the world, or more?

questions.why: Strong arguments mix questions, concessions, and evidence.

questions.stem: True or false: In “The Rainy Picnic,” when Adam says “What a perfect day for a picnic,” he really thinks the day is perfect.

questions.stem: In “The Rainy Picnic,” what does Dad mean when he says, “It is a little damp”?

The sand is dry, so it is a good place to sit.
His hat is new, so he does not want it to get wet.

bus drivers who will not follow the school's schedule
students who refuse to wake up early for their classes
leaders who hide a problem instead of truly solving it

questions.stem: Which TWO features show that “School Solves Lateness Forever” is satire rather than a real news report? Choose two.

questions.stem: What do Nada's final words in “The Solar Oven” reveal about her? Choose two.
options: She wants to take credit for inventing the oven.
She will not help unless Rami builds a new oven.

questions.stem: Part A: What is the author's actual view in “In Praise of the Notification”?

partA.stem: Part A: What is the author's actual view in “In Praise of the Notification”?

options.label: A
options.text: Notifications are useful because they share important news.

options.label: B
options.text: Researchers have proved that alerts improve memory.

options.label: C

options.label: D
options.text: Families should use phones more often during dinner.

partB.stem: Part B: Which sentence from the passage best supports the answer to Part A?

questions.stem: In “In Praise of the Notification,” what is the effect of following “news of extraordinary importance” with a list that includes a discount on sunglasses and a photographed sandwich?
options: The contrast between grand language and trivial examples exposes how unimportant most alerts are.
The examples show that the author enjoys receiving many different kinds of messages each day.

questions.stem: Which statement best summarizes the author's central claim in “Shade Is Infrastructure”?

questions.stem: Which statement best summarizes the central idea of “The House of Wisdom”?
options: Baghdad's new supply of paper was the main reason the caliphs decided to build a royal library.
Baghdad's House of Wisdom was destroyed in 1258, which ended all scientific progress in the region.
Baghdad's scholars translated Greek texts because they had few original ideas of their own.

questions.why: The central idea joins preservation, new discovery, and lasting influence.

questions.stem: Select two sentences from “The House of Wisdom” whose ideas are most essential to a summary of the article's central idea.

segments.text: At the center of this transformation stood the Bayt al-Hikma, or House of Wisdom, an institution that began as a royal library and gradually expanded into a hub for translation, research, and debate.

Although the institution itself was destroyed during the Mongol siege of 1258, the ideas it preserved and generated had already traveled to Cordoba, Cairo, and eventually Europe, influencing scientific thought for centuries.
The availability of paper, which had recently spread from Central Asia, made copying books faster and cheaper, allowing knowledge to circulate among scholars across the empire.
Scholars working there translated Greek, Persian, and Indian texts on mathematics, medicine, and astronomy into Arabic, often comparing several manuscripts to establish the most reliable version.

questions.why: What the institution was and why it mattered are the core of any summary.

questions.stem: For an objective summary of “The House of Wisdom,” classify each statement.

rows.text: The institution became a center of translation and research.

questions.stem: Which statement most accurately summarizes the author's position in “The Promise and Limits of Citizen Science”?

questions.stem: Select the sentence from “The Promise and Limits of Citizen Science” that best captures the essay's overall claim for a one-sentence summary.

questions.stem: Which TWO details best support the idea that teenagers' late bedtimes are not caused by laziness? Choose two.
options: Melatonin is released about two hours later during puberty.
Attendance improved in some districts with later start times.
A teen in bed at ten may lie awake for hours.
Specialists recommend eight to ten hours of sleep.
questions.why: Only the melatonin details explain why teens cannot fall asleep early.

questions.stem: Part A: According to the article, why do many teenagers have trouble falling asleep early?

partA.stem: Part A: According to the article, why do many teenagers have trouble falling asleep early?

options.label: A
options.text: They lack the discipline to go to bed on time each night.

options.label: B
options.text: Their brains release the sleep hormone later than before.

options.label: C
options.text: They sleep too much during the day at school.

options.label: D
options.text: Their schools give them too much homework at night.

partB.stem: Part B: Which sentence from the passage best supports the answer to Part A?

options.label: A
options.text: During puberty, the brain begins releasing melatonin, the hormone that signals sleepiness, roughly two hours later than it did in childhood.

options.label: B
options.text: Students who must wake at six o'clock frequently sleep fewer than seven hours, although specialists recommend between eight and ten.

options.label: C
options.text: In several districts that adopted this change, attendance improved and students reported feeling more alert during lessons.

options.label: D
options.text: Families can also help by limiting bright screens in the evening, since artificial light further delays the release of melatonin.

questions.why: The later release of melatonin, not laziness, explains why teens cannot fall asleep early.

questions.stem: Which statement best expresses the central idea of “The Paper Mills of Baghdad”?
options: The House of Wisdom translated Greek, Persian, and Indian works into Arabic.
Papermaking spread slowly from Samarkand to Baghdad and finally to Spain.
Paper was cheaper than parchment and lasted longer than papyrus in humid places.
Affordable paper made possible the spread of learning in Abbasid Baghdad.
questions.why: The other choices are true details, but only the first covers the whole article.

questions.stem: Select TWO sentences from “The Paper Mills of Baghdad” that together best express the central idea.

segments.text: When papermaking reached Baghdad in the late eighth century, it transformed the intellectual life of the Abbasid capital.
Historians sometimes describe paper as a humble technology, yet in Baghdad it functioned as the infrastructure upon which an entire culture of learning was constructed.
Paper, made from linen rags and plant fibers, was cheap and could be produced in huge amounts.
Book markets grew, and copyists could reproduce a lengthy manuscript within weeks rather than months.
The results were remarkable.

questions.why: The opening and closing sentences frame the article's claim; the others supply supporting details.

questions.stem: Part A: How does paragraph 2 develop the central idea of the article?

partA.stem: Part A: How does paragraph 2 develop the central idea of the article?

options.label: A
options.text: It compares the strengths of parchment and papyrus in detail.

options.label: B
options.text: It argues that translators were more important than papermakers.

options.label: C
options.text: It gives examples of how cheap paper changed government, trade, and scholarship.

options.label: D
options.text: It explains the steps used to make paper from linen rags.

partB.stem: Part B: Which sentence from the passage best supports the answer to Part A?

options.label: A
options.text: Before paper, scholars depended on parchment, which required the skins of numerous animals and was therefore expensive, or on papyrus, which was imported from Egypt and deteriorated in humid conditions.

options.label: B
options.text: Scholars at the House of Wisdom translated Greek, Persian, and Indian works into Arabic, and those translations circulated widely because paper made duplication affordable.

options.label: C
options.text: Historians sometimes describe paper as a humble technology, yet in Baghdad it functioned as the infrastructure upon which an entire culture of learning was constructed.

options.label: D
options.text: Paper, made from linen rags and plant fibers, was cheap and could be produced in huge amounts.

questions.why: This sentence ties a specific effect of paper directly to the spread of learning.

questions.stem: For “The Paper Mills of Baghdad,” decide whether each statement is the central idea, a supporting detail, or not stated.

rows.text: Paper became the foundation of Baghdad's culture of learning.
Ink on paper could not be altered without leaving traces.
The first paper mill in Baghdad opened around 794.
Paper replaced parchment in Europe before it reached Baghdad.

questions.why: A central idea covers the whole text; a detail supports it; some statements are not in the text at all.

questions.stem: What is the main purpose of the bracketed timeline in “The Paper Mills of Baghdad”?
options: to explain why government offices preferred paper for their official records
to show that the House of Wisdom closed when papermaking reached Spain
to show where Baghdad fits in the spread of papermaking
to prove that paper was invented in Baghdad before it reached any other city
questions.why: The timeline places Baghdad's mill within a larger movement of the technology.

questions.stem: Which statement best expresses the central idea of “The Neglected Art of Maintenance”?
options: Innovation is less important than maintenance and should receive less public funding.
Engineers who maintain infrastructure deserve public ceremonies like those for new buildings.
Because value depends on continued function, maintenance deserves more respect.
Cities should stop building desalination plants and focus only on repairing their old pipes.
questions.why: The author argues for valuing maintenance without rejecting innovation, as paragraph 3 makes clear.

questions.stem: Part A: What is the main function of paragraph 3 in developing the central idea?

partA.stem: Part A: What is the main function of paragraph 3 in developing the central idea?

options.label: A
options.text: It shifts the topic from infrastructure to the history of invention.

options.label: B
options.text: It qualifies the argument so it is not read as an attack on innovation.

options.label: C
options.text: It admits that the author's earlier claims were exaggerated.

options.label: D
options.text: It introduces new evidence about the cost of water systems.

partB.stem: Part B: Which sentence from the passage best supports the answer to Part A?

options.label: A
options.text: Societies tend to celebrate invention and neglect maintenance.

options.label: B
options.text: This imbalance is not merely a matter of recognition; it shapes budgets, careers, and ultimately the reliability of the infrastructure on which ordinary life depends.

options.label: C
options.text: None of this implies that innovation is unimportant.

options.label: D
options.text: Consider city water systems.

questions.why: The author anticipates a misreading and narrows the claim.

questions.stem: For “The Neglected Art of Maintenance,” classify each statement by its role in the argument.

rows.text: A technology's value depends on its continued functioning.
Many cities lose treated water through leaking pipes.
Innovation is not unimportant.
Repairing pipes rarely attracts political enthusiasm.

questions.why: The claim is the author's main point, evidence supports it, and the concession limits it.

questions.stem: Select TWO sentences from “The Neglected Art of Maintenance” that most fully state the author's central idea.

segments.text: This imbalance is not merely a matter of recognition; it shapes budgets, careers, and ultimately the reliability of the infrastructure on which ordinary life depends.
Rather, a technology's value depends on its continued functioning, and a culture that rewards only novelty will gradually inherit a landscape of magnificent, deteriorating machines.
Consider city water systems.

Ribbon-cutting ceremonies accompany the opening of every bridge, hospital, and water network, but no comparable ceremony honors the engineer who inspects corroded cables or the technician who replaces a failing pump before it disrupts an entire neighborhood.
Societies tend to celebrate invention and neglect maintenance.

questions.why: These sentences state why neglect matters and what follows from it; the opening sentence names the topic but not the full claim.

questions.stem: Why does the author include the example of the desalination plant in paragraph 2?
options: to prove that desalination is the most expensive way for any city to produce water
to argue that political leaders understand engineering better than the public does
to describe how coastal cities first began to remove salt from seawater
to show how attention to novelty can distort practical choices
questions.why: The example shows a visible new project winning out over a cheaper, invisible repair.

questions.stem: True or false: In “Rain in the Desert,” the sand turns dark brown when the rain falls.
questions.why: The story says the sand turned dark brown.

questions.stem: For “Rain in the Desert,” decide what each part helps you see, hear, or feel.

rows.text: Plink, plink, plink!
The rain was cold on their arms.
Tiny yellow flowers opened in the sun.

questions.why: Some words help us see, some help us hear, and some help us feel.

questions.stem: Select the sentence from “Rain in the Desert” that helps you hear the rain.

segments.text: Dark clouds came over the desert.
Plink, plink, plink!
The sand turned dark brown.
Reem smiled.

questions.why: Plink is a sound word.

questions.stem: Which picture best shows the end of “Rain in the Desert”?
options: green plants and yellow flowers on the sand
two children running out into the cold rain
dark gray clouds high over an empty desert
big drops of rain falling down onto the sand
questions.why: At the end, plants and flowers grow and the desert looks like a garden.

questions.stem: Put the pictures of “Rain in the Desert” in the order they happen.
sequence: Dark clouds cover the desert sky.
Rain drops fall on the sand.
Reem and her brother play in the rain.
Yellow flowers open in the sun.
questions.why: The story goes from clouds, to rain, to play, to flowers.

questions.stem: For “The Night Market,” decide which sense each detail mostly appeals to.

rows.text: lanterns of red, blue, and amber glass
the sharp scent of cardamom
each ring echoed off the walls
his white beard glowing in the lantern light

questions.why: Sensory words help the reader see, hear, and smell the market.

questions.stem: Select the sentence from “The Night Market” that best helps the reader picture how quiet the children are.

segments.text: Around him, a circle of children leaned forward so quietly that Khalid could hear the lanterns creak in the breeze.
When they reached the far corner, Khalid stopped.
On his right, a man tapped a copper pot with a small hammer, and each ring echoed off the walls.
As the sun sank behind the old city wall, the empty square slowly came alive.

questions.why: If you can hear lanterns creak, the crowd must be very silent.

questions.stem: The phrase “drifted up like tiny clouds of dust” helps the reader picture that the turmeric
options: is turning the night sky a bright orange color
is falling to the ground in heavy wet lumps
is a light powder that floats into the air
is being thrown into the air by the spice seller
questions.why: Comparing the powder to dust clouds shows it is fine and floats.

questions.stem: Match each phrase from “The Night Market” to what it helps the reader picture.

pairs.left: unrolled striped carpets across the stones
each ring echoed off the walls
pairs.right: a sound bouncing around the square

pairs.left: his white beard glowing in the lantern light
pairs.right: the storyteller lit up in the dark

pairs.left: the warm sweetness of fresh bread
pairs.right: a pleasant smell from a nearby stall

questions.why: Each detail builds one part of the picture in the reader's mind.

questions.stem: Part A: How does the mood of the scene change when Khalid reaches the far corner?

partA.stem: Part A: How does the mood of the scene change when Khalid reaches the far corner?

options.label: A
options.text: It changes from busy and noisy to calm and hushed.

options.label: B
options.text: It changes from crowded with children to empty of people.

options.label: C
options.text: It changes from quiet and sleepy to loud and dangerous.

options.label: D
options.text: It changes from dark and empty to bright and full of rain.

partB.stem: Part B: Which sentence from the passage best supports the answer to Part A?

options.label: A
options.text: As the sun sank behind the old city wall, the empty square slowly came alive.

options.label: B
options.text: Merchants unrolled striped carpets across the stones, and lanterns of red, blue, and amber glass swayed from wooden poles above their heads.

options.label: C
options.text: Around him, a circle of children leaned forward so quietly that Khalid could hear the lanterns creak in the breeze.

options.label: D
options.text: On his left, a spice seller scooped orange turmeric into paper cones, and the powder drifted up like tiny clouds of dust.

questions.why: The noise of the market gives way to the hush around the storyteller.

questions.stem: In “The Pearl Diver,” the simile “like a door of green glass” helps the reader picture
options: the green color of the oysters on the seabed
the water sealing the diver off from the world above
a wooden door on the deck of the old dhow
a window that the diver can see the gulls through
questions.why: A closing door shows the diver passing into a separate, silent world.

questions.stem: For “The Pearl Diver,” decide which sense each image mostly appeals to.

rows.text: a heavy, humming silence
ribbons of light that tremble and bend
a clip of turtle shell pinching his nose
his lungs begin to burn
silver fish that scatter

questions.why: Images can appeal to sight, sound, or touch.

questions.stem: Put the images of “The Pearl Diver” in the order they appear.
sequence: a stone tied to the diver's ankle
the surface closing over him
silver fish scattering like coins
sand rising in soft gray clouds
the blinding gold of morning
questions.why: The poem follows the diver down to the seabed and back up.

questions.stem: Which TWO images from “The Pearl Diver” help the reader picture light? Choose two.
options: the sand rising around his fingers in soft gray clouds
the blinding gold of morning
ribbons of light that tremble and bend
a heavy, humming silence
questions.why: Both images describe light, first underwater and then above the surface.

questions.stem: Part A: Which picture best matches the last stanza of “The Pearl Diver”?

partA.stem: Part A: Which picture best matches the last stanza of “The Pearl Diver”?

options.label: A
options.text: a tired but happy diver being pulled up into bright sunlight

options.label: B
options.text: a lonely diver searching the sand for lost oysters

options.label: C
options.text: a frightened diver sinking slowly toward the dark seabed

options.label: D
options.text: a calm diver resting quietly on the deck of the dhow

partB.stem: Part B: Which sentence from the passage best supports the answer to Part A?

options.label: A
options.text: On the seabed he moves slowly, the sand rising around his fingers in soft gray clouds, as he pries the rough oysters loose and drops them into the basket at his chest.

options.label: B
options.text: Down he sinks through ribbons of light that tremble and bend, past silver fish that scatter like coins tossed from a careless hand.

options.label: C
options.text: The surface closes over him like a door of green glass, and the noise of the gulls and the creaking ropes fades into a heavy, humming silence.

options.label: D
options.text: When his lungs begin to burn, he tugs the rope, and the men above haul him upward into the blinding gold of morning, gasping, dripping, and laughing at the sky.

questions.why: Gasping shows he is tired, laughing shows joy, and gold light shows the bright morning.

questions.stem: In “Fog on the Plateau,” the phrase “like a giant green staircase” helps the reader picture
options: a row of tall juniper trees standing on a hill
flat fields cut in steps down a steep slope
a narrow trail that the hikers climb all morning
a stone stairway built into the side of the cliff
questions.why: Terraced fields rise in level steps, much like stairs.

questions.stem: Put the descriptions of the fog in “Fog on the Plateau” in the order they appear, showing how it changes.
sequence: resting quietly in the valleys
thin, curling threads between the trees
a pale wall that swallows the trail
so thick the narrator can barely see her fingers
questions.why: The fog grows from a quiet presence into a blinding wall.

questions.stem: Select TWO sentences from “Fog on the Plateau” that best help the reader picture how thick the fog has become.

segments.text: I reached out and could barely see my own fingers.
The terraced fields we had admired all morning, stepping down the mountainside like a giant green staircase, had vanished entirely.
Hessa stopped so abruptly that I nearly collided with her overstuffed backpack.
By midafternoon, the fog that had been resting quietly in the valleys below the Asir plateau began to climb.
Hessa pulled the compass from her pocket, its needle trembling, and we continued cautiously forward, one deliberate step at a time.

questions.why: Losing sight of whole fields and even one's own fingers shows how dense the fog is.

questions.stem: For “Fog on the Plateau,” decide which sense each detail mostly appeals to.

rows.text: the steady drip of moisture from the branches
cold and damp against my face
a pale wall that swallowed the trail
the faint, bitter smell of wet stone

questions.why: The author uses several senses to put the reader inside the fog.

questions.stem: Part A: What feeling do the sensory details in the second paragraph most help the reader experience?

partA.stem: Part A: What feeling do the sensory details in the second paragraph most help the reader experience?

options.label: A
options.text: relief that the long, hot hike is finally over

options.label: B
options.text: a growing unease as the familiar world disappears

options.label: C
options.text: excitement at seeing the baboons up close

options.label: D
options.text: boredom at walking through the same fields again

partB.stem: Part B: Which sentence from the passage best supports the answer to Part A?

options.label: A
options.text: Even the baboons that had been barking from the cliffs had fallen silent, and the only sound was the steady drip of moisture from the branches above our heads.

options.label: B
options.text: The air was cold and damp against my face, and it carried the faint, bitter smell of wet stone.

options.label: C
options.text: By midafternoon, the fog that had been resting quietly in the valleys below the Asir plateau began to climb.

options.label: D
options.text: At first it moved in thin, curling threads that slipped between the juniper trees, but within minutes it had thickened into a pale wall that swallowed the trail ahead of us.

questions.why: The sudden silence of the animals makes the scene feel strange and uneasy.

questions.stem: In “The Glassblower,” the simile “like honey reluctant to fall” helps the reader picture the molten glass as
options: sweet-smelling and golden yellow
thick and slow-moving
thin and running quickly off the iron pipe
brittle and ready to break into pieces
questions.why: Honey that hesitates to drip is heavy and slow, like soft hot glass.

questions.stem: For “The Glassblower,” decide what each image mainly helps the reader picture.

rows.text: a fierce, trembling white that made the surrounding walls seem to waver
He turned the pipe constantly, almost lazily
a delicate vase stood cooling on the bench
a single patient breath

questions.why: Images in the scene build three pictures: the furnace, the craftsman, and the vase.

questions.stem: Part A: What does the detail about the glassblower's forearms help the reader picture?

partA.stem: Part A: What does the detail about the glassblower's forearms help the reader picture?

options.label: A
options.text: a man who has worked near fire for many years

options.label: B
options.text: a man who is new to the craft and still learning

options.label: C
options.text: a man who is careless and often injures himself

options.label: D
options.text: a man who is too weak to lift the iron pipe

partB.stem: Part B: Which sentence from the passage best supports the answer to Part A?

options.label: A
options.text: The bead swelled into a translucent bubble, faintly blue, through which I could see the distorted outline of the doorway behind him.

options.label: B
options.text: He turned the pipe constantly, almost lazily, and blew into its far end with a single patient breath.

options.label: C
options.text: The workshop was little more than a cave of heat.

options.label: D
options.text: Then, with a pair of blackened tongs, he pinched and pulled the softened glass, and within a minute a delicate vase stood cooling on the bench, still ticking softly as it released its heat.

questions.why: Many small scars and effortless, relaxed movements together suggest long experience.

questions.stem: Select the sentence from “The Glassblower” that best helps the reader see that the glass has become thin and clear.

segments.text: The bead swelled into a translucent bubble, faintly blue, through which I could see the distorted outline of the doorway behind him.
The workshop was little more than a cave of heat.
He turned the pipe constantly, almost lazily, and blew into its far end with a single patient breath.
Then, with a pair of blackened tongs, he pinched and pulled the softened glass, and within a minute a delicate vase stood cooling on the bench, still ticking softly as it released its heat.

questions.why: Seeing the doorway through the bubble shows the glass is now see-through.

questions.stem: Why does the author end the scene with the vase “still ticking softly as it released its heat”?
options: to show that the vase has a crack and will soon shatter
to explain that the glassblower is in a hurry to leave
to suggest that the workshop is full of clocks and machines
to let the reader hear the object cooling after the heat
questions.why: The quiet sound contrasts with the roaring furnace and shows the glass cooling.

questions.stem: In “Dawn in the Empty Quarter,” the phrase “an absence of stars along the horizon” helps the reader picture
options: dark dunes blocking the lower part of the sky
a traveler who cannot find the way by starlight
a cloudy night sky with no stars visible at all
the moment the sun first appears in the east
questions.why: The dunes are visible only as dark shapes where the stars stop.

questions.stem: For “Dawn in the Empty Quarter,” decide what each detail mainly helps the reader picture.

rows.text: a thin seam of copper
slides down each slope with the deliberateness of a tide
the eye cannot judge distance
a deep, bruised violet

questions.why: The author builds the scene through color, movement, and size.

questions.stem: Select TWO sentences from “Dawn in the Empty Quarter” that most help the reader picture the contrast between light and darkness on the dunes.

segments.text: The first crests to catch the light ignite like the edges of burning paper, while the hollows between them remain a deep, bruised violet.

As the sun rises, the boundary between light and shadow slides down each slope with the deliberateness of a tide, revealing ripples in the sand so regular that they resemble the grain of polished wood.
Nothing in the Empty Quarter prepares a traveler for the abruptness of its dawns.
The silence, which at night felt protective, becomes immense and slightly unnerving in daylight.
Without trees, buildings, or any object of familiar size, the eye cannot judge distance, and a dune that appears to be a short walk away may require the entire morning to reach.

questions.why: Both sentences set lit crests against shaded hollows and show the line between them moving.

questions.stem: Part A: What does the comparison “with the deliberateness of a tide” help the reader visualize?

partA.stem: Part A: What does the comparison “with the deliberateness of a tide” help the reader visualize?

options.label: A
options.text: water collecting in the hollows between dunes

options.label: B
options.text: shadows flickering quickly across the desert

options.label: C
options.text: sand blowing across the dunes in rolling waves

options.label: D
options.text: light moving down the dunes slowly and steadily

partB.stem: Part B: Which sentence from the passage best supports the answer to Part A?

options.label: A
options.text: The first crests to catch the light ignite like the edges of burning paper, while the hollows between them remain a deep, bruised violet.

options.label: B
options.text: As the sun rises, the boundary between light and shadow slides down each slope with the deliberateness of a tide, revealing ripples in the sand so regular that they resemble the grain of polished wood.

options.label: C
options.text: For hours the dunes lie under a darkness so complete that their enormous ridges can be sensed only as an absence of stars along the horizon; then, within minutes, a thin seam of copper appears in the east, and the desert assembles itself out of shadow.

options.text: Nothing in the Empty Quarter prepares a traveler for the abruptness of its dawns.

questions.stem: Which TWO details help the reader understand why the desert's size is hard to picture in daylight? Choose two.
options: A dune that seems close may take all morning to reach.
The ripples in the sand resemble the grain of polished wood.
The silence felt protective during the night.
There are no trees, buildings, or objects of familiar size.
questions.why: Without familiar objects for comparison, distances fool the eye.

questions.stem: Choose the word that best completes the sentence: First, ____ the two pictures to see how they are the same.
options: compare
forget
hide
questions.why: To compare is to look at how things are alike or different.

questions.stem: Match each school word (sort, describe, count) to its meaning.
questions.why: These words tell you what to do in class.

questions.stem: True or false: In the sentence “Predict what will happen next,” the word predict means to make a smart guess about what comes later.
questions.why: To predict is to guess what will happen using clues.

questions.stem: Does each sentence use the word “label” correctly?

rows.text: Label each part of the plant.
I label my lunch with a spoon.
The label on the jar says honey.

questions.why: A label is a name or tag that tells what something is.

questions.stem: Mona said, “The main idea of my book is that bees help plants grow.” What does main idea mean?
options: the name of the person who wrote it
the most important point
the longest sentence of all
the first word on the page
questions.why: The main idea is what something is mostly about.

questions.stem: Choose the word that best completes the sentence: The scientist recorded her ____ after watching the ants for three days.
options: invitations
decorations
celebrations
observations
questions.why: Observations are things you notice by watching closely.

questions.stem: Match each academic word (evidence, conclude, summarize, infer) to its meaning.

pairs.right: facts that show something is true
decide after thinking about the facts
tell the most important parts briefly
figure out using clues and what you know

questions.why: These words name the thinking you do when you read and study.

questions.stem: In the sentence “The class must identify three causes of erosion,” what does identify most likely mean?
options: count the number of
name or point out
argue against
draw a picture of
questions.why: To identify something is to name it or point it out.

questions.stem: Which TWO sentences use the word “analyze” correctly? Choose two.
options: We will analyze the data to find a pattern.
The baby analyzed loudly because she was hungry.
Ahmed analyzed the poem line by line to understand it.
Please analyze the door when you leave the room.
questions.why: To analyze is to study something closely, part by part.

questions.stem: Decide whether the academic word “structure” in each sentence means how something is built or how writing is organized.

rows.text: The bridge's steel structure can hold heavy trucks.
The essay's structure moves from problem to solution.
A bird's nest has a strong, woven structure.
The report's structure uses headings for each section.

questions.why: Structure can mean the way an object or a piece of writing is put together.

questions.stem: Which word best replaces “shows” to make this sentence more academic: “The graph shows that rainfall dropped by half”?
options: proves wrong
screams
guesses
indicates
questions.why: Indicates is a precise academic verb for what data shows.

questions.stem: Choose the word that best completes the sentence: Although the two desert plants look different, they share a ____ feature: both store water in thick leaves.
options: common
minor
random
rare
questions.why: A common feature is one that both things share.

questions.stem: Match each academic verb (justify, contrast, cite, evaluate) to the task it describes.

pairs.right: give reasons that support a choice
show how two things are different
name the source of a quotation or fact
judge how good or useful something is

questions.why: Task verbs in questions tell you exactly what kind of answer to give.

questions.stem: Which part of this sentence about an author's message uses an academic word incorrectly?
segments: but she never states it directly.
questions.why: Writers imply (suggest) ideas; readers infer (figure them out).

options.text: paints colorful pictures of

partB.stem: Part B: Which clue in the sentence best supports the answer to Part A?
