options.text: the word museum, which names a place

options.label: B

options.label: C

questions.stem: Choose the word that best completes the sentence: The new bus lane had a significant ____ on traffic; commute times fell by twenty minutes.
options: import
impact
interval
instinct
questions.why: An impact is a strong effect on something.

questions.stem: Which sentence uses the word “derive” correctly?
options: We derived loudly in the stands when our team scored.

The bus will derive at the main station at exactly noon.
questions.why: To derive from something is to come from it or be based on it.

questions.stem: Classify each word as a general academic word or a domain-specific (subject) word.

rows.text: analyze
photosynthesis
significant
hypotenuse
sequence

questions.why: General academic words appear in every subject; domain-specific words belong to one field.

questions.stem: Which THREE words could replace “important” in “Ibn Sina made an important contribution to medicine” without changing its meaning? Choose three.
options: trivial
significant
temporary
notable
major
similar
questions.why: Significant, major, and notable all mean having great value or effect.

questions.stem: Part A: What does “allocate” mean in the sentence “The school will allocate more funds to the science lab next year, leaving less for sports”?

partA.stem: Part A: What does “allocate” mean in the sentence “The school will allocate more funds to the science lab next year, leaving less for sports”?

options.label: A
options.text: to spend without any planning

options.label: B
options.text: to give out for a particular purpose

options.label: C
options.text: to collect from many sources

options.label: D
options.text: to save for an emergency

partB.stem: Part B: Which phrase in the sentence best helps a reader determine that meaning?

options.label: A
options.text: will

options.label: B
options.text: next year

options.label: C
options.text: The school will

options.label: D
options.text: more funds to the science lab

questions.why: Money is directed to a specific use, so allocate means to assign for a purpose.

questions.stem: Choose the word that best completes the sentence: The researchers were careful not to ____ their findings beyond the small group of villages they had actually studied.
options: generalize
illustrate
document
verify
questions.why: To generalize is to apply a finding more widely than the evidence allows.

questions.stem: In the sentence “Critics argued that the report’s conclusions were undermined by its reliance on a single, outdated survey,” what does undermined mean?
options: delayed
supported
weakened
summarized
questions.why: Relying on one outdated survey makes conclusions weaker.

questions.stem: Which part of this sentence about a city water study uses an academic word illogically?
questions.why: Ambiguous means open to more than one meaning, so readers would not all agree.

questions.stem: Match each academic transition (in contrast, as a consequence, to illustrate, in addition) to its function.
questions.why: Academic transitions show the logical link between ideas.

questions.stem: Which TWO sentences use “adverse” correctly? Choose two.
options: The team was adverse to changing its training schedule.
An adverse wind carried the sailboat quickly toward shore.
The drought had adverse effects on the date harvest.
Some patients reported adverse reactions to the new medicine.
questions.why: Adverse means harmful or working against; averse means unwilling.

questions.stem: Choose the word that best completes the sentence: The historian’s account is ____: it presents only evidence that flatters the expedition’s leader and omits the crew’s complaints.
options: tendentious
comprehensive
chronological
empirical
questions.why: Tendentious writing is slanted to promote one point of view.

questions.stem: In the sentence “The committee’s response was perfunctory, a two-line reply to a forty-page proposal,” what does perfunctory most nearly mean?
options: delayed and reluctant
precise and formal
hostile and dismissive
minimal and careless
questions.why: A two-line reply to forty pages shows little effort or care.

questions.stem: For each sentence, decide whether “qualify” means to limit or modify a claim or to meet a requirement.

rows.text: The author qualifies her praise by noting the study’s small sample.
Only students with a B average qualify for the program.
He qualified his argument with the phrase “in most cases.”
The runner qualified for the final by finishing second.

questions.why: In academic writing, to qualify a claim is to limit how far it reaches.

questions.stem: Part A: In the sentence “Although the theory was initially dismissed as speculative, subsequent observations substantiated it,” what does substantiated mean?

partA.stem: Part A: In the sentence “Although the theory was initially dismissed as speculative, subsequent observations substantiated it,” what does substantiated mean?

options.label: A
options.text: raised new doubts about

options.label: B
options.text: provided evidence that confirmed

options.label: C
options.text: described in greater detail

options.label: D
options.text: replaced with a simpler idea

partB.stem: Part B: Which phrase in the sentence provides the strongest contrast clue for that meaning?

options.label: A
options.text: dismissed as speculative

options.label: B
options.text: the theory was

options.label: C
options.text: observations

options.label: D
options.text: subsequent

questions.why: Although sets up a contrast: first doubted, later confirmed.

questions.stem: Which THREE revisions replace the informal phrase in “The data kind of backs up the claim” with precise academic language? Choose three.
options: The data tentatively corroborate the claim.
The data are kind of supportive of the claim.
The data partially support the claim.
The data offer limited support for the claim.
The data totally back the claim up.
The data sort of prove the claim.
questions.why: Academic writing replaces vague, casual hedges with precise qualifiers.

sets.skill: Action, Main, Helping and Linking Verbs

questions.stem: Choose the action verb that best completes the sentence: The frog ____ into the pond.
options: jumps
green
happy
questions.why: An action verb tells what someone or something does.

questions.stem: True or false: In the sentence “Sara kicks the ball,” the action verb is kicks.
questions.why: Kicks tells what Sara does.

questions.stem: Is each word from the sentence “The big dog runs fast” an action verb or not?

rows.text: runs
dog
big

questions.why: Runs is the only word that shows an action.

questions.stem: Which sentence has an action verb?
options: The sea is very big today.
The sea is blue.
Ali is my best friend.
Ali swims in the sea.
questions.why: Swims shows something Ali does.

questions.stem: Which word is the helping verb in the sentence “We are painting a picture”?
options: painting
are
picture
We
questions.why: Are helps the main verb painting.

questions.stem: Choose the helping verb that best completes the sentence: By next week, the students ____ finished their science projects.
options: has
will have
was
is
questions.why: Will have helps show an action finished by a future time.

questions.stem: Decide whether the verb in capital letters in each sentence about soup and a camel is an action verb or a linking verb.

rows.text: The soup TASTES salty.
Omar TASTES the soup carefully.
The camel LOOKS tired.
The camel LOOKS for water.

questions.why: A linking verb connects the subject to a word that describes it.

questions.stem: Which TWO sentences contain a helping verb? Choose two.
options: The hawk was circling above the dunes.
Mariam speaks three languages well.
The hawk circled above the dunes.
Mariam can speak three languages.
questions.why: Was and can help the main verbs circling and speak.

questions.stem: Match each sentence about the kitten to the kind of verb shown in capital letters.
questions.why: Is before sleeping helps the main verb; seems links the kitten to sleepy.

questions.stem: Find the error in the verb phrase of this sentence about a soccer team.
questions.why: A singular subject like team takes the helping verb has.

questions.stem: In the sentence “The museum guide had already explained the history of the astrolabe,” what is the main verb?
options: explained
guide
had
already
questions.why: Explained is the main verb; had is the helping verb.

questions.stem: Decide whether “grew” is used as an action verb or a linking verb in each sentence.

rows.text: The farmer grew dates and figs.
The sky grew dark before the storm.
The audience grew restless during the delay.
My brother grew three centimeters this year.

questions.why: Grew is linking when it means became.

questions.stem: Choose the verb phrase that correctly completes the sentence: The ancient library ____ by fire, but many scrolls were saved.
options: has damage
damaging
was damaged
were damaged
questions.why: Was is the helping verb that agrees with library and pairs with damaged.

questions.stem: Which THREE words in the sentence “The engineers should have been testing the bridge more carefully” are helping verbs? Choose three.
options: should
have
bridge
testing
carefully
been
questions.why: Should, have, and been all help the main verb testing.

questions.stem: Part A: In the sentence “The old map appeared accurate, but it was missing two islands,” how is appeared used?

partA.stem: Part A: In the sentence “The old map appeared accurate, but it was missing two islands,” how is appeared used?

options.label: A
options.text: as a helping verb

options.label: B
options.text: as an action verb

options.label: C
options.text: as a linking verb

options.label: D
options.text: as a noun

partB.stem: Part B: Which test supports the answer to Part A?

options.label: A
options.text: Appeared names a person, place, or thing.

options.label: B
options.text: Appeared shows something the map physically did.

options.label: C
options.text: Appeared can be replaced with seemed and still make sense.

options.label: D
options.text: Appeared comes before another verb in a verb phrase.

questions.why: If seem or is can replace the verb, it is linking.

questions.stem: Choose the word that correctly completes the sentence: The lemon juice smelled ____ after sitting in the sun.
options: sours
sourness
sour
sourly
questions.why: A linking verb is followed by an adjective, not an adverb.

questions.stem: Which part of this sentence about a desert hike contains an error after a linking verb?
questions.why: Felt is a linking verb here, so it takes the adjective bad.

questions.stem: Which sentence uses “remained” as a linking verb?
options: Only crumbs remained on the plate.
The guests remained in the courtyard.
Two students remained after class to help.
The weather remained calm all morning.
questions.why: Calm describes the weather, so remained links them.

questions.stem: Match each sentence about the robotics club to the role of the word “has.”

pairs.left: The club has built five robots.
pairs.right: helping verb forming a perfect tense

pairs.left: The club has to finish by Friday.
pairs.right: part of a phrase meaning must

questions.why: The same word can be a main verb or a helping verb.

questions.stem: Classify the verb in capital letters in each sentence about Ibn al-Haytham.

rows.text: Ibn al-Haytham STUDIED how light travels.
His ideas BECAME the basis of modern optics.
He WAS writing his Book of Optics in Cairo.
His experiments SEEM simple today.

questions.why: Was before writing is helping; became and seem are linking.

questions.stem: Choose the option that correctly completes the sentence with a linking verb and its complement: After weeks of training, the young falcon ____.
options: grew with confident
grew confident
grew confidently
confidently grew
questions.why: Grew means became here, so it takes the adjective confident.

questions.stem: Which TWO sentences contain a verb that functions as a linking verb? Choose two.
options: The alarm sounded at exactly six o'clock.
The visitors stayed in the courtyard until dusk.
The proposal sounded reasonable to the council.
The courtyard stayed cool despite the heat.
questions.why: Sounded and stayed link when followed by an adjective describing the subject.

questions.stem: Which part of this sentence about a research team contains an error in the verb phrase?
questions.why: An if-clause about the past uses had, not would have.

questions.stem: In “Neither the captain nor the sailors could have predicted the sudden storm,” which choice correctly identifies the verb phrase?
options: have predicted: a linking verb and a main verb
could have: a main verb and a linking verb
could have predicted: two helping verbs and a main verb
predicted the sudden storm: an action verb and its object
questions.why: Could and have help the main verb predicted.

questions.stem: True or false: In the sentence “The solution proved effective,” proved functions as a linking verb because effective describes the subject.
questions.why: Proved means turned out to be, linking solution to effective.

questions.stem: Decide how “turned” functions in each sentence about the autumn harvest.

rows.text: The leaves turned golden in late October.
The farmer turned the soil before planting.
The conversation turned serious when prices came up.
The cart turned sharply at the gate.

questions.why: Turned is linking when it means became.

questions.stem: Choose the verb form that correctly completes the sentence: Had the engineers ____ the warning, the dam might not have failed.
options: been heeded
heeded
heeding
heed
questions.why: After the helping verb had, the main verb takes the past participle.

questions.stem: Part A: In the sentence “The explanation she offered appeared plausible but proved, on closer inspection, deeply flawed,” what is the function of proved?

partA.stem: Part A: In the sentence “The explanation she offered appeared plausible but proved, on closer inspection, deeply flawed,” what is the function of proved?

options.label: A
options.text: an action verb showing what the subject did to an object

options.label: B
options.text: a linking verb connecting the subject to a description

options.label: C
options.text: a main verb showing an action in the past

options.label: D
options.text: a helping verb forming a verb phrase with flawed

partB.stem: Part B: Which reason best supports the answer to Part A?

options.label: A
options.text: On closer inspection names the action the subject performs.

options.label: B
options.text: Proved is followed by a direct object that receives the action.

options.label: C
options.text: Proved combines with appeared to form a single verb phrase.

options.label: D
options.text: Deeply flawed describes the explanation rather than receiving an action.

questions.why: Proved links the explanation to the description deeply flawed.

questions.stem: Which part of this sentence about the mountain expedition contains a verb error?
questions.why: An action finished before another past action needs the helping verb had.

questions.stem: Which THREE sentences contain a verb that functions as a linking verb? Choose three.
options: The negotiators grew weary as talks dragged on.
The proposal remained on the table for months.
The proposal, though ambitious, remained feasible.
The witness proved her claim with documents.
The old manuscript proved authentic after testing.
The farmers grew drought-resistant wheat.
questions.why: A linking verb is followed by a word that describes the subject, not an object or a place.

questions.stem: True or false: In the sentence “The cat ate the fish,” the cat is the one doing the action.
questions.why: The cat did the eating.

questions.stem: In the sentence “The cake was made by Mom,” who made the cake?
options: Mom
the oven
the baker
the cake
questions.why: The word by tells who did the action.

questions.stem: In each sentence about Ali and Huda, where is the doer of the action?

rows.text: Ali threw the ball.
The ball was thrown by Ali.
The kite was flown by Huda.
Huda flew the kite.

questions.why: Sometimes the doer comes first; sometimes it comes after by.

questions.stem: Choose the word that completes the sentence: The window was broken ____ the wind.
options: at
by
on
questions.why: By tells who or what did the action.

questions.stem: Match each sentence about the garden to the sentence that means the same thing.

pairs.right: The plants were watered by Sami.
The roses were picked by Mona.
The grass was cut by Dad.

questions.why: Both sentences tell the same thing in a different order.

questions.stem: Choose the verb that correctly completes the passive sentence: The packages ____ by the mail carrier every morning.
options: are delivered
delivers
is delivering
delivered
questions.why: A passive verb uses a form of be plus a past participle.

questions.stem: Decide whether each sentence about the school fair is active or passive.

rows.text: The students painted the posters.
The posters were painted by the students.
The tickets were sold at the door.
Our teacher hung the banner.

questions.why: In passive voice, the subject receives the action.

questions.stem: Which sentence is written in the active voice?
options: The kitten was rescued by firefighters.
The kitten was carried down the ladder.
The kitten was rescued yesterday.
The firefighters rescued the kitten.
questions.why: In active voice, the doer (firefighters) is the subject.

questions.stem: Which TWO sentences are in the passive voice? Choose two.
options: The fish were caught by the fishermen at dawn.
The bridge was built in 1990.
The fishermen caught fish at dawn.
The workers built the bridge in 1990.
questions.why: Was built and were caught are passive verbs.

questions.stem: Which part of this passive sentence about the science fair has an error?
questions.why: The plural subject projects needs were.

questions.stem: Which sentence correctly changes “The storm damaged several boats” to the passive voice?
options: Several boats are damaging by the storm.
The storm was damaged by several boats.
Several boats damaged the storm.
Several boats were damaged by the storm.
questions.why: The object boats becomes the subject, and the verb becomes were damaged.

questions.stem: Choose the verb phrase that correctly completes the sentence in the passive voice: The new desalination plant ____ next year.
options: will open by
will be opening
opens
will be opened
questions.why: Future passive is will be plus a past participle.

questions.stem: Put the steps for changing “The chef prepared the meal” into the passive voice in order.
sequence: Find the object of the verb: the meal.
Move the object to the subject position.
Add a form of be with the past participle: was prepared.
Add “by” and the original doer: by the chef.
questions.why: The object moves up, the verb changes, and the doer moves after by.

questions.stem: Part A: Why might a writer choose the passive sentence “The ancient coins were discovered in 1952” instead of an active one?

partA.stem: Part A: Why might a writer choose the passive sentence “The ancient coins were discovered in 1952” instead of an active one?

options.label: A
options.text: Active voice cannot be used with past events.

options.label: B
options.text: The person who found the coins is unknown or unimportant.

options.label: C
options.text: The writer wants to show who found the coins.

options.label: D
options.text: Passive sentences are always shorter than active ones.

partB.stem: Part B: Which feature of the sentence supports the answer to Part A?

options.label: A
options.text: It uses the past tense verb were.

options.label: B
options.text: It includes a specific year.

options.label: C
options.text: It does not name who discovered the coins.

options.label: D
options.text: It begins with an article, The.

questions.why: Passive voice is useful when the doer is unknown or less important.

questions.stem: Classify each sentence about the robotics team as active or passive.

rows.text: The robot was programmed by two students.
Two students programmed the robot.
The trophy has been awarded to our team.
Our team is building a new robot.

questions.why: Is building is active; the team does the building.

questions.stem: Choose the verb phrase that correctly completes the passive sentence: The results of the survey ____ before the meeting starts.
options: will posting
will have posted
will have been posted
have been posting
questions.why: Future perfect passive is will have been plus a past participle.

questions.stem: Which THREE sentences are in the passive voice? Choose three.
options: The tower had stood for two hundred years.
Mistakes were made during the count.
The workers are repairing the trail this week.
The old tower had been restored before the festival.
The festival was exciting for everyone.
The trail is being repaired this week.
questions.why: Passive needs be plus a past participle with the subject receiving the action.

questions.stem: Which part of this sentence about the stadium renovation contains a passive-voice error?
questions.why: Passive voice needs the past participle renovated.

questions.stem: Which revision changes “The decision was made by the committee after a long debate” to the active voice?
options: The decision had been made by the committee after debate.
The committee made the decision after a long debate.
The decision was made after a long debate.
After a long debate, the decision was made by the committee.
questions.why: In active voice, the doer (the committee) becomes the subject.

questions.stem: True or false: The sentence “The museum was quiet in the morning” is in the passive voice because it contains the verb was.
questions.why: Quiet is an adjective, not a past participle, so the sentence is not passive.

questions.stem: Decide whether each sentence about the oil spill cleanup uses the active or passive voice.

rows.text: Volunteers had cleaned most of the beach by noon.
Most of the beach had been cleaned by noon.
The birds were being washed with mild soap.
Experts warned that recovery would take years.

questions.why: Had been cleaned and were being washed are passive forms.

questions.stem: Revise “It was decided by the council that the market would close early” into the active voice: ____ that the market would close early.
options: Deciding by the council
It was decided
The council was decided
The council decided
questions.why: Active voice puts the doer, the council, as the subject.

questions.stem: Part A: A news report states, “Mistakes were made in the handling of the budget.” What is the most likely effect of the passive voice here?

partA.stem: Part A: A news report states, “Mistakes were made in the handling of the budget.” What is the most likely effect of the passive voice here?

options.label: A
options.text: It emphasizes the officials who made the mistakes.

options.label: B
options.text: It makes the mistakes sound more serious than they were.

options.label: C
options.text: It shows that the mistakes happened very recently.

options.label: D
options.text: It avoids naming who is responsible for the mistakes.

partB.stem: Part B: Which feature of the sentence best supports the answer to Part A?

options.label: A
options.text: The sentence uses the plural noun mistakes.

options.label: B
options.text: No doer appears after the verb phrase were made.

options.label: C
options.text: The sentence includes the phrase of the budget.

options.label: D
options.text: The verb were is in the past tense.

questions.why: Leaving out the doer can hide responsibility.

questions.stem: Which part of this sentence about the stolen manuscript contains an error in the passive construction?
questions.why: Passive perfect uses had been plus the past participle stolen.

questions.stem: Which sentence uses the passive voice most appropriately?
options: My homework was finished by me before dinner.
A great time was had by all of us at the party.
The ball was kicked by me into the goal.
Rice was first grown in Asia long ago.
questions.why: Passive voice fits when the doer is unknown; the others hide an obvious doer awkwardly.

questions.stem: Which TWO sentences use the passive voice effectively to keep the focus on the most important subject? Choose two.
options: A decision was reached by me to study engineering.
The cake was eaten by my brothers before I could taste it.
After the earthquake, the hospital was evacuated within twenty minutes.
The rare manuscript was rediscovered in a library basement in 1998.
questions.why: Passive voice works when the receiver of the action matters more than the doer.

questions.stem: Choose the verb phrase that best completes the sentence: Had the warning signs ____ sooner, the bridge could have been closed before the collapse.
options: be recognized
recognized
being recognized
been recognized
questions.why: The signs receive the action, so the past perfect passive had been recognized is needed.

questions.stem: Which part of this sentence about the city transit plan contains an error in the passive construction?
questions.why: Progressive passive uses being plus a past participle.

questions.stem: Part A: A writer revises “Researchers have observed that the glacier is retreating” to “It has been observed that the glacier is retreating.” What is the main effect of this revision?

partA.stem: Part A: A writer revises “Researchers have observed that the glacier is retreating” to “It has been observed that the glacier is retreating.” What is the main effect of this revision?

options.label: A
options.text: It shifts attention away from the researchers toward the observation itself.

options.label: B
options.text: It strengthens the claim by adding a new source of evidence.

options.label: C
options.text: It changes the claim from a past event to a future one.

options.label: D
options.text: It makes the claim more precise by naming the observers.

partB.stem: Part B: Which change in the revision best supports the answer to Part A?

options.label: A
options.text: The verb observed is replaced with a stronger verb.

options.label: B
options.text: The doer of the action is removed and replaced with It.

options.label: C
options.text: The present perfect tense is changed to the future tense.

options.label: D
options.text: The clause that the glacier is retreating is shortened.

questions.why: An impersonal passive removes the doer and spotlights the finding.

questions.stem: For each sentence about the ancient frankincense route, decide whether the verb is active, passive, or a linking verb with an adjective.

rows.text: Caravans carried frankincense across the desert.
Frankincense was carried across the desert by caravans.
The route was dangerous in summer.
The route had been abandoned by the tenth century.
Merchants were eager to find safer paths.

questions.why: Be plus a past participle is passive; be plus an adjective is linking.

sets.skill: Adjectives, Articles and Order of Adjectives

questions.stem: Choose the word that completes the sentence: I saw ____ owl in the tree.
options: a
many
an
questions.why: Use an before a word that starts with a vowel sound.

questions.stem: True or false: In the sentence “The tall boy ran,” the word tall is an adjective.
questions.why: Tall describes the boy.

questions.stem: Is each word from “The little brown hen laid an egg” an adjective or not?

rows.text: little
brown
hen
laid

questions.why: Adjectives describe nouns, like little and brown.

questions.stem: Which sentence uses a or an correctly?
options: We ate a apple.
We saw an big cat.
We ate an apple.
We saw an dog.
questions.why: Apple starts with a vowel sound, so we use an.

questions.stem: Which sentence puts the describing words in the right order?
options: I have two small dogs.
I have dogs two small.
I have two dogs small.
I have small two dogs.
questions.why: Number words come first, then size, then the noun.

questions.stem: Choose the adjective that best completes the sentence: The desert at noon is ____, so hikers carry plenty of water.
options: gentle
freezing
scorching
soggy
questions.why: Scorching means very hot.

questions.stem: Which THREE words are adjectives in the sentence “The curious students examined an ancient clay pot”? Choose three.
options: clay
curious
students
examined
pot
ancient
questions.why: Curious, ancient, and clay all describe nouns.

questions.stem: Find the error in this sentence about a museum visit.
questions.why: Ancient begins with a vowel sound, so it takes an.

questions.stem: Put the adjectives red, big, and beautiful in the correct order to describe a kite.
sequence: beautiful
big
red
questions.why: Opinion comes before size, and size comes before color.

questions.stem: Decide whether each word in capital letters in these sentences about stone and summer is used as an adjective or a noun.

rows.text: We sat on the STONE wall.
He threw a STONE into the lake.
The SUMMER days are long.
SUMMER is my favorite season.

questions.why: A noun can act as an adjective when it describes another noun.

questions.stem: Choose the phrase that correctly orders the adjectives: Grandfather gave me ____ for my birthday.
options: a lovely wooden old box
a wooden old lovely box
a lovely old wooden box
an old lovely wooden box
questions.why: Order: opinion, age, material.

questions.stem: Which sentence uses articles correctly?
options: She waited an hour for a bus to arrives.
She waited an hour for the bus.
She waited a hour for an bus to arrive.
She waited the hour for an bus arriving.
questions.why: Hour starts with a vowel sound (silent h), so it takes an.

questions.stem: Match each adjective type to its example in the phrase “three tiny round Japanese tea cups.”
questions.why: Adjectives follow the order quantity, size, shape, origin, purpose.

questions.stem: Which part of this sentence about a shopping trip contains an adjective-order error?
questions.why: Color comes before material.

questions.stem: Which TWO sentences use comparative or superlative adjectives correctly? Choose two.
options: This puzzle is more harder than the last one.
Of the two kites, Sara's is the most colorful.
Mount Everest is higher than K2.
The cheetah is the fastest land animal.
questions.why: Do not use more with -er, and compare two things with more, not most.

questions.stem: For each sentence about the new observatory, decide whether a or an is used correctly.

rows.text: An university in Riyadh built the observatory.
The astronomers used a unique telescope.
It took them an hour to adjust the lens.
They recorded a honest account of their results.

questions.why: Choose a or an by the first sound, not the first letter.

questions.stem: Choose the phrase that correctly completes the sentence: The craftsman carved ____ for the palace door.
options: an elegant large rectangular cedar panel
a large elegant cedar rectangular panel
a cedar large elegant rectangular panel
an rectangular elegant large cedar panel
questions.why: Order: opinion, size, shape, material.

questions.stem: Which part of this sentence about a camping trip contains an error with adjectives?
questions.why: A noun is described by an adjective (quiet), not an adverb.

questions.stem: Which sentence correctly uses commas between adjectives?
options: It was a long difficult, climb.
It was a long, difficult climb.
It was, a bright red sports car.
It was a bright, red, sports car.
questions.why: Use a comma between coordinate adjectives, never before the noun.

questions.stem: True or false: In the phrase “a happy, energetic puppy,” a comma belongs between the adjectives because their order could be reversed.
questions.why: Coordinate adjectives can switch places and take a comma.

questions.stem: Which TWO phrases need a comma between the adjectives? Choose two.
options: a cold windy morning
three small boats
a thoughtful patient teacher
a bright red kite
questions.why: Coordinate adjectives can be reversed or joined with and.

questions.stem: Choose the word that correctly completes the sentence: There were ____ errors in the second draft than in the first.
options: lesser
fewer
less
littler
questions.why: Use fewer with things you can count.

questions.stem: Which part of this sentence about the falconry exhibition contains an error?
questions.why: Unique begins with a y sound, so it takes a.

questions.stem: Which sentence places all the adjectives in the correct order?
options: She wore a beautiful long white cotton dress.
She wore a long beautiful cotton white dress.
She wore a cotton beautiful long white dress.
She wore a white long beautiful cotton dress.
questions.why: Order: opinion, size, color, material.

questions.stem: Decide whether each sentence about the school trip uses an -ed or -ing adjective correctly.

rows.text: The students were bored by the long lecture.
The tour of the ruins was very interested.
The tired divers rested on the boat.
Everyone felt exciting about the launch.

options.text: It tells where students keep their reading books.

questions.why: Support should show why the opinion is a good idea.

questions.stem: Faisal is writing an opinion paragraph about why his town needs a new library. Select the sentence that does NOT belong in his paragraph.

segments.text: Our town needs a new library.
The old library is too small for all the people who visit.
A bigger library could have a room for homework help.
My favorite food is grilled fish with rice.
A new library would make our town a better place to learn.

questions.why: Every sentence in an opinion paragraph should support the opinion.

questions.stem: Which sentence is an arguable claim that could guide an argumentative essay?
options: Schools should replace vending machines with healthy snack stations.
Many schools have vending machines placed near their crowded cafeterias.
Some vending machines accept coins, and others accept cards.
A vending machine is a device that sells snacks and cold drinks to students.
questions.why: A claim takes a position that reasonable people could disagree with.

questions.stem: A student claims, “Schools should install water refill stations.” Which two pieces of evidence are most relevant and credible? Choose two.
options: Refill stations come in several colors, such as blue and silver.
A school district found that refill stations cut plastic bottle waste by forty percent in one year.
My cousin says the water at his school tastes strange.
A city health office reported that students drank more water after refill stations were added.
questions.why: Relevant, credible evidence comes from reliable sources and directly supports the claim.

questions.stem: Rana is writing about why her school should start a robotics club. Select the sentence in her paragraph that acknowledges a counterclaim.

segments.text: A robotics club would help students practice problem-solving.
Some parents worry that the club would take time away from homework.
However, meetings would be held only once a week for one hour.
Members would also learn to work as a team.

questions.why: A counterclaim presents an opposing view that the writer then answers.

questions.stem: Choose the transition that best introduces the writer's response: Some people argue that video games waste time. ____, studies show that certain puzzle games improve problem-solving skills.
options: However
Therefore
Similarly
For instance
questions.why: However signals a contrast between the counterclaim and the writer's response.

questions.stem: Sort each sentence from an essay about school start times as a claim, a counterclaim, or evidence.

rows.text: Middle schools should begin classes at 8:30 instead of 7:30.
Critics say a later start would make sports practice end after dark.
One study found that students who started later were absent less often.
Others argue that families would struggle to adjust their morning schedules.

questions.why: A claim states the position, a counterclaim opposes it, and evidence supports it with facts.

questions.stem: Choose the word that keeps a formal style: The survey data ____ that teens who sleep nine hours earn higher test scores.
options: totally prove
kinda show
sort of say
suggest
questions.why: Argumentative writing uses precise, formal language.

questions.stem: Match each part of an argument about city parks to its example.

pairs.right: Our city should build more neighborhood parks.
A 2023 study found that residents near parks exercised more often.
Some council members say parks cost too much to maintain.
Yet volunteer groups could reduce maintenance costs significantly.

questions.why: Each part of an argument plays a different role in persuading readers.

questions.stem: Part A: A student writes, “Everyone in my class loves the new cafeteria menu, so every student in the country must love it.” What is the main weakness in this reasoning?

partA.stem: Part A: A student writes, “Everyone in my class loves the new cafeteria menu, so every student in the country must love it.” What is the main weakness in this reasoning?

options.label: A
options.text: It describes the cafeteria menu in too much detail.

options.label: B
options.text: It presents a counterclaim without a rebuttal.

options.label: C
options.text: It draws a broad conclusion from a very small group.

options.label: D
options.text: It uses formal language that is hard to read.

partB.stem: Part B: Which revision best fixes the weakness identified in Part A?

options.label: A
options.text: Everyone in my class truly loves the new menu, so all students everywhere must love it.

options.label: B
options.text: Most students in my class enjoy the new menu, which suggests it may be popular at our school.

options.label: C
options.text: The new cafeteria menu has rice dishes, salads, and fresh fruit every day.

options.label: D
options.text: Students in every country deserve a cafeteria menu that they will love.

questions.why: Strong reasoning matches the size of the conclusion to the size of the evidence.

questions.stem: Yusuf is arguing that his school should add solar panels. Select the sentence that rebuts an opposing view.

segments.text: Our school should install solar panels on the gym roof.
Solar panels could provide much of the electricity the gym uses.
Some people think solar panels are too expensive to install.
However, the panels would pay for themselves through lower bills within eight years.

questions.why: A rebuttal answers a counterclaim with reasons or evidence.

questions.stem: Put the sentences of Huda's argument about planting trees along city streets in the most logical order.
sequence: Our city should plant trees along every main street.
Trees can lower street temperatures by several degrees in summer.
Cooler streets mean people can walk to shops instead of driving.
Some residents worry that tree roots will crack sidewalks.
However, planting deep-rooted species in wide beds prevents most damage.
questions.why: A strong paragraph moves from claim to evidence and explanation, then addresses and rebuts a counterclaim.

questions.stem: A writer argues that the city should replace diesel buses with electric buses. Which sentence most effectively rebuts the counterclaim that electric buses cost too much to buy?
options: Many cities around the world have already purchased electric buses in recent years.
Although they cost more at first, electric buses save enough on fuel and repairs to cover the difference within a decade.
Diesel buses produce exhaust that can make the air harder to breathe on hot days.
Electric buses are much quieter than diesel buses, which riders and shop owners in busy, crowded neighborhoods would appreciate.
questions.why: An effective rebuttal answers the specific concern, which here is cost.

questions.stem: Identify the reasoning flaw in each statement from a debate about technology in schools.

rows.text: Two students cheated using tablets, so tablets make all students dishonest.
Test scores rose after the school bought new chairs, so the chairs raised the scores.
Either we ban phones completely or students will never learn anything.
The day the new Wi-Fi was installed, attendance dropped, so the Wi-Fi caused the absences.

questions.why: Recognizing faulty reasoning helps writers build and test stronger arguments.

questions.stem: A draft claim reads, “Technology is bad for teenagers.” Which two revisions turn it into a precise, defensible claim? Choose two.
options: Teenagers who use screens for more than three hours after 9 p.m. tend to sleep less, so families should set nightly screen limits.
Schools should teach teenagers to evaluate online sources because unreliable websites spread false health information.
Some teenagers use technology, and some teenagers do not use it very much.
Technology is very, very bad for all teenagers in every possible way.
questions.why: A defensible claim is specific, limited in scope, and supported by a reason.

questions.stem: Find and correct the error in this sentence from an argument about a desalination plant.
segments: uses less energy than the old one,
however the city should approve it
questions.why: A sentence that begins with because should not also use however; the two transitions contradict each other.

questions.stem: Part A: A writer claims that a school should adopt a four-day week and supports it only with the sentence “Students I talked to said they would like it.” What is the best way to strengthen this support?

partA.stem: Part A: A writer claims that a school should adopt a four-day week and supports it only with the sentence “Students I talked to said they would like it.” What is the best way to strengthen this support?

options.label: A
options.text: Repeat the claim in stronger, more emotional words.

options.label: B
options.text: Add the names of the students the writer asked.

options.label: C
options.text: Add data from schools that have tried a four-day week.

options.label: D
options.text: Remove the support so the claim stands alone.

partB.stem: Part B: Why would the change in Part A strengthen the argument?

options.label: A
options.text: It shortens the paragraph so readers finish quickly.

options.label: B
options.text: It replaces personal preference with evidence of actual results.

options.label: C
options.text: It makes the claim sound more urgent and exciting.

options.label: D
options.text: It shows the writer personally knows many students.

questions.why: Evidence about outcomes is more convincing than what people say they would like.

questions.stem: Choose the word that creates an appropriately qualified claim: Remote instruction ____ improve outcomes for students in isolated villages, provided that reliable internet access is in place.
options: can
could never
will always
must certainly
questions.why: A qualified claim avoids overstatement and admits conditions.

questions.stem: Classify the main rhetorical appeal in each sentence from an argument for protecting coastal mangroves.

rows.text: Mangroves can store up to four times more carbon per hectare than many inland forests.
As a marine biologist who has surveyed the Red Sea coast for twenty years, I have watched these forests shrink.
Imagine a child returning to a beach where the herons no longer nest.
Where mangroves were cleared, storm damage to nearby homes doubled within a decade.

questions.why: Logos appeals to logic, ethos to credibility, and pathos to emotion.

questions.stem: Dana is drafting an editorial in favor of restoring coastal mangroves. Select the sentence that most weakens her credibility with skeptical readers.

segments.text: Mangroves shelter young fish that later support local fishing fleets.
A regional survey found that restored sites recovered within seven years.
Anyone who opposes this plan clearly does not care about the future.
Restoration costs would be shared by the fisheries and the tourism board.

questions.why: Attacking opponents' motives instead of their reasons is an ad hominem that damages a writer's credibility.

questions.stem: Part A: An argument states, “The city should extend library hours because more students will use the library in the evening.” What unstated assumption does this argument rely on?

partA.stem: Part A: An argument states, “The city should extend library hours because more students will use the library in the evening.” What unstated assumption does this argument rely on?

options.label: A
options.text: Library staff would prefer to work in the evening.

options.label: B
options.text: The library has enough books for every student.

options.label: C
options.text: Students currently cannot visit during the hours the library is open.

options.label: D
options.text: Evening is the best time of day to study.

partB.stem: Part B: Which finding would most seriously weaken the argument in Part A?

options.label: A
options.text: Other cities have libraries that close earlier in the day.

options.label: B
options.text: A survey shows most students already visit after school and leave before closing time.

options.label: C
options.text: The library recently added new computers and study tables.

options.label: D
options.text: Many students say they enjoy reading in quiet places.

questions.why: An argument is only as strong as its hidden assumptions; evidence against an assumption weakens the conclusion.

questions.stem: A writer argues that the national museum should offer free admission and must answer readers who worry about lost revenue. Which two strategies would address those readers most effectively? Choose two.
options: Concede that revenue may fall at first, then explain how longer visits raise shop and café sales.
Cite museums that replaced ticket income with donations and grants after going free.
Restate the claim more forcefully at the end of each paragraph.
Point out that people who worry about money do not truly value culture.
questions.why: Effective arguments respect opposing concerns and answer them with evidence or reasoned concessions.

questions.stem: Which sentence uses capital letters correctly?
options: My friend Ali lives in Riyadh.
My friend ali lives in riyadh.
My Friend Ali Lives in Riyadh.
my friend Ali lives in Riyadh.
questions.why: Begin a sentence with a capital, and capitalize names of people and places.

questions.stem: Choose the word that is written correctly: We went to the zoo on ____.
options: mONDAY
monday
Monday
questions.why: Days of the week begin with a capital letter.

questions.stem: Find the mistake in the sentence about playing in the park on the weekend.
questions.why: Saturday is the name of a day, so it needs a capital letter.

questions.stem: Does each word need a capital letter in a sentence?

rows.text: jeddah
apple
sara
school

columns.text: Does not need a capital letter

questions.why: Names of people and places need capital letters.

questions.stem: Read: “my sister and i visited egypt.” Which three words need capital letters? Choose three.
options: i
and
sister
egypt
visited
my
questions.why: Capitalize the first word, the word I, and the name of a place.

questions.stem: Find and correct the capitalization error in the sentence about Huda Saleh's book.
questions.why: Capitalize the first word and important words in a book title.

questions.stem: Choose the correct words to complete the sentence: My family visited ____ during the spring holiday.
options: the red sea coast
The Red sea Coast
the Red Sea coast
questions.why: Red Sea is a proper noun; coast is a common noun here.

questions.stem: Which sentence is capitalized correctly?
options: yesterday Mom and i went to the market.
Yesterday Mom and I went to the market.
Yesterday my Mom and I went to the market.
Yesterday mom and I went to the Market.
questions.why: Mom is capitalized when used as a name, but not after my.

questions.stem: Should the word in capital letters be capitalized in each phrase?

rows.text: MARS in “a trip to MARS”
RIVER in “a long, muddy RIVER”
NILE in “the NILE River”
PLANET in “a small PLANET”

questions.why: Proper nouns name specific things; common nouns do not.

questions.stem: True or false: In the sentence “We drove north to visit Uncle Fahad,” the word north should be capitalized.
questions.why: Directions are lowercase when they tell which way someone moves.

questions.stem: Choose the correct capitalization: The ____ is the longest river in Africa.
options: Nile river
nile river
Nile River
questions.why: When river is part of a specific name, both words are capitalized.

questions.stem: Find and correct the capitalization error in the sentence about a cousin's summer classes.
questions.why: School subjects are lowercase unless they are languages or course titles.

questions.stem: Which two sentences are capitalized correctly? Choose two.
options: We visited the Masmak Fortress in the spring.
We visited the Masmak fortress in the Spring.
My Grandfather was born in the eastern province.
My grandfather was born in the Eastern Province.
questions.why: Capitalize full names of places and regions; seasons and common nouns stay lowercase.

questions.stem: Decide whether each sentence about a doctor's visit uses titles correctly.

rows.text: Doctor Amal Hassan gave the talk.
The Doctor gave a talk about healthy eating.
We thanked Dr. Hassan after class.
My uncle is a Doctor at the hospital.

questions.why: A title is capitalized only when it comes before a name.

questions.stem: Which sentence correctly capitalizes a quotation?
options: Coach Salem said, “practice starts at six.”
coach Salem said, “Practice starts at six.”
Coach Salem said, “Practice starts at six.”
Coach salem said, “Practice Starts at six.”
questions.why: Capitalize the first word of a full quoted sentence and a title used with a name.

questions.stem: Find and correct the capitalization error in the sentence about how people worked and traveled.
questions.why: Names of historical periods and events are capitalized.

questions.stem: Choose the correct capitalization: Many families in the ____ travel to the mountains of Abha in summer.
options: Middle East
middle east
Middle east
questions.why: The names of world regions are proper nouns.

questions.stem: Read: “during ramadan, my aunt reads arabic poetry from the abbasid era.” Besides the first word, which three words need capital letters? Choose three.
options: ramadan
abbasid
aunt
arabic
era
poetry
questions.why: Names of months, languages, and historical dynasties are capitalized.

questions.stem: Should the word in capital letters be capitalized in each sentence about a road trip?

rows.text: SUMMER in “We left in early SUMMER.”
ARABIC in “We sang ARABIC songs.”
SOUTH in “Turn SOUTH at the gas station.”
SOUTHEAST ASIA in “Next year we will visit SOUTHEAST ASIA.”

questions.why: Seasons and directions are lowercase; languages and named regions are capitalized.

questions.stem: True or false: In the title “The Journey of Ibn Battuta Across the World,” the word “of” should be capitalized.
questions.why: Short prepositions such as of are lowercase in titles unless they are the first or last word.

questions.stem: Choose the correct capitalization: The ____ approved a new plan for protecting coral reefs.
options: United nations
united nations
United Nations
questions.why: Every main word in the name of an organization is capitalized.

questions.stem: Find and correct the capitalization error in the sentence about Reem's report on trade routes.
questions.why: General school subjects are not capitalized unless they name a language or a specific course.

questions.stem: Which two sentences about family stories and a museum trip are capitalized correctly? Choose two.
options: Our class visited the science museum in the spring.
Our class visited the Science Museum in the Spring.
Last night, my Grandfather told us about pearl diving.
Last night, Grandfather told us about pearl diving.
questions.why: Family words are capitalized only when used as names; seasons and generic places stay lowercase.

questions.stem: Decide whether each sentence about a university schedule is capitalized correctly.

rows.text: She is taking Physics II this term.
He hopes to study Engineering in college.
We studied the history of the Abbasid Caliphate.
The Fall semester begins in September.

questions.why: Specific course titles and historical names are capitalized; general fields and seasons are not.

questions.stem: Which sentence correctly capitalizes an interrupted quotation?
options: “When the tide rises,” said the captain, “We will leave the harbor.”
“when the tide rises,” said the captain, “we will leave the harbor.”
“When the tide rises,” said the Captain, “We will leave the harbor.”
“When the tide rises,” said the captain, “we will leave the harbor.”
questions.why: The second part of a single interrupted sentence continues in lowercase.

questions.stem: Choose the correctly capitalized title: The scholar Ibn Sina wrote ____, a medical encyclopedia used for centuries.
options: The canon of medicine
The Canon of Medicine
the Canon Of Medicine
questions.why: In title case, capitalize the first word and major words but not short prepositions.

questions.stem: Find and correct the capitalization error in the sentence about the treaty delegates.
segments: the delegates from the European union
questions.correction: the delegates from the European Union
questions.why: Every main word in the official name of a political organization is capitalized.

questions.stem: Select the sentence about the desert research trip that is capitalized correctly.

segments.text: The team crossed the empty quarter in the Winter of 2021.
Professor Nasser led the team across the Empty Quarter.
The Professor said the Dunes were higher than in previous years.
They reported to the ministry of environment, water and agriculture.

questions.why: A title before a name and the name of a specific desert are capitalized; seasons and common nouns are not.

questions.stem: Should the word in capital letters be capitalized in each sentence?

rows.text: GOVERNOR in “The GOVERNOR of the province opened the bridge.”
GOVERNOR in “Yesterday GOVERNOR Hamad opened the bridge.”
BRONZE in “Tools from the BRONZE Age were found.”
WESTERN in “Rain fell across WESTERN parts of the country.”

questions.why: Titles are capitalized before names; descriptive directions stay lowercase; named eras are capitalized.

questions.stem: True or false: In the sentence “Last night I read ‘How Falcons See the World’ in a magazine,” the title is capitalized correctly.
questions.why: In title case, major words are capitalized and a short article like the stays lowercase.

questions.stem: Choose the word that best completes the sentence: I wore my coat ____ it was cold.
options: or
because
but
questions.why: Because tells why something happened.

questions.stem: Which group of words is a complete sentence?
options: The bird in the tall tree.
When the bird built a nest.
The bird built a nest.
Because the big nest.
questions.why: A complete sentence tells who and what happened, and it makes sense alone.

questions.stem: Match each sentence beginning about a rainy school day to the ending that makes the most sense.

pairs.right: so I would not get wet.

questions.why: Joining words like because, when, and so connect ideas.

questions.stem: True or false: “When the bell rang” is a complete sentence.
questions.why: It does not tell what happened when the bell rang.

questions.stem: Is each group of words about a picnic a complete sentence?

rows.text: We ate lunch under a tree.
After we ate lunch.
Because the sun was hot.
Dad brought cold juice.

questions.why: A complete sentence makes sense by itself.

questions.stem: Choose the word that best completes the sentence: ____ the sun set, the camels rested near the tents.
options: After
But
And
So
questions.why: After begins a clause that tells when something happened.

questions.stem: Which two sentences are complex sentences? Choose two.
options: The road near our school was flooded.
The bus was late, and we waited outside.
We read a book while we waited for the bus.
Because the road was flooded, the bus came late.
questions.why: A complex sentence has one independent clause and at least one dependent clause.

questions.stem: Select the part of the sentence about the falcon that is a dependent clause.

segments.text: The falcon
dove quickly toward the ground
because it saw a small lizard.

questions.why: A dependent clause has a subject and verb but cannot stand alone.

questions.stem: Find and correct the error in the sentence about Faris and the race.
questions.why: Do not use but after a because clause; the two ideas are cause and effect.

questions.stem: Is each clause from the sentences about a science fair independent or dependent?

rows.text: we built a model volcano
when the judges arrived
since our project was ready
Maha explained the results

questions.why: An independent clause can stand alone; a dependent clause begins with a word like when or since.

questions.stem: Which sentence is a complex sentence?
options: The museum closed early; the guards locked the doors.
The museum near the old market closed early today.
The museum closed early, and the visitors went home.
The museum closed early because a storm was coming.
questions.why: A complex sentence joins an independent clause and a dependent clause.

questions.stem: Classify each sentence about a camping trip as simple, compound, or complex.

rows.text: We set up our tent beside the dunes.
The wind grew strong, so we moved the tent.
Although the night was cold, we slept well.
After we ate dinner, my brother told jokes.

questions.why: Compound sentences join independent clauses; complex sentences include a dependent clause.

questions.stem: Choose the pronoun that correctly begins the clause: The scientist ____ discovered the new species of lizard spoke at our school.
options: whose
who
whom
which
questions.why: Who is the subject of the clause and refers to a person.

questions.stem: Find and correct the punctuation error in the sentence about the museum that opened last year.
questions.why: A nonrestrictive clause beginning with which is set off by commas on both sides.

questions.stem: Which two sentences contain an adverb clause? Choose two.
options: The coach said that the match would be canceled.
The players rested whenever the coach blew the whistle.
If the rain continues, the match will be canceled.
The player who scored the goal is my neighbor.
questions.why: An adverb clause tells when, why, how, or under what condition.

questions.stem: Choose the word that correctly completes the sentence: The well, ____ water was once shared by the whole village, has been restored.
options: whose
which
who's
that
questions.why: Whose shows possession; the water belongs to the well.

questions.stem: Identify the type of the clause in quotation marks in each sentence.

rows.text: The book “that I borrowed” is overdue.
“Before the library closed,” I returned it.
The librarian asked “why I was late.”
We visited the town “where my father grew up.”

questions.why: Adjective clauses describe nouns, adverb clauses modify verbs, and noun clauses act as nouns.

questions.stem: Which choice uses a dependent clause to show that one event caused another?
options: The dam was repaired; the farms also received water again.
The dam was repaired before the farms received water again.
The dam was repaired, and the farms received water again.
Since the dam was repaired, the farms received water again.
questions.why: Since can introduce a clause that explains a cause.

questions.stem: Find and correct the error in the sentence about the engineer and the water pump.
questions.why: Whom is used when the pronoun is the object of the verb in the clause.

questions.stem: Part A: In the sentence “We will support whatever the team decides,” what is the function of the clause “whatever the team decides”?

partA.stem: Part A: In the sentence “We will support whatever the team decides,” what is the function of the clause “whatever the team decides”?

options.label: A
options.text: It describes the noun team.

options.label: B
options.text: It acts as the subject of the sentence.

options.label: C
options.text: It tells when we will support someone.

options.label: D
options.text: It acts as the direct object of the verb.

partB.stem: Part B: Which sentence contains a clause with the same function as the clause in Part A?

options.label: A
options.text: The judges announced who had won the prize.

options.label: B
options.text: The student who won the prize thanked her teacher.

options.label: C
options.text: When the prize was announced, the crowd cheered.

options.label: D
options.text: The prize went to the team that built the robot.

questions.why: A noun clause can serve as the direct object, receiving the action of the verb.

questions.stem: Which two sentences are punctuated correctly? Choose two.
options: My oldest brother, who lives in Dammam, is an engineer.
Students who finish early may read quietly.
My oldest brother who lives in Dammam, is an engineer.
Students, who finish early, may read quietly.
questions.why: Commas set off nonrestrictive clauses but not restrictive ones.

questions.stem: Is the clause in each sentence about the expedition restrictive or nonrestrictive?

rows.text: The guide who knew the desert best led the way.
Our guide, who had crossed the desert twelve times, led the way.
The map that showed the old wells was lost.
The oasis at Al-Ula, which we reached at noon, was cool and green.

questions.why: A restrictive clause identifies which one; a nonrestrictive clause adds extra information.

questions.stem: Select the compound-complex sentence about the coral reef survey.

segments.text: The divers counted fish along the reef.
The divers counted fish, and the scientists recorded the water temperature.
When the divers returned, the scientists compared the data, and the results surprised everyone.
Although the water was cloudy, the divers finished the survey.

questions.why: A compound-complex sentence has two independent clauses and at least one dependent clause.

questions.stem: Choose the word that correctly begins the noun clause: Few visitors realized ____ the fortress had been built without a single iron nail.
options: whose
which
what
that
questions.why: That introduces a noun clause that states a fact.

questions.stem: Which revision correctly fixes the fragment “Although the divers had mapped most of the wreck and photographed its cargo.”?
options: The divers, although they had mapped most of the wreck and its cargo.
Although the divers had mapped most of the wreck and photographed its cargo too.
Although mapped most of the wreck, and photographed its cargo, the divers.
Although the divers had mapped most of the wreck, they never found its bell.
questions.why: A dependent clause must be attached to an independent clause to form a complete sentence.

questions.stem: Part A: Which revision best combines “The expedition reached the oasis at dusk. The expedition had lost two camels in a sandstorm.” so that reaching the oasis is the main idea?

partA.stem: Part A: Which revision best combines “The expedition reached the oasis at dusk. The expedition had lost two camels in a sandstorm.” so that reaching the oasis is the main idea?

options.label: A
options.text: The expedition, which reached the oasis at dusk, had lost two camels in a sandstorm.

options.label: B
options.text: Because the expedition reached the oasis at dusk, it had lost two camels in a sandstorm.

options.label: C
options.text: Although it had lost two camels in a sandstorm, the expedition reached the oasis at dusk.

options.label: D
options.text: The expedition reached the oasis at dusk, and it had lost two camels in a sandstorm.

partB.stem: Part B: Why is the revision in Part A the most effective?

options.label: A
options.text: It gives both ideas equal weight by joining them with a conjunction.

options.label: B
options.text: It makes the loss of the camels the central idea of the sentence.

options.label: C
options.text: It explains that losing the camels caused the arrival.

options.label: D
options.text: It places the less important idea in a dependent clause and shows contrast.

questions.why: The main idea belongs in the independent clause; subordinate ideas belong in dependent clauses.

questions.stem: Find and correct the pronoun error in the sentence about presenting the committee's findings.
questions.why: The pronoun is the subject of asks within its clause, so whoever is correct even after a preposition.

questions.stem: Identify the type of the clause in quotation marks in each sentence about Al-Biruni.

rows.text: “That Al-Biruni measured the Earth's radius so accurately” still amazes scientists.
He worked in an era “when few instruments existed.”
“Wherever he traveled,” he recorded local customs and languages.
Historians debate “how he calculated the height of the mountain.”

questions.why: Clause type depends on function: a noun clause names, an adjective clause modifies a noun, an adverb clause modifies a verb or sentence.

questions.stem: Which sentence uses subordination to express concession most precisely?
options: The bridge was rated safe, and engineers closed it for a second inspection.
Even though the bridge was rated safe, engineers closed it for a second inspection.
Because the bridge was rated safe, engineers closed it for a second inspection.
The bridge was rated safe, so engineers closed it for a second inspection.
questions.why: Even though signals a concession: the second idea happens despite the first.

questions.stem: In which two sentences does the dependent clause function as a noun? Choose two.
options: Whether the satellite survives reentry depends on its heat shield.
The engineers could not explain why the signal had faded.
Because the heat shield cracked, the satellite burned up.
The satellite, which was launched in 2019, sent its final signal.
questions.why: A noun clause can serve as a subject or object, unlike adjective and adverb clauses.

questions.stem: Your group is talking about a class pet. Mona is speaking. What should you do?
options: Listen and wait for your turn.
Walk away and sit by yourself.
Look out the window and play.
Talk at the same time as Mona.
questions.why: Good group members listen and take turns.

questions.stem: Is each action a good way to act in a group talk about the class library?

rows.text: Looking at the person who is talking
Shouting so others cannot speak
Saying “I agree with Ali”
Playing with toys while others talk

questions.why: Good group members look, listen, and share kindly.

questions.stem: Sami says, “I like fish best.” Choose a kind way to answer: “____”
options: That is a silly idea.
Why do you like fish?
Stop talking now.
questions.why: Asking a question shows you are listening and want to learn more.

questions.stem: True or false: In a group talk about the class garden, it is good to ask a question when you do not understand.
questions.why: Asking questions helps everyone understand.

questions.stem: Which two things does a good group member do in a talk about a class trip? Choose two.
options: Takes turns speaking
Laughs at other ideas
Talks the whole time
Stays on the topic
questions.why: Good speakers take turns and talk about the topic.

questions.stem: Hessa says the class should collect cans for recycling. Choose the response that best builds on her idea: Omar says, “____”
options: Cans are boring, so I do not care.
I already said that we should not recycle.
I agree, and we could also collect plastic bottles.
Let's talk about the football match instead.
questions.why: Building on an idea means adding something connected to it.

questions.stem: Match each role in a group discussion about a class project to its job.

pairs.right: keeps the group focused on the task
makes sure the group finishes on time
shares the group's ideas with the class

questions.why: Each role helps the group work well together.

questions.stem: Put the steps for a group discussion about a book the class read in the best order.
sequence: Read the book and mark important parts before meeting.
Take turns sharing ideas about the book.
Ask questions about each other's ideas.
Sum up what the group agreed on.
questions.why: Preparing first and summing up last helps a discussion succeed.

questions.stem: A group is discussing how to keep the school library quiet. Is each comment on topic or off topic?

rows.text: We could put signs that say “Quiet, please.”
My new shoes are very comfortable.
Students could use the study room for group work.
I watched a great movie last weekend.

questions.why: On-topic comments help the group answer its question.

questions.stem: Which question best asks a group member to explain an idea more clearly?
options: Do you want to be the group leader today?
Why are you always talking in our group?
Can you give an example of what you mean?
Can we please change the topic right now?
questions.why: Asking for an example helps a speaker explain more.

questions.stem: Khalid says, “We should test plants with different amounts of light.” Which two responses paraphrase his point before adding a new idea? Choose two.
options: So you think light amount is the key variable; we could also measure how tall each plant grows.
I think we should test plants, too, since everyone likes plants.
You're saying we should change only the light; maybe we should keep the water the same for every plant.
Light is fine, but I really want to build a volcano model for the fair.
questions.why: Paraphrasing shows you understood the speaker before you add your own idea.

questions.stem: Select the comment in the group discussion about a water-saving campaign that shows a student changing her view after hearing new information.

segments.text: Rania: I think posters are the best way to reach students.
Fahad: A survey last year showed most students ignore posters in the halls.
Rania: That's a good point, so maybe short announcements would work better than posters.
Salma: We could ask the art club to help us.

questions.why: Good discussers revise their views when they hear new evidence.

questions.stem: Rashid starts talking about his weekend during a discussion about the science fair. Choose the leader's most respectful response: “____”
options: Rashid, you always get off topic, and it is annoying.
Never mind, Rashid, we will ignore that comment.
Let's just stop the discussion because we are wasting time.
That sounds fun, Rashid. How could it connect to choosing our experiment?
questions.why: Redirecting politely keeps the discussion focused and respectful.

questions.stem: Is each comment in a discussion about adding a school garden supported by evidence or not?

rows.text: A study found that school gardens help students eat more vegetables.
Gardens are just better than anything else.
Our principal said the empty lot behind the gym gets six hours of sun.
Everyone will love the garden, I'm sure.

questions.why: Supporting comments with evidence makes a discussion more useful.

questions.stem: Which group rule would best help a class discussion reach decisions fairly?
options: The loudest member decides what the group will do.
Members vote right away before anyone speaks.
Each member shares a view before the group votes.
Only the members who agree may share their views.
questions.why: Hearing every voice before deciding makes decisions fair.

questions.stem: Two classmates have shared different ideas for the class trip. Choose the question that best connects their ideas: “____”
options: Can we hear from someone who has not spoken yet about lunch?
Could the museum visit and the beach cleanup happen on the same day?
Why don't we just pick whatever the teacher wants us to do?
Which of you has the better idea, and why is the other one wrong?
questions.why: Questions that connect ideas help the group find common ground.

questions.stem: Match each discussion move in a conversation about school recycling to an example.

pairs.right: When you say “cut waste,” do you mean paper, plastic, or both?
So your main point is that bins should be closer to classrooms.
I see your point, but what evidence shows students will use the bins?
So far we agree on more bins and a weekly reminder.

questions.why: Different discussion moves serve different purposes.

questions.stem: Part A: In a discussion about a new school schedule, Lama says, “That idea is wrong, and nobody should listen to it.” What is the main problem with her comment?

partA.stem: Part A: In a discussion about a new school schedule, Lama says, “That idea is wrong, and nobody should listen to it.” What is the main problem with her comment?

options.label: A
options.text: It summarizes the discussion too early.

options.label: B
options.text: It agrees too quickly with the speaker.

options.label: C
options.text: It asks too many questions at once.

options.label: D
options.text: It dismisses an idea without giving a reason.

partB.stem: Part B: Which revision best improves Lama's comment?

options.label: A
options.text: I don't like that idea, so let's move on to the next one.

options.label: B
options.text: I disagree because a later start would make the bus schedule harder for families.

options.label: C
options.text: That idea is wrong, and I think everyone here knows it.

options.label: D
options.text: Maybe that idea is fine, but I still think it is wrong.

questions.why: Disagreeing respectfully means giving reasons, not dismissing others.

questions.stem: Put the steps a group should take to settle a disagreement about its project topic in the best order.
sequence: Have each member explain the reasons for their choice.
Identify where the ideas agree and differ.
Weigh the evidence for each option.
Agree on a decision and record it.
questions.why: Understanding views and evidence before deciding leads to fair decisions.

questions.stem: Which two comments qualify a speaker's view after hearing new evidence? Choose two.
options: Given the survey results, I think the uniform rule could work for younger grades.
I still support longer recess, but maybe only on days without tests.
I was right from the start, so the new evidence doesn't matter.
I agree with everything everyone has said so far today.
questions.why: Qualifying a view means adjusting it to fit new evidence while keeping what is still valid.

questions.stem: In a discussion about banning single-use plastics, Ziad says, “The ban will hurt small shops.” Which response best moves the discussion forward by probing his reasoning?
options: Let's move on, since we have already talked about the shops a lot.
I don't think that matters much compared to protecting the oceans.
Which costs do you expect the shops to face, and could any support offset them?
That's true; small shops always struggle when the rules change suddenly.
questions.why: Probing questions ask a speaker to explain and test their reasoning.

questions.stem: Decide whether each comment in a seminar on renewable energy moves the discussion forward or shuts it down.

rows.text: How does your point about cost connect to Maryam's point about jobs?
We've heard enough about wind power; it's obviously useless.
Can someone offer evidence that challenges what we've said so far?
There's no reason to discuss this further because the answer is clear.

questions.why: Questions that connect and challenge ideas keep a discussion productive.

questions.stem: Select the comment in the seminar on reducing food waste that best synthesizes the group's ideas.

segments.text: Noor: Cafeterias throw away a lot of uneaten bread.
Tariq: Smaller portions could reduce what students leave behind.
Huda: Leftovers could go to local food banks instead of the trash.
Ali: So we have two strategies, serving less and donating more, and both target uneaten food.

questions.why: Synthesizing combines several speakers' points into one connected idea.

questions.stem: True or false: In a group project on reducing food waste, roles and deadlines should be decided only by the most confident member.
questions.why: Effective groups set roles and deadlines together so everyone is responsible.

questions.stem: Part A: During a debate on homework limits, a student keeps repeating her opinion without responding to classmates. Which norm is she failing to follow?

partA.stem: Part A: During a debate on homework limits, a student keeps repeating her opinion without responding to classmates. Which norm is she failing to follow?

options.label: A
options.text: speaking loudly enough for everyone to hear

options.label: B
options.text: responding to others' points with relevant evidence

options.label: C
options.text: preparing notes before the discussion begins

options.label: D
options.text: allowing the moderator to keep track of time

partB.stem: Part B: Which comment would best show that she now follows that norm?

options.label: A
options.text: As I already said three times, homework should be limited.

options.label: B
options.text: Can we vote now, since I've explained my opinion clearly?

options.label: C
options.text: I just think homework limits are the most important issue we face.

options.label: D
options.text: Omar's data on sleep is useful, but it doesn't address students with after-school jobs.

questions.why: Strong discussers respond directly to others' points with evidence.

questions.stem: Part A: In a seminar on city planning, two classmates make claims that seem to contradict each other: one says new roads reduce traffic, and the other says new roads increase traffic. What is the best next move?

partA.stem: Part A: In a seminar on city planning, two classmates make claims that seem to contradict each other: one says new roads reduce traffic, and the other says new roads increase traffic. What is the best next move?

options.label: A
options.text: Ask both speakers what evidence and time frame their claims are based on.

options.label: B
options.text: Ask the class to vote on which speaker is right.

options.label: C
options.text: Move on to a different topic so the conflict does not grow.

options.label: D
options.text: Agree with the speaker who sounds more confident.

partB.stem: Part B: Why is the move in Part A most effective?

options.label: A
options.text: It may reveal that both claims are true under different conditions.

options.label: B
options.text: It rewards the speaker who presented the idea first.

options.label: C
options.text: It ensures the most popular opinion becomes the group's view.

options.label: D
options.text: It prevents the discussion from becoming uncomfortable.

questions.why: Examining evidence can resolve apparent contradictions instead of forcing a winner.

questions.stem: A discussion on regulating artificial intelligence has included only students who favor strict rules. Which two moves would best broaden the range of perspectives? Choose two.
options: Repeat the strongest argument for strict rules so everyone remembers it.
Summarize the agreement so far and close the discussion early.
Present a credible argument for lighter rules and ask the group to respond.
Ask a quieter member who has not spoken to share any reservations.
questions.why: Seeking out quieter voices and opposing arguments makes a discussion more complete.

questions.stem: A group member states a conclusion that the evidence does not fully support. Choose the response that best identifies the gap: “____”
