options: The data show a link in two cities, but do we know whether it holds elsewhere?
Let's not worry about evidence and just finish the report on time.
That conclusion is completely wrong, and I strongly disagree with it.
Great point; I think we can include that conclusion in our report.
questions.why: Pointing out what the evidence does not show strengthens the group's reasoning.

questions.stem: Decide whether each comment in a seminar on water conservation helps resolve a disagreement or deepens it.

rows.text: We both want lower usage; we differ only on whether fines or rewards work better.
Your side never cares about families' budgets.
Could we test both approaches in two neighborhoods and compare results?
There's no point arguing with someone who ignores the facts.

questions.why: Finding shared goals and proposing tests helps resolve disagreements.

questions.stem: Match each comment from a seminar on desert agriculture to the discussion skill it shows.

pairs.right: Taken together, Huda's point on drip irrigation and Sami's on crop choice suggest a combined strategy.
We have cost data, but nothing on how long these systems last.
Reem, you grew up on a farm; how would farmers respond to this?
Let's each find one study before Thursday and compare them.

questions.why: Advanced discussers use specific moves to deepen and advance a conversation.

questions.stem: Join the sentences “I have a cat. I have a dog.” Choose the word: I have a cat ____ a dog.
options: but
or
and
questions.why: And joins two things that go together.

questions.stem: Which sentence best joins “The sun is hot. The sun is bright.”?
options: The sun is hot and bright.
The sun is hot or the sun is.
The sun hot is and bright.
The sun is hot, the sun bright.
questions.why: When two sentences tell about the same thing, join the describing words with and.

questions.stem: Match each pair of short sentences about animals to the sentence that joins them.

pairs.left: The cat is small. The cat is soft.
pairs.right: The cat is small and soft.

pairs.left: Sara has a bird. Sara has a fish.
pairs.right: Sara has a bird and a fish.

pairs.left: I ran fast. I did not win.
pairs.right: I ran fast, but I did not win.

questions.why: Joining sentences makes writing smoother.

questions.stem: True or false: “Ali likes apples, and Ali likes grapes” is the best way to join “Ali likes apples. Ali likes grapes.”
questions.why: The best way is “Ali likes apples and grapes.”

questions.stem: Choose the word that best joins each pair of sentences about the weekend.

rows.text: We went to the park. We played ball.
I wanted to swim. The pool was closed.
Mom made rice. Dad made soup.
It was sunny. It was cold.

questions.why: Use and for ideas that go together; use but for ideas that are different.

questions.stem: Combine “Noor likes science. Reem likes science.” Choose the words: ____ like science.
options: Noor and Reem
Noor, Reem
Noor or Reem
questions.why: Two subjects doing the same action can be joined with and.

questions.stem: Which two sentences correctly combine “The storm was strong. We stayed home.”? Choose two.
options: The storm was strong but we stayed home.
The storm was strong, so we stayed home.
The storm was strong, we stayed home.
Because the storm was strong, we stayed home.
questions.why: Use so or because to show cause and effect, with the right comma.

questions.stem: Find and correct the error in the sentence about the camel crossing the sand.
questions.why: Two complete thoughts need a joining word, not just a comma.

questions.stem: Which joining word best combines each pair of sentences about the school play rehearsal?

rows.text: Maha forgot her lines. She kept going.
The stage lights broke. We practiced in the hall.
We can practice today. We can practice tomorrow.
Fahad was nervous. He spoke clearly.

questions.why: But shows contrast, so shows a result, and or shows a choice.

questions.stem: Which sentence best combines “The turtle swam to the shore. The turtle laid her eggs in the sand.”?
options: The turtle swam to the shore, the turtle laid her eggs.
The turtle swam, and to the shore she laid her eggs in sand.
Swimming to the shore, the eggs were laid in the sand.
The turtle swam to the shore and laid her eggs in the sand.
questions.why: When the subject is the same, join the two actions with and.

questions.stem: Which sentence best combines “Ibn Battuta was a traveler from Morocco. He visited more than forty countries.”?
options: Ibn Battuta, a traveler from Morocco, visited over forty countries.
Ibn Battuta was a traveler, and Morocco, he visited forty countries.
A traveler from Morocco, over forty countries visited Ibn Battuta.
Ibn Battuta was a traveler from Morocco he visited forty countries.
questions.why: An appositive phrase can rename a noun and combine two sentences smoothly.

questions.stem: Choose the word that best combines the ideas: ____ the desert is dry, many plants survive there by storing water.
options: Although
Because
Since
Unless
questions.why: Although shows a contrast between the two ideas.

questions.stem: Which two sentences correctly combine “The team trained hard. The team lost the final match.”? Choose two.
options: The team trained hard, yet it lost the final match.
Although the team trained hard, it lost the final match.
The team trained hard, so it lost the final match.
Because the team trained hard, it lost the final match.
questions.why: Yet and although show contrast; so and because wrongly suggest cause.

questions.stem: Is each sentence about Ibn al-Haytham's work correctly combined or a run-on/comma splice?

rows.text: Ibn al-Haytham studied light, and he wrote about how eyes see.
He tested his ideas, he used careful experiments.
Because he tested ideas carefully, he is called an early scientist.
His book was translated into Latin it influenced later scholars.

questions.why: Clauses must be joined with a conjunction or correct punctuation.

questions.stem: Find and correct the error in the sentence about Ibn al-Haytham's famous book.
questions.why: A comma alone cannot join two independent clauses.

questions.stem: Choose the phrase that best combines the sentences “The diver checked her equipment. She jumped into the sea.”: ____ the diver jumped into the sea.
options: She checked her equipment,
Her equipment checked and
Having checked her equipment,
Checked her equipment,
questions.why: A participial phrase can combine sentences when it describes the subject.

questions.stem: Part A: Which sentence best combines “The bridge was built in 1920. The bridge is made of stone. The bridge crosses the river.”?

partA.stem: Part A: Which sentence best combines “The bridge was built in 1920. The bridge is made of stone. The bridge crosses the river.”?

options.label: A
options.text: The bridge was built in 1920, it is stone, it crosses the river.

options.label: B
options.text: Built of stone, the river is crossed by the bridge from 1920.

options.label: C
options.text: The bridge was built in 1920 and is stone and crosses the river.

options.label: D
options.text: The stone bridge, built in 1920, crosses the river.

partB.stem: Part B: Why is the answer to Part A the most effective?

options.label: A
options.text: It reduces repetition by turning two sentences into modifiers.

options.label: B
options.text: It keeps all three sentences as separate independent clauses.

options.label: C
options.text: It joins the sentences with and to show they are equal.

options.label: D
options.text: It makes the river the subject so the sentence is clearer.

questions.why: Turning less important ideas into modifiers creates concise sentences.

questions.stem: Which sentence best combines “Maha found a fossil. The fossil was in the cliff. The fossil was of a sea creature.”?
options: Maha found a fossil, and the fossil was in the cliff.
Maha found the fossil of a sea creature in the cliff.
Maha found a fossil in the cliff, it was a sea creature.
In the cliff, a fossil was found, which was a sea creature.
questions.why: Prepositional phrases can combine several details into one clear sentence.

questions.stem: Which two sentences correctly combine “The market opens at dawn. Farmers bring fresh dates.”? Choose two.
options: The market opens at dawn; farmers bring fresh dates.
The market opens at dawn; and farmers bring fresh dates.
When the market opens at dawn, farmers bring fresh dates.
The market opens at dawn, farmers bring fresh dates.
questions.why: A dependent clause or a semicolon can correctly join related ideas.

questions.stem: Select the sentence that combines “The library has a new reading room. The room overlooks the garden.” without changing the meaning.

segments.text: The library has a new reading room that overlooks the garden.
The library overlooks the garden and has a reading room.
The garden overlooks the library's new reading room.
The library has a garden, and the room is new.

questions.why: A relative clause can combine ideas while keeping the original meaning.

questions.stem: Which sentence best combines “The rover landed on Mars in 2021. It has collected rock samples. The samples may show signs of ancient life.”?
options: Landing on Mars in 2021, rock samples were collected that may show signs of ancient life.
The rover landed on Mars in 2021, it collected samples, and they may show ancient life.
The rover, which may show signs of ancient life, landed on Mars in 2021 with samples.
Since landing on Mars in 2021, the rover has collected rock samples that may show signs of ancient life.
questions.why: Combine ideas so the relationships are clear and each modifier is attached to the right noun.

questions.stem: Choose the transition that correctly combines the sentences: The city expanded its metro lines; ____, traffic in the center decreased.
options: for instance
nevertheless
in contrast
consequently
questions.why: Consequently shows that the second idea results from the first.

questions.stem: Is each combined sentence about the solar farm effective or flawed?

rows.text: Covering two square kilometers, the solar farm powers thousands of homes.
Covering two square kilometers, thousands of homes are powered.
The solar farm, which opened last year, already exceeds its goals.
The farm opened last year, it already exceeds its goals.

questions.why: Effective combining avoids dangling modifiers and comma splices.

questions.stem: Find and correct the error in the sentence about the archaeologists' work.
questions.why: Combined actions should use parallel verb forms.

questions.stem: Part A: Which sentence best combines “The peregrine falcon is fast. It can dive at over 300 kilometers per hour. This makes it the fastest animal on Earth.”?

partA.stem: Part A: Which sentence best combines “The peregrine falcon is fast. It can dive at over 300 kilometers per hour. This makes it the fastest animal on Earth.”?

options.label: A
options.text: Able to dive at over 300 kilometers per hour, the peregrine falcon is the fastest animal on Earth.

options.label: B
options.text: The peregrine falcon is fast; it is the fastest animal; it dives at 300 kilometers per hour.

options.label: C
options.text: Diving at over 300 kilometers per hour, the Earth's fastest animal is fast.

options.label: D
options.text: The peregrine falcon is fast, and it can dive at over 300 kilometers per hour, and this makes it fastest.

partB.stem: Part B: What makes the answer to Part A effective?

options.label: A
options.text: It removes repetition and shows how the speed explains the record.

options.label: B
options.text: It places the main idea in a separate sentence for emphasis.

options.label: C
options.text: It uses several conjunctions to give each idea equal weight.

options.label: D
options.text: It keeps every original word so no information is lost.

questions.why: Strong combining removes redundancy and makes logical relationships clear.

questions.stem: Part A: Which revision best combines “The council approved the desalination plant. Critics had warned about its effect on marine life. The council required a monitoring program.”?

partA.stem: Part A: Which revision best combines “The council approved the desalination plant. Critics had warned about its effect on marine life. The council required a monitoring program.”?

options.label: A
options.text: Because critics warned about marine life, the council approved the plant and required monitoring.

options.label: B
options.text: The council approved the plant, critics had warned about marine life, and the council required monitoring.

options.label: C
options.text: Approving the desalination plant, critics' warnings about marine life required a monitoring program.

options.label: D
options.text: Despite critics' warnings about marine life, the council approved the desalination plant but required a monitoring program.

partB.stem: Part B: Why is the revision in Part A the most effective?

options.label: A
options.text: It presents the three ideas as equal events in time order.

options.label: B
options.text: It makes the critics' warnings the reason for the approval.

options.label: C
options.text: It shows both the contrast with the critics and the condition attached to approval.

options.label: D
options.text: It places the most information in a single participial phrase.

questions.why: Skilled combining uses subordination and conjunctions to show exact logical relationships.

questions.stem: Which two sentences correctly combine “Al-Jazari designed water clocks. His designs used gears and floats. Engineers still study them.” without errors? Choose two.
options: Al-Jazari designed water clocks whose gears and floats engineers still study.
Designing water clocks with gears and floats, engineers still study Al-Jazari.
Engineers still study the water clocks of Al-Jazari, whose designs used gears and floats.
Al-Jazari designed water clocks, his designs used gears and floats, engineers still study them.
questions.why: Correct combinations keep modifiers next to the words they describe and avoid comma splices.

questions.stem: Choose the option that best combines the ideas while keeping them parallel: The new policy aims to lower costs, ____, and to reduce waste.
options: service will improve
to improve service
for improving service
improving service
questions.why: Items in a series should share the same grammatical form.

questions.stem: Select the sentence that best combines “The expedition mapped the reef. The reef had never been surveyed. The mapping took three months.”

segments.text: Over three months, the expedition mapped the previously unsurveyed reef.
The reef, never surveyed, was mapped, and it took the expedition three months.
Mapping the reef for three months, it had never been surveyed before.
The expedition mapped the reef, it had never been surveyed, this took three months.

questions.why: The most effective combination is concise, clear, and grammatically correct.

questions.stem: Which sentence most effectively combines “Many students struggle with algebra. Some schools now use visual models. Test scores at those schools have risen.”?
options: Because many students struggle with algebra, some schools use visual models, and scores there have risen.
Some schools use visual models; algebra is a struggle for students; scores rose.
Struggling with algebra, visual models have raised test scores at some schools.
Many students struggle with algebra, and some schools use visual models, and scores have risen.
questions.why: Subordination shows that one idea caused the next, unlike a string of and clauses.

questions.stem: Choose the common noun that completes the sentence: I drink milk from a ____.
options: cup
happy
run
questions.why: A cup is a thing, so it is a noun.

questions.stem: Which TWO words are common nouns? Choose two.
options: ball
blue
teacher
jump
questions.why: Ball and teacher name a thing and a person.

questions.stem: True or false: In the sentence “The cat sleeps on the mat,” the word mat is a common noun.
questions.why: Mat names a thing, and it is not a special name.

questions.stem: Is each word a common noun or a proper noun: school, Riyadh, dog, Sara?

rows.text: school
Riyadh
dog
Sara

questions.why: Special names of people and places are proper nouns and start with a capital letter.

questions.stem: Find the mistake in the sentence about the park.
questions.why: Park is a common noun here, so it does not need a capital letter.

questions.stem: Which word is a common noun in the sentence “Yusuf carefully packed his telescope before sunset”?
options: packed
Yusuf
telescope
carefully
questions.why: Telescope names a thing; Yusuf is a proper noun.

questions.stem: Choose the word that correctly completes the sentence: Both ____ on our street planted palm trees this spring.
options: Families
families
familys
family's
questions.why: The plural of family is families, and it is not capitalized.

questions.stem: Classify each noun from the sentence “The crew sailed the Red Sea in July with a captain named Faisal.”

rows.text: crew
Red Sea
July
captain
Faisal

questions.why: Names of specific seas, months, and people are proper nouns.

questions.stem: Match each common noun to the kind of thing it names: engineer, harbor, compass, courage.
questions.why: Nouns can name people, places, things, or ideas.

questions.stem: Find the error in the sentence about the museum visit.
questions.why: Class is a common noun, so it is lowercase.

questions.stem: Choose the noun that best completes the sentence: The ____ of the bridge took three years because the engineers had to work around the tides.
options: constructive
constructed
construction
construct
questions.why: Construction is the noun form; the others are a verb and an adjective.

questions.stem: Which word is an abstract common noun in the sentence “The athletes showed great patience during the heavy rain at the stadium”?
options: patience
rain
stadium
athletes
questions.why: Patience names a quality you cannot see or touch.

questions.stem: Sort the nouns from the sentence “Dr. Hayat Sindi, a scientist from Mecca, designed a tool to test health in poor villages.”

rows.text: scientist
Mecca
tool
villages
Hayat Sindi

questions.why: General words for people, things, and places are common nouns.

questions.stem: Find the error in the sentence about the desert expedition.
questions.why: Explorers is a common noun; Empty Quarter is a proper name.

questions.stem: Which TWO sentences write every common noun correctly without a capital letter? Choose two.
options: The Mountain behind our town is covered in snow.
We asked the librarian for books about coral reefs.
My uncle works as a pilot for a national airline.
Our Principal, Mr. Hamad, opened the science fair.
questions.why: Common nouns like principal and mountain stay lowercase unless they begin a sentence.

questions.stem: Choose the word that correctly completes the sentence: The new laboratory received several pieces of ____ from the university.
options: equipment's
equipments
equipmentes
equipment
questions.why: Equipment is an uncountable noun, so it has no plural -s.

questions.stem: Which sentence uses a collective noun as its subject?
options: The players celebrated after the final whistle.
Khalid celebrated after the final whistle.
The team celebrated after the final whistle.
Everyone celebrated after the final whistle.
questions.why: Team names a group acting as one unit.

questions.stem: Decide whether each noun is usually countable or uncountable in “The guide gave us advice, two maps, some luggage tags, and information about the weather.”

rows.text: advice
maps
tags
information
weather

questions.why: Uncountable nouns like advice and information have no plural form.

questions.stem: Find the error in the sentence about the research report.
questions.why: Information is uncountable, so it cannot take many or a plural -s.

questions.stem: Which THREE sentences use common nouns correctly? Choose three.
options: The committee met on Tuesday to plan the festival.
We studied the history of the Abbasid period in class.
Our Coach told the team to stretch before practice.
The furnitures in the new library are made of oak.
My grandmother is a nurse at the city hospital.
questions.why: Coach is a common noun here, and furniture has no plural -s.

questions.stem: Which sentence capitalizes the common nouns correctly?
options: The governor of the Province spoke at the opening.
The governor of the province spoke at the opening.
The Governor of the Province spoke at the opening.
The Governor of the province spoke at the opening.
questions.why: Titles and place words used without a name are common nouns.

questions.stem: Choose the noun form that best completes the sentence: The ____ of the new desalination plant has lowered water costs for thousands of residents.
options: efficiency
efficiently
efficiencies'
efficient
questions.why: Efficiency is the noun that can act as the subject.

questions.stem: Find the error in the sentence about the marine survey.
segments: including a rare bloom of algae.
questions.why: The plural of phenomenon is phenomena.

questions.stem: Classify each noun from “The jury reached its verdict after hours of discussion, and the crowd outside cheered” as concrete or abstract.

rows.text: jury
verdict
discussion
crowd

questions.why: Concrete nouns name people or things you can perceive; abstract nouns name ideas or decisions.

questions.stem: Which TWO sentences match the collective noun with a correct verb and pronoun? Choose two.
options: The class has finished their projects early this week.
The herd moves toward the river when the dry season begins.
The orchestra tunes its instruments before every concert.
The fleet were anchored in the harbor because of its repairs.
questions.why: A collective noun acting as one unit takes a singular verb and the pronoun its.

questions.stem: Choose the word that correctly completes the sentence in formal writing: The survey's ____ were clear: most residents wanted more shaded walkways.
options: data's
datas
data
datum
questions.why: In formal writing, data is the plural of datum and takes were.

questions.stem: Which sentence uses the common noun criterion correctly?
options: The judges agreed that originality was the most important criterions.
The judges agreed that originality was the most important criterion.
The judges agreed that originality was the most important criteria.
The judges agreed that originality were the most important criterions.
questions.why: Criterion is singular; criteria is the plural.

questions.stem: Find the error in the sentence about the science symposium.
questions.why: A title used without a person's name is a common noun and stays lowercase.

questions.stem: Decide whether each sentence about family and school capitalizes its nouns correctly.

rows.text: We drove north along the coast to visit my Aunt.
My uncle, Dr. Saleh, visited our school.
My mother studied at a University in Jeddah.
The museum's Arabic manuscripts date from the ninth century.

questions.why: Aunt after my and university after a are common nouns, while names and proper adjectives like Arabic are capitalized.

questions.stem: Part A: In the sentence “The council debated the proposal for hours, yet its members could not reach an agreement,” which word is a collective noun?

partA.stem: Part A: In the sentence “The council debated the proposal for hours, yet its members could not reach an agreement,” which word is a collective noun?

options.label: A
options.text: members

options.label: B
options.text: council

options.label: C
options.text: proposal

options.label: D
options.text: agreement

partB.stem: Part B: Why is the pronoun its correct in this sentence?

options.label: A
options.text: It refers to the agreement the members wanted.

options.label: B
options.text: It refers to the council acting as a single unit.

options.label: C
options.text: It refers to the members as separate individuals.

options.label: D
options.text: It refers to the proposal that was being debated.

questions.why: A collective noun treated as one group takes the singular pronoun its.

questions.stem: Choose the word that completes the sentence: A horse is ____ than a cat.
options: bigger
big
biggest
questions.why: Use -er to compare two things.

questions.stem: Choose the word that completes the sentence: Mona is the ____ runner in our class.
options: fast
fastest
faster
questions.why: Use -est to compare more than two.

questions.stem: True or false: The sentence “My bag is more heavier than your bag” is correct.
questions.why: Say heavier, not more heavier.

questions.stem: Match each word to the form that compares three or more things: tall, small, happy.
questions.why: Add -est to compare three or more things.

questions.stem: Find the mistake in the sentence about the sun.
questions.why: Short words like hot add -er instead of using more.

questions.stem: Which sentence compares two things correctly?
options: The falcon flew more higher than the pigeon.
The falcon flew more high than the pigeon.
The falcon flew higher than the pigeon.
The falcon flew highest than the pigeon.
questions.why: Higher compares two things; do not add more.

questions.stem: Choose the word that completes the sentence: Of all the dates we tasted, the ones from Al-Ahsa were the ____.
options: sweetest
sweeter
sweet
most sweetest
questions.why: Of all means many things, so use the -est form.

questions.stem: Does each sentence about the school race compare two things or more than two?

rows.text: Ali ran faster than Omar.
Huda ran the fastest of all the girls.
The red team was stronger than the blue team.
This was the longest race of the year.

questions.why: The -er form compares two; the -est form compares three or more.

questions.stem: Find the error in the sentence about the two kittens.
questions.why: When only two things are compared, use the -er form.

questions.stem: Which TWO sentences use good, better, or best correctly? Choose two.
options: Sara's drawing is better than mine.
Today I feel more good than yesterday.
Of the three songs, this one is the goodest.
This is the best soup I have ever tasted.
questions.why: Good changes to better and best; it never takes more or -est.

questions.stem: Choose the words that complete the sentence: Of all the swimmers, Reem breathed the ____ during the long race.
options: more steadily
most steadily
steadier
steadiest
questions.why: Steadily is an adverb, and of all calls for the superlative most.

questions.stem: Which sentence uses a comparative adverb correctly?
options: The new train runs more quieter than the old one.
The new train runs most quietly than the old one.
The new train runs more quietly than the old one.
The new train runs quietlier than the old one.
questions.why: Adverbs ending in -ly use more to compare two actions.

questions.stem: Find the error in the sentence about the robotics contest.
questions.why: Do not use more together with an -er ending.

questions.stem: Decide whether the comparing word in each sentence is an adjective or an adverb.

rows.text: The mountain trail was steeper than we expected.
Khalid answered more confidently than before.
This is the most useful app on my phone.
The wind blew harder after sunset.

questions.why: Adjectives compare nouns; adverbs compare how actions happen.

questions.stem: Which TWO sentences contain an illogical comparison? Choose two.
options: Jeddah's weather is warmer than Abha.
Our library's books are newer than the city library.
Our library's books are newer than those in the city library.
Jeddah's weather is warmer than Abha's weather.
questions.why: Compare like with like: weather with weather, books with books.

questions.stem: Choose the words that complete the sentence: The second experiment was ____ than the first because the students measured each sample twice.
options: most accurate
more accurately
accurater
more accurate
questions.why: Accurate describes the experiment (a noun), and two things call for more.

questions.stem: Find the error in the sentence about the two bridges.
questions.why: With only two bridges, use the comparative more.

questions.stem: Which sentence makes a logical comparison?
options: Mount Everest is more taller than other mountains in the world.
Mount Everest is taller than any mountain in the world.
Mount Everest is taller than any other mountain in the world.
Mount Everest is the tallest of any other mountain in the world.
questions.why: Add other so Everest is not compared with itself.

questions.stem: Decide whether each sentence uses bad, badly, worse, or worst correctly.

rows.text: Rashid felt bad after missing the bus.
The storm was worse than the forecast predicted.
Of the three drafts, the first was the worse.
The team played badder in the second half.

questions.why: Bad becomes worse and worst; three items need worst.

questions.stem: Match each base word to its correct superlative form: little, many, well, far.
questions.why: Some comparing words have irregular forms that must be memorized.

questions.stem: Choose the words that best complete the sentence: Of the four proposals for the new park, the one with the shaded walking paths was clearly the ____.
options: most practical
more practical
practicalest
most practically
questions.why: Four proposals call for the superlative adjective most practical.

questions.stem: Which revision corrects the illogical comparison in the sentence “The population of Riyadh is larger than Jeddah”?
options: Riyadh's population is the largest than Jeddah.
The population of Riyadh is larger than that of Jeddah.
The population of Riyadh is larger than the city of Jeddah is.
The population of Riyadh is larger than Jeddah is.
questions.why: That of Jeddah makes the sentence compare population with population.

questions.stem: Find the error in the sentence about the two candidates.
questions.why: Between two calls for the comparative form.

questions.stem: Which TWO sentences use comparisons correctly? Choose two.
options: Her second essay was less wordy than her first.
The coach said Ahmed ran most fastest of all.
The drone flew farther than the instructor expected.
This solution is more unique than the others.
questions.why: Absolute adjectives like unique cannot be compared, and double superlatives are wrong.

questions.stem: Decide whether each comparison about places, animals, and students is logical or illogical.

rows.text: The museum's collection is larger than the library's.
A cheetah's speed is greater than a horse.
Ali studies more than any other student in his class.
Ali studies more than any student in his class.

questions.why: A logical comparison compares like things and does not compare something with itself.

questions.stem: Choose the word that correctly completes the sentence: The final draft was ____ organized than the earlier versions, though it still needed a stronger conclusion.
options: better
best
more well
more better
questions.why: Well becomes better in the comparative; do not add more.

questions.stem: Which sentence avoids an ambiguous comparison?
options: Fatima helps her younger brother more than her cousin does help.
Fatima helps more her younger brother than her cousin.
Fatima helps her younger brother more than she helps her cousin.
Fatima helps her younger brother more than her cousin.
questions.why: Repeating she helps makes clear who is being compared.

questions.stem: Find the error in the sentence about the two studies.
segments: that the results of the second study
questions.correction: than those of the first study.
questions.why: Results must be compared with results, not with a study.

questions.stem: Which THREE sentences use comparisons correctly and logically? Choose three.
options: The new vaccine proved more effective than any other treatment tested.
The architect's design was more perfect than the others.
His report was more thorough than any report submitted to the panel.
Of the two routes, the coastal road is the less crowded.
Her argument was stronger than her opponent's.
questions.why: Use the comparative for two, avoid comparing absolutes, and exclude the item from its own group.

questions.stem: Part A: Which revision of the sentence “The ancient library in Timbuktu held more manuscripts than any library in West Africa” makes the comparison logical?

partA.stem: Part A: Which revision of the sentence “The ancient library in Timbuktu held more manuscripts than any library in West Africa” makes the comparison logical?

options.label: A
options.text: …than the most libraries in West Africa.

options.label: B
options.text: …than all libraries in West Africa.

options.label: C
options.text: …than any other library in West Africa.

options.label: D
options.text: …than any libraries in Africa did.

partB.stem: Part B: Why is the original sentence illogical?

options.label: A
options.text: It uses a superlative form to compare only two things.

options.label: B
options.text: It compares a library with manuscripts instead of libraries.

options.label: C
options.text: It compares the library with a group that includes itself.

options.label: D
options.text: It uses a double comparative that repeats more and -er.

questions.why: Timbuktu is in West Africa, so the sentence needs other.

questions.stem: Choose the word that best joins the ideas: I wanted to play outside, ____ it was raining.
options: but
and
so
questions.why: But shows that the second idea is different from what you wanted.

questions.stem: Choose the word that best joins the ideas: The bell rang, ____ we went to class.
options: or
so
but
questions.why: So tells what happened because the bell rang.

questions.stem: True or false: “I like apples, and my brother likes bananas” is a compound sentence.
questions.why: It joins two complete ideas with a comma and and.

questions.stem: Match each sentence start to the best ending: I was hungry, so… / We can walk, or… / Sami is tall, but…
questions.why: So shows a result, or shows a choice, and but shows a difference.

questions.stem: Find the mistake in the sentence about the beach.
questions.why: And adds an idea; but is for ideas that are different.

questions.stem: Which sentence is a compound sentence?
options: The strong wind and the high waves frightened the fishermen.
The fishermen returned to the harbor because of the wind.
When the wind grew strong, the fishermen returned to the harbor.
The wind grew strong, so the fishermen returned to the harbor.
questions.why: A compound sentence joins two complete sentences with a comma and a conjunction.

questions.stem: Find the error in the sentence about the science project.
segments: Laila built a model of the moon
her partner painted the craters gray.
questions.correction: Laila built a model of the moon,
questions.why: Put a comma before the conjunction that joins two complete sentences.

questions.stem: Decide whether each sentence about the class trip is simple or compound.

rows.text: We visited the aquarium on Monday.
We saw sharks, and our teacher took photos.
The guide showed us a turtle and a ray.
The bus was late, but we still arrived on time.

questions.why: A compound sentence has two complete thoughts, each with its own subject and verb.

questions.stem: Choose the conjunction that best completes the sentence: The road was covered in sand, ____ the drivers had to slow down.
options: but
so
or
nor
questions.why: So shows the result of the sandy road.

questions.stem: Which TWO sentences use a comma and a conjunction correctly to join two complete thoughts? Choose two.
options: The kite rose quickly and, the children cheered.
The kite rose quickly, and the children cheered.
I studied hard, the test was still difficult.
I studied hard, yet the test was still difficult.
questions.why: The comma goes before the conjunction, and a comma alone cannot join two sentences.

questions.stem: Choose the conjunction that best shows the relationship between the ideas: Saeed had never sailed before, ____ he volunteered to steer the boat across the bay.
options: or
for
yet
so
questions.why: Yet shows a surprising contrast.

questions.stem: Find the error in the sentence about the football team.
questions.why: Winning is a result of practice, so the conjunction should show cause and effect.

questions.stem: Which choice best combines the sentences? “The museum opened a new space exhibit. Hundreds of students visited it in the first week.”
options: The museum opened a new space exhibit, or hundreds of students visited it in the first week.
The museum opened a new space exhibit, but hundreds of students visited it in the first week.
The museum opened a new space exhibit hundreds of students visited it in the first week.
The museum opened a new space exhibit, and hundreds of students visited it in the first week.
questions.why: And adds a related idea; the version without a comma and conjunction is a run-on.

questions.stem: Decide which conjunction best fits each sentence about the camping trip.

rows.text: The tent was small, ____ all four of us fit inside.
It started to rain, ____ we moved under the rocks.
Faris gathered wood, ____ Samir lit the fire.
The night was cold, ____ our blankets kept us warm.

questions.why: Choose and to add, but to contrast, and so to show a result.

questions.stem: Which TWO sentences about the space flight are punctuated correctly? Choose two.
options: The satellite launched on time and, the crew celebrated.
The engine failed, the crew made an emergency landing.
The satellite launched on time, and the crew celebrated.
The engine failed; the crew made an emergency landing.
questions.why: Join two sentences with a comma plus a conjunction, or with a semicolon.

questions.stem: Choose the conjunction that best completes the sentence: The students could present their findings on Monday, ____ they could submit a written report by Wednesday.
options: yet
for
so
or
questions.why: Or shows a choice between two options.

questions.stem: Find the error in the sentence about the desert garden.
segments: is planted with cactus and desert sage.
questions.why: A comma alone cannot join two sentences; for adds the reason.

questions.stem: Put these parts in order to build a correctly punctuated compound sentence about the volcano.
sequence: The volcano had been quiet for a century,
yet
scientists continued
to monitor it closely.
questions.why: The first clause and comma come before the conjunction, then the second clause.

questions.stem: Decide whether each sentence about the robotics club is a correct compound sentence or a run-on sentence.

rows.text: The club meets on Tuesdays, and new members are welcome.
The club meets on Tuesdays new members are welcome.
Our robot was finished; we tested it in the hallway.
Our robot was finished, we tested it in the hallway.

questions.why: Two clauses need a comma and conjunction or a semicolon between them.

questions.stem: Which choice best combines the sentences to show contrast? “Ibn Battuta traveled for nearly thirty years. He never lost his desire to return home.”
options: Ibn Battuta traveled for nearly thirty years, and he never lost his desire to return home.
Ibn Battuta traveled for nearly thirty years, for he never lost his desire to return home.
Ibn Battuta traveled for nearly thirty years, yet he never lost his desire to return home.
Ibn Battuta traveled for nearly thirty years, so he never lost his desire to return home.
questions.why: Yet shows that the second idea contrasts with the first.

questions.stem: Choose the punctuation and conjunction that correctly join the clauses: The researchers expected the coral to recover quickly____ the water temperature remained unusually high.
options: , but
but,
, so
; but,
questions.why: A comma goes before but when it joins two independent clauses.

questions.stem: Find the error in the sentence about the harbor project.
questions.why: Use a comma, not a semicolon, before a coordinating conjunction.

questions.stem: Which TWO sentences use a semicolon and a conjunctive adverb correctly? Choose two.
options: The bridge was closed for repairs, therefore, traffic moved slowly.
The data were incomplete; however, the team published early results.
The bridge was closed for repairs; therefore, traffic moved slowly.
The data were incomplete; however the team, published early results.
questions.why: Use a semicolon before and a comma after a conjunctive adverb that joins clauses.

questions.stem: Which choice best combines the sentences? “Al-Khwarizmi wrote about algebra. His work was translated into Latin. European scholars studied it for centuries.”
options: Al-Khwarizmi wrote about algebra, but his work was translated into Latin, yet European scholars studied it for centuries.
Al-Khwarizmi wrote about algebra his work was translated into Latin, so European scholars studied it for centuries.
Al-Khwarizmi's writing on algebra was translated into Latin, and European scholars studied it for centuries.
Al-Khwarizmi wrote about algebra, or his work was translated into Latin, and European scholars studied it for centuries.
questions.why: It combines all three ideas smoothly with a logical conjunction and no run-on.

questions.stem: Decide what relationship the conjunction shows in each sentence about the expedition.

rows.text: The guides warned of a sandstorm, so the team waited at camp.
The camels were tired, yet they carried the supplies another ten miles.
We could cross the dunes at night, or we could wait for cooler weather.
The map was old, but its landmarks were still accurate.

questions.why: But and yet contrast, so shows a result, and or offers a choice.

questions.stem: Choose the conjunction that best expresses the logical relationship: The committee had approved the budget months earlier, ____ no construction had begun by the end of the year.
options: yet
for
so
and
questions.why: Yet signals that the second clause is an unexpected contrast.

questions.stem: Find the error in the sentence about the solar project.
questions.why: A conjunctive adverb like consequently needs a semicolon before it to join clauses.

questions.stem: Which THREE sentences are correctly punctuated compound sentences? Choose three.
options: Some critics praised the design; others called it impractical.
The forecast predicted calm seas, but the ferry was delayed anyway.
The archive was fragile, nevertheless, the scholars handled every page.
The archive was fragile, so the scholars photographed every page.
The forecast predicted calm seas but, the ferry was delayed anyway.
questions.why: Comma plus conjunction or a semicolon joins clauses; nevertheless after a comma creates a splice.

questions.stem: Part A: Which revision best corrects the sentence “The study lasted three years, the results were never published, the funding ran out before the final report”?

partA.stem: Part A: Which revision best corrects the sentence “The study lasted three years, the results were never published, the funding ran out before the final report”?

options.label: A
options.text: The study lasted three years, and the results were never published, so the funding ran out before the final report.

options.label: B
options.text: The study lasted three years, but the results were never published, for the funding ran out before the final report.

options.label: C
options.text: The study lasted three years, the results were never published; the funding ran out before the final report.

options.label: D
options.text: The study lasted three years but the results were never published, the funding ran out before the final report.

partB.stem: Part B: Why is the conjunction for the best choice in the second part of the revision?

options.label: A
options.text: It shows that the funding and the results were unrelated events.

options.label: B
options.text: It shows that the funding problem explains why the results were not published.

options.label: C
options.text: It shows a choice between publishing results and ending the study.

options.label: D
options.text: It shows that the results caused the funding to run out early.

questions.why: For introduces a reason, which matches the logic of the ideas.

questions.stem: Which sentence uses coordination most effectively to show that the second idea is unexpected?
options: The drought lasted two years, so the oasis never ran dry.
The drought lasted two years, and the oasis never ran dry.
The drought lasted two years, yet the oasis never ran dry.
The drought lasted two years, for the oasis never ran dry.
questions.why: Yet signals contrast; so and for would make the drought a cause or an effect.

questions.stem: Choose the compound word that completes the sentence: I brush my teeth with a ____.
options: teeth
toothbrush
brushing
questions.why: Toothbrush is made of two words: tooth and brush.

questions.stem: Match each first word with a second word to make a compound word: sun, rain, foot, cup.
questions.why: Two small words join to make sunflower, rainbow, football, and cupcake.

questions.stem: Which TWO words are compound words? Choose two.
options: garden
sandbox
window
bedroom
questions.why: Bed + room and sand + box are two words put together.

questions.stem: True or false: The word playground is made of the two words play and ground.
questions.why: Play + ground = playground.

questions.stem: Is each word a compound word or not a compound word: seashell, happy, starfish, table?

rows.text: seashell
happy
starfish
table

questions.why: Seashell and starfish are each made of two words.

questions.stem: What does the compound word sandstorm mean?
options: a storm of blowing sand
a quiet day in the desert
a castle made of sand
sand that is very wet
questions.why: The two parts, sand and storm, tell the meaning.

questions.stem: Choose the compound word that best completes the sentence: At night, the sailors watched the ____ flash its warning beam from the rocky shore.
options: moonbeam
sunlight
lighthouse
headlight
questions.why: A lighthouse is a tower with a light that warns ships.

questions.stem: Decide whether each pair of words forms a closed compound (one word) or an open compound (two words).

rows.text: basket + ball
ice + cream
high + school
note + book

questions.why: Some compounds are written as one word and some stay as two words.

questions.stem: Find the error in the sentence about the weekend.
questions.why: Grandmother is a closed compound written as one word.

questions.stem: Match each compound word to its meaning: waterfall, homework, daydream, handshake.

pairs.right: water dropping from a high place

questions.why: The two smaller words in a compound give clues to its meaning.

questions.stem: Choose the correctly written compound word to complete the sentence: My ____ helped me plan the surprise party for our teacher.
options: class-mate
class mate
classmate
questions.why: Classmate is a closed compound.

questions.stem: Which sentence uses a hyphenated compound correctly?
options: My sisterinlaw teaches chemistry at the university.
My sister-in law teaches chemistry at the university.
My sister-in-law teaches chemistry at the university.
My sister in-law teaches chemistry at the university.
questions.why: Sister-in-law needs hyphens between all of its parts.

questions.stem: Classify each compound in the sentence “The well-known author stopped by the post office to mail her notebook.”

rows.text: well-known
post office
notebook

questions.why: Compounds can be closed (one word), open (two words), or hyphenated.

questions.stem: Find the error in the sentence about the soccer match.
questions.why: Someone, meaning an unknown person, is a closed compound written as one word.

questions.stem: Which TWO sentences use the compound word correctly? Choose two.
options: Maybe the bus will arrive early today.
The answer maybe hidden in the last chapter.
Everyday chores teach children responsibility.
I water the plants everyday before school.
questions.why: Everyday and maybe are modifiers; every day and may be are used for time and verbs.

questions.stem: Choose the word or words that correctly complete the sentence: The researchers checked the equipment ____ before the launch.
options: every-day
every day
everyday
questions.why: Every day (two words) tells how often something happens.

questions.stem: True or false: In the sentence “The team needs a new set up for the laboratory,” the compound set up is written correctly.
questions.why: As a noun, setup is one word; set up is the verb.

questions.stem: Match each sentence about the computer lab to the correct form: set up, setup, log in, or login.

pairs.left: We will ____ the computers before class.
Use your new ____ to open the account.
You must ____ before the quiz starts.

questions.why: The open form is usually the verb, and the closed form is usually the noun.

questions.stem: Find the error in the sentence about the science fair.
questions.why: A compound adjective before a noun is hyphenated.

questions.stem: Which sentence correctly uses a hyphenated compound adjective?
options: The museum displayed a hand drawn map of the old trade routes.
The museum displayed a hand-drawn map of the old trade routes.
The museum displayed a hand-drawn-map of the old trade routes.
The museum displayed a handdrawn map of the old trade-routes.
questions.why: Hyphenate the two-word modifier, but not the noun it describes.

questions.stem: Choose the correct form to complete the sentence: The architect presented a ____ plan for the waterfront park.
options: long-termed
long term
long-term
longterm
questions.why: A compound modifier before a noun is hyphenated.

questions.stem: Find the error in the sentence about the market report.
questions.why: Well-known is hyphenated when it comes before the noun.

questions.stem: Decide whether the compound in each sentence about the research schedule is written correctly.

rows.text: The data were collected over a three-month period.
The study lasted three-months.
Her work is well known among scientists.
The up to date figures were released Monday.

questions.why: Hyphenate compound modifiers before a noun, but not ordinary noun phrases or most modifiers after the verb.

questions.stem: Which TWO sentences use a compound modifier correctly? Choose two.
options: The coach gave a last minute speech before kickoff.
The newly-built stadium seats forty thousand fans.
The newly built stadium seats forty thousand fans.
The team adopted a data-driven approach to training.
questions.why: Do not hyphenate after an -ly adverb, but do hyphenate other compound modifiers before a noun.

questions.stem: Which sentence uses the compound word breakdown correctly?
options: Our old car might breakdown on the long desert highway.
If the talks breakdown tonight, the two companies will not reach an agreement.
Machines often breakdown when sand gets into the gears.
The engineer gave a detailed breakdown of the project costs.
questions.why: Breakdown is a noun; the verb is written as two words, break down.

questions.stem: Choose the word that correctly completes the sentence: The committee's decision was hardly a ____ conclusion, since members debated it for weeks.
options: forgone
fore-gone
foregone
forgoing
questions.why: Foregone means decided in advance; forgone means given up.

questions.stem: Find the error in the sentence about the clinic.
questions.why: Follow-up is hyphenated when it modifies a noun.

questions.stem: Decide whether each compound in the sentences about the startup company is used correctly.

rows.text: The startup secured funding in its first year.
We plan to startup a recycling business next year.
The company's turnaround surprised investors.
Sales will turnaround once the new product launches.
Her well-reasoned argument convinced the panel.

questions.why: Closed forms like startup and turnaround are nouns; the verbs are start up and turn around.

questions.stem: Part A: In the sentence “The lab replaced its out-of-date equipment, but the new devices are not yet up to date with the latest software,” why are the two compounds written differently?

options.label: B

options.label: C

questions.stem: Which sentence says the idea in the fewest words?

The dog is big.

The cat is sleeping and is asleep.
The cat drank milk.
The cat, it drank milk.

The team, which won, won the game.

options: return back
free gift
small gift
walk home

questions.why: Short words often say the same thing as long phrases.

options: In a surprising manner
In a way that was surprising
Surprisingly
Surprisingly and unexpectedly
questions.why: One adverb does the work of the longer phrases.

questions.stem: Which revision of the sentence “The reason why the game was canceled was because of the storm” is the most concise?
options: Because of the storm was the reason the game was canceled.
The game was canceled because of the storm.

finished
past history

history

options: Most students prefer morning classes.

During the time of the earthquake, the bridge collapsed down.

options: explained
gave an explanation of
made an explanation about
provided an explaining of
questions.why: A strong verb is shorter than a weak verb plus a noun.

questions.why: A library is already a building, so is a building that is extra.

I think that the school day should start later in the morning.
I think the school day should start later.
The school day should start later.
questions.why: Each revision removes words that repeat or add nothing.

questions.stem: Decide whether each sentence about the solar car is concise or wordy.

The car, which was solar-powered in nature, was fast in terms of its speed.
Engineers tested the car for six weeks.
It is a fact that the engineers tested the car for a period of six weeks.

questions.why: Phrases like in nature, in terms of, and it is a fact that add no meaning.

options: made the decision
came to the decision
decided
reached a decision
questions.why: A single verb is more concise than a verb plus a noun.

questions.stem: Which revision is the most concise version of the sentence “There are many scientists who believe that the reef can still be saved if action is taken quickly” that keeps its meaning?

Many scientists believe that the reef can be saved.

options: The new innovation was completely unique when it was first introduced.

The innovation was introduced in 2019.
The unique innovation was introduced in 2019.

Her proposal reduces costs without sacrificing safety.

questions.why: Empty openers, repeated nouns, and noun-heavy verb phrases make writing wordy.

questions.stem: Decide whether each revision of “The engineers basically conducted an analysis of the samples in order to determine their actual composition” is the best revision, still wordy, or loses meaning.

rows.text: The engineers analyzed the samples to determine their composition.

The engineers analyzed the samples.
The engineers basically analyzed the samples in order to find out their actual composition.

questions.why: The best revision cuts filler words without removing the purpose of the analysis.

questions.stem: A student writes: “The historian's book, which is a volume that runs to six hundred pages, is a work that traces the history of the spice trade from its earliest beginnings.” Which revision is most concise while keeping all key information?

questions.stem: Read: “The once-vibrant fishing village is now moribund: its young people have moved to the cities, its school has closed, and only a few boats remain.” Moribund means ____.

crowded with visitors
newly rebuilt

questions.stem: Read: “The scientist’s explanation was lucid; even students who had never studied chemistry could follow every step.” Which TWO words are closest in meaning to lucid? Choose two.

understandable
technical
lengthy

questions.stem: Decide whether each sentence uses “ephemeral” in a way that fits its meaning, “lasting a very short time.”

questions.why: Thousands or millions of years contradict a short life.

questions.stem: Part A: Read: “The new manager’s policies were draconian: employees were fined for arriving even one minute late, and breaks were cut to five minutes.” What does draconian most likely mean?

questions.stem: Read: “Her rebuttal was so trenchant that her opponent, usually quick with a reply, could only nod and concede the point.” What does trenchant most likely mean?

lengthy and full of detail

questions.stem: Read: “The committee’s decision seemed capricious; it approved the design on Monday, rejected it on Wednesday, and approved it again on Friday without new information.” Capricious means ____.

changing suddenly without reason

questions.stem: Select two sentences about the scholar Al-Khwarizmi that best help define “erudite.”

He had mastered mathematics, astronomy, and geography.

questions.stem: For each sentence, decide whether the context supports reading “sanguine” as “hopeful” or as “blood-red.”

questions.stem: True or false: In “The lemon tasted sour,” the word sour tells how something tastes.

questions.stem: Choose the word that helps you hear the rain: The rain went ____ on the roof.

pitter-patter

questions.stem: Which sense does each phrase about the beach use?

rows.text: blue waves
crashing waves
warm sand
squawking gulls

questions.why: Colors are seen, sounds are heard, warmth is felt.

questions.stem: Which sentence uses the best describing words?
options: The fluffy white cat napped in the sun.
The cat was on the mat.
There is a cat by the door.
My family has a cat at our home in the city.

questions.stem: Which TWO words describe how a cold drink feels? Choose two.
options: chilly
icy
loud
sweet

questions.stem: Choose the most precise verb: The hungry falcon ____ toward the rabbit.
options: got
moved
went
plunged
questions.why: Plunged shows a fast, steep dive.

questions.stem: Which sentence best appeals to the sense of touch?

The rough bark scraped Faisal’s palms.
Birds sang loudly from the top of the old tree.
The ripe dates in the tree smelled sweet and rich.

questions.stem: Identify the sense in each detail from a description of a spice market.

rows.text: pyramids of golden turmeric
the sharp scent of cloves
merchants calling out prices
the warm aroma of cardamom

questions.why: Scent and aroma are smells; calling is a sound; golden is seen.

questions.stem: Which part of the sentence about the thunder should be revised to use more vivid language?
questions.why: Boomed is more vivid than made a noise.

questions.stem: Put the sentences describing a desert sunrise in an order that moves from dark to bright.
sequence: A thin gray line appeared at the edge of the sky.
The gray softened into pink and pale orange.
A golden rim of sun rose above the dunes.
Bright light spilled across the sand, and the day grew hot.
questions.why: The description follows the light as it grows.

questions.stem: Choose the word that creates the strongest image: Wind ____ through the cracked walls of the abandoned fort.
options: passed
moaned
blew
went
questions.why: Moaned adds sound and a lonely feeling.

questions.stem: Match each phrase about a thunderstorm to the sense it appeals to.

pairs.left: a metallic smell before the rain

questions.why: Each detail points to one of the five senses.

questions.stem: Which part of the sentence about the diver should be replaced with more precise sensory language?
segments: and the light faded to a dim blue-green.
questions.why: Nice is vague; colder tells what the diver feels.

questions.stem: Which TWO revisions of “The market was busy” use the most vivid sensory details? Choose two.
options: The market was very, very busy and full of things.
Shoppers jostled past stalls heaped with glossy eggplants.
Voices bargained over the clatter of carts and the hiss of frying bread.
The market had a lot of people in it on that day.
questions.why: Specific sights and sounds make the scene vivid.

questions.stem: Part A: Read: “The kettle shrieked, and the smell of mint drifted from the kitchen.” Which senses does the sentence appeal to?

options.label: C
options.text: drifted

options.label: D
options.text: smell

questions.why: Shrieked is a sound; mint is a smell.

questions.stem: Which revision of “The old car made noise” uses the most precise sensory language?
options: The old car was noisy when it went up the hill.
The car, which was old, made a lot of noise.
The old car coughed and rattled up the hill.
The old car made a very loud and bad noise.
questions.why: Coughed and rattled name the exact sounds.

questions.stem: Select the sentence about the night fishing trip that uses figurative sensory language.

My uncle checked the nets twice.
We returned before sunrise with twelve fish.

questions.stem: Classify each phrase describing a waterfall as literal or figurative description.

rows.text: water falling sixty meters
a curtain of white thunder
mist that wet our faces
the river leaping off the cliff like a startled deer

questions.why: Figurative phrases compare the water to something else.

questions.stem: A student is describing a bakery. Which THREE details appeal to senses other than sight? Choose three.
options: a red-and-white striped awning
the crackle of crust being sliced
shelves lined with round loaves
golden pastries in the window
the yeasty warmth of rising dough
flour soft as powder between her fingers
questions.why: Warmth, crackle and softness appeal to smell, hearing and touch.

questions.stem: Part A: Read: “The abandoned station sagged under the desert sun, its windows blind with dust and its sign creaking on one rusted hinge.” What mood does the descriptive language create?

partA.stem: Part A: Read: “The abandoned station sagged under the desert sun, its windows blind with dust and its sign creaking on one rusted hinge.” What mood does the descriptive language create?

options.label: A
options.text: tense and dangerous

options.label: B
options.text: lonely and neglected

options.label: C
options.text: calm and refreshing

options.label: D
options.text: cheerful and busy

partB.stem: Part B: Which phrase contributes most to this mood?

options.text: under the desert sun

options.label: B
options.text: its windows blind with dust

options.label: C
options.text: The abandoned station

options.label: D
options.text: its sign

questions.why: Dust-covered windows suggest no one cares for the place.

questions.stem: Choose the word that best keeps the tense, threatening mood: Across the valley, storm clouds ____ over the ridge like an army preparing to attack.
options: appeared
massed
floated
drifted
questions.why: Massed fits the army image; floated and drifted feel gentle.

questions.stem: Decide whether each detail from a description of a hospital waiting room creates a mood of anxiety or comfort.

rows.text: the clock ticking too loudly
a soft blanket draped over a chair
fluorescent lights buzzing overhead
the smell of fresh cardamom coffee

questions.why: Harsh sounds create tension; soft, warm details comfort.

questions.stem: Which part of the sentence about the hushed library breaks the solemn mood and should be revised?
segments: its tall shelves casting long shadows,
questions.why: Slang breaks the quiet, serious mood.

questions.stem: A writer wants to show that a character is exhausted after a long race. Which sentence does this most effectively through sensory detail?
options: Her legs burned, and each breath scraped her throat like sand.
She was extremely tired after running in the very long race.
After the race she sat down on the bench because she was quite worn out.
She felt exhausted, which is how runners feel after races.
questions.why: Burning legs and a scraped throat let readers feel the exhaustion.

questions.stem: Part A: Read: “The city at noon was a furnace: heat rose off the asphalt in shimmering waves, and the air tasted of dust and diesel.” How does the sensory language develop the description?

partA.stem: Part A: Read: “The city at noon was a furnace: heat rose off the asphalt in shimmering waves, and the air tasted of dust and diesel.” How does the sensory language develop the description?

options.label: B
options.text: It uses smell alone to show how polluted cities have become.

options.text: It focuses only on sight to show how bright the city is.

options.label: D

options.label: A

options.label: B
options.text: heat rose off the asphalt

options.label: C
options.text: shimmering waves

options.label: D
options.text: the air tasted of dust and diesel

questions.why: Several senses together make the heat overwhelming.

melted

Molten glass hung from the pipe like a drop of honey.
Bellows wheezed, tools rang against the anvil, and the fire roared.

questions.why: Wheezed, rang and roared are sound words.

the sharp, sour sound of the alarm

a bright orange shirt

questions.stem: A writer revises “The marsh was quiet” to “The marsh held its breath; not a reed stirred, and even the frogs had fallen silent.” What does the revision accomplish?
options: It adds scientific facts about the specific plants and animals that usually live in coastal marshes.
It shortens the description so that the reader moves quickly to the action.
It changes the setting from a quiet marsh to a noisy one full of animals.
It replaces a flat statement with images that make the silence feel tense and expectant.
questions.why: Holding its breath suggests waiting for something to happen.

options.text: slackened

options.label: D

questions.why: Slackened ropes show tension being released at day’s end.

noun
adjective

valiant
rash

questions.stem: Using the entry “ob·jec·tive (adjective) not influenced by feelings; (noun) a goal,” classify how “objective” is used in each sentence.

questions.stem: Put the steps for using a thesaurus to replace the overused word “good” in an essay in a logical order.

Check a dictionary to confirm the word’s exact meaning.

slender
gaunt

finding a synonym for “procedure” in an essay

questions.stem: True or false: “What is your favorite color?” is a good question to look up in books.

How do bees make honey?

questions.stem: Can each question about the moon be answered by looking it up?

questions.stem: Decide whether each question for a report on the Red Sea is too broad, too narrow, or just right.
