Do I like oryx?
What are all the animals in Asia?
questions.why: The revision names one animal and one problem.

questions.stem: Which question would best guide research for a report on the inventor Al-Jazari?
options: How did Al-Jazari’s water-powered machines influence later engineers?
Was Al-Jazari the smartest person ever to live?
What year is it in the country where Al-Jazari lived?
Did Al-Jazari enjoy building toys and small machines with his friends when he was young?
questions.why: It is focused and can be answered with evidence.

questions.stem: Classify each question for a project on sleep and students as researchable or not researchable.

rows.text: How does screen time before bed affect students’ sleep?
Is sleeping boring?
How many hours of sleep do doctors recommend for teenagers?
Which dream would I like to have tonight?

questions.why: Researchable questions can be answered with facts and data.

questions.stem: Which TWO questions for a report on the Hejaz Railway are researchable rather than opinion-based? Choose two.
options: Was the Hejaz Railway the most beautiful railway?
How did the railway change travel times across the region?
Would traveling by train be more fun than by car?
When was the Hejaz Railway built, and why?
questions.why: Dates, reasons and effects can be supported with sources.

questions.stem: Part A: Yusuf is researching solar energy. Which research question is most effective?

partA.stem: Part A: Yusuf is researching solar energy. Which research question is most effective?

options.label: A
options.text: Do solar panels exist in Saudi Arabia?

options.label: B
options.text: Is solar energy better than everything else?

options.label: C
options.text: What is solar energy?

options.label: D
options.text: How have solar panels changed energy use in Saudi homes since 2015?

partB.stem: Part B: Why is the question in Part A the most effective?

options.label: A
options.text: It can be answered with one word.

options.label: B
options.text: It is focused and can be answered with evidence.

options.label: C
options.text: It covers every type of energy on Earth.

options.label: D
options.text: It asks for the writer’s personal feelings.

questions.why: A good question has a clear focus and needs evidence.

questions.stem: The question ____ cannot be answered through research because it asks for an opinion.
options: When were the first modern Olympics held?
Which Olympic sport is the most exciting to watch?
How many countries competed in the 2020 Games?
questions.why: Most exciting is a matter of opinion.

questions.stem: Select the research question about desalination that is most likely to be answerable with credible sources.

segments.text: Is desalination cool?
How much energy do desalination plants in Saudi Arabia use per liter of water?
Will everyone love desalination someday?
Why is desalination the best invention ever?

questions.why: It asks for measurable facts.

questions.stem: Which part of the research question about the history of coffee needs revision?
segments: and why do I like it so much?
questions.why: Personal feelings do not belong in a research question.

questions.stem: A student’s question is “How did the printing press change the spread of knowledge in Europe between 1450 and 1550?” Which TWO features make it strong? Choose two.
options: It can be answered with a simple yes or no.
It sets a clear time frame.
It asks about effects rather than a single fact.
It asks for the student’s personal opinion.
questions.why: A time frame and a focus on effects make it researchable and deep.

questions.stem: Part A: Which revision best narrows the research question “How does pollution affect the environment?”

partA.stem: Part A: Which revision best narrows the research question “How does pollution affect the environment?”

options.label: A
options.text: What is pollution?

options.label: B
options.text: Is pollution bad for the environment?

options.label: C
options.text: How does pollution affect the whole environment on Earth?

options.label: D
options.text: How does plastic waste affect sea turtles along the Red Sea coast?

partB.stem: Part B: What makes the revision in Part A more effective?

options.label: A
options.text: It focuses on the writer’s feelings.

options.label: B
options.text: It names a specific pollutant, animal, and place.

options.label: C
options.text: It can be answered with yes or no.

options.label: D
options.text: It uses more words than the original.

questions.why: Naming specifics makes a question manageable.

questions.stem: Which research question about electric cars is most free of bias?
options: How have gas car makers misled the public about emissions?
How do the lifetime emissions of electric and gasoline cars compare?
Why do foolish drivers still buy gasoline cars today?
Why are electric cars so much better for everyone than old gasoline cars?
questions.why: It compares without assuming an answer.

questions.stem: Evaluate each question for a research paper on urban heat islands.

rows.text: How do tree-planting programs affect summer temperatures in Riyadh neighborhoods?
What is weather?
Why are city planners failing to stop urban heat?
How much does reflective roofing lower indoor temperatures in hot cities?

questions.why: Effective questions are focused and do not assume a conclusion.

questions.stem: Which THREE questions could serve as sub-questions for “How has desalination affected water security in the Arabian Peninsula?” Choose three.
options: What share of drinking water in the region comes from desalination?
Which desalination plant has the most attractive design?
What environmental costs do desalination plants create?
How do rivers in South America form deltas?
How has desalination capacity changed since 1990?
Is water more delicious than juice?
questions.why: Sub-questions must stay on topic and be answerable with evidence.

questions.stem: Arrange the questions about the Silk Road from broadest to most focused.
sequence: What was life like in the past?
What was trade like in the ancient world?
What goods moved along the Silk Road?
How did paper from China change book-making in ninth-century Baghdad?
questions.why: Each step narrows the time, place or subject.

questions.stem: Part A: A student plans a report with the question “Why do people like social media?” What is the main weakness of the question?

partA.stem: Part A: A student plans a report with the question “Why do people like social media?” What is the main weakness of the question?

options.label: A
options.text: It can be answered with a single statistic.

options.label: B
options.text: It is too broad and assumes all people like social media.

options.label: C
options.text: It is too narrow to find any information.

options.label: D
options.text: It focuses on a single country.

partB.stem: Part B: Which revision best fixes this weakness?

options.label: A
options.text: Do people use social media?

options.label: B
options.text: Why does everybody love social media so much?

options.label: C
options.text: How do teenagers in Riyadh describe their reasons for using photo-sharing apps?

options.label: D
options.text: What is social media?

questions.why: The revision names a group, a place and a type of app without assuming.

questions.stem: Which part of the research question about microplastics should be revised to remove bias?
questions.why: Loaded words assume the answer before the research begins.

questions.stem: Which research question is most likely to produce a complex, arguable thesis?
options: What are the ten Arabic numerals that people still use today?
Which Italian merchants and bankers were the first to write the number zero in their records?
How did Arabic numerals reshape European commerce, and why was their adoption slow?
In what year did Fibonacci publish the book Liber Abaci in Italy?
questions.why: It asks how and why, inviting analysis rather than one fact.

questions.stem: Evaluate each question proposed for a paper on artificial intelligence in hospitals.

rows.text: How accurate are AI tools at reading chest X-rays compared with radiologists?
What is the future of technology?
Will AI doctors replace all humans by 2200?
How have AI scheduling systems affected wait times in Saudi hospitals since 2018?

questions.why: Questions about the distant future cannot be answered with present evidence.

questions.stem: A student narrows “How does sleep affect learning?” Which TWO revisions are both focused and researchable? Choose two.
options: How does sleep affect every part of human health and learning?
Is sleep the most important thing in a student’s life?
What does research show about naps and recall among university students?
How does sleeping fewer than seven hours affect memory test scores in high school students?
questions.why: Focused questions name a group and a measurable effect.

questions.stem: Part A: A student proposes: “To what extent did public investment drive the growth of renewable energy in Morocco between 2009 and 2020?” What is the strongest feature of this question?

partA.stem: Part A: A student proposes: “To what extent did public investment drive the growth of renewable energy in Morocco between 2009 and 2020?” What is the strongest feature of this question?

options.label: A
options.text: It invites an evaluative argument supported by evidence.

options.label: B
options.text: It avoids any specific time period.

options.label: C
options.text: It requires no outside sources.

options.label: D
options.text: It can be answered with a single fact.

partB.stem: Part B: Which revision would most weaken the question?

options.label: A
options.text: How did the Noor solar complex affect output after 2016?

options.label: B
options.text: Which policies most affected wind power growth after 2009?

options.label: C
options.text: To what extent did private investment also drive this growth?

options.label: D
options.text: Is renewable energy in Morocco good?

questions.why: “To what extent” asks for weighing evidence; a yes-or-no value question does not.

questions.stem: Is each sentence a simile or not a simile? (A simile uses like or as.)

rows.text: The baby is as quiet as a mouse.
The baby is sleeping.
Her hair is soft like a cloud.
The cat ate its food.

questions.why: A simile compares two things using like or as.

questions.stem: Choose the word that makes a simile: The camel was as tall ____ a tree.
options: than
and
as
questions.why: The pattern as tall as compares the camel to a tree.

questions.stem: In the sentence “The sun smiled at us,” what is the sun doing that only people can do?
options: shining
setting
rising
smiling
questions.why: Only people smile, so the sun is given a human action.

questions.stem: True or false: “I am so hungry I could eat a whole camel!” is an exaggeration, not a real fact.
questions.why: No one could eat a whole camel; the speaker exaggerates to show great hunger.

questions.stem: Match each figurative phrase about the weather to what it really means.

pairs.right: The wind was soft and quiet.

pairs.left: The rain danced on the roof.
pairs.right: The rain tapped lightly on the roof.

pairs.left: It is as hot as an oven.

questions.why: Figurative phrases describe real things in a colorful way.

questions.stem: Which sentence contains a metaphor?
options: The classroom was busy like a beehive.
The bees buzzed loudly outside the classroom.
The classroom had many busy students.
The classroom was a beehive of activity.
questions.why: A metaphor says one thing IS another, without like or as.

questions.stem: In the sentence “When Amal saw her test score, her heart was a balloon,” the metaphor shows that Amal felt ____.
options: empty and lost
light and happy
sick and tired
angry and loud
questions.why: A balloon floats up, so her heart felt light with joy.

questions.stem: Which TWO sentences use hyperbole? Choose two.
options: I asked you twice to close the door.
My backpack is heavier than my brother's.
I have told you a million times to close the door.
My backpack weighs a ton today.
questions.why: Hyperbole is an extreme exaggeration that is not meant literally.

questions.stem: Label each sentence about the desert as a simile, a metaphor, or personification.

rows.text: The sand dunes were waves frozen in place.
The dunes rolled like an ocean of gold.
The desert wind howled its angry song.
At noon the sand was as bright as a mirror.

questions.why: Like/as signals a simile; is/were signals a metaphor; human actions signal personification.

questions.stem: Part A: Read the sentence: “The old bicycle groaned as Faisal pedaled up the hill.” What kind of figurative language is used?

partA.stem: Part A: Read the sentence: “The old bicycle groaned as Faisal pedaled up the hill.” What kind of figurative language is used?

options.label: A
options.text: metaphor

options.label: B
options.text: personification

options.label: C
options.text: hyperbole

options.label: D
options.text: simile

partB.stem: Part B: Which word in the sentence creates this figurative language?

options.label: A
options.text: old

options.label: B
options.text: hill

options.label: C
options.text: pedaled

options.label: D
options.text: groaned

questions.why: Groaning is a human sound, so the bicycle is personified.

questions.stem: Select the sentence in this description of a sandstorm that uses personification.

segments.text: The sky turned a dull orange by noon.
The wind grabbed at our scarves and refused to let go.
We covered our faces and walked toward the shelter.
Inside, we waited for the storm to pass.

questions.why: Grabbing and refusing are human actions given to the wind.

questions.stem: Which sentence uses a simile to show that a runner was very fast?
options: Khalid ran faster than every other runner in the race.
Khalid's legs ached for hours after he crossed the finish line.
Khalid was a falcon as he crossed the finish line first.
Khalid flew past the finish line like a falcon diving for prey.
questions.why: The word like compares Khalid's speed to a diving falcon.

questions.stem: In the sentence “Her words were daggers that cut through the cheerful mood,” the metaphor suggests that her words were ____.
options: quiet and calm
funny and surprising
hurtful and sharp
long and confusing
questions.why: Daggers cut and wound, so the words were hurtful.

questions.stem: Match each sentence about the sea to the type of figurative language it uses.

pairs.left: The waves applauded as the boat came home.
The coral reef was a crowded city under the sea.
The water was as clear as glass.
There were a billion fish around the boat.

questions.why: Each device works differently: human action, direct comparison, like/as, or exaggeration.

questions.stem: Part A: Read the sentence: “The library was a sleeping giant, its long halls silent and its doors closed for the summer.” What does the metaphor suggest about the library?

partA.stem: Part A: Read the sentence: “The library was a sleeping giant, its long halls silent and its doors closed for the summer.” What does the metaphor suggest about the library?

options.label: A
options.text: It is frightening to visitors.

options.label: B
options.text: It is huge but quiet and inactive.

options.label: C
options.text: It is old and falling apart.

options.label: D
options.text: It is full of noisy readers.

partB.stem: Part B: Which detail from the sentence best supports the answer to Part A?

options.label: A
options.text: for the summer

options.label: B
options.text: its long halls silent

options.label: C
options.text: its doors

options.label: D
options.text: The library

questions.why: Silent halls show that the giant building is asleep, or inactive.

questions.stem: Decide whether each sentence about a football match uses hyperbole or a metaphor.

rows.text: The stadium roared loud enough to wake the whole planet.
The goalkeeper was a wall that no shot could break.
We waited ten thousand years for the final whistle.
The midfield was a chessboard, and our captain was the master player.

questions.why: Hyperbole exaggerates; a metaphor states that one thing is another.

questions.stem: Which sentence uses personification to create a feeling of danger?
options: The cliffs were tall and steep beside the narrow path.
The cliffs leaned over the path, waiting for a careless step.
The cliffs were as sharp as broken glass along the path.
The cliffs were a million meters high above the narrow path.
questions.why: Leaning and waiting are human actions that make the cliffs seem threatening.

questions.stem: Which TWO sentences use figurative language to show that a scientist was determined? Choose two.
options: Dr. Salma was a bulldozer, pushing through every failed experiment.
Her lab was as quiet as a library late at night.
Her patience was an anchor that held firm through years of setbacks.
Dr. Salma repeated the experiment forty times before it worked.
questions.why: Both metaphors show strength that does not give up; the others are literal or about something else.

questions.stem: True or false: The sentence “The news hit the village like an earthquake” is a metaphor because it compares news to an earthquake.
questions.why: It uses like, so it is a simile, not a metaphor.

questions.stem: Part A: Read the sentence: “Time crawled through the last hour of the exam, dragging its heavy feet.” What effect does the figurative language create?

partA.stem: Part A: Read the sentence: “Time crawled through the last hour of the exam, dragging its heavy feet.” What effect does the figurative language create?

options.label: A
options.text: It suggests that the students finished the exam early.

options.label: B
options.text: It makes the hour seem slow and difficult to endure.

options.label: C
options.text: It shows that the exam was easy for the students.

options.label: D
options.text: It explains why the clock in the room was broken.

partB.stem: Part B: Which words in the sentence create this effect?

options.label: A
options.text: the last hour

options.label: B
options.text: of the exam

options.label: C
options.text: crawled; dragging its heavy feet

options.label: D
options.text: Time

questions.why: Crawling and dragging heavy feet personify time as moving slowly and painfully.

questions.stem: Choose the word that best completes the extended metaphor: “Memory is a desert archive; each storm buries some pages and ____ others.”
options: uncovers
forgets
burns
writes
questions.why: Storms both bury and uncover things in sand, so uncovers keeps the metaphor consistent.

questions.stem: Which revision turns the plain sentence “The city was busy at night” into personification?
options: The city never closed its eyes, humming to itself until dawn.
The city was a beehive that buzzed until dawn.
The city had a billion cars rushing around until dawn.
The city at night was like a beehive, buzzing busily until dawn.
questions.why: Closing eyes and humming are human actions; the others are a simile, a metaphor, and hyperbole.

questions.stem: Select two sentences in this description of an old lighthouse that use personification.

segments.text: The lighthouse stood at the edge of the cliff for two hundred years.
Every night it kept watch over the restless sea, refusing to sleep.
Its stone walls were cracked and covered in salt.
Sailors trusted its single eye to guide them past the rocks.
Its light reached about thirty kilometers.

questions.why: Keeping watch, refusing to sleep, and having an eye give the lighthouse human traits.

questions.stem: Match each figurative sentence about technology to the meaning it most likely suggests.

pairs.left: My phone is a leash that keeps me tied to work.
pairs.right: Technology can limit a person's freedom.

pairs.left: The new app spread through the school like wildfire.
The old computer wheezed through every task.
pairs.right: A machine worked slowly and with difficulty.

pairs.left: This laptop weighs less than a feather.

questions.why: Interpret figurative language by asking what the two things have in common.

questions.stem: Part A: Read the sentence: “Ibn Battuta's curiosity was a compass that never stopped spinning, pointing him toward one more city, one more coast.” What does the metaphor suggest about Ibn Battuta?

partA.stem: Part A: Read the sentence: “Ibn Battuta's curiosity was a compass that never stopped spinning, pointing him toward one more city, one more coast.” What does the metaphor suggest about Ibn Battuta?

options.label: A
options.text: He wanted to return home after visiting each city.

options.label: B
options.text: His restless curiosity kept leading him to new places.

options.label: C
options.text: He depended on a compass to find his way at sea.

options.label: D
options.text: He often became lost and confused during his travels.

partB.stem: Part B: Which part of the sentence most strongly supports the answer to Part A?

options.label: A
options.text: Ibn Battuta's curiosity

options.label: B
options.text: pointing him toward one more city, one more coast

options.label: C
options.text: a compass

options.label: D
options.text: never stopped spinning

questions.why: The compass points him to new cities, showing curiosity directing his travels.

questions.stem: True or false: The sentence “The stadium held perhaps forty thousand people” is hyperbole because the number is very large.
questions.why: A large but realistic estimate is literal; hyperbole is deliberate, impossible exaggeration.

questions.stem: In which sentence does hyperbole serve mainly to criticize rather than to praise?
options: The committee took a geological age to approve a single bench for the park.
The architect's design was so elegant it could make a mountain feel humble.
The volunteers' kindness was a lamp that lit the darkest streets.
The new bridge glittered like a necklace across the river at night.
questions.why: A geological age mocks the committee's slowness; the other sentences praise.

questions.stem: Classify each sentence about a scientist's discovery by the main figurative device it uses.

rows.text: The data refused to cooperate, hiding its pattern behind random noise.
Al-Biruni's measurements were a ladder that later astronomers climbed.
The answer arrived as quietly as dawn over an empty desert.
The equation sat on the board, daring anyone to solve it.
Each failed trial was a stone in the foundation of her success.

questions.why: Look for like/as (simile), a direct identity (metaphor), or human behavior (personification).

questions.stem: Read these lines from an original poem: “The highway is a river of light / that never reaches the sea; / it murmurs to the sleeping town / of places it will never be.” Which THREE statements about the figurative language are accurate? Choose three.
options: The image suggests constant movement without a final destination.
The highway is compared directly to a river in a metaphor.
The highway is given the human ability to murmur.
The town is personified as awake and listening closely.
The lines exaggerate the highway's length for humorous effect.
A simile with the word like compares the town to the sea.
questions.why: The highway is a river (metaphor) that murmurs (personification) and never arrives.

questions.stem: Part A: Read the sentence: “Progress, that tireless engine, rolls forward over the old souqs, and few stop to ask what it flattens beneath its wheels.” What attitude toward progress does the figurative language most likely convey?

partA.stem: Part A: Read the sentence: “Progress, that tireless engine, rolls forward over the old souqs, and few stop to ask what it flattens beneath its wheels.” What attitude toward progress does the figurative language most likely convey?

options.label: A
options.text: admiration for the speed of modern progress

options.label: B
options.text: confusion about how engines and wheels work

options.label: C
options.text: indifference to changes in the old markets

options.label: D
options.text: concern that progress destroys valued things

partB.stem: Part B: Which phrase from the sentence best supports the answer to Part A?

options.label: A
options.text: what it flattens beneath its wheels

options.label: B
options.text: over the old souqs

options.label: C
options.text: that tireless engine

options.label: D
options.text: rolls forward

questions.why: Flattening the old markets shows the writer worries about what progress destroys.

questions.stem: Would you say each sentence to a friend or to a teacher?

rows.text: Hey, wanna play?
Good morning, Ms. Noor.
May I please borrow a pencil?
See ya later!

questions.why: We use polite, formal words with teachers and casual words with friends.

questions.stem: Match each informal word to its formal word.
questions.why: Formal English uses complete, standard words.

questions.stem: Choose the polite words to ask a teacher for help: “____ help me with this word?”
options: Hey, can ya
Could you please
You gotta
questions.why: Could you please is a polite, formal way to ask.

questions.stem: Which is the best way to greet the school principal?
options: Yo, Mr. Saleh!
Hi, buddy!
Good morning, Mr. Saleh.
Hey there, Mr. Saleh, what's up?
questions.why: A principal should be greeted politely and formally.

questions.stem: True or false: “Thanks a bunch!” is a polite and formal way to thank a guest speaker.
questions.why: A formal thank-you would be “Thank you very much for visiting us.”

questions.stem: Decide whether each sentence about a school trip is formal or informal.

rows.text: The museum visit was informative.
The museum was kinda boring.
We were grateful for the guide's help.
The guide was a cool dude.

questions.why: Slang such as kinda and cool dude is informal.

questions.stem: Which sentence is written in formal English for a school report?
options: You won't believe how long camels can last without water!
Camels can go for ages without a drink, which is awesome.
Camels can travel for many days without drinking water.
Camels are, like, super good at going without water.
questions.why: Reports use clear, standard words without slang.

questions.stem: Choose the most formal words to complete the sentence for a class presentation: “The results of our survey ____ that most students walk to school.”
options: tell ya
indicate
kinda show
pretty much say
questions.why: Indicate is a precise, formal verb.

questions.stem: Mona is writing an email to invite a scientist to speak at her school. Which TWO sentences are formal enough for this email? Choose two.
options: Just tell us whenever you're free, okay?
It'd be awesome if you could swing by our class.
Please let us know which date works best for you.
We would be honored if you could visit our class.
questions.why: An invitation to an adult guest should be polite and formal.

questions.stem: Find the part that is too informal in this sentence from a science report: “The experiment showed that plants grow faster in sunlight, which is totally cool.”
questions.why: Totally cool is slang and does not belong in a report.

questions.stem: Choose the best words for a formal science report: “The scientists ____ the samples for three weeks.”
options: checked out
observed
looked at stuff in
kept an eye on
questions.why: Observed is the precise, formal choice.

questions.stem: Match each informal phrase to a formal replacement suitable for an academic essay.
questions.why: Academic writing prefers single, precise verbs and words.

questions.stem: Find the informal part of this sentence from a book review for the school website: “The novel's main character faces many challenges, but she totally nails it by the final chapter.”
questions.why: Totally nails it is slang; overcomes them keeps a formal tone.

questions.stem: True or false: Contractions such as can't and won't are usually acceptable in a friendly message but are often avoided in a formal research report.
questions.why: Formal academic writing usually spells out cannot and will not.

questions.stem: Which revision makes the sentence “Kids these days spend way too much time on their phones” appropriate for a formal argument essay?
options: Lots of kids spend a really huge amount of time on their phones.
Young people are always on their phones, which is a massive problem.
Kids nowadays spend way more time than they should on their phones.
Many young people spend an excessive amount of time on their phones.
questions.why: Excessive and young people replace the slang way too much and kids.

questions.stem: Decide whether each sentence would fit better in a formal email to a company or in a casual message to a cousin.

rows.text: I am writing to request information about your internship program.
Guess what? I'm applying for an internship!
Thank you for considering my application.
Can't wait to hear back from them, fingers crossed.

questions.why: Match the register to the audience and purpose.

questions.stem: Choose the phrase that keeps a formal tone: “The council's decision, ____, will affect thousands of residents.”
options: no offense to them
although well intended
which, honestly, was kind of dumb
even though they meant well and all
questions.why: Although well intended is concise and formal.

questions.stem: Which THREE changes would make this sentence more formal: “So, basically, the city's gotta fix the roads 'cause they're super dangerous”? Choose three.
options: Replace the city's gotta with the city must.
Replace super dangerous with hazardous.
Add an exclamation point at the end.
Replace the city's with the city is.
Replace roads with streets.
Remove the words So, basically.
questions.why: Remove filler words and replace slang with standard vocabulary.

questions.stem: Find the part that shifts to an informal tone in this sentence from a history essay: “In the ninth century, the House of Wisdom in Baghdad attracted scholars from many regions, and it was seriously the place to be.”
segments: the House of Wisdom in Baghdad
and it was seriously the place to be.
questions.correction: and it became a major center of learning.
questions.why: Seriously the place to be is conversational slang.

questions.stem: Part A: Read the draft sentence from a formal presentation: “Recycling programs are a no-brainer for our city.” Which problem does the sentence have?

partA.stem: Part A: Read the draft sentence from a formal presentation: “Recycling programs are a no-brainer for our city.” Which problem does the sentence have?

options.label: A
options.text: It uses too many technical terms for the audience.

options.label: B
options.text: It presents a fact instead of a claim.

options.label: C
options.text: It uses slang that is too informal for the audience.

options.label: D
options.text: It does not include a subject or a verb.

partB.stem: Part B: Which revision best fixes the problem identified in Part A?

options.label: A
options.text: Recycling programs are a no-brainer, in my opinion, for our city.

options.label: B
options.text: Recycling programs are a sensible choice for our city.

options.label: C
options.text: Recycling is a total no-brainer for any city like ours.

options.label: D
options.text: Our city really, really needs recycling programs.

questions.why: No-brainer is slang; a sensible choice states the claim formally.

questions.stem: Choose the word that best fits the formal register of this sentence: “The committee will ____ the proposal before the final decision.”
options: evaluate
run through
eyeball
mull over a bit
questions.why: Evaluate is precise and formal.

questions.stem: A student is writing a cover email for a summer research program. Which sentence best maintains a formal, professional tone?
options: I'm honestly super excited because this program sounds amazing and perfect for me.
I think I would totally be a great fit for your awesome research program this summer.

questions.stem: Find the part with an inappropriately informal tone in this sentence from a research paper on solar energy: “Although initial installation costs remain high, solar panels reduce long-term energy expenses, and in sunny regions they pay for themselves in no time flat.”
segments: Although initial installation costs remain high,
solar panels reduce long-term energy expenses,
and in sunny regions they pay for themselves
questions.why: In no time flat is an idiom too casual for a research paper.

questions.stem: Select two sentences in this paragraph from a formal report on water use that shift into an informal tone.

segments.text: Agriculture accounts for the largest share of freshwater use in the region.
Farmers have begun adopting drip irrigation to conserve resources.
Honestly, it's about time they figured that out.
Drip systems deliver water directly to plant roots.
This approach can lower water use by up to half, which is pretty awesome.

questions.why: Honestly, about time, and pretty awesome are casual and opinionated.

questions.stem: True or false: Writing in the passive voice, such as “Mistakes were made,” automatically makes a sentence formal and appropriate for any academic audience.
questions.why: Formality comes from word choice and audience; passive voice can also make writing vague.

questions.stem: In which situation would a writer most reasonably choose an informal register?
options: a summary of research findings submitted to a university journal
a complaint sent to the customer service department of an airline
a personal blog post sharing tips with fellow students about study habits
a grant proposal requesting funds from a national science foundation
questions.why: A peer audience in a personal blog allows a relaxed, conversational tone.

questions.stem: Match each informal expression to the formal equivalent that best preserves its meaning in an academic essay.
questions.why: A formal equivalent must keep the exact meaning of the idiom.

questions.stem: Classify each revision of “The study's findings are kind of shaky” by its register.

rows.text: The study's findings are not fully reliable.
The study's findings are pretty sketchy.
The findings of the aforementioned study are, in a manner of speaking, of a nature lacking in reliability.
The study's conclusions rest on limited evidence.

questions.why: Good formal writing is precise and concise, not slangy or inflated.

questions.stem: A graduate is writing a speech for a formal ceremony attended by officials and families. Which TWO sentences strike the most appropriate register, formal but not stiff? Choose two.
options: Shout-out to all the teachers who put up with us for four whole years!
Tonight we honor the teachers whose patience shaped who we have become.
Pursuant to the aforementioned achievements, gratitude is hereby extended to all faculty.
We leave this school grateful, prepared, and ready to serve our communities.
questions.why: The best register respects the occasion without sounding like a legal document.

questions.stem: Part A: Read the sentence from a formal opinion column: “Critics who dismiss the new transit plan as a waste of money simply haven't done their homework.” Which phrase is least consistent with a formal register?

partA.stem: Part A: Read the sentence from a formal opinion column: “Critics who dismiss the new transit plan as a waste of money simply haven't done their homework.” Which phrase is least consistent with a formal register?

options.label: A

options.label: B

options.label: C

options.label: D
options.text: a waste of money

partB.stem: Part B: Which revision best maintains a formal register while keeping the writer's claim?

options.label: B

options.label: C

options.label: D
options.text: Critics who dismiss the new transit plan are mistaken, period.

questions.why: Haven't done their homework is a casual idiom; overlooked key evidence makes the same point formally.

questions.stem: Is each group of words a complete sentence or not a complete sentence?

rows.text: The bird sings.
Under the big tree.
My brother reads a book.
Ran to the park.

questions.why: A complete sentence tells who or what and what happens.

questions.stem: Choose the words that finish the sentence: “The little camel ____.”
options: so tall and
in the sand
drinks water
questions.why: The sentence needs an action word, drinks.

questions.stem: Which is a complete sentence?
options: The little green frog near the pond.
Into the pond.
The frog jumps into the pond.
Jumps into the pond quickly.
questions.why: It has a naming part (the frog) and an action part (jumps).

questions.stem: True or false: “At the beach with my dad.” is a complete sentence.
questions.why: It does not tell what happened, so it is not complete.

questions.stem: Find the part that needs a fix in “I like apples I like grapes too.”
questions.why: Two sentences need an end mark between them.

questions.stem: Which TWO are sentence fragments? Choose two.
options: The bus was late this morning.
Because the bus was late.
After the long soccer game in the rain.
We played soccer in the rain.
questions.why: A fragment is missing a complete thought.

questions.stem: Choose the word that correctly joins the two sentences: “Laila finished her homework, ____ she went outside to play.”
options: then
she
and
questions.why: A comma plus and correctly joins two complete sentences.

questions.stem: Label each group of words about a science fair as a complete sentence, a fragment, or a run-on.

rows.text: Our volcano model won second place.
Mixing baking soda with vinegar.
The volcano erupted everyone clapped.
While the judges watched closely.

questions.why: Fragments are incomplete; run-ons join sentences without correct punctuation.

questions.stem: Which is the best way to fix the run-on sentence “The storm was loud we hid under the blanket”?
options: The storm was loud and, we hid under the blanket.
The storm was loud we hid, under the blanket.
The storm, was loud we hid under the blanket.
The storm was loud, so we hid under the blanket.
questions.why: A comma and so correctly joins the two sentences.

questions.stem: Find the part that makes this a run-on: “Our class visited the aquarium we saw a shark at feeding time.”
questions.why: Two complete thoughts need a joining word or an end mark.

questions.stem: Select the sentence fragment in this paragraph about sea turtles.

segments.text: Sea turtles return to the same beaches to lay their eggs.
Scientists are still studying how they find their way.
Possibly by sensing the Earth's magnetic field.
Many turtle nests are now protected by volunteers.

questions.why: It has no subject or main verb.

questions.stem: Decide whether each sentence about a basketball tournament is correct or a run-on.

rows.text: Our team lost the first game, but we won the next three.
The coach called a time-out the players gathered around her.
The final was close, our captain scored in the last second.
Although we were tired, we played with energy.

questions.why: A comma alone cannot join two independent clauses.

questions.stem: Choose the punctuation that correctly fixes the run-on: “The desert can be extremely hot during the day____ it can be freezing at night.”
options: , however
; however,
however,
questions.why: A semicolon before however and a comma after it join the clauses correctly.

questions.stem: Which revision correctly fixes the fragment in “The students cheered loudly. When the robot climbed the ramp.”?
options: The students cheered loudly. When the robot, climbed the ramp.
The students cheered loudly when the robot climbed the ramp.
The students cheered loudly; when the robot climbed the ramp.
The students cheered loudly, when the robot. Climbed the ramp.
questions.why: Attach the dependent clause to the main clause.

questions.stem: Part A: Read the sentence: “The museum opened a new exhibit on Al-Jazari, it features working models of his water clocks.” What is the error in the sentence?

partA.stem: Part A: Read the sentence: “The museum opened a new exhibit on Al-Jazari, it features working models of his water clocks.” What is the error in the sentence?

options.label: A
options.text: It is missing a subject.

options.label: B
options.text: It has no error.

options.label: C

options.label: D
options.text: It is a comma splice.

partB.stem: Part B: Which revision corrects the error?

options.label: A
options.text: The museum opened a new exhibit on Al-Jazari; it features working models of his water clocks.

options.label: B
options.text: The museum opened a new exhibit on Al-Jazari, featuring, working models of his water clocks.

options.label: C
options.text: The museum opened a new exhibit, on Al-Jazari, it features working models of his water clocks.

options.label: D
options.text: The museum opened a new exhibit on Al-Jazari it features working models of his water clocks.

questions.why: A semicolon can join two closely related independent clauses.

questions.stem: True or false: “Having studied the map carefully before the hike through Wadi Rum.” is a complete sentence because it is long and has a verb form.
questions.why: A participle phrase has no subject and main verb, so it is a fragment.

questions.stem: Match each word group about recycling to the best description.

pairs.left: Plastic bottles that are collected each week.
The bins were full, nobody emptied them.
The bins were full nobody emptied them.
The bins were full, so the workers emptied them.

questions.why: A comma splice has a comma; a fused sentence has no punctuation at all.

questions.stem: Which TWO revisions correctly fix the run-on “Solar panels are becoming cheaper more families are installing them”? Choose two.
options: Solar panels are becoming cheaper, so more families are installing them.
Solar panels are becoming cheaper, more families are installing them.
Because solar panels are becoming cheaper, more families are installing them.
Solar panels are becoming cheaper so, more families are installing them.
questions.why: Use a comma with a conjunction or make one clause dependent.

questions.stem: Which sentence is complete and correctly punctuated?
options: Although the bridge was old, and engineers decided to repair it rather than replace it.
Because the bridge was old and engineers decided to repair it rather than replace it.
The bridge was old, engineers decided to repair it rather than replace it.
Although the bridge was old, engineers decided to repair it rather than replace it.
questions.why: A dependent clause followed by an independent clause forms a complete sentence.

questions.stem: Find the error in this sentence about a marathon: “The marathon began at dawn, thousands of runners crowded the street, and the city cheered as they passed.”
segments: thousands of runners crowded the street,
questions.why: The first two independent clauses are joined by only a comma.

questions.stem: Choose the option that correctly completes the sentence without creating a run-on: “The researchers tested the water at twelve sites____ only two met safety standards.”
options: but,
; but,
, but
questions.why: A comma before the conjunction but joins two independent clauses.

questions.stem: Classify each sentence about a coding competition.

rows.text: The team that finished first, whose code ran in under a second.
The judges reviewed every program, then they announced the winners.
Although the problem looked simple, most teams needed the full three hours.
The final round, which began at noon, lasted three hours.
Debugging took longer than expected the team still submitted on time.

questions.why: Then is not a conjunction, so a comma before it creates a splice.

questions.stem: Select two sentences in this paragraph about early aviation that are fragments.

segments.text: In the ninth century, Abbas ibn Firnas attempted to glide from a hill near Córdoba.
Wearing a frame of wood and silk covered with feathers.
Later writers reported that he stayed in the air for a short time.
His landing, however, was rough.
A reminder that a safe landing matters as much as a takeoff.

questions.why: Neither word group has a subject with a main verb.

questions.stem: True or false: The sentence “Stop.” is a fragment because it contains only one word.
questions.why: It is a command with the understood subject you, so it is complete.

questions.stem: Part A: Read the sentences: “The new law protects mangrove forests along the coast. Which serve as nurseries for many fish species.” What is the problem with the second group of words?

partA.stem: Part A: Read the sentences: “The new law protects mangrove forests along the coast. Which serve as nurseries for many fish species.” What is the problem with the second group of words?

options.label: A
options.text: It joins two independent clauses with only a comma.

options.label: B
options.text: It is a dependent clause punctuated as a sentence.

options.label: C

options.label: D
options.text: It is an independent clause missing a conjunction.

partB.stem: Part B: Which revision best corrects the problem?

options.label: A
options.text: The new law protects mangrove forests along the coast. Serving as nurseries for many fish species.

options.label: B
options.text: The new law protects mangrove forests along the coast, which serve as nurseries for many fish species.

options.text: The new law protects mangrove forests along the coast which, serve as nurseries for many fish species.

options.label: D
options.text: The new law protects mangrove forests along the coast; which serve as nurseries for many fish species.

questions.why: Attach the relative clause to the sentence with a comma.

questions.stem: Find the error in this sentence about the observatory at Maragha: “Built in the thirteenth century, the observatory at Maragha housed instruments of remarkable precision, its astronomers produced tables that scholars used for generations.”
segments: the observatory at Maragha housed instruments of remarkable precision,
questions.why: Two independent clauses joined by only a comma form a comma splice.

questions.stem: Which revision of the run-on “The drought lasted three years the farmers adopted new irrigation methods” is correct and best shows the relationship between the ideas?
options: The drought lasted three years, the farmers adopted new irrigation methods.
The drought lasted three years, and, the farmers adopted new irrigation methods.
The drought lasted three years; however the farmers adopted new irrigation methods.
Because the drought lasted three years, the farmers adopted new irrigation methods.
questions.why: Because shows cause and effect and creates a correct complex sentence.

questions.stem: Which THREE of these word groups are complete sentences? Choose three.
options: Seldom has a single invention changed daily life so quickly.
The surgeon who pioneered the technique, having trained in Damascus for a decade.
What the committee decided surprised no one.
Go.
Whereas earlier maps had relied on rumor and guesswork.
A discovery that, despite decades of skepticism, finally changed the field.
questions.why: Length does not decide completeness; a subject and a main verb do.

questions.stem: Decide whether each sentence about the history of paper is correct or contains a fragment or run-on error.

rows.text: Papermaking spread from China to Samarkand, and by the late eighth century Baghdad had its own paper mills.
Paper replaced parchment in many offices, it was cheaper and easier to produce.
A material so cheap and portable that it transformed record keeping across the region.
Not only did paper lower costs, but it also made books far more common.
Scholars copied texts quickly, libraries grew larger as a result.

questions.why: Check every sentence for a main clause and for correctly joined clauses.

questions.stem: Part A: Read the draft: “The expedition reached the summit at dawn. Exhausted but triumphant, their flags whipping in the wind.” Why is the second word group incorrect?

partA.stem: Part A: Read the draft: “The expedition reached the summit at dawn. Exhausted but triumphant, their flags whipping in the wind.” Why is the second word group incorrect?

options.label: A

options.label: B
options.text: It uses a participle as a main verb, creating a run-on.

options.label: C

options.label: D
options.text: It contains a dangling modifier but is otherwise complete.

partB.stem: Part B: Which revision corrects the error while keeping the writer's meaning?

options.text: The expedition reached the summit at dawn; exhausted but triumphant, their flags whipping in the wind.

options.label: B

options.text: The expedition reached the summit at dawn. Exhausted but triumphant; their flags whipping in the wind.

questions.why: The modifiers must attach to a main clause; a semicolon still needs an independent clause after it.

questions.stem: Match each number root to what it means.
questions.why: Number roots tell how many.

questions.stem: The root bi means “two.” A bicycle has ____ wheels.
options: four
three
two
questions.why: Bi means two.

questions.stem: The root tri means “three.” What is a tricycle?
options: a bike with four wheels
a bike with three wheels
a bike with two wheels
a bike with one big wheel
questions.why: Tri means three, so a tricycle has three wheels.

questions.stem: True or false: The root graph means “write,” so an autograph is a name that a person writes.
questions.why: An autograph is a person's own written name.

questions.stem: Does each word have the root tele, which means “far”?

rows.text: telephone
television
table
tiger

questions.why: Tele words are about things far away.

questions.stem: Match each Greek or Latin root to its meaning.
questions.why: Knowing a root helps you guess the meaning of many words.

questions.stem: The root port means “carry.” Choose the word that best completes the sentence: Trucks ____ dates from the farm to the market.
options: transport
support
report
questions.why: Transport means to carry across from one place to another.

questions.stem: The root therm means “heat.” What does a thermos most likely do?
options: keeps drinks hot or cold
writes notes in a notebook
measures how far you walk
shows pictures of the sky
questions.why: A thermos controls the heat of a drink.

questions.stem: Which TWO words have a root that means “to see”? Choose two.
options: spectator
sonic
audience
vision
questions.why: Vis and spect mean see; son means sound and aud means hear.

rows.text: geology
biology
hydrant
biome
geography

questions.why: The root tells what the word is about.

options: erupt
interrupt
corrupt

questions.stem: Decide whether each word contains the root meaning “sound” (phon) or the root meaning “light” (photo).

rows.text: symphony
photograph
microphone
photosynthesis

questions.why: Phon relates to sound; photo relates to light.

questions.stem: The Greek root chron means “time.” Which word means “arranged in the order in which events happened”?
options: chronic
synchronous
anachronistic
chronological
questions.why: Chronological order follows time from first to last.

questions.stem: Find the word that is used incorrectly because of its root: “The biologist used a telescope to study the tiny cells, which were invisible without magnification.”
questions.why: Tele means far; micro means small, so a microscope views tiny cells.

questions.stem: Part A: Read the sentence: “The new bridge is a structure that is meant to be durable, lasting for more than a century.” The Latin root dur means “hard” or “lasting.” What does durable mean?

options.label: C

options.label: D

questions.stem: The root bene means “good” and mal means “bad.” A ____ tumor is not harmful to the body.
options: malignant
benevolent
malicious
benign

questions.stem: Match each word built from the root graph or gram (“write”) to its meaning.

pairs.right: a written account of a person's life
a written message sent over a distance
an instrument that records earthquake movement

questions.stem: The Latin root aud means “hear.” Which TWO words contain this root with that meaning? Choose two.
options: auditorium
applaud
audacious
audible
questions.why: Audacious comes from a root meaning bold, and applaud comes from plaud, to clap.

questions.stem: True or false: The words manuscript and manufacture share the Latin root man, meaning “hand,” because both originally referred to things done by hand.
questions.why: A manuscript was written by hand, and manufacture once meant made by hand.

questions.stem: The Greek root path means “feeling,” and the prefix sym- means “together with.” What does sympathy most likely mean?
options: a lack of interest in others
sharing in another person's feelings
a feeling of being very tired
a strong dislike of other people's habits
questions.why: Sym + path means feeling together with someone.

questions.stem: The root ver means “truth.” In the sentence “The journalist worked to ____ every claim before publishing her report,” which word fits best?
options: revere
verbalize
diversify
verify
questions.why: Verify means to confirm that something is true.

questions.stem: Classify each word by the meaning of its Latin root.

rows.text: conductor
transmit
infer
deduce
emissary

questions.why: Separate the prefix from the root to find the core meaning.

questions.stem: The Greek root anthrop means “human,” and the Greek root phil means “love.” Which word describes a person who donates generously to improve the lives of others?
options: philanthropist
philosopher
anthropologist
misanthrope
questions.why: A philanthropist loves humanity and acts to help people.

questions.stem: Find the word that is misused because of its Greek or Latin roots: “The geneticist's lecture on ancient fossils of extinct animals was so fascinating that the audience listened in rapt silence.”
segments: on ancient fossils of extinct animals
that the audience listened in rapt silence.
questions.why: Paleo means ancient; a paleontologist studies fossils, while a geneticist studies genes.

questions.stem: The Greek roots pan (“all”) and demos (“people”) form pandemic. Which word built from demos describes a disease regularly found among the people of a particular region?
options: demographic
endemic
pandemic
epidemic

rows.text: metamorphosis
circumscribe
reflexive
amorphous
inflection

questions.why: Find the root inside the prefixes and suffixes.

questions.stem: Which THREE words share the Latin root cred, meaning “believe” or “trust”? Choose three.
options: credulous
incredible
decree
credentials
accrue
crescendo

questions.stem: Match each word built from the Latin root vid/vis (“see”) or the Greek root scope (“look at”) to its meaning.

pairs.right: a person who imagines future possibilities
an instrument that shows changing patterns
an instrument for seeing above an obstacle

questions.why: Improvise means not foreseen, and provident means seeing ahead.

questions.stem: Choose the right word: We ate ____ cookies after lunch.
options: to
too
two

pairs.right: the star that lights the day

questions.stem: Which word sounds like “flower” but means the powder used to make bread?
options: flow
flour
flier
floor
questions.why: Flour and flower are homophones.

questions.stem: Is the word their or there used correctly in each sentence?

Their dog is brown.
I put the box their.
There cat is sleeping.

questions.why: There tells where; their tells who owns something.

questions.stem: True or false: In “The bat flew out of the cave,” the word bat means a stick used to hit a ball.

questions.stem: Choose the correct word: “Please ____ the bread into pieces for the birds.”
options: brick
break
brake

questions.stem: Decide which meaning of the homograph bow is used in each sentence.

The branches bow under the weight of the ripe fruit.
A bow held her hair in place.

questions.why: Other words in the sentence show which meaning fits.

questions.stem: Which TWO sentences use the homophone correctly? Choose two.
options: The sky was a bright, clear blew.
We road our bikes to the park.
We rode our bikes to the park.
The wind blew the sand across the road.
questions.why: Blew is the past of blow; blue is a color. Rode is the past of ride; road is a street.

questions.stem: In the sentence “The doctor wound a bandage around the wound,” how are the two words wound different?
options: They are spelled differently and mean the same thing.
They have the same meaning but are said in different ways.
They sound the same but are spelled differently and mean different things.
They are spelled the same but have different sounds and meanings.

segments: a hole room of old maps.
questions.correction: a whole room of old maps.
questions.why: Whole means all of something; a hole is an opening.

questions.stem: Choose the correct homophone: “The pyramid's ____ is a perfect square.”
options: bays
bass
base

questions.stem: Match each homophone to the sentence it correctly completes.

Honesty is an important ____ in our family.
The bus remained ____ during the sandstorm.
She wrote the thank-you note on blue ____.

questions.why: Stationary means not moving; stationery is writing paper.

questions.stem: Decide whether each pair of words is a pair of homophones or a pair of homographs.

lead (a metal) / lead (to guide)
tear (to rip) / tear (from crying)
weather / whether

questions.stem: Which sentence uses their, there, or they're correctly?
