partA.stem: Part A: Read the sentence: “The desert wind was so strong that the hikers had to wind their scarves tightly around their faces.” How is the second wind pronounced, and what does it mean?

options.label: A
options.text: It rhymes with pinned and means “to wrap.”

options.label: B
options.text: It rhymes with kind and means “moving air.”

options.label: C
options.text: It rhymes with kind and means “to wrap.”

options.label: D
options.text: It rhymes with pinned and means “moving air.”

partB.stem: Part B: Which words in the sentence help show the meaning of the second wind?

options.label: A
options.text: their scarves tightly around their faces

options.label: B
options.text: The desert wind was so strong

options.label: C
options.text: the hikers had to

options.label: D
options.text: so strong that

questions.why: Wrapping scarves around faces shows that wind means to wrap.

questions.stem: Choose the word that correctly completes the sentence: “The doctors hope the new medicine will ____ the patients faster.”
options: heel
heal
he'll
questions.why: Heal means to make healthy; a heel is part of the foot.

questions.stem: True or false: In “The farmers will produce more dates this year than last year,” the homograph produce is a noun meaning fruits and vegetables.
questions.why: After will, produce is a verb (pro-DUCE) meaning to grow or make.

questions.stem: Which TWO sentences use the homograph present as a verb (pronounced pre-ZENT)? Choose two.
options: Grandmother gave each child a small present.
Everyone in the class was present for the test.
The museum plans to present an award to the young inventor.
The students will present their research to the judges.
questions.why: As a verb, present means to show or give formally.

questions.stem: Select the sentence in this paragraph about a camel race that contains a misused homophone.

segments.text: The race began just after sunrise.
Each camel wore a colorful saddle.
Halfway through, the fastest camels reached there top speed.
By mid-morning, the winners were known.

questions.why: Their shows possession; there tells where.

questions.stem: Find the homophone error in this sentence about a sailing race: “The sailors pulled hard on the ropes as the boat sailed passed the lighthouse.”
questions.why: Past means beyond; passed is the past tense of pass.

questions.stem: Decide how the homograph object is used in each sentence.

rows.text: Several residents object to the new parking rules.
The archaeologists found a bronze object in the sand.
The object of the game is to reach the oasis first.
No one will object if you leave early.

questions.why: The stress and the part of speech change with the meaning.

questions.stem: Find the error in this sentence from a report on water conservation: “The city council complemented residents for reducing their water use by nearly a fifth.”
questions.why: Compliment means to praise; complement means to complete.

questions.stem: Which sentence uses every homophone correctly?
options: The engineer sited a study to explain why the cite was chosen.
The engineer cited a study to explain why the sight was chosen.
The engineer cited a study to explain why the site was chosen.
The engineer sighted a study to explain why the site was chosen.
questions.why: Cite means to quote as evidence; site means a location.

questions.stem: Which THREE sentences about a research trip use every homophone correctly? Choose three.
options: The team planned to pour over the maps all night.
The guide led us down a steep path to the cave.
The divers could not bare the cold water for long.
Everyone was allowed to speak aloud in the meeting.
The captain decided to wave the fee for students.
The researchers waited for the tide to turn before they tied the boat.
questions.why: Bear means endure, pore means study closely, and waive means cancel.

questions.stem: Part A: Read the sentence: “The new coach was determined to refuse every shortcut, even though the refuse from the old stadium still covered the field.” What does the second refuse mean?

partA.stem: Part A: Read the sentence: “The new coach was determined to refuse every shortcut, even though the refuse from the old stadium still covered the field.” What does the second refuse mean?

options.label: A
options.text: a place of safety

options.label: B
options.text: a strong rejection

options.label: C
options.text: trash or waste material

options.label: D
options.text: a group of players

partB.stem: Part B: Which clue in the sentence best signals this meaning?

options.label: A
options.text: was determined to

options.label: B
options.text: every shortcut

options.label: C
options.text: from the old stadium still covered the field

options.label: D
options.text: The new coach

questions.why: Something that covers a field from an old stadium is waste; REF-use is a noun.

questions.stem: Choose the word that correctly completes the sentence: “The harsh criticism did not ____ the young architect; she calmly revised her design.”
options: phrase
faze
phase
questions.why: Faze means to disturb or unsettle; a phase is a stage.

questions.stem: Decide whether each homograph in these sentences about a museum exhibit is stressed on the first or the second syllable.

rows.text: The curator was content with the final display.
The exhibit's content focused on early navigation tools.
Each label described a minute detail of the astrolabe.
The tour lasted only one minute longer than planned.
Visitors were asked not to record the guide's talk.

questions.why: Meaning and part of speech decide the stress: con-TENT (pleased) vs. CON-tent (material).

questions.stem: Select two sentences in this paragraph about a historian's research that contain a misused homophone.

segments.text: The historian spent months poring over records from the old port of Jeddah.
She was careful not to let her personal opinions affect her conclusions.
Each new document seemed to compliment the evidence she had already found.
Her final report treated each trading family as a discrete case study.
Several scholars later sited her work in their own studies.

questions.why: Complement means to complete, and cite means to quote; poring, affect, and discrete are correct.

questions.stem: Which sentence correctly uses both words in the pair council and counsel?
options: The counsel sought legal council before approving the new park.
The counsel sought legal counsel before approving the new park.
The council sought legal counsel before approving the new park.
The council sought legal council before approving the new park.
questions.why: A council is a group; counsel is advice.

questions.stem: True or false: In “The painter mixed colors on her palate before starting the mural,” every word is used correctly.
questions.why: A palette holds paint; the palate is the roof of the mouth.

questions.stem: True or false: The number word “twenty-one” is written with a hyphen.
questions.why: Number words from twenty-one to ninety-nine use a hyphen.

questions.stem: Choose the correct way to write the number: Sara has ____ crayons.
options: twentytwo
twenty two
twenty-two
questions.why: Two-word numbers like twenty-two are joined with a hyphen.

questions.stem: Does each number word about Sara's crayons need a hyphen?

rows.text: the word for 45 (forty five)
the word for 12 (twelve)
the word for 21 (twenty one)
the word for 100 (one hundred)

questions.why: Only numbers like 21 to 99 that join two number words need a hyphen.

questions.stem: Which sentence uses hyphens correctly?
options: I have a five year-old cat.
I have a five-year-old cat.
I have a five-year old cat.
I have a five year old-cat.
questions.why: All three words that describe the cat are joined: five-year-old.

questions.stem: Which TWO sentences use dots ( . . . ) to show a pause? Choose two.
options: Stop! The road is very wet.
Ali ran fast to the big park.
“Wait . . . I hear a bird,” said Mona.
“Um . . . I forgot my bag,” said Ali.
questions.why: Three dots can show that a speaker stops for a moment.

questions.stem: Choose the correct punctuation: The ____ runner won the race.
options: twelve-year-old
twelve year-old
twelve-year old
twelve year old
questions.why: Words that work together to describe a noun are joined with hyphens.

questions.stem: Which sentence uses a dash correctly to show a sudden break in thought?
options: I packed—my bag wait, where is my water bottle?
I packed my bag—wait, where is my water bottle?
I packed my—bag wait, where is my water bottle?
I packed my bag wait—, where is my water bottle?
questions.why: The dash goes exactly where the thought breaks off.

questions.stem: Tell which mark is used in each sentence about the school trip.

rows.text: We took a well-planned trip to the museum.
The guide—a tall woman with a cheerful voice—led us inside.
“The next room is . . .” she said, and then she stopped.
My best friend is a fast-moving swimmer.

questions.why: A hyphen joins words, a dash sets off extra information, and an ellipsis shows a pause or missing words.

questions.stem: Find the mistake in the sentence about the lifeguard's rule.
questions.why: Well-known comes before the noun it describes, so it needs a hyphen.

questions.stem: Which TWO sentences use an ellipsis correctly? Choose two.
options: The sign said, “Visitors must . . . stay on the path.”
We bought apples . . . , bananas, and grapes at the market.
The sign said, “Visitors must stay on the path . .”
“I think . . . no, I am sure the answer is seven,” said Reem.
questions.why: An ellipsis has three dots and shows a pause or words left out.

questions.stem: Which sentence correctly uses a hyphen in a compound modifier?
options: The museum opened a-hands on exhibit about falcons.
The museum opened a hands-on exhibit about falcons.
The museum opened a hands on-exhibit about falcons.
The museum opened a hands-on-exhibit about falcons.
questions.why: Only the words that form the modifier (hands-on) are joined, not the noun.

questions.stem: Choose the punctuation that best introduces the list: Ibn Battuta visited many lands ____ Egypt, Persia, India, and China.
questions.why: A dash can introduce a list that explains what came before it.

questions.stem: Is the hyphen correct in each sentence about the science fair?

rows.text: Our project used a solar-powered fan.
The judges were very-impressed by it.
Hamad wrote a two-page report.
The results were clearly-shown on a chart.

questions.why: Do not hyphenate an adverb like very or one ending in -ly.

questions.stem: Find the punctuation error in the sentence about the uncle who is a pilot.
questions.why: Interrupting information that opens with a dash must close with a dash.

questions.stem: A student shortens this quotation: “The camel, which can drink up to 100 liters of water in a few minutes, is well suited to desert life.” Which version uses an ellipsis correctly?
options: “The camel which . . . is well suited to desert life.”
“The camel, . . . a few minutes, is well suited to desert life.”
“The camel can drink . . . 100 liters of water in a few minutes.”
“The camel . . . is well suited to desert life.”
questions.why: An ellipsis may remove a whole clause, but the words left must stay grammatical and keep the meaning.

questions.stem: The ____ scientist Ibn al-Haytham studied how light enters the eye.
options: eleventh-centuries
eleventh century
eleventh-century
questions.why: A compound adjective before a noun takes a hyphen.

questions.stem: Does each word made from a prefix need a hyphen?

rows.text: self + confident
re + build
ex + captain
pre + Islamic
un + usual

questions.why: Self- and ex- take hyphens, and so does a prefix before a capital letter.

questions.stem: Find the error in the sentence about the first- and second-place winners.
questions.why: In a suspended compound, the first word keeps its hyphen: first- and second-place.

questions.stem: Which revision correctly uses punctuation to set off and emphasize the final phrase? “Only one thing could stop the rally driver a sudden sandstorm.”
options: Only one thing could stop the rally—driver a sudden sandstorm.
Only one thing could stop the rally driver; a sudden sandstorm.
Only one thing could stop the rally driver - a sudden - sandstorm.
Only one thing could stop the rally driver—a sudden sandstorm.
questions.why: A single dash before a final phrase sets it off with strong emphasis.

questions.stem: Which THREE sentences use dashes, hyphens, or ellipses correctly? Choose three.
options: The robot's arm—made of light aluminum—lifted the box with ease.
Faisal paused. “I suppose . . . we could try again.”
The well-trained falcon returned to its owner.
The robot's arm—made of light aluminum, lifted the box with ease.
The falcon was highly-trained by its owner.
questions.why: Pair dashes, use an ellipsis for a pause, and never hyphenate an -ly adverb.

questions.stem: Choose the punctuation that correctly completes the sentence: Patience, precision, and curiosity ____ these were the qualities that made al-Biruni a great scientist.
questions.why: A dash links an opening list to the clause that sums it up.

questions.stem: Which sentence about the new bridge uses hyphens correctly?
options: The newly built bridge carries a high-speed rail line.
The newly-built bridge carries a high-speed-rail line.
The newly-built bridge carries a high speed rail line.
The newly built bridge carries a high speed-rail line.
questions.why: Do not hyphenate an -ly adverb, but do hyphenate a compound adjective like high-speed.

questions.stem: Find the error in the sentence about the suspension bridge built in 2019.
questions.why: A number and unit that describe a noun are joined with a hyphen.

questions.stem: Decide whether each sentence about the coral reef survey is punctuated correctly.

rows.text: The divers—all trained volunteers—counted the fish.
The divers—all trained volunteers, counted the fish.
The survey covered a two-kilometer-long stretch of reef.
The survey's results were widely-reported in the news.
The leader wrote, “Our count . . . shows a strong recovery.”

questions.why: Dashes come in matching pairs, and -ly adverbs are never hyphenated.

questions.stem: Part A: A student quotes this sentence: “The ancient harbor, which traders from India and East Africa visited every year, slowly filled with silt after the river changed course.” Which shortened quotation uses an ellipsis correctly without changing the meaning?

partA.stem: Part A: A student quotes this sentence: “The ancient harbor, which traders from India and East Africa visited every year, slowly filled with silt after the river changed course.” Which shortened quotation uses an ellipsis correctly without changing the meaning?

options.label: A
options.text: “The ancient harbor, which traders . . . visited every year, slowly filled with silt.”

options.label: B
options.text: “The ancient harbor, which traders from India . . . slowly filled with silt after the river changed course.”

options.label: C
options.text: “The ancient harbor . . . slowly filled with silt after the river changed course.”

options.label: D
options.text: “The ancient harbor . . . filled with silt . . . the river changed course.”

partB.stem: Part B: Which statement best explains why the answer to Part A is correct?

options.label: A
options.text: It removes a complete nonessential clause, so the rest is still grammatical and keeps the original meaning.

options.label: B
options.text: It places the ellipsis at the end, which is the only position where omissions are allowed.

options.label: C
options.text: It keeps every comma from the original, which is required whenever an ellipsis is used.

options.label: D
options.text: It removes the cause of the event, which makes the quotation shorter and easier to read.

questions.why: An ellipsis is correct when the remaining words are grammatical and faithful to the source.

questions.stem: Her argument relies on a ____ distinction between data and evidence.
options: hard to define-
hard to-define
hard-to define
hard-to-define
questions.why: Every word of a phrase used as a modifier before a noun is linked by hyphens.

questions.stem: Which sentence is punctuated correctly?
options: The new policy—which, according to its critics, ignores rural schools—passed by a narrow margin.
The new policy—which according to its critics, ignores rural schools—passed by a narrow margin.
The new policy—which, according to its critics, ignores rural schools, passed by a narrow margin.
The new policy, which, according to its critics, ignores rural schools—passed by a narrow margin.
questions.why: An interruption opened with a dash must close with a dash, and commas inside it must also be paired.

questions.stem: Decide whether each bracketed phrase about research should be hyphenated.

rows.text: a [carefully planned] experiment
a [long term] study of drought
a study that matters over the [long term]
a [twenty first century] skill set

questions.why: Hyphenate compound modifiers before a noun, but not -ly adverbs or phrases used as nouns.

questions.stem: Find the hyphen error in the sentence about the city's transit plan.
questions.why: An -ly adverb never takes a hyphen, even before a past participle.

questions.stem: A writer quotes from this sentence: “Al-Khwarizmi, whose name gave us the word algorithm, wrote a book on solving equations that scholars across Europe would study for centuries.” Which TWO quotations use an ellipsis accurately and grammatically? Choose two.
options: “Al-Khwarizmi . . . wrote a book on solving equations that scholars across Europe would study for centuries.”
Al-Khwarizmi “wrote a book on solving equations that scholars . . . would study for centuries.”
“Al-Khwarizmi . . . would study for centuries.”
“Al-Khwarizmi, whose name gave us the word algorithm . . . scholars across Europe would study for centuries.”
“Al-Khwarizmi . . . gave us the word algorithm . . . for centuries.”
questions.why: An omission must leave a grammatical sentence that does not distort what the source says.

questions.stem: True or false: If someone says it is “raining cats and dogs,” it is raining very hard.
questions.why: This idiom means a very heavy rain, not real animals.

questions.stem: Sami said, “I am all ears.” What does Sami mean?
options: He wants to wash his ears.
He cannot hear very well.
He is ready to listen.
He has very big ears.
questions.why: Being all ears means listening closely.

questions.stem: Mom said the test was “a piece of cake.” This means the test was ____.
options: very sweet
very easy
very long
questions.why: A piece of cake means something is easy.

questions.stem: Match each idiom about feelings to its meaning.
questions.why: Idioms use pictures in words to tell how someone feels.

questions.stem: Is each sentence about cake and horses using the real meaning or an idiom?

rows.text: Ali ate a piece of cake at lunch.
The math quiz was a piece of cake.
Dad said, “Hold your horses!”
The farmer fed his horses hay.

questions.why: An idiom means something different from what the words say.

questions.stem: Match each proverb about good habits to its meaning.

pairs.right: Doing something often helps you get better.
What you do shows more than what you say.

pairs.left: The early bird catches the worm.
pairs.right: People who start early often succeed.

questions.why: A proverb is a short saying that gives advice.

questions.stem: Lina finished her project the night before it was due, just ____.
options: under the weather
in the nick of time
once in a blue moon
on thin ice
questions.why: In the nick of time means just before it is too late.

questions.stem: Read the sentence: “Omar was skating on thin ice when he forgot his homework for the third time.” What does the idiom mean?
options: He was moving very quickly to class.
He was skating on a frozen pond.
He was feeling cold and tired that day.
He was close to getting into trouble.
questions.why: Skating on thin ice means being in a risky situation.

questions.stem: Is each saying about the school play an idiom or an adage?

rows.text: break a leg
Better late than never.
spill the beans
Honesty is the best policy.

questions.why: An idiom is a phrase with a hidden meaning; an adage is a wise saying.

questions.stem: Which TWO sentences use an idiom that means “to give away a secret”? Choose two.
options: Khalid let the cat out of the bag before the party.
Khalid was all thumbs when he wrapped the gift.
Nadia spilled the beans about the surprise party.
Nadia hit the books before the big science test.
questions.why: Spill the beans and let the cat out of the bag both mean telling a secret.

questions.stem: After weeks of arguing, the two teams decided to ____ and work together on the project.
options: beat around the bush
bury the hatchet
add fuel to the fire
cut corners
questions.why: Bury the hatchet means to stop fighting and make peace.

questions.stem: Which situation best illustrates the proverb “Don't count your chickens before they hatch”?
options: Yousef enters the contest again after losing the first time.
Yousef spends his prize money before the contest results are announced.
Yousef shares the prize money he won with the classmates who helped him.
Yousef saves part of his allowance every week for a new bicycle.
questions.why: The proverb warns against depending on something before it actually happens.

questions.stem: Match each idiom about work and effort to its meaning.
questions.why: Each idiom describes a way of working.

questions.stem: Decide whether each sentence about the robotics club uses its idiom correctly.

rows.text: Hana was on the fence about joining, so she took a day to decide.
Hana was on the fence about joining, so she signed up right away.
The coach told us to hit the ground running on the first day.
The robot broke, so the whole team was over the moon.

questions.why: The rest of the sentence must fit the idiom's meaning.

questions.stem: Part A: Read the sentence: “When the new student offered to help with the mural, Reem gave him the cold shoulder.” What does the idiom gave him the cold shoulder mean?

partA.stem: Part A: Read the sentence: “When the new student offered to help with the mural, Reem gave him the cold shoulder.” What does the idiom gave him the cold shoulder mean?

options.label: A
options.text: ignored him on purpose

options.label: B
options.text: thanked him warmly

options.label: C
options.text: gave him a jacket

options.label: D
options.text: told him to paint faster

partB.stem: Part B: Which change to the sentence about Reem would show the opposite of the idiom's meaning?

options.label: A
options.text: Reem welcomed him with a smile.

options.label: B
options.text: Reem kept her eyes on her brush.

options.label: C
options.text: Reem turned away without a word.

options.label: D
options.text: Reem acted as if he were not there.

questions.why: Giving someone the cold shoulder means being unfriendly, so the opposite is a warm welcome.

questions.stem: The principal's speech about the new schedule was so vague that many parents felt he was ____.
options: beating around the bush
burning bridges
going against the grain
hitting the nail on the head
questions.why: Beating around the bush means avoiding the main point.

questions.stem: Match each adage to the situation it best fits.

pairs.left: Too many cooks spoil the broth.
pairs.right: A group project fails because everyone gives orders.

pairs.left: Every cloud has a silver lining.
pairs.right: A cancelled trip gives a tired family time to rest.

pairs.left: Where there's a will, there's a way.
pairs.right: A student with no computer finishes her report at the library.

pairs.left: Make hay while the sun shines.
pairs.right: A shop owner orders more umbrellas the day the rainy season begins.

questions.why: An adage expresses a general truth that fits many real situations.

questions.stem: Which sentence uses the idiom “the tip of the iceberg” correctly?
options: The tip of the iceberg was the best part of the meal, so we ordered it again.
The leaking pipe was just the tip of the iceberg; the whole house needed repair.
Because the test was just the tip of the iceberg, everyone finished it in five minutes.
She reached the tip of the iceberg by climbing to the top of the tower.
questions.why: The tip of the iceberg is a small visible part of a much larger problem.

questions.stem: Find the part of the sentence about the chess final that does not fit the idiom.
questions.why: A dark horse is a competitor who wins or does well unexpectedly.

questions.stem: Which THREE expressions are proverbs or adages that give advice, rather than idioms? Choose three.
options: under the weather
Look before you leap.
a dime a dozen
over the moon
Don't put all your eggs in one basket.
Haste makes waste.
questions.why: Proverbs are complete sayings with advice; idioms are phrases with figurative meanings.

questions.stem: The scientist's discovery ____ in the study of desert plants.
options: broke new ground
jumped the gun
fell on deaf ears
threw in the towel
questions.why: Broke new ground means did something new and important.

questions.stem: In the sentence “The mayor's promise to fix the roads turned out to be a double-edged sword,” what does the idiom suggest about the promise?
options: It was broken quickly and caused only disappointment.
It brought both benefits and harmful consequences.
It was made twice to two different groups of voters.
It was so strong that no one could argue against it.
questions.why: A double-edged sword has both good and bad effects.

questions.stem: Classify each saying about time and patience by the advice it gives.

rows.text: Rome wasn't built in a day.
Strike while the iron is hot.
Good things come to those who wait.
He who hesitates is lost.
Slow and steady wins the race.

questions.why: Proverbs can give opposite advice, so read each one for its own message.

questions.stem: Part A: Read the sentence: “Critics argued that the committee's report merely scratched the surface of the water shortage.” What do the critics mean?

partA.stem: Part A: Read the sentence: “Critics argued that the committee's report merely scratched the surface of the water shortage.” What do the critics mean?

options.label: A
options.text: The report exaggerated how serious the shortage was.

options.label: B
options.text: The report described damage to the land's surface.

options.label: C
options.text: The report dealt with the problem only in a shallow way.

options.label: D
options.text: The report solved only the easiest part of the problem.

partB.stem: Part B: Which revision of the sentence about the committee keeps the same meaning without an idiom?

options.label: A
options.text: Critics argued that the committee's report covered the water shortage in exhaustive detail.

options.label: B
options.text: Critics argued that the committee's report hid the true causes of the water shortage.

options.label: C
options.text: Critics argued that the committee's report examined the water shortage only superficially.

options.label: D
options.text: Critics argued that the committee's report blamed the water shortage on damaged land.

questions.why: Scratching the surface means treating something without depth.

questions.stem: Which TWO sentences use an idiom in a way that fits its meaning? Choose two.
options: After losing the first round, the debate team regrouped instead of throwing in the towel.
Because the plan was foolproof, the team was skating on thin ice the whole time.
The two companies saw eye to eye, so their dispute dragged on for years.
The fundraiser was a drop in the bucket, covering the entire cost of the new library.
The senior engineer's warning fell on deaf ears, and the design flaw went uncorrected.
questions.why: Check whether the context agrees with or contradicts what the idiom means.

questions.stem: The board's decision to cancel the scholarship program, announced the same week tuition rose, only ____.
options: bore fruit
added insult to injury
broke the ice
cleared the air
questions.why: Adding insult to injury means making a bad situation worse.

questions.stem: Match each proverb to the principle it most nearly expresses.

pairs.left: A chain is only as strong as its weakest link.
pairs.right: A system's reliability depends on its least reliable part.

pairs.left: The pen is mightier than the sword.
pairs.right: Persuasion and ideas can achieve more than force.

pairs.left: Necessity is the mother of invention.
pairs.right: Hardship often drives people to create new solutions.
Quiet people may have great depth of thought or feeling.

questions.why: A proverb compresses a general principle into a memorable image.

questions.stem: A columnist writes: “By funding the stadium while closing two libraries, the council has robbed Peter to pay Paul.” What criticism does the idiom express?
options: The council wasted more on the stadium than the libraries ever cost.
The council spent public money on projects that benefit only athletes.
The council met one need only by taking resources from another.
The council took funds without permission from the people who earned them.
questions.why: Robbing Peter to pay Paul means solving one problem by creating another.

questions.stem: Decide whether each sentence about the research team uses its idiom accurately.

rows.text: The lead researcher played devil's advocate, defending a theory she privately doubted to test her team's reasoning.
Because the results were a foregone conclusion, the team waited anxiously, unsure what they would find.
By calling the proposal merely “adequate,” the committee damned it with faint praise.
The new data were a red herring, leading the team directly to the true cause of the error.

questions.why: A foregone conclusion is certain, and a red herring misleads, so those contexts contradict the idioms.

questions.stem: Part A: Read this sentence: “Some critics dismiss solar desalination as pie in the sky, yet three coastal plants are already supplying fresh water to nearby towns.” What does the idiom pie in the sky suggest about the critics' view?

partA.stem: Part A: Read this sentence: “Some critics dismiss solar desalination as pie in the sky, yet three coastal plants are already supplying fresh water to nearby towns.” What does the idiom pie in the sky suggest about the critics' view?

options.label: A
options.text: They think the technology works but is not needed.

options.label: B
options.text: They consider the technology too expensive to maintain.

options.label: C
options.text: They believe the technology depends on sunny weather.

options.label: D
options.text: They consider the technology an unrealistic hope.

partB.stem: Part B: How does the rest of the sentence about solar desalination respond to the critics?

options.label: A
options.text: It explains how the technology turns seawater into vapor.

options.label: B
options.text: It admits that the critics' concerns about cost are valid.

options.label: C
options.text: It offers evidence that the technology is already practical.

options.label: D
options.text: It suggests that the coastal towns are too small to matter.

questions.why: Pie in the sky means an impossible dream; working plants are evidence against that view.

questions.stem: True or false: A report about frogs should tell facts about frogs.
questions.why: A report gives true facts about its topic.

questions.stem: Mona is writing a report about bees. Which sentence is the best first sentence?
options: Do you like to eat sweet honey with your bread?
My little brother is afraid of all the bees.
I saw a big bee sitting on my window last week.
Bees are busy insects that help plants grow.
questions.why: A good first sentence tells what the report is about.

questions.stem: Put the steps of Ali's how-to report on planting a seed in order.
sequence: First, fill a cup with soil.
Next, push the seed into the soil.
Then, water the seed.
Last, put the cup in the sun.
questions.why: Words like first, next, then, and last show the order of steps.

questions.stem: Does each sentence belong in a report about camels?

rows.text: Camels can walk a long way without water.
Camels have long legs and humps.
My favorite color is blue.
I want a new bike.

questions.why: Every sentence in a report should be about the topic.

questions.stem: Huda's report is about the moon. Which TWO sentences give facts about the moon? Choose two.
options: I like to look at the moon with my dad.
The moon is so pretty at night.
The moon goes around the Earth.
The moon has no air.
questions.why: A fact can be proved true; a feeling cannot.

questions.stem: Choose the transition that best connects the ideas: The desert is very hot during the day. ____, many animals sleep in burrows until night.
options: However
As a result
In contrast
For instance
questions.why: As a result shows that the second idea is caused by the first.

questions.stem: Which sentence would be the best topic sentence for a paragraph about how solar panels work?
options: Some people think solar panels look strange on rooftops.
My uncle put four shiny new solar panels on his roof last year.
Solar panels are the coolest and most exciting invention I have ever seen.
Solar panels change sunlight into electricity that people can use.
questions.why: A topic sentence states the main idea the paragraph will explain.

questions.stem: Put the sentences of Faisal's paragraph about how a sandstorm forms in a logical order.
sequence: Sandstorms form when strong winds blow across dry land.
First, the wind lifts loose grains of sand into the air.
Then, the wind carries the sand for many kilometers.
Finally, the sand drops back to the ground when the wind slows.
questions.why: Start with the main idea, then explain the steps in time order.

questions.stem: Is each sentence for Noura's report on sea turtles a fact that informs or an opinion?

rows.text: Sea turtles lay their eggs on sandy beaches.
Sea turtles are the most beautiful animals in the sea.
Some sea turtles live for more than fifty years.
Everyone should love sea turtles.

questions.why: Informative writing uses facts, not the writer's opinions.

questions.stem: Omar is writing a report about how honeybees make honey. Which TWO details would best support his topic? Choose two.
options: Bees collect nectar from flowers and carry it back to the hive.
Inside the hive, bees fan the nectar with their wings until it thickens.
Honey tastes delicious on warm bread in the morning.
Bears in cartoons often steal honey from beehives.
Some people are afraid of bees because they can sting.
questions.why: Supporting details must explain the topic, which here is how honey is made.

questions.stem: Choose the most precise word for a science report: Al-Biruni ____ the size of the Earth using a mountain and simple geometry.
options: found out about
did
calculated
guessed
questions.why: Precise verbs make informative writing clear and accurate.

questions.stem: Which sentence best maintains a formal style for a report on renewable energy?
options: Wind turbines make a ton of power and they're really clean, you know?
Wind turbines are super awesome because they don't make gross pollution.
Honestly, wind turbines are way better than anything else out there.
Wind turbines generate electricity without releasing harmful gases.
questions.why: Formal style avoids slang, contractions, and personal comments.

questions.stem: Put the sentences of a paragraph about how pearl divers in the Gulf once worked in a logical order.
sequence: For centuries, pearl diving was an important industry in the Arabian Gulf.
Divers set out in wooden boats called dhows at the start of the summer season.
Each diver held his breath and sank to the seabed with a stone tied to his foot.
After gathering oysters, he tugged a rope so that a partner could pull him up.
Today, cultured pearls have largely replaced this dangerous work.
questions.why: Begin with the topic, follow the process in order, and end with a closing idea.

questions.stem: For a report on the invention of the printing press, decide whether each sentence is a main idea or a supporting detail.

rows.text: The printing press changed how knowledge spread across Europe.
Gutenberg's press could print about 3,600 pages a day.
Before the press, books were copied by hand.
Books became cheaper, so more people learned to read.

questions.why: The main idea is the broad point; details give facts that support it.

questions.stem: Part A: A student wrote this conclusion for a report on coral reefs: “Coral reefs are home to about a quarter of all ocean species. Also, reefs are pretty.” What is the main weakness of this conclusion?

partA.stem: Part A: A student wrote this conclusion for a report on coral reefs: “Coral reefs are home to about a quarter of all ocean species. Also, reefs are pretty.” What is the main weakness of this conclusion?

options.label: A
options.text: It uses formal language instead of everyday words.

options.label: B
options.text: It repeats the exact title of the report.

options.label: C
options.text: It ends with an informal opinion instead of summing up the main ideas.

options.label: D
options.text: It includes too many facts and numbers for a closing.

partB.stem: Part B: Which sentence would make the strongest conclusion for the coral reef report?

options.label: A
options.text: Because reefs shelter so much ocean life, protecting them helps protect the health of the entire sea.

options.label: B
options.text: I hope you enjoyed reading my report about coral reefs.

options.label: C
options.text: Reefs are found in warm, shallow water around the world.

options.label: D
options.text: Some fish that live on reefs are bright orange and yellow.

questions.why: A strong conclusion sums up why the main ideas matter.

questions.stem: Choose the transition that best shows the relationship: Early camera lenses were heavy and expensive. ____, modern smartphone lenses are tiny and cost only a few dollars to make.
options: For example
Consequently
By contrast
Similarly
questions.why: By contrast signals a difference between two ideas.

questions.stem: Decide which organizational structure each report topic would most likely use.

rows.text: how overfishing has reduced fish populations in the Red Sea
the similarities and differences between falcons and hawks
the major events in the life of Ibn Battuta
why sea levels are rising along coastlines

questions.why: Match the structure to the kind of relationship the topic explains.

questions.stem: Find the part of the sentence that breaks the formal style of Rana's report on volcanoes.
questions.why: Informative writing uses precise, formal words instead of casual phrases.

questions.stem: A student is writing a report explaining how desalination plants make seawater drinkable. Which sentence is LEAST relevant and should be removed?
options: Saudi beaches are popular with tourists in the winter months.
Most plants use a process called reverse osmosis to remove salt.
The leftover salty water, called brine, is returned to the sea.
In reverse osmosis, seawater is pushed through very fine filters.
questions.why: Every sentence must help explain the topic of the report.

questions.stem: Which THREE revisions would most improve an introduction that begins, “This report is about bridges. Bridges are things that go over stuff.”? Choose three.
options: Move the definition of a bridge to the final paragraph.
Add the writer's personal feelings about crossing bridges.
Open with a surprising fact about a famous bridge.
Replace vague words such as “things” and “stuff” with precise terms.
Use more casual language to sound friendly.
State the main points the report will explain.
questions.why: A strong introduction hooks the reader, uses precise words, and previews the main points.

questions.stem: Choose the transition that most precisely shows the relationship: Glaciers in the Alps have lost a large share of their ice over the past century; ____, several mountain villages now face summer water shortages.
options: similarly
for instance
consequently
nevertheless
questions.why: Consequently shows that the second idea is an effect of the first.

questions.stem: Which sentence most effectively introduces evidence from an expert in a report on urban heat?
options: “Can be up to 10 degrees warmer than nearby farmland.” This is what one person once said about the topic of cities.
Dr. Lina Saeed is a researcher. She said cities “can be up to 10 degrees warmer than nearby farmland,” too.
Climate researcher Dr. Lina Saeed found that city surfaces “can be up to 10 degrees warmer than nearby farmland.”
Cities can be up to 10 degrees warmer than farmland, which I personally think proves my whole point about heat.
questions.why: Introduce a quotation smoothly by naming the expert and blending the words into your sentence.

questions.stem: Decide whether each sentence would be appropriate in an objective report on electric cars.

rows.text: Electric cars produce no tailpipe emissions.
Only foolish drivers still buy gasoline cars.
Battery production requires mining lithium and cobalt.
Electric cars are obviously the best choice for everyone.
Charging times range from 30 minutes to several hours.

questions.why: Objective writing presents facts without insults or the writer's bias.

questions.stem: Arrange the sentences to form a coherent paragraph explaining how the astrolabe was used.
sequence: The astrolabe was one of the most important scientific instruments of the medieval Islamic world.
Its main part was a brass disk marked with a map of the sky.
To use it, an observer sighted a star through a rotating arm called the alidade.
By lining up the star's angle with the markings, the observer could then determine the local time.
As a result, travelers and astronomers relied on the device for centuries.
questions.why: Pronouns like its and transitions like as a result show how each sentence depends on the one before.

questions.stem: Part A: A student's draft reads: “Coffee was first grown in Yemen. It spread to Egypt and Turkey. It became popular in Europe. Today it is grown in more than seventy countries.” What is the best way to improve this draft?

partA.stem: Part A: A student's draft reads: “Coffee was first grown in Yemen. It spread to Egypt and Turkey. It became popular in Europe. Today it is grown in more than seventy countries.” What is the best way to improve this draft?

options.label: A
options.text: Add transitions that show how and when coffee spread.

options.label: B
options.text: Add the writer's favorite way to drink coffee.

options.label: C
options.text: Change the order to start with today's coffee farms.

options.label: D
options.text: Combine all four sentences into one very long sentence.

partB.stem: Part B: Which revision of the coffee draft best applies the improvement from Part A?

options.label: A
options.text: Coffee was first grown in Yemen; from there, it spread to Egypt and Turkey, and by the 1600s it had become popular in Europe.

options.label: B
options.text: Today coffee is grown in more than seventy countries, but it started in Yemen.

options.label: C
options.text: Coffee was grown in Yemen, Egypt, Turkey, and Europe, and now it is grown in seventy countries.

options.label: D
options.text: Coffee, which I enjoy, was first grown in Yemen and then spread elsewhere.

questions.why: Transitions show the reader how ideas connect in time and logic.

questions.stem: Choose the word that most precisely and accurately conveys the claim: Satellite data ____ that the Aral Sea lost about 90 percent of its surface area between 1960 and 2010.
options: prove beyond all doubt
imagine
feel
indicate
questions.why: Precise academic verbs match the strength of the evidence without overstating it.

questions.stem: A writer is drafting a report on how microplastics enter the food chain. Which THREE sentences provide the strongest support? Choose three.
options: Plastic was invented in the early twentieth century.
One survey found microplastics in most of the sardines it sampled.
Laboratory tests show that particles can remain in fish tissue for weeks.
Plankton swallow plastic fragments, which then pass to the fish that eat them.
Recycling bins are now common in most schools.
Many people feel uneasy about eating seafood these days.
questions.why: The strongest support is specific, relevant evidence about the exact topic.

questions.stem: Which revision most effectively eliminates wordiness while preserving meaning? “Due to the fact that the dam was built, there were many villages that were forced to relocate to other places.”
options: Because the dam was built, many villages had to relocate.
The dam was built, and so many villages, they had to move elsewhere.
Villages relocated.
Due to the dam being built, there were villages forced to relocate places.
questions.why: Concise writing cuts empty phrases but keeps every important idea.

questions.stem: Classify the role each sentence would play in a report on the decline of desert aquifers.

rows.text: Groundwater in the Arabian Peninsula is being used faster than it can refill.
Water levels in many wells in the region have dropped sharply in recent decades.
This drop shows that pumping far exceeds the slow natural recharge from rare rainfall.
Satellite gravity measurements recorded a steady loss of underground water from 2003 to 2016.

questions.why: Strong expository paragraphs state an idea, give evidence, and explain what the evidence shows.

questions.stem: Find the part of the sentence about expansion joints in desert bridges that uses an illogical transition.
segments: to keep desert bridges from cracking.
questions.why: The joints are added because of the expansion, so a cause-effect transition is needed.

questions.stem: Yesterday, I ____ a big fish.
options: seen
saw
seed
questions.why: The past tense of see is saw.

questions.stem: True or false: “Mom goed to the store” is the correct way to say it.
questions.why: The past tense of go is went: Mom went to the store.

questions.stem: Match each verb to its past tense form.
questions.why: Irregular verbs do not add -ed in the past tense.

questions.stem: Which sentence is correct?
options: Ali drawed a picture of a camel.
Ali drew a picture of a camel.
Ali drawn a picture of a camel.
Ali drewed a picture of a camel.
questions.why: The past tense of draw is drew.

questions.stem: Find the mistake in the sentence about Huda's tooth.
questions.why: The past tense of fall is fell.

questions.stem: Sara has ____ three books this month.
options: read
readed
reading
questions.why: Read keeps the same spelling in the past and with has.

questions.stem: Match each verb to the form used with has or have.
questions.why: Many irregular verbs have a special form used after has or have.

questions.stem: Is the verb in brackets correct in each sentence about the soccer game?

rows.text: The ball [flew] over the goal.
Our coach has [spoke] to the team.
We [brung] water for everyone.
Our team [won] the game.

questions.why: Has spoken and brought are the correct forms.

questions.stem: Which sentence uses the past tense of the verb “catch” correctly?
options: Majed caughted the ball with one hand.
Majed catched the ball with one hand.
Majed caught the ball with one hand.
Majed has catch the ball with one hand.
questions.why: The past tense of catch is caught.

questions.stem: Find the mistake in the sentence about lunch on the bus.
questions.why: After had, use the past participle eaten.

questions.stem: The old well had ____ dry by the end of the summer.
options: gone
go
went
goed
questions.why: After had, use gone, not went.

questions.stem: Decide whether each verb in brackets about the field trip is the simple past or the past participle.

rows.text: We [rode] the bus to the museum.
The guide had [ridden] that route many times.
The bell [rang] at noon.
By noon, the bell had [rung] twice.

questions.why: The past participle is the form used with has, have, or had.

questions.stem: Which sentence uses the verb correctly?
options: The tired hikers laid down under a palm tree.
The tired hikers lied down under a palm tree.
The tired hikers lay down under a palm tree.
The tired hikers layed down under a palm tree.
questions.why: Lay is the past tense of lie, meaning to rest.

questions.stem: Find the verb error in the sentence about the fishermen and the tide.
questions.why: Drag is a regular verb: its past tense is dragged.

questions.stem: Which TWO sentences about the swimming race use irregular verbs correctly? Choose two.
options: The judges had already chosen the winner when the lights went out.
The crowd had began to cheer before the finish.
Reem swam faster than she had ever swum before.
Reem swum the last lap with great speed.
questions.why: Use swam and began alone, and swum and begun after had.

questions.stem: The ice on the pond had ____ during the cold night.
options: frozed
frozen
freezed
froze
questions.why: After had, use the past participle frozen.

questions.stem: Match each verb description to the correct form.
questions.why: Lie and rise are irregular; lay and raise follow their own patterns.

questions.stem: Decide whether each sentence about the storm uses the correct verb form.

rows.text: The wind had blown the sign across the road.
The old tree was shook by the wind.
Water had sprung from a broken pipe.
The children had hid under the stairs.

questions.why: Use shaken and hidden after was or had.

questions.stem: Which sentence uses the past perfect form correctly?
options: Before the race started, the runners had drinked plenty of water.
Before the race started, the runners had drunk plenty of water.
Before the race started, the runners drunk plenty of water.
Before the race started, the runners had drank plenty of water.
questions.why: The past participle of drink is drunk, used after had.

questions.stem: Find the verb error in the sentence about the scientists' plan.
questions.why: After had, use the past participle written.

questions.stem: The ancient ship had ____ in shallow water before divers discovered it.
options: sank
sunk
sinked
questions.why: Sank is the past tense; sunk is used after had.

questions.stem: Classify each sentence about the archaeological dig by its verb error, if any.

rows.text: The team dug carefully around the wall.
A worker had strove to lift the stone.
Sand slid into the trench, and they sweeped it out.
They had borne the heat for weeks.

questions.why: Strive becomes striven after had, and sweep becomes swept in the past tense.

questions.stem: Which sentence uses a form of “lie” or “lay” correctly?
options: The documents had layed in the archive for centuries before anyone studied them.
The documents had lain in the archive for centuries before anyone studied them.
The documents had lied in the archive for centuries before anyone studied them.
The documents had laid in the archive for centuries before anyone studied them.
questions.why: Lain is the past participle of lie, meaning to rest.

questions.stem: Find the verb error in the sentence about the diplomat's remarks.
questions.why: A passive verb needs the past participle forgotten.

questions.stem: Which THREE sentences use irregular past participles correctly? Choose three.
options: The athletes had swam the length of the pool twice.
The coach had forbidden phones during practice.
The wind had torn the tent from its poles.
The old photographs had shrank in the heat.
The bell had been rung three times before class began.
questions.why: After had, use rung, forbidden, torn, swum, and shrunk.

questions.stem: Having ____ his comfortable post at the court, the scholar traveled to study the stars.
options: forsaken
forsook
forsaked
forsake
questions.why: Having requires the past participle forsaken.

questions.stem: Which sentence uses verb forms correctly throughout?
options: The pond had shrinked so much that the birds that had once flocked there flew elsewhere.
The pond had shrank so much that the birds that had once flocked there flew elsewhere.
The pond had shrunk so much that the birds that had once flocked there flew elsewhere.
The pond had shrunk so much that the birds that had once flocked there flown elsewhere.
questions.why: Use shrunk after had and the simple past flew without a helper.

questions.stem: Decide whether each sentence from the expedition's journal is correct as written or needs revision.

rows.text: The explorers had wrung every drop of water from their cloths.
The guide had foretold the storm days earlier.
Their camels had strayed and had went beyond the dunes.
The sun had already sank below the horizon.
The stars shone brightly after the storm had passed.

questions.why: After had, use gone and sunk, not the simple past forms.

questions.stem: Find the verb error in the sentence about the committee's delay.
questions.why: The past participle of bear is borne.

questions.stem: Part A: Read the sentence: “After the river had overflown its banks, the villagers fled to the hills, where they had sought shelter before.” Which word is used incorrectly?

partA.stem: Part A: Read the sentence: “After the river had overflown its banks, the villagers fled to the hills, where they had sought shelter before.” Which word is used incorrectly?

options.label: A
options.text: overflown

options.label: B
options.text: fled

options.label: C
options.text: sought

options.label: D
options.text: shelter

partB.stem: Part B: Which revision corrects the error in the sentence about the river?

options.label: A
options.text: After the river had overflowed its banks

options.label: B
options.text: After the river had overflowen its banks

options.label: C
options.text: After the river overflown its banks

options.label: D
options.text: After the river had overflew its banks

questions.why: Overflow is regular (overflowed); overflown is the participle of overfly, meaning to fly over.

questions.stem: True or false: In the word “cake,” the final e is silent.
questions.why: A silent e at the end often makes the vowel say its name.

questions.stem: Choose the word with a long a sound: I want to ____ with my friends.
options: pat
play
pet
questions.why: The letters ay in play make the long a sound.

questions.stem: Does each word have a short a or a long a sound?

rows.text: cat
rain
map
game

questions.why: Ai and a-consonant-e spell long a; a alone between consonants is usually short.

questions.stem: Match each word to the letters that make its first sound.
questions.why: Two letters together can make one new sound.

questions.stem: Which TWO words have the same vowel sound as “moon”? Choose two.
options: moan
book
blue
spoon
questions.why: Oo in spoon and ue in blue make the same sound as in moon.

questions.stem: Choose the correct spelling: The ____ of the new library will take two years.
options: construction
constructsion
constructshun
questions.why: The ending /shun/ after t is usually spelled -tion.

questions.stem: Match each prefix to its meaning.
questions.why: Knowing a prefix helps you figure out a new word.

questions.stem: Does c in each word make a hard /k/ sound or a soft /s/ sound?

rows.text: camel
city
cactus
ceiling
pencil

questions.why: C is usually soft before e, i, or y and hard before a, o, or u.

questions.stem: How is the word “basket” divided into syllables?
options: bask-et
bas-ket
ba-sket
b-asket
questions.why: When two consonants are between vowels, divide between them.

questions.stem: Which TWO words have a silent letter? Choose two.
options: window
wrist
inland
island
twist
questions.why: The w in wrist and the s in island are not spoken.

questions.stem: Choose the correct spelling: The fossil was barely ____ under the sand.
options: visibel
visable
visible
questions.why: Visible keeps the -ible ending from its Latin root.

questions.stem: Match each Greek or Latin root to its meaning.
questions.why: Roots carry the core meaning of many English words.

questions.stem: Decide whether ch in each word sounds like /ch/ (chair), /k/ (school), or /sh/ (machine).

rows.text: chemist
chef
chimney
orchestra
parachute

questions.why: Ch is /k/ in many Greek words and /sh/ in many French words.

questions.stem: Which word has the stress on the second syllable?
options: pyramid
signal
camel
volcano
questions.why: Volcano is said vol-CA-no.

questions.stem: Part A: In the word “transportation,” what does the root port mean?

partA.stem: Part A: In the word “transportation,” what does the root port mean?

partB.stem: Part B: Which word uses the root port with the same meaning as in transportation?

options.label: B

options.label: C

options.label: D

questions.stem: Choose the correct spelling: The scientist's ____ that the water was safe proved correct.
options: insistince
insistence
insistance
questions.why: Insist forms insistent and insistence with -ent/-ence.

questions.stem: Match each suffix to the part of speech it usually forms.
questions.why: Suffixes often signal a word's part of speech.

questions.stem: Decide which ending (-tion, -sion, or -cian) correctly completes each word.

rows.text: musi__ (a person who plays music)
explo__ (a sudden burst)
informa__ (facts)
electri__ (a person who fixes wires)
deci__ (a choice)

questions.why: -cian names a person; -sion often follows words ending in d or de.

questions.stem: The word “photosynthesis” combines photo (light) and synthesis (putting together). Which meaning is most accurate?
options: measuring light with a camera
breaking food apart in darkness
putting things together using light
taking a series of pictures of plants
questions.why: Combine the meanings of the parts to find the meaning of the whole word.

questions.stem: Which THREE words contain a prefix that means “not”? Choose three.
options: irregular
illustrate
irrigate
impossible
illegal
important
questions.why: Il-, im-, and ir- can mean not, but only when the rest is a word whose meaning is reversed.

questions.stem: Choose the correctly spelled word: The town's water supply became a ____ issue during the drought.
options: contentious
contencious
contentous
questions.why: Contention becomes contentious, keeping the t before -ious.

questions.stem: Decide which root each science word contains.

rows.text: dehydrate
biodegradable
thermostat
symbiosis
hydraulic

questions.why: Look for the root inside prefixes and suffixes.

questions.stem: In which sentence is the word in brackets stressed on the second syllable?
options: Ali set the [record] for the fastest lap.
The poetry [contest] drew forty entries this year.
The athletes will [contest] the referee's decision.
The [present] for my teacher is wrapped.
questions.why: Many two-syllable verbs are stressed on the second syllable, while the nouns are stressed on the first.

questions.stem: Find the misspelled word in the sentence about the museum's trade-route display.
questions.why: Exhibit keeps the silent h from its Latin root.

questions.stem: Part A: The word “incredulous” is built from in- (not), cred (believe), and -ulous (inclined to). What does incredulous most likely mean?

partA.stem: Part A: The word “incredulous” is built from in- (not), cred (believe), and -ulous (inclined to). What does incredulous most likely mean?

options.label: A
options.text: deserving of trust

options.label: B
options.text: impossible to believe

options.label: C
options.text: unwilling or unable to believe something

options.label: D

partB.stem: Part B: Which sentence uses incredulous correctly?

options.label: A
options.text: The judges looked incredulous when the young inventor said her robot cost only ten riyals.

options.label: B
options.text: The story was so incredulous that no one believed it.

options.label: C
options.text: The incredulous weather forced the match to stop.

options.label: D
options.text: Her incredulous kindness made everyone trust her.

questions.why: Incredulous describes a person who doubts; incredible describes something hard to believe.

questions.stem: Choose the correct spelling: The professor's comments were ____, brief and to the point.
options: sucinct
succint
succinct
questions.why: Succinct is spelled with a double c (suc-cinct) and ends in -cinct.

questions.stem: Match each word to the meaning built from its Greek or Latin parts.

pairs.right: to sail all the way around
something placed in the wrong time

questions.why: Combining the meanings of word parts reveals a word's meaning.

questions.stem: Decide whether the letters gh in each word are silent, sound like /f/, or sound like /g/.

rows.text: drought
tough
ghost
thorough
laughter

questions.why: Gh is /g/ at the start of a word and is silent or /f/ elsewhere.

questions.stem: Which word contains an assimilated prefix, one whose last letter changed to match the first letter of the root?
options: disagree
collaborate
unaware
reconstruct
questions.why: Com- becomes col- before l, as in collaborate.

questions.stem: Which THREE words contain a Greek or Latin root meaning “to write”? Choose three.
options: grapefruit
inscription
autograph
scrupulous
manuscript
scrutinize
questions.why: Script and graph mean write; words that only look similar have different roots.

questions.stem: [Picture: a small boat with a white sail floating on the sea.] Which word names the picture?
options: sandcastle
sailboat
seashell
starfish
questions.why: A boat that moves with a sail is a sailboat.

questions.stem: [Picture: a girl uses a tool with a long handle and stiff bristles to sweep leaves off a path.] The girl is using a ____.
options: broom
bucket
shovel
questions.why: A broom has a long handle and bristles for sweeping.

questions.stem: True or false: A picture of water falling from dark clouds matches the meaning “soft white flakes of frozen water.”
questions.why: Water falling from clouds is rain; soft white flakes are snow.

questions.stem: Match each picture of a desert animal to the meaning that fits it.

pairs.left: [Picture: a tall animal with one big hump on its back]
pairs.right: a large animal that can go a long time without water

pairs.left: [Picture: a small fox with very big ears]
pairs.right: a little wild dog that hears very well

pairs.left: [Picture: a bird with a hooked beak and sharp claws]
pairs.right: a fast bird that hunts other animals

questions.why: Look at the special body part in each picture and find the meaning that tells about it.

questions.stem: Decide which meaning fits each pictured school object: “a tool for writing” or “a tool for cutting.”

rows.text: [Picture: a pencil]
[Picture: a pair of scissors]
[Picture: a crayon]
[Picture: a paper cutter with a sharp edge]

questions.why: Pencils and crayons make marks; scissors and paper cutters cut.

questions.stem: [Picture: a stream of water flowing over the edge of a high cliff into a pool far below.] Which word matches the picture?
options: waterway
whirlpool
waterfront
waterfall
questions.why: A waterfall is water dropping over a steep edge.

questions.stem: [Picture: a scientist looks through a tube with lenses at a tiny drop of pond water on a glass slide.] The scientist is using a ____, a tool that makes very small things look larger.
options: periscope
telescope
stethoscope
microscope
questions.why: A microscope magnifies tiny objects on a slide; a telescope shows faraway objects.

questions.stem: Match each picture of a landform to its definition.

pairs.left: [Picture: land with water all around it]
pairs.right: land surrounded by water on all sides

pairs.left: [Picture: a low area of land between two mountains]
pairs.right: a low area between hills or mountains

pairs.left: [Picture: a tall hill of sand shaped by the wind]
pairs.right: a mound of sand built up by wind

pairs.left: [Picture: a high, flat area of land with steep sides]
pairs.right: a large, raised area of fairly flat land

questions.why: Match the shape in each picture to the words that describe that shape.

questions.stem: Decide whether each picture shows a “mammal” (an animal that feeds its young milk) or a “reptile” (a cold-blooded animal with scaly skin).

rows.text: [Picture: a camel calf drinking milk from its mother]
[Picture: a lizard warming itself on a rock]
[Picture: a sea turtle crawling up a sandy beach]
[Picture: a dolphin leaping beside its calf]

questions.why: Use the definitions: milk-fed young means mammal; scaly, cold-blooded means reptile.

questions.stem: [Picture: a farmer stands beside rows of date palms; a narrow channel carries water from a well to the roots of each tree.] Which TWO definitions describe things shown in the picture? Choose two.
options: harvest: the season when crops are gathered and stored
irrigation: supplying land with water through channels or pipes
orchard: an area of land where fruit trees are grown
drought: a long period with little or no rain
questions.why: The channel shows irrigation and the rows of palms are an orchard; no gathering or dry land is shown.

questions.stem: [Picture: a stone structure with tall arches carries a channel of flowing water across a valley toward a city.] Which term matches the picture?
options: dam
aqueduct
canal lock
reservoir
questions.why: An aqueduct is a structure built to carry water over a long distance.

questions.stem: True or false: A picture of a wide area where a river splits into many small channels before reaching the sea matches the definition of “delta.”
questions.why: A delta forms where a river spreads out and drops sediment at its mouth.

questions.stem: [Picture: a narrow strip of land with sea on both sides connects two large areas of land.] The name of this landform, a narrow strip of land that joins two larger land areas, is ____.
options: estuary
peninsula
archipelago
isthmus
questions.why: An isthmus links two larger landmasses; a peninsula is attached on only one side.

questions.stem: Match each picture of an early scientific instrument to its definition.

pairs.left: [Picture: a brass disk with a rotating arm, held up to sight a star]
pairs.right: an instrument for measuring the height of stars to find time and position

pairs.left: [Picture: a glass tube of liquid with marks along its side]
pairs.right: an instrument that measures how hot or cold something is

pairs.left: [Picture: a magnetized needle floating in a bowl of water, pointing north]
pairs.right: a device that shows direction using Earth's magnetism

pairs.left: [Picture: a glass container letting sand flow from its top half to its bottom half]
pairs.right: a device that measures a fixed amount of time

questions.why: Notice what each instrument is doing in the picture, then match it to its purpose.

questions.stem: [Picture: a coastline seen from above shows a curved bay of calm water, a rocky point of land sticking out into the sea, and a line of coral just under the surface offshore.] Which THREE definitions name features in the picture? Choose three.
options: reef: a ridge of rock or coral near the water's surface
glacier: a slow-moving mass of ice on land
bay: a body of water partly enclosed by land
oasis: a fertile spot in a desert where water is found
cape: a point of land extending into the sea
canyon: a deep valley with steep rock walls
questions.why: Each correct definition names something you can see in the coastal picture.

questions.stem: [Picture: a wooden ship with a single large triangular sail carrying goods along a coast of the Arabian Gulf.] Which term best matches the picture?
options: dhow
barge
canoe
raft
questions.why: A dhow is a traditional sailing ship with a triangular sail.

questions.stem: [Picture: a thick stone support built out from the side of a tall wall, pushing against it to keep it from leaning outward.] The structure shown is a ____, a support that strengthens a wall from the outside.
options: column
foundation
beam
buttress
questions.why: A buttress presses against a wall from outside; a column stands on its own.

questions.stem: Match each picture of a weather instrument to its definition.

pairs.left: [Picture: a set of cup-shaped arms spinning on a pole]
[Picture: a sealed metal box with a needle that moves as air pressure changes]
[Picture: an open cylinder with a ruler marked on its side]
[Picture: a cloth cone on a pole that swings with the breeze]

questions.why: Each instrument's shape shows what it measures: spinning cups catch wind, a cylinder catches rain.

questions.stem: Decide whether each picture shows “erosion” (the wearing away of rock or soil) or “deposition” (the dropping of sediment in a new place).

rows.text: [Picture: waves cutting a hollow into the base of a cliff]
[Picture: a fan of sand and mud spread where a river slows at a lake]
[Picture: wind blasting grains of sand against a rock pillar]
[Picture: a sandbar building up on the inside bend of a river]

questions.why: Material being removed is erosion; material piling up is deposition.

questions.stem: Part A: [Picture: a field on a steep hillside is cut into a series of flat, step-like levels, each held up by a low stone wall.] Which term matches the picture?

partA.stem: Part A: [Picture: a field on a steep hillside is cut into a series of flat, step-like levels, each held up by a low stone wall.] Which term matches the picture?

options.label: A
options.text: strip mining

options.label: B
options.text: crop rotation

options.label: C
options.text: terrace farming

options.label: D
options.text: contour plowing

partB.stem: Part B: Which detail in the picture best supports the answer to Part A?

options.label: A
options.text: the steep slope of the hillside

options.label: B
options.text: the flat, step-like levels held up by stone walls

options.label: C
options.text: the low height of the stone walls

options.label: D
options.text: the farmer working in the field

questions.why: Terraces are flat steps cut into a slope; a steep slope alone could fit contour plowing too.

questions.stem: [Picture: a horizontal beam sticks out from a cliff wall, supported only at the end fixed into the rock, with a walkway on top hanging over the canyon.] Which term matches the structure in the picture?
options: arch
suspension bridge
cantilever
truss
questions.why: A cantilever is supported at only one end.

questions.stem: [Picture: a cross-section of the ground shows a layer of water-soaked sand and gravel between two layers of solid clay, with a well drilled down into the wet layer.] The water-soaked layer is an ____, an underground layer of rock or sediment that holds and transmits water.
options: aquifer
aqueduct
estuary
outcrop
questions.why: An aquifer stores groundwater that wells can reach.

questions.stem: Decide which term from a cell-biology chart matches each picture: “mitosis” (one cell dividing into two identical cells), “osmosis” (water moving across a membrane), or “diffusion” (particles spreading from high to low concentration).

rows.text: [Picture: a cell pinching in the middle to form two matching cells]
[Picture: a raisin swelling as water passes through its skin]
[Picture: a drop of dye spreading evenly through a glass of still water]
[Picture: a red blood cell shrinking in very salty water]

questions.why: Osmosis is specifically water crossing a membrane; diffusion is any particles spreading out.

questions.stem: [Picture: a museum display shows a hand-drawn chart of a coastline with compass roses and lines radiating across the sea; beside it sits a brass instrument with a curved scale and a small telescope.] Which TWO definitions name objects shown in the display? Choose two.
options: almanac: a yearly book listing tides, sunrise times, and star positions
chronometer: a highly accurate clock used to find longitude at sea
sextant: an instrument that measures the angle between a star and the horizon
portolan: a navigational chart showing coastlines and compass directions between ports
questions.why: All four are navigation tools, but only the chart and the angle-measuring instrument appear in the display.

questions.stem: Part A: [Picture: four drawings in a row show a caterpillar, a hanging case wrapped around it, the case splitting open, and a butterfly drying its wings.] Which definition best matches what the full set of drawings shows?

partA.stem: Part A: [Picture: four drawings in a row show a caterpillar, a hanging case wrapped around it, the case splitting open, and a butterfly drying its wings.] Which definition best matches what the full set of drawings shows?

options.label: A
options.text: camouflage: coloring or shape that helps an animal blend into its surroundings

options.label: B
options.text: metamorphosis: a major change in body form during an animal's development

options.label: C
options.text: hibernation: a deep, sleep-like state that saves energy in cold seasons

options.label: D
options.text: migration: the seasonal movement of animals from one region to another

partB.stem: Part B: Which detail of the drawings best supports the answer to Part A?

options.label: A
options.text: the caterpillar becoming a butterfly inside a case

options.label: B
options.text: the drawings being arranged in a row

options.label: C
options.text: the butterfly drying its wings at the end

options.label: D
options.text: the case hanging from a branch

questions.why: The change from caterpillar to butterfly is a change in body form.

questions.stem: [Picture: an architectural drawing shows a curved row of wedge-shaped stones forming an arch, with one central stone at the very top highlighted in red.] Which term names the highlighted stone?
options: capstone
lintel
cornerstone
keystone
questions.why: The keystone is the central top stone that locks an arch in place.

questions.stem: [Picture: a diagram of a hillside shows a thin slice of soil peeled back to reveal distinct layers, from dark topsoil down through lighter clay to cracked bedrock.] The diagram illustrates a soil ____, a vertical section showing the layers, or horizons, of the ground.
options: outcrop
stratum
profile
sediment
questions.why: A soil profile is the whole vertical sequence; a stratum is only one layer.

questions.stem: Decide which term each picture of a rock formation matches: “mesa” (a broad, flat-topped hill with steep sides), “butte” (an isolated flat-topped hill taller than it is wide), or “hoodoo” (a thin spire of rock topped by a harder cap).

rows.text: [Picture: a wide, table-like landform stretching several kilometers]
[Picture: a lone, tower-shaped hill with a flat top, narrower than its height]
[Picture: a slender column of soft rock balancing a flat stone on top]
[Picture: a flat-topped highland whose width is many times its height]

questions.why: Compare width and height: mesas are wide, buttes are narrow and tall, hoodoos are thin spires.

questions.stem: [Picture: a historical illustration shows a scholar in a dark room with a tiny hole in one wall; an upside-down image of the street outside appears on the opposite wall, and on a table a glass globe of water bends a beam of sunlight.] Which TWO definitions name phenomena or devices the illustration actually depicts? Choose two.
options: camera obscura: a darkened chamber in which light through a small opening projects an inverted image
refraction: the bending of light as it passes from one medium into another
eclipse: the blocking of light from one celestial body by another
reflection: the bouncing back of light from a smooth, polished surface
questions.why: The pinhole room is a camera obscura and the water globe bends light; no mirror or eclipse appears.

questions.stem: Part A: [Picture: a coastal scene shows a long ridge of sand running parallel to the shore, separated from the mainland by a shallow body of calm water; a narrow gap in the ridge lets the tide flow in and out.] Which pair of terms most precisely names the two main features?

partA.stem: Part A: [Picture: a coastal scene shows a long ridge of sand running parallel to the shore, separated from the mainland by a shallow body of calm water; a narrow gap in the ridge lets the tide flow in and out.] Which pair of terms most precisely names the two main features?

options.label: A
options.text: spit and bay

options.label: B
options.text: barrier island and lagoon

options.label: C
options.text: sandbar and estuary

options.label: D
options.text: isthmus and strait

partB.stem: Part B: Which detail in the picture best distinguishes the answer to Part A from the other choices?

options.label: A
options.text: the ridge runs parallel to the shore, cut off from the mainland by shallow water

options.label: B
options.text: the tide flows in and out through a narrow gap

options.label: C
options.text: the ridge is made entirely of sand and is long

options.label: D
options.text: the water closest to the shore is calm and quiet

questions.why: A spit stays attached to land, while a barrier island is separated from the mainland by a lagoon.

questions.stem: In the sentence “The bat flew out of the cave at night,” the word bat means ____.
options: to hit something hard
a stick used to hit a ball
a small animal with wings
questions.why: Something that flies out of a cave is the animal.

questions.stem: In which sentence does the word ring mean “a circle of metal worn on a finger”?
options: Ring the bell for lunch.
Mama wears a gold ring.
I hear the bell ring.
The phone will ring soon.
questions.why: A ring you wear is a circle of metal.

questions.stem: True or false: In “I can open the can,” the word can has the same meaning both times.
questions.why: The first can means 'am able to'; the second is a metal container.

questions.stem: Match each sentence with the meaning of the word light.
questions.why: Other words in the sentence tell which meaning of light fits.

questions.stem: Decide what the word bark means in each sentence: “the sound a dog makes” or “the outside of a tree.”

rows.text: The puppy has a loud bark.
The bark felt rough.
Birds pecked at the bark.
We heard a bark at the door.

questions.why: Words like loud and heard point to sound; rough and pecked point to a tree.

questions.stem: “The coach told us to stand on the right side of the field.” In this sentence, right means ____.
options: at once
a fair claim to something
correct or true
the side opposite the left
questions.why: Side of the field tells us right is a direction.

questions.stem: In which sentence does the word current mean “a steady flow of water in one direction”?
options: The news report covers current events.
An electric current runs through the wire.
The swimmers fought a strong current.
The current price of dates is low.
questions.why: Swimmers fight the moving water of a current.

questions.stem: Match each sentence with the meaning of the word scale.

pairs.left: The fish's scale shone like silver.
pairs.right: a thin plate covering the skin of a fish

pairs.left: Climbers will scale the rocky cliff.
Weigh the flour on the kitchen scale.
The map uses a scale of one centimeter to one kilometer.
pairs.right: the ratio of map distance to real distance

questions.why: Context words like fish, climbers, weigh, and map show which meaning is used.

questions.stem: Which TWO sentences use the word match to mean “a contest between players or teams”? Choose two.
options: He struck a match to light the lantern.
Our school won the chess match.
The tennis match lasted three hours.
Her scarf is a good match for her coat.
questions.why: Won and lasted three hours point to a contest.

questions.stem: Decide whether the word fair in each sentence means “just and honest,” “light in color,” or “an event with rides and displays.”

rows.text: The referee made a fair call.
