The science fair opens on Monday.
Her fair skin burns in the sun.
Everyone got a fair share of the dates.

questions.why: A fair call or share is just; a science fair is an event; fair skin is light.

questions.stem: “The old bridge can no longer bear the weight of heavy trucks.” In this sentence, bear means ____.
options: put up with a feeling
give birth to
hold up or support
a large furry animal
questions.why: A bridge bears weight by supporting it.

questions.stem: In which sentence does the word draft mean “a first version of a piece of writing”?
options: The team will draft three new players.
Maha shared her draft with her teacher.
A cold draft blew under the door.
The ship's draft is too deep for the harbor.
questions.why: A draft shared with a teacher is an early version of writing.

questions.stem: True or false: In “Please file the reports in the cabinet” and “Use a metal file to smooth the edge,” the word file has the same meaning.
questions.why: The first file means to store papers; the second is a tool for smoothing.

questions.stem: Which TWO sentences use the word yield with the same meaning as in “The date palms yield a large crop each summer”? Choose two.
options: Drivers must yield to people in the crosswalk.
The old gate finally yielded under the pressure.
This mine still yields high-quality copper.
The new wheat seeds yield twice as much grain.
questions.why: Here yield means produce; the other choices mean give way.

questions.stem: Decide what the word cell means in each sentence: “the smallest unit of a living thing,” “a device that produces electricity,” or “a box in a table or grid.”

rows.text: Each cell in the leaf contains chloroplasts.
The calculator runs on a solar cell.
Type the total in the last cell of the spreadsheet.
A red blood cell carries oxygen.

questions.why: The topic of each sentence (biology, power, spreadsheets) signals the meaning.

questions.stem: “The scientist will present her findings at the conference in Riyadh.” In this sentence, present means ____.
options: existing or happening now
in attendance at a place
a gift given to someone
formally show or describe to others
questions.why: Findings are presented, or shown, to an audience.

questions.stem: In which sentence does the word sound mean “in good condition; not damaged”?
options: Engineers declared the old bridge sound.
Her plan sounds reasonable to the whole team.
The sound of drums filled the stadium.
Ships crossed the sound between the islands.
questions.why: A sound bridge is safe and undamaged.

questions.stem: Match each sentence with the meaning of the word charge.

pairs.left: The phone needs a full charge.
The museum does not charge for entry.
pairs.right: to ask a price for something

pairs.left: Ms. Lina is in charge of the science club.
The horses began to charge across the plain.

questions.why: Each context (phone, museum, club, horses) points to a different meaning.

questions.stem: The word table can mean (a) a piece of furniture, (b) to postpone discussing something, or (c) an arrangement of data in rows and columns. Which TWO sentences use meaning (c)? Choose two.
options: The committee voted to table the proposal.
The table shows rainfall for each month.
Copy the multiplication table into your notebook.
We set the table before the guests arrived.
questions.why: Rainfall data and multiplication facts are organized in rows and columns.

questions.stem: Decide whether the word mean in each sentence means “average,” “unkind,” or “intend.”

rows.text: The mean temperature in July was 44°C.
I did not mean to interrupt you.
Teasing a younger student is mean.
Find the mean of 4, 8, and 12.

questions.why: Numbers signal average; actions toward people signal unkind; 'did not mean to' signals intend.

questions.stem: “The engineers must address the cracks in the dam before the rainy season.” In this sentence, address means ____.
options: write a location on an envelope
deal with or attempt to solve
speak formally to an audience
the place where someone lives
questions.why: Engineers address cracks by fixing them.

questions.stem: In which sentence is the word novel used to mean “new and unusual”?
options: The novel won a prize for its vivid and memorable characters.
The library added a novel about a sailor's journey across the sea.
Her first novel took six years to write and two to publish.
Researchers tested a novel method for cleaning seawater.
questions.why: A novel method is a new one, not a book.

questions.stem: True or false: In “The scientist's account of the eclipse was precise,” the word account means “a record of money kept in a bank.”
questions.why: Here account means a description or report of an event.

questions.stem: Which THREE sentences use the word conduct to mean “to transmit heat or electricity”? Choose three.
options: Guides conduct visitors through the old fort.
His conduct during the match earned praise.
Copper wires conduct electricity efficiently.
Metal pans conduct heat to the food quickly.
Seawater can conduct an electric current.
The students will conduct an experiment on plant growth.
questions.why: Only heat and electricity are transmitted; the others mean carry out, behavior, or lead.

questions.stem: Part A: Read the sentence: “Although the evidence was slight, the researchers felt it was enough to support a fresh look at the old theory.” What does slight mean in this sentence?

partA.stem: Part A: Read the sentence: “Although the evidence was slight, the researchers felt it was enough to support a fresh look at the old theory.” What does slight mean in this sentence?

options.label: A
options.text: small in amount or degree

options.label: B
options.text: thin and delicate in build

options.label: C
options.text: an act of disrespect

options.label: D
options.text: to treat someone rudely

partB.stem: Part B: Which phrase in the sentence best supports the answer to Part A?

options.label: A
options.text: “the old theory”

options.label: B
options.text: “the researchers”

options.label: C
options.text: “Although … felt it was enough”

options.label: D
options.text: “a fresh look”

questions.why: Although signals a contrast: the evidence was small, yet still enough.

questions.stem: “The engineers measured the pitch of the roof to make sure rainwater would drain quickly.” In this sentence, pitch means ____.
options: the steepness of a slope
a sticky black substance
a field for playing sports
how high or low a sound is
questions.why: Drainage depends on how steep the roof is.

questions.stem: Decide which meaning the word check has in each sentence: “to stop or hold back,” “to examine for accuracy,” or “a mark showing something is done.”

rows.text: The new levee checked the spread of the floodwater.
Please check each calculation twice.
Put a check beside each completed task.
A hard frost checked the growth of the young plants.

questions.why: A levee or frost holds something back; calculations are examined; a task gets a mark.

questions.stem: In which sentence is the word qualify used to mean “to limit a statement by adding conditions”?
options: Two more years of training will qualify him to work as a pilot.
Only athletes in the top ten will qualify for the final round.
These results qualify as the most reliable data the team has.
She chose to qualify her claim by noting the small sample.
questions.why: Qualifying a claim narrows it with a condition or exception.

questions.stem: Which TWO sentences use the word bound with the same meaning as in “Rising sea levels are bound to change the shape of the coastline”? Choose two.
options: The old manuscripts were bound in leather covers.
If the dam keeps leaking, the valley is bound to flood.
The gazelle cleared the fence in a single bound.
The ship was bound for the port of Jeddah.
With such careful planning, the expedition was bound to succeed.
questions.why: Bound to + verb means certain to; the others mean headed for, tied together, or a leap.

questions.stem: Part A: Read the sentence: “The historian's argument was sound in its logic, yet its conclusions were tempered by the scarcity of surviving records.” What does tempered most likely mean in this sentence?

partA.stem: Part A: Read the sentence: “The historian's argument was sound in its logic, yet its conclusions were tempered by the scarcity of surviving records.” What does tempered most likely mean in this sentence?

options.label: A
options.text: mixed in proper amounts

options.label: B
options.text: made angry or upset

options.label: C
options.text: made stronger by heating

options.label: D
options.text: limited or made less extreme

partB.stem: Part B: Which phrase in the sentence best supports the answer to Part A?

options.label: A
options.text: “by the scarcity of surviving records”

options.label: B
options.text: “The historian's argument”

options.label: C
options.text: “sound in its logic”

options.label: D
options.text: “its conclusions”

questions.why: Few records would limit how strong the conclusions could be.

questions.stem: Omar is writing about his trip to the beach. Which sentence is the best beginning?
options: I like to eat apples and bananas.
The end of my day was a lot of fun.
Last Friday, my family drove to the beach.
Many people like to swim at beaches in summer.
questions.why: A good beginning tells who, when, and where the events start.

questions.stem: Choose the best word to finish Ali's sentences: “We built a tall sandcastle. ____, a big wave knocked it down.”
options: Suddenly
Because
Before
questions.why: Suddenly shows that something happened quickly and by surprise.

questions.stem: True or false: “Finally, I put my tooth under my pillow and smiled” is a good ending for a narrative about losing a tooth.
questions.why: It wraps up the events and shows how the writer felt.

questions.stem: Put the sentences about Lina planting a seed in order.
sequence: First, Lina dug a small hole.
Next, she dropped a seed into it.
Then she watered the soil.
After many days, a green sprout came up.
questions.why: Time words like first, next, then, and after many days show the order.

questions.stem: Hessa is writing a narrative about her first day at a new school. Which TWO sentences tell how she felt? Choose two.
options: My hands shook as I walked in.
The school has two floors.
I smiled when a girl said hello.
My bag is blue and new.
questions.why: Shaking hands and smiling show feelings; the others only describe things.

questions.stem: Choose the transition that best shows a change in time in Yusuf's narrative: “We searched the whole market for Grandpa's lost key. ____, we found it hanging on the door of his shop.”
options: In contrast
Similarly
At last
For example
questions.why: At last shows that time has passed after a long search.

questions.stem: Which sentence best shows, rather than tells, that Reem was nervous before her race?
options: Reem tapped her foot and kept retying her shoes.
Reem felt very nervous before her race started.
Reem thought the race would be long and hard.
Reem was in a race at school on a Thursday.
questions.why: Showing uses actions that let the reader figure out the feeling.

questions.stem: Find the verb that shifts tense incorrectly in this sentence about Saeed's falcon, and fix it.
questions.why: Keep all the actions in the past tense: spread, circled, landed.

questions.stem: In Bader's narrative about a football match, decide whether each sentence is dialogue or description.

rows.text: “Pass it to me!” Bader called.
The grass was wet from the morning sprinklers.
The ball curved toward the corner of the goal.
“We did it!” the team shouted.

questions.why: Dialogue is the exact words a character says, inside quotation marks.

questions.stem: Put the events of Mariam's narrative about a sandstorm in the order that makes the most sense.
sequence: The sky in the west turned orange.
Mariam's father told everyone to go inside.
Wind and sand rattled the windows for an hour.
When it was quiet, they stepped out and saw sand piled against the gate.
questions.why: Events follow cause and time: warning sign, reaction, storm, aftermath.

questions.stem: Choose the phrase that best completes Faisal's narrative so it shows a shift in setting: “Faisal waved goodbye to the crowded harbor. ____, the dhow drifted alone under a sky full of stars.”
options: By nightfall
For instance
As a result
In other words
questions.why: By nightfall signals a change in time and place.

questions.stem: Which sentence would best open a narrative about a girl who discovers an old map in her grandmother's house?
options: This is a narrative about a girl named Dana and an old map that she found.
Dana is a twelve-year-old girl who lives in Jeddah with her parents and grandmother.
The paper crackled as Dana unfolded it, and a faded red X stared back at her.
Maps are useful tools that people have used for many centuries around the world.
questions.why: Starting in the middle of an action with sensory detail hooks the reader.

questions.stem: Find and fix the punctuation error in this line of dialogue from Majid's narrative.
segments: the guide replied, “just past those dunes.”
questions.why: A comma goes inside the closing quotation mark before a dialogue tag.

questions.stem: Select the sentence in Huda's first-person draft that shifts out of her point of view.

segments.text: I opened the lab door slowly.
The robot I had built sat silent on the bench.
She pressed the red switch and held her breath.
A low hum filled the room.

questions.why: Huda narrates with I, so switching to she breaks the point of view.

questions.stem: Rana's narrative about a lost camel ends with “And then I woke up, and it was all a dream.” Which TWO revisions would make a stronger ending? Choose two.
options: Rana lists every place she searched, in order, from first to last.
Rana leads the camel home and realizes her patience mattered more than speed.
Rana meets a new character who appears only in the final sentence.
Rana ties the camel's rope tightly and promises to check the gate every night.
questions.why: Strong endings resolve the conflict and show what the character learned or will do.

questions.stem: Choose the most precise verb for Nawaf's narrative: “The old fisherman ____ the heavy net onto the deck, his arms trembling.”
options: got
moved
put
hauled
questions.why: Hauled shows the effort of pulling something heavy.

questions.stem: Which revision of the sentence “The market was busy” uses the most vivid sensory details?
options: The market was very, very busy with many different kinds of people on that day.
There were lots of people at the market buying and selling all sorts of things.
Spices perfumed the air as sellers called out prices over the clatter of carts.
Many people visited the market, which is very popular in the city every weekend.
questions.why: Smell, sound, and specific images make a scene vivid.

questions.stem: Put these sentences from Lamia's narrative about a science fair in the most logical order.
sequence: Lamia carried her solar oven to the table, hoping the clouds would stay away.
By noon, the judges had not reached her yet, and the sun was fading.
Just as the first judge arrived, a ray of light broke through.
The chocolate inside the oven melted perfectly, and the judge smiled.
questions.why: The order builds tension toward the climax and then resolves it.

questions.stem: For Turki's narrative about climbing Jabal Sawda, decide whether each sentence mainly develops character, setting, or plot.

rows.text: Turki always counted his steps when he was afraid.
Mist wrapped the juniper trees along the rocky path.
Halfway up, the trail split and the sign was missing.
He laughed at himself for packing three snacks and no map.

questions.why: Habits reveal character, place details build setting, and new problems move the plot.

questions.stem: Part A: Read the sentences from Abeer's narrative: “Abeer stared at the blank page. The competition closed at midnight. She picked up her pen, set it down, and picked it up again.” What is the main purpose of the last sentence?

partA.stem: Part A: Read the sentences from Abeer's narrative: “Abeer stared at the blank page. The competition closed at midnight. She picked up her pen, set it down, and picked it up again.” What is the main purpose of the last sentence?

options.label: A
options.text: to introduce a new problem for Abeer

options.label: B
options.text: to describe the setting of Abeer's room

options.label: C
options.text: to show Abeer's hesitation and build tension

options.label: D
options.text: to explain how the competition works

partB.stem: Part B: Which detail best supports the answer to Part A?

options.label: A
options.text: the blank page that Abeer stares at

options.label: B
options.text: the fact that Abeer is entering a competition

options.label: C
options.text: the repeated action of picking up and setting down the pen

options.label: D
options.text: the deadline of midnight for the competition

questions.why: Repeating an action shows a character who cannot decide, which slows the moment and builds tension.

questions.stem: Choose the transition that best signals a flashback in Saad's narrative: “Saad gripped the steering wheel of the desert rover. ____, when he was eight, he had built his first car from cardboard and bottle caps.”
options: Moments later
Eventually
Meanwhile
Years earlier
questions.why: Years earlier moves the reader back in time, along with the past perfect had built.

questions.stem: Which line of dialogue best reveals a character's personality rather than simply giving information?
options: “The radio says the winds will reach sixty kilometers an hour,” Fahad reported.
“Another sandstorm?” Fahad grinned. “Perfect—now it's an adventure.”
“We should stay inside the tent until the storm passes,” Fahad told the group.
“The sandstorm will arrive at four o'clock this afternoon,” Fahad read aloud.
questions.why: Fahad's eager reaction to danger shows he loves adventure.

questions.stem: Find the part of this sentence from Nasser's narrative that creates a dangling modifier, and fix it.
questions.correction: As Nasser peered through the telescope,
questions.why: The opening phrase must describe the person doing the action, not the rings.

questions.stem: A writer wants to slow the pace at the climax of a narrative, when a diver first sees a sunken ship. Which TWO strategies would best achieve this? Choose two.
options: Summarize the dive in one sentence and move on to the next day.
Include the diver's thoughts as she hesitates before swimming closer.
Describe the diver's sensations moment by moment in longer, detailed sentences.
Add a list of the equipment the diver packed the night before.
questions.why: Detailed sensations and inner thoughts stretch an important moment; summary and unrelated detail do not.

questions.stem: Part A: Read the ending of Jamal's narrative: “Jamal set the broken compass on his grandfather's desk. He did not need it anymore; he knew the way home.” What does the ending most suggest?

partA.stem: Part A: Read the ending of Jamal's narrative: “Jamal set the broken compass on his grandfather's desk. He did not need it anymore; he knew the way home.” What does the ending most suggest?

options.label: A
options.text: Jamal has decided never to travel far from his home again.

options.label: B
options.text: Jamal plans to repair the compass and return it to his grandfather later.

options.label: C
options.text: Jamal has gained confidence and no longer depends on outside guidance.

options.label: D
options.text: Jamal is upset that the gift from his grandfather has been broken.

partB.stem: Part B: Which phrase best supports the answer to Part A?

options.label: A
options.text: “he knew the way home”

options.label: B
options.text: “the broken compass”

options.label: C
options.text: “his grandfather's desk”

options.label: D
options.text: “Jamal set”

questions.why: Knowing the way home without a compass shows Jamal's new inner confidence.

questions.stem: Choose the ending that best keeps the narrator's restrained, understated tone: “When the results were posted, Dalia read her name at the top of the list, folded the paper once, and ____.”
options: screamed with uncontrollable joy
felt like the happiest person alive
danced wildly around the hallway
slipped it into her pocket
questions.why: A quiet action matches the calm, understated tone of the sentence.

questions.stem: A narrative alternates between a scientist in Cairo in 1020 and a student in present-day Riyadh who reads the scientist's notes. Which choice would best connect the two timelines?
options: telling every section in the past tense to keep the time simple
giving both characters the same name so readers are not confused
ending each section with an image echoed at the start of the next
placing a list of dates at the top of the first section only
questions.why: Echoed images create links between alternating timelines without confusing readers.

questions.stem: Find the verb error that confuses the time sequence in this sentence from Amal's narrative, and fix it.
questions.why: An action earlier than another past action needs the past perfect.

questions.stem: Decide which narrative technique each sentence from Waleed's narrative mainly uses: foreshadowing, flashback, or symbolism.

rows.text: Waleed did not notice the hairline crack spreading across the dam's wall.
He remembered the summer his father first taught him to read the river.
The single palm, still standing after the flood, seemed to promise the village a future.
Years later, he would wish he had listened to the old engineer's warning.

questions.why: Hints of future trouble foreshadow, memories are flashbacks, and objects standing for ideas are symbols.

questions.stem: Select two sentences in Nora's draft about a robotics race that tell emotions directly instead of showing them.

segments.text: Nora was extremely frustrated with the broken engine.
Grease blackened her fingers to the knuckles.
She hurled the wrench, then picked it up and wiped it clean.
She felt sad that the race was only two days away.
Outside, the other teams' engines roared to life.

questions.why: Naming a feeling (frustrated, sad) tells; actions like hurling the wrench show.

questions.stem: Choose the word that makes the sentence correct: I don't have ____ pencils.
options: none
no
any
questions.why: Don't is already a negative, so use any.

questions.stem: Which sentence is correct?
options: We don't have no milk.
We don't have none milk.
We don't have any milk.
We doesn't have any milk.
questions.why: Use only one negative word in a sentence.

questions.stem: True or false: “I can't find nothing” uses two negative words.
questions.why: Can't and nothing are both negative words.

questions.stem: Find the mistake in the sentence about Sara's lunch box.
questions.why: Didn't is already negative, so no should be any.

questions.stem: Is each sentence about the empty park correct or incorrect?

rows.text: Nobody is on the swings.
There isn't nobody here.
I don't see anyone.
We can't find no ball.

questions.why: A correct sentence has only one negative word.

questions.stem: Choose the word that correctly completes the sentence: The baker hasn't sold ____ of the cakes yet.
options: any
nothing
none
no
questions.why: Hasn't is negative, so pair it with any.

questions.stem: Which revision corrects the double negative in “Khalid never says nothing during science class”?
options: Khalid never says anything during science class.
Khalid doesn't never say anything during science class.
Khalid never doesn't say nothing during class.
Khalid never says nothing at all during class.
questions.why: Keep never and change nothing to anything.

questions.stem: Which TWO sentences use negatives correctly? Choose two.
options: She didn't tell nobody about the surprise.
There was hardly any water left in the bottle.
We couldn't hardly see the trail in the dark.
Neither of the boys wanted to leave the museum.
questions.why: Hardly is already negative, so it cannot be paired with not.

questions.stem: Find and fix the double negative in the sentence about the hiking trip.
questions.why: Hadn't is negative, so no must become any.

questions.stem: Decide whether each sentence about the class trip has a double negative or uses negatives correctly.

rows.text: Nobody forgot their water bottle.
The guide didn't give us no maps.
I won't ever forget the view.
We didn't see nothing at the top.

questions.why: Won't ever is correct; didn't with no or nothing is a double negative.

questions.stem: Choose the words that correctly complete the sentence: The students ____ hear the speaker over the noise of the fans.
options: couldn't hardly
could not scarcely
could barely
couldn't barely
questions.why: Barely is already negative, so it needs a positive verb.

questions.stem: Which sentence avoids a double negative?
options: There was not hardly any shade along the coastal road.
There was scarcely any shade along the coastal road.
There wasn't no shade at all along the coastal road.
There wasn't scarcely any shade along the coastal road.
questions.why: Scarcely is negative on its own, so wasn't is not needed.

questions.stem: Find and fix the negative error in the sentence about the museum visit.
questions.why: None already makes the sentence negative, so never becomes ever.

questions.stem: True or false: Read literally, “The scientists didn't find no evidence of water” means the scientists found some evidence of water.
questions.why: Two negatives cancel in logic, which is why double negatives can confuse readers.

questions.stem: Match each sentence containing a double negative with its correct revision.
questions.why: Replace the second negative with a positive word, or remove the not.

questions.stem: Choose the word that correctly completes the sentence: Neither the coach nor the players had ____ doubt about the plan.
options: no
any
never
none
questions.why: Neither already makes the sentence negative.

questions.stem: Which revision of “The engineers didn't find no cracks in neither of the bridges” is correct?
options: The engineers didn't find any cracks in neither bridge.
The engineers found no cracks in neither of the bridges.
The engineers didn't find no cracks in either of the bridges.
The engineers didn't find cracks in either of the bridges.
questions.why: Keep one negative (didn't) and use the positive either.

questions.stem: Which THREE sentences use negatives correctly? Choose three.
options: There aren't scarcely any parking spaces left.
We could hardly believe the size of the sea turtle.
Not one of the seedlings survived the frost.
Nobody never visits the old lighthouse.
The desert fox rarely drinks any water at all.
The pilot couldn't see nothing through the fog.
questions.why: Rarely, not one, and hardly each stand as the only negative.

questions.stem: Decide whether each sentence about the coral reef is correct or contains a double negative.

rows.text: Divers shouldn't touch any of the coral.
The reef doesn't have hardly any fish this year.
No one has ever counted every species there.
The water wasn't barely warm enough.

questions.why: Hardly and barely are negatives and should not be paired with not.

questions.stem: Find and fix the error in the sentence about the falcon trainer.
questions.why: Hadn't is already negative, so no becomes any.

questions.stem: Choose the word that correctly completes the sentence: Without ____ warning, the dune shifted and buried part of the road.
options: no
nothing
any
none
questions.why: Without is a negative word, so it takes any.

questions.stem: Which sentence contains a double negative?
options: The report doesn't mention many of the risks.
The report doesn't mention scarcely any of the risks.
The report fails to mention a single one of the major risks.
The report mentions scarcely any of the risks.
questions.why: Doesn't and scarcely are two negatives in the same clause.

questions.stem: True or false: The sentence “It is not unusual for gazelles to travel long distances” is an incorrect double negative.
questions.why: Not un- is an accepted way to state something mildly (litotes), not an error.

questions.stem: Decide whether each sentence about the research data uses an acceptable negative construction or a nonstandard double negative.

rows.text: The result was not insignificant.
The team couldn't find nothing wrong with the data.
The plan is not without risks.
Researchers haven't hardly begun the analysis.
Nobody disagreed with none of the findings.

questions.why: Not with a negative prefix or 'without' is acceptable; two negative words like couldn't + nothing are not.

questions.stem: Find and fix the negative error in the sentence about the solar-panel test.
segments: Although the test ran for six hours,
questions.why: Didn't is negative, so no more must become any more.

questions.stem: Choose the word that correctly completes the sentence: The committee has not approved the budget, ____ has it set a date for the next review.
options: so
and
or
nor
questions.why: After a negative clause, nor continues the negative and takes inverted word order.

questions.stem: Which sentence uses negation correctly to state its intended meaning, that some volunteers stayed late?
options: Hardly none of the volunteers left before sunset.
None of the volunteers didn't leave before sunset.
All of the volunteers didn't leave before sunset.
Not all of the volunteers left before sunset.
questions.why: Not all clearly means some stayed; all ... didn't is ambiguous.

questions.stem: Decide what each sentence about the expedition's supplies actually means: “some supplies remained” or “no supplies remained.”

rows.text: Not all of the supplies were used.
None of the supplies were left.
The team did not fail to use every supply.
It is not true that nothing remained.

questions.why: Work out each negative step by step: not fail to use every supply means every supply was used.

questions.stem: Which TWO sentences contain a nonstandard double negative? Choose two.
options: The proposal is not without its critics, however.
Hardly no one questioned the accuracy of the old star maps.
The data couldn't scarcely support such a broad conclusion.
Few of the samples showed any sign of contamination.
Not one of the samples failed to meet the standard.
questions.why: Couldn't + scarcely and hardly + no one stack negatives; the others are deliberate, acceptable negation.

questions.stem: Find and fix the negative error in the sentence about the restoration team's findings.
questions.why: Scarcely is already negative, so not must be removed.

questions.stem: Mom looked out the window and said, 'It is raining cats and dogs!' What does she mean?
options: The pets are playing in the rain.
It is raining very hard.
Cats and dogs are falling from the sky.
It will stop raining soon.
questions.why: 'Raining cats and dogs' is a fun way to say it is raining a lot.

questions.stem: Ali skipped his snack and said, 'I could eat a horse!' He means he is ____.
options: not hungry
very hungry
a horse rider
very tired
questions.why: Saying you could eat a horse means you are very hungry.

questions.stem: True or false: When Sara says 'I am all ears,' she means she is ready to listen.
questions.why: 'All ears' means listening closely.

questions.stem: Match each everyday phrase to what it means: 'a piece of cake,' 'hit the hay,' and 'in hot water.'
questions.why: These phrases do not mean exactly what the words say.

questions.stem: Does each sentence use words with a real meaning or a nonliteral (pretend) meaning?

rows.text: The cake was hot from the oven.
That test was a piece of cake.
Dad gave me a hand with my heavy bag.
I washed my hands before lunch.

questions.why: A nonliteral phrase means something different from its exact words.

questions.stem: Read the sentence: 'When the coach announced the final score, the whole team was on cloud nine.' What does 'on cloud nine' mean?
options: nervous and worried
floating high above
extremely happy
very confused
questions.why: The team just heard good news, so they were very happy.

questions.stem: Khalid kept putting off his science project, and now he is ____ to finish it before Sunday.
options: letting the cat out of the bag
racing against the clock
keeping his chin up
breaking the ice
questions.why: 'Racing against the clock' means hurrying because time is short.

questions.stem: Which TWO sentences use a nonliteral phrase that means 'to feel nervous'? Choose two.
options: Before lunch, Mona saw butterflies in the school garden.
Before her talk, Mona had butterflies in her stomach.
Faisal's knees were knocking as he waited for his turn at the spelling bee.
Faisal knocked on the door before he entered the classroom.
questions.why: Butterflies in your stomach and knocking knees describe nervousness, not real butterflies or knocking.

questions.stem: Select the sentence about the school garden that uses a nonliteral phrase.

segments.text: The students planted tomatoes in April.
Each morning they watered the young plants.
Mr. Saleh said the class had a green thumb.
By June, the tomatoes were red and ripe.

questions.why: 'A green thumb' means being good at growing plants.

questions.stem: Find the part of the sentence about the math quiz that uses a common phrase incorrectly.
questions.why: The phrase for something easy is 'a piece of cake.'

questions.stem: Read the sentence: 'After weeks of arguments, the two teams finally agreed to bury the hatchet and share the practice field.' What does 'bury the hatchet' mean in this sentence?
options: to start a new contest
to hide important tools
to give up the field
to end a disagreement
questions.why: Agreeing to share the field shows the argument has ended.

questions.stem: Part A: Read the sentence: 'Laila's report on coral reefs was so thorough that her teacher said she had left no stone unturned.' What does 'left no stone unturned' mean?

partA.stem: Part A: Read the sentence: 'Laila's report on coral reefs was so thorough that her teacher said she had left no stone unturned.' What does 'left no stone unturned' mean?

options.label: A
options.text: She collected rocks from the beach.

options.label: B
options.text: She searched every possible source.

options.label: C
options.text: She forgot to check some facts.

options.label: D
options.text: She worked very quickly.

partB.stem: Part B: Which words in the sentence best help the reader understand the phrase?

options.label: A
options.text: Laila's report

options.label: B
options.text: coral reefs

options.label: C
options.text: her teacher

options.label: D
options.text: so thorough

questions.why: 'So thorough' is a context clue showing she checked everything.

questions.stem: Classify each sentence about the robotics club as using an idiom, a simile, or hyperbole.

rows.text: Yousef was as quiet as a mouse while the robot moved.
The new member quickly learned the ropes.
We waited a million years for the battery to charge.
The motor hummed like a sleepy bee.

questions.why: A simile uses like or as, hyperbole exaggerates, and an idiom has a set nonliteral meaning.

questions.stem: The scientist did not want to ____, so she waited for every test result before announcing the discovery.
options: break the ice
jump the gun
call it a day
hit the books
questions.why: 'Jump the gun' means to act too soon.

questions.stem: Read the sentences: 'The new stadium cost an arm and a leg. Still, fans agreed it was worth every riyal.' Which TWO statements about the phrase 'cost an arm and a leg' are accurate? Choose two.
options: It shows the fans thought the price was too high.
It means workers were hurt while building it.
It means the stadium was very expensive.
It exaggerates to make a point about the price.
questions.why: The phrase means 'very expensive,' and 'Still' shows the fans accepted the cost.

questions.stem: True or false: In the sentence 'The new manager runs a tight ship,' the phrase means the manager is strict and well organized.
questions.why: 'Run a tight ship' means to manage something with strict order.

questions.stem: Read the sentence: 'When the museum's funding was cut, the curator knew the summer exhibit was hanging by a thread.' What does 'hanging by a thread' suggest?
options: The exhibit had many hanging decorations.
The exhibit was close to being canceled.
The exhibit was ready to open early.
The exhibit used delicate fabric displays.
questions.why: Losing funding put the exhibit in danger of failing.

questions.stem: When the engineer explained why the bridge needed extra supports, the reason finally ____ for Omar.
options: fell through
wore thin
blew over
sank in
questions.why: 'Sank in' means it was finally understood.

questions.stem: Part A: Read the sentences: 'Everyone expected the rookie to crack under pressure. Instead, she sank three free throws in the final minute.' What does 'crack under pressure' mean?

partA.stem: Part A: Read the sentences: 'Everyone expected the rookie to crack under pressure. Instead, she sank three free throws in the final minute.' What does 'crack under pressure' mean?

options.label: A
options.text: win easily against others

options.label: B
options.text: fail because of stress

options.label: C
options.text: play with great strength

options.label: D
options.text: break a piece of equipment

partB.stem: Part B: Which words from the sentences best help the reader understand the meaning?

options.label: A
options.text: in the final minute

options.label: B
options.text: the rookie to

options.label: C
options.text: Everyone expected the rookie

options.label: D
options.text: Instead, she sank three free throws

questions.why: 'Instead' shows she did the opposite of failing under stress.

questions.stem: Find the part of the sentence about the chess final that uses a nonliteral phrase incorrectly.
segments: hid her plans from her rival,
and won the match by a wide hair.
questions.correction: and won the match by a hair.
questions.why: The idiom for winning barely is 'by a hair'; adding 'wide' breaks it.

questions.stem: Read the sentence: 'The council's promise to repair the harbor before winter turned out to be a castle in the air.' What does the phrase suggest about the promise?
options: It was an unrealistic plan that never became real.
It was an ambitious plan finished ahead of schedule.
It was a plan that the public strongly opposed.
It was a plan designed to protect the coastline.
questions.why: A 'castle in the air' is a dream that cannot be achieved.

questions.stem: Read the sentence: 'Critics dismissed the young inventor's water-harvesting device, but she refused to throw in the towel, and two years later her design was supplying entire farms.' Which TWO conclusions about 'throw in the towel' are supported? Choose two.
options: The phrase means to clean up after a failed test.
The phrase means to quit or give up.
The word 'but' signals that she did the opposite of quitting.
The phrase shows that the critics later praised her work.
questions.why: The contrast word 'but' and her later success show she did not give up.

questions.stem: Decide whether the nonliteral phrase in each sentence about the debate team creates a positive or a negative tone.

rows.text: Their closing argument was a breath of fresh air.
Their opening remarks fell flat with the judges.
The captain's research was the backbone of the team's case.
One weak statistic opened a can of worms during questioning.

questions.why: The connotation of each phrase sets the tone.

questions.stem: Although the startup had little money, its founders refused to ____; they spent every riyal on testing rather than on advertising.
options: raise the bar
break new ground
cut corners
turn the tables
questions.why: 'Cut corners' means to do something cheaply or carelessly, which the founders avoided.

questions.stem: Read the sentence: 'The documentary's final scene, in which an old fisherman returns to an empty harbor, drives home the cost of overfishing.' Which choice best explains the effect of 'drives home'?
options: It hints that the harbor will soon be rebuilt.
It stresses the point so viewers fully grasp it.
It shows the fisherman traveling back to his house.
It suggests the film ends in a hurried manner.
questions.why: To 'drive home' a point is to make it clear and forceful.

questions.stem: The engineer's report was praised for its clarity, but one reviewer noted that its optimistic budget ____, given the rising cost of steel.
options: struck a chord
broke the mold
went the extra mile
did not hold water
questions.why: An idea that does not 'hold water' cannot survive examination.

questions.stem: Part A: Read the sentence: 'The historian argued that the explorer's famous map was less a discovery than a house of cards, built on secondhand reports that collapsed under scrutiny.' What does 'a house of cards' suggest about the map?

partA.stem: Part A: Read the sentence: 'The historian argued that the explorer's famous map was less a discovery than a house of cards, built on secondhand reports that collapsed under scrutiny.' What does 'a house of cards' suggest about the map?

options.label: A
options.text: It was carefully built from many separate expeditions.

options.label: B
options.text: Its claims depended on weak sources that failed when examined.

options.label: C
options.text: It was hidden away by the explorer for many years.

options.label: D
options.text: It was beautifully decorated but rarely used by sailors.

partB.stem: Part B: Which part of the sentence best supports the answer to Part A?

options.label: A
options.text: built on secondhand reports that collapsed under scrutiny

options.label: B
options.text: the explorer's famous map

options.label: C
options.text: less a discovery than

options.label: D
options.text: The historian argued

questions.why: The phrase about collapsing reports extends the image of a fragile house of cards.

questions.stem: Read the sentence: 'With the deadline looming, the editor told the writers to stop gilding the lily and submit their articles.' Which THREE statements are accurate? Choose three.
options: 'Gilding the lily' means adding needless decoration to something already good.
The editor thinks the articles still need major changes first.
'Looming' presents the deadline as a threatening shape drawing near.
'Gilding the lily' means rushing to finish careless and weak work.
The editor believes the articles are already good enough to submit.
'Looming' suggests that the deadline has already passed by.
questions.why: To gild the lily is to over-improve something already fine; 'looming' makes the deadline feel close and threatening.

questions.stem: Find the part of the sentence about the trade negotiations that uses a mixed-up idiom.
segments: they quickly got down to brass tacks
and nipped the problem in the bush.
questions.correction: and nipped the problem in the bud.
questions.why: The idiom is 'nip it in the bud,' meaning to stop a problem early.

questions.stem: Decide whether each sentence about the archaeological dig uses its nonliteral phrase correctly or incorrectly.

rows.text: The grant was generous, but compared with the cost of the excavation it was a drop in the bucket.
The tomb was only the tip of the iceberg, since it was the very last thing the team ever found.
When the funding ran out, the director went back to the drawing board and redesigned the project.
The volunteers were on thin ice, so the dig went smoothly and safely all summer.

questions.why: 'Tip of the iceberg' means a small part of something bigger, and 'on thin ice' means in a risky position.

sets.skill: Nouns: Common, Proper, Concrete, Abstract, Collective

questions.stem: Which word is a noun?
options: happy
run
desk
quickly
questions.why: A noun names a person, place, or thing; a desk is a thing.

questions.stem: True or false: In the sentence 'Sara lives in Riyadh,' the word Riyadh is a proper noun.
questions.why: Riyadh names a special place, so it is a proper noun with a capital letter.

questions.stem: Sort the words from Ahmed's list: is each one a common noun or a proper noun?

rows.text: city
Jeddah
teacher
Mr. Saleh

questions.why: Proper nouns name a special person or place and start with a capital letter.

questions.stem: Find the mistake in the sentence about Lina's trip to Dubai.
questions.why: The name of a city is a proper noun, so it needs a capital letter.

questions.stem: Choose the word that names a group: A ____ of birds flew over the school.
options: sky
flock
nest
bird
questions.why: A flock is a group of birds; it is a collective noun.

questions.stem: Choose the abstract noun that best completes the sentence: The firefighters showed great ____ when they entered the smoky building.
options: helmets
trucks
courage
water
questions.why: Courage is an idea or feeling you cannot touch, so it is abstract.

questions.stem: Classify each noun from the sentence 'The team felt pride when the crowd cheered for the trophy' as concrete or abstract.

rows.text: team
pride
crowd
trophy

questions.why: Concrete nouns can be seen or touched; pride is a feeling.

questions.stem: Which TWO words are collective nouns? Choose two.
options: happiness
committee
player
herd
questions.why: A herd and a committee each name a group.

questions.stem: Find the part of the sentence about the science fair that has a capitalization error.
questions.why: 'School' here is a common noun, so it is not capitalized.

questions.stem: Match each noun to the type it best shows: Red Sea, fleet, honesty, and school.
questions.why: Each noun can be sorted by what kind of thing it names.

questions.stem: Which sentence contains an abstract noun used as the subject?
options: The desk held a large puzzle.
The puzzle pieces sat in a box on Rami's desk.
Rami solved the puzzle quickly.
Patience helped Rami solve the puzzle.
questions.why: Patience is an abstract noun, and it is the subject of 'helped.'

questions.stem: Choose the verb that agrees with the collective noun: The jury ____ reached its decision after two days.
options: have
were
has
are
questions.why: The jury acts as one unit (its decision), so it takes a singular verb.

questions.stem: Sort the nouns in the sentence 'The Arabian Peninsula has a long history of trade, and a caravan of camels once carried spices across it' by type.

rows.text: Arabian Peninsula
history
caravan

questions.why: A caravan is a group, history is an idea, and Arabian Peninsula names a specific place.

questions.stem: Read the sentence: 'With great skill and patience, the sailors guided the dhow toward Muscat.' Which TWO words are common concrete nouns? Choose two.
options: dhow
skill
sailors
patience
questions.why: Sailors and a dhow can be seen; skill and patience are abstract.

questions.stem: Find the part of the sentence about the museum visit that has a capitalization error.
segments: took us to the Saudi National Museum.
questions.why: School subjects such as science are common nouns unless they are languages or course titles.

questions.stem: True or false: In the sentence 'The orchestra tunes its instruments before every concert,' the word orchestra is a collective noun.
questions.why: An orchestra is a group of musicians, so it is a collective noun.

questions.stem: Which word from the sentence 'Her curiosity about the desert led Professor Aziz to study the dunes of the Empty Quarter' is an abstract noun?
options: curiosity
Empty Quarter
desert
dunes
questions.why: Curiosity is a quality, not something you can see or touch.

questions.stem: Choose the word that best completes the sentence: After years of practice, the young swimmer's ____ finally earned her a place on the national team.
options: dedicate
dedication
dedicating
dedicated
questions.why: The possessive 'swimmer's' must be followed by a noun, and 'dedication' is the abstract noun.

questions.stem: Classify each noun in the sentence 'The committee praised the bravery of the volunteers who cleaned the beach at Al Khobar' as concrete or abstract.

rows.text: committee
bravery
volunteers
beach

questions.why: Bravery is a quality; the other nouns name people or places you can see.

questions.stem: Which THREE sentences use a collective noun correctly with a singular verb? Choose three.
options: The committee have finished its report.
Our family travels to Abha every summer.
The team are wearing its new uniforms.
The herd moves slowly across the plain.
The audience clap loudly after each song.
The class is taking its final exam today.
questions.why: When a group acts as one unit, the collective noun takes a singular verb.

questions.stem: In which sentence does the word 'light' function as a concrete noun?
options: We packed light for the short trip to Taif.
The scholar's research shed light on a mystery about ancient trade.
The light from the lighthouse swept across the dark water.
Her light mood lifted everyone's spirits at dinner.
questions.why: Light you can see is concrete; 'shed light' is figurative and abstract, and the others are not nouns.

questions.stem: Decide how the noun 'body' is used in each sentence about groups and people.

rows.text: The student body voted for a new council president.
Regular exercise keeps the body strong.
The governing body of the league approved new rules.
The diver's body cut cleanly through the water.

questions.why: The same word can be a collective noun or a concrete noun depending on context.

questions.stem: Find the part of the sentence about the research team that contains a noun error.
segments: at the Conference on Desert Agriculture
questions.why: Months are proper nouns and must be capitalized.

questions.stem: Choose the word that correctly completes the sentence: The scientist's ____ about the data led her to repeat the experiment three times.
options: skeptically
skeptic
skepticism
skeptical
questions.why: After a possessive, the sentence needs the abstract noun 'skepticism.'

questions.stem: Read the sentence: 'A delegation from Oman brought a gift of frankincense as a symbol of friendship.' Which TWO statements about its nouns are accurate? Choose two.
options: 'Oman' is a common noun.
'Delegation' is a collective noun.
'Frankincense' is an abstract noun.
'Friendship' is an abstract noun.
questions.why: A delegation is a group, and friendship is an idea; Oman is proper and frankincense is concrete.

questions.stem: Which sentence contains a proper noun, a collective noun, and an abstract noun?
options: A large group of students from our school visited the Jeddah Book Fair on Tuesday.
The fair's organizers felt joy when crowds arrived.
The authors at the fair signed books for eager readers.
The panel at the Jeddah Book Fair discussed the value of reading.
questions.why: Panel is collective, Jeddah Book Fair is proper, and value is abstract.

questions.stem: Classify each noun from the sentence 'The fleet's arrival filled the harbor at Yanbu with excitement' by its most specific type.

rows.text: fleet
arrival
excitement
Yanbu

questions.why: Arrival (an event) and excitement (a feeling) are abstract; a fleet is a group of ships.

questions.stem: Find the part of the sentence about the Abbasid scholars that contains an error in noun use.
segments: scholars at the house of wisdom
questions.correction: scholars at the House of Wisdom
questions.why: The House of Wisdom is the name of a specific institution, so it is a proper noun.

questions.stem: Part A: Read the sentence: 'The board's decision reflected a growing concern for safety among the staff.' How many collective nouns does the sentence contain?

partA.stem: Part A: Read the sentence: 'The board's decision reflected a growing concern for safety among the staff.' How many collective nouns does the sentence contain?

options.label: A
options.text: none

options.label: B
options.text: one

options.label: C
options.text: three

options.label: D
options.text: two

partB.stem: Part B: Which pair of words from the sentence are the collective nouns?

options.label: A
options.text: concern and staff

options.label: B
options.text: board and staff

options.label: C
options.text: decision and concern

options.label: D
options.text: board and safety

questions.why: A board and a staff are both groups of people; decision, concern, and safety are abstract.

questions.stem: Choose the verb that agrees with the collective noun when its members act separately: After the long meeting, the staff ____ returning to their own offices.
options: are
was
is
has been
questions.why: When members of a group act as individuals ('their own offices'), the collective noun takes a plural verb.

questions.stem: Choose the word that best completes the sentence: I like to run, jump, and ____.
options: swimming
swam
swim
questions.why: Run, jump, and swim all have the same form.

questions.stem: Which sentence lists the actions the same way?
options: We ate, playing, and sang at the party.
We ate, played, and sang at the party.
We eating, played, and sang at the party.
We ate, played, and singing at the party.
questions.why: Ate, played, and sang all end the same way to show the past.

questions.stem: True or false: The sentence 'Huda likes reading, drawing, and to paint' lists all the actions the same way.
questions.why: It should say 'reading, drawing, and painting.'

questions.stem: Find the part that does not match in the sentence about Fahad at the beach.
questions.why: Dug, swam, and ate all match.

questions.stem: Which TWO sentences list the actions the same way? Choose two.
options: The cat eats, sleeps, and plays.
The cat eats, sleeping, and plays.
My brother likes singing and dancing.
My brother likes singing and to dance.
questions.why: Words in a list should have the same form.

questions.stem: Which sentence has parallel structure?
options: Nora enjoys hiking, biking, and swimming.
Nora enjoys hiking, to bike, and swims.
Nora enjoys hiking, biking, and to swim.
Nora enjoys to hike, biking, and swimming.
questions.why: All three activities end in -ing.

questions.stem: Choose the words that best complete the sentence: The coach told us to stretch first, drink water often, and ____.
options: rested between drills
resting between drills
rest between drills
we should rest between drills
questions.why: Stretch, drink, and rest all have the same form.

questions.stem: Find the part of the sentence about the class garden that breaks parallel structure.
segments: and were picking the ripe beans.
questions.why: Pulled, watered, and picked are all simple past verbs.

questions.stem: Decide whether each sentence about the school library is parallel or not parallel.

rows.text: Students can read, study, or research in the library.
The library is quiet, bright, and has comfort.
You may borrow books, magazines, or videos.
The librarian helps with finding books and to check them out.

questions.why: Items joined by and or or should have the same grammatical form.

questions.stem: Match each sentence beginning about the field trip to the ending that keeps it parallel.

pairs.left: We came to learn, to explore, and
The guide was friendly, patient, and

questions.why: Each ending matches the form of the items before it.

questions.stem: Which revision corrects the faulty parallelism in the sentence 'The new park is large, shady, and it has many benches'?
options: The new park is large, shady, and it is having many benches.
The new park, being large and shady, it has many benches.
The new park is large, shady, and full of benches.
The new park is large, it is shady, and many benches.
questions.why: Large, shady, and full are all adjectives.

questions.stem: Choose the phrase that keeps the sentence parallel: Ibn Battuta traveled not only across North Africa but also ____.
options: Central Asia was visited
he visited Central Asia
through Central Asia
to visit Central Asia
questions.why: After 'not only across...', 'but also through...' matches with another prepositional phrase.

questions.stem: Find the part of the sentence about the volunteer project that breaks parallel structure.
segments: The volunteers planned to collect litter,
before the end of the month.
questions.correction: and to paint the playground walls
questions.why: The series uses 'to' + verb, so every item needs that form.

questions.stem: Which TWO sentences about the solar car contest use correct parallel structure? Choose two.
options: The judges looked at speed, design, and safety.
The judges looked at speed, design, and whether it was safe.
The team wanted to build the car quickly and testing it carefully.
The team wanted to build the car quickly and to test it carefully.
questions.why: Paired or listed items must share the same grammatical form.

questions.stem: For each sentence about the camping trip, identify the type of element repeated in parallel.

rows.text: We hiked, cooked, and rested.
We went to relax, to explore, and to learn.
The night was cold, clear, and silent.
Our tents were small, light, and sturdy.

questions.why: Parallel structure repeats the same kind of word or phrase.

questions.stem: Choose the phrase that completes the sentence in parallel form: The museum guide suggested that we either join the morning tour or ____.
options: we could explore the galleries on our own
explore the galleries on our own
the galleries could be explored on our own
exploring the galleries on our own
questions.why: Either join... or explore: both parts begin with a base verb.

questions.stem: Which sentence about the robotics team uses parallel structure correctly?
options: The robot was designed to lift boxes, to sort them, and stacking them neatly.
The robot was designed for lifting boxes, to sort them, and stacking them neatly.
The robot was designed to lift boxes, sorting them, and to stack them neatly.
The robot was designed to lift boxes, to sort them, and to stack them neatly.
questions.why: All three items use 'to' + verb.

questions.stem: Find the part of the sentence about the marathon runner that contains faulty parallelism.
segments: Training for the marathon taught Reem
questions.why: Each item in the series should begin with 'how to.'

questions.stem: True or false: The sentence 'Al-Khwarizmi was known for his work in algebra, his studies of astronomy, and for creating geography tables' uses correct parallel structure.
questions.why: The last item should be 'his geography tables' to match the other noun phrases.

questions.stem: Select the sentence about the desert expedition that uses correct parallel structure.

segments.text: The explorers packed water, food, and they brought maps.
They hoped to reach the oasis, to rest, and refilling their tanks.
The guide was patient, experienced, and knew the dunes well.
By evening, they had crossed the dunes, reached the oasis, and set up camp.

questions.why: Crossed, reached, and set up are all past-tense verb phrases.

questions.stem: Which sentence about the city's water plan uses parallel structure correctly?
options: The plan aims to reduce waste, to recycle water, and to educate residents.
The plan aims to reduce waste, recycle water, and residents being educated.
The plan aims at reducing waste, to recycle water, and the education of residents.
The plan aims to reduce waste, recycling water, and educating of residents.
questions.why: Each goal uses 'to' + verb.

questions.stem: Choose the phrase that best completes the sentence in parallel form: The report concluded that solar panels are cheaper to install, easier to maintain, and ____.
options: lasting longer than diesel generators
more reliable than diesel generators
have more reliability than diesel generators
they last longer than diesel generators
questions.why: Cheaper, easier, and more reliable are all comparative adjectives.

questions.stem: Find the part of the sentence about the new library policy that breaks parallel structure.
segments: that students return books on time,
that they keep noise to a minimum,
and to report any damaged materials.
questions.correction: and that they report any damaged materials.
questions.why: Every item in the series must be a 'that' clause.

questions.stem: Which THREE revisions of the sentence 'The scientist was praised for her accuracy, she was patient, and because she wrote clearly' correct its faulty parallelism? Choose three.
options: The scientist was praised for her accuracy, her patience, and her clear writing.
The scientist was praised for being accurate, patient, and clear in her writing.
The scientist was praised for her accuracy, being patient, and because she wrote clearly.
The scientist was praised for accuracy, she was patient, and her clear writing.
The scientist was praised because she was accurate, patient, and clear in her writing.
The scientist was praised for her accuracy and patience, and because she wrote clearly.
questions.why: A correct revision uses all nouns, all adjectives, or one clause that holds a parallel list.

questions.stem: For each sentence about the debate tournament, decide whether the elements joined by the correlative conjunction are parallel.

rows.text: Our team prepared both by reading articles and by practicing rebuttals.
The judges were neither impressed by the evidence nor did they accept the logic.
Either we revise the opening or we lose the round.
The captain not only researched the topic but also she coached the speakers.

questions.why: The words after each part of a correlative pair must have the same structure.

questions.stem: Part A: Read the sentence: 'The architect's design was celebrated for its elegance, for its efficiency, and because it respected the traditional courtyard houses of Najd.' What is the main problem with this sentence?

partA.stem: Part A: Read the sentence: 'The architect's design was celebrated for its elegance, for its efficiency, and because it respected the traditional courtyard houses of Najd.' What is the main problem with this sentence?

options.label: A
options.text: Its verb does not agree with its subject.

options.label: B
options.text: It uses too many commas in the series.

options.label: C
options.text: Its first item is a sentence fragment.

options.label: D
options.text: Its final item breaks the parallel series.

partB.stem: Part B: Which revision best corrects the problem identified in Part A?

options.label: A
options.text: The architect's design was celebrated for its elegance, for its efficiency, and for its respect for the traditional courtyard houses of Najd.

options.label: B
options.text: The architect's design was celebrated for being elegant, for its efficiency, and its respect of the courtyard houses of Najd.

options.label: C
options.text: The architect's design was celebrated because it was elegant, for its efficiency, and respecting the courtyard houses of Najd.

options.label: D
options.text: The architect's design was celebrated for its elegance, its efficiency, and because of respecting the courtyard houses of Najd.

questions.why: Three 'for its' phrases create a fully parallel series.

questions.stem: Find the part of the sentence about the climate summit that contains faulty parallelism.
segments: The delegates agreed that cutting emissions is urgent,
that funding clean energy is essential,
should not only pledge money but also delivering it.
questions.correction: should not only pledge money but also deliver it.
questions.why: 'Not only pledge' must be balanced by 'but also deliver.'

questions.stem: Choose the option that maintains parallel structure: To lead well, a manager must listen more than she speaks, act more than she promises, and ____.
options: more credit given than she takes
give more credit than she takes
giving more credit than taking it
credit should be given more than taken
questions.why: Each item follows the pattern verb + 'more than she' + verb.

questions.stem: Read the sentence: 'Ibn al-Haytham argued that knowledge comes not from accepting authority but from testing claims, observing results, and to doubt one's own assumptions.' Which TWO statements accurately describe the sentence? Choose two.
options: The phrase 'to doubt one's own assumptions' breaks the parallel series of -ing phrases.
The 'not from... but from' pair is correctly parallel in the sentence.
The series would be parallel if 'observing results' became 'to observe results'.
The 'not from... but from' pair should be changed to 'not from... but by'.
questions.why: The fix is 'doubting one's own assumptions'; changing a different item would still leave the series mixed.

questions.stem: Which sentence about the historian's lecture is both parallel and most concise?
options: The lecture traced the city's rise, its decline, and its revival.
The lecture traced the city's rise, how it declined, and its revival.
The lecture traced the rise of the city, and the decline, and also it revived.
The lecture traced how the city rose, its decline, and the way that it revived.
questions.why: Three possessive noun phrases make the series parallel and brief.

questions.stem: Which group of words is a complete sentence?
options: The bird sings.
In the big tree.
The bird in the tree.
Up and away.
questions.why: A sentence tells who and what they do.

questions.stem: True or false: 'In the park' is a complete sentence.
questions.why: It does not tell who did something or what happened.

questions.stem: Is each group of words about Omar's dog a complete sentence or only part of a sentence?

rows.text: Omar's dog runs fast.
under the table
The dog barks.
with a red ball

questions.why: A complete sentence has a naming part and an action part.

questions.stem: Choose the words that make a complete sentence: ____ played in the sand.
options: In the morning
The children
Next to the sea
questions.why: The sentence needs a naming part that tells who played.

questions.stem: Match each beginning to an ending to make a sentence about the farm.
questions.why: Each sentence needs a naming part and an action part that make sense together.

questions.stem: Which group of words is a dependent clause?
options: during the long storm
when the rain stopped
the rain stopped quickly
after the heavy rain
questions.why: It has a subject and verb but begins with 'when,' so it cannot stand alone.

questions.stem: Decide whether each group of words about the science museum is a phrase or a clause.

rows.text: inside the dark planetarium
the lights dimmed
before the show began
with excited voices

questions.why: A clause has a subject and a verb; a phrase does not.

questions.stem: Choose the clause that best completes the sentence: We stayed inside ____.
options: during the strong dust storm
because the dust storm was strong
the dust storm strong
strong dust storm outside
questions.why: Only 'because the dust storm was strong' has a subject and a verb.

questions.stem: Which TWO groups of words are independent clauses? Choose two.
options: after the team won the match
finishing her model
Layla finished her model
the team won the match
questions.why: An independent clause has a subject and verb and can stand alone.

questions.stem: Find the part of the sentences about the wet field that creates a fragment.
questions.why: A dependent clause must be joined to an independent clause.

questions.stem: In the sentence 'The students who entered the contest designed robots that could climb stairs,' what is the function of 'who entered the contest'?
options: It is a prepositional phrase showing location.
It is an independent clause that stands alone.
It is an adverb clause telling when they designed.
It is an adjective clause describing students.
questions.why: It begins with 'who' and tells which students.

questions.stem: Classify each group of words from sentences about the falcon show as a prepositional phrase, adjective clause, or adverb clause.

rows.text: over the crowd
that its trainer raised
when the whistle blew
whose wings were spotted

questions.why: Adjective clauses describe nouns; adverb clauses tell when, why, or how.

questions.stem: Choose the word that turns the first clause into a dependent clause that fits the meaning: ____ the well was old, it still gave fresh water.
options: And
Because
Although
So
questions.why: 'Although' shows contrast and makes the first clause dependent.

questions.stem: Find the part of the sentence about the hiking trip that contains a dangling modifier.
questions.correction: As the students hiked up the mountain,
questions.why: The view was not hiking; the opening must name who was hiking.

questions.stem: Which TWO sentences contain an adverb clause? Choose two.
options: Watching the sunrise, we sat quietly on the dune.
We left early so that we could watch the sunrise.
Before the guests arrived, Maha set the table.
The book that Maha borrowed is about volcanoes.
questions.why: Adverb clauses tell why, when, or how; 'that Maha borrowed' is an adjective clause and 'Watching the sunrise' is a phrase.

questions.stem: True or false: In the sentence 'Swimming in the cold sea, the diver spotted a turtle,' the words 'Swimming in the cold sea' form a participial phrase.
questions.why: The phrase acts as an adjective describing the diver.

questions.stem: Which sentence contains a gerund phrase used as the subject?
options: The coins that Faris collected are very old.
Collecting old coins is Faris's favorite hobby.
Faris is collecting old coins for his museum.
Faris, collecting old coins, visited the market.
questions.why: A gerund phrase acts as a noun; here it is the subject of 'is.'

questions.stem: Identify the type of verbal phrase in each sentence about the chess club.

rows.text: Winning the final match was Salma's goal.
Salma practiced daily to improve her openings.
Focused on the board, Salma ignored the noise.
Salma's plan was to defend her title.

questions.why: Gerunds act as nouns, participles as adjectives, and infinitives begin with 'to.'

questions.stem: Choose the option that correctly completes the sentence with a noun clause: The coach announced ____.
options: practice starting an hour earlier
that practice would start an hour earlier
an hour earlier for practice
to an hour earlier practice
questions.why: A noun clause has a subject and verb and can act as the object of 'announced.'

questions.stem: Find the part of the sentence about the new bridge that creates a comma splice.
segments: it shortens the trip by an hour.
questions.correction: and it shortens the trip by an hour.
questions.why: Two independent clauses cannot be joined by a comma alone.

questions.stem: In the sentence 'Whoever finishes the experiment first must record the results carefully,' what is the function of the clause 'Whoever finishes the experiment first'?
options: It acts as the object of 'record'.
It modifies the noun 'results'.
It acts as the subject of the sentence.
It tells when the results are recorded.
questions.why: The noun clause is the subject of the verb 'must record.'

questions.stem: Classify each sentence about the coral reef survey by its structure.

rows.text: Divers counted the fish along the reef.
The water was clear, so the divers saw far.
Because the reef was healthy, the fish were abundant.
The team photographed corals that had begun to bleach.
Some corals were white, and others were bright green.

questions.why: Compound sentences join independent clauses; complex sentences add a dependent clause.

questions.stem: Read the sentence: 'The archaeologists, having studied the site for years, finally found the wall that the ancient traders had built.' Which TWO statements are accurate? Choose two.
options: 'that the ancient traders had built' is a noun clause acting as the object.
'having studied the site for years' is an independent clause in the sentence.
'having studied the site for years' is a participial phrase modifying 'archaeologists.'
'that the ancient traders had built' is an adjective clause modifying 'wall.'
questions.why: The participial phrase describes the archaeologists, and the 'that' clause tells which wall.

questions.stem: Choose the best way to combine 'The satellite orbits Earth every ninety minutes' and 'It sends weather images to scientists': The satellite, ____, sends weather images to scientists.
options: which orbits Earth every ninety minutes
and it orbits Earth every ninety minutes
orbits Earth every ninety minutes
it orbits Earth every ninety minutes
questions.why: A nonrestrictive 'which' clause adds the detail without a run-on.

questions.stem: Find the part of the sentence about the bridge engineer that uses the wrong relative pronoun.
questions.why: Use 'who' for a clause that describes a person.

questions.stem: Part A: Read the sentence: 'What the committee finally recommended surprised everyone who had attended the early meetings.' What is the function of the clause 'What the committee finally recommended'?

partA.stem: Part A: Read the sentence: 'What the committee finally recommended surprised everyone who had attended the early meetings.' What is the function of the clause 'What the committee finally recommended'?

options.label: A
options.text: subject of the verb 'surprised'

options.label: B
options.text: object of the verb 'attended'

options.label: C
options.text: object of the verb 'recommended'

options.label: D
options.text: modifier of the noun 'everyone'

partB.stem: Part B: Which feature of the sentence best supports the answer to Part A?

options.label: A
options.text: The clause comes before the main verb and names what did the surprising.

options.label: B
options.text: The clause begins with a word that often introduces questions.

options.label: C
options.text: The clause contains the adverb 'finally'.

options.label: D
options.text: The clause contains the past-tense verb 'recommended'.

questions.why: A noun clause placed before the main verb and naming its doer acts as the subject.

questions.stem: Identify how the dependent clause functions in each sentence about the space agency.

rows.text: The agency announced that the launch would be delayed.
The rocket, which carried three satellites, lifted off at dawn.
Although the winds were strong, the launch went smoothly.
Engineers studied why the engine had overheated.
The crew stayed alert until the capsule landed safely.

questions.why: Noun clauses act as objects or subjects, adjective clauses describe nouns, and adverb clauses modify verbs.

questions.stem: Which THREE sentences punctuate their relative clauses correctly? Choose three.
options: Our principal, who studied in Dammam, teaches one physics class.
Riyadh which is the capital of Saudi Arabia has grown rapidly.
Riyadh, which is the capital of Saudi Arabia, has grown rapidly.
Students, who finish early, may begin the bonus problem.
The book, that I borrowed, is about Ibn Sina's medicine.
Students who finish early may begin the bonus problem.
questions.why: Nonessential clauses take commas; essential clauses and 'that' clauses do not.

questions.stem: Find the part of the sentence about the research grant that turns it into a sentence fragment.
questions.why: 'Although' makes the whole group dependent, so no independent clause remains.

questions.stem: Which revision of 'The pilot landed the plane. The storm had grown stronger. Everyone cheered.' best uses clauses to show how the ideas are related?
options: The pilot landed the plane, the storm had grown stronger, and everyone cheered.
Although the storm had grown stronger, the pilot landed the plane, and everyone cheered.
Because the pilot landed the plane, the storm had grown stronger, and everyone cheered.
The storm had grown stronger, which the pilot landed the plane, so everyone cheered loudly.
questions.why: 'Although' shows the landing happened despite the storm.

questions.stem: Ali will tell the class about his pet fish. What should he do first?
options: Look at the floor the whole time.
Plan what he wants to say.
Forget to bring his notes.
Talk as fast as he can.
questions.why: Good speakers plan before they speak.

questions.stem: True or false: When you speak to the class, you should talk loudly and clearly so everyone can hear.
questions.why: A clear, strong voice helps listeners understand.

questions.stem: Sara is giving a short talk about her favorite fruit. Which TWO things should she do? Choose two.
options: Speak in a clear voice.
Look at her classmates.
Turn her back to the class.
Mumble her words softly.
questions.why: Looking at the audience and speaking clearly help them listen.

questions.stem: Put the steps for Hamad's talk about camels in order.
sequence: Pick a topic: camels.
Find facts about camels.
Practice the talk at home.
Give the talk to the class.
questions.why: First choose and learn, then practice, then present.

questions.stem: During Mona's talk about the moon, is each action done by a good speaker or a good listener?

rows.text: Mona speaks clearly.
Yasir looks at Mona and stays quiet.
Mona shows a picture of the moon.
Dana asks a question at the end.

questions.why: Speakers share clearly; listeners pay attention and ask questions.

questions.stem: Reem is planning a presentation about recycling for her classmates. Which question should she ask herself first?
options: How fast can I finish talking?
What color should my poster's border be?
What do my listeners already know?
Which friend will sit in front?
questions.why: Thinking about the audience helps a speaker choose what to say.

questions.stem: Choose the best opening line for Yousef's presentation about sea turtles: ____
options: Sea turtles. That is my topic. Okay, here it is.
My presentation is done, thank you for listening.
Did you know some sea turtles swim over 10,000 kilometers each year?
Um, so, I am going to talk about turtles I guess.
questions.why: A surprising fact grabs the audience's attention.

questions.stem: Put the parts of Lina's presentation on desert plants in the best order.
sequence: Ask a question to grab attention.
State the main idea: desert plants save water in clever ways.
Give three examples with facts.
Sum up the main idea and thank the audience.
questions.why: A presentation has an opening, a main idea, support, and a conclusion.

questions.stem: Decide whether each choice would help or hurt Tariq's presentation about volcanoes.

rows.text: Using a labeled diagram of a volcano
Reading every word from his notes
Making eye contact with the audience
Talking very quickly to finish early

questions.why: Visuals and eye contact help; reading and rushing lose listeners.

questions.stem: Hessa's science talk must last three minutes, but her practice run took six minutes. Which TWO changes would best help her? Choose two.
options: Speak twice as fast during the talk.
Add more facts to each section.
Keep only her strongest examples.
Cut details that do not support her main idea.
questions.why: Cutting extra details keeps the talk on time without rushing.

questions.stem: Basil is presenting to younger students about how solar panels work. Which choice best fits his audience?
options: Use technical terms such as 'photovoltaic efficiency'.
Show a long chart of energy data from ten years.
Read aloud from an engineering book chapter.
Use simple words and a hands-on model of a panel.
questions.why: Young listeners need simple language and concrete examples.

questions.stem: Choose the best transition for Nadia's presentation as she moves from causes to effects of water shortages: ____ we know why water is scarce, let's look at how it affects farmers.
options: In contrast,
Even though
For example,
Now that
questions.why: 'Now that' signals a move from one section to the next.
