questions.stem: Decide whether each piece of support is relevant or not relevant to Majid's presentation on the benefits of school gardens.

rows.text: A study showing gardens improve students' science scores
A story about his cousin's favorite cartoon
Photos of vegetables grown by students at his school
The price of a new soccer ball

questions.why: Support must connect directly to the main claim.

questions.stem: Find the part of Huda's note card on Al-Biruni that should be revised for a formal presentation.
segments: who measured the size of Earth
and he was, like, super smart
questions.why: Formal presentations avoid slang such as 'like' and 'super.'

questions.stem: Which TWO actions would best help Faisal answer audience questions after his presentation on electric cars? Choose two.
options: Restate each question before answering it.
Prepare for likely questions by reviewing extra facts.
Answer every question with 'I do not know.'
Skip any questions that seem difficult to answer.
questions.why: Restating and preparing help a speaker answer clearly.

questions.stem: True or false: When citing a statistic in a presentation, a speaker should name the source so the audience can judge its credibility.
questions.why: Naming sources lets listeners judge whether evidence is trustworthy.

questions.stem: Mariam's presentation argues that her city should add more bike lanes. Which claim would be strongest to include?
options: City data show that bike accidents fell 30% on streets with lanes.
I have always enjoyed riding my bike on weekends.
Many residents have said in casual conversations that bike lanes look nice.
Bike lanes are popular in some other countries.
questions.why: Specific data from a reliable source is the strongest support.

questions.stem: Put the steps for preparing Omar's presentation on the history of the Hejaz Railway in a logical order.
sequence: Research reliable sources about the railway.
Organize the facts into an outline.
Create slides with key dates and images.
Rehearse while timing the presentation.
questions.why: Research comes first, then organizing, designing visuals, and rehearsing.

questions.stem: Choose the best way for Lama to end her presentation on reducing food waste: ____
options: So start today: plan meals, store food wisely, and share extra food with neighbors.
And that is pretty much everything I found on the internet about food waste.
I forgot to mention a few more facts, but we are out of time now.
Okay, I think I am done, so does anyone have any questions?
questions.why: A strong conclusion gives the audience a clear call to action.

questions.stem: For each slide in Saad's presentation on desert foxes, decide whether it shows good or poor slide design.

rows.text: A slide with a clear photo and a short label
A slide with three paragraphs in small print
A slide with one key fact in large type
A slide with bright, flashing animations on every word

questions.why: Good slides are simple and easy to read from a distance.

questions.stem: Khalid is presenting a proposal to the school board to extend library hours. Which choice would best adapt his presentation to this audience?
options: Open with the cost and the expected benefit to student achievement.
Open with a joke about late-night studying to help relax the board members.
Open by describing his personal love of reading as a child.
Open with a long history of libraries in the ancient world.
questions.why: Decision makers care most about costs and results.

questions.stem: Part A: Dana's presentation claims that her school should switch to reusable water bottles. During rehearsal, a classmate says her argument 'feels one-sided.' What should Dana add?

partA.stem: Part A: Dana's presentation claims that her school should switch to reusable water bottles. During rehearsal, a classmate says her argument 'feels one-sided.' What should Dana add?

options.label: A
options.text: a second slide that repeats her main claim in larger letters

options.label: B
options.text: a counterclaim about cost, answered with evidence of long-term savings

options.label: C
options.text: more personal stories about how much she likes her own bottle

options.label: D
options.text: a list of the stores and brands that sell reusable bottles

partB.stem: Part B: Which sentence would best introduce that addition?

options.label: A
options.text: As I said before, we should switch to reusable bottles.

options.label: B
options.text: Some may argue that new bottles cost too much, but the savings appear within one term.

options.label: C
options.text: I have used my green bottle every day since Grade 6.

options.label: D
options.text: Reusable bottles come in many bright colors and fun designs.

questions.why: Addressing an opposing view and answering it makes an argument more balanced.

questions.stem: Which THREE delivery choices would most strengthen a formal presentation on the history of pearl diving in the Gulf? Choose three.
options: Turning to face the screen most of the time
Reading each slide word for word
Varying pace and pausing after key points
Using slang to sound relaxed and friendly
Using a timeline visual that the speaker explains
Making steady eye contact across the room
questions.why: Pacing, explained visuals, and eye contact keep a formal audience engaged.

questions.stem: Find the part of Zaid's outline sentence on desalination that contains an unsupported generalization.
segments: supply much of Saudi Arabia's drinking water,
that brine discharge requires careful management.
questions.why: Claims like 'every expert agrees' overstate the evidence.

questions.stem: Decide whether each revision to Abeer's presentation on smartphone use improves or weakens her credibility.

rows.text: Citing a 2025 study from a university research center
Saying 'Everybody knows phones are bad for sleep'
Acknowledging that phones can also help students learn
Using a statistic without naming where it came from

questions.why: Credible speakers cite sources and treat other views fairly.

questions.stem: Choose the most effective closing for Sultan's presentation urging the city to protect its mangrove forests: ____
options: Mangroves are trees that grow in salty water near the coasts of many different countries around the world.
There are some other topics about the coast that I could have discussed today if there had been time.
If we lose these forests, we lose the coast's natural shield, its nurseries for fish, and a piece of our heritage.
In conclusion, my presentation was about mangroves, which I have now finished explaining to all of you.
questions.why: A strong close uses a memorable parallel series that ties the issue to the audience's values.

questions.stem: Part A: Rana must present the same research on heat-resistant crops to two groups: farmers and university scientists. What is the most important adjustment between the two presentations?

partA.stem: Part A: Rana must present the same research on heat-resistant crops to two groups: farmers and university scientists. What is the most important adjustment between the two presentations?

options.label: A
options.text: Shorten the presentation for farmers because they are less interested in the topic.

options.label: B
options.text: Use the same slides for both but speak more loudly to the larger group of listeners.

options.label: C
options.text: Remove all numbers from both versions so that no listener becomes confused.

options.label: D
options.text: Shift vocabulary and evidence: practical results for farmers, methods and data for scientists.

partB.stem: Part B: Which slide title would best suit the scientists' version?

options.label: A
options.text: How These Seeds Can Save You Money This Year

options.label: B
options.text: Trial Design and Yield Data Across Three Growing Seasons

options.label: C
options.text: Fun Facts About Wheat and Other Grains

options.label: D
options.text: Why I Have Always Loved Studying Plants

questions.why: Effective speakers match content and language to each audience's purpose.

questions.stem: A speaker presenting on the life of Ibn Battuta notices listeners looking at their phones midway through. Which TWO responses are most effective? Choose two.
options: Pose a question that invites the audience to imagine one of his journeys.
Stop and tell the audience members that they are being rude.
Speed up so that the presentation ends sooner than was planned.
Move to a vivid visual, such as a map of his route, and explain it.
questions.why: Re-engaging listeners with interaction or strong visuals works better than rushing or scolding.

questions.stem: Classify each technique in Walid's presentation on renewable energy as an appeal to logic, emotion, or credibility.

rows.text: Comparing the cost per kilowatt-hour of solar and oil
Describing a child in a village receiving electricity for the first time
Mentioning his internship at a national energy laboratory
Presenting a graph of falling solar panel prices since 2010

questions.why: Data appeals to logic, stories to emotion, and expertise to credibility.

questions.stem: Find the part of Noor's thesis for her presentation on online learning that should be revised to be more precise.
segments: is kind of good in some ways
questions.why: A thesis should make a clear, specific claim, not a vague one.

questions.stem: Match each word to the word that rhymes with it in a poem about the sea.
questions.why: Rhyming words end with the same sound.

questions.stem: Finish the rhyming lines: “I saw a little cat. / It slept upon a ____.”
options: rug
bed
mat
questions.why: Mat ends with the same sound as cat.

questions.stem: True or false: A poem can use words that sound alike at the end of lines, like “tree” and “bee.”
questions.why: Many poems use rhyming words at the ends of lines.

questions.stem: Which TWO words help a reader hear the sounds in a poem about rain? Choose two.
options: table
pitter-patter
blue
splash
questions.why: Sound words like splash let the reader hear the rain.

questions.stem: Ali wants to write a poem about the wind. Which line uses the senses best?
options: I will now write about the wind today.
The cool wind whistles past my ears.
The wind is a thing that I know about.
Wind is air and it moves around a lot.
questions.why: Cool and whistles tell how the wind feels and sounds.

questions.stem: Sort each line from a poem about a desert night as a simile or a metaphor.

rows.text: The moon is a silver coin.
The stars glitter like sugar.
The dunes are sleeping camels.
The wind hums like a kettle.

questions.why: A simile uses like or as; a metaphor says one thing is another.

questions.stem: Choose the word that completes the rhyme: “The falcon circles in the sky, / Its sharp eyes watching from up ____.”
options: above
there
top
high
questions.why: High rhymes with sky and fits the meaning.

questions.stem: Hana is writing a poem about her grandmother's garden. Which TWO lines use vivid sensory details? Choose two.
options: Mint leaves release a sharp, cool smell.
The garden is very nice and I like it.
Bees hum softly over yellow squash blossoms.
My grandmother has a lot of plants there.
questions.why: Sensory details name what we smell, hear, see, taste, or touch.

questions.stem: Which revision of the line “The ocean was big” creates the strongest image for a poem?
options: The ocean was big, and it was also quite large.
The ocean stretched, a blue blanket to the sky.
The ocean was very, very, very big and wide.
The ocean was bigger than anything I had seen.
questions.why: A metaphor with color paints a picture instead of repeating big.

questions.stem: Yusuf's four-line poem about rain should rhyme in pairs (AABB). Which line breaks the rhyme pattern?
segments: The rain came down upon the hill,
and all the birds sat very still.
The puddles shone like silver light,
and then the sky turned dark at noon.
questions.correction: and then the sky grew dark as night.
questions.why: In AABB, line 4 must rhyme with line 3 (light / night).

questions.stem: Match each poetic device to the example line about a lighthouse.

pairs.right: The lighthouse keeps its patient watch
Waves crash and whoosh against the rocks
Its beam swings like a slow pendulum

questions.why: Each device shapes sound or meaning in a different way.

questions.stem: Arrange these lines of a short poem about a date palm so it moves from the roots up to the crown.
sequence: Deep roots drink from hidden water,
the rough trunk climbs through the heat,
green fronds open like fans,
and golden dates hang near the sky.
questions.why: The poem follows the tree from the ground upward.

questions.stem: Choose the verb that gives the strongest image in this line about a storm: “Lightning ____ across the black sky.”
options: was
moved
went
slashed
questions.why: Slashed is a strong, specific verb that shows sudden, sharp motion.

questions.stem: A student wants the final line of a poem about moving to a new city to show mixed feelings. Which line does this best?
options: I carry the old street in my pocket as I walk the new one.
I am sad about leaving but also happy, and I feel both of them.
Moving is something that many families do every year.
My new city has tall buildings and many busy roads.
questions.why: An image of carrying the old street while walking the new one shows both feelings without naming them.

questions.stem: Read these lines from a draft about a marathon runner. Select the line that uses enjambment, letting the sentence run on into the next line.

segments.text: My legs are heavy, but my heart
still pounds a steady drum.
The finish line is far away.
I run.

questions.why: The first line stops mid-sentence, so the meaning carries into the next line.

questions.stem: Decide whether each line from a draft about a coral reef uses imagery or states a plain fact.

rows.text: Parrotfish crunch the coral with beaked mouths.
Coral reefs cover less than one percent of the ocean floor.
Sea fans sway like green flags in the current.
Many reef fish live in warm, shallow water.

questions.why: Imagery appeals to the senses; plain facts give information.

questions.stem: True or false: In a free-verse poem about a camel, the writer must keep a regular rhyme scheme in every stanza.
questions.why: Free verse does not need regular rhyme or meter.

questions.stem: Choose the word that continues the extended metaphor: “My city is a beehive: / workers stream from every cell, / and the streets ____ until evening.”
options: shine
sleep
flow
hum
questions.why: Hum continues the beehive comparison.

questions.stem: A student is revising a poem about a desert caravan to create a slow, tired rhythm. Which TWO revisions best achieve this? Choose two.
options: Add commas and pauses so each line moves slowly.
Shorten every line to one quick, sharp word.
Use exclamation points at the end of every line.
Replace short, quick words with long, heavy ones like “plodding” and “weary.”
questions.why: Long words and pauses slow the reader down.

questions.stem: Which revision of the line “The old house was quiet” best creates a mood of loneliness?
options: The house was old, and it did not make much noise.
Dust settles on chairs that no one pulls out anymore.
The old house was really extremely quiet and very still.
Nobody lived in the old house, so it was quiet.
questions.why: The image of unused chairs suggests loneliness without stating it.

questions.stem: Match each sound device to the line about a waterfall that shows it.

pairs.right: Low foam flows over hollow stone
The spray at play along the bay
It falls. It rises. It falls again.

questions.why: Sound devices repeat vowels, consonants, or rhymes, or create pauses.

questions.stem: A sonnet draft about fishermen should keep iambic pentameter (ten syllables per line). Which line breaks the meter?
segments: The tide returns to claim the sleeping shore,
and gulls cry out above the silver foam;
each wave arrives and asks a little more,
while fishermen who worked since dawn now row their boats toward home.
questions.correction: while weary fishermen row slowly home.
questions.why: The last line has too many syllables; the revision keeps ten and the rhyme with foam.

questions.stem: A poet wants a poem about an aging falconer to end with an ambiguous, reflective tone. Which TWO closing lines best achieve this? Choose two.
options: Tomorrow the sky will be the same, and I will not.
I slip the hood on the bird, or on myself.
The falcon flew away and never came back, the end.
And so he was very sad because he was getting old.
questions.why: Ambiguous lines invite reflection instead of stating a feeling directly.

questions.stem: Which revision most effectively replaces the cliché in the line “Her heart was as cold as ice” in a poem about a stern teacher?
options: Her voice was a locked door with the key inside.
Her heart was very cold, colder than ice is.
Her heart was as cold as the snow on a winter peak.
She had a heart that was frozen like a lake.
questions.why: A fresh metaphor replaces the cliché; the others keep the tired cold-heart idea.

questions.stem: A student's poem about a city at night repeats the refrain “and still the lights stay on.” What is the most likely purpose of repeating it at the end of each stanza?
options: to explain in detail how electricity reaches each building in the city at night
to show that the poet ran out of new ideas for ending each stanza
to make every stanza the same length as the first one
to emphasize the city's restless energy and build a sense of persistence
questions.why: A refrain builds emphasis and a feeling that something continues.

questions.stem: A poet drafting an elegy for a retired ship's captain wants a concrete image that suggests the abstract idea of loss. Select the line that does this best.

segments.text: His compass still points north on the kitchen shelf.
He was a man who felt a deep sense of loss.
Grief is a difficult and complicated feeling.
We will always remember him in our hearts.

questions.why: An unused compass is a concrete object that quietly suggests absence.

questions.stem: Classify each revision a poet might make to a villanelle about drought as a change mainly to form or mainly to tone.

rows.text: Restoring the second refrain so it closes the final stanza
Replacing “dry” with “parched and pleading” to deepen desperation
Cutting a line so the tercet has exactly three lines
Shifting the final image from cracked earth to a single green shoot

questions.why: Form concerns structure; tone concerns attitude and feeling.

questions.stem: A poet wants the closing line about a scientist's unfinished notebook to be compressed and resonant. Choose the best ending: “Her equations end mid-page, ____.”
options: and she did not finish writing all of them
which was sad for everyone who knew her
the pencil still waiting
because she ran out of time to complete them
questions.why: A brief image suggests loss more powerfully than explaining it.

questions.stem: A sonnet begins by praising the speed of modern travel. Which THREE choices would most strengthen its volta (turn)? Choose three.
options: Add a fact about the top speed of commercial aircraft
Move from images of jets to an image of a slow walk with a grandparent
Begin line 9 with “Yet” to signal a shift in thought
Remove the rhyme from the final couplet without changing ideas
Change the tone from celebratory to quietly questioning
Keep praising speed with stronger adjectives through line 14
questions.why: A volta shifts thought, imagery, and tone.

questions.stem: Order these steps a poet would follow to revise a free-verse poem about pearl divers, from first draft to final polish.
sequence: Read the draft aloud to hear where the rhythm stalls
Cut abstract words and replace them with concrete images
Adjust line breaks to emphasize key words at line ends
Proofread punctuation and spacing for consistency
questions.why: Revise big issues of sound and content first, then line breaks, then proofread.

questions.stem: Choose the word that completes the sentence: That is ____ ball.
options: Sara
Saras
Sara's
questions.why: Add 's to show that the ball belongs to Sara.

questions.stem: True or false: In “the cat's bowl,” the bowl belongs to the cat.
questions.why: The 's shows the cat owns the bowl.

questions.stem: Match each phrase to the possessive that means the same thing.
questions.why: The owner comes first with 's.

questions.stem: Which sentence uses a possessive noun correctly?
options: My brothers bike is blue.
My brother's bike is blue.
My brother bike's is blue.
My brother bikes is blue.
questions.why: Brother's shows the bike belongs to him.

questions.stem: Find the mistake in this sentence about Nora's lunch.
questions.why: Nora owns the lunch box, so add an apostrophe: Nora's.

questions.stem: Decide whether each possessive noun names one owner or more than one owner.

rows.text: the girl's notebook
the girls' notebooks
the teacher's desk
the players' uniforms

questions.why: An apostrophe after the s shows a plural owner.

questions.stem: Choose the correct possessive: All of the ____ caps were the same color.
options: students'
student's
studentses'
students
questions.why: Many students own caps, so add an apostrophe after the s.

questions.stem: Find the error in the sentence about the children's garden.
questions.why: Children is already plural, so add 's.

questions.stem: Which TWO sentences use possessive nouns correctly? Choose two.
options: The mens' shoes were by the door.
The women's team practiced early.
The two dogs' leashes were tangled.
The bird's sang in the green trees.
questions.why: Irregular plurals take 's; regular plurals take s'.

questions.stem: Which sentence uses an apostrophe correctly?
options: The geeses feathers floated on the pond.
The geese's feathers floated on the pond.
The geeses' feathers floated on the pond.
The geese feather's floated on the pond.
questions.why: Geese is an irregular plural, so it takes 's.

questions.stem: Which sentence correctly shows that two sisters share one room?
options: Hudas and Reem room faces the garden.
Huda and Reem's room faces the garden.
Huda and Reems room faces the garden.
Huda's and Reem's room faces the garden.
questions.why: For joint ownership, only the last name takes 's.

questions.stem: True or false: “Huda's and Reem's bikes” shows that each girl owns her own bike.
questions.why: When each name takes 's, the ownership is separate.

questions.stem: Choose the correct form: My ____ car is parked outside.
options: sister-in-laws'
sisters-in-law
sister-in-law's
sister's-in-law
questions.why: For a compound noun, add 's to the last word.

questions.stem: Find the error in the sentence about the museum's exhibit.
questions.why: One museum owns the exhibit, so write museum's.

questions.stem: Decide whether each phrase about a science fair is written correctly or incorrectly.

rows.text: the judges' decision
the class's display
the childrens' projects
the womens' booth

questions.why: Irregular plurals like children and women take 's.

questions.stem: Choose the correct possessive: The ____ trip to the observatory was postponed because of clouds.
options: astronomy club's
astronomy's club
astronomy clubs's
astronomy clubs
questions.why: One club owns the trip, so add 's to club.

questions.stem: Find the error in this sentence about a family's farm.
questions.why: The whole family is plural (the Ahmads), so the apostrophe follows the s.

questions.stem: Which sentence correctly uses a possessive with a unit of time?
options: After a weeks' rest, the runner returned to training.
After a weeks rest, the runner returned to training.
After a week's rest, the runner returned to training.
After a week rest's, the runner returned to training.
questions.why: One week is singular, so write week's.

questions.stem: Decide whether each phrase about inventors shows joint ownership or separate ownership.

rows.text: Ali and Omar's invention
Ali's and Omar's notebooks
the Wright brothers' airplane
Sara's and Lina's science kits

questions.why: One 's at the end shows joint ownership; 's on each name shows separate ownership.

questions.stem: Which TWO sentences correctly use possessive nouns? Choose two.
options: James's report on Al-Biruni was excellent.
The bus's brakes squealed at the corner.
The Joneses's garden was full of roses.
The Smith's car is parked outside their home.
questions.why: Singular nouns ending in s still take 's; a plural family name takes only an apostrophe.

questions.stem: True or false: In “The researchers' and the engineers' goals were different,” the apostrophes show that the two groups had separate goals.
questions.why: Each group has its own possessive, so the goals are separate.

questions.stem: Choose the correct form: Both of my ____ offices are on the fifth floor.
options: sisters-in-law's
sister-in-law's
sisters'-in-law
sister-in-laws'
questions.why: Pluralize the main word (sisters), then add 's at the end of the compound.

questions.stem: Find the error in the sentence about a company rule.
questions.why: Two weeks is plural, so the apostrophe follows the s.

questions.stem: Which sentence uses a possessive before a gerund correctly?
options: The coach was pleased about Faisals' improving so quickly.
The coach was pleased about Faisal improving's so quickly.
The coach was pleased about Faisal's improving so quickly.
The coach was pleased about Faisals improving so quickly.
questions.why: In formal writing, a noun before a gerund takes the possessive form.

questions.stem: Which THREE sentences use possessives correctly? Choose three.
options: Somebody elses' bag was left behind.
The editor in chief's comments were brief.
The childrens's choir sang first.
Everyone else's tickets arrived on time.
The committee's decision surprised the members.
The two companies's profits rose sharply.
questions.why: Add 's to the last word of a phrase; plurals ending in s take only an apostrophe.

questions.stem: Which sentence is correctly punctuated?
options: The director of the museums speech opened the ceremony.
The director of the museum speech's opened the ceremony.
The director's of the museum speech opened the ceremony.
The director of the museum's speech opened the ceremony.
questions.why: With a phrase like director of the museum, the 's goes on the last word.

questions.stem: Choose the form that best completes the sentence: The project's success depended on ____ careful work over many years.
options: Dr. Hassan's and Dr. Malik
Dr. Hassan and Dr. Maliks'
Dr. Hassan and Dr. Malik's
Dr. Hassans and Dr. Maliks
questions.why: Shared work is joint ownership, so only the last name takes 's.

questions.stem: Find the error in the sentence about the Ibn Sina exhibit.
questions.why: Ibn Sina owns the texts, so the name needs 's.

questions.stem: Decide whether each sentence about a research team correctly uses a possessive or needs revision.

rows.text: The team's members disagreed about their methods.
The two labs's policies on safety are identical.
A month's worth of data was lost in the power cut.
The scientist's who published first received credit.

questions.why: Use 's only to show possession, and use s' for regular plurals.

questions.stem: Which TWO revisions correctly remove the awkward chain of possessives in “the city's museum's director's announcement” while keeping its meaning? Choose two.
options: the citys museum director announcement
the announcement by the director of the city's museum
the city museum director's announcement
the city's museums' director's announcement
questions.why: An of-phrase or a noun used as an adjective can replace stacked possessives.

questions.stem: Choose the word that tells more about how the puppy moved: The puppy ____ across the grass.
options: was
did
raced
went
questions.why: Raced tells exactly how the puppy moved.

questions.stem: Match each plain phrase to a more exact word.
questions.why: One exact word can replace a plain phrase.

questions.stem: True or false: “The bird sang” tells more than “The bird did something.”
questions.why: Sang is an exact word; did something is not.

questions.stem: Which sentence gives the clearest picture?
options: The gray cat napped in the warm sun.
It was a cat and it was very nice.
The animal did a thing outside today.
The cat was there in some place outside.
questions.why: Gray, napped, and warm sun help the reader see the cat.

questions.stem: Which TWO words are more exact than “nice” to describe a sunny day at the beach? Choose two.
options: okay
bright
breezy
fine
questions.why: Bright and breezy tell what the day was like.

questions.stem: Choose the most precise verb: The hungry camel ____ the dry leaves from the bush.
options: munched
got
had
took
questions.why: Munched shows exactly how the camel ate.

questions.stem: Decide whether each sentence for a school science report has a formal tone or an informal tone.

rows.text: The plant grew three centimeters in one week.
Our plant got super huge, like, really fast!
We measured the soil temperature each morning.
Honestly, the bean thing was kind of cool.

questions.why: Formal writing avoids slang and chatty words.

questions.stem: Find the part that should be more formal in this sentence from a report on Ibn al-Haytham.
segments: and came up with tons of
questions.why: Tons of is slang; a report needs formal words.

questions.stem: Which revision makes the sentence “The storm was bad” more precise?
options: The storm was very, very bad on that awful day.
The storm was the worst thing in a while.
The sandstorm blocked the sun for three hours.
The storm was really bad and it was not good at all.
questions.why: Specific details tell exactly how the storm was bad.

questions.stem: Which TWO sentences would fit best in a polite request to the principal for a school garden? Choose two.
options: A garden would help students learn about plants and soil.
We would appreciate the chance to plant vegetables near the library.
Everyone knows a garden is way better than nothing.
Give us a garden, because the yard is totally boring.
questions.why: A polite request uses respectful words and clear reasons.

questions.stem: Match each vague phrase to the most precise replacement for a report on Red Sea coral reefs.

pairs.right: bleaching on a third of the reef

questions.why: Numbers and specific terms make writing precise.

questions.stem: Choose the word with the most fitting connotation for a news report about a careful rescue: The divers gently ____ the trapped turtle from the net.
options: took
grabbed
yanked
freed
questions.why: Freed fits the gentle, positive meaning; yanked and grabbed suggest roughness.

questions.stem: Find the part that shifts the tone in this sentence from a formal report on solar energy.
questions.why: Seriously awesome is informal and breaks the formal style.

questions.stem: Which sentence is the most concise way to say “In my personal opinion, I think that the experiment was not successful at all”?
options: The experiment, in my view, was not at all successful.
I personally think the experiment was not very successful.
The experiment failed.
In my opinion, I believe the experiment was unsuccessful.
questions.why: Concise writing removes repeated and unneeded words.

questions.stem: A student is writing an objective summary of a debate about school uniforms. Which TWO sentences keep an objective tone? Choose two.
options: Supporters made the only sensible argument in the room.
Supporters argued that uniforms reduce morning decisions.
Opponents said uniforms limit personal expression.
Opponents whined that uniforms are uncomfortable.
questions.why: An objective tone reports ideas without judging them.

questions.stem: Decide whether each word has a positive or negative connotation when used to describe a determined athlete.

rows.text: persistent
stubborn
dedicated
obsessed

questions.why: Words with similar meanings can carry different feelings.

questions.stem: Choose the phrase that best maintains the formal style: The committee will ____ the proposal at next week's meeting.
options: mess with
consider
check out
go over
questions.why: Consider is formal and precise.

questions.stem: Part A: Read the sentence: “The new desalination plant, though costly, delivers clean water to thousands of homes.” What is the tone of the sentence?

partA.stem: Part A: Read the sentence: “The new desalination plant, though costly, delivers clean water to thousands of homes.” What is the tone of the sentence?

options.label: A
options.text: balanced and informative

options.label: B
options.text: playful and humorous

options.label: C
options.text: angry and critical

options.label: D
options.text: sad and regretful

partB.stem: Part B: Which phrase from the sentence best supports the answer to Part A?

options.label: A
options.text: new desalination plant

options.label: B
options.text: delivers clean water

options.label: C
options.text: thousands of homes

options.label: D
options.text: though costly

questions.why: Admitting a drawback while stating a benefit creates a balanced tone.

questions.stem: Find the part with imprecise wording in this sentence about Al-Khwarizmi.
questions.why: Did stuff is vague; helped is precise.

questions.stem: Which revision best eliminates the redundancy in “The two twins were both identical and looked exactly alike”?
options: The two twins were both identical.
The twins were identical.
The two twins looked exactly alike.
The twins were both alike and identical.
questions.why: Twins already means two, and identical means exactly alike.

questions.stem: Which word best replaces “said” to show reluctance in this sentence: “I suppose I can help,” Kareem said.
options: insisted
announced
conceded
declared
questions.why: Conceded means agreed unwillingly.

questions.stem: Choose the phrase that best keeps the measured, objective tone of a scientific abstract: The data ____ a link between soil salinity and reduced crop yields.
options: suggest
prove beyond any doubt
scream out
totally show
questions.why: Scientific writing uses cautious, precise verbs like suggest.

questions.stem: Find the part that disrupts the consistent style of this sentence from a formal museum guide.
segments: and was, like, a total game-changer.
questions.why: Slang breaks the formal style of the rest of the sentence.

questions.stem: Decide whether each revision of a cover letter for a marine research internship improves precision or creates wordiness.

rows.text: “I helped with research” → “I recorded water-temperature data for six weeks”
“I am interested” → “I am very much interested and quite keen and eager”
“good at computers” → “proficient in spreadsheet analysis”
“I can start soon” → “I am able to begin at a point in time that is soon”

questions.why: Precise revisions add specific information; wordy ones add only length.

questions.stem: A writer is revising a formal research paper on falconry. Which THREE revisions improve style and precision? Choose three.
options: Change “peregrine falcons” to “those cool birds”
Change “hunt” to “do their thing”
Change “they're super smart” to “they demonstrate keen problem-solving”
Change “trained” to “taught real good”
Change “really fast” to “at speeds exceeding 300 km/h”
Change “a bunch of birds” to “a flock of twelve falcons”
questions.why: Precise revisions use specific, formal language.

questions.stem: Which revision of “The policy had a big effect on a lot of people” is most precise for an academic essay?
options: The policy impacted a large number of people in a big and important way.
The policy's effect on people was big, important, and felt by many of them.
The water-rationing policy altered daily routines for nearly 40,000 residents.
The policy had a very significant and enormous effect on many different people everywhere.
questions.why: Precise writing names the policy, the effect, and the number affected.

questions.stem: Part A: Read this sentence from a speech at a science-fair awards ceremony: “Some will call these projects modest; I call them the first quiet steps of discovery.” What is the speaker's tone?

partA.stem: Part A: Read this sentence from a speech at a science-fair awards ceremony: “Some will call these projects modest; I call them the first quiet steps of discovery.” What is the speaker's tone?

options.label: A
options.text: admiring and encouraging

options.label: B
options.text: humorous and teasing

options.label: C
options.text: dismissive and doubtful

options.label: D
options.text: neutral and detached

partB.stem: Part B: Which word or phrase from the sentence most clearly creates this tone?

options.label: A
options.text: modest

options.label: B
options.text: first quiet steps of discovery

options.label: C
options.text: Some will call

options.label: D
options.text: these projects

questions.why: The speaker reframes modest projects as the beginning of discovery, which encourages the students.

questions.stem: Find the part where diction undercuts the solemn tone of this sentence from a eulogy for a beloved teacher.
segments: she guided students with patience and grace,
a pretty big hole in our school.
questions.correction: a silence our halls will long remember.
questions.why: Pretty big is casual and clashes with the solemn tone.

questions.stem: A writer wants to convey restrained irony in a review of an overpriced, underpowered phone. Which TWO sentences best achieve this? Choose two.
options: The camera captures colors that exist nowhere in nature, a bold artistic choice.
This phone is terrible and nobody should ever buy it under any circumstances.
The phone has a battery, a camera, and a screen, along with several apps.
Its battery lasts nearly until lunch, an impressive feat for the price of a small car.
questions.why: Restrained irony praises on the surface while signaling criticism.

questions.stem: Choose the phrase that most precisely captures the nuance: The scholar's reply was ____: every word was polite, yet each one quietly dismissed her rival's theory.
options: completely indifferent
warmly enthusiastic
coolly courteous
openly hostile
questions.why: Coolly courteous captures politeness with an undertone of rejection.

questions.stem: Match each word with a prefix to its meaning.
questions.why: Un- can mean not or the opposite of; re- means again.

questions.stem: Choose the word that means “tie again”: Sam had to ____ his shoe.
options: untie
retie
tied
questions.why: Re- means again, so retie means tie again.

questions.stem: True or false: The prefix un- in “unsafe” means “not.”
questions.why: Unsafe means not safe.

questions.stem: Sort these words by what their prefix means: un- (not) or re- (again).

rows.text: unkind
refill
unfair
reread

questions.why: Un- means not; re- means again.

questions.stem: What does the word “preheat” mean in “Mom will preheat the oven”?
options: not heat
heat again
heat too much
heat before
questions.why: Pre- means before.

questions.stem: Choose the prefix that makes the sentence make sense: The bridge was ____safe, so the city closed it.
options: mis
un
pre
re
questions.why: Unsafe means not safe, which is why the bridge was closed.

questions.stem: Match each prefix to its meaning.
questions.why: Knowing a prefix helps you figure out a new word.

questions.stem: Which TWO words have a prefix that means “not”? Choose two.
options: rebuild
preview
dishonest
impossible
questions.why: Im- and dis- can both mean not.

questions.stem: Find the word with the wrong prefix in the sentence about a lost map.
questions.why: Mis- means wrongly, so misread means read wrongly.

questions.stem: In “The team will preview the new stadium before the game,” what does “preview” mean?
options: see the wrong way
see ahead of time
not see at all
see once again
questions.why: Pre- means before.

questions.stem: Decide what the prefix means in each science word: anti-, inter-, or sub-.

rows.text: antibiotic
international
submarine
subsoil
antifreeze

questions.why: Anti- means against, inter- means between, and sub- means under.

questions.stem: Choose the word that best completes the sentence: Pearl divers often stayed ____ for more than a minute.
options: remerged
emerged
submerged
merged
questions.why: Sub- means under, so submerged means under the water.

questions.stem: The prefix trans- means “across.” Which word most likely means “to send across a distance”?
options: submit
recommit
permit
transmit
questions.why: Trans- (across) + mit (send) = send across.

questions.stem: Find the error in prefix use in this sentence about Ibn Battuta.
segments: to many people of his time.
questions.why: Before p, the prefix in- becomes im-.

questions.stem: Which TWO words contain a prefix meaning “one”? Choose two.
options: tricycle
unicycle
bicycle
monorail
questions.why: Uni- and mono- mean one; bi- means two and tri- means three.

questions.stem: Match each Greek or Latin prefix to its meaning.
questions.why: Greek and Latin prefixes appear in many academic words.

questions.stem: Choose the word that best fits: Because both teams agreed to the new rules, it was a ____ agreement.
options: collateral
bilateral
multilateral
unilateral
questions.why: Bi- means two, and two teams agreed.

questions.stem: True or false: The prefix counter- in “counterbalance” means “with” or “together.”
questions.why: Counter- means against or opposite.

questions.stem: Decide whether the prefix in each word means “before” or “after.”

rows.text: prehistoric
postwar
antechamber
postscript
foresee

questions.why: Pre-, ante-, and fore- mean before; post- means after.

questions.stem: Using your knowledge of prefixes, what does “malnourished” most likely mean in “The rescued camel was malnourished”?
options: poorly fed
fed before others
fed too often
fed again
questions.why: Mal- means bad or poorly.

questions.stem: In the sentence “The witness's account was incoherent, so the investigators could not use it,” which meaning of the prefix in- applies?
options: not
into
very
within
questions.why: Incoherent means not coherent, which is why the account could not be used.

questions.stem: Which THREE words contain a prefix that means “not”? Choose three.
options: overcast
interact
precede
irreversible
nonessential
illegible
questions.why: Ir-, non-, and il- can all mean not.

questions.stem: Choose the word that best completes the sentence: The scientist's claim was ____: no experiment could ever show whether it was true or false.
options: falsifiable
misfalsified
refalsified
unfalsifiable
questions.why: Un- (not) + falsifiable (able to be tested and disproved) = cannot be tested.

questions.stem: Decide whether the prefix in each word means “in / into” or “not.”

rows.text: inhale
inaccurate
import
immobile
inject

questions.why: The prefixes in- and im- can mean into or not; context and root decide.

questions.stem: Find the word whose prefix makes this sentence about a dam project illogical.
segments: the project ran out of money
questions.why: Running out of money means the cost was guessed too low, so under- is needed.

questions.stem: Using its prefix, what does “hypoallergenic” most likely mean in “The hospital ordered hypoallergenic pillows”?
options: tested again for allergies
less likely to cause allergies
more likely to cause allergies
completely free of allergies
questions.why: Hypo- means under or less, not completely free.

questions.stem: Match each word to the meaning its prefix contributes.
questions.why: Prefixes like ante-, anti-, pseudo-, omni-, and retro- shape meaning.

questions.stem: Choose the word whose prefix makes the sentence logical: The historian argued that the date on the manuscript was an ____, since paper of that type did not exist until a century later.
options: antecedent
chronometer
anachronism
synchronism
questions.why: Ana- (back) + chron (time): something placed in the wrong time.

questions.stem: Which TWO sentences use a prefixed word correctly in context? Choose two.
options: The noisy crowd was inaudible from every seat in the stadium.
The predecessor of the invention came after it and improved it.
The committee's decision was irrevocable, so no appeal was possible.
The guide spoke through an interpreter at the multilingual conference.
questions.why: Inaudible means cannot be heard, and pre- in predecessor means before.

questions.stem: Find the part where a prefix creates a contradiction in this sentence about medieval astronomy.
segments: that later astronomers relied on them
questions.why: Astronomers would rely on precise measurements, not imprecise ones.

questions.stem: Choose the word that tells where the cat is: The cat is ____ the box.
options: the
and
in
questions.why: In is a preposition that tells where.

questions.stem: True or false: In “The ball rolled under the bed,” the word “under” tells where the ball went.
questions.why: Under is a preposition that tells where.

questions.stem: Match each position word to its opposite.
questions.why: Position words can have opposites.

questions.stem: Which TWO words are prepositions in “The boy ran across the park after school”? Choose two.
options: after
boy
ran
across
questions.why: Across tells where and after tells when.

questions.stem: Which sentence tells WHEN Lina reads?
options: Lina reads on the sofa.
Lina reads before bed.
Lina reads with her dad.
Lina reads in her room.
questions.why: Before bed tells when.

questions.stem: Decide whether each prepositional phrase about a trip to the souq tells where or when.

rows.text: inside the spice shop
after lunch
near the fountain
during the holiday

questions.why: Prepositional phrases can tell where or when.

questions.stem: Choose the correct preposition: The team was proud ____ its win.
options: with
of
at
for
questions.why: We say proud of.

questions.stem: Find the mistake in the sentence about Maha's science interest.
questions.why: We say interested in.

questions.stem: Which THREE phrases in “After the storm, the fishermen sailed toward the harbor with their nets” are prepositional phrases? Choose three.
options: with their nets
toward the harbor
After the storm
the fishermen
sailed toward
questions.why: A prepositional phrase starts with a preposition and ends with its object.

questions.stem: Which sentence uses “between” or “among” correctly?
options: Rana shared the dates between her five cousins.
Rana shared the dates among her five cousins.
Rana divided the job among her and her brother.
Rana stood among the two tall palm trees.
questions.why: Use among for three or more and between for two.

questions.stem: Choose the preposition that completes the sentence correctly: The new stadium is similar ____ the old one in size.
options: with
as
to
from
questions.why: We say similar to.

questions.stem: Decide whether each prepositional phrase in these sentences about a falcon acts as an adjective or an adverb.

rows.text: “with the hood” in “The falcon with the hood waited quietly.”
“toward the field” in “The falcon dove toward the field.”
“near the window” in “The perch near the window was empty.”
“At dawn” in “At dawn, the falcon hunted.”

questions.why: Adjective phrases describe nouns; adverb phrases tell where, when, or how.

questions.stem: Find the error in the sentence about the hiking trip.
questions.why: The object of a preposition takes an object pronoun (me).

questions.stem: Which sentence places the phrase “with a long tail” so that it clearly describes the lizard?
options: The lizard with a long tail ate the cricket.
The lizard ate the cricket with a long tail.
With a long tail, the cricket was eaten.
The lizard ate with a long tail the cricket.
questions.why: Place a prepositional phrase right after the noun it describes.

questions.stem: Which TWO sentences use pronouns correctly after a preposition? Choose two.
options: The teacher sat beside Ahmed and I.
The coach gave the medals to Omar and me.
The secret stayed between her and them.
The gift was from my sister and she.
questions.why: Pronouns after prepositions take object forms: me, her, them.

questions.stem: Choose the correct preposition: The museum is famous ____ its collection of ancient astrolabes.
options: by
about
for
of
questions.why: We say famous for.

questions.stem: Decide whether the word in capitals acts as a preposition or an adverb in each sentence about a desert hike.

rows.text: We climbed UP the dune.
The sun came UP early.
Hamad walked AROUND the camp.
The wind swirled AROUND all night.

questions.why: A preposition has an object; an adverb does not.

questions.stem: Find the unnecessary word in this question about the new library.
questions.why: Where already means at what place, so at is not needed.

questions.stem: Which sentence uses the idiomatic preposition correctly?
options: Fahad is capable in leading the robotics team.
Fahad is capable at leading the robotics team.
Fahad is capable for leading the robotics team.
Fahad is capable of leading the robotics team.
questions.why: We say capable of.

questions.stem: Which TWO sentences avoid a misplaced prepositional phrase? Choose two.
options: With binoculars, the scientist watched the flamingos.
I saw a camel driving to Riyadh on the highway.
In the newspaper, I read about the new metro line.
The teacher handed out maps to students with colored borders.
questions.why: Place a phrase where it clearly modifies the right word.

questions.stem: Choose the preposition that is standard in formal writing: The proposal was not in accordance ____ the safety guidelines.
options: by
with
to
of
questions.why: The standard phrase is in accordance with.

questions.stem: Which revision best reduces the string of prepositional phrases in “The report on the effects of the use of plastic in the oceans of the world”?
options: The report on how plastic affects the world's oceans
The report regarding effects of the use of plastic in oceans
The report about the effects of the use of ocean plastic
The report on the effects of plastic use in world oceans of the planet
questions.why: Turning phrases into a verb and a possessive removes stacked of-phrases.

questions.stem: Find the error in the sentence about the research grant.
questions.why: Whoever is the subject of submits, even though the clause follows a preposition.

questions.stem: Decide whether each sentence about learning and museums places its prepositional phrase clearly or leaves it misplaced or dangling.

rows.text: At the age of six, my father taught me to swim.
At the age of six, I learned to swim from my father.
The museum displays a telescope used by Ulugh Beg in a glass case.
In a glass case, the museum displays a telescope used by Ulugh Beg.

questions.why: An introductory phrase must describe the subject right after it.

questions.stem: Which THREE sentences use prepositions correctly in formal writing? Choose three.
options: She is averse against taking unnecessary risks.
The results were independent from the variables.
Her conclusions differ from those of her advisor.
The data are consistent with earlier findings.
The author's argument is centered around one claim.
The team was oblivious to the approaching storm.
questions.why: Standard forms are consistent with, differ from, oblivious to, independent of, averse to, and centered on.

questions.stem: Which sentence uses a compound preposition correctly in formal written English?
options: With regards to the budget, the board made no changes.
With regard to the budget, the board made no changes.
Regarding to the budget, the board made no changes.
In regards of the budget, the board made no changes.
questions.why: The standard forms are with regard to, in regard to, and regarding.

questions.stem: Choose the word that completes the sentence correctly: The award, shared by Dr. Saleh and ____, recognized a decade of research on desert locusts.
options: mine
myself
I
me
questions.why: The object of the preposition by takes the object pronoun me.

questions.stem: Find the redundant preposition in the sentence about the explorer's archive.
segments: in which the letters of the explorer
questions.why: In which already supplies the preposition, so a second in is redundant.

questions.stem: Which TWO sentences correctly end with a preposition, a construction acceptable in formal English when moving it would be awkward? Choose two.
options: This is the problem the engineers must deal with.
Where did the researchers go to?
The instrument she relied on had been calibrated that morning.
Which lab is the sample at?
questions.why: A final preposition is fine when needed, but not when it is redundant after where.

questions.stem: Decide whether each sentence about a historian's research uses the preposition that its meaning requires.

rows.text: The historian's account is based on letters from the period.
The findings are contingent to further testing.
Her theory was predicated on a single manuscript.
The museum was indifferent of public opinion.
The scholar was preoccupied with dating the coins.

questions.why: Correct idioms are contingent on and indifferent to.

questions.stem: Choose the word that best completes the sentences: Sara has a new bike. ____ is red.
options: She
They
It
questions.why: It stands for one thing, the bike.

questions.stem: Read: “Ali and Omar went to the park. They played ball.” Who does the word They stand for?
options: the ball
Ali and Omar
the park
only Ali, the first boy
questions.why: They stands for more than one person: Ali and Omar.

questions.stem: Which word, he or she, can take the place of each name: Ahmed, Mona, my grandfather, Aunt Laila?

rows.text: Ahmed
Mona
my grandfather
Aunt Laila

questions.why: Use he for a boy or man and she for a girl or woman.

questions.stem: Find the mistake in the sentence about Mom baking bread.
questions.why: Mom is a woman, so the pronoun is she.

questions.stem: True or false: In “The birds built a nest, and it sang all day,” the word it is the right word for the birds.
questions.why: Birds means more than one, so the pronoun should be they.

questions.stem: Choose the pronoun that best completes the sentence: The team members packed ____ bags after the game.
options: his
its
our
their
questions.why: Team members is plural, so it takes their.

questions.stem: Which sentence uses a pronoun that agrees with its antecedent?
options: Each girl brought its own notebook to class.
Each girl brought them own notebook to class.
Each girl brought her own notebook to class.
Each girl brought our own notebook to class.
questions.why: One girl needs the singular pronoun her.

questions.stem: Match each sentence about a falcon, a project, and scientists to the antecedent of its pronoun.

pairs.left: The falcon spread its wings over the dunes.
Huda and I finished our project early.

questions.why: The antecedent is the noun the pronoun replaces.

questions.stem: Find the pronoun error in the sentence about the museum visit.
questions.why: Students is plural, so the pronoun must be they.

questions.stem: Which TWO sentences have a pronoun that does NOT agree with its antecedent? Choose two.
options: The girls finished their drawings early.
The dog wagged their tail happily.
The tree dropped its leaves in autumn.
The box of crayons lost their lid.
questions.why: Box and dog are singular things, so each needs its.

questions.stem: Choose the pronoun that correctly completes the sentence: Each of the robots completed ____ task in under a minute.
options: theirs
its
their
it's
questions.why: Each is singular, and a robot is a thing, so its is correct.

questions.stem: Which sentence contains an unclear (ambiguous) pronoun?
options: When Faisal met Khalid at the airport, he was tired.
When Faisal arrived at the airport, he was tired.
Khalid noticed that Faisal looked tired at the airport.
Faisal was tired when he met Khalid at the airport.
questions.why: He could mean Faisal or Khalid, so the reader cannot tell.

questions.stem: Find the pronoun error in the sentence about the film crew's cameras.
questions.why: One is singular, so the pronoun must be it.

questions.stem: Decide whether each sentence about the science fair uses pronouns clearly or has an unclear pronoun.

rows.text: Mariam told Reem that her poster had won.
Mariam told Reem, “Your poster won.”
The judges praised the robot and gave it first prize.
They say the fair will move to the gym next year.

questions.why: A pronoun is unclear when it could point to two nouns or to no noun at all.

questions.stem: Part A: Read the sentence: “After the fishermen pulled the nets onto the boats, they were full of silver fish.” What is the problem with the sentence?

partA.stem: Part A: Read the sentence: “After the fishermen pulled the nets onto the boats, they were full of silver fish.” What is the problem with the sentence?

options.label: A
options.text: The pronoun they could refer to the nets or the boats.

options.label: B
options.text: The pronoun they does not agree in number with fishermen.

options.label: C
options.text: The sentence has no antecedent for any of its pronouns.

options.label: D
options.text: The pronoun they should be the object form them.

partB.stem: Part B: Which revision best fixes the problem?

options.label: A
options.text: After the fishermen pulled the nets onto the boats, them were full of silver fish.

options.label: B
options.text: After the fishermen pulled the nets onto the boats, the nets were full of silver fish.

options.label: C
options.text: After the fishermen pulled them onto the boats, they were full of silver fish.

options.label: D
options.text: After the fishermen pulled the nets onto the boats, it was full of silver fish.

questions.why: Replacing they with the nets removes the doubt.

questions.stem: Choose the pronoun that correctly completes the sentence: Neither the coach nor the players had packed ____ uniforms.
options: their
his
its
questions.why: With neither…nor, the pronoun agrees with the nearer antecedent, players.

questions.stem: Which TWO sentences use pronouns that agree with their antecedents? Choose two.
options: Every one of the trucks needs their tires checked.
Either Salma or Dana will present her findings first.
The jury delivered its verdict after an hour.
Neither of the windows had their shutters closed.
questions.why: Every one and neither are singular, so they need its.

questions.stem: Find the vague pronoun in the sentence about desert foxes.
questions.why: It has no antecedent; name who is giving the information.

questions.stem: Which sentence avoids a vague pronoun?
options: At the gate they told Hamad that he had forgotten his own badge.
Hamad forgot his badge at the gate, and that mistake delayed the group.
Hamad forgot his badge at the gate, which delayed the entire group.
Hamad and Saad reached the gate, and he had forgotten his badge.
questions.why: Naming that mistake gives the pronoun a clear meaning.

questions.stem: Put these sentences about a solar car in an order that makes every pronoun clear.
sequence: Engineering students in Dhahran built a solar car.
They tested it on a long desert highway.
Its panels collected energy even in the late afternoon.
This success convinced the team to enter a national race.
questions.why: Each pronoun needs its antecedent to come first.

questions.stem: Choose the word that correctly completes the sentence: The panel of experts released ____ report on coral bleaching on Monday.
options: there
its
their
it's
questions.why: A collective noun acting as one unit takes the singular its.

questions.stem: Which revision best corrects the unclear pronoun in “When the archive moved the manuscripts to the new library, it was damaged”?
options: When the archive moved the manuscripts to the new library, one of the manuscripts was damaged.
When it moved the manuscripts to the new library, the archive was damaged.
When the archive moved the manuscripts to the new library, they was damaged.
When the archive moved the manuscripts to the new library, it was badly damaged during the long move.
questions.why: Naming one of the manuscripts removes the doubt about what was damaged.

questions.stem: Select the sentence about the coastal desalination plant that contains a pronoun with no clear antecedent.

segments.text: The plant on the coast turns seawater into drinking water.
Engineers monitor its pumps around the clock.
In the local newspaper, they claim the plant will double its output.
Its managers plan to open a second site next year.

questions.why: They has no antecedent; the writer should name who makes the claim.

questions.stem: Find the pronoun error in the sentence about the falcon and the hawk.
segments: Both the falcon and the hawk
questions.why: Two antecedents joined by and need a plural pronoun.

questions.stem: Classify each sentence about the robotics league by whether its pronoun agrees with its antecedent.

rows.text: The league announced its new rules on Sunday.
Each of the robots had their battery replaced.
Neither of the drones could finish its route.
Every competitor's laptop had their charger attached.

questions.why: Each, neither, and every competitor's laptop are singular things that take its.

questions.stem: Choose the pronoun that correctly completes the sentence: Neither the ministry nor the regional councils have published ____ budgets for next year.
options: its
their
there
his
questions.why: The pronoun agrees with the nearer antecedent, councils, which is plural.

questions.stem: Which TWO sentences contain a pronoun error? Choose two.
options: If the students do not return the lab goggles promptly, they will be cleaned by the staff.
Whoever finishes the experiment first should record the results before leaving.
The council, having reviewed every bid, announced its decision on Thursday.
The committee members, each of whom had read the proposal, raised its objections.
