questions.stem: Find the pronoun error in the sentence about the documentary and its sources.
segments: Neither the documentary nor the books it was based on
questions.why: The pronoun agrees with the nearer antecedent, books, so it must be their.

questions.stem: Which sentence is written so that every pronoun has one clear antecedent?
options: The pilot and the inspector argued, which meant the report was revised that night.
After the pilot spoke with the inspector, she revised the report that night.
The pilot told the inspector, “I will revise my report tonight.”
The pilot told the inspector that he would revise his report tonight.
questions.why: Quoting the pilot's words makes I and my point only to the pilot.

questions.stem: Part A: Read the sentence: “The architects presented models of the new towers to the city planners, and they were impressed by their energy-saving design.” Which statement best describes the pronoun problem?

partA.stem: Part A: Read the sentence: “The architects presented models of the new towers to the city planners, and they were impressed by their energy-saving design.” Which statement best describes the pronoun problem?

options.label: A
options.text: Both they and their could point to more than one plural noun.

options.label: B
options.text: The pronoun their should be the contraction they're.

options.label: C
options.text: The pronoun they disagrees in number with architects.

options.label: D
options.text: The sentence has no plural noun for they to refer to.

partB.stem: Part B: Which revision best removes the problem?

options.label: A
options.text: The architects presented models of the new towers to the city planners, and them were impressed by their design.

options.label: B
options.text: The architects presented them to the city planners, and they were impressed by their energy-saving design.

options.label: C
options.text: The architects presented models of the new towers to the city planners, and they were impressed by its energy-saving design.

options.label: D
options.text: The architects presented models of the new towers to the city planners, who were impressed by the towers' energy-saving design.

questions.why: Using who for the planners and naming the towers gives each reference one clear antecedent.

questions.stem: Choose the word that completes the sentence: I have ____ apples in my bag.
options: two
to
too
questions.why: Two is the number 2.

questions.stem: Match each contraction to the two words it stands for: can't, I'm, it's, we're.
questions.why: A contraction joins two words and uses an apostrophe for the missing letters.

questions.stem: Choose the word that completes the sentence: The kids put on ____ coats.
options: there
their
they're
questions.why: Their shows that the coats belong to the kids.

questions.stem: Which sentence is correct?
options: Dont forget your hat.
Do'nt forget your hat.
Don't forget you're hat.
Don't forget your hat.
questions.why: Don't needs an apostrophe where the o in not was, and your shows ownership.

questions.stem: True or false: In the sentence “Its raining, so take an umbrella,” the word Its is spelled correctly.
questions.why: It is raining shortens to It's, with an apostrophe.

questions.stem: Choose the word that completes the sentence: The camel lifted ____ head to sniff the wind.
options: its
it's
its'
questions.why: Its with no apostrophe shows ownership.

questions.stem: Decide which word belongs in each blank in these sentences about a beach trip.

rows.text: The shells are over ___ by the rocks.
The twins packed ___ snorkels.
___ going to swim after lunch.
Is ___ a lifeguard today?

questions.why: There is a place, their shows ownership, and they're means they are.

questions.stem: Find the mistake in the sentence about the new science lab.
questions.why: You're means you are.

questions.stem: Which TWO sentences use to, too, or two correctly? Choose two.
options: The soup was too hot to eat.
I have to many books to carry.
She bought too new pencils today.
We walked to the library after lunch.
questions.why: Too means also or very, and two is a number.

questions.stem: Match each sentence about a soccer match to the word that completes it.
questions.why: Whose and your show ownership; who's and you're are contractions.

questions.stem: Choose the word that completes the sentence: The scientists say ____ still studying how the comet formed.
options: they're
there
their
questions.why: They're means they are.

questions.stem: Find the mistake in the sentence about the company's drone.
questions.why: The possessive its has no apostrophe.

questions.stem: Which THREE sentences are written correctly? Choose three.
options: The parrot cleaned it's feathers.
Who's notebook is on the floor?
The players left their bags in the gym.
Their going to the museum tomorrow.
It's been a long week for the volunteers.
Whose turn is it to feed the fish?
questions.why: Use whose, their, and its for ownership; use who's, they're, and it's for contractions.

questions.stem: For each sentence about a desert hike, choose the correct word.

rows.text: Check ___ water supply before noon.
If ___ tired, rest in the shade.
___ map shows two wells ahead.
Call when ___ at the camp.

questions.why: Your shows ownership; you're means you are.

questions.stem: Which sentence uses contractions and possessive pronouns correctly?
options: It's clear that the team's plan worked, and there proud of it's results.
Its clear that the team's plan worked, and they're proud of it's results.
It's clear that the team's plan worked, and they're proud of its results.
It's clear that the teams plan worked, and their proud of its results.
questions.why: It's = it is, they're = they are, and its shows ownership.

questions.stem: Choose the word that correctly begins the sentence: ____ responsible for locking the laboratory tonight?
options: Who's
Who
Whose
questions.why: Who's means who is, which the sentence needs.

questions.stem: True or false: The sentence “The council will decide whose proposal is strongest” uses whose correctly.
questions.why: Whose shows ownership of the proposal.

questions.stem: Select the sentence about the coral reef survey that contains a homophone error.

segments.text: The divers counted fish along the reef's edge.
They're reports show that the reef is recovering.
Its colors have returned in several areas.
The team plans to return there next spring.

questions.why: The possessive is their reports, not they're.

questions.stem: Find the mistake in the sentence about the two runners.
questions.why: Their shows that the times belong to the runners.

questions.stem: Which revision correctly fixes every error in “Your welcome to join us, but its to late to sign up for the trip”?
options: Your welcome to join us, but it's too late to sign up for the trip.
You're welcome to join us, but it's too late to sign up for the trip.
You're welcome to join us, but it's to late to sign up for the trips.
You're welcome to join us, but its too late to sign up for the trips.
questions.why: The sentence needs you're, it's, and too.

questions.stem: Choose the word that correctly completes the sentence: The novelist, ____ latest book explores life on a pearl-diving ship, will speak at the festival.
options: who is
which's
whose
who's
questions.why: Whose shows that the book belongs to the novelist.

questions.stem: Decide whether each sentence about the archaeology dig is correct or contains a homophone error.

rows.text: The team's findings exceeded their expectations.
It's too early to say who's tools these were.
The site has lost much of its original wall.
Their are fragments of pottery in every layer.
They're hoping to finish before the summer heat.

questions.why: Whose shows ownership, and there introduces something that exists.

questions.stem: Which TWO words are used incorrectly in “Whose ready to explain why the satellite lost it's signal over there?” Choose two.
options: there
it's
explain
Whose
questions.why: The sentence needs Who's (who is) and the possessive its.

questions.stem: Find the mistake in the sentence about the engineers' calculations.
questions.why: Their shows that the calculations belong to the engineers.

questions.stem: Which sentence about the solar project contains no errors in pronouns, contractions, or homophones?
options: Whoever's design wins, the city will install their panels on schools, to.
Whose ever design wins, the city will install its panels on school's too.
Whoever's design wins, the city will install its panels on schools, too.
Who's ever design wins, the city will install it's panels on schools, too.
questions.why: Whoever's, its, and too are each used correctly in the first sentence.

questions.stem: Choose the word that correctly completes the sentence: The board, ____ members rarely agree, approved the plan unanimously.
options: whom
who's
whose
which
questions.why: Whose is the possessive relative pronoun: the members of the board.

questions.stem: Find the mistake in the sentence about the researchers' methods.
questions.why: Whose shows possession; who's means who is.

questions.stem: Which THREE sentences are free of errors in pronouns, contractions, and homophones? Choose three.
options: It's the city's oldest library, and its reading room still uses its original lamps.
The judges, whose decisions are final, say they're ready to announce the winners.
Two of the volunteers stayed late, too, to finish counting the birds.
The company, who's profits rose, thanked it's employees at the meeting.
The council members said there satisfied with the bridge's new design.
Your either too early or too late for the noon ferry to the island.
questions.why: Check every its/it's, whose/who's, their/there/they're, your/you're, and to/too/two.

questions.stem: Part A: Read the sentence: “The orchestra, who's conductor trained in Vienna, will perform it's new program at the festival, and there tickets sold out.” How many homophone errors does the sentence contain?

partA.stem: Part A: Read the sentence: “The orchestra, who's conductor trained in Vienna, will perform it's new program at the festival, and there tickets sold out.” How many homophone errors does the sentence contain?

options.label: A
options.text: one

options.label: B
options.text: three

options.label: C
options.text: four

options.label: D
options.text: two

partB.stem: Part B: Which revision corrects all of them?

options.label: A
options.text: The orchestra, who's conductor trained in Vienna, will perform its new program at the festival, and their tickets sold out.

options.label: B
options.text: The orchestra, whose conductor trained in Vienna, will perform its new program at the festival, and its tickets sold out.

options.label: C
options.text: The orchestra, whose conductor trained in Vienna, will perform its new program at the festival, and they're tickets sold out.

options.label: D
options.text: The orchestra, whose conductor trained in Vienna, will perform it's new program at the festival, and their tickets sold out.

questions.why: Who's, it's, and there are all wrong; the possessives whose and its fix them.

questions.stem: True or false: In “Each nation sent its strongest athletes, and it's clear the competition will be close,” both its and it's are used correctly.
questions.why: Its shows ownership, and it's means it is.

questions.stem: Which mark should go at the end? Where is my red cap____
questions.why: A question ends with a question mark.

questions.stem: Which sentence uses commas correctly in a list?
options: I like apples, grapes, and dates.
I, like apples, grapes and dates.
I like, apples grapes and dates.
I like apples grapes, and, dates.
questions.why: Commas go between the things in a list.

questions.stem: Which end mark does each sentence about the sun, the bus, and a whale need?

rows.text: The sun is hot today
Can you help me
Wow, look at that big whale
We ride the bus to school

questions.why: Telling sentences get a period, questions get a question mark, and strong feelings get an exclamation point.

questions.stem: Find the mistake in the sentence about where we live.
questions.why: Put a comma between a city and its country.

questions.stem: True or false: The sentence “Yes I can come to your party.” needs a comma after Yes.
questions.why: A comma follows yes or no at the start of a sentence.

questions.stem: Choose the punctuation that correctly completes the sentence: After the long hike____ we rested under a palm tree.
questions.why: A comma follows an introductory phrase.

questions.stem: Which TWO sentences use commas correctly? Choose two.
options: My sister, likes to paint.
We saw camels goats, and sheep.
Omar, please pass the salt.
When the rain stopped, we went outside.
questions.why: Use commas after a name you speak to and after an opening clause.

questions.stem: Find the comma mistake in the sentence about the museum.
questions.why: Every item in a series needs a comma after it.

questions.stem: For each sentence about a class trip, decide whether a comma is needed.

rows.text: Yes we will leave at eight.
We will leave at eight.
Before we ate lunch we visited the fort.
Huda and Sara sat together on the bus.

questions.why: Commas follow yes and introductory clauses, but not simple subjects.

questions.stem: Which sentence correctly uses commas to set off the name of the person being spoken to?
options: Do you know Faisal, where the map is?
Do you, know Faisal where the map is?
Do you know, Faisal, where the map is?
Do you know Faisal where, the map is?
questions.why: A name in direct address is set off by commas on both sides.

questions.stem: Choose the punctuation that correctly completes the sentence: The camping list included three items____ a tent, a lantern, and a compass.
questions.why: A colon introduces a list after a complete sentence.

questions.stem: Find the punctuation error in the sentence about the trained falcon.
segments: which had been trained for years
questions.correction: , which had been trained for years,
questions.why: A nonessential which clause is set off by commas.

questions.stem: Which TWO sentences correctly use commas in a compound sentence? Choose two.
options: The test was difficult, but most students passed it.
Most students studied hard, and passed the difficult test.
The wind grew stronger so, the sailors lowered the sails.
The wind grew stronger, so the sailors lowered the sails.
questions.why: Put the comma before the conjunction that joins two complete sentences.

questions.stem: Select the sentence about Rania's science fair project that is punctuated correctly.

segments.text: Rania built a model, of a wind turbine.
Her model, which used recycled parts won first place.
The judges praised its design, its cost, and its clear labels.
Next year she plans to build, a solar oven.

questions.why: Commas separate items in a series but do not split a verb from its object.

questions.stem: Which sentence correctly uses a semicolon?
options: The library closed early; because the storm knocked out power.
The library; closed early because the storm knocked out power.
The library closed early because; the storm knocked out power.
The library closed early; the storm had knocked out the power.
questions.why: A semicolon joins two complete, closely related sentences.

questions.stem: Choose the punctuation that belongs in the blank: The old fort was quiet____ only the wind moved through its gates.
questions.why: A semicolon joins two independent clauses; a comma alone makes a comma splice.

questions.stem: Classify each sentence about the robotics club as correctly punctuated or as a comma splice.

rows.text: The club met on Tuesday, the robot was not ready.
The club met on Tuesday, but the robot was not ready.
The motor overheated; the team replaced it.
The team replaced the motor, it worked perfectly.

questions.why: Two sentences joined only by a comma form a comma splice.

questions.stem: Find the punctuation error in the sentence about cousin Tariq.
questions.why: An appositive needs a comma at both ends.

questions.stem: Match each sentence about a marine biologist to the comma rule it shows.

pairs.left: Dr. Amal Saleh, a marine biologist, studies sea turtles.
However, the turtles return every spring.
She tagged turtles in Oman, Qatar, and Bahrain.
The nests were safe, but the eggs hatched late.

questions.why: Each comma has a job; naming the rule helps you place commas correctly.

questions.stem: Which sentence about the satellite is punctuated correctly?
options: On July 4, 2024 the satellite, sent its first image from orbit.
On July 4, 2024, the satellite sent its first image from orbit.
On July 4 2024, the satellite sent its first image from orbit.
On July, 4, 2024 the satellite sent its first image from orbit.
questions.why: A full date takes a comma after the day and after the year.

questions.stem: Choose the punctuation that correctly completes the sentence: The team visited Riyadh, Saudi Arabia____ Muscat, Oman; and Doha, Qatar.
questions.why: When items in a series already contain commas, semicolons separate the items.

questions.stem: Which TWO sentences use commas correctly with essential and nonessential clauses? Choose two.
options: The Nile which flows north, empties into the Mediterranean Sea.
The Nile, which flows north, empties into the Mediterranean Sea.
Students who finish early may begin the bonus problem.
The river that, flows past our city floods every spring.
questions.why: Essential clauses take no commas; nonessential clauses take a pair.

questions.stem: Find the punctuation error in the sentence about the delayed launch.
questions.why: Two independent clauses cannot be joined by a comma alone.

questions.stem: Part A: Read the sentence: “The new library, designed by a team of young architects uses sunlight to cool its reading rooms.” What punctuation error does the sentence contain?

partA.stem: Part A: Read the sentence: “The new library, designed by a team of young architects uses sunlight to cool its reading rooms.” What punctuation error does the sentence contain?

options.label: A
options.text: A comma is missing after architects to close the descriptive phrase.

options.label: B
options.text: The sentence is a run-on that needs a semicolon after library.

options.label: C
options.text: A colon should introduce the phrase about the architects.

options.label: D
options.text: A comma is needed after library and again after rooms.

partB.stem: Part B: Which rule explains the correction?

options.label: A
options.text: A semicolon must separate items that contain commas.

options.label: B
options.text: A comma must separate two independent clauses.

options.label: C
options.text: A nonessential phrase must be set off by a pair of commas.

options.label: D
options.text: A comma must follow every introductory word.

questions.why: An interrupting phrase that opens with a comma must close with one.

questions.stem: Which revision correctly punctuates “The documentary however left several questions unanswered”?
options: The documentary; however, left several questions unanswered.
The documentary, however left several questions, unanswered.
The documentary however, left several questions unanswered.
The documentary, however, left several questions unanswered.
questions.why: An interrupting word like however is set off by commas on both sides.

questions.stem: Choose the punctuation that correctly completes the sentence: The committee raised only one concern about the plan____ its cost.
questions.why: A colon after a complete clause can introduce a single explaining item.

questions.stem: Which THREE sentences are punctuated correctly? Choose three.
options: The delegates came from Amman, Jordan; Cairo, Egypt; and Tunis, Tunisia.
The lab, which had already lost a week repeated the test on Monday.
Because the samples were contaminated, the lab, which had already lost a week, repeated the test.
The proposal was ambitious, expensive, and, in the end, impossible to fund.
Al-Biruni measured the earth's radius, his method used a mountain and the horizon.
The researchers concluded, that the coral could recover within a decade.
questions.why: Watch for unpaired commas, comma splices, and commas that split a verb from its object.

questions.stem: Find the punctuation error in the sentence about Ibn Sina.
segments: whose medical encyclopedia was studied for centuries
questions.correction: whose medical encyclopedia was studied for centuries,
questions.why: A nonessential clause opened by a comma must be closed by a comma.

questions.stem: Decide whether each sentence about the map archive project is punctuated correctly.

rows.text: The archivists' goal was simple: preserve every map before the move.
The fragile maps, those drawn before 1800, were scanned first.
Several volunteers—most of them students, worked through the night.
The project's director asked, whether the scans could be finished by June.
Funding was limited; nevertheless, the team finished early.

questions.why: Paired marks must match, and no comma comes before an indirect question.

questions.stem: Part A: Read the sentence: “The guide warned us that the trail, though beautiful was steep, narrow, and in places, crumbling.” What is wrong with the punctuation?

partB.stem: Part B: Which version corrects the error?

options.label: C

options.label: D

questions.stem: Why is this joke funny? “Why did the cookie go to the doctor? It felt crummy.”
options: Crummy sounds like crumb and also means feeling bad.
Cookies can really visit a doctor's office.
Doctors like to eat cookies when they are at work.
The cookie was baked in the oven for too long.
questions.why: Crummy is about crumbs and about feeling sick.

questions.stem: Match each word to the word that sounds the same but means something different: sea, flower, pair, knight.
questions.why: Words that sound the same but mean different things are used in many jokes.

questions.stem: True or false: The joke “The bee was a good speller because it knew its B's” plays on the insect bee and the alphabet's B.
questions.why: Bee and B sound the same, which makes the joke.

questions.stem: Finish the joke with the word that has two meanings: Why did the student bring a ladder to class? She wanted to go to high ____.
options: school
desks
class
questions.why: High school is a kind of school, and a ladder takes you high.

questions.stem: Is each sentence about a clock or our class a pun (a joke with a word that has two meanings) or not a joke?

The clock on the wall says it is noon.
Our class went to see the camels.

questions.why: Four seconds sounds like for seconds, which means more food.

questions.stem: Choose the word that makes the pun work: The math book looked sad because it had too many ____.
options: pages
problems
numbers
questions.why: Problems means math questions and also troubles.

questions.stem: What makes this sentence a pun? “The astronaut skipped lunch because she wanted to wait for launch.”
options: The sentence explains a real rule that astronauts follow.
The word skipped shows the astronaut was moving fast.
Launch sounds like lunch, so the joke plays on both words.
Astronauts may not eat any food before a space flight.
questions.why: A pun can use two words that sound almost alike.

questions.stem: Match each pun about a tailor, a ruler, a tree, and a calendar to the word that has a double meaning.

pairs.left: The tailor's work was sew good.
A ruler is a great leader because it always measures up.
The tree did its homework because it wanted to turn over a new leaf.
The calendar was nervous because its days were numbered.

questions.why: In each pun, one word fits two meanings at once.

questions.stem: Which TWO sentences are puns? Choose two.
options: The fish swam slowly near the bottom of the coral reef.
I used to be a baker, but I could not make enough dough.
The baker sold warm bread to every family on the street.
The fish failed math because it was always below sea level.
questions.why: Dough means bread mix and money; sea level sounds like C level.

questions.stem: Select the line of this joke about a bicycle that contains the pun.

segments.text: Why did the bicycle fall over?
It had been riding all day.
It was two tired.
Its owner fixed it the next morning.

questions.why: Two tired sounds like too tired, and a bicycle has two tires.

questions.stem: Choose the word that creates a pun: The lazy kangaroo was a ____ potato.
options: pouch
couch
sofa

The banker lost interest in her job.
The cheetah could never hide because he was always spotted.
When the fog lifted, the city was mist by everyone.

questions.stem: Read: “Writing with a broken pencil is pointless.” Which two meanings of pointless create the wordplay?
options: having no eraser left and having no bright color
being made of wood and being of little value
having no paper nearby and having no straight lines
having no sharp tip and having no purpose
questions.why: A broken pencil has no point, and the task has no point.

questions.stem: True or false: In “The lighthouse keeper was a bright person,” the word bright can mean both clever and giving off light.

options.label: C

options.label: D

questions.stem: Put the lines of this riddle about a student and her clock in order so the wordplay comes at the end.

Her teacher had told her to be on time,
so she took the advice literally.

questions.stem: Which sentence uses a pun to describe an electrician?

The electrician's work was careful, and customers returned to her every year.
The electrician's work was expensive, but customers still trusted her advice.

questions.stem: Complete the pun: The geologist lost her job because she took her work for ____.
options: gravel
granite
sand

questions.stem: Which TWO sentences contain a pun? Choose two.
options: Atoms cannot be trusted because they make up everything.
The pharmacist's jokes were so bad they were a hard pill to swallow.
The pharmacist explained how often to take each tablet with water.
The chemist mixed the solutions carefully before the test began.
questions.why: Make up and hard pill to swallow each carry a literal and a figurative meaning.

questions.stem: Decide whether the key words in each sentence about a chef carry one meaning or two meanings.

rows.text: The chef was so stressed that she reached her boiling point.
The chef boiled water for the rice.
The chef chopped onions until her eyes watered.
The chef retired because she had bigger fish to fry.

questions.why: A pun uses a phrase that fits both the cooking and the feeling.

questions.stem: Why is the sentence “The archaeologist's career was in ruins” an example of wordplay?

questions.stem: Select the sentence about Nadia the weather reporter that contains a pun.

questions.stem: Match each sentence about an optometrist, snakes, a racecar, and silence to the type of wordplay it uses.

pairs.left: The optometrist fell into the lens grinder and made a spectacle of himself.
Seven slithering snakes slid silently south.
The racecar's name, Kayak, reads the same backward.
The silence in the hall was deafening.

questions.why: Wordplay can use meaning, sound, spelling, or contradiction.

questions.stem: Part A: In the sentence “The dentist's speech at the conference was mostly filler,” which word is the pun?

partA.stem: Part A: In the sentence “The dentist's speech at the conference was mostly filler,” which word is the pun?

options.label: B
options.text: mostly

options.label: C
options.text: filler

options.label: D

partB.stem: Part B: Which two meanings does the pun combine?

options.label: A

options.label: B

options.label: C

questions.why: Filler describes weak speech and a dental filling.

questions.stem: Complete the pun: When the clockmaker retired, he said he finally had some ____ on his hands.
options: time
money
work
tools
questions.why: Time on his hands means free time, and clocks have hands.

questions.stem: Which sentence contains zeugma, in which one word governs two others in different senses?
options: She looked for her keys and her ticket on the crowded platform.
She lost her keys and her temper on the crowded platform.
She held her keys tightly and her ticket even more tightly.
She lost her keys on the platform and then found them again.
questions.why: Lost applies literally to keys and figuratively to temper.

questions.stem: Match each sentence about travelers, patients, skills, and surgeons to the form of wordplay it shows.

pairs.left: The traveler packed his bag and his worries into the same small trunk.
The patient insisted that his allergy was a pigment of his imagination.
Work hard on your skills, and your skills will work hard for you.
The surgeon's jokes kept the whole ward in stitches.

questions.why: Zeugma stretches one verb, malapropism swaps a sound-alike word, chiasmus reverses a pattern, and a pun doubles a meaning.

questions.stem: Which TWO sentences contain a malapropism, the mistaken use of a word that sounds like the correct one? Choose two.
options: After the long trip, my brother lost his luggage and his patience.
The coach said our win was a foregone conclusion.
After the long trip, my brother fell into a deep comma on the couch.
The coach said our win was a foregone confusion.
questions.why: Confusion and comma are sound-alike errors for conclusion and coma; the last choice is zeugma, not a malapropism.

questions.stem: Part A: Read the sentence: “When the old mapmaker retired, he said he had finally found his place in the world.” What is the most likely purpose of the wordplay?

partA.stem: Part A: Read the sentence: “When the old mapmaker retired, he said he had finally found his place in the world.” What is the most likely purpose of the wordplay?

options.label: A
options.text: to show that the mapmaker had been lost for many years

options.label: B
options.text: to add gentle humor while suggesting the mapmaker feels content

options.label: C
options.text: to criticize the mapmaker for leaving his profession

options.label: D
options.text: to explain how maps are used to locate places

partB.stem: Part B: Which two meanings of found his place create the effect?

options.label: A
options.text: located a spot on a map, and felt at peace with his life

options.label: B
options.text: marked a page in a book, and finished his reading

options.label: C
options.text: won an award, and earned a high position at work

options.label: D
options.text: discovered his home address, and returned to his village

questions.why: The phrase fits a mapmaker's job and a person's sense of belonging.

questions.stem: Classify the wordplay in each sentence about travelers.

rows.text: She caught the early train and a terrible cold.
The pilot's landing was so smooth that passengers called it plane sailing.
The guide said the old statues were in perfect condiment.
He packed his maps and his hopes before dawn.

questions.why: Zeugma uses one verb in two senses; a malapropism swaps in a wrong sound-alike word.

questions.stem: Which sentence uses quotation marks correctly?
options: “Mom said, Time for bed.”
Mom “said,” Time for bed.
Mom said, Time for bed.”
Mom said, “Time for bed.”
questions.why: Quotation marks go around only the words Mom says.

questions.stem: Which mark goes in the blank? Ali said____ “I like the rain.”
questions.why: A comma comes after said, before the quotation.

questions.stem: Does each sentence about Sara, Dad, and the cat need quotation marks?

rows.text: Sara said let's play.
Sara wanted to play.
Dad asked can you help me?
The cat sat on the mat.

questions.why: Use quotation marks only when someone's exact words are shown.

questions.stem: Find the mistake in the sentences about Nora running fast.
questions.why: Every quotation needs closing marks at the end.

questions.stem: True or false: Quotation marks go around the exact words a person says.
questions.why: Quotation marks show a speaker's exact words.

questions.stem: Choose the correct punctuation: “Where did you find that shell____ asked Mariam.
questions.why: The question mark belongs to the spoken question, so it goes inside.

questions.stem: Find the mistake in the sentence about the tide.
questions.why: Commas go inside the closing quotation marks.

questions.stem: Which TWO sentences are punctuated correctly? Choose two.
options: Grandma asked “Would you like some dates”?
“We should leave now,” said Dad.
“We should leave now” said Dad.
Grandma asked, “Would you like some dates?”
questions.why: Use a comma between the quote and the speaker, and keep the question mark inside.

questions.stem: Put these lines of dialogue between Yusuf and Mr. Hassan in a logical order.
sequence: “Mr. Hassan, may I borrow a ruler?” asked Yusuf.
“Of course,” said Mr. Hassan. “Here you are.”
“Thank you,” Yusuf replied, smiling.
“Please return it after class,” Mr. Hassan reminded him.
questions.why: Dialogue follows the order of a real conversation: request, answer, thanks, reminder.

questions.stem: Which sentence correctly shows a split quotation?
options: “After lunch, said Coach Amal, we will practice passing.”
“After lunch,” said Coach Amal, “we will practice passing.”
“After lunch,” said Coach Amal, “We will practice passing.”
“After lunch” said Coach Amal “we will practice passing.”
questions.why: When one sentence is split, the second part starts with a lowercase letter.

questions.stem: Choose the correct way to complete the sentence: Did the guide really say ____
options: “The cave is closed today”?
“The cave is closed today.”?
“The cave is closed today?”
questions.why: When the whole sentence is the question, the question mark goes outside.

questions.stem: Find the mistake in the dialogue about Rania's experiment.
questions.why: A new sentence inside quotation marks begins with a capital letter.

questions.stem: For each title in a book report, decide whether it needs quotation marks or italics.

rows.text: a short story called The Silver Falcon
a novel called The Desert Clock
a poem called Morning at the Harbor
a magazine called Young Explorer

questions.why: Short works take quotation marks; long works take italics.

questions.stem: Select the sentence about Khalid's chess match that is punctuated correctly.

segments.text: “Check,” said Khalid, moving his knight forward.
His opponent sighed, “I didn't see that coming”.
“Is it over?” whispered a younger player?
“Not yet” Khalid replied, “there are still moves left.”

questions.why: The comma goes inside the closing mark, and the speaker tag follows it.

questions.stem: Part A: Which sentence about the pilot is an indirect quotation that needs NO quotation marks?

partA.stem: Part A: Which sentence about the pilot is an indirect quotation that needs NO quotation marks?

options.label: A
options.text: The pilot announced, we will land early.

options.label: B
options.text: The pilot said, I will land the plane early.

options.label: C
options.text: The pilot said, the flight will land early.

options.label: D

partB.stem: Part B: Which sentence correctly turns it into a direct quotation?

options.label: A
options.text: The pilot said, “The flight will land early”.

options.label: B
options.text: The pilot said that, “The flight will land early.”

options.label: C
options.text: The pilot said, “The flight will land early.”

options.label: D
options.text: The pilot said “that the flight would land early.”

questions.why: Indirect speech uses that and no marks; direct speech uses the exact words in quotation marks.

questions.stem: Which sentence correctly punctuates a quotation within a quotation?
options: Leen said, “The guide told us, ‘Stay on the path.”’
Leen said, “The guide told us, ‘Stay on the path.’”
Leen said, “The guide told us, “Stay on the path.””
Leen said, “The guide told us, Stay on the path.”
questions.why: Single marks go inside double marks, and they close first.

questions.stem: Find the mistake in the sentence about the new planetarium.
questions.why: The question belongs to Salem's words, so the mark goes inside.

questions.stem: Which TWO sentences correctly punctuate dialogue that is interrupted by a speaker tag? Choose two.
options: “The storm,” the captain warned, “Will reach the coast by noon.”
“We tried,” said Noor. “The door would not open.”
“The storm,” the captain warned, “will reach the coast by noon.”
“We tried,” said Noor, “the door would not open.”
questions.why: Continue one sentence in lowercase; start a new sentence after a period.

questions.stem: Match each sentence of Hana's dialogue to the punctuation rule it shows.

pairs.right: An exclamation point inside the quotation replaces the comma.
A comma follows the speaker tag before the quotation.
A question mark goes outside when the whole sentence asks.
A comma inside the closing mark ends the spoken part.

questions.why: Placement of marks depends on what belongs to the speaker.

questions.stem: Decide whether each sentence about a museum visit is a direct or an indirect quotation.

rows.text: The curator explained that the vase was a thousand years old.
“This vase is a thousand years old,” the curator explained.
Hessa asked whether photos were allowed.
Hessa asked, “Are photos allowed?”

questions.why: Direct quotations repeat exact words in quotation marks; indirect ones report them.

questions.stem: Choose the punctuation that correctly completes the sentence: The engineer called the design “elegant but fragile____ a phrase the team repeated for weeks.
questions.why: In American usage, commas go inside closing quotation marks.

questions.stem: Find the mistake in the sentence about the mayor and the tunnel.
segments: When the reporter asked about the delay,
questions.why: A quotation woven into a that clause begins with a lowercase letter.

questions.stem: Which TWO sentences punctuate titles and quotations correctly? Choose two.
options: In the chapter “Salt and Stars,” the author describes sailing at night.
The poem “Wind over Najd” ends with the line “and the sand remembers”.
In the chapter “Salt and Stars”, the author describes sailing at night.
The poem “Wind over Najd” ends with the line “and the sand remembers.”
questions.why: Commas and periods go inside closing quotation marks.

questions.stem: Part A: Read the sentence: Hamad asked, “Who said, ‘The best map is the one you draw yourself’?” Why is the question mark placed where it is?

partA.stem: Part A: Read the sentence: Hamad asked, “Who said, ‘The best map is the one you draw yourself’?” Why is the question mark placed where it is?

options.label: A
options.text: The whole sentence is a question asked by the narrator.

options.label: B
options.text: The question belongs to Hamad's words, not to the saying he quotes.

options.label: C
options.text: Question marks always go outside every quotation mark.

options.label: D
options.text: The saying that Hamad quotes is itself a question.

partB.stem: Part B: Which sentence follows the same rule?

options.label: A
options.text: Laila asked, “Did the guide really say, ‘The tide is safe?’”

options.label: B
options.text: Laila asked, “Did the guide really say, ‘The tide is safe’?”

options.label: C
options.text: Laila asked, “Did the guide really say, ‘The tide is safe’”?

options.label: D
options.text: Laila asked “Did the guide really say ‘The tide is safe’?”

questions.why: Place a question mark with the words that actually ask the question.

questions.stem: Decide whether each sentence about Dana's debate team is punctuated correctly.

rows.text: “Facts,” Dana insisted, “are not opinions.”
Dana insisted that “facts are not opinions.”
“Do you agree”? asked the moderator.
The coach called our closing “brilliant”; then she listed its flaws.
Dana insisted, “facts are not opinions”.

questions.why: Semicolons go outside closing marks; periods and question marks of the speaker go inside.

questions.stem: Choose the punctuation that correctly completes the sentence: The critic praised three qualities in Salwa's essay “Tides of Memory____ its honesty, its structure, and its restraint.
questions.why: Colons and semicolons go outside closing quotation marks.

questions.stem: Find the error in the way the writer adds a clarifying word to a quotation about the dam.
segments: twice the water of the old one.”
questions.why: Words a writer inserts into a quotation go in square brackets, not parentheses.

questions.stem: Which THREE sentences use quotation marks and related punctuation correctly? Choose three.
options: The poet's line “the dunes keep their own calendar” suggests patience.
The poet wrote that “The dunes keep their own calendar.”
Critics called the film “bold;” others found it slow.
The professor asked, “Is the theory elegant”?
The guide's warning—“Do not leave the marked path”—was ignored by two hikers.
Did the professor really call the theory “elegant”?
questions.why: Put question marks with the words that ask, semicolons outside, and lowercase for blended quotations.

questions.stem: Part A: A student wants to shorten this quotation: “The observatory, which was built in 1259 under the direction of the astronomer Nasir al-Din al-Tusi, attracted scholars from many lands.” Which version is correct?

partA.stem: Part A: A student wants to shorten this quotation: “The observatory, which was built in 1259 under the direction of the astronomer Nasir al-Din al-Tusi, attracted scholars from many lands.” Which version is correct?

options.label: A
options.text: “The observatory [. . .] attracted scholars from many lands”.

options.label: B
options.text: “The observatory attracted scholars from many lands.”

options.label: C
options.text: “The observatory . . . attracted scholars from many lands.”

options.label: D
options.text: “The observatory, attracted scholars from many lands.”

partB.stem: Part B: Why is that version correct?

options.label: A
options.text: A comma shows where a quotation has been shortened.

options.label: B
options.text: An ellipsis shows that words were removed without changing the meaning.

options.label: C
options.text: Words may be removed from a quotation without any mark.

options.label: D
options.text: Brackets show that the writer added words of her own.

questions.why: Omitted words must be marked with an ellipsis.

questions.stem: Which sentence correctly integrates a quotation into the writer's own sentence?
options: The traveler's journal describes the river as one that “bends like a bow before reaching the sea.”
The traveler's journal describes the river as one that “bends like a bow before reaching the sea”.
The traveler's journal describes the river as one that: “bends like a bow before reaching the sea.”
The traveler's journal describes the river as one that, “Bends like a bow before reaching the sea.”
questions.why: A blended quotation needs no comma or colon, starts lowercase, and keeps the period inside.

questions.stem: Mia wants to learn how frogs grow. Which is the best place to look?
options: a storybook about a talking frog
a science book about frogs
a map of the town park
a cookbook with pictures of food
questions.why: A science book gives true facts about real frogs.

questions.stem: True or false: A dictionary is a good place to find what a word means.
questions.why: A dictionary tells what words mean.

questions.stem: Sara wants to know if it will rain tomorrow. She should check ____.
options: an old photo album
a joke book
a weather report
questions.why: A weather report tells what the weather will be.

questions.stem: Would each one help Omar learn facts about the moon?

rows.text: a book called All About the Moon
a video from a space museum
a song about a sleepy cat
a poem about his new bike

questions.why: Good sources are about the topic and give facts.

questions.stem: Match each question with the best place to find the answer.
questions.why: Each kind of source answers a different kind of question.

questions.stem: Which source would most likely give reliable facts about sea turtles?
options: a blog post by someone who saw a turtle once
a cartoon movie with a turtle as the hero
a website from a marine science center
an advertisement for a toy turtle
questions.why: Experts who study sea life are the most reliable source.

questions.stem: Khalid is writing a report on the Saudi desert. To find the page about sand dunes in a long book, he should use the ____.
options: index
copyright page
dedication
title page
questions.why: An index lists topics and the pages where they appear.

questions.stem: Decide whether each source about the Apollo 11 moon landing is a primary source or a secondary source.

rows.text: an astronaut's diary from the mission
a 2020 encyclopedia entry about the landing
a photograph taken on the moon
a textbook chapter on space travel

questions.why: Primary sources come from people who were there; secondary sources are written later.

questions.stem: Lina is researching how honeybees make honey. Which TWO questions would best guide her research? Choose two.
options: How do bees turn nectar into honey inside the hive?
What colors are the flowers in my own garden?
Do I like honey on my bread in the morning?
What do bees collect from flowers to make honey?
questions.why: Good research questions focus on the topic and can be answered with facts.

questions.stem: Put the steps of a research project about volcanoes in the best order.
sequence: Choose a question: Why do volcanoes erupt?
Find two or three reliable sources.
Take notes in your own words.
Write the report and list your sources.
questions.why: Research starts with a question and ends with a report that credits sources.

questions.stem: Which search term would most likely give the most useful results for a report on how solar panels produce electricity?
options: how solar panels make electricity
solar panel prices at local stores
pictures of solar panels on houses
the temperature at the sun's surface
questions.why: The best search term matches the exact research question.

questions.stem: Hassan copied a sentence word for word from a website into his report. To avoid plagiarism, he must ____.
options: add his own opinion right after it
move it to the end of his report
put it in quotation marks and name the source
change one or two words and keep it
questions.why: Exact words need quotation marks and a citation.

questions.stem: Classify each note from Reem's research about the Hejaz Railway as a verifiable fact or an opinion.

rows.text: The railway opened in 1908.
It was the most beautiful railway ever built.
It linked Damascus and Medina.
Everyone should visit the old stations.

questions.why: Facts can be checked in other sources; opinions are judgments.

questions.stem: Faisal found a website about coral reefs. Which TWO clues suggest the site is credible? Choose two.
options: It names the marine biologist who wrote it.
It was updated last month and lists its sources.
It has bright colors and many fun animations.
It says its facts are true in large letters.
It sells snorkeling gear on every single page.
questions.why: Credible sources name qualified authors, stay current, and show where facts come from.

questions.stem: Part A: Amal's note says, “Dates are healthy.” Her source said, “100 grams of dates provide about 7 grams of fiber,” as reported in a 2021 nutrition study. What is the main problem with her note?

partA.stem: Part A: Amal's note says, “Dates are healthy.” Her source said, “100 grams of dates provide about 7 grams of fiber,” as reported in a 2021 nutrition study. What is the main problem with her note?

options.label: A
options.text: It leaves out the specific evidence and its source.

options.label: B
options.text: It uses too many numbers from the study.

options.label: C
options.text: It copies the source word for word.

options.label: D
options.text: It disagrees with what the source said.

partB.stem: Part B: Which revision of the note is best?

options.label: A
options.text: Dates give about 7 g of fiber per 100 g (2021 nutrition study).

options.label: B
options.text: Dates are healthy, and almost everyone likes them.

options.label: C
options.text: 100 grams of dates provide about 7 grams of fiber.

options.label: D
options.text: Dates are very, very healthy for everyone.

questions.why: Good notes keep the specific fact and record where it came from.

questions.stem: Which source is likely the most credible for a report on the health effects of energy drinks?
options: a magazine ad featuring a famous athlete
a review article in a medical journal
a video made by an energy drink company
a post on a social media fitness page
questions.why: Medical journals are reviewed by experts and have no product to sell.

questions.stem: True or false: When you paraphrase a source in your own words, you still need to cite it.
questions.why: The idea still belongs to the source, so it must be credited.

questions.stem: Match each research term with its meaning.

pairs.right: restating an idea in your own words
a source's exact words inside quotation marks
information that identifies where an idea came from
a one-sided view that favors one position

questions.why: Knowing these terms helps you use sources honestly.

questions.stem: Put the steps for evaluating a website about electric cars in a logical order.
sequence: Identify who wrote or published the site.
Check the author's qualifications and purpose.
Compare its facts with two other reliable sources.
Decide whether to use the information in the report.
questions.why: Evaluate the author first, then check the facts, then decide.

questions.stem: Which part of this research sentence should be revised to keep it objective?
segments: A World Health Organization report found
that about one in four adults
which proves that everyone is lazy.
questions.correction: which suggests many adults could benefit from more activity.
questions.why: Research writing reports evidence without exaggerated personal judgments.

questions.stem: A student researching water scarcity in the Arabian Peninsula finds a statistic in a 2009 report. What is the strongest reason to look for a newer source?
options: Water use and supply data can change significantly over time.
A newer source will automatically agree with the older report.
Government reports cannot be used in serious academic research.
Older reports are usually written by less qualified authors overall.
questions.why: Current data matters most for topics that change quickly.

questions.stem: Part A: A student's research question is “Does daily reading improve vocabulary in middle school students?” Which source would provide the strongest evidence?

partA.stem: Part A: A student's research question is “Does daily reading improve vocabulary in middle school students?” Which source would provide the strongest evidence?

options.label: A
options.text: a bookstore's list of best-selling novels for teenagers

options.label: B
options.text: an interview with one student who loves reading novels

options.label: C
options.text: a two-year study comparing readers and non-readers in 40 schools

options.label: D
options.text: an opinion column titled “Reading Makes You Smarter”

partB.stem: Part B: Which feature of that source makes it strongest?

options.label: A
options.text: It is popular with a great many readers.

options.label: B
options.text: It uses a large sample collected over a long period.

options.label: C
options.text: It includes a personal story readers can relate to.

options.label: D
options.text: It states its claim in a memorable title.

questions.why: Large, long-term studies give stronger evidence than single stories or opinions.

questions.stem: A student is researching whether school start times affect teen sleep. Which THREE sources would be most appropriate? Choose three.
options: a university researcher's data on attendance after a schedule change
an alarm-clock company's blog post on morning routines
a popular movie about a student who always oversleeps
a peer-reviewed sleep study of 2,000 high school students
a social media poll of the student's own friends
a national health agency report on adolescent sleep
questions.why: Strong sources are expert, data-based, and free of commercial bias.

questions.stem: For a paper on desalination in Saudi Arabia, decide whether each detail is relevant to the claim “Desalination supplies much of the kingdom's drinking water.”

the number of desalination plants on the Red Sea coast
the history of pearl diving in the Gulf
the average summer temperature in Abha

questions.why: Relevant evidence directly supports the specific claim.

questions.stem: Choose the verb that best integrates the source into the sentence: Marine biologist Dr. Salma Idris ____ that rising water temperatures “have bleached nearly a third of the reef.”
options: guesses wildly
proves forever
feels like
reports
questions.why: A neutral signal verb such as reports accurately introduces a source.

questions.stem: A student's paper claims that a city's new bus network reduced traffic. Her only source is a press release from the city's transportation office. What is the most significant weakness?
options: Government offices almost never publish statistics about city traffic.
Press releases are too brief to contain any data that could be verified.
The source is written for general readers rather than transportation experts.
The source may present the project favorably because the office created it.
questions.why: A source that judges its own project may be biased, so independent evidence is needed.

questions.stem: A student claims that remote work increases productivity. Which TWO pieces of evidence would most directly strengthen this claim? Choose two.
options: company data showing that tasks completed per week rose after remote work began
a survey in which most workers say they prefer working from home
a chief executive's statement that remote work is the future of business
an article describing how remote workers save time on commuting
a study measuring the output of 500 employees before and after switching to remote work
questions.why: Productivity claims need measures of output, not preferences or predictions.

questions.stem: Find the part of this sentence that misrepresents its source, a study that found a correlation between exercise and higher test scores.

questions.stem: Classify each way of using sources in a research paper on the Islamic Golden Age.

summarizing a historian's argument in new words with a citation
rewording a historian's paragraph sentence by sentence without a citation
using another student's outline as your own without credit

questions.stem: Choose the right way to write the time: School starts at ____.

The recipe needs one more thing: honey.
The team: won the game on Friday.
questions.why: A colon should follow a complete sentence.
