semicolon (;)
colon (:)
questions.why: Use a semicolon before a conjunctive adverb such as however that joins two clauses.

questions.stem: Find the error in the sentence about the trip.
questions.why: When list items contain commas, separate the items with semicolons.

questions.stem: Which TWO sentences are punctuated correctly? Choose two.
options: Rain fell all morning; because the field was soaked.
The coach gave: one instruction to the team.
The coach gave one instruction: keep your eyes on the ball.
Rain fell all morning; the match was postponed.
questions.why: A colon follows a complete clause; a semicolon joins two complete clauses.

questions.stem: True or false: In the sentence “I enjoy several hobbies: reading, swimming, and chess,” the colon is used correctly.
questions.why: A complete clause comes before the colon, and a list follows it.

questions.stem: Which revision correctly combines these sentences with a semicolon? “Al-Jazari designed many machines. His water clock was among the most famous.”
options: Al-Jazari designed many machines; and his water clock was among the most famous.
Al-Jazari designed; many machines, his water clock was among the most famous.
Al-Jazari designed many machines; his water clock was among the most famous.
Al-Jazari designed many machines, his water clock; was among the most famous.
questions.why: A semicolon alone joins two related independent clauses.

questions.stem: Choose the punctuation that correctly completes the sentence: The scientist's advice was simple____ test every idea twice.
options: semicolon (;)
comma (,)
colon (:)
questions.why: A colon introduces an explanation of what came before.

questions.stem: Decide whether each sentence about the robotics team is punctuated correctly or incorrectly.

rows.text: The team had one goal: win the regional final.
The robot was fast; it was also accurate.
The team needed: wires, batteries, and sensors.
The robot stalled; when the battery died.

questions.why: A colon needs a complete clause before it; a semicolon needs complete clauses on both sides.

questions.stem: Find the error in the sentence about the marathon.
segments: they pushed toward the finish line.
questions.why: Use a semicolon before nevertheless when it joins two clauses.

questions.stem: Match each sentence about the desert hike with the reason for its punctuation.

pairs.left: We packed water; the heat was intense.
pairs.right: semicolon joining two related independent clauses

pairs.left: We packed three things: water, hats, and maps.
The guide said one thing: stay on the trail.
pairs.right: colon introducing an explanation or emphasis

pairs.left: We met hikers from Taif, Saudi Arabia; Salalah, Oman; and Aqaba, Jordan.
pairs.right: semicolons separating list items that contain commas

questions.why: Each use of a semicolon or colon has a specific job.

questions.stem: Which sentence about the archive uses a colon correctly?
options: Among the treasures in the archive were: maps and a few letters.
The archive held one treasure, which was: a map drawn by al-Idrisi.
The archive held one treasure above all: a map drawn by al-Idrisi.
The archive held: maps, letters, and a journal written by al-Idrisi.
questions.why: A colon must follow a complete independent clause.

questions.stem: Find the error in the sentence about the experiment.
questions.why: A dependent clause cannot stand before a semicolon; use a comma.

questions.stem: Which THREE sentences use semicolons correctly? Choose three.
options: The plan seemed perfect; in practice, however, it failed.
Our speakers came from Cairo, Egypt; Fez, Morocco; and Tunis, Tunisia.
Because the plan failed; we tried a new method.
The library closes at noon on Friday; it reopens on Saturday.
The speakers were; a doctor, an engineer, and a poet.
She studied very hard; for the final exam in June.
questions.why: Semicolons join independent clauses or separate complex list items, never a clause from a fragment.

questions.stem: Choose the punctuation that best shows that the second clause explains the first: The experiment produced only one clear conclusion____ heat speeds up the reaction.
options: colon (:)
comma (,)
question mark (?)
semicolon (;)
questions.why: A colon signals that what follows explains or specifies what came before.

questions.stem: Part A: Read the sentence “The expedition faced two problems, the water supply was low, and the camels were tired.” What is the main error?

partA.stem: Part A: Read the sentence “The expedition faced two problems, the water supply was low, and the camels were tired.” What is the main error?

options.label: A
options.text: The sentence needs no punctuation after “problems.”

options.label: B
options.text: A colon is needed after “problems” to introduce the explanation.

options.label: C
options.text: The comma after “low” should be changed to a colon.

options.label: D
options.text: A semicolon is needed after the word “expedition.”

partB.stem: Part B: Which revision best corrects the sentence?

options.label: A
options.text: The expedition faced two problems; the water supply was low; and the camels were tired.

options.label: B
options.text: The expedition faced two problems, the water supply was low; and the camels were tired.

options.label: C
options.text: The expedition faced: two problems, the water supply was low and the camels were tired.

options.label: D
options.text: The expedition faced two problems: the water supply was low, and the camels were tired.

questions.why: A colon introduces the two problems that the first clause announces.

questions.stem: Which revision of the sentence “The committee reached a decision, the festival will be moved to March” is correct and best shows that the second clause explains the first?
options: The committee reached a decision; and the festival will be moved to March.
The committee reached a decision: the festival will be moved to March.
The committee reached a decision, so: the festival will be moved to March.
The committee reached: a decision, the festival will be moved to March.
questions.why: A colon fixes the comma splice and signals that the decision is being explained.

questions.stem: Find the error in the sentence about the conference panel.
segments: and Dr. Lina Haddad, a physician.
questions.why: Items that contain internal commas must all be separated by semicolons.

questions.stem: Decide whether each use of a colon or semicolon in these sentences about urban planning is correct or incorrect.

rows.text: The planners proposed a bold idea: close the old road to cars.
The city grew rapidly; consequently, traffic worsened.
The proposal, which included: parks and bike lanes, passed.
Traffic worsened; as the city kept growing.
The report raised one question: who will pay for the new trains?

questions.why: Colons follow complete clauses; semicolons never introduce a dependent clause.

questions.stem: Which TWO sentences about the observatory are punctuated correctly? Choose two.
options: The astronomers included: a student, a professor, and a retired pilot.
The telescope was old; nevertheless, it revealed remarkable detail.
The observatory had one rule: no lights after sunset.
The telescope was old, nevertheless, it revealed remarkable detail.
The sky was clear; which made viewing easy for everyone.
questions.why: Watch for colons after verbs, semicolons before relative clauses, and comma splices with nevertheless.

questions.stem: True or false: The sentence “The author's argument rests on a single premise: that cities, not nations, will shape the next century” uses the colon correctly.
questions.why: A complete clause precedes the colon, and what follows explains the premise.

questions.stem: Which is a complete sentence?
options: On the soft mat today.
The sleepy cat on the soft mat.
Sleeps on the mat all day.
The cat sleeps on the mat.
questions.why: A sentence tells who and what they do.

questions.stem: Choose the end mark for this asking sentence: Do you like apples____
questions.why: An asking sentence ends with a question mark.

questions.stem: Is each sentence about the park a telling sentence or an asking sentence?

rows.text: We play at the park.
Can we go to the park?
The park has a big slide.
Where is the slide?

questions.why: Asking sentences end with a question mark.

questions.stem: True or false: “Wow, what a big fish!” is a sentence that shows strong feeling.
questions.why: An exclamation shows strong feeling and ends with !

questions.stem: Find the mistake in the sentence about the bird.
questions.why: A sentence begins with a capital letter.

questions.stem: Which sentence is a command (imperative sentence)?
options: Please close the window before the dust blows in.
Did you close the window before the dust blew in?
The window was closed before the dust blew in.
What a lot of dust blew in through the window!
questions.why: A command tells someone to do something.

questions.stem: Classify each sentence about the camel race.

rows.text: The race begins at sunrise.
Which camel is the fastest?
What an amazing finish that was!
The winner gets a trophy.

questions.why: Statements, questions, and exclamations have different purposes and end marks.

questions.stem: Which TWO groups of words are sentence fragments? Choose two.
options: Running along the beach at sunset.
The children ran along the beach.
The tide came in very quickly.
Because the tide was coming in.
questions.why: A fragment is missing a subject, a verb, or a complete thought.

questions.stem: Find the part that causes the run-on in the sentence about the library.
segments: The library opened a new room
it is full of science books
questions.correction: The library opened a new room, and
questions.why: Join two complete sentences with a comma and a conjunction.

questions.stem: Choose the word that best joins the ideas into one compound sentence: The wind was strong, ____ the boat stayed in the harbor.
options: although
because
so
until
questions.why: So shows that the strong wind caused the boat to stay.

questions.stem: Which sentence is a complex sentence?
options: We lit the lanterns and waited for the power.
When the power went out, we lit the lanterns.
The power went out; we lit the lanterns quickly.
The power went out, and we lit the lanterns.
questions.why: A complex sentence has one independent clause and at least one dependent clause.

questions.stem: Classify each sentence about the coral reef by its structure.

rows.text: Coral reefs protect coastlines from waves.
Reefs are colorful, but they are fragile.
Because the water warmed, the coral turned white.
Divers study the reef, and students learn from their data.
Fish that live on reefs depend on coral for shelter.

questions.why: Count independent and dependent clauses to find a sentence's structure.

questions.stem: Part A: Which choice best describes the group of words “The students who entered the robotics contest.”?

partA.stem: Part A: Which choice best describes the group of words “The students who entered the robotics contest.”?

options.label: A
options.text: It is a complete simple sentence.

options.label: B
options.text: It is a fragment because it has no main verb.

options.label: C
options.text: It is a run-on sentence with two clauses.

options.label: D
options.text: It is a compound sentence missing a comma.

partB.stem: Part B: Which revision makes it a complete sentence?

options.label: A
options.text: The students who entered the robotics contest and the judges.

options.label: B
options.text: The students who entered the robotics contest won second place.

options.label: C
options.text: The students, who entered the robotics contest.

options.label: D
options.text: The students who entered. The robotics contest.

questions.why: The subject needs a main verb such as won to make a complete sentence.

questions.stem: Which TWO sentences are compound sentences? Choose two.
options: Although the pool was closed, Huda swam in the sea.
The falcon dove, and the pigeon escaped.
The falcon and the pigeon flew over the dunes.
Huda wanted to swim, but the pool was closed.
questions.why: A compound sentence joins two independent clauses.

questions.stem: Find the part that creates a comma splice in the sentence about the volcano.
questions.correction: The volcano erupted at dawn, and
questions.why: A comma alone cannot join two independent clauses.

questions.stem: Which sentence is a compound-complex sentence?
options: The bridge was old, but it held the weight of the heavy trucks easily.
Although the bridge was old, it held the weight of the heavy trucks.
Although the bridge was old, it held, and the trucks crossed safely.
The old bridge held the weight of the trucks during the long storm.
questions.why: A compound-complex sentence has two independent clauses and at least one dependent clause.

questions.stem: Choose the subordinating conjunction that best shows the relationship: ____ the satellite reached orbit, engineers celebrated in the control room.
options: Although
Whereas
After
Unless
questions.why: After shows the order of events.

questions.stem: Decide whether each item about the solar car project is a complete sentence, a fragment, or a run-on.

rows.text: The team tested the solar car in the desert heat.
Hoping to break the school speed record.
The car was light it was also very fast.
Since the panels were cleaned every morning.

questions.why: Fragments lack a complete thought; run-ons join clauses without punctuation.

questions.stem: Match each sentence about Ibn Battuta with its structure.

pairs.left: Ibn Battuta traveled across Africa and Asia.
Ibn Battuta traveled for decades, and he wrote about his journeys.
Because he kept careful notes, his book is still read today.
Although he faced dangers, he kept going, and he reached China.

questions.why: Structure depends on the number and kind of clauses.

questions.stem: True or false: “Whenever the market opens early on Fridays” is a complete sentence.
questions.why: It is a dependent clause with no main clause, so it is a fragment.

questions.stem: Which revision best corrects the run-on sentence “The tide was rising quickly the fishermen pulled their boats onto the sand”?
options: The tide was rising quickly the fishermen, pulled their boats onto the sand.
Because the tide was rising quickly, the fishermen pulled their boats onto the sand.
The tide was rising quickly, so, the fishermen then pulled all of their boats onto the sand.
The tide was rising quickly, the fishermen pulled their boats onto the sand.
questions.why: Subordinating one clause fixes the run-on and shows cause and effect.

questions.stem: Which TWO sentences correctly use subordination to show cause and effect? Choose two.
options: The dam was repaired, the valley no longer floods.
Since the dam was repaired, the valley no longer floods.
The valley no longer floods, although the dam was repaired.
The crops survived because farmers switched to drip irrigation.
questions.why: Since and because signal cause; although signals contrast.

questions.stem: Part A: Read the sentences “The new museum opened in Riyadh. It displays ancient manuscripts. Scholars from many countries visit it.” Which structure would best combine the ideas while showing that the manuscripts are the reason scholars visit?

partA.stem: Part A: Read the sentences “The new museum opened in Riyadh. It displays ancient manuscripts. Scholars from many countries visit it.” Which structure would best combine the ideas while showing that the manuscripts are the reason scholars visit?

options.label: A
options.text: a compound sentence joined by “or”

options.label: B
options.text: a fragment beginning with “Displaying”

options.label: C
options.text: a complex sentence with a subordinate clause

options.label: D
options.text: three simple sentences joined by commas

partB.stem: Part B: Which sentence best combines the ideas?

options.label: A
options.text: Displaying ancient manuscripts in the new museum in Riyadh for many scholars.

options.label: B
options.text: The new museum opened in Riyadh, it displays ancient manuscripts, scholars visit it.

options.label: C
options.text: Scholars from many countries visit the new Riyadh museum because it displays ancient manuscripts.

options.label: D
options.text: The new museum opened in Riyadh, or it displays ancient manuscripts for scholars.

questions.why: A because-clause shows the cause-and-effect relationship clearly.

questions.stem: Classify the function of each sentence from a speech about recycling.

rows.text: Bring your empty bottles to the collection bins on Thursday.
Our school threw away four tons of plastic last year.
How many of those bottles could have been reused?
Imagine a campus with no litter at all.
Recycling saves both energy and money.

questions.why: Imperatives give directions or invitations, even when they begin with a verb like imagine.

questions.stem: Find the part that makes the sentence about the explorers a fragment.
questions.why: A participle such as having crossed cannot serve as the main verb.

questions.stem: Which sentence about the archaeological dig has a compound-complex structure?
options: The team dug carefully, and they found a coin, a lamp, and a broken clay jar.
Because the site was fragile, the team dug slowly with brushes and small tools.
The team dug carefully because the site was fragile, and they found a coin.
Digging carefully at the fragile site, the team found a coin beside an old lamp.
questions.why: Two independent clauses plus a because-clause make it compound-complex.

questions.stem: Find the part that leaves the sentence about the hospital without a main clause.
segments: Although the hospital was founded in 1931
and has expanded several times since then,
which is why its original wing still stands.
questions.why: Every clause here is dependent until a main clause is supplied.

questions.stem: Which THREE sentences are grammatically complete? Choose three.
options: That the bridge survived the earthquake surprised the engineers.
The engineers, surprised that the bridge had survived the earthquake.
Exhausted after the climb, the hikers rested in the shade.
Because the exhausted hikers rested in the shade after the climb.
Whoever finishes the survey first and leaves the room early.
Whoever finishes the survey first may leave early.
questions.why: A noun clause can be a subject, but every sentence still needs a main verb and an independent clause.

questions.stem: Classify each sentence from a report on water conservation by its structure.

rows.text: Farmers in the region, facing drought and rising costs, adopted drip irrigation.
Water use fell sharply, yet crop yields remained stable.
What surprised researchers was how quickly the farmers adapted.
Rainfall decreased; the aquifer, however, held steady.
Drip lines deliver water directly to the roots of each plant.

questions.why: Long phrases do not add clauses; noun clauses make a sentence complex.

questions.stem: True or false: “The question of whether the old souq should be restored, a debate that has divided the city for years” is a complete sentence.
questions.why: It has a long subject and an appositive but no main verb.

sets.skill: Singular, Plural and Irregular Plural Nouns

questions.stem: Choose the right word: I saw three ____ at the farm.
options: sheepes
sheeps
sheep
questions.why: Sheep is the same for one or more than one.

questions.stem: Which word means more than one child?
options: childs
childrens
childes
children
questions.why: The plural of child is children.

questions.stem: Is each word about one thing or more than one thing?

rows.text: box
boxes
mouse
mice

questions.why: Plural nouns name more than one.

questions.stem: Match each word to its plural form: foot, tooth, man.
questions.why: Some plurals change the vowel instead of adding -s.

questions.stem: Find the mistake in the sentence about the dishes.
questions.why: Add -es to words that end in sh.

questions.stem: Which sentence uses the correct plural form?
options: The wolfes howled at the moon.
The wolfs howled at the moon.
The wolves howled at the moon.
The wolvs howled at the moon.
questions.why: Wolf changes f to v and adds -es.

questions.stem: Choose the correct plural: The farmer picked ten ripe ____ from the trees.
options: peach's
peaches
peachies
peachs
questions.why: Add -es to nouns that end in ch.

questions.stem: Decide whether each plural noun (babies, leafs, heroes, monkies, geese) is spelled correctly.

rows.text: babies
leafs
heroes
monkies
geese

questions.why: Leaf becomes leaves; monkey keeps the y because a vowel comes before it.

questions.stem: Which TWO nouns have the same form in the singular and the plural? Choose two.
options: fish
goose
mouse
deer
questions.why: Deer and fish do not change; goose and mouse become geese and mice.

questions.stem: Find the error in the sentence about the museum.
questions.why: Knife changes f to v and adds -s.

questions.stem: Which sentence uses plural nouns correctly?
options: Both of my sister-in-laws visited the ranchs.
Both of my sister-in-law visited the ranches.
Both of my sisters-in-laws visited the ranches.
Both of my sisters-in-law visited the ranches.
questions.why: In compound nouns, the main word (sister) becomes plural.

questions.stem: Match each singular noun with its correct plural: cactus, crisis, phenomenon, ox.
questions.why: Many irregular plurals come from Latin, Greek, or Old English.

questions.stem: Choose the correct plural: The two ____ of the nature club met in the library.
options: secretarys
secretaries
secretary's
secretaryies
questions.why: For a consonant + y ending, change y to i and add -es.

questions.stem: True or false: The plural of “potato” is “potatos.”
questions.why: Potato adds -es: potatoes.

questions.stem: Find the error in the sentence about the zoo.
questions.why: Goose has the irregular plural geese.

questions.stem: Which sentence contains an incorrectly formed plural?
options: The criteria for the award were announced in May.
The data from the trials were published in May.
The analysises of the data were published in May.
The analyses of the data were published in May.
questions.why: The plural of analysis is analyses.

questions.stem: Classify how each plural is formed: chiefs, pianos, tomatoes, radii, hooves.

rows.text: chief → chiefs
piano → pianos
tomato → tomatoes
radius → radii
hoof → hooves

questions.why: Some -f and -o nouns simply add -s; others change form.

questions.stem: Which THREE sentences use plural nouns correctly? Choose three.
options: The scientists examined several vertebrae from the fossil.
The fungis spread slowly across the damp wall.
The thiefs escaped before the guards arrived.
The bacteria multiplied quickly in the warm dish.
Several mother-in-laws attended the ceremony.
Two passersby stopped to help the injured cyclist.
questions.why: Fungi, mothers-in-law, and thieves are the correct plurals.

questions.stem: Find the error in the sentence about the photo exhibit in our town.
segments: and an exhibit of old photoes.
questions.correction: and an exhibit of old photos.
questions.why: Photo is a shortened word and adds only -s.

questions.stem: Choose the noun that correctly completes the sentence: Each of the ____ received a certificate at the reunion.
options: alumnus
alumni
alumnis
questions.why: After “each of the,” use the plural alumni.

questions.stem: Which revision corrects the noun error in “The criterion for the scholarship are listed below”?
options: The criteria for the scholarship are listed below.
The criterion for the scholarship are listing below.
The criterions for the scholarship are listed below.
The criterias for the scholarship are listed below.
questions.why: Criteria is the plural of criterion and agrees with are.

questions.stem: Part A: Which word in the sentence “Several new phenomenon were observed by the researchers” is in the wrong number?

partA.stem: Part A: Which word in the sentence “Several new phenomenon were observed by the researchers” is in the wrong number?

options.label: A
options.text: several

options.label: B
options.text: researchers

options.label: C
options.text: phenomenon

options.label: D
options.text: were

partB.stem: Part B: Which form should replace it?

options.label: A
options.text: phenomenas

options.label: B
options.text: phenomena

options.label: C
options.text: phenomenons

options.label: D
options.text: phenomenon's

questions.why: Several requires a plural, and the plural of phenomenon is phenomena.

questions.stem: Decide whether the noun in capital letters in each sentence is singular or plural.

rows.text: The CRITERIA for entry are strict.
This STIMULUS caused a reaction.
The FUNGI grew under the logs.
One THESIS was rejected.
Two OASES lay along the route.

questions.why: Words from Latin and Greek often form plurals with -a, -i, or -es.

questions.stem: Which TWO plural forms are correct? Choose two.
options: attorneys general
editor in chiefs
attorney generals
editors in chief
questions.why: In compound nouns, the main noun is made plural.

questions.stem: Find the error in the sentence about the economic report.
questions.why: Nouns ending in -is change -is to -es: crisis, crises.

questions.stem: Which sentence uses nouns and verbs that agree in number correctly?
options: The data from both survey suggests that the hypotheses was sound.
The datum from both surveys suggest that the hypothesis were sound.
The datas from both surveys suggests that the hypothesises were sound.
The data from both surveys suggest that the hypotheses were sound.
questions.why: In formal writing data and hypotheses are plural and take plural verbs.

questions.stem: Find the error in the sentence about the conference.
questions.why: Three panels produced three reports, so the plural analyses is needed.

questions.stem: Classify each plural noun: curricula, brothers-in-law, species, nuclei, aircraft.

rows.text: curricula
brothers-in-law
species
nuclei
aircraft

questions.why: Irregular plurals follow several different patterns.

questions.stem: Which THREE sentences from a science report use plural nouns correctly? Choose three.
options: Each of the two stimulus produced a response.
Both vertebrae showed signs of an old injury.
The larvae emerged from the eggs after nine days.
Several crisis in the colony were recorded.
The two larvas were placed under the lens.
The researchers studied several bacteria in each sample.
questions.why: Larva, vertebra, bacterium, crisis, and stimulus all have irregular plurals.

questions.stem: Choose the correct word: The museum's two ____ on desert ecology drew record crowds.
options: symposia
symposium
symposias
questions.why: Symposia is the plural of symposium.

sets.skill: Sound Devices: Alliteration, Onomatopoeia and Repetition

questions.stem: Which word is a sound word, like the sound a bee makes?
options: yellow
fly
buzz
bee
questions.why: Buzz sounds like the noise it names.

questions.stem: Is each word a sound word or not a sound word?

rows.text: bang
table
splash
green

questions.why: Sound words copy real sounds.

questions.stem: Which TWO words start with the same sound as “sun”? Choose two.
options: moon
tree
sand
silly
questions.why: Sand and silly begin with the s sound.

questions.stem: True or false: In “Big brown bears bounce,” many words begin with the same sound.
questions.why: Big, brown, bears, and bounce all begin with b.

questions.stem: Choose the sound word for a dog: The dog said, “____!”
options: Woof
Wing
Wet
questions.why: Woof is the sound a dog makes.

questions.stem: Which sentence uses alliteration?
options: Silly snakes slide slowly south.
The snake moved across the hot sand.
A long green snake hid under a rock.
Snakes are reptiles that shed their skin.
questions.why: Alliteration repeats the same beginning sound in nearby words.

questions.stem: Match each line with the sound device it shows.
questions.why: Sound words, repeated first sounds, and repeated words are different devices.

questions.stem: Decide whether each word from the lines “The clock went tick. The rain went drip. The cat sat still.” is onomatopoeia.

rows.text: tick
drip
sat
still

questions.why: Onomatopoeia words imitate sounds.

questions.stem: Choose the word that best continues the alliteration: “Bright blue balloons ____ above the beach.”
options: rose
floated
drifted
bobbed
questions.why: Bobbed begins with b like the other words.

questions.stem: Select the sentence that uses repetition to show how long the walk felt.

segments.text: We walked and walked and walked across the sand.
The sun was hot above us.
Finally, we reached the shady oasis.

questions.why: Repeating walked makes the walk seem long.

questions.stem: What is the main effect of the onomatopoeia in the line “Thud! The heavy door slammed shut behind us”?
options: It lets the reader hear the sudden, heavy sound.
It creates a calm and peaceful mood for the reader.
It shows that the door was painted a dark color.
It explains why the characters went into the room.
questions.why: Thud imitates the sound, so the reader hears the moment.

questions.stem: Part A: Read the lines “The wind whistled through the window, / Whoosh, whoosh, it wailed all night.” Which sound devices appear in these lines?

partA.stem: Part A: Read the lines “The wind whistled through the window, / Whoosh, whoosh, it wailed all night.” Which sound devices appear in these lines?

options.label: A
options.text: repetition and metaphor

options.label: B
options.text: rhyme and simile only

options.label: C
options.text: alliteration and onomatopoeia

options.label: D
options.text: simile and onomatopoeia

partB.stem: Part B: Which words from the lines best show alliteration?

options.label: A
options.text: it, all, night

options.label: B
options.text: wind, whistled, window, wailed

options.label: C
options.text: the, window, all

options.label: D
options.text: through, the, all, night

questions.why: The repeated w sound is alliteration; whoosh is onomatopoeia.

questions.stem: Which TWO lines use alliteration? Choose two.
options: Pale petals parted in the morning breeze.
The waves came in and went back out again.
Restless waves rolled toward the rocky reef.
Petals fell from the tree in the evening.
questions.why: Alliteration repeats beginning consonant sounds in nearby words.

questions.stem: Classify the main sound device in each line about a thunderstorm.

rows.text: Boom! Crash! The sky split open.
Dark, dense clouds drifted down.
Rain, rain, rain, all through the night.
Sizzle went the lightning on the wire.

questions.why: Look for sound words, repeated first sounds, or repeated words.

questions.stem: Select the line in this stanza about a market that uses onomatopoeia.

segments.text: The spices sit in sacks of gold,
The sellers call out, young and old,
Clang, clang, the copper pots collide,
And shoppers wander far and wide.

questions.why: Clang imitates the sound of metal pots.

questions.stem: Read the line “Again the drums, again the drums, again they call us home.” What is the most likely purpose of the repetition?

to show that the speaker cannot count the drums
to build a steady rhythm and stress the call home
to describe exactly what the drums are made of

options: burned
waited
glowed
crackled
questions.why: Crackled imitates the sound of the fire.

questions.stem: Decide whether each line about the city at night uses alliteration.

rows.text: Taxis tumble through the tunnels.
Lights glow above the quiet road.
Silent streets stretch south.
A bus waits near the corner.

questions.why: Alliteration needs several nearby words with the same first sound.

questions.stem: Read the lines “Click, click, the keyboard counts the hours; / click, click, the deadline creeps.” How does the repeated onomatopoeia contribute to the meaning?
options: It shows that the keyboard is broken and needs repair.
It mimics steady typing and suggests time pressure building.
It contrasts the noise of the office with outdoor sounds.
It reveals that the speaker truly enjoys working late at night.
questions.why: The repeated click works like a clock, adding to the sense of pressure.

questions.stem: Which TWO lines use sound devices to create a harsh, aggressive tone? Choose two.
options: Crack, crunch, the bulldozers crush the coastline.
Murmuring, the meadow hums its mellow song.
Soft sand slips softly through the sleepy hours.
Grinding gears growl and grate against the gravel.
questions.why: Hard k and g sounds feel harsh; soft s and m sounds feel gentle.

questions.stem: Part A: Read this line from a speech: “We will build, and we will learn, and we will not turn back.” What is the main purpose of the repetition of “we will”?

partA.stem: Part A: Read this line from a speech: “We will build, and we will learn, and we will not turn back.” What is the main purpose of the repetition of “we will”?

options.label: A
options.text: to show that the speaker is unsure

options.label: B
options.text: to emphasize shared determination

options.label: C
options.text: to contrast the past with the present

options.label: D
options.text: to list the speaker's daily tasks

partB.stem: Part B: Which revision would most weaken that effect?

options.label: A
options.text: We will build! We will learn! We will not turn back!

options.label: B
options.text: We will build; we will learn; we will not turn back.

options.label: C
options.text: We will build, learn, and not turn back.

options.label: D
options.text: We will build, and we will learn, and we will never turn back.

questions.why: Removing the repeated we will removes the drumbeat of determination.

questions.stem: Classify each line about a factory by its main sound device.

rows.text: Clank, whirr, thump: the machines wake.
Workers walk wearily toward the west gate.
Again and again and again, the press comes down.
Steel sheets slide smoothly from the rollers.
Hiss! Steam escapes the valve.

questions.why: Identify whether the sound comes from imitation, first sounds, or repeated words.

questions.stem: Choose the word that both continues the alliteration and keeps the gentle mood: “Morning mist moves ____ over the marsh.”
options: harshly
mildly
mournfully
quickly
questions.why: Mildly repeats the m sound and keeps the calm feeling; mournfully alliterates but adds sadness.

questions.stem: Read the lines “Silence, then the slow, insistent ssss of sand against the tent— / silence, then the sand again.” What effect does the combination of sound devices create?
options: It makes the sandstorm feel relentless and inescapable.
It suggests the sandstorm has suddenly come to an end.
It creates a cheerful rhythm for a desert celebration.
It shows the speaker is angry about the poorly made tent.
questions.why: The hissing s-sounds and the repeated pattern make the storm seem endless.

questions.stem: Part A: In the lines “Tick. The ward is still. Tick. A nurse's step. / Tick. Each second stretches, swollen, slow,” how does the author use sound devices to develop meaning?

partA.stem: Part A: In the lines “Tick. The ward is still. Tick. A nurse's step. / Tick. Each second stretches, swollen, slow,” how does the author use sound devices to develop meaning?

options.label: A
options.text: The repetition shows that the speaker is counting the patients.

options.label: B
options.text: The ticking shows that the hospital clock is broken and very loud.

options.label: C
options.text: The ticking and s-sounds make time seem to drag during a tense wait.

options.label: D
options.text: The s-sounds suggest that the nurse is whispering a secret to someone.

partB.stem: Part B: Which phrase most clearly shows the slowing of time through alliteration?

options.label: A
options.text: “stretches, swollen, slow”

options.label: B
options.text: “A nurse's step”

options.label: C
options.text: “Each second”

options.label: D
options.text: “Tick. The ward is still.”

questions.why: The drawn-out s-sounds slow the reader down, just as time slows for the speaker.

questions.stem: Which THREE statements accurately describe the lines “Hammer, hammer, hammer on the anvil of the noon; / harder, hotter, heavier, the beat of labor's tune”? Choose three.
options: The lines rely mainly on onomatopoeia such as “anvil” and “noon.”
The alliteration of h-sounds suggests heavy breathing and strain.
The repeated “hammer” imitates the steady rhythm of work.
The repetition shows that the worker is bored and wants to stop.
The h-sounds create a soft, soothing, and sleepy mood.
The words “harder, hotter, heavier” build intensity.
questions.why: Repetition, alliteration, and rising comparatives work together to show hard labor.

questions.stem: Select two lines in this stanza about a harbor where sound devices most clearly echo the motion of the water.

segments.text: Lap, lap, the low tide licks the stones,
The fishermen mend their nets at dawn,
Slosh and settle, slosh and settle,
The gulls have gone, the boats are drawn.

questions.why: Lap and slosh imitate water, and their repetition copies the rhythm of waves.

questions.stem: Decide whether each claim about the line “Buzz, buzz, the busy bazaar never sleeps” is accurate or inaccurate.

rows.text: “Buzz” is onomatopoeia that suggests the noise of the crowd.
The b-sounds create alliteration.
Repeating “buzz” makes the market seem quiet and empty.
“Never sleeps” is an example of onomatopoeia.

questions.why: Buzz imitates crowd noise; never sleeps is personification, not a sound word.

questions.stem: Choose the correct spelling to complete the sentence: The ____ swam in the pond.
options: duk
duc
duck

options: fsh
fish
fishh

questions.stem: Sort the words “cap,” “cape,” “kit,” and “kite” by their vowel sound.

cape
kit
kite

questions.why: A silent e at the end makes the vowel say its name.

questions.why: Drop the silent e before adding -ing.

questions.stem: Which TWO words are spelled correctly? Choose two.
options: siting
bakeing
hopping
running
questions.why: Double the last consonant after a short vowel (run → running); drop the silent e (bake → baking).

questions.stem: Choose the correct spelling to complete the sentence: The baby ____ when she is hungry.
options: cries
cryes
crys
questions.why: When a word ends in a consonant plus y, change y to i and add -es.

questions.stem: Which spelling of the word meaning “to get” is correct?
options: resieve
receeve
recieve
receive
questions.why: Use i before e except after c: receive.

questions.stem: Sort the words “action,” “vision,” “motion,” and “decision” by how their ending is spelled.

rows.text: action
vision
motion
decision

questions.why: The /zhun/ sound, as in vision, is usually spelled -sion.

questions.stem: Find the misspelled word in the sentence about the soccer game.
questions.why: Begin is stressed on its last syllable, so the n doubles before -ing.

questions.stem: Part A: Which word correctly completes the sentence? “The two ____ shared one big tent on the camping trip.”

partA.stem: Part A: Which word correctly completes the sentence? “The two ____ shared one big tent on the camping trip.”

options.label: A

options.label: B

options.label: C

options.label: D

partB.stem: Part B: Which rule explains the answer to Part A?

options.label: A
options.text: When a word ends in a vowel plus y, just add -s to the end.

questions.stem: Which spelling of the word meaning “apart” is correct?
options: seperete
seperate

options: accessible
accessable
accesible
acessible
questions.why: Accessible has double c, double s, and ends in -ible.

questions.stem: Decide whether each word is spelled with -ance or -ence: “attend_nce,” “differ_nce,” “confid_nce,” “appear_nce.”

rows.text: attend_nce
differ_nce
confid_nce
appear_nce

questions.why: Related words help: different → difference, confident → confidence.

questions.stem: Find the misspelled word in the sentence about Layla’s science fair project.
questions.why: Definitely is built from definite + -ly.

questions.stem: Which THREE words are spelled correctly? Choose three.
options: beleive
weird
cieling
neighbor
height
freind
questions.why: Neighbor, weird, and height are exceptions to “i before e”; the correct spellings are friend, believe, and ceiling.

questions.stem: Choose the correct spelling to complete the sentence: The hikers decided to ____ with the climb despite the wind.
options: proceede
proseed
procede
proceed
questions.why: Only three common words end in -ceed: exceed, proceed, succeed.

questions.stem: Which sentence has every word spelled correctly?
options: The comittee will recommend a new schedule.
The committee will recommend a new schedule.
The commitee will recomend a new schedule.
The committee will reccommend a new schedule.
questions.why: Committee has double m, double t, double e; recommend has one c and double m.

questions.stem: Find the misspelled word in the sentence about the new hotel.
questions.why: Accommodate has double c and double m.

questions.stem: Part A: Which word correctly completes the sentence? “The sudden storm was a rare ____ in the desert town.”

partA.stem: Part A: Which word correctly completes the sentence? “The sudden storm was a rare ____ in the desert town.”

options.label: A
options.text: occurrence

options.label: B
options.text: occurrance

options.label: C
options.text: occurence

options.label: D
options.text: ocurrence

partB.stem: Part B: Why is the r doubled in the correct answer to Part A?

options.label: A
options.text: The suffix -ence always requires a double consonant right in front of it.

options.label: B
options.text: Every word that ends in r doubles the r before any suffix is added to it.

options.label: C
options.text: The stress in occur falls on the last syllable, so the r doubles before a vowel suffix.

options.label: D
options.text: The r doubles because the base word has more than two syllables in it.

questions.why: Occur is stressed on -cur, so the final r doubles before -ence.

questions.stem: Which spelling of the word meaning “easy to see” is correct?
options: noticeable
noticeible
noticable
notisable

questions.stem: Choose the correct spelling to complete the sentence: The ____ student double-checked every answer before submitting the exam.
options: conscienscious
conscientious
consciencious
conscientous
questions.why: Conscientious is science + -tious: con-sci-en-tious.

questions.stem: Decide whether each base word keeps or drops its final e when the suffix is added.

rows.text: courage + ous → courageous
hope + ing → hoping
manage + able → manageable
argue + ment → argument
value + able → valuable

questions.why: The e usually drops before a vowel suffix but stays after soft c or g; argument is an exception.

questions.stem: Find the misspelled word in the sentence about the orchestra’s performance.

options: privilege
maintenance
millenium
embarrass
perseverence
harrass

options: supersead
supersede
superseed
supercede
questions.why: Supersede is the only common English word ending in -sede.

questions.stem: Which sentence uses the correct plural spelling?
options: The researchers observed several unusual phenomena near the reef.
The researchers observed several unusual phenomenon near the reef.
The researchers observed several unusual phenomenons near the reef.
The researchers observed several unusual phenomenas near the reef.
questions.why: Phenomenon is Greek; its plural is phenomena.

questions.stem: Match each misspelled word borrowed from French with its correct spelling.
questions.why: French borrowings keep French letter patterns such as -ai-, -z-, and -eur.

questions.stem: Find the misspelled word in the sentence about the vaccination campaign.
questions.why: Inoculate has one n and one c.

questions.stem: Choose the verb that completes the sentence: The bird ____ on the branch.
options: sits
sitting
sit

questions.stem: Which sentence is correct?
options: The boy play in the park.
The boys is playing in the park.
The boys plays in the park.
The boys play in the park.
questions.why: Boys is more than one, so the verb is play.

questions.stem: Does each verb phrase go with “My friend” or with “My friends”?

rows.text: reads a book
ride bikes
eats lunch
draw pictures

questions.why: One friend reads; two or more friends ride.

questions.stem: Find the mistake in the sentence about Sara and Mona walking to school.
questions.why: Two people joined by and need the verb walk.

questions.stem: Which TWO sentences are correct? Choose two.
options: The cat drinks milk.
The dogs barks at night.
My sister like apples.
The ducks swim in the lake.
questions.why: One cat drinks; many ducks swim.

questions.stem: Choose the verb that completes the sentence: Each of the players ____ a water bottle.
options: has
have
having
questions.why: Each is singular, so it takes has.

questions.stem: Which sentence uses the correct verb?
options: The box of crayons were on the shelf.
The box of crayons are on the shelf.
The boxes of crayons is on the shelf.
The box of crayons is on the shelf.
questions.why: The subject is box, not crayons, so the verb is is.

questions.stem: Find the mistake in the sentence about the students singing on the bus.
questions.why: Students is plural, so it needs were.

questions.stem: Decide whether each subject takes “is” or “are.”

rows.text: Everybody in my class
My brother and I
The team
The pencils in my bag

questions.why: Everybody and team are singular; compound subjects with and are plural.

questions.stem: True or false: In the sentence “Either my cousins or my uncle is driving us to the beach,” the verb “is” is correct.
questions.why: With either…or, the verb agrees with the closer subject, uncle.

questions.stem: Which sentence uses subject-verb agreement correctly?
options: One of the camels drinks from the trough first.
One of the camel drinks from the trough first.
One of the camels drink from the trough first.
One of the camels are drinking from the trough first.
questions.why: The subject is one, so the verb is drinks.

questions.stem: Choose the verb that completes the sentence: The news about the new library ____ exciting.
options: is
are
were
questions.why: News looks plural but is singular.

questions.stem: Find the error in the sentence about the coach traveling with the swimmers.
questions.why: Phrases like along with do not change the subject; coach is singular.

questions.stem: Which TWO sentences use the correct verb? Choose two.
options: Neither of the answers are correct.
There are three falcons on the fence.
Here comes the twins from next door.
Mathematics is my favorite subject.
questions.why: Neither is singular (is); in “Here come the twins,” the subject twins is plural.

questions.stem: For each sentence about the airport and the classroom, choose the verb that agrees with the subject.

rows.text: Every student and teacher (has / have) a badge.
Both the pilot and the co-pilot (has / have) landed.
Somebody in the stands (has / have) dropped a hat.
A few of the questions (has / have) two answers.

questions.why: Every and somebody are singular; both and a few are plural.

questions.stem: Choose the verb that completes the sentence: Neither the students nor the teacher ____ the answer.
options: have known
knows
know
questions.why: With neither…nor, the verb agrees with the closer subject, teacher.

questions.stem: Which sentence about the museum uses the correct verb?
options: The number of visitors to the museum have doubled.
A number of visitors to the museum has complained.
The number of visitors to the museum has doubled.
The number of visitors to the museums have doubled.
questions.why: “The number” is singular; “a number” is plural.

questions.stem: Find the error in the sentence about the falcons at the festival.
questions.why: In an inverted sentence the subject (falcons) comes after the verb, so the verb is were.

questions.stem: Part A: Which verb correctly completes the sentence? “Each of the robots built by the engineering club ____ a different task.”

options.label: A

options.label: B

options.label: C

options.label: D

options.label: B
options.text: club

options.label: C

options.label: D
options.text: task

questions.stem: Decide whether each sentence about science and travel is correct or incorrect in subject-verb agreement.

rows.text: Physics requires careful measurement.
Several of the climbers has reached the summit.
Fifty kilometers is a long way to walk.
The scissors on the desk is sharp.

questions.why: Physics and an amount of distance are singular; several and scissors are plural.

questions.stem: Which sentence about the old albums uses subject-verb agreement correctly?
options: The quality of the photograph in the old albums are remarkable.
The quality of the photographs in the old albums are remarkable.
The qualities of the photograph in the old album is remarkable.
The quality of the photographs in the old albums is remarkable.
questions.why: The subject is quality, which is singular.

questions.stem: Choose the verb that completes the sentence: Not only the director but also the actors ____ been invited to the ceremony.
options: have
has
is
questions.why: With not only…but also, the verb agrees with the closer subject, actors.

questions.stem: Find the error in the sentence about the collection of ancient manuscripts.
segments: that scholars have studied for decades
questions.why: The subject is collection, singular, despite the long modifiers.

questions.stem: Which TWO sentences use subject-verb agreement correctly? Choose two.
options: Every one of the volunteers were thanked by name.
What the scientists discovered was a new species of lizard.
Each of the delegates who attend the summit receives a schedule.
There remains several questions about the budget.
questions.why: Each and a noun clause take singular verbs; questions (plural) needs remain; every one needs was.

questions.stem: Part A: Which revision corrects the agreement error in the sentence “The effect of the new irrigation methods on desert farms have been studied carefully”?

partA.stem: Part A: Which revision corrects the agreement error in the sentence “The effect of the new irrigation methods on desert farms have been studied carefully”?

options.label: A
options.text: Change “have” to “has.”

options.label: B
options.text: Change “methods” to “method.”

options.label: C
options.text: Change “farms” to “farm.”

options.label: D
options.text: Change “been” to “being.”

partB.stem: Part B: Why is the revision in Part A needed?

options.label: A
options.text: The verb must agree with “methods,” the plural noun closest to it.

options.label: B
options.text: The subject is “farms,” which is plural and needs a plural verb form.

options.label: C
options.text: The phrase “on desert farms” makes the whole subject plural in meaning.

options.label: D
options.text: The subject is “effect,” which is singular, not “methods” or “farms.”

questions.why: The verb agrees with the head noun effect, not nouns inside prepositional phrases.

questions.stem: Choose the verb that completes the sentence: Ten liters of water ____ enough for each hiker on the desert trail.
options: are
were
is
questions.why: An amount treated as one quantity takes a singular verb.

questions.stem: Which sentence about the expedition uses subject-verb agreement correctly?
options: The expedition’s leader, as well as her two guides, were praised for the rescue.
The expedition’s leader, as well as her two guides, was praised for the rescue.
The expedition’s leaders, as well as their guide, was praised for the rescue.
The expedition’s leader, together with her guides, have been praised for the rescue.
questions.why: As well as and together with do not create a compound subject; leader is singular.

questions.stem: Find the error in the inverted sentence about the final report for the city council.
segments: is a summary of the findings
questions.correction: are a summary of the findings
questions.why: The inverted subject is compound (a summary and a list), so the verb must be are.

questions.stem: Which TWO sentences about Hana have verbs that agree with their subjects? Choose two.
options: Hana is the only one of the students who volunteers at the clinic.
Hana is one of the students who volunteer at the clinic.
Hana is one of the students who volunteers at the clinic.
Hana is the only one of the students who volunteer at the clinic.
questions.why: In “one of the students who…,” who refers to students (plural); in “the only one who…,” who refers to one (singular).

questions.stem: Part A: Which verb correctly completes the sentence? “What the new data reveal ____ that the glacier is retreating faster than predicted.”

partA.stem: Part A: Which verb correctly completes the sentence? “What the new data reveal ____ that the glacier is retreating faster than predicted.”

options.label: A
options.text: are

options.label: B
options.text: is

options.label: C
options.text: were

options.label: D
options.text: have been

partB.stem: Part B: Why is the answer to Part A correct?

options.label: A
options.text: The subject is “data,” which is plural, so the main verb must also be plural.

options.label: B
options.text: The verb must agree with “predicted,” the last word in the full sentence.

options.label: C
options.text: The subject is “glacier,” which is singular and comes right after the main verb.

options.label: D
options.text: The subject is the whole clause “What the new data reveal,” which is treated as singular.

questions.why: A noun clause used as a subject takes a singular verb, even if a plural noun appears inside it.

questions.stem: What is the subject (who or what the sentence is about) in “The puppy wags its tail”?

wags its tail
wags
its tail

questions.stem: Choose the predicate that completes the sentence: My grandmother ____.

in the kitchen
bakes bread
questions.why: A predicate tells what the subject does.

questions.stem: Sort these sentence parts about the school day into subjects and predicates.

rows.text: My teacher
rings the bell
The children
eat lunch outside

questions.why: Subjects name who; predicates tell what they do.

questions.stem: True or false: In the sentence “The camel walks across the sand,” the predicate is “walks across the sand.”
questions.why: The predicate tells what the camel does.

questions.stem: Which TWO groups of words are complete sentences with a subject and a predicate? Choose two.
options: Birds fly south.
The sun shines.
The big red ball.
Runs to the park.
questions.why: A sentence needs both who/what and what it does.

questions.stem: Choose the words that make the sentence complete: ____ planted twenty palm trees near the school.
options: Very green and tall
The students in our class
Near the tall gate
questions.why: The sentence needs a subject that tells who planted.

questions.stem: What is the simple subject of the sentence “The tall boy in the blue shirt scored the winning goal”?
options: scored
goal
shirt
boy
questions.why: The simple subject is the main noun: boy.

questions.stem: Decide whether each part of “The old fisherman from Jeddah repaired his nets on the beach” is in the complete subject or the complete predicate.

rows.text: The old fisherman
from Jeddah
repaired his nets
on the beach

questions.why: Everything describing the fisherman is in the subject; the verb and what follows is the predicate.

questions.stem: This group of words about the new library has no predicate. Which part should be changed to make a complete sentence?
questions.correction: and quiet reading rooms opened today.
questions.why: Adding a verb (opened) gives the subject a predicate.

questions.stem: Which TWO sentences have a compound subject? Choose two.
options: Dolphins and whales breathe air.
The goats ate and slept all day.
My cousin swam in the warm sea.
Ahmed and his sister fed the goats.
questions.why: A compound subject has two subjects joined by and.

questions.stem: What is the simple predicate in “The engineers at the plant have tested the new solar panels”?
options: the new solar panels
engineers
tested the new solar panels
have tested
questions.why: The simple predicate is the verb with its helping verb: have tested.

questions.stem: Choose the words that complete the sentence so that it has a compound predicate: The desert fox ____.

environment
important

begin
happen
protect
desert (noun)

options: volc-a-no
vol-can-o
vo-lca-no
vol-ca-no

options: unb-
break
un-
-able
brea
-kable

questions.stem: True or false: The word “geography” has four syllables: ge-og-ra-phy.

questions.stem: In the word “photosynthesis,” the stressed syllable is ____.
options: to
the
syn
pho

options: navigation
telescopes
carpenters
wonderful

questions.stem: Classify each science word by its number of syllables: octopus, crustacean, invertebrate, evaporation.

rows.text: octopus
crustacean
invertebrate
evaporation

questions.stem: Which word pair shows the stressed syllable moving when a suffix is added?
options: comfort → comfortable
happy → happiness
govern → government
music → musician
questions.why: MU-sic becomes mu-SI-cian; the others keep stress on the first syllable.

questions.stem: When the noun “produce” (PRO-duce, fresh fruit and vegetables) is used as a verb, its stress moves and it is pronounced ____.
options: PRO-DUCE
pro-duce with no stress
PRO-duce
pro-DUCE
questions.why: Noun-verb pairs like this often shift stress to the second syllable in the verb.

questions.stem: For each word pair from a geology report, decide whether the stressed syllable stays the same or shifts.

rows.text: geology → geological
mineral → minerals
history → historic
erode → erosion
volcano → volcanoes

questions.why: Suffixes like -ical and -ic often pull stress toward the end of the word.

questions.stem: Which THREE words have five syllables? Choose three.
options: independent
unforgettable
electricity
communicate
international
alternative
questions.why: E-lec-tric-i-ty, un-for-get-ta-ble, and in-ter-na-tion-al each have five syllables.

questions.stem: Find the incorrect stress mark in a student's pronunciation notes for “The export of dates increased.”
questions.why: As a noun, export stresses the first syllable; as a verb it is ex-PORT.

questions.stem: In the word “photography,” the primary stress falls on the ____ syllable.
options: third (pho-tog-RA-phy)
second (pho-TOG-ra-phy)
fourth (pho-tog-ra-PHY)
first (PHO-tog-ra-phy)
questions.why: Words ending in -graphy stress the syllable just before -graphy.

questions.stem: Match each word in the photograph word family to its syllable count and stress pattern.
questions.why: Suffixes change both the syllable count and where the stress falls.

questions.stem: Identify the stressed syllable of each heteronym as it is used in the phrase.

rows.text: desert in “crossed the hot desert”
desert in “will not desert their team”
object in “a strange object”
object in “I object to the plan”
present in “to present the award”

questions.why: In these heteronyms, the noun stresses the first syllable and the verb the second.

questions.stem: Which word pair follows the same stress shift as “analyze → analysis” (AN-a-lyze → a-NAL-y-sis)?
options: decide → decision
atom → atomic
excel → excellent
inform → information
questions.why: A-tom → a-TOM-ic moves the stress from the first to the second syllable.

questions.stem: Which TWO words have their primary stress on the third syllable? Choose two.
options: calendar
develop
engineer
volunteer
questions.why: En-gi-NEER and vol-un-TEER stress the final -eer syllable; de-VEL-op and CAL-en-dar do not.

questions.stem: True or false: “big” and “large” are synonyms.
questions.why: Synonyms are words that mean almost the same thing.

questions.stem: Match each word to its antonym (opposite): hot, up, fast.
questions.why: Antonyms are words with opposite meanings.

questions.stem: Choose the word that means the same as “little”: The puppy is very ____.
options: tall
loud
small
questions.why: Little and small are synonyms.

questions.stem: Are the words in each pair synonyms or antonyms: happy/glad, wet/dry, start/begin, open/shut?

rows.text: happy – glad
wet – dry
start – begin
open – shut

questions.why: Same meaning = synonyms; opposite meaning = antonyms.

questions.stem: Which word is the opposite of “empty”?
options: round
clean
heavy
full
questions.why: An empty cup has nothing in it; a full cup is filled.

questions.stem: Choose the antonym that best completes the sentence: The first part of the hike was easy, but the climb to the top was ____.
options: difficult
pleasant
simple
quick
questions.why: The word but signals a contrast, so the opposite of easy fits.

questions.stem: Which is the best synonym for “ancient” in the sentence “The museum displayed ancient pottery from Mada'in Salih”?
options: very large
very costly
very old
very rare
questions.why: Ancient means from a time long ago.

questions.stem: Which TWO words are synonyms for “brave”? Choose two.
options: fearless
timid
courageous
careless
questions.why: Courageous and fearless both describe someone who faces danger.

questions.stem: Sort each word as a synonym or an antonym of “generous.”

rows.text: giving
selfish
stingy
charitable

questions.why: Generous people share freely; selfish and stingy people do not.

questions.stem: Find the word that does not fit the meaning in this sentence: “Although the falcon looked fragile, it was actually very weak.”
questions.why: Although signals a contrast, so the word must be an antonym of fragile.

questions.stem: Match each word from a desert nature report to its synonym.
questions.why: Each pair has nearly the same meaning.

questions.stem: Choose the antonym of “abundant” that best completes the sentence: After the long drought, fresh water in the oasis became ____.
options: scarce
valuable
plentiful
murky
questions.why: A drought makes water hard to find, the opposite of abundant.

questions.stem: Which pair of words are antonyms?
options: gather – collect
rapid – swift
fragile – delicate
reluctant – eager
questions.why: Reluctant means unwilling; eager means very willing.

questions.stem: True or false: In the sentence “The cautious diver checked her equipment twice,” the word “reckless” could replace “cautious” without changing the meaning.
questions.why: Reckless is an antonym of cautious, so it would reverse the meaning.

questions.stem: Which TWO words could replace “examined” in the sentence “The scientist examined the fossil under a microscope” without changing its meaning? Choose two.
options: inspected
ignored
studied
polished
questions.why: Inspected and studied both mean looked at closely.

questions.stem: Choose the synonym that best fits the formal tone: The committee will ____ the new library plans on Monday.
options: glance at
review
skim
mess with
questions.why: Review is formal and means to examine carefully.

questions.stem: In a report on the inventor Al-Jazari, decide whether each word is a synonym or an antonym of “innovative.”

rows.text: inventive
conventional
original
outdated

questions.why: Innovative means new and creative; conventional and outdated mean the opposite.

questions.stem: Which word is the best antonym for “transparent” in the sentence “The jellyfish's transparent body made it hard to see”?
options: clear
opaque
glowing
fragile
questions.why: Opaque means light cannot pass through, the opposite of transparent.

questions.stem: Which THREE words are antonyms of “temporary”? Choose three.
options: passing
permanent
momentary
brief
enduring
lasting
questions.why: Temporary means short-lived; the antonyms describe something that lasts.

questions.stem: Find the word that creates a contradiction in this sentence about a marathon runner: “Exhausted after the race, the runner felt energetic and collapsed on the grass.”
questions.why: Energetic is an antonym of exhausted, so it contradicts the rest of the sentence.

questions.stem: Which word is the closest synonym for “meticulous” in the sentence “The meticulous engineer checked every weld on the bridge”?
options: talented
efficient
cautious
thorough
questions.why: Meticulous means paying close attention to every detail; cautious is related but means avoiding risk.

questions.stem: Choose the synonym whose connotation best fits: The critic praised the documentary's ____ account of the pearl divers' daily lives, noting that it avoided exaggeration.
options: tactless
harsh
candid
blunt
questions.why: All four suggest honesty, but only candid carries a positive connotation.

questions.stem: Each word below is a synonym of “stubborn.” Decide whether it has a positive or a negative connotation.

rows.text: determined
inflexible
tenacious
obstinate

questions.why: Synonyms can share a meaning but differ in the feeling they suggest.

questions.stem: Which TWO words are antonyms of “lucid” in the sentence “The professor gave a lucid explanation of black holes”? Choose two.
options: confusing
brilliant
detailed
obscure
questions.why: Lucid means clear and easy to understand.

questions.stem: Match each word from an account of a historic voyage to its antonym.
questions.why: Each pair names opposite qualities: too little/enough, unfriendly/welcoming, careful/careless, brief/wordy.

questions.stem: Choose the synonym that keeps both the meaning and the formal register: The historian's argument was ____ by new evidence from the archive.
options: backed up
patched
okayed
corroborated
questions.why: Corroborated means confirmed and suits formal academic writing.

questions.stem: In the sentence “Ibn Battuta's travel account is replete with vivid detail,” which word is the best synonym for “replete”?
options: decorated
filled
completed
weakened
questions.why: Replete means abundantly filled; it only looks like complete.

questions.stem: Decide whether each pair of words are synonyms or antonyms.

rows.text: ephemeral – transient
laconic – garrulous
mitigate – exacerbate
ubiquitous – pervasive
venerate – revere

questions.why: Laconic (few words) opposes garrulous (talkative); mitigate (ease) opposes exacerbate (worsen).

questions.stem: Part A: In the sentence “Far from being frugal, the sultan's builders spent lavishly on marble and gold,” what does “frugal” most likely mean?

options.label: B
options.text: sparing with money

options.label: C

options.label: D

options.label: A
options.text: builders

options.label: B
options.text: lavishly

options.label: C
options.text: marble

options.label: D
options.text: spent

questions.why: Far from signals contrast with spent lavishly, so frugal means careful with money.

questions.stem: A writer wants to replace “criticized” in “The engineer criticized the plan” with words that suggest harsh, public criticism. Which TWO words work best? Choose two.
options: critiqued
questioned
denounced
condemned
questions.why: Denounced and condemned are synonyms with a stronger, harsher connotation.

questions.stem: True or false: You can use a computer to type a story.
questions.why: Computers and tablets let us type and save our writing.

questions.stem: Which key do you press on a keyboard to make a space between words?
options: the enter key
the shift key
the space bar
the delete key
questions.why: The long space bar puts a space between words.

questions.stem: Match each computer key to what it does.

pairs.right: erases the letter before the cursor

questions.why: Each key has its own job when you type.

questions.stem: Put the steps for typing and sharing a class story about your pet in order.
sequence: Open a new document.
Type your story.
Check for mistakes.
Print or share it.
questions.why: Open, write, check, and then share.

questions.stem: Does each tool help you type words or add a picture to your story about the beach?

rows.text: keyboard
camera photo
“Insert Picture” button
voice typing (speaking words)

questions.why: Some tools add words and some add pictures.

questions.stem: To fix a word with a red squiggly line under it, a writer should use the ____ tool.
options: font color
page border
spell check
questions.why: A red line usually marks a spelling mistake.

questions.stem: Fatima is typing a report about camels. Which tool should she use to find a better word for “big”?
options: print preview
thesaurus
calculator
word count
questions.why: A thesaurus suggests synonyms.

questions.stem: Put the steps for adding a photo of the Edge of the World cliffs to a slideshow in order.
sequence: Click the slide where the photo should go.
Choose “Insert,” then “Image.”
Select the photo file from the folder.
Resize the photo so it fits the slide.
questions.why: Pick the place, insert, choose the file, then adjust it.

questions.stem: For Yusuf's class newsletter, decide whether each action keeps his work safe or shares it with others.

rows.text: saving the file with a clear name
emailing the file to the teacher
posting it on the class website
making a backup copy on a USB drive

questions.why: Saving and backing up protect work; emailing and posting publish it.

questions.stem: Mona is making a slideshow about coral reefs for her class. Which TWO choices make the slides easier to read? Choose two.
options: Fill each slide with long paragraphs.
Use many different fonts and colors.
Put only a few key points on each slide.
Use a large, simple font.
questions.why: Clear fonts and short points help an audience read slides quickly.

questions.stem: Which is the best way to give credit for a photo of a sand dune found online and used in a school blog post?
options: Write the photographer's name and the website under it.
Crop the photo so nobody recognizes where it came from.
Use it without a caption because it is online.
Change the colors so it looks like a new photo.
questions.why: Writers must credit the creator and source of images they use.

questions.stem: To let three classmates edit the same science report at the same time, Khalid should ____.
options: print three copies of the report
share the online document with editing rights
save the report on his desktop
email a PDF that cannot be edited
questions.why: Shared online documents allow several people to work together at once.

questions.stem: For a report on sea turtles, decide whether each website is likely a reliable or a less reliable source.

rows.text: a national marine science agency site
an anonymous comment under a video
a university biology department page
a pop-up ad selling turtle toys

questions.why: Expert, accountable sources are more reliable than anonymous or commercial ones.

questions.stem: Find the error in this tip about using a word processor: “To undo your last change, press Ctrl+Z, and to copy text, press Ctrl+P.”
questions.why: Ctrl+C copies; Ctrl+P prints.

questions.stem: Which THREE word-processor features help a writer revise the organization of a long report on renewable energy? Choose three.
options: cut and paste to move paragraphs
comments to mark where ideas need support
adding a decorative border
headings that show in a navigation pane
changing the page color
making every line bold
questions.why: Organization tools move and label ideas; decoration does not improve structure.

questions.stem: True or false: Turning on “Track Changes” in a shared document lets a writer see, accept, or reject each edit a peer makes.
questions.why: Track Changes records edits so the writer stays in control.

questions.stem: A student wants readers of her online article about Ibn al-Haytham to jump to a museum page for more information. What should she add?
options: a hyperlink
a text box
a page break
a footnote number
questions.why: A hyperlink takes readers directly to another web page.

questions.stem: Before publishing a class podcast about the history of the dhow, the team should ____ so that listeners who are deaf can follow it.
options: post a written transcript
add background music
raise the volume
shorten the episode
questions.why: A transcript makes audio content accessible.

questions.stem: Put the steps for publishing a class blog post about a beach cleanup in a logical order.
sequence: Draft the post in a document.
Ask a peer to review it using comments.
Revise and proofread the post.
Add photos with captions and credits.
Click “Publish” on the class blog.
questions.why: Draft, get feedback, revise, add media, then publish.

questions.stem: For a multimedia presentation about the Hejaz Railway, decide which tool best fits each purpose.

rows.text: showing how passenger numbers changed over ten years
showing the route from Damascus to Medina
letting the audience hear an interview with a historian
comparing travel times across several years

questions.why: Choose the medium that presents each kind of information most clearly.

questions.stem: To keep a long research paper on desalination consistent, a writer should format the section titles with built-in ____, which also allow an automatic table of contents.
options: larger fonts
bold text
text boxes
heading styles
questions.why: Heading styles format titles consistently and feed the table of contents.

questions.stem: Which choice is the best reason to use a citation manager when writing a research paper on solar power?
options: It removes the need to read each of your sources carefully.
It formats sources consistently and reduces citation errors.
It automatically finds the most popular websites about your topic.
It checks that every source you use agrees with your thesis.
questions.why: Citation managers organize and format references; they do not judge or read sources.

questions.stem: A student is publishing an online article about water use in Riyadh. Decide whether each action is ethical or unethical.

rows.text: embedding a government chart with a link to its source
copying a paragraph from a blog without quotation marks
using a Creative Commons photo and following its license
editing a quote so the expert seems to say the opposite

questions.why: Ethical publishing credits sources and represents them accurately.

questions.stem: A group is co-writing a shared online report about falconry. Which TWO practices best prevent members from losing or overwriting each other's work? Choose two.
options: downloading separate copies and merging them from memory
having everyone edit the same paragraph at once
using the version history to restore earlier drafts
assigning each member a section and using comments for suggestions
questions.why: Version history and clear roles protect shared work.

questions.stem: Select the sentence in Huda's email to her teacher that is NOT appropriate for formal digital communication.

segments.text: Dear Ms. Salem,
I have attached my final report on coral bleaching as a PDF.
lol sorry it's late, my wifi was being super annoying!!
Please let me know if the file does not open.
Sincerely, Huda Al-Harbi

questions.why: Formal emails avoid slang, text abbreviations, and extra punctuation.

questions.stem: A writer publishing a digital essay about urban heat islands wants readers who use screen readers to understand a key graph. What should she add?
options: a larger version of the graph in the appendix
a brighter color scheme for the graph lines
alt text that states the graph's main trend
an animation that shows the graph being drawn
questions.why: Screen readers read alt text aloud; visual changes do not help.

questions.stem: When adapting a print article about Al-Khwarizmi into a web version, the writer should ____ because online readers tend to scan rather than read every line.
options: remove all hyperlinks to keep readers on the page
break long paragraphs into shorter chunks with subheadings
increase the word count to add more detail
use a single long block of text for continuity
questions.why: Short chunks and subheadings suit how people read on screens.

questions.stem: Decide whether each feature of a digital research report on desert agriculture mainly supports credibility or accessibility.

rows.text: links to peer-reviewed sources
captions on embedded videos
a date showing when the data was last updated
high color contrast between words and background
an author note listing credentials

questions.why: Credibility features build trust; accessibility features let more people use the work.

questions.stem: Put the steps for publishing a student journal paper on water conservation through an online review system in a logical order.
sequence: Submit the draft through the journal's online portal.
Receive reviewer comments through tracked changes.
Revise the paper and respond to each comment.
Approve the final proof before release.
The paper is published with a permanent link.
questions.why: Digital publishing moves from submission through review and revision to release.

options.label: A
options.text: The link should open in the same browser tab.

options.label: B

questions.stem: True or false: “Mr.” is the short way to write “Mister.”

questions.stem: Choose the correct greeting for a thank-you note: ____ Grandma,
options: Deer
Dear
dear

The big red Bus
the big red bus
the Big Red bus

Greeting (Dear Uncle Ali,)

Signature (Sara)

Journey To The Center Of The Earth
Journey to The Center of the earth
Journey to the Center of the Earth
questions.why: Short words like to, the, and of stay lowercase unless they come first.

a chapter: The First Storm

your friend.

mr. Hamad

Laila read “The Silent Lighthouse” in one sitting.
Laila read “The silent lighthouse” in one sitting.

questions.stem: In a formal business letter, the inside address comes ____.

before the sender's own address
after the signature at the bottom
after the heading and before the salutation

Inside address
Salutation
Body
Complimentary close and signature
questions.why: Formal letters follow a fixed order from heading to signature.

A Guide to Falcons And Hawks

The Boy Who Mapped the Stars
Secrets Of The Coral Reef

questions.stem: Choose the correct abbreviation for the title in this sentence: ____ Huda Karim, a chemistry professor, judged the science fair.
options: dr.
Dr.
Doc.
Dr

newspaper: The Daily Coast
magazine article: How Bees Talk
book-length poem: The Long Road Home

The meeting begins at 9:00 A.M on Thursday.

questions.stem: Which salutation is most appropriate for a formal letter to an organization when the recipient's name is unknown?

Bridges Across the Gulf
“Bridges across The Gulf”
“Bridges Across The Gulf”
questions.why: Speech titles go in quotation marks, and short words like the stay lowercase.

questions.stem: Which TWO sentences correctly follow abbreviation rules for formal writing? Choose two.

Dr. Mariam Ali, Ph.D., led the study.
Many famous space missions have been run by NASA.
The team arrived in Calif. on Tuesday.

questions.stem: In MLA style, the title of a short web page within a larger website is placed in ____, while the website's name is placed in italics.
options: italics
bold type
all capital letters
quotation marks
