questions.stem: Find the error in the opening of a formal business letter written in American style.
questions.why: American business letters use a colon after the salutation; a comma is for friendly letters.

questions.stem: Which sentence follows standard rules for introducing an abbreviation in formal academic prose?
options: The WHO issued a report, and the WHO (World Health Organization) later revised it.
The WHO (World Health Organization) issued a report; the World Health Org. later revised it.
The World Health Organization (WHO) issued a report; WHO later revised it.
The W.H.O. issued a report; the World Health Organization (WHO) later revised it.
questions.why: Spell out the full name first with the abbreviation in parentheses, then use the abbreviation consistently.

questions.stem: Part A: Nawaf is writing a formal letter of application to a university engineering program. Which closing best fits?

options.label: C

options.label: D

questions.stem: Which THREE choices format titles correctly in academic writing? Choose three.
options: a full-length film in quotation marks: “The Long Voyage”
a short poem in italics: Morning Tide
a newspaper headline in italics: Rain Returns to Abha
a book chapter in quotation marks: “The Age of Sail”
an online journal in italics: Desert Ecology Review
a podcast episode in quotation marks: “Voices of the Souq”

questions.stem: True or false: A dictionary lists words in ABC order.
questions.why: Dictionaries are in alphabetical order so words are easy to find.

questions.stem: Put these animal words in ABC order, as they would appear in a dictionary: goat, zebra, ant, camel.

camel
goat
zebra

questions.stem: Where should you look to find what the word “oasis” means?
options: a calendar
a dictionary
a phone book
a sticker book
questions.why: A dictionary tells what words mean.

questions.stem: In a dictionary, the word “bird” comes ____ the word “boat.”
options: on top of
after
before

rows.text: to find how to spell “elephant”
to find where Egypt is
to find what “desert” means
to find a map of the Red Sea

options: mango
market
meadow
match

questions.stem: Match each reference source to the question it answers best.

pairs.right: How do desert foxes survive the heat?

questions.why: Each reference source is made for a different kind of question.

questions.stem: A dictionary entry shows “ca·ra·van (KAIR-uh-van).” What do the dots in “ca·ra·van” show?
options: where the stress falls
which letters are silent
where the syllables break
where to stop reading
questions.why: Dots in an entry word divide it into syllables.

questions.stem: Decide whether each word comes before or after the guide word “honey” in a dictionary.

rows.text: hawk
horse
hold
hope

questions.why: Compare letter by letter until the letters differ.

questions.stem: Read this dictionary entry: “light (adj.) 1. not heavy 2. pale in color (n.) 3. brightness from the sun or a lamp.” Which TWO sentences use “light” with meaning 2? Choose two.
options: The walls were painted light green.
She wore a light blue scarf.
The light from the lamp was warm.
The box was light enough to carry.
questions.why: Meaning 2 describes a pale color.

questions.stem: Which resource would be best for checking how the word “desalination” is pronounced and divided into syllables?
options: a thesaurus
a dictionary
a book of maps
an almanac
questions.why: A dictionary shows syllables and pronunciation.

questions.stem: Select the definition in this dictionary entry for “current” that fits the sentence “Swimmers were pulled away by a strong current.”

segments.text: cur·rent (KUR-uhnt)
adj. 1. happening now
n. 2. a flow of water or air in one direction
n. 3. a flow of electricity
[from Latin currere, ‘to run’]

questions.why: In the sentence, current is a noun naming moving water.

questions.stem: A thesaurus lists “daring, fearless, reckless” as words related to “brave.” Which word best completes this positive description? The ____ firefighter calmly entered the building to rescue the child.
options: fearless
nervous
careless
reckless
questions.why: Fearless is positive; reckless suggests danger from not thinking.

questions.stem: Decide which part of a nonfiction book about volcanoes a reader should use for each task.

rows.text: to find the meaning of “magma”
to find every page that mentions Mount Etna
to see what chapter 4 is called
to define “lava dome”

questions.why: A glossary defines terms, an index lists pages for topics, and a table of contents lists chapters.

questions.stem: A dictionary entry reads: “ex·ca·vate (EKS-kuh-vayt) v. -vat·ed, -vat·ing. to dig out and remove; to uncover by digging. [from Latin excavare, ‘to hollow out’]” Which TWO facts does the entry give? Choose two.
options: The word is most often used as a noun.
The word has three syllables.
The word has the synonym “bury.”
The word comes from Latin.
questions.why: The brackets give the origin and the dots show three syllables; v. means verb.

questions.stem: In a dictionary or thesaurus entry, the abbreviation “syn.” introduces ____.
options: the word's origin
words with similar meanings
words with opposite meanings
the plural form
questions.why: Syn. stands for synonyms; ant. stands for antonyms.

questions.stem: A student writes, “The new law had a strong affect on fishing.” A dictionary shows that “affect” is usually a verb and “effect” is usually a noun. Which revision is correct?
options: The new law had a strong effect on fishing.
The new law strongly effect the fishing.
The new law had a strong affected on fishing.
The new law had a strongly affect on fishing.
questions.why: After a strong, a noun is needed, so effect is correct.

questions.stem: Select the meaning from this dictionary entry for “bank” that fits the sentence “The heron waited on the bank of the river.”

segments.text: bank n. 1. a business that keeps and lends money
2. the sloping land beside a river or lake
3. a large supply kept for use, as in a blood bank
v. 4. to tilt an airplane while turning

questions.stem: Match each word part from a dictionary's etymology notes to its meaning.
questions.why: Etymology notes show Greek and Latin parts that build many English words.

questions.stem: A writer wants to know whether “nauseous” is accepted in formal English. Which part of a dictionary entry should she check?
options: the etymology in brackets
the pronunciation in parentheses
the usage note in the entry
the guide words at the top

questions.stem: The etymology “[from Arabic al-jabr, ‘reunion of broken parts’]” in a dictionary entry tells a reader that the English word “algebra” ____.
options: was invented in English
is used only in Arabic
has a synonym in Arabic
was borrowed from Arabic

rows.text: How should I cite a translated book?
Is “canon” the right spelling for a body of medical writing?
What is a more precise word than “good” for his treatments?
Should book titles be italicized in my citations?
What part of speech is “physician”?

questions.why: Dictionaries define and spell, thesauruses offer word choices, and style manuals set formatting rules.

questions.stem: A thesaurus lists these synonyms for “change”: alter, modify, transform, revolutionize. Which TWO best complete the sentence “The engineer made small adjustments to ____ the design while keeping its purpose”? Choose two.
options: modify
transform
revolutionize
alter
questions.why: Modify and alter suggest small changes; transform and revolutionize suggest complete ones.

questions.stem: A historical dictionary, which records a word's uses over time with dated quotations, is most useful when a scholar needs to ____.
options: check the spelling of a common word
look up a city's current population
find a quick list of everyday synonyms
trace how a word's meaning changed over centuries
questions.why: Historical dictionaries document how meanings developed.

questions.stem: Select the two definitions in this dictionary entry for “sanction” that, as nouns, have nearly opposite meanings.

segments.text: sanc·tion (SANGK-shuhn)
n. 1. official permission or approval
n. 2. a penalty for breaking a rule or law
v. 3. to give official approval to
[from Latin sanctio, ‘decree’]

questions.why: Sanction can mean both approval and punishment, so context decides.

questions.stem: A student finds “decimate” defined as “1. (historical) to kill one in every ten; 2. to destroy a large part of.” Which sentence uses the word in its current, common sense?
options: The locust swarm decimated the region's wheat crop.
The class decimated the cake into ten equal slices.
The coach decimated the team by benching one player in ten.
The farmer decimated his savings by spending ten riyals.
questions.why: Today decimate usually means to destroy a large part of something.

questions.stem: A researcher writing about the history of the word “algorithm” uses several sources. Decide which source best serves each purpose.

explaining how algorithms are used in computer science
deciding whether to capitalize a term in a citation
finding when the word first appeared in English

questions.why: Match the research need to the reference built for it.

questions.stem: Read this usage note: “Disinterested traditionally means ‘impartial’; many careful writers object to its use as ‘uninterested.’” Which TWO sentences use “disinterested” as the note recommends? Choose two.

The judges were disinterested, so neither school felt cheated.
The disinterested students yawned through the lecture.

questions.why: In careful usage, disinterested means having nothing to gain, not bored.

questions.stem: Is each sentence about the class trip telling something or giving a command?

Line up by the door.
The bus was yellow.
Hold my hand.

questions.stem: Which sentence gives a command?
options: The window is open.
Mom opened the window.
Close the window, please.
Is the window open now?

options: Take off
Taking off
Took off
questions.why: A command uses the plain verb: Take off.

questions.why: Sentences can tell, ask, or command.

questions.stem: Match each sentence about the science fair to its verb mood.

pairs.left: Our poster explains how clouds form.
Will the judges visit every table?

questions.why: Imperative gives commands, indicative states facts, interrogative asks.

questions.stem: Which sentence is in the imperative mood?
options: Did you measure the water before pouring?
If you measure the water, it will not spill.
Measure the water before you pour it.
You measured the water before pouring it.
questions.why: The imperative gives a direct command with the base verb.

rows.text: The match starts at four o'clock.
Pass the ball to Yusuf.
Who scored the first goal?
Our team won by two points.

questions.why: Statements are indicative, commands imperative, questions interrogative.

questions.stem: Choose the verb that completes the conditional sentence: If it rains tomorrow, we ____ the picnic indoors.
options: holding
will hold
hold been
held
questions.why: A real condition about the future uses will + verb.

questions.stem: Which TWO sentences about the library are in the conditional mood? Choose two.
options: Return the book by Friday.
If you return the book late, you will pay a small fee.
The library closes at six o'clock.
We would read more if the library stayed open later.
questions.why: Conditional sentences show what happens or would happen under a condition.

questions.stem: Which sentence is in the conditional mood?
options: The ship arrived sooner because the winds were calm.
Watch the ship arrive in the calm harbor today.
The ship would arrive sooner if the winds were calmer.
Did the ship arrive sooner because the winds were calm?
questions.why: Would + verb shows a result that depends on a condition.

If the sensor failed, the robot would stop.
The robot completed the course in two minutes.
Tighten every bolt on the frame.

questions.stem: Choose the verb that shows a wish that is contrary to fact: Layla wishes she ____ able to swim like her cousin.
options: has been
will be
were
is
questions.why: Wishes about unreal situations use the subjunctive were.

options: be
was
will be
is

If I be the captain, I would change the schedule.
If I was the captain, I would change the schedule.
If I were the captain, I would change the schedule.
questions.why: Contrary-to-fact conditions use were for all subjects.

options: The guide asked that each visitor stay behind the rope.
It is essential that she arrive before the doors close.
It is essential that she arrives before the doors close.
The guide asked that each visitor stays behind the rope.
questions.why: In that-clauses after demands and necessity, use the base verb with no -s.

questions.why: Recommended that calls for the subjunctive base form extend.

First, you should preheat the oven, and then grease the pan.
First, you preheat the oven, and then grease the pan.
First, preheat the oven, and then grease the pan.

Read the instructions carefully, and then sign the form.
Read the instructions carefully, and you should then sign the form.

options.text: The engineers asked that the bridge was inspected, and they would repair it if any cracks are found.

options.label: B

approved
approve
approves

options.label: C

play
played

The baby slept.

has finished
finishes

Khalid is visiting the museum today.
